en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The Great Commentary on the Path of Purification (First Part)
The Introduction to the Work:
He who is garlanded with the rays of the True Dhamma,
having utterly destroyed the darkness of great delusion, has awakened the lotus-like assembly of those to be trained.
Having paid homage to that Buddha-sun of great majesty, who is free from all defilements, whose form is distinguished by supreme knowledge, whose dawn is pure compassion, who illuminates the world,
and who shines with the rays of his virtues— I shall now explain the Dhamma.
And the noble Saṅgha, which is in full bloom like a pure lotus pond—
by the power of whatever merit has been generated through these offerings to the Triple Gem,
may I be free from obstacles everywhere.
Requested by the wise Elder Dāṭhānāga, who was firm in mind,
perfected in virtue and conduct, and pure in speech—
the Lord of purified conduct [spoke] that unsurpassed purity.
Having attained it, he taught it with a mind uplifted by compassion.
The means for her attainment is the *Visuddhimagga*,
adorned with the method of purification, which was spoken [by him] with its sequence of words thoroughly purified.
[This work] is perfectly pure, unconfused, and a precise determination of the meaning;
it does not contradict the doctrine of the Mahāvihāravāsins.
Relying upon that ancient and orderly path of exposition, [I have composed this].
"We shall provide a pure commentary on the meaning,
following the method of the Discourses (Tantinayā). Therefore, O virtuous ones, listen as we analyze its meaning for one who desires the long endurance of the True Dhamma."
Commentary on the Discourse on the Introduction, etc.:

1. Having first set aside that Sutta passage upon which this *Visuddhimagga* is established, the following—beginning with "Established in virtue"—is intended to explain its meaning in various ways by way of determining its introduction and so forth.
It has been undertaken. For one who expounds the Dhamma, first the introduction (*nidāna*) must be stated;

thereafter, the purpose (*payojana*), the summary of the meaning (*piṇḍattha*), the meaning of the words (*padattha*), the connection (*sambandha*), the intention (*adhippāya*), the objection (*codanā*), and the resolution (*sodhana*) must be stated. It was in this very manner that the Teacher proceeded.
Herein, the passage beginning with "it is said that the Blessed One... is the determination of the introduction and the purpose of the teaching, [leading to] the *Visuddhimagga*.
"‘They will speak,’ etc., is the extraction of the summarized meaning; ‘Standing firm in virtue,’ etc., is the elucidation of the intended connection between the word-meanings;
‘What is virtue? etc., is the objection; and what follows is the resolution. This same method applies to the discourses on concentration and wisdom as well.
But why are the verses of the response placed at the beginning here, rather than the verses of the question? For is it not the case that the response is preceded by the question?"

It is said: It should be understood that this is because it establishes the auspicious nature of its subject matter; because it elucidates the quality of being "good in the beginning" and so forth for the Teaching;
because it dispels obstacles by warding off dangers and other calamities; and because it comprises the doctrines to be further expounded herein. Here it may be asked:
Why has this discourse on the Path of Purification been commenced with a treatment of the subject matter (*vatthu*), rather than with a eulogy of the Teacher (*satthūthomana*)?
It is said: because it does not exist as a separate commentary or the like. For this is not a separate commentary on the *Dīghanikāya* and so forth, such as the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* and others;
nor is it a distinct treatise (*pakaraṇa*), like the *Abhidhammāvatāra*, *Sumatāvatāra*, and so on.
Rather, it is a specific refinement of those very commentaries, such as the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*. Therefore he says: "The *Visuddhimagga* stands in the midst," and so forth.
Alternatively, it should be understood that this discourse is preceded by praise rather than being preceded by a narrative account.

For in the Dispensation, the description of a narrative is not merely for its own sake as it is in the world; rather, because it is a description of the excellence of the Dispensation, it proceeds as something that points toward the proclamation of the Teacher’s qualities by way of revealing the state of the Teacher’s unerring teaching of the Dhamma. Thus he will say: "To this extent, the three..."
“Training,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “the cause for the state of a stream-enterer and so on”:
here, by the word “and so on” (*ādi*), all *arahants* are included—just as all *sakadāgāmins* and *anāgāmins* are—because no specific distinction is mentioned.

Therefore, it should be understood that the virtues conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) of all three types of Bodhisattvas are included here by the expression “being established in virtue,” and so forth.

For all three of them, in their final existence, there was specifically the perception of the terror of *saṃsāra*; having established themselves each in their respective moral discipline (*sīla*) and having exerted themselves in serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), their practice was identical in its unraveling of the tangle of craving (*taṇhājaṭā*).
Alternatively, by means of the general statement, "He shall unravel this tangle," the unravelling of the tangle of craving is both preeminent and unsurpassed.

It has been grasped. In this context, that which is unsurpassed by virtue of the abandonment of defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*) constitutes the Teacher’s perfection of abandonment;
and by reason of that, his perfection of knowledge. Through both of these, his perfection of power and so forth are also implied because they are inseparable from them.
Thus, it should be understood that this discourse is preceded by praise. Alternatively, this discourse consists solely of praise.
It should be understood that this commentary was undertaken preceded by a praise of the Teacher, beginning with the words,
"His range of knowledge is unimpeded regarding all phenomena," because it was composed to manifest the Teacher's capacity to provide answers in accordance with the intention of the questioner;
and it is the custom of the Master to begin his commentaries in a manner consistent with the doctrine to be explained.
At the commencement of the commentary, there is praise of the Teacher. Therefore, for this reason, the eulogy proceeds in this manner here.

Having first set down the verse of response while extracting the reason for the mode of praise being stated, and having shown both the form and the meaning of the question-verse by way of an introductory inquiry into its origin, [the author proceeds] with that question.
Having placed foremost the praise of the Blessed One—which illuminates his capacity for unerring exposition—the commentary on the intended doctrine is now undertaken.
Therefore, he said: "Having established oneself in virtue," and so forth. Regarding that, the meaning of the verse will be made clear later.

As for the word "iti" (thus) and the others: this particle *iti* has many distinct meanings, such as cause, conclusion, the opposite of the meaning of a word, manner, determination, illustration, and so on.
For instance, this [particle] occurs in the sense of a reason in such passages as: "Bhikkhus, it is because it is afflicted (*ruppati*) that it is called 'form' (*rūpa*).
It occurs in the sense of concluding a discourse in such passages as: "Therefore, bhikkhus, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things.
I have compassion for you, thinking: 'How may my disciples be heirs to the Dhamma, not heirs to material things?'"
In such passages as “Thus, or in such a manner, he abstains from dancing, singing, music, and the viewing of spectacles,” it has the sense of *ādi* (and so forth).

In such passages as “‘Māgaṇḍiya’ is the designation, the appellation, the description, the conventional term, the name, the naming, the denomination, the linguistic expression, the phrasing, and the utterance of that brahmin,” it has the sense of the reversal of the meaning of the word (*padatthavipariyāya*). And in the passage: “Thus, monks, there is danger...”
In such contexts as: "The fool is fearful, the wise man is fearless; the fool is beset by calamity, the wise man is free from calamity;
the fool is beset by misfortune, the wise man is free from misfortune," [the term *idappaccayatā* is used]. Furthermore, Ānanda, when asked, "Is there a specific condition for aging and death?
one should answer, "There is. And if it should be asked, "By what condition is there aging and death? [one should answer, "With birth as condition..."]
In such passages as "‘Old age and death,’ this is what should be said," it has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), meaning "certainty" (*sanniṭṭhāna*).
In such passages as "‘It exists,’ Kaccāna, this is one extreme; ‘it does not exist,’ Kaccāna, this is the second extreme," it has the sense of illustration (*nidassana*).

Here too, it should be understood in the sense of illustration; it is also appropriate to say it signifies "manifestation" (*pakāra*). However, the first word *iti* [in the phrase *jarāmaraṇanti*] serves to conclude the discourse (*parisamāpana*).
It should be seen. *Hi* is used for emphasis. *Idaṃ* is a term denoting what is near or present, because it brings face-to-face the Sutta passage as it has been attained. Regarding *vuttaṃ*:

this word *vutta* is seen with and without prefixes (*upasagga*) in such senses as sowing, planting, leveling, extracting hair, livelihood, existence, liberation, speaking, proceeding, entreating, and telling. For instance, this [word] is used thus:
"Cows are born for him; what is sown in his field grows."
“He eats the fruit of what has been sown, he who does not betray his friends”—in such passages, it occurs in the sense of sowing.
“But it was not yet reaped,” etc.—in such passages, it refers to leveling the ground for sowing with ivory pegs and the like.

“The young brahmin student Kāpaṭika, with shorn hair”—in such passages, it refers to the removal of hair. “With hair as thin as a leaf, living on the gifts of others, having become like a deer... [and so forth].

In such passages as “he dwells with his mind,” it refers to the maintenance of life. In such passages as “Just as a withered leaf, detached from its stalk, is incapable of becoming green again,” it refers to the state of being released from bondage.
In such passages as “For whom this ancient mantra-word has been sung, uttered, and rehearsed,” it refers to that which has proceeded by way of the sacred word. However, in common worldly usage...
In such passages as “The virtue has been told, the Pārāyana has been told,” it refers to an exhortation. In such passages as “But this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Bhikkhus, be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things,’” it refers to a statement. Here too, it should be understood as referring to a statement.
Therefore, [the phrase] “Thus indeed, in this very way, this sutta was taught” should be understood as the state of having taught the verses exactly as they were laid down.
He demonstrates it. Or, he retains the manner in which it was taught.
"Why" (*kasmā*) is used in the ablative case (*nissakka*) to indicate a reason. "But" (*pana*) is merely a rhetorical ornament. By both [terms], he asks for the cause.
"This" (*etaṃ*) refers back to the aforementioned words of the Sutta. "Was stated" (*vuttaṃ*) indicates the basis for the question. Regarding its meaning, for himself...

Having stated "this" with reference to the state of revolving within the intellect (*buddhi*), the Blessed One then said "this [very thing]" (*etad*) with reference to the specific mode in which he had spoken.
By this entire statement, the introduction (*nidāna*) to the teaching is illuminated.

Following that, in order to clarify the teacher, the place, the time, and the recipients of that teaching, the words beginning with "it is said that [he spoke] to the Blessed One" were uttered. Therein:
*Kirāti* is a particle used in the sense of "repeatedly hearing. By this, it indicates that the meaning being stated is heard again and again.
*Rattibhāge* means in one portion of the night; the intention is [the middle watch]. Because his name is not well-known, like that of Vessavaṇa and others, he is called *aññataro* (a certain one).
*Devaputto* is simply a deity (*devo*). *Saṃsayasamugghāṭatthaṃ* means for the purpose of uprooting the arrow of doubt (*vicikicchā-salla*).

The construction is: "He asked. By the phrase "for the purpose of uprooting doubt," he shows that among the five kinds of questions, this is a question for cutting through uncertainty (*vimaticchedanā-pucchā*).
To show the very meaning by which craving (*taṇhā*) is called a "tangle" (*jaṭā*), the words beginning with "of the net-like" (*jāliniyā*) were spoken.
For she possesses a net consisting precisely of her own constituent parts, which are the eight hundred varieties of the movements of craving (*taṇhā-vicari-ta*).
"It exists" is what is called "the net.
Now, in order to show its occurrence in the form of a tangle, the passage beginning with "For that... was stated.
Therein, the phrase "regarding objects such as visible forms" indicates the sphere of its activity, because there is no object of craving apart from the sixfold objects beginning with visible forms.

"By way of lower and higher" means by way of their occurrence at times with a visible-form object, at times up to a mental-object (dhamma) object, at times with a mental-object object, and at times down to a visible-form object;
thus it is by way of occurrence both below and above. Furthermore, the sequence of lower and higher should be understood here according to the order of the teaching.
At times in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), at times in the fine-material sphere existence (rūpabhava), and at times in the immaterial sphere existence (arūpabhava). At times...
Or in the formless existence... [and so on] ...or sometimes in the sense-sphere existence; thus here the occurrence should be understood according to the sequence from below upwards.
Because all conditioned phenomena have the nature of breaking up moment by moment, their repeated arising is what is meant here by "sewing together" (saṃsibbana);
hence it is said, "because of arising again and again. As for the phrase "in the sense of sewing together," this refers to the connection by which it is like a tangle (jaṭā).
"Jaṭā" refers to the likeness of the tangle of cravings; this is the demonstration of that. Herein, the meaning is as follows:

just as the branches of a thicket of reeds, as well as sheaths, stores, and so forth, which are interwoven and bound together by their own parts, are called "tangles" (jaṭā), so too craving is [called a tangle] because its intrinsic nature is to bind together—or rather, there is the reading "in the sense of being interwoven."
The meaning is: "by way of being woven together by itself. For this craving proceeds by weaving itself together with itself, just like a silkworm.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Craving for form is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world;
herein this craving, when arising, arises; herein, when settling, it settles," and so forth. These beings [think]: "It is mine..."
Thinking that an object grasped as "this" is not different from themselves, they make it internal.

Since the word *anta* has the meaning of "internal," craving (*taṇhā*) arising even toward one’s own requisites is called "inner tangle" (*antojaṭā*). For a renunciant, the bowl and so forth are personal requisites;
for a householder, the elephant and so forth are personal requisites.
“Self” (*atta*) means that which is the object of conceit; thus it is *attabhāva*, the pentad of the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*). Some say it is the body.
The mode in which craving arises with respect to one’s own selfhood and so forth—such as “My selfhood is beautiful,” or “May my selfhood be like that of so-and-so”—is to be understood as such.
One’s own eyes and so forth are the internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*). One’s own...
And there are the external bases, such as visible forms and so forth, belonging to others.

Or else, all internal bases—such as the eye and so forth—belonging to others, whether included within their own continuity or that of another; likewise for the external bases, such as visible forms and so forth.

Furthermore, the state of being an "inner tangle" and an "outer tangle" of craving should be understood even with respect to its occurrence in limited and sublime states of existence. For the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) is [the basis] for any defilement whatsoever.
Because it is not suppressed and is thus in no way liberated, it serves as a specific condition for internal grasping; therefore, it is called "internal" (*ajjhatta*) or "within" (*anto*).
By contrast, the realms of form and formlessness are called "external" (*bahiddhā*) or "without" (*bahi*). Thus the Blessed One said:
"A person with internal fetters, a person with external fetters. [This distinction is made] by way of the difference in objects and the difference in the mode of occurrence.

And although craving is divided into many different types, it is grasped as a single unity by way of its common characteristic of being a "tangle" (*jaṭā*); thus it is said, "by that tangle which arises in this manner.
Furthermore, being comprised within the continuity of beings (*sattasantāna*) referred to as "the world" (*pajā*), it proceeds by repeatedly tangling and binding;
therefore he says, "the world is entangled by the tangle. For, in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*),...
Even though there is no aggregate apart from its constituent parts, yet since a single part is not called an "aggregate," he spoke thus—"just as, for example, by means of bamboo twigs and so forth...
woven together"—showing the simile and the subject of the simile by treating the aggregate as distinct from its parts.
The connection is with the phrase "this tangle. By weaving them together without leaving even one of the three realms remaining, it is "the triple realm" (*tedhātuka*).
"Standing entangled": by this he indicates its vast scope and the extreme difficulty of disentangling it. By the phrase "Who is able to disentangle it?
he shows that the word "vijaṭeyya" (should disentangle) has the sense of a potentiality (*satti*), not the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*) or the like.
Thus, the connection is that when asked "What is the internal tangle? and so forth, the Blessed One spoke this verse to that son of the gods.

Thinking, “Edisova should answer this question,” he spoke the words beginning with “one whose range of knowledge is unimpeded regarding all phenomena,” thereby showing the Teacher’s excellence through his qualities.
Therein, “regarding all phenomena” (*sabbadhammesu*) means regarding all knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhamma*) distinguished by their divisions such as the past and so forth.

“One whose range of knowledge is unimpeded” (*appaṭihatañāṇacāro*) means one whose movement of knowledge is unhindered because it proceeds without attachment due to the abandonment of all obstructions to the knowable. By this, [he is shown] in the three times...
By the very inclusion of the first three unique qualities through the manifestation of unimpeded knowledge and power (*appaṭihata-ñāṇatā-vibhāvana*),
it should be understood that the remaining unique qualities of the Blessed One are also included, because they share the same characteristic and are inseparable from them. They "play" (*dibbanti*)—
meaning they sport and dally with the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) and so forth, or they dwell among them— or [they are so called] because of their fitness for overcoming adversaries.
They are called *devas* because they desire to conquer; they engage in commerce by bestowing honor, wealth, and so forth, and by accepting gifts, while providing instruction on various matters;
they shine with a radiance attained through the power of their connection to an abundance of merit; they proceed without obstruction toward whatever object they intend;
and they are capable of accomplishing whatever they desire. Alternatively, they are *devas* because they are worthy of being honored (*devanīyā*).

They are called *devas* because they are to be approached as a refuge and ultimate resort by those seeking deliverance from various misfortunes, or because they are to be praised, or because they are desirable due to their possession of exceptional beauty.
They are threefold: conventional deities (*sammutideva*), deities by birth (*upapattideva*), and deities by purification (*visuddhideva*).

But the Blessed One, through his unsurpassed play of supernormal knowledge (*abhiññākīḷā*), by means of the supreme divine, brahma, and noble abidings (*vihāra*), and by the accomplishment of his desire for victory over the five kinds of Māra pertaining to his own and others' continuums—
By means of his preeminent conventional excellence— consisting of the right practice of the sovereignty of mind, the seven treasures, and so forth,
as well as his unwavering confidence, honor, giving, and receiving— and by means of his splendor known as the radiance of the body of supreme wisdom,

and by means of the movement of the body of knowledge which is not shared by others, he was engaged in the conquest of Māra, the possession of all the qualities of omniscience, and the accomplishment of the welfare of all.

Because he possesses an unobstructed spear (satti) and because he is to be approached as a refuge by the world including the devas, because he is to be praised, and because he is desirable through his affectionate nature, he stands having surpassed all those devas with his virtues;
thus, being the best and supreme among those devas, he is the "God of Gods" (devadeva). He is the god more worthy of worship than all other devas.
Alternatively, he is the "God of Gods" (Devadeva) because, having attained the state of a pure deity or the ornament of the qualities of omniscience,
he is a god superior to other gods;
and because he surpasses the qualities of the countless Sakka-s and Great Brahmas in immeasurable world-systems, he is preeminent.
One who is superior (*atisaya*) or more excellent than the *Sakkas* and the *Brahmās* is the "Super-Sakka" among the Sakkas and the "Super-Brahmā" among the Brahmās.

Because he cannot be obstructed by anyone in the world with its devas regarding his specific excellence in knowledge, abandonment, and teaching, and because he is free from fear from any quarter, he is "confident through the four grounds of self-confidence" (*catuvesārajjavisārado*).
With reference to this, it was said: "To you who claim to be a perfectly enlightened Buddha..."
"These phenomena have not been fully awakened to"—regarding such things, indeed, I dwell having attained fearlessness, whether it be a recluse or [anyone else].

Because he is endowed with the ten powers of knowledge, beginning with the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhānañāṇa*), he is the "Bearer of the Ten Powers" (*dasabaladhara*). It is with reference to this that it was said:
"In this world, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible," and so forth.
Regarding whatever is called "the knowable," because his knowledge is unobstructed in every respect therein, he possesses "unobstructed knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*).

Furthermore, because he is endowed with the eye of knowledge capable of seeing all that directly—as if looking at an *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of one's hand from every side and in every aspect—he is "all-seeing" (*samantacakkhu*);
this is the meaning of "omniscient" (*sabbaññū*). By these two terms, however, the subsequent...
Two uncommon knowledges are included here. The Blessed One is so called because of such reasons as his fortunate nature.
Whatever else is to be said on this matter will be explained in detail later in the exposition of the recollection of the Buddha.
And here, by the phrase "the unimpeded range of knowledge regarding all phenomena," [the text refers to] the Blessed One’s [response] to questions concerning the three times.
Since his capacity for answering questions has been demonstrated, there might be the suspicion that even the Blessed One is capable of answering the questions of deities;

to dispel that, he is called "the God of Gods" (*devadeva*). Furthermore, thinking, "Sakka, the Lord of Devas, who is a god superior to other gods, answers the questions of deities—what then is the distinction between him and this [Buddha]? in order to dispel such thoughts, [he is so designated].

It is said, "the supreme among the Sakkas. Since the Brahmās such as Sanaṅkumāra answer the questions asked even by Sakka, it is said, "the supreme among the Brahmās," in order to prevent those who might think, "What then is his superiority? from entertaining that notion.
And this distinction of his has become manifest through the four grounds of self-confidence and the ten powers of knowledge.
To show that [these qualities] exist for the purpose of vision, it is said: "the bearer of the four... [etc.]...
And to show that these various knowledges are established simultaneously with the attainment of this twofold knowledge, it is said: "possessing unobstructed knowledge, possessing the universal eye.

Demonstrating that this twofold knowledge is established by virtue of the destruction of faults—which is itself accomplished through the accumulation of the equipment of merit and knowledge—he spoke the word "Bhagavā" (the Blessed One).
Thus, the purpose for grasping these terms and their sequential order should be understood.

As for this final pair of knowledges—the knowledge of non-obstruction and the knowledge of omniscience—they are not distinct in meaning. Indeed, that single knowledge is spoken of in two ways by way of its objects and its modes of activity, in order to show that it is not shared by others.
Omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) has as its object all conventional phenomena, both conditioned and unconditioned, without exception;

because there is no obstruction therein, it is also called "unobstructed knowledge" (anāvaraṇañāṇa) by way of its unimpeded range. Whatever else needs to be said on this matter, we shall explain later in the description of the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati).
2. One who seeks and searches for the great aggregate of virtue and so forth is a *mahesi*; this refers to the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*). By that *mahesi*.
"Expounding" means explaining and detailing. "As it really is" means without error. "The divisions of virtue and so forth" refers to the classification of virtue, concentration, wisdom, and the rest.
"Very difficult to obtain" means it is truly hard to find because it is to be attained only during the ninth moment, which is free from the eight unfavorable occasions.

“Comprising virtue and so forth” means comprising the three aggregates beginning with virtue. For the Noble Path is comprised by the three aggregates because it is partial, like a kingdom is comprised by a city; but the three aggregates are not comprised by the Noble Path because they are complete. Indeed, this has been said:
“Friend Visākha, the three aggregates are not comprised by the Noble Eightfold Path; rather, by the three [aggregates]...”
"Furthermore, friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is subsumed within the aggregates.

It is secure because it cannot be obstructed by the thieves of the defilements. It is straight because it avoids the two extremes and because it abandons the crookedness of the body such as deceit and so forth.
It is a path because it proceeds by way of destroying all defiled phenomena, and because it leads to Nibbāna.
And it is the "path" because it is to be sought by those who desire Nibbāna. "For the sake of purification" means for the sake of Nibbāna, or for the state of purification;

that is to say, for Arahantship. "Not knowing things as they really are" means not understanding according to reality that such a thing—characterized by this nature, having this function, and possessing this purpose—is to be attained through the successive series of purifications beginning with purification of virtue. [It is so called] because of all defilement and because of saṃsāra.
They are called "desirous of purity" (*suddhikāmā*) because they desire and long for purification and liberation. The word *api* is used in the sense of inclusion;
it shows that they are not satisfied with mere virtue alone, but are also desirous of complete purification.
"Here" means in this teaching. Although these practitioners (*yogin*) are striving through their application and dedication to mental development (*bhāvanā*), they do so directed toward purification.
The construction is: "Even while practicing, they do not attain purification because they have not mastered the means. "Of them" refers to the yogis.

Granted that this *Visuddhimagga* (Path of Purification) brings joy to everyone who is intent upon hearing, memorizing, and mastering it due to its universal excellence, yet it is an especially great cause for the delight of yogis;
thus he says, "bringing joy to them. [This is] by means of the views of outsiders and other schools...
"Of perfectly pure determination" (*suvisuddhavinicchayaṃ*) means because of its non-confusion and because its determination is thoroughly purified.

"Of the Mahāvihāravāsins" indicates the school that serves as his own support. "Dependent on the method of exposition" (*desanānayanissitaṃ*) means dependent on the method of the commentary on the Dhamma.
And here, by the phrase "the cause of their gladness" and so forth, [he shows] purity, which is Nibbāna, through the purification from all stains of defilement.

It shows that this is the discourse-path of the Mahāvihāravāsins, which brings about joy because it leads unerringly to the goal for practitioners who aspire [to it], and which is a thoroughly correct and pure determination established by those of superior knowledge who have practiced rightly.
It should be connected thus: "Listen attentively as I speak attentively."
And here, by the phrase "of this verse now," the basis for the exposition of the *Visuddhimagga* is indicated;
by "spoken by the Great Sage," its authoritative status is indicated; by "the meaning according to reality, distinguished by virtue and so forth," the unerring summary-meaning is indicated;
by "very difficult to obtain... for the practitioner," the motive is indicated; and by "causing joy to them," [the result is indicated].

By the phrase "for this purpose," he shows the motive; and by the phrase "expounding the meaning with a very pure determination, based on the method of teaching of the Mahāvihāravāsins, with care," he shows the manner of performance.

Then, with the words "all you virtuous ones who desire purification, listen attentively," he enjoins the virtuous people to listen with care. For the prosperity of the Dispensation is dependent upon careful listening.

3. Since the discourse on the Path of Purification—which proclaims the state of a recluse (sāmañña) that is the common goal of the path of purification revealed through the analysis of the meaning of the words—arouses delight when being spoken, [Buddhaghosa] began with the words "Therein, purification... in order to clarify the Path of Purification according to the meaning of the terms.
Therein, the phrase "therein" (*tattha*) refers to the word "Path of Purification" (*visuddhimagga*) in the statement: "I shall speak the Path of Purification."
It is said therein: "Free from all stains" means free from and secluded from all stains of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, as well as all stains of defilement (*saṃkilesa*).
For that very reason, it is "absolutely pure," meaning it is purified at all times and in every way.
That by which one seeks, searches for, and attains the aforementioned purity is the "Path of Purification" (*Visuddhimagga*).
Therefore he said: "The 'path' (magga) is called the means of realization. The *Visuddhimagga* should be understood, in the primary sense, as the supramundane path;
however, because it is the means to that, the preliminary path is so called, as are the series of discourses based upon it.
This *Visuddhimagga* was taught by the Teacher through various methods, owing both to the elegance of his teaching and to the inclinations of those to be trained.
In order to show that this is one particular method among them, the passage beginning with "So panāyam" (But as for this... is commenced.
Therein, the phrase "katthaci" means in some Sutta. By the restrictive particle "eva" in "vipassanāmattavaseneva," it excludes serenity (*samatha*).

For serenity is its counterpart, and not virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. Furthermore, by the word "matta" (mere/only) in the sense of excluding qualifications, it excludes concentration (*samādhi*) along with its specific attributes.
Thus, having established that this is the teaching for one whose vehicle is insight (*vipassanā-yānika*), it is not merely concentration (*samādhi*) alone;

for insight is not possible without momentary concentration (*khaṇika-samādhi*). And "insight" should be understood as all three kinds of contemplation (*anupassanā*), not merely the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*);

for the realization of the truths (*saccābhisamaya*) is not possible by the mere seeing of impermanence. As for that which [is mentioned] in the verse regarding the characteristic of impermanence alone...
The grasping has been performed; this refers to one for whom that very [characteristic] becomes more clearly manifest as it presents itself.
For such a person, having made the other two characteristics even more distinct and having comprehended them, they attain distinction, and not merely the characteristic of impermanence alone.

"All formations" (*sabbe saṅkhārā*) refers to all formations belonging to the three planes; for these are what must be comprehended by insight. "Impermanent" (*aniccā*) means they are not permanent, unstable, fleeting, and fragile, breaking apart moment by moment.
"With wisdom" (*paññāya*) means with the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*); one sees and comprehends them.

Then, subsequently—that is, at a later time following the arising of the knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*) and the other stages—one becomes disenchanted (*nibbindati*) with suffering (*dukkhe*), precisely because of that aspect of impermanence.

When it is said, "All conditioned phenomena" regarding what is seen, one becomes disenchanted with suffering—consisting of the five aggregates belonging to the three planes—and acquires the knowledge of disenchantment (*nibbidāñāṇa*).
"This is the path to purification": this means that this contemplation of disenchantment, being the cause for dispassion and the other [factors], is the means for attaining Nibbāna.
"By way of jhāna and wisdom" means by way of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
And here, "jhāna" refers to the jhāna that serves as the foundation for insight. "In whom" means in which person. Regarding the phrase "jhāna and wisdom," this is the meaning:
the person who, having made jhāna the foundation and established insight, brings it to its fulfillment—he indeed is one who is near to Nibbāna.
Thus, being well-trained, he attains Nibbāna unreservedly in its vicinity.

"Kamma" refers to the volition of the Path; for it brings about the purification of beings through its nature of leading to the diminution of defilements. "Vijjā" (knowledge) is right view. "Sīla" (virtue) consists of right speech and right action.
"Uttama-jīvitaṃ" (the supreme livelihood) is right livelihood. "Dhamma" refers to the remaining four factors.
The factors of the Noble Path. Alternatively, "action" (*kamma*) refers to right action (*sammākammanta*), because of the statement:

"Friend Visākha, that which is right view and that which is right intention—these factors are included in the aggregate of wisdom. "True knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the inclusion of right view and right intention.
"Dhamma" refers to concentration (*samādhi*), as it is said: "Such is the nature of those Blessed Ones..."

As in the passages beginning with "there were," by the inclusion of that [term], one should understand that right effort and right mindfulness are also included, based on the statement: "And whatever, friend Visākha, is right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these states are comprised within the aggregate of concentration.
"Virtue" refers to right speech and right livelihood. "The supreme life" refers to such a noble person (ariyapuggala).
It should be understood that the Noble Eightfold Path is described here by the statement, "Life is the supreme life.
"By way of virtue and so forth" means by way of virtue, concentration, wisdom, and energy. "At all times" means at every moment from the time of undertaking [the precepts] onwards.
"Endowed with virtue" means endowed and possessed of the perfection of the fourfold purification of virtue (*cātupārisuddhisīla*). "Possessing wisdom" refers to both mundane and supramundane wisdom.
"Endowed with wisdom": well-composed through the concentration associated with that [wisdom]. "With energy aroused":
one who has exerted energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states.
"Resolute": one whose mind is indifferent toward body and life because it is directed toward Nibbāna. "The flood..."
The fourfold flood, beginning with the flood of sensual desire, or indeed the great flood of saṃsāra itself.
"The single way" (*ekāyana*) means the one path. Here, the word *ayana* is used in the sense of "path"; therefore, the meaning is:
"Monks, this path is a single track, not a forked road. Or else, it is so called because it goes to or reaches the one [goal], which is Nibbāna.
It is "the one-way path" (*ekāyana*) because it is to be traversed (*ayitabba*) or practiced (*paṭipajjitabba*) by one person alone, having abandoned the company of crowds;

or alternatively, it is a "way" (*ayana*) because one goes (*ayanti*) by means of it. It is "the one-way path" because it is the way of the One, the Blessed One, the Supreme; or because it was brought forth by Him;
or because it is the way within this very single Dhamma and Discipline. "For the purification of beings" means [purification] from the stains of passion and so forth.
And for the sake of the purification and cleansing of sentient beings from the defilements such as covetousness and improper greed.

*Yadidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is "those which are these. Since that which was previously called the "Path"—by way of its characteristic of refuge and its status as the Path—has fourfold divisions according to the objects such as the body and so forth, it is stated as "the four foundations of mindfulness" (*cattāro satipaṭṭhānā*). [The phrase] "in the case of the right efforts and so forth... [is used].
Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of delight in diligence (*appamādābhirati*) and so forth is to be understood.
For the *Visuddhimagga* has been taught in some places by way of delight in diligence and the rest as well. As it is said:
"A bhikkhu who delights in diligence, seeing fear in negligence..."
“Unfit for decline, he is close indeed to Nibbāna.

Regarding this: the word *tatra* (there) refers to that verse. The detailed commentary (*vitthārasaṃvaṇṇanā*) to be stated below stands in the place of the exposition (*niddesa*) and sub-exposition (*paṭiniddesa*);

whereas the more concise explanation of the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*) stands in the place of the summary (*uddesa*). Therefore, he says, “This is the concise commentary. Of what has been thus indicated...

For indeed, the exposition and further exposition of the meaning are easy to perform and easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "established in virtue" (*sīle patiṭṭhāya*): here, "virtue" (*sīla*) refers to wholesome virtue (*kusalasīla*).
Although even unwholesome states are referred to as "virtue" in such passages as, "And what, master carpenter, are unwholesome virtues?";

nevertheless, because they are unfit to serve as the foundation for the cultivation of the mind and wisdom that is currently being discussed, even the virtues of mere ritual action (*kiriyasīla*) [are not intended].
Since the others are impossible, it is only wholesome virtue (*kusalasīla*) that is intended here.
In such passages as "fulfilling virtue," the word "fulfilling" means guarding, or increasing; the sense is that one restrains oneself in all respects and does not transgress.
For one who has become thus, by not abandoning that [virtue], one is said to be "established" therein. Indeed, regarding the phrase "in virtue":

This is the locative case used in the sense of a support (*ādhāre bhumma*). "Having established" (*patiṭṭhāya*): establishment is twofold, by way of the distinction between support (*nissaya*) and decisive support (*upanissaya*).
Therein, establishment as decisive support is mundane; the other is supramundane in the case of grasping without breaking [the continuity].

However, in the case of grasping with breaking [the continuity], there is establishment as support and decisive support according to the manner of co-nascent factors and of preceding and succeeding factors in the arising of mundane states of consciousness.

Just as it is possible [in the case of mundane states], so too in the case of supramundane states, a foundation consisting of the virtue of the lower paths and fruits is possible as a decisive support (*upanissaya-paṭṭhāna*).

And when the word "foundation" (*patiṭṭhā*) is intended to mean a decisive support, its meaning should be understood according to the sense of a prior temporal action, as in the phrases "having relied upon faith" (*saddhaṃ upanissāya*), and so forth. Therefore he said: "But previously indeed his bodily action..."

“Verbal action and livelihood are perfectly pure. However, when the support as a foundation (nissayapatiṭṭhā) is intended, the meaning should be understood in terms of simultaneous activity, as in the passage beginning, “dependent on the eye,” and so forth.
For right speech and the others serve as supporting conditions (nissayapaccaya) for their associated factors, such as right view, precisely by way of co-nascence (sahajāta).

A *nara* is one who leads (*neti*), thus a man. For just as a being who has become the primary nature (*pakati*) is called a "man" (*purisa*) because he lies (*seti*) or proceeds in a high place (*puri*) in the sense of being superior to the other nature, so too is he called a "man" (*nara*) in the sense of leading.
Indeed, even a person who is a son or a brother stands in the position of a leader for his mother, paternal aunt, and elder sisters, let alone for anyone else.
Regarding the others: because she goes toward a man (*nara*), or because she belongs to a man, she is a woman (*nārī*).

Although she too possesses the capacity to disentangle the tangle of craving (*taṇhājaṭā*) as much as he does, the author says "man" (*naro*) to indicate the being who is primarily [the subject] here, just as one says "the Teacher of gods and men" (*satthā devamanussānam*).
In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is stated "a man is a being" (*naro ti satto*) to show that, without distinction, the term refers to a person (*puggala*).
“Possessing wisdom” (*sapañño*): he proceeds together with wisdom that has become a result (*vipāka*), thus he is “possessing wisdom.
For it is by means of that wisdom—which, from the very beginning, proceeds extensively as a continuous stream—that this being deserves to be specifically called “possessing wisdom.
Indeed, even resultant wisdom (*vipākapaññā*), through its excellence as a continuity, serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the arising of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāpaññā*).

Because that [wisdom] is absent in those with rootless or two-rooted consciousnesses. It is appropriate to say "possessing wisdom" (*sapañño*) by way of the wisdom known as *sampajañña* (clear comprehension), which performs its respective functions.

However, since in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) the word "skilled" (*nipaka*) is taken to mean "protective wisdom" (*pārihārika-paññā*), the meaning stated here is specifically in terms of resultant wisdom (*vipāka-paññā*). [This refers to] the wisdom of the kamma-born, three-rooted rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

"In the three-rooted rebirth-linking born of kamma, wisdom is discerned"—thus, the term "three-rooted" (tihetuka) should be connected with the term "rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi), not with the term "wisdom" (paññā). For there is no such thing as wisdom that is itself three-rooted.

Wisdom that arises from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards is called "wisdom in rebirth-linking" because it is rooted in that [rebirth-linking], not because it occurs only at the precise moment of rebirth-linking.

It is called *citta* because it thinks (*cinteti*) and closely contemplates (*upanijjhāyati*) an object; thus, it is concentration (*samādhi*). For that [concentration] has the function of close contemplation to a preeminent degree.
Indeed, initial application (*vitakka*) and the other factors do not accomplish that purpose without concentration, whereas concentration accomplishes it even without them.

Furthermore, it is called *citta* because it is accumulated (*cita*) by conditions through the attainment of a state of proficiency and strength, and likewise because it accumulates (*cinoti*) the continuum in such a way; thus, it is concentration.

Because of the diversity of mind through the first jhāna and so forth, and because of the production of mind by means of the various kinds of psychic power (iddhividha) and so on, the designation "mind" (citta) is indeed applicable to concentration (samādhi) even without instruction from another.

However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is stated—taking the word *citta* to be conventionally established in the sense of consciousness—that "here, concentration is indicated under the heading of 'mind'. [This is said] by way of its modes according to its true nature.

“Wisdom” (paññā) means that which knows. Although it is of many kinds according to its divisions such as the wholesome and so forth, because of the word “develop” (bhāvaya), it is intended here as that which is to be developed;
to show this, it is called “insight” (vipassanā). Furthermore, the word “develop” should be applied to each [term]:
“developing the mind and developing wisdom. Are these two mundane, or...
Or is it supramundane? It should be regarded as supramundane from the perspective of the highest description.
For when one cultivates that [concentration], it is said that at the moment of the Noble Path, one disentangles the tangle of craving by way of its total eradication; it is not mundane.
However, even mundane states are included here as "uninterrupted" (ānantariya) because they cannot exist without mundane serenity and insight. For one whose vehicle is serenity...

For indeed, without the three doors of liberation, the attainment of the supramundane (lokuttara) can never occur for either of the two types of concentration—namely, that which is distinguished as access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā), or the other, momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi). Therefore, he said: "cultivating both concentration and insight.
In this context, when mundane serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are intended, then the word "cultivating" (bhāvaya) refers to the act of cultivation.
The statement regarding the state of being a cause means "the causes for development. For it is by those causes for development that the act of disentangling occurs.

However, when the supramundane states are intended, there is merely a description of the present state of development; for the disentangling of the tangle of craving occurs at the very same time as both types of development.
“Zealous and discerning”: this is a praise of the qualities that assist the aforementioned meditation.
For one who is devoted to the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*), these three qualities—energy, mindfulness, and clear comprehension—are of great benefit.

Indeed, a subject of meditation supported by energy, when guarded by mindfulness and clear comprehension, does not fall away and brings about further distinction. This is because of the establishment of a firm foundation.
And herein, faith is established because virtue has faith as its decisive support, as do energy and the others.
For one who does not have faith in the object of faith, the aforementioned energy and so forth are impossible, and likewise with concentration.

Just as faith is established through energy and the others by way of being their cause, so too is concentration established through them by way of being their fruit. This is because when energy and the others are perfected, [concentration follows].
He is indeed accomplished in concentration, because that [concentration] is absent for one who is not concentrated. But how is mindfulness established here? By the inclusion of the term *nipaka*.
For mindfulness that has attained a state of sharpness and clarity is called "discernment" (*nepakka*). As it is said: "Endowed with supreme mindfulness and discernment.
However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), this meaning is shown as "discernment is wisdom" (*paññā*). By the inclusion of that very term...

Mindfulness is indeed included [therein], for there is no wisdom devoid of mindfulness. However, others say that since "possessing wisdom" (*sapañño*) already includes protective wisdom (*pārihārika-paññā*), they explain the word "discerning" (*nipako*) as having the meaning of "mindful" (*sato*).
Although the abandoning of defilements is indeed an exertion (*ātāpana*) common to right view and the other factors as well, the term *ātāpa*—like the term *ātappa*—[is used here specifically].
"It is established in energy itself," he said, "one who is ardent is one who possesses energy.

Alternatively, because energy—which functions by way of exertion toward the associated states for the sake of abandoning opposing factors—possesses an exceptional quality of such burning (*ātāpana*), it is energy alone that is so described, and not other states.
Furthermore, this vowel *ī* in the word *ātāpī* is an indicator of praise or of excellence. "One who possesses energy" (*vīriyavā*).
The word *vā* (or) should also be understood in that same sense. By this, possession of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*) is expressed. Therefore he said:

"in the sense of burning and scorching the defilements. Here, by the inclusion of the term "burning" (*ātāpana*), he refers to the element of initiative (*ārambha-dhātu*), taking it as the initial arousal of energy;
and by the inclusion of the term "scorching" (*paritāpana*), he refers to the elements of launching and striving (*nikkama-parakkama-dhātu*), [which function] entirely against their opposites.

It is so called by way of its having emerged and its successive attainment of distinction. It is "discerning" (*nipaka*) because it dries up or withers away its opposite, or because it protects and preserves itself;
thus it is one who is fully aware. They are "those engaged in the maintenance" (*pārihārikā*) because they are devoted to the preservation of the meditation subject.
She is "the leader in all duties" (*sabbakiccapariṇāyikā*) because she guides all tasks, such as going forward and so forth, by means of clear comprehension of purposefulness and the rest.
It is the guide for all these duties: the learning of the meditation subject, questioning about it, the commencement of development,
the method of attention, and therein, thoroughness, constancy, suitability, skill in the sign, self-exertion, lack of shrinking in the interval, the balancing of the faculties,
the attainment of evenness of energy, and the application of evenness of energy.
The leader in all duties. "He sees fear" (bhayaṃ ikkhati) is thus called a *bhikkhu*;

by this general statement of the characteristics of a *bhikkhu*, it is shown that the state of being a *bhikkhu* consists solely in one's practice (*paṭipatti*), and not in such things as being a mendicant (*bhikkhaka*) or wearing the distinctive robes.
For in this way, the inclusion of novices (*sāmaṇera*) and others who have completed their tasks, as well as those practicing the path who have not yet gone forth, is accomplished.
Furthermore, the meaning should be understood here in terms of practice. Alternatively, he is called a *bhikkhu* because he "splits" (*bhindati*) evil, unwholesome states.
"He disentangles this" refers to the person of wisdom who, having established himself in virtue, being ardent and prudent, develops the mind and wisdom—as it has been said;
the connection is that such a *bhikkhu* disentangles this tangle of craving. Now...
In order to show that this "unbraiding" is comparable to the unbraiding of a bamboo thicket, the text refers back to the qualities such as virtue mentioned in the verse with the words,
"By means of this virtue," and so forth. Since the qualities of virtue and the rest— occurring at various moments and mixed together within the continuum of the practitioner—
are what are grasped by the verse, one who takes them collectively says, "Endowed with six qualities."
He said: "Indeed, those six factors are not found together in a single continuum at a single moment.
And because the verse was spoken with reference to a person (*puggala*), he therefore spoke the words beginning with 'Just as if a man' while presenting a simile also with reference to a person.
In that context, *sunisitam* means well-sharpened; the meaning is exceedingly keen. [This refers to] the whetstone for the sword."
Both the making of it exceedingly sharp and its being lifted by the strength of the arm are stated as a simile after having been established as actual facts;
showing both of these in relation to the subject of the simile, he said: "Well-sharpened on the stone of concentration...
lifted by the hand of wisdom. For it is through the quality of concentration that wisdom becomes keen. Therefore the Blessed One said: "One who is concentrated..."
“He understands it as it really is. And his energy is a supporting factor because of its exerting nature.
“He would disentangle” means he would be able to disentangle. For when insight leading to emergence is present, the practitioner is indeed capable of disentangling the tangle of craving.
And here, “disentangling” is abandonment by way of complete cutting off; thus he said, “he would cut it away and shatter it.”
One who is worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇā*) is "worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyya*). One who is both foremost (*agga*) and worthy of offerings is "foremost worthy of offerings" (*aggadakkhiṇeyya*).
Alternatively, the foremost offering is the "foremost offering" (*aggadakkhiṇā*); one who is worthy of that is "foremost worthy of offerings. 5. *Tatra*: in that verse. *Ayaṃ*:
this practitioner (*yogāvacara*) who is called both "man" (*nara*) and "monk" (*bhikkhu*). Again...
*Therein*: in that aforementioned wisdom (*paññā*). *His*: of the bhikkhu. This is a genitive case used in the sense of the agent; the meaning is "by him.

There is nothing further to be done for the attainment of distinction because of the absence of the three-rooted rebirth-wisdom (*tihetuka-paṭisandhi-paññā*). Therefore he said: "For that [wisdom] was already accomplished by the power of previous karma alone.
*By him*: by the yogi. In meditation, by one who acts with persistence due to the state of energy (*vīriya*) being continuously active.
"By way of wisdom" means by way of the wisdom consisting of the ninefold factors already mentioned.

One who is habitually disposed to perform whatever is to be done solely through clear comprehension (*sampajañña*), or for whom there exists such a mode of clear comprehension therein, or who is a maker or producer of clear comprehension—that is, of non-delusion—is "one who acts with clear comprehension" (*sampajānakārī*); [the phrase] "by that one acting with clear comprehension" refers to him. "In this regard" means in this [state].

In this verse, because energy is a constituent factor (*aṅga*) in the accomplishment of virtue and the other qualities, it is not mentioned separately; rather, it is stated as "by way of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

Having stated the summarized meaning of the teaching in its undivided form with the words "he shows the Path of Purification" (*Visuddhimaggaṃ dasseti*), the passage beginning with "to this extent" (*ettāvatā*) is stated in order to show that same teaching again in its divided form.
Therein, "to this extent" means by means of this much teaching. "Trainings" (*sikkhā*) is in the sense of that which is to be trained in.

Training (*sikkhā*). And here, training should be understood as cultivation (*āsevana*). One who cultivates by way of restraint and so forth through the factors of virtue (*sīla*) and the rest is said to "train" (*sikkhati*) in them.
The teaching (*sāsana*) is the teaching of practice (*paṭipatti*). The decisive support (*upanissaya*) is the powerful cause.

Avoidance (*vajjana*) is non-approach. Cultivation (*sevanā*) is development (*bhāvanā*). The opposite (*paṭipakkha*) is the opposite of that which is to be abandoned. Although it says "in virtue" (*sīle*) in this verse—

This was stated in a general sense, not specifically as "in higher virtue" (*adhisīla*). However, since that [virtue] is intended here as the foundation for disentangling the tangle of craving, it is said:

"By means of virtue, the training in higher virtue is explained. For virtue that leads to existence (*bhava*) is merely virtue, whereas virtue that leads to non-existence (*vibhava*) is the training in higher virtue.
This is because a general designation applies to a specific instance. The same principle applies to the remaining trainings as well.

"By virtue" means by virtue that constitutes the training in higher morality (*adhisīla-sikkhā*). For that [virtue], by virtue of its uniqueness, demonstrates the excellence at the beginning of the Dispensation (*sāsana*), and not merely the mere practice of restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*).
Therefore it is said: "Virtue well-purified is the non-doing of all evil. "Of the wholesome" (*kusalānam*) means of those skilled in the Path (*magga*).
Or, "of the wholesome" means of those that are blameless (*anavajja*). By this, the states of the Noble Fruits (*ariya-phala-dhamma*) are also [included].
The inclusion is established. "The non-doing of all evil" means the non-performance and non-transgression of everything that is blameworthy.
By this, the inclusion of the entire range of virtue (sīla), divided into positive conduct (cāritta) and prohibitive conduct (vāritta), is effected;

for even the failure to do what ought to be done is indeed blameworthy. "Because it is stated at the beginning" means because concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā) are mentioned at the beginning of the verse. This refers to their status as the beginning.
This is because it is the root of those superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma). Alternatively, "ādivacanaṃ" means the statement of the beginning.
By the word "beginning" (ādi), the inclusion of such things as "virtue, concentration, wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation" should be understood.
Because virtue is purified, it brings about qualities such as non-remorse by distancing causes such as remorse; thus, it is said: "Because it brings about qualities such as non-remorse."
By this it should be understood that not only is the excellence of virtue (*sīla*) elucidated, but its foundational nature as well;
for in the Sutta, the successive conditionality of [virtue]—beginning with non-regret and culminating in the knowledge and vision of liberation—is stated.

"By concentration" means by concentration which constitutes the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*). This is said because [concentration] functions by encompassing the entire Dispensation (*sāsana*).

Because the virtue to be practiced at the beginning is taken by the first word of the verse, and the wisdom to be practiced at the conclusion is taken by the third word, concentration—which is to be practiced in the middle—is understood by elimination through the second word. Thus it is said:
"Concentration is in the middle of the Dispensation because of the statement beginning with 'the undertaking of the wholesome,'" and this does not refer to the word *kusala* itself.

Because it is dependent on the method of concentration (*samādhi*). For one who possesses prior support (*pubbūpanissaya*), the capacity for directed application (*abhinīhāra*) through the possession of the eight factors such as concentration, and the bringing of qualities such as the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*), occurs.

When the wisdom of the supreme path (*aggamaggapaññā*) has been attained, that for which one went forth is brought to completion; thus, wisdom is the culmination of the Dispensation (*sāsana*). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "This is the benefit of training..."
“Monks, the holy life is lived with faith as its dominant factor, wisdom as its culmination, and liberation as its essence.
The purification of one’s own mind (*sacittapariyodāpana*) consists in the complete eradication of all defilements from one’s own mind.
When the function of wisdom has thus reached its pinnacle, there remains nothing further to be done; therefore, wisdom is the culmination of the Teaching.
It should be understood [as follows]. "Because it brings about the state of suchness" (*tādibhāvāvahanato*):

it is "such" (*tādi*) because there is an absence of attraction toward desirable things and gains, etc., and an absence of aversion toward undesirable things and losses, etc.; or else, it is "such" because it is the same toward desirable and undesirable objects whether they have come within the range of perception or not.
The state of being such is "the state of suchness" (*tādibhāva*); it is because of its bringing about that state. "By the wind" (*vātena*) means by reason of the wind.
"Does not blow" means it does not move. "Does not stir" means it does not quiver; the intention is, "How could there be movement?

The word *tathā* (thus) has the sense of summarizing the mode of manifestation of those [qualities], just as virtue and so forth are the manifestors of the training in higher virtue and so on, so too is the proximate cause (*upanissaya*) for the state of possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*) and so forth.
This is because virtue, while being purified by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, [is so manifested].
And by the power of the knowledge of being the owner of one’s own kamma, one is purified from the stains of defilement and reaches fulfillment;
therefore, when the perfection of virtue (sīlasampadā) is being accomplished, it establishes the power of mindfulness and the power of knowledge by way of being a supporting condition (upanissaya).

Thus, its status as a supporting condition for the three types of clear knowledge (vijjā) should be understood through its provision of a homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu). For, through mindfulness and discernment (satinepaka), the clear knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-vijjā) is accomplished.

Through clear comprehension (*sampajañña*), which consists in the habitual performance of all duties with full awareness, there is the accomplishment of the second true knowledge (*vijjā*) by means of the continuous pursuit of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth (*cutūpapāta-ñāṇa*).

Through the absence of transgression, because of the actuality of the abandonment of defilements (*saṃkilesa*), there is the accomplishment of the third true knowledge by way of the purity of intention (*ajjhāsaya-suddhi*) as a necessary condition for turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).

Without the fulfillment of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*paññā*) already previously accomplished, the virtue (*sīla*) [of one who has not yet reached the path] cannot serve as a necessary condition for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*).
This should be illustrated by those whose taints are destroyed through dry insight (sukkha-vipassaka-khīṇāsava).

It is said, "not beyond that," considering that virtue is not a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), just as concentration and wisdom are.

Because of the statement, "One who is concentrated understands things as they truly are," the perfection of concentration is the decisive support (upanissaya) for the six higher knowledges. Concentration is [the support] for the analytical insights, just as wisdom is.
It is said that it is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), as stated in the phrase "not beyond that.

According to the statement, "Abundance indeed arises from yoga," the perfection of wisdom (*paññā-sampatti*)—cultivated through prior application (*pubbayoga*), living with a teacher, the local language, penetration (*kāosalla*), grasping [the meaning], and interrogation—is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the various analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

Since even the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*paccekabodhi*) and perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*) depend upon the perfection of wisdom, there is nothing that cannot be attained through wisdom.
Because there is no distinction [in the result], and because that specific variety of analytical knowledge (*paṭisambhidā*) has an exclusive cause,
it is stated as "not by another cause" rather than "nothing beyond that," as was said previously. And here,
since it is stated, "relying indeed upon the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampatti*)," for whomsoever [there is] the entirety of that which constitutes the unfolding of concentration (*samādhi*)...
The six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) do not succeed; for him, there is no perfection of concentration (*samādhi-sampadā*) by way of the ultimate limit.

Although the three true knowledges (*vijjā*) are a partial aspect of the direct knowledges, only those three true knowledges that have arisen from the perfection of virtue (*sīla-sampatti*) are included here.

For just as the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*) arise from the perfection of wisdom (*paññā-sampatti*), [they are attained] through the path itself for one endowed with the necessary support (*upanissaya*).
They succeed precisely at the moment of the Path (magga), because they are to be acquired only at that time.

Thus, the three types of higher knowledge (tisso vijjā) arising from the perfection of virtue (sīla-sampatti) and the six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā) arising from the perfection of concentration (samādhi-sampatti) succeed by means of the Path itself for one who possesses the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya).
Therefore, their attainment should be understood as occurring through the very attainment of the Path. This applies to both Paccekabuddhas and Sammāsambuddhas.
For these specific attainments of these noble ones are indeed comparable to the attainment of the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha or of a Sammāsambuddha.

The fact that right practice in the Vinaya, Sutta, and Abhidhamma serves as a necessary condition (*upanissaya*) for the attainment of the state of one possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*), and so forth, should also be understood according to the method already stated.
Because one whose virtue is perfected lacks the pursuit of sensual pleasures, it is said that through virtue one avoids the first extreme. For the most part...
For beings, due to the cause of sensual desire, even through acts such as killing living beings, their modes of activity become impure.

Since for one who has attained the bliss of jhāna there is no possibility of physical exhaustion, the avoidance of the second extreme by means of concentration is stated, because the body is pervaded by the sublime matter produced by jhāna.
"By wisdom" refers to path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*). For, according to the highest description, the noble path alone is definitively the middle way of practice.
[This is] the name. Even so, the avoidance of the two extremes must be clarified by way of mundane wisdom (*lokiya-paññā*) as well.
Since virtue causes one who possesses it to be reborn only in the happy destinies (*kamasugati*), it is the cause for liberation from the four states of misery (*apāya*);
thus he said: "By virtue, the means for transcending the states of misery is made manifest. For the abstention from killing living beings and so forth—

It brings about the affliction of miserable rebirths. Concentration (samādhi), by producing [the mind] only in the sublime plane for one who possesses it, liberates one from the entire realm of sense-desire (kāmabhava);
thus it is said: "By means of concentration, the method for transcending the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) is revealed.
For [concentration] is the suppressor of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and the other [hindrances] which provide support to sense-sphere karma.

Jhāna brings about the defilements of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*). Nor should access-jhāna (*upacārajjhāna*) be indicated here, because absorption-concentration (*appanāsamādhi*) is intended.
Nor is there any occasion for the statement: "Just as the existence of the woeful states (*apāyabhava*) is to be transcended by virtue, so too is it to be transcended by concentration.

For one who is transcending even the existence of happy destinies (*sugatibhava*), what need is there to mention the transcending of the miserable destinies? Thus, it is the means for transcending all forms of existence.

The means for transcending all nine types of existence, beginning with the existence of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*), is through virtue and concentration; yet even though these existences have been transcended by virtue and concentration, they are not truly transcended because their cause has not been abandoned.
However, because that cause has been thoroughly abandoned by wisdom, they are indeed transcended.

"By way of abandonment as a factor" (*tadaṅgappahānavasena*) means, for example, as darkness is [dispelled] by the light of a lamp, so too [is it dispelled] by each respective wholesome factor pertaining to the bases of meritorious action.

By way of abandoning each respective unwholesome factor. "By means of concentration through the abandoning of suppression" means by way of the prevention of the occurrence of those various factors such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), through concentration—distinguished as access and absorption—just as water-weeds on the surface of the water are removed by striking them with a jar.
"By wisdom" means by the wisdom of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). "By way of abandoning through eradication" refers to the four Noble Paths.

Because it has been cultivated, for one possessing that respective path within their own continuum, it functions by way of the abandonment consisting in the absolute non-occurrence—defined as eradication—of the mass of defilements belonging to the side of origination, which were described in the passage beginning with "for the abandoning of the various views.
It is the counteragent to the transgression of defilements; that is, it is the counteragent to the phenomena of corruption, or to karma and defilements, at the doors of body and speech.
Transgression (*vītikkama*) is overstepping; its opposite is revealed by virtue (*sīla*), because virtue has non-transgression as its essential nature.
The arising of defilements in the mind, having exhausted the occurrence of the wholesome by way of providing them an opportunity, is "obsession" (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
Concentration suppresses that; thus it is said: "By concentration, the opposite of obsession is revealed."

Because concentration abandons the active outbursts [of defilements], and because they lie latent (anusenti) in the continuum (santāna) by way of being unabandoned, they are called *anusayas*—meaning they are ready to arise when they encounter their respective causes.
These should be understood as the seven defilements, such as sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), which have become firmly rooted and are ready to arise upon obtaining a corresponding cause.
Since these are abandoned in every respect by the wisdom of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga-paññā*), it is said: "By means of wisdom, the antidote to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) is revealed."
Bodily misconduct and so forth are called *duccarita* because they are badly practiced, or because they are practices defiled by the *kilesas*.
That very [misconduct], wherever it arises, defiles that mental continuum (*santāna*), oppresses it, and afflicts it; thus, it is *saṃkileso*.

Its purification is through virtue (*sīla*) by way of abandoning it through its specific antidote (*tadaṅgavasena*), since virtue is the opposite of transgression. Regarding the defilement of craving (*taṇhāsaṃkilesa*):

Purification from the defilement of craving is abandonment by way of suppression, because concentration is the opposite of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), and because it is the direct antithesis to craving.
Purification from the defilement of views is abandonment by way of eradication,

because wisdom is the opposite of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), and because wisdom— which grasps things as they truly are— is the opposite of those modes of view which grasp things incorrectly.
Because it is the direct opposite.

"Cause" means the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). "One who fulfills the precepts" refers to the non-transgression of the major training rules of morality—namely, the *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa* offenses—which constitute the primary morality because they form the beginning of the holy life of the Path.

Because he is able to fulfill completely whatever must be done regarding the precepts by emerging from them immediately upon committing minor and secondary offenses, he is called "one who fulfills the precepts.
The word "likewise" (*tathā*) links this to the phrase "one who fulfills the precepts" in the case of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*).
For these two noble ones [the once-returner and the non-returner] have abandoned sensual lust and ill will, which are obstacles to concentration.

Because the delusion that obstructs wisdom and conceals the truths has not been entirely eradicated, even while developing concentration and wisdom, they perform only a portion, a measure, or a limited part of what must be done regarding concentration and wisdom;
thus, those who act only to a limited extent in concentration and wisdom are nevertheless called "those who fulfill their conduct in the precepts. (The Non-returner)
But because sensual lust and ill will have been utterly eradicated, he is one who fulfills concentration.
Because delusion has been thoroughly and completely destroyed, the Arahant is one who fulfills wisdom.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Here, monks, a monk is one who fulfills the precepts, but is only partially accomplished in concentration and only partially accomplished in wisdom.
He commits those minor and lesser training rules and then emerges from them. Why is that?
Because, monks, I have not declared this to be a case of incapacity. As for those training rules...”
These are the fundamentals of the holy life, which are in conformity with the holy life; therein he is steadfast in virtue and firm in virtue, training himself by undertaking the rules of training.

With the total destruction of three fetters, he becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment. Furthermore, monks, here a monk [is established] in the virtues... (as before)... [and so on].
With the complete destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a once-returner;

having come back to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering. Furthermore, monks, here a monk is one who fulfills virtuous behavior, is one who fulfills concentration, and is one who practices wisdom to a moderate degree. He trains himself in those training rules... [as before] ...in the precepts of training.
Thus, with the five lower fetters abandoned... [he is] of a nature not to return from that world.
Furthermore, monks, here a monk is one who fulfills his conduct in the precepts, fulfills his conduct in concentration, and fulfills his conduct in wisdom.

He trains himself in those training rules regarding the minor and lesser matters... he trains in the rules of training. Through the destruction of the taints... [he realizes for himself with direct knowledge...]
“...and dwells having attained [it].
Having asked “How? and having analyzed the training and so forth, the words beginning with “Thus” were spoken to conclude the very same meaning that was stated.
Therein, “others” refers to the three seclusions (*viveka*), the three roots of the wholesome (*kusalamūla*), the three gateways to liberation (*vimokkhamukha*), and the three faculties (*indriya*).
These and others, such as the various triads of qualities other than the triad of trainings;
"of such a kind" means of the same nature as the triads of trainings and so forth that have been explained here by way of virtue and the rest.
For here, because it is virtue based on turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) that is intended, bodily seclusion is revealed by virtue.

There is seclusion of the mind through concentration, and seclusion from the substrata through wisdom. Likewise, by means of virtue, the wholesome root of non-hatred is manifested, because virtue has endurance as its primary characteristic and non-violence as its intrinsic nature.
By means of concentration, the wholesome root of non-greed is manifested, because concentration is the opposite of greed and has non-greed as its primary characteristic. But by means of wisdom—
It is non-delusion itself. And by means of virtue, the door to the signless liberation is revealed.

For, relying on the perfection of virtue which is dominated by non-hatred, the contemplation of impermanence—which sees the danger in hatred—is easily accomplished; and the contemplation of impermanence is the door to the signless liberation.
By means of concentration, the door to the desireless liberation [is revealed]; by means of wisdom, the door to the void liberation.

For the exertion based on non-greed, which is the escape from sensual desires, succeeds with ease through the contemplation of suffering for one who, relying on the perfection of concentration, sees the danger in sensual pleasures;
and the contemplation of suffering is the gateway to the desireless liberation. Relying on the perfection of wisdom, the contemplation of non-self succeeds with ease;
and the contemplation of non-self is the gateway to the emptiness liberation. Likewise...
