"In minute measures" means in measures of the smallest atom (*paramāṇu*). "In the various occurrences of unwholesome states of mind and so forth, consisting of training rules (*sekhiya*) committed unintentionally" means in the various occurrences of unwholesome states of mind and so forth that consist of training rules committed unintentionally; thus, the inclusion of the term "unintentionally" should be understood as a qualification of the training rules.
Furthermore, by the inclusion of the term "training rules," the observances (*vatta*) mentioned in the *Vattakkhandhaka* and other sections are also included here.
Indeed, they are intended as "sekhiyā" (rules of training) in the sense that one must train on their periphery.

For this reason, no specific limit for the sekhiyas was established in the Mātikā, unlike the cases of the pārājikas and so forth. By establishing it thus, the inclusion of the term "unintentionally" (*asañcicca*) in the phrase "having unintentionally committed a sekhiya offense" becomes justified.
For among the seventy-five sekhiyas included in the Mātikā, there is no such thing as "non-release through perception" (*no-saññā-vimokkho*).
There is a name for it; and here, by the very inclusion of "unintentionally," ignorance and lack of mindfulness are also included.
However, some say that by including "having committed [an offense] unintentionally" here, mindless offenses (*acittakāpatti*) are thereby grasped;

but that is merely their own opinion, because even among the heavy offenses (*garukāpatti*), there exists the state of being mindless in certain cases, and because of the distinction of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna-vikamma*) and the distinction of confession (*desanā-vikamma*).
Or rather, it is because here the lightest of all faults (vajja) is intended. Therefore he said: "Those faults which are trifling, minor, light, and considered light," and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of those [precepts] that are not to be transgressed and lead to non-offense for the sake of purification through restraint by the Pātimokkha should be understood.
One whose nature is to see fear [even in the slightest fault]... even a mere atom...
The nature of seeing [an offense] is such that one might treat even a slight fault as being like Mount Sineru, sixty-eight hundred thousand yojanas in height;
or conversely, the nature of seeing [an offense] is such that one might treat even the lightest mere wrong speech (*dubbhāsita*) as being like a defeat (*pārājika*).

"Whatever" refers to any training rule, including those classified as original formulations (*mūlapaññatti*), subsequent formulations (*anupaññatti*), universal formulations (*sabbatthapaññatti*), or partial formulations (*padesapaññatti*).
The virtue that is to be practiced and fulfilled. "Having properly undertaken" means having correctly, with diligence, and in every respect, undertaken it.
Now, is this perfection of conduct and resort included within the Pātimokkha virtue, or is it not so included?
It is included. If this is so, why was it stated again? Addressing this objection, he says: "And here," and so forth.

The Description of the Virtue of Restraint of the Faculties (Indriyasaṃvara-sīla) 15. The virtue of restraint of the faculties serves as a prerequisite for the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha; it must be cultivated only when that [latter] exists.
Thus it is said: "He is a bhikkhu established in the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha. For when this [virtue of restraint of the faculties] has been accomplished...
The virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is well-guarded and well-protected, like a crop with its thorn-fence well-arranged.
"By way of cause" means by way of the specific (asādhāraṇa) cause. For a fruit is designated by way of its specific cause, just as one says "a barley sprout" or "the sound of a drum.
Or else, this is a statement regarding that which depends [on a cause], using the conventional expression for the support itself.
"Just as 'the beds cry out' [is a metaphorical expression]. "Form" refers to the form base (*rūpāyatana*). Regarding the phrase "having seen a form with the eye":
if the eye itself were to see the form, then those possessing other types of consciousness would also see it; but this is not the case. Why?
Because the eye is devoid of consciousness (*acetana*). Therefore he said: "The eye does not see the form because it is without mind. Now, as for consciousness...
One might think that consciousness would see form even when it is behind a wall or similar obstacles because of its non-obstructive nature;
however, this is not the case, since there is no seeing by all types of consciousness. Therefore he said: "Consciousness does not see, because it is devoid of the eye.
In this regard, just as consciousness dependent on the eye sees, and not anything else, and that [seeing] occurs only when [the object] is not obstructed by something such as a wall—

It does not arise where there is an obstruction to light. However, where there is no obstruction—as in the case of crystal, a womb, a membrane, and so forth—it certainly arises even when the object is concealed.
Thus, it is the eye presided over by consciousness that sees, and not just any [eye];
it is with reference to the eye presided over by consciousness that this was said: "Having seen a form with the eye."
"In the collision with the object at the door" means when there is a collision between the door and its object;
the intended meaning is that the visible form has come into the range of the eye.

"By the consciousness based on the sensitive organ" means by the consciousness that arises depending upon the sensitive eye-organ, which is called "eye-consciousness. "Sees" means looks at. [This occurs] in dependence upon the sensitive eye-organ.
For when consciousness illuminates a visible-form object assisted by light by means of its inherent quality as a support, the person possessing that consciousness is said to "see the form.
Herein, this illumination is the discernment of the object according to its true nature, which is called "perception through direct experience" (*paccakkhato gahaṇa*).
This is like the piercing of a target with an arrow, wherein [the success] depends on the arrow's constituent parts.

Just as there is the expression "he pierces with a bow," so too, when the seeing of form is accomplished by consciousness, such a statement as "the eye sees form" is called a "figurative expression" (*sasambhārakathā*).
A "figurative expression" means a discourse accompanied by the causal factors; the meaning is that it is a discourse associated with the causes of seeing.
Alternatively, it is a discourse concerning seeing together with its equipment, hence a "figurative expression. Therefore, because [it is] by the [consciousness] alone...
There is no seeing of forms by means of the eye alone or by consciousness alone; therefore [it is said].

Regarding the phrase "the sign of woman or man": here, what is grasped by way of the form dependent on the female continuum consists of the shape, the lack of development of the flesh of the breasts, the absence of facial hair, the binding of the hair, the wearing of clothing, the movement of the limbs, and so forth.
And all of this is the "female sign" because it serves as the cause for the perception of "woman. By the reverse of what has been stated, the "male sign" is to be understood.
Regarding the phrase "or the beautiful sign, etc.": here, the "beautiful sign" is the desirable aspect that serves as the cause for the arising of lust.
By the word "etc.," there is an inclusion of the "repulsive sign" and so forth; that, however, is the undesirable aspect and so on, which serves as the cause for the arising of hatred and the like.

This is how it should be understood. While it is true that in this passage covetousness and ill will are presented in their own specific forms within the text, the inclusion of the sign of equanimity (*upekkhā-nimitta*) should also be intended;
for even delusion, which arises through a lack of equanimity, constitutes a lack of restraint. Indeed, he will later state:
"either forgetfulness or ignorance. And here, "the sign of equanimity" refers to the equanimity of ignorance.
The object that has become the basis for it should be understood as such by way of not regarding it [as beautiful].
Thus, in brief, the cause of lust, hatred, and delusion is stated to be "the sign of the beautiful" and so forth. Therefore he said:
"the sign which has become the basis for the defilements. It settles at the mere sight [of it], as in the Sutta: "In what is seen, there will be the mere seen."
In the manner already described, as soon as the sense-sphere of visible form is grasped by eye-consciousness and the [subsequent] cognitive processes (*vīthicitta*), it ceases;
one does not thereafter conceptualize any aspect such as beauty and so forth. "By making manifest" means by making distinct, by making clear.
For one who conceptualizes beauty and so forth in the hands and other limbs of an object that is dissimilar [to oneself], [the meditation fails].
The defilements arising there again and again become manifest; thus they are called their "secondary characteristics" (*anubyañjana*).
Furthermore, these are the modes of arrangement of the primary and derived material phenomena (*bhūta-upādāya-rūpa*) as they are situated in such and such ways.
For apart from that, there is no such thing as a "hand" or the like existing in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*). Therefore it was said: "Hand, foot... [etc.]..."
"It does not grasp the aspect. But what does it grasp? He says: "It grasps only that which is real therein.
Whatever exists in that body—the mere elements and derived matter such as head hair, body hair, and so forth—it grasps that exactly as it is.
To provide an illustration of grasping the aspect of foulness therein, he cites the story of the Elder Mahātissa, beginning with the words "The resident of Cetiyapabbata," and so on.

In that context, "well-adorned and well-graced" means thoroughly adorned and thoroughly graced. Adornment (*maṇḍana*) refers to beautifying with such things as jewelry that are brought forth for the purpose;

they say that "gracing" (*pasādhana*) is the restoration of the body by means of anointing it and so forth, while "adornment" (*pasādhana*) is the decoration with jewelry, garments, ornaments, and the like.
Adornment is the filling out of deficient parts. "With perverted mind" (*vipallatthacittā*).
"With a mind perverted by passion": while the Elder was walking along, attending solely to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he looked back because of the "thorn" of sound;
following the sound of laughter, he wondered, "What is this? and looked back. "The perception of foulness" (*asubhasaññā*) refers to the perception of a skeleton (*aṭṭhikasaññā*).
For at that time, the Elder was maintaining the skeleton meditation subject (*aṭṭhikakammaṭṭhāna*). "He attained arahantship": the Elder [attained it].

It is said that as she was laughing, by the very sight of her teeth and bones, because her preliminary development (*pubbabhāga-bhāvanā*) had been well-cultivated, she attained the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) and an especially superior access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*).

Remaining right there, she attained the first jhāna, took that as a basis, and by increasing insight (*vipassanā*), reached the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*) through the succession of the paths. [She attained] the perception of what was before (*pubba-saññā*).
"He recollected" means that he recalled and brought to mind the meditation subject on bones (*aṭṭhika-kammaṭṭhāna*) as it had been previously undertaken and was being practiced from time to time.
"Along the path" means along the way, step by step following her.
It is said that because the Elder was so proficient in his meditation, by the mere sight of the tooth-bone, her entire body appeared to him as a collection of bones.
He did not perceive that as "woman" or "man. Therefore he said, "I do not recall... [omission] ...on the great highway.

Having stated, "due to which lack of restraint of the eye-faculty," it was further said, "for the purpose of closing that eye-faculty with the bolt of mindfulness," and not for the sake of non-restraint itself. That is to say: that which is due to the lack of restraint of the eye-faculty.
The following after covetousness and so forth has been shown; it is stated with the understanding that this occurs specifically because of one whose faculty of the eye is unrestrained.
For the faculty of the eye is the primary cause for the following after covetousness and so forth by way of the eye-door, just as it is for the consciousness occurring through that same door.
When the faculty of the eye is unrestrained, those [defilements] follow after it.
That non-restraint is said to be caused by the eye-faculty being unrestrained.

For the phrase *yatvādhikaraṇaṃ* means "on account of which eye-faculty" (*yassa cakkhundriyassa kāraṇā*). And of what kind [of faculty] is it the cause? Of that which is unrestrained. And what is unrestrained?
The construction here is as follows: "For the sake of the restraint of that eye-faculty through whose lack of restraint covetousness and the other [unwholesome states] flow in."

However, regarding the moment of adverting (*javana-kkhaṇa*), if it is asked why "immorality" (*dussīlya*) and so forth were not mentioned again, the answer is that everything has already been stated right here;
thus, it should be understood as applying to all six doors according to what is possible. For immorality, in the sense of bodily and verbal misconduct, does not exist in the five doors;
therefore, non-restraint in the form of immorality occurs by way of the mind door, while the remaining forms of non-restraint occur by way of the six doors.

It should be applied as follows: Since forgetfulness (*muṭṭhasacca*) and the other factors are unwholesome states that are the opposites of mindfulness, their arising might occur at the five sense-doors;

however, misconduct (*dussīlya*), which consists of bodily and verbal transgressions, cannot arise there, because the impulsion consciousnesses (*javana*) of the five doors do not produce intimation (*aviññatti*).
Furthermore, the five types of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), such as misconduct, are the opposites of the five types of restraint, such as the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*).
They are stated as being the opposites of the restraints (*saṃvara*). "When that exists" means when that lack of restraint (*asaṃvara*) exists.
"In what way" means: by what manner does the lack of restraint arising in the impulsion (*javana*) come to be called "lack of restraint of the eye-faculty"?

That is the meaning of the question "how is it illustrated? By the phrase beginning with "in what way," [it is shown that] when there is a lack of restraint at the city gate, for those things connected to it...

Just as there is non-restraint (asaṃvuta-tā) regarding doors and so forth when a house is unsecured, so too, when there is non-restraint in the impulsion (javana), there is non-restraint in the doors and so forth connected to it.

In this way, the commonality of non-restraint in one thing with non-restraint in another is merely being illustrated; it does not indicate a commonality between preceding and succeeding moments, nor a commonality between the internal and the external.
Alternatively, when the door-moment, the bhavaṅga, and so forth are present, the impulsion arising again is treated as if it were "external," being analogous to the gate of a city.

It has been stated that the other [object] is like a house and so forth within a city. For, by way of being a condition, even though the preceding [state], such as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), has already ceased at the time of the impulsion (javana), it is indeed called "existent" for the production of the result, just like the eye and so forth. Indeed, it is not only that which is currently existing which is called "existent.
And regarding the phrase "having made it external," this refers to the fact that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramattha), the impulsion itself is external.
And although the other [the mind] does not possess an internal state [in the sense of being always present], according to such statements as, "Bhikkhus, this mind is luminous,
but it is defiled by adventitious defilements," the impulsion (javana) that arises from time to time is adventitious and thus external,
while the other, whose intrinsic nature is the opposite of that, is internal; this is one way of explaining it.

This was stated because [non-restraint] "occurs. Or, it is because when a javana (impulsive consciousness) arises as non-restraint, subsequently the door-moments, the bhavaṅga (subconsciousness), and so forth, become the causes for that non-restraint.
For, through the arising of non-restraint, the state of being its cause is manifested in the door-moments, the bhavaṅga, and so forth.

Having entered by means of the javana—which is like a city gate—there occurs the robbing of the thieves of immorality and the like within the door-moments, the bhavaṅga, and so forth, which is the destruction of the goods of wholesomeness.
It has been explained. For, in whichever door non-restraint arises, it proceeds precisely by severing the state of those doors and so forth as supports for restraint.
The connection between the doors, the bhavaṅga, and so forth with the impulsion (javana) should be understood as being due to their inclusion within a single continuum.
And herein, when a visible object has entered the range at the eye-door, there are seven occurrences of wholesome or unwholesome impulsion by way of the determined [process] and so forth.

Once it has arisen and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has subsided, a mind-door impulsion (manodvārika-javana) arises seven times with respect to that same object in accordance with the preceding process;

then, once the life-continuum has again subsided, the impulsion runs seven times at that same door, depending on that same object, determining it as "woman" or "man" and so forth by way of appreciation of the sense-faculties (pasāda-rañjana) and the rest. While proceeding in this manner—
With reference to the impulsion (javana), it was said: "When unvirtuousness and so forth arise during the impulsion, and there is non-restraint therein, the door is also unguarded," and so on.
But regarding that impulsion: "When virtue and so forth" means when virtue-restraint, mindfulness-restraint, knowledge-restraint, patience-restraint, and energy-restraint have arisen.
For just as unvirtuousness and so forth arise for one who does not establish the protection of mindfulness beforehand, [so too do their opposites arise when those restraints are present].
In the same way, it should be understood that the arising of virtue and the other [factors] occurs even more so for one who establishes the protection of mindfulness.
Regarding sounds and the rest as well, the signs (*nimitta*) and secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*) should be understood as appropriate.

For, having heard a sound with the ear-consciousness, one does not grasp the sign—which is the basis for defilement—whether it be "the voice of a woman," "the voice of a man," or anything desirable, undesirable, and so forth.

It settles upon the mere hearing [of the sound]. Furthermore, it does not grasp even that aspect which is designated as the "subsequent characteristic" (*anubyañjana*)—a term derived from its being a subsequent manifestation of defilements such as the sound of singing—which is established by way of its dullness or intensity and is divided into the sixfold scale beginning with *ṣaḍja*.

The same should be stated accordingly for odors and so forth. However, in the case of the mind-door, the mind-door consists of the mind-door adverting consciousness and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

When that door has the Dhamma as its object and it comes into range, it should be connected with the passage beginning, "having known [it] by means of the impulsive consciousness (javana-manoviññāṇa).
That which has defilement as its following is "defilement-following" (kilesānubandha); that itself is the grasping of signs and so forth.

Therefore, it has the characteristic of avoiding that grasping of signs and so forth followed by defilement; thus, it has the characteristic of avoiding the grasping of signs and so forth followed by defilement. By the word "and so forth" (ādi),...
He grasps the secondary details.
16. The commentary on the virtue of purity of livelihood:
"Vutta" means previously stated here by way of enumeration; for thus [it was said]: "The six things prescribed on account of livelihood..."

Having extracted the phrase "of the training rules" (*sikkhāpadānaṃ*), the passage beginning with "those which" (*yāni tāni*) was commenced in order to show them according to the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
Therein, the connection is: "those six training rules which were thus prescribed. "For the sake of livelihood" (*ājīvahetu*) means for the purpose of one's subsistence;
it refers to the intention: "In this way, I shall live without being exhausted by the [necessities of] requisites. "For the cause of livelihood" (*ājīvakāraṇā*) is a synonym for that same term.
"One who has evil desires" (*pāpiccho*) means one who is possessed by a wicked desire for the recognition of non-existent qualities.

"Overpowered by desire" (*icchāpakato*) means overcome, afflicted, or overwhelmed by desire. "Non-existent" (*asantaṃ*) means that which does not exist. "Unarisen" (*abhūtaṃ*) means that which has not yet arisen. Because it has not arisen, it is "non-existent";
thus the latter term is an explanatory reason for the former. "Superhuman states" (*uttarimanussadhammaṃ*)...
The Dhamma of superior human beings, or that which is superior and elevated above the human condition.
"He boasts" (ullapati) means he speaks with an inflated life-span; for morality is the life-span of a bhikkhu, and it vanishes at the very moment he speaks in such a manner.
Therefore he said: "There is an offense entailing defeat" (āpatti pārājikassa), meaning there is an offense designated as a *pārājika* for him who is known by the name of a *pārājika*.
The meaning of *ullapanā* is the act of committing a transgression. “He engages in matchmaking” (*sañcarittaṃ samāpajjati*) means he enters into the state of being a go-between;
the intention is that he reports a man’s thoughts to a woman, or a woman’s thoughts to a man.
The connection, namely “by way of the transgression of these six training rules,” has already been shown below.

"In 'kuhanā' and so forth" refers to the citation of the words from the scriptural passage (pāḷi) listed below. "This scriptural passage" refers to this explanatory passage (niddesa-pāḷi) found in the Vibhaṅga.
17. "Requisites such as robes are obtained" means they are gains (lābhā). When these very things are given with care and respect, they are honors (sakkārā).
"The sound of fame spread abroad" is renown (kittisaddo). "That gain, honor, and renown"—of one who is dependent upon these.
Here, "craving" (taṇhā) is intended as the basis; thus he says, "of one who yearns.
"Desiring to display non-existent qualities" means desiring to cause others to esteem qualities such as faith that do not exist within oneself.

For wicked desire (pāpicchatā) is characterized by the esteem of non-existent qualities, and it is characterized by a lack of moderation in receiving [offerings]. "Of one who is overcome by desire" means by wicked desire.
“Apakato” means one who has departed from right livelihood. And because such a person is afflicted by a calamity regarding livelihood, it is said:
“The meaning is ‘of one who is afflicted.
Deceit itself is the basis for the production of requisites; thus, it is the “basis of deceit. All three types of this [deceit] are mentioned therein.
The meaning should be understood as follows: "to show by means of this foundational text. "Only for one who has need of them" means only for one who has need of those robes and so forth.
"By the rejection" means because of the rejection of the robes and so forth. "Assa" means "it would be.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and by the acceptance," he includes the previously mentioned "rejection."
“Desire for more” (*bhiyyokamyatā*) means having many desires. “That” (*yaṃ*) is a reference to the action; therefore, the construction here is:
“that which is the wearing [of robes] after sewing them into a *saṅghāṭi* is what is appropriate for a recluse. “Market goods” (*pāpaṇikāni*) refers to things discarded from a shop.
“Rags” (*nantakāni*) refers to pieces of cloth that have been cast away. “Having gathered” (*uñchitvā*) means having collected by means of gleaning.
"Having collected. "By means of gleaning" means by what is obtained through the practice of gleaning.
"Requisites for life known as medicine, which serve as conditions for one who is ill" refers to the medicinal requisites for the sick.
"Putimutta" is a name for all cow-urine, whether old or not old. "By means of putimutta" means by that which has been released in a state of decay, discarded by others.
Or with putrid cow urine. "One who speaks of the ascetic qualities" (*dhutavāda*) means one who speaks of the ascetic virtues (*dhutaguṇa*) to others.
"In the presence" (*sammukhībhāva*) means because of being present before one's eyes; the meaning is "because it is obtainable.
"Bordering chatter" (*sāmantajappana*) is the muttering [of praise] by placing oneself near the attainment of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*). "Of great influence" (*mahesakkha*)...
The intention is that he is of great power by virtue of his attainment of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
Having stated "friend" (*mitta*) in a general sense, he further qualifies it as "one seen and one associated with. For a friend who is merely seen is "one seen" (*sanditṭha*);

one who possesses firm devotion is "associated with" (*sambhatta*). "Companion" (*sahāya*) means one who goes together; the meaning is "comrade" (*sakha*). Indeed, those who have taken the seven steps together are called "comrades" (*sakha*).
A *vihāra* is an entire residence delimited by a wall. An *aḍḍhayoga* is a long palace;
some also say it is a palace shaped like a garuḷa. A *pāsāda* is a square palace. A *hammiya* is a palace with a flat roof. A *kūṭāgāra* is a palace that must be constructed with two gables.
An *aṭṭa* is a special type of dwelling consisting of four or five stories, suitable for repelling rival kings.
A *māḷa* is a specific type of dwelling comprised of a single roof and possessing many corners.
An *uddaṇḍa* is said by some to be a long hall without inner chambers and with a single door; others, however, say that a *vihāra* is a long-faced palace (*pāsāda*).
An *aḍḍhayoga* is a lodging with a roof on one side; it is said that its wall on one side is higher than on the other.
*Ānīca*: by that, it becomes a dwelling with a roof on one side. A *pāsāda* is a long or square mansion. A *hammiya* has a flat roof and is provided with a courtyard (*candika*).
A *guhā* is simply a mountain cave. A *leṇa* is a shelter enclosed by a door. A *kūṭāgāra* is any kind of mansion supported by a central pillar (*kaṇṇikā*).
An *aṭṭa* is a house with thick walls, which does not have rafters but [is constructed] with bricks...
This is what constitutes a *chadana*. Some also say it is constructed in the shape of a watchtower (*aṭṭālaka*). A *māḷa* is a dwelling built in a circular form.
An *uddaṇḍa* is a particular type of shelter which is also called a "storehouse" (*bhaṇḍasālā*) or a "granary" (*udosita*). An *upaṭṭhānasālā* is a place for assembly.
*Koraja* is the useless restraint of bodily and verbal movements caused by the base dust of evil desire (*pāpicchatā*).
One who has that [shame] is *korajika*. One whose body is restrained through hypocrisy (*kohañña*) is *korajika*;
one who is excessively or frequently shameless is *korajikakorajika*. Some say it means "excessively suspicious. One who is excessively deceitful is *kuhakakuhaka*;
the meaning is "one who is preeminently deceptive. One who is excessively talkative is *lapakalapaka*. He is a "mouth-blower" by virtue of being *korajikakorajika* and so forth.
One who is esteemed by others merely on account of his own mouth and the words he utters— such a person,
making himself out to be like another by means of such a state, speaks words such as "this is a recluse.
The words "profound," and so forth, are stated because that speech is connected with superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*).

"By that which was done with the intention of being esteemed" means: by that which was done with the intention, "How indeed might people esteem me as 'noble' or 'one who has attained distinction'? "He steadies his gait" means:
he establishes his own gait carefully, like the gait of those who have attained distinction; he is as if walking mindfully and clearly comprehending. "Having resolved" means:
“May they know me as an arahant”—having fixed his mind thus, or having made this aspiration. “As if concentrated” means as if concentrated by means of jhāna-concentration.
“A meditator in public” means one who sits as if having attained concentration in a place within the range of sight of people;
a meditator in a place visible to the public. “Consisting of the postures” means consisting of the stabilization of the postures.
"By what is termed the use of requisites" means by that which is described as the use of requisites produced through improper means;
or, it is by that use of requisites which is to be reckoned (saṅkhātabba) or described (kathitabba). Speaking in one's own presence while acting as if it were someone else is "sāmantajappita.
By shortening the vowel *ā* to *a*, it is called "aṭṭhapanā. This is hypocrisy (*kuhana*).
*Kuhāyanā* is the conduct or activity of one who is *kuha* (deceitful); or, the conduct, course, or action of a person who is *kuha* is *kuhāyanā*.
One who deceives (*kuheti*) or one who is deceived by deceit (*kuhena*) is *kuhita*; such a person is a *kuhaka* (a deceiver).

"Of one who is questioned" means of one who is asked, "Who is Tissa? Who is honored by the king? "Having raised up" means having lifted up or promoted [himself] through the attainment of wealth and so forth.

*Unnahanā* means binding higher and higher, wrapping around. It is said that two monks, having entered a certain village and sat down in a rest-house, called out to a young girl. When she had come, one of them asked the other:
"Venerable sir, whose daughter is this girl? [The other replied: "She is the daughter of our supporter, Telakandarikā; of her..."
“When my mother went to the house, she gave me ghee as if from a jar; this woman also gives from a jar like my mother,” he cried out.
It is with reference to this that it is said: “The story of Telakaṇḍarika should be told here.
“In accordance with the Dhamma” means in accordance with the appropriate measure (*mattā*). For the appropriate measure is called “Dhamma. As it has been said:
“The virtuous say that well-spoken speech is supreme; one should speak the Dhamma, not non-Dhamma—that is the second. By this, he speaks of much idle chatter;
or rather, speech that is true or otherwise well-spoken should be understood as “Dhamma.
A person whose conduct is like bean soup is a “bean-soup person” (*muggasūpya*). Therefore he said: “This person is called a ‘bean-soup person. [The conduct] of a messenger...
*Pāribhaṭyaṃ* is that very state of being a parasite (*pāribhaṭyatā*).
One who acts or lives by means of signs is a *nimittaka*; the state of such a person is *nemittikatā*. *Obhāsa* is the making known of one’s own desires.
What, then, is this? It is talk connected with requisites, such as: “Today, requisites for the monks have become difficult to obtain,” and so forth.
*Sāmantajappā* (indirect solicitation) is speaking in the vicinity of a desired object.
*Akkosana* (abuse) is reviling by means of the ten grounds for abuse, thinking, "He might give [the gift] even out of fear of being abused. Likewise for derision and the rest.
*Upekkhanā* (neglect) is casting aside the status of a donor and so forth from among the lay followers (*upāsakas*). *Khipanā* (reproach) is a word of censure; furthermore, that—
Having mocked the statement, he says, "It is 'mockery' (uppaṇḍanā). "Causing to fall" (pāpanā) means establishing [the charge] of being a non-giver or of having a bad reputation.
One whose habit is to eat the back-flesh of others is a "back-biter" (parapiṭṭhimaṃsika); the state of being such is "back-bitingness" (parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā).
"Anointing" (abbhaṅga) means an ointment. It is like seeking fragrance by rubbing [something], for it is not obtained without rubbing.

Just as there is gain from pressing a scent, so too should it be understood that there is gain from pressing out the requisites that would otherwise not be obtained if one did not press out the virtues of others.

*Nijigīsana* is the desire to deceive and seize a great deal by means of a small gain; its state is *nijigīsanatā*. It is either the mode of occurrence of that very desire, or the act of searching that arises simultaneously with it.
*Aṅga* refers to the science practiced for the sake of limbs such as hands and feet. *Nimitta* refers to the science of omens (*nimittasattha*). *Uppāta* refers to...
The science dependent on portents such as the falling of meteors, the burning of the quarters of the sky, and earthquakes; "dreams" refers to the science of dream interpretation;

"marks" refers to the science of knowing the bodily marks of women and men; "mouse-gnawed" refers to the science of knowing that when there is a mouse-bite in a specific part of cloth or other items, such-and-such a result occurs;
and [the science of] when an oblation has been offered with this or that fire among the fires of the forest and so forth.
"Aggihoma" is the performance of an oblation by means of fire, [thinking] "this is what is called *aggi*. By this same method, *dabbihoma* (oblation with sacrificial grass) is to be understood.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *thusahoma* (oblation of husks) and other wrong livelihoods mentioned in the Suttas is to be seen.
Because the virtue of purity of livelihood is accomplished through energy (*vīriya*), it is described as "the effort in seeking requisites. Of that—
Purity is the state of being blameless; it is that quality by which one obtains requisites in a righteous and equitable manner.
For one who is indolent is not able to seek requisites according to the proper method.
This concludes the commentary on virtue dependent on requisites.
18. *Paṭisaṅkhā* (reflecting) is a designation formed by the elision of the *ya*-sound, as in the expression “*sayaṃ abhiññā*” (direct knowledge by oneself), and so forth.
Here, showing that the word *yoniso* has the sense of “means,” he says: “by means of the method (*upāyena pathenā*).

Having stated “having reflected and known (*paṭisaṅkhāya ñatvā*),” he says “the meaning is ‘having reviewed’ (*paccavekkhitvā*)” and so on, in order to show that this reflection is an act of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa*).

It has been said: "Just as ‘having reflected’ (*paccavekkhitvā*) means having reflected upon each respective purpose, such as warding off cold, that is, having seen it with knowledge (*ñāṇena*), so too ‘having considered’ (*paṭisaṅkhāya*) means having considered each respective purpose, that is, having known it.
For here the word *saṅkhā* is a synonym for knowledge (*ñāṇa*). And in this context, ‘consideration’ (*paṭisaṅkhā*)..."
The phrase beginning with "yoniśo" (properly) is indeed spoken in reference to the time of using requisites;
however, others say that through reflection by way of the elements (*dhātu*) or by way of repulsiveness (*paṭikūla*), virtue dependent on requisites is purified.
Some say it is "broken"; others, however, say it is "mastered" from the very first—this should be investigated. The singular number in "cīvaraṃ" (robe) indicates its unity alone.
It is stated as "whatever among the inner robe (antaravāsaka) and so forth" with the intention of being a general term (*vācaka*);

however, because it is a generic word (*jātisadda*), it appears in the Pāḷi in the singular number. Thus, it can be understood as a collective inclusion of all those robes that must be carried by the yogin;
or rather, "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) is an expression that exhaustively includes everything without exception, not a statement of indefinite restriction.

“‘He wears it as an undergarment or he wraps it around’—this ‘assignment’ (vikappana) is a demonstration of the distinction between ‘utilization’ (paribhoga) as a mode of employment and its actual use.
Having established that, the inclusion of utilization should be understood by way of using it for lying down, sitting, making a robe, building a hut, and so forth.
‘The limit of purposes’ (payojanānaṃ mariyādā) means the boundary of purposes; the statement regarding the restriction that defines that [boundary] is what is meant.”
...the purpose ... [and so on] ... the statement. Now, in order to explain that rule by opening it up, it was said: “For only this much,” and so forth.
Therein, by means of the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), he prohibits the use of clothing for the sake of play, ornamentation, delay, dancing, and the like.
Therefore he said: “There is nothing more than this. For some beings wear and put on clothes out of a sense of play.
And: as, for example, urban people established in their youth; some, by way of adornment, such as those who live off their beauty and so forth;

the *vilambakas*, by way of hanging [ornaments]; the *bhojas* and others, by way of dramatic performance (*naṭambara*); internal disturbance of the elements (*dhātu*) that gives rise to cold, disease, and so forth;
"by way of the transformation of the season" means by way of the shifting of the season, through the arising of a discordant cold season. By the word "or" (*vā*),...

The inclusion [of the phrase] should be understood as referring to that which occurs during the winter season and so forth by way of the falling of snow; the intention is not that it produces coldness.
However, in order to show that purpose for which this removal [of heat] reaches its ultimate point, the words beginning with "afflicted by cold" were spoken.
"In all cases" refers to all the remaining purposes, such as "for the warding off of heat" and so on. Even though the heat of the sun...
"Heat" (*uṇha*) is mentioned; however, because it is included by the mention of "sunlight," it is stated as "the heat of fire.
One might think that the heat of a forest fire can be warded off by covering the body with a robe; therefore, he says, "its occurrence should be understood in forest fires and the like.
"Gnats" (*ḍaṃsa*) refers to brown flies. Since they have the habit of biting, they are called "biting flies" (*ḍaṃsanamakkhikā*).
“Snakes and so forth” refers to snakes, centipedes, scorpions, spiders, crabs, and the like. “Contacted venom” means the poison of contact.
For snakes are of three kinds: those with venom in their bite (*daṭṭhavisā*), those with venom in their touch (*phuṭṭhavisā*), and those with venom in their sight (*diṭṭhavisā*).
Of these, only the first two are included here, in order to encompass such creatures as the centipede and others as well. “Fixed purpose” means that which is certain and applicable at all times.
The purpose [is as follows]: shame is disturbed and shamelessness becomes established. Therefore he said, "it perishes.

Alternatively, it is called *kopinaṃ* because it deserves to be covered like a well. And since it is both shame (*hirī*) in the sense of that which ought to be shunned and a covering (*kopinaṃ*), the meaning here should be understood as "shame-covering" (*hirikopinaṃ*).
The word *ca* in the phrase "and of that" (*tassa ca*) has the sense of collecting the purposes mentioned previously.
"Whatever food" (*yaṃ kiñci āhāraṃ*) means any substance to be taken in, classified as hard food, soft food, and so forth.
One who goes about for alms—that is, for begging—is a *piṇḍola*; the occupation of such a person is *piṇḍolya*. By that *piṇḍolya*, meaning by the practice of wandering for alms.

"From having fallen" (*patitattā*) means from having been cast [into the bowl]. "Alms-food" (*piṇḍapāta*) is the food consisting of alms that has been placed in the bowl; or, it is the falling (*pāta*) of the alms (*piṇḍa*).
A gathering of those who have obtained alms from house to house. In phrases such as “there is no sport,” even an action done impulsively is called “sport” (*davā*);
therefore, to provide a qualification, he said, “for the sake of sport, for the purpose of play. Boxers are those who engage in boxing.
By the word “etcetera,” those who engage in wrestling and so forth are included. It means “for the purpose of intoxication with strength.”
Pride arising by relying on strength is "pride of strength" (*balamada*). Its purpose is for the sake of producing that [strength]; this is the meaning.
Regarding "the sign of pride of manliness" (*porisamadanimitta*): "pride of manliness" (*porisamada*) refers to the conceit of a man, the pride that arises thinking, "I am a man.
Some say that pride proceeding from the capacity to engage in unrighteous conduct, or even lust itself, is "pride of manliness."
That is the sign. "Antepurikā" refers to the king's concubines. "Vesīs" refers to those who live by their beauty, being suitable for the company of all [men].
"Maṇḍana" here means the perfection of the limbs; thus he says, "the cause for the fullness of the major and minor limbs," meaning the causes for their nourishment and growth.
"Naṭā" refers to stage-actors. "Naccakā" refers to dancers, acrobats, and so forth. "Vibhūsana" means the production of splendor.
He said: "The sign of the clear complexion. This is the phrase.
"For the purpose of abandoning the decisive support for delusion" means for the sake of abandoning the state of being a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for delusion.

For through lust there is delusion, and it increases delusion; therefore, by avoiding that [lust], there is the non-supporting of delusion. "For the purpose of abandoning the decisive support for hatred" means...

This was stated by way of the cause of hatred for one who has seen the danger in strength and for one who has seen the danger in manliness; however, by way of the other [the person of dull faculties], it should be said:

"for the purpose of abandoning the underlying tendency of lust. While the rejection of adornment and embellishment may also be for the sake of abandoning the underlying tendency of delusion, it is stated as "for the purpose of abandoning the underlying tendency of lust" because it is the direct opposite of the state of being an underlying tendency for lust. Even though...

For some, when directed toward the intoxication of their own sport, there indeed arises in another the fetter of aversion and so forth, as in the case of the gods corrupted by mental malice (*manopadosika*).
However, for those in whom specific evil states such as lust, delusion, and pride arise especially on account of their own intoxication with sport—referring to them, it was said:
"for the purpose of preventing the arising of fetters in oneself," and [it follows] "in dependence upon adornment and embellishment."
"Even in another person, lust, delusion, and so forth arise in a specific manner"; thus it is said, "for the purpose of preventing the arising of fetters in another as well.
Regarding the phrase "through improper practice": here, setting aside the pursuit of sensual pleasure, all forms of wrong practice constitute improper practice.
By the first two phrases, [the text refers] to improper practice; by the latter two, to the pursuit of sensual pleasure.

They say that "abandonment" has been stated [in relation to each]. However, because of the statement, "And by all four of these," it should be understood that the abandonment of both has been stated by means of all [four].
Even amorous play is indeed included within sporting; likewise, even manly pride is simply a cause for the pursuit of sensual pleasure (*kāmasukhallikānuyoga*).

"Of that which consists of the four great elements" means of that which is dependent upon the four great elements. "Of the material body" means of the aggregate of the fourfold continuity of matter (*rūpa*).
"By way of stability" means for the purpose of stability. Since that stability of his is intended in the sense of continuity, he says "the purpose of continuous stability.
"By way of occurrence" means by way of the occurrence of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). For the life-faculty is defined as "sustenance" and "maintenance.
And its non-interruption occurs through the application of nutriment. [This lasts] for the body for a longer time, up until the end of the lifespan.
Showing that "maintenance" means enduring for a long time, he said, "for the sake of remaining for a long period.
Now, in order to make the meaning just stated even clearer, he said, "like a house pillar," and so forth. Herein, this is the construction:
just as the owner of an old house provides a support for the house for the sake of its not falling down, and just as a cartwright applies oil to the axle—
He does this for the sake of its maintenance; in this way, the yogi partakes of and consumes almsfood for the sake of the body’s stability and for the sake of its sustenance.
By this, he shows that "stability" means non-falling and "sustenance" means continued existence.
The phrase "not for amusement, intoxication, adornment, or embellishment" demonstrates the purpose excluded by the restriction "only so far as."
"Stasis" (*ṭhiti*) means that by means of this, the appropriated phenomena persist; thus he says, "Stasis is a designation for the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

For in that way, that vitality (*āyu*) is pointed out as "stasis. The meaning is: for the purpose of maintaining stasis—that is, for the sake of the functioning of the life-faculty, which has acquired the conventional designation "stasis" because it is the cause of the body's persistence. Therefore he says, "for the purpose of causing the life-faculty to continue."
"In the sense of affliction" means in the sense of oppression, or in the sense of disease; for hunger is the supreme disease. "For the purpose of cessation" means for the purpose of subsiding.
The connection is as follows: just as one who has a wound uses an ointment, so too, when heat, cold, and so forth prevail, one partakes of cold and heat as a remedy for them.
Excluding the holy life of the Path, that which is to be practiced according to the Dispensation is comprised within the three trainings.
“Instruction is the holy life of the Dispensation,” he said, referring to “both the holy life of the entire Dispensation and the holy life of the Path.
“For the purpose of assistance” means for the purpose of repeatedly assisting, that is, for the purpose of bringing about accomplishment.

“Relying on bodily strength” means relying on the mere measure of bodily strength that serves as the cause for fulfilling the specific qualities already undertaken. Therefore, he said: “By way of devotion to the three trainings,” and so forth.
Just as husband and wife seeking to cross a wilderness, or those seeking to cross a river or the ocean,
consume even their own son’s flesh and so forth— being neither greedy nor infatuated, but considering only the accomplishment of that specific purpose because it cannot be achieved without it—
so too this person is merely seeking to cross the wilderness of existence, being neither greedy nor infatuated.
"He partakes of almsfood because it would not be possible [to live] without it"—this is the correlation with the simile.
*Iti* is a particle used in the sense of "manner. By means of it, the manner of partaking of the almsfood being consumed is grasped;
thus he said, "In this way, by this manner of partaking of almsfood. *Purāṇaṃ* (old) refers to its being prior in time to the actual eating.
"Old": "I shall ward off" means "I will ward off. The construction is: "He partakes [of food] thinking, 'I will not give rise to new feeling.
To the questions "Of what kind? and "In what manner? he says: "With immeasurable... like a certain person.
"Immeasurable food-conditioned" (*aparimitabhojanapaccayā*) means that which has immeasurable, unlimited food as its condition; that [food] conditioned by immeasurable food, for himself...
The meaning is: caused by eating an amount of food that exceeds the capacity of the digestive heat (*gahaṇī-teja*).
One who, having eaten much, is unable to stand up due to his own natural constitution and says, "Bring me a hand," is *āharahatthaka*.
One who, having eaten, even when standing up, is unable to put on his lower garment because his belly is so excessively distended, is *alaṃsāṭaka*. One who...
One who, being unable to rise after eating, rolls about right there, is a "one who rolls on the spot" (tatravaṭṭaka).
One who consumes food only as far as the mouth-cavity, so that it can be pecked at by crows, is a "crow-pecker" (kākamāsaka).
One who, being unable to hold it in the mouth after eating, vomits it right back up, is a "vomiter after eating" (bhuttavamitaka). [He is] like one of these.
Alternatively, "old feeling" refers to a feeling that arises due to the condition of not having eaten; he partakes [of food] thinking, "I shall ward this off.
"New feeling" refers to a feeling that arises due to the condition of eating too much; he partakes [of food] thinking, "I shall not let this arise.
Alternatively, "new feeling" refers to a feeling that arises due to the condition of not having eaten; while that [feeling] has not yet arisen...
One pursues [food] solely for the purpose of its non-arising. The phrase "arising due to lack of eating" is a qualification of *khuddā* (hunger).
It is intended to show that the cessation of which must be effected by eating.

Among the feelings arising from the condition of not having eaten and those arising from the condition of having eaten, the former are the feelings characterized by hunger as they occur in their natural course. That...
For [hunger] arises by way of further intensification in one who does not eat. Even the latter pains, such as the burning and piercing sensations in the limbs, are merely signs of hunger;
for those would not have arisen previously even with food as their condition, and thus they will not arise now either—this is the distinction between them.
Furthermore, the fact that these are signs of cruelty is the distinction of cruelty itself.
"Whatever feeling": it afflicts at this present time. "Depending on unsuitable and immoderate food" means that it arises by way of the practice of consuming food that is unsuitable and immoderate.
"By way of the condition of past karma" means that it is fit to arise by way of the causal condition of past karma—namely, what was done in a previous birth—due to a failure in one's conduct.
Avoiding that [unwholesome state] and establishing oneself through the perfection of application destroys the conditions for painful feeling and constitutes its repelling;
thus he said: "Destroying its condition, may I repel that old feeling.
Improper use is the use of requisites without reflecting upon them. That itself, by way of having accumulated karma, is the accumulation of karma. Depending on that—
The construction is as follows: because it arises in the future, in a later time, depending [on conditions], that which is called "new feeling" (*navavedanā*) [is so designated].
"By way of appropriate enjoyment" means by way of enjoying the requisites after having reflected upon them;

thus, one does not produce the unwholesome action of inappropriate enjoyment—which is the root of that new feeling—by not generating it at all in any way whatsoever. "To this extent" refers to: "Thus..."

By the two phrases beginning with "ancient" (*purāṇa*), or by the four phrases beginning with "for the cessation of violence" (*vihiṃsūparatiyā*), there is an inclusion of appropriate enjoyment, because the enjoyment of requisites suitable for those who have gone forth has been described.
The abandonment of devotion to self-mortification is stated because of the mention of warding off the suffering of hunger and so forth.
[This refers to] bodily pleasure which serves as a condition for the bliss of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and the like.
By not relinquishing [the requisites], the non-abandonment of righteous happiness is also illustrated.

A danger that might sever the life-faculty or destroy the postures through the use of what is unsuitable or in excessive measure does not exist when there is the use of what is suitable and in moderation.
This being so, the longevity of the body—characterized by its persistence over a long period of time—[is maintained].
Showing the meaning that "there will be maintenance through sustenance," he said: "By means of limited enjoyment... [etc]... there will be.
A disease that is neither curable nor incurable is a "maintainable disease" (*yāpyaroga*); one who has such a disease is "one with a maintainable disease" (*yāpyarogī*).
For he constantly resorts to medicine, and this person is likewise. If "maintenance" (*yātrā*) is the same as "sustenance" (*yāpanā*), then it was also [the case] previously.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of maintenance" (*yāpanāya*), what is the distinction here? Previously, "for the sake of maintenance" was intended as the maintenance of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*);
however, here it refers to maintenance or sustenance (*yātrā*) defined as the non-interruption of all four postures.
Seeking requisites through a wrong livelihood, which is censured by the Buddha, is improper seeking. [This concerns] the donors and the objects to be given...
Receiving without knowing one’s own measure, or receiving for the sake of squandering what has been given out of faith, is improper receiving;
or it is that by which one incurs an offense. Improper use is the use [of requisites] without having reflected upon them.
The avoidance of these should be understood by way of producing the necessary conditions in accordance with the Dhamma and with justice. For, in accordance with the Dhamma...
Seeking requisites, receiving them in accordance with the Dhamma, and using them after reflecting upon them—this is called blamelessness.
*Arati* means discontent; it is a lack of delight in secluded lodgings and in superior wholesome qualities. *Tandi* is drowsiness and sleep.
*Vijambhitā* is the stretching of the body due to being overcome by sloth and torpor. *Viññūgarahā* is censure by the wise.
For one person indeed commits what is blameworthy while thinking it is blameless;
having eaten an excessive amount under the thought, "I have obtained [food]," and being unable to digest it, he suffers from purging upwards, purging downwards, and so forth.
Consequently, all the bhikkhus in the monastery become preoccupied with attending to his body and searching for medicine. Others ask them, "What is this? and...
Having heard such things as, "So-and-so’s belly is bloated," people criticize him, saying, "At all times he is of such a nature that he does not even know the capacity of his own stomach.
Thus, he makes what is blameless seem blameworthy. Instead of doing this, he partakes [of food] thinking, "There will be blamelessness.
For, having understood one's own natural constitution, strength, and so forth, one should consider how [the food] will affect one's aversion and other states.
"By means of non-existence, there will be physical ease and blamelessness"—thinking thus, he partakes only in moderation.
"As much as is needed for food" refers to the accomplishment of its purpose; "filling the belly to satiety" refers to eating until the stomach is full;

by avoiding such "eating until the belly is full," he avoids *yāvad-attha-udara-ādehakam-bhojanaṃ*. Regarding "the pleasure obtainable from lying down": this refers to the pleasure obtained through reclining on a bed.
The pleasure of lying down (*seyyasukha*) is the pleasure arising for one who lies down turning from side to side;
the pleasure of reclining (*passasukha*) is the pleasure arising from sleeping with drowsiness (*middha*); the pleasure of sloth (*middhasukha*) is the pleasure arising from that very sleep.

From the abandoning of these pleasures of lying down, etc., there is the cultivation of the body’s fitness for the four postures (*iriyāpatha*), which is called "the cultivation of the body’s fitness for the four postures."

Therefore, the dwelling in the postures is pleasant and a comfortable abiding. In order to support the definition of "comfortable abiding" stated in the final alternative—or indeed in all alternatives—by means of scripture, it is said:
"For it has also been said," and so forth. For in all three alternatives, comfortable abiding is described precisely by way of moderate consumption of nutriment.
“By this much” means by the three phrases beginning with “sustenance” (*yātrā*). “And there will be sustenance for me” is an indication of the grasping of the purpose;

for it is through sustenance that one applies oneself to the use of food. A comfortable dwelling (*phāsuvihāra*) caused by not abandoning righteous happiness (*dhammika-sukha*) is the middle way because it avoids the two extremes.
At this point, however, eight factors are to be combined.
“Not for sport” is one factor; “not for intoxication” is one; “not for adornment” is one; “not for beautification” is one;
“only for the maintenance and sustenance of this body” is one; “for the cessation of affliction and for support of the holy life” is one;
“thus I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings” is one.
“‘And there will be sustenance for me’—this is one [factor]. ‘Blamelessness and a comfortable dwelling’—this, in this context, is the benefit of eating.
However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: ‘The four factors mentioned below are indeed prohibitions, whereas the eight factors mentioned above are to be combined together.
In that regard, ‘only as long as there is the maintenance of this body’ is one factor; ‘for its sustenance’ is [another].”
One [portion] is for the cessation of harmfulness; one is for the support of the holy life (*brahmacariya*); one is for the thought, "I shall eliminate old feelings";
one is for the thought, "I shall not give rise to new feelings"; one is for the thought, "There shall be sustenance for me"; and one is for blamelessness.
However, a comfortable dwelling (*phāsuvihāra*) is the benefit of food. Thus, it is endowed with eight factors.
One who consumes food while reflecting wisely is said to "make use of almsfood with proper reflection.
By using the locative case in the phrase "in whatever [place]" (*yattha yattha*), the word *sena* indicates its function as denoting the locus of an action. The same applies to the word *āsana*.
In the expression "in a half-roofed house, etc.," the word "etc. includes palaces and so forth, as well as beds and the like. "In whatever monastery" (*yattha yattha vihāre*)...
Or, having brought [the phrase] "dwells in" (*āsatī*) from such contexts as "half-yoga huts" (*aḍḍhayogādi*), it should be connected with "monastery half-yoga huts," etc. Here, by the word "etc.
(*ādi*), the inclusion of benches, mats, and so forth should be understood. "In the sense of enduring" (*parisahanaṭṭhena*) means in the sense of overcoming;

the meaning is "in the sense of warding off. "The seasonal danger itself" (*utuparissaya*) means that the seasons themselves—cold, heat, and so forth—when they are unsuitable, constitute a seasonal danger according to the method already stated.
The meaning is: for the purpose of dispelling that seasonal danger, for the purpose of preventing its arising when it has not yet arisen, and for the purpose of calming it when it has already arisen.
Having withdrawn the mind from various objects, its proper seclusion (*paṭisallāna*) in a single object that serves as a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is "seclusion";
delighting in and finding pleasure therein is "delight in seclusion" (*paṭisallānārāma*), and it is for that purpose.
For a secluded lodging is conducive to the development of a yogi because of its state as an empty dwelling. To clarify these two points, it is said:
"That which causes bodily affliction and mental distraction," and so forth. Therein, "for the sake of the happiness of solitude" means:

happiness caused by solitude is "the happiness of solitude"; for that purpose. It is the happiness arising through the absence of the defilement of socializing with groups and the defilement of socializing with people.
If the seasonal element itself is the seasonal peril, then with reference to the objection—

“Since cold and heat have already been mentioned as the ‘counteracting of cold and heat,’ why is the ‘dispelling of the seasonal peril’ stated separately?”— he says, “Granted, however,” and so forth. In that context,

by the phrase “the dispelling of the seasonal peril is certain,” he indicates that the cold and heat mentioned in the passage “for the counteracting of cold, for the counteracting of heat” are not fixed.
He shows that while [certain dangers] arise only occasionally, the danger of the climate (utu-parissaya) is intended here as being present at all times.
"Of the kind described" means of the kind already mentioned— namely, "cold and so forth," and "unwholesome"—

referring to manifest dangers such as those arising from sitting in an open space or at the foot of a tree due to lack of protection and the state of having unsecured doors, etc., and non-manifest dangers such as the sight of unsuitable forms, etc.

And they might cause affliction to the body and mind of a bhikkhu. In a protected lodging where they do not cause affliction—having known thus means having known it to be free from both kinds of danger;
the connection is that a bhikkhu should be understood as one who makes use [of such a place] after knowing this.
It is the state of being an antidote to disease, which is characterized by the disturbance of the elements or by the painful feeling caused thereby.
The sense of counteracting. Therefore he said, "the meaning is 'in the sense of going against'"; what is meant is "in the sense of pacifying.
"Of anything whatsoever" means of any one among the [remedies] such as ghee and so forth. For the intention is that it is for the pacification of the disorder of that which is suitable.
It is the work of a physician because it must be performed by him. Therefore he said, "because it is authorized by him. "By the requisites of a city" means...

Having surrounded the city, it is guarded by sentries. The seven "requisites of a city" are said to be: the open gateway, the enclosure, the rampart, the wall, the watchtower, the crossbar, and the level ground at the base of the wall. The "requisite of virtue" (*sīlaparikkhāra*) is the ornament of perfectly purified virtue.
For here, the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is intended by the term "chariot," and its factors—right speech and so forth—are called "requisites" in the sense of being ornaments.
"Requisites for life" (jīvitaparikkhārā) means the causes for the continued existence of life. "To be procured" (samudānetabbā) means they must be properly brought forth from above and sought after.
It is also a "retinue" (parivāro) because it wards off obstacles from all sides. Therefore he said:
"Because of protecting life... and so forth.
In this context, *antara* means an opening or gap; the meaning is "space.
It is so called because it protects like attendants who stand surrounding one's own masters, not allowing an interval for enemies. *Assa* refers to life.
*Kāraṇabhāvato* means by virtue of being the cause for its long-term continuation; for medicine that acts as an elixir (*rasāyana*) indeed causes life to persist for a very long time.

Even though unarisen painful feelings are warded off by the use of medicine, they are not [considered] arisen because they perish by their very nature once they have arisen; however, those that are similar to what has arisen are called "arisen.
For such a designation is applied to things similar to them, just as one says "that same partridge" or "those same medicines. Therefore it was said: "Of those that have arisen."

"Of those born, become, and produced. Because that disturbance of the elements (*dhātukkhobha*) is their source from the moment of conception onwards, they are "originated from that" (*taṃsamuṭṭhāna*).

Having stated "painful feeling" (*dukkhavedanā*), it is said "feeling that is unwholesome-resultant" (*akusalavipākavedanā*) in order to distinguish it from the fact that there is also a painful feeling whose intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is unwholesome.
In the sense of afflicting, it is "affliction" (*byābādha*); affliction itself is "afflictiveness" (*byābajjha*).
“Dukkha” means suffering. “Abyābajjha” means that which is free from affliction (byābajjha), that is, the state of being without suffering.

Therefore he said, “for the sake of the supreme state of being free from affliction,” meaning for the sake of the supreme state of being without suffering. That “suffering” refers to the suffering characterized by illness.
To show that it is precisely the dependence upon and the utilization of requisites such as robes and so forth, he said, “depending upon and relying on them.”

Having said this, it is stated: "while consuming. "Pavattanti" means they live. For living is indeed "pavattana" (functioning), which is why the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is called "having functioning as its essence" (*pavattanarasa*).
*Catupārisuddhisampādanavidhivaṇṇanā* (Commentary on the Method for Accomplishing the Fourfold Purity)

19. Thus, having explained virtue (sīla) through its divisions such as the restraint of the Pātimokkha, the passage beginning with “In this way, in this [virtue]... is commenced in order to further demonstrate it by way of its means of accomplishment (sādhana).
Therein, that by which something is accomplished or achieved is the “means of accomplishment” (sādhana);

one for whom faith is the means of accomplishment is “one whose means of accomplishment is faith” (saddhāsādhano). But is it not the case that the restraint of the Pātimokkha cannot exist even without energy, mindfulness, and wisdom?
"Is it not accomplished? [The reply is: "It is true that it is not accomplished; however, this was said with reference to faith being a specific cause. To show this, he said:
"Because the formulation of the training rules (sikkhāpada-paññatti) lies beyond the domain of disciples.

Indeed, the formulation of training rules appropriate to each respective offense when the matter has descended into distinctions such as grave or light is not within the domain of disciples; it belongs to the Buddhas.
This is the scope [of the Buddha]. Let alone the laying down of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-ppaññāpana*), even the timing for that is not within the scope of the disciples;
it is the scope of the Buddhas alone. Demonstrating this, he said: "And here, the refusal of the request for the laying down of the training rules is the illustration.
For it has been said: "Wait, Sāriputta, wait, Sāriputta! Only the Tathāgata..."

"In that regard, he will know the proper time. Here, the word *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). By it, the inclusion of such statements as "We do not prescribe what has not been prescribed;
we do not abolish what has been prescribed; having undertaken them, we conduct ourselves according to the training rules as they have been laid down" should be understood.
"By faith" means by means of conviction regarding the Teacher and by the manifestation of faith in the Dhamma.
The intended meaning is: "even for life, let alone for the requisites of life.
"Like a hen her egg" means like a female *kikī* bird her own egg; it is said that she protects the egg even at the cost of her own life.
"Like a yak its tail" means like the *camari* deer its own tail. It is said that when the *camari* deer is pursued by a hunter...
While being nurtured, they even sacrifice their own lives to protect their own hair that has become entangled in thorny bushes and the like.
This should be connected [to the simile] by bringing in the phrase "like a beloved only son.
For just as a householder with an only son protects that only son, and one with an only eye protects that only eye most thoroughly, so too do those who guard their virtue.

This was said by way of compassion. "Well-behaved" (*supesalā*) means those whose virtue is very dear to them. "Always" (*sadā*) means at all times—during the periods of youth, middle age, and old age.
"Respectful" (*sagāravā*) is by way of the six kinds of reverence; the meaning is "possessing reverence and honor.

"In this very way" (*evameva kho*) means just as the great ocean is of a fixed nature and does not overstep its shore, so too [is it with these disciples]. "My disciples" (*mama sāvakā*) is said with reference to noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*), for they are of constant virtue. "In this matter" (*imasmiṃ atthe*) refers to the non-transgression of virtue even for the sake of one's life.

The Mahāvattaniaṭavī is the Viñjhāṭavī forest. Some say it is a forest on the slopes of the Himalayas. "An elder" refers to a certain elder who was not well-known by name or clan. They went and laid him down, thinking, "Let no one report this.
"With a rotten creeper" means with a *gaḷocī* creeper. "One whose head is level" means one whose life has reached its end.

For he whose head of defilements—namely ignorance—is exhausted by the path of Arahantship through the sequence of the paths, [is so called] at the nineteenth moment of reviewing knowledge that follows.
When one has established oneself and crossed over the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the life-faculty—the head of the cycle—exhausts itself at the moment of the death-consciousness (cuticitta).
Because of this equality of the two occasions, he is called "one whose head is level with his life" (jīvitasamasīsī). That elder attained final Nibbāna in such a manner. Therefore it is said:

"Having become one whose head was level [with his life], he attained final Nibbāna. It is said that the Elder Abhaya was possessed of great supernormal powers (mahābhiñña); therefore, he had a cetiya constructed.
They say: "Even so" means that he would rather give up his own life than break [the precepts], would not break them, and would not transgress them.
"Of the faculties established through mindfulness" means, even more so, of the faculties established by way of protection through mindfulness already present.
"Not to be followed" means because they cannot be pursued by covetousness and the like by way of the sense-doors. "Excellent" means supreme.
"Heated" means hot. "Blazing" means glowing from the very beginning. "Flaming" means burning all around.
"Become a single mass of flame" means having become one continuous blaze. "Completely rubbed" means rubbed in every way; the meaning is "polished.
This should be connected by bringing in the word "not" (*na tveva*). "In forms" means in the objects of form. "Grasping the sign according to the details" means...
The apprehension of signs such as beauty (*subha*) occurs through the gradual production and manifestation of defilements by way of their secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*).

Alternatively, "by way of secondary characteristics" means by way of the secondary characteristics such as hands and feet; "apprehension of signs" refers to the grasping of signs such as those of a woman or a man, or beauty and so forth.
"Of consciousness proceeding through the eye-door, etc. means of consciousness proceeding by way of the eye-door and so on. "Of consciousness" refers to impulsion-consciousness (*javana-viññāṇa*).
The connection is that [the practice] must be accomplished by one who restrains the grasping of signs and so forth.

"Not having the surrounding branches properly arranged" means not having the enclosure of the fence properly constructed. "By those who carry off what belongs to others" means by thieves who seize the property of others.
"He pierces through completely" means he penetrates it entirely, entering into it.
"Regarding 'in forms' (rūpesu)": this means by way of form, with form as the cause or sign. "The faculty protects from the arising of harm"—this is the grammatical connection.

The same applies to the remaining [faculties]. "For these are the doors": these refer to the doors of the eye and so forth. They are "open" because they are not secured by the bolt of mindfulness; for that very reason, they are "unprotected.
By way of metaphorical designation (*kāraṇūpacāra*), they are said to "slay the one possessing them" by acting as the cause for the arising of defilements.

It has been said. Or, these [objects] such as visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth are the doors that serve as the objective supports (*ārammaṇa*) for the defilements (*kilesa*), namely the eye-door and the others.

Of what nature are they when "open" and "unprotected"? It is stated by way of metaphorical attribution (*kāraṇūpacāra*) that they "strike" the possessor of those [doors] because of the cause—the unguarded state of the eyes and so forth.
"House" (*agāra*) means a dwelling. "Ill-thatched" (*ducchanna*) means not properly covered. "Uncultivated" (*abhāvita*) means devoid of supramundane cultivation (*lokuttara-bhāvanā*).
The meaning of the side of purification beginning with the words "has been accomplished" (*sampādita*) should be understood as the opposite of what was stated [regarding the side of defilement].
However, this total non-arising of defilements is an extremely exalted teaching, because it is similar to that which has already arrived by means of the path.
"It should be accomplished" means it should be accomplished through the purity of resolve, thinking, "I shall not do so again."

“Now, by one who has gone forth” (adhunāpabbajitena) means by one who has not long been ordained; the sense is “by one newly ordained. “I am burning with sensual lust” (kāmarāgena ḍayhāmi) means I am being consumed by the fire of sensual lust.
And showing that this burning is currently present in the mind, he said, “my mind is burning.
“Please” (sādhu) is an expression of entreaty. “Extinguishing” (nibbāpana) refers to the means for its extinguishing. “Gotama,” he addresses the Elder by his clan name.
"Due to perversion of perception" means: because of the perversion of perception that occurs [thinking] "the beautiful in the unattractive," it is the sign of perverted perception.
What kind of sign should you avoid? Avoid the sign of beauty associated with lust—that which has become the cause for the arising of lust—and do not attend to it.
Not only should you refrain from attending to the sign of beauty, but furthermore, through the cultivation of the unattractive (*asubha-bhāvanā*),...
“Develop your own mind. How? Develop it so that it becomes one-pointed and well-concentrated;

that is, just as it becomes one-pointed through the absence of distraction regarding the meditation object of foulness (asubha), and well-concentrated through being properly absorbed—develop it in this way.

Having thus shown the suppression of sensual lust through the development of serenity (samatha), the following passage beginning with “formations” (saṅkhāre) is now given to show the method for its eradication.
It has been said. Therein, "view all formations as other": view all formations as "other" because they cannot be controlled by you.
Furthermore, view them as suffering because they are oppressed by arising and passing away due to their impermanence;

view them as not-self because they lack the nature of a self and are devoid of a self. Thus, having applied the three characteristics and increasing insight, [proceed] according to the sequence of the paths.
"Completely extinguish your great lust by means of the fourth path; because it overcomes the three realms and possesses a vast domain, bring this great lust to rest.
Do not burn again and again as you do now"—thus he urged him toward the more firm removal of lust.
Having thus shown the method for accomplishing the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties, [he said]: "In this way, that is well accomplished."
In order to demonstrate this method, he points out the elders who fulfilled that requirement with the words beginning "Furthermore" (*apicā*).
In that context, the phrase "a roof never before looked upon" is said because, in every respect, the elder was one who looked only as far as a yoke’s length ahead.
But does the elder not clean his lodging? For it is said: "The ceiling must first be removed," and [this applies to] the resident pupils and others.
In this way they cleaned his lodging—the *nāgara* tree.
"In that village" means in the great village. "Those with young children" refers to those women whose sons and daughters were still nursing;
[the king] caused them to be marked. That is, having had the breasts bound with breast-patches, he caused them to be marked with the royal seal. The King.
Wishing to see the Elder for a longer time, he made a delay by saying, "I shall take the precepts tomorrow.
When it was time for the Elder to pay homage to the King and the Queen, he would merely show the gesture of salutation; however, he did not distinguish between them as "woman" or "man.
Therefore he said, "I do not make a distinction. [The King thought: "Oh, how perfectly pure in virtue this noble one truly is!"
He stood there holding a staff-lamp. Because of his attainment of what is suitable, the meditation subject became exceedingly pure and manifest, appearing as perfectly clear as a lamp.
"Making the entire mountain resound" means making the whole mountain ring out with a single sound due to the earthquake; some say it was because of the deities dwelling there giving their applause.
"Bhanta" means unsettled. "Bāla" means a young child. "Utrasta" means terrified by the separation from his kinsmen.
"Visagaṇḍakaroga" refers to the disease of the breast-nipple; some also say it refers to diseases such as erysipelas.
"Yato pabbajito" means from the time he went forth; the meaning is "from the moment of his ordination. "Indriyāni" refers to the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties.
For when these are split, the faculties (*indriya*) are also said to be split due to the absence of protection;
or rather, the very faculties that serve as the doors for grasping signs and secondary characteristics are called "split" because they give rise to harm for one who possesses them.
Conversely, they should be understood as "unsplit. Alternatively, the improper application of the faculties is their splitting, while their proper application is their non-splitting.
"Others": this refers to Mahāmitta Thera, as in the case of Mitta Thera. "Vare" means excellent.

In the phrase "likewise by energy," the word "likewise" (tathā) qualifies energy; just as mindfulness has the characteristic of blamelessness and is the means for achieving restraint of the sense faculties, so too does energy have the characteristic of blamelessness and is the means for achieving purity of livelihood. This qualification depends specifically on energy.
