It is to be seen. For this very reason, it is said: "of one who has rightly exerted energy. Seeking in an improper way is *anesanā* (wrong seeking), because it is comprised within the aforementioned wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*).

That itself is *appatirūpa* (unbecoming) because it is not suitable for the Teacher’s dispensation; that wrong seeking is *appatirūpa*. Alternatively, *appatirūpa* is that which is contrary to what is fitting (*patirūpa*);
for one who has undertaken the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), it is contrary to the rule of those ascetic practices. Of whom? [Of one who has undertaken them.]

This is a practice that agitates the effacement of some. In this context, the word *ca* (and) is indicated as being elided, [meaning] "having abandoned improper means and what is unbecoming. The connection is: "these must be accomplished by one who is avoiding [them] while practicing [the path].
By the phrase "in the arising of purity," the fact that the teaching of the Dhamma and so forth originate from a pure basis is illustrated; thus, [it is said] "by the teaching of the Dhamma, etc."

"...of those who have confidence in his virtues," it is said. By the word "etc. (ādi), one should understand the inclusion of great learning, the fulfillment of the observances, excellence in deportment, and so forth.
The same method applies here as well to the phrase "of those who have confidence in his ascetic qualities" (dhutaguṇa).

By the word "etc. in the phrase "by alms-round practice, etc.," the inclusion of the conduct of friends, companions, and rag-robe wearers, and so forth, should be understood. [The phrase] "in accordance with the rules of the ascetic practices" (dhutaṅga-niyama) [is explained as follows].
The meaning is: "in accordance with" (anulomavasena) means by way of conformity to the practice fixed upon the various ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and "by way of non-disturbance" (avikopanavasena).

It is said, "for the sake of allaying a single disease," and so forth, to show that a wrong livelihood is possible only for one who has great desire (mahiccha), and not for one who has few desires (appiccha); for when fewness of desires has reached its highest excellence, the occurrence of wrong livelihood is simply impossible.
In this context, "rotten haritakī" refers to [a preparation] infused with rotten urine (pūtimutta).

Or it is myrobalan fruit discarded because it has become rotten. One who possesses the noble lineage (*ariyavaṃsa*) is called "one of the noble lineage" (*ariyavaṃsika*); or, one who is devoted to the noble lineage is "one of the noble lineage.
Because greed for requisites has been cast far away, he is both supreme and one of the noble lineage; thus, he is a "supreme one of the noble lineage" (*uttama-ariyavaṃsika*).
"Of anyone whatsoever" (*yassa kassaci*) means of anyone among those who have undertaken or not undertaken the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
"Sign" (nimitta) means making a sign such that the intention is understood in accordance with the conditions intended.
"Hinting" (obhāsa) means indicating in such a way that the intention becomes clear without speaking directly.
"Indirect talk" (parikathā) means speaking by way of a circuitous or figurative expression. "Likewise arisen" means arisen by way of the sign and so forth.
“The door has been given”: by way of the heading “illness,” the door for its use has been granted. Therefore, it is permissible to use it even when one is not ill;
the meaning is that there is no offense. Thus he said, “Even though there is no offense,” and so forth. “It is not permissible”:
for one established in the practice of effacement (*sallekha*), it is not permissible; the intention is that it would disturb the effacement. “But as for the livelihood...”
By the phrase "he is angry," they say that for one who observes the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) related to lodgings, signs and so forth are not permitted.
Others say that they are likewise not permitted even for one who observes other ascetic practices.
"Not doing" means not doing even within the scope of what is individually permitted. "Except elsewhere" means setting those aside.
Having abandoned living in a group, the Great Elder dwelt in a forest region in the attainment of the supreme fruit, which is the pinnacle of the seclusion of tranquility;
thus he is described as "cultivating solitude. A wind-affliction dependent on the stomach is a "stomach-wind-affliction" (*udaravātābādha*).
That whose milk is undiluted is "undiluted-milk" (*asambhinnakhīra*); that very thing being rice-porridge is "undiluted-milk-rice-porridge" (*asambhinnakhīrapāyāsa*).
The meaning is: "boiled rice porridge cooked with milk unmixed with water. *Tassa* means "of that porridge. *Uppattimūlaṃ* refers to the cause of its arising, namely his own verbal utterance:
"Friends, in my time as a householder, my mother would mix ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, and give me unadulterated milk-rice porridge;
by that, I was comfortable. [He said: "It is not fit for consumption..."
Why was it said, “almsfood”? Is it not the case that for the Elder there was no arising of such thoughts as the manifestation of light and so forth? It is true that there were none;

however, certain worldlings, being unaware of his inner intention (*ajjhāsaya*), might have thought otherwise, and future fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārino*) might likewise follow in the footsteps of his views.
Therefore, he rejected [the idea]. Furthermore, the Great Elder’s [realization] had reached the highest excellence.

The practice of ascetic self-effacement (*sallekhapaṭipatti*). For instance, based on the words of a young bhikkhu, "To whom would what is well-prepared not be pleasing?", [the elder] did not eat solid food until his final *parinibbāna*.
"Expansion through verbal intimation" means the cause for the utterance of speech; for sound proceeds by way of making meaning known.
Even though there is no actual intimation (*viññatti*), because it functions as a condition for that [action] through some causal factor, it proceeds by way of verbal intimation alone;
thus it is called "the manifestation of verbal intimation" (*vacīviññattivipphāra*). "Bhutto" means "if I were one who has eaten. "Sā" refers to "it" (*assā*).
This is an elided form of the vowel *a*, as in expressions such as "evaṃsa te. "Antaguṇa" means the entrails. "Bahicare" means "he would move outside."
If it were to go outside after emerging from its dwelling in order to take up its range of movement, he spoke thus in accordance with worldly convention to demonstrate his extreme fewness of wishes.
For in the world, those who reproach one for gluttony—unfit food—say:
"What indeed, are his intestines wandering outside? "I gratify" (*ārādhemī*) means that from the very beginning I succeed; the meaning is that I bring [him] under my control.
It is said that while traveling on a road during a time of famine, the Elder Mahātissa—

his body exhausted and weakened by the interruption of his meals and the fatigue of the journey— lay down at the foot of a certain ripe mango tree where many mango fruits had fallen here and there. There, a certain elder lay follower approached the Elder.
Recognizing his exhaustion, he gave him mango juice to drink, placed him upon his own back, and carried him to his dwelling. The Elder said:
“Neither father nor mother, neither kinsman nor friend, would perform such a service for the sake of one who is virtuous.”

Having exhorted himself, begun the process of contemplation (*sammasana*), and increased his insight (*vipassanā*), he realized *arahantship* right there on the back of that elephant in the sequence of the paths.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "The story of the Great Elder Tissa, the Mango-Eater, should also be told here.
"In every way" means in every manner: both by way of improper search (*anesanā*) and by way of the arising of the thought (*cittuppatti*).
The intention is that it is even more so by way of the agitation of body and speech. Therefore he said, "by improper means," and so forth.

"Seeing the danger and the benefit" refers to seeing the danger—such as the offense of using [requisites] like a debt—in the case of unreflective use, and seeing the benefit in its opposite, namely, reflective use. Because this concerns the category of requisites, it was stated:
“Regarding ‘in the requisites’ (paccayesu): even a remote cause is spoken of as a cause by virtue of its causal nature, just as it is said that ‘the meal was prepared with grass.

In order to show that when that [cause] by which a monk’s so-called ‘unreflective enjoyment’ occurs is excluded, the morality based on requisites (paccaya-sannissita-sīla) is accomplished and purified, the passage beginning with ‘therefore’ (tasmā) was stated.
In that context, by the very use of the word ‘greed’ (gedha), ‘craving for requisites’ (paccaya-gedha) is implied.”
Delusion should also be understood as being "taken up" because it occurs together with [the other defilements] and because it is their supporting condition (*upanissaya*).

The phrase "arisen in accordance with the Dhamma and justice" is a demonstration of the purity of the *origination* of the requisites, not a demonstration of the purity of virtue based on the requisites (*paccayasannissita-sīla-visuddhi*).
For virtue based on the requisites consists in using them after having considered their proper purpose. Since...
However, those requisites must be used by a bhikkhu only when they have been acquired through a proper method; therefore it is said:

“requisites obtained in accordance with the Dhamma and in a righteous manner. “By the method already stated” means by the method stated in the passage beginning, “for the warding off of cold,” and so forth.
“Or by way of the elements” means that these things, such as robes and the like, which exist according to their respective conditions, are merely elements (*dhātu*), and the one who uses them is—

Or, by way of attention to the elements (*dhātumanasikāra*), as in the phrase "and the person. Or, by way of the repulsive (*paṭikūla*): first, by way of the perception of the repulsiveness of food in the case of alms-food;

or else, by way of attention to the repulsive in this manner: "All these things, such as robes and so forth, are not inherently disgusting, yet having come into contact with this putrid body, they become exceedingly disgusting. Beyond that—

“From the time of acquisition onwards. Because it has been purified from the very beginning by wisdom, its use is indeed blameless, like alms-bowls and robes that have been set aside after being formally resolved upon.
This statement regarding “purification from the beginning” is intended to show the purity through reflection;
it is not intended to prohibit reflection at the time of use. Therefore he said, “Even at the time of use,” and so forth. Therein, “at that time” means at the time of use.
In reviewing [the practice], one acts with certainty; it is decisive and free from doubt.

What is called "enjoyment by theft" is the enjoyment of what belongs to another who is unworthy. Even in the Blessed One’s own teaching, requisites are permitted for the virtuous, not for the immoral.
For the donors as well, their relinquishment is intended only for the virtuous, not for the immoral. As for oneself...

Because it anticipates that the causes will yield great fruit. Thus, because it has not been authorized by the Teacher and because it has not been relinquished by the donors, the use of what belongs to one of immoral conduct is "use by theft" (*theyyaparibhoga*).
Use by way of debt is "debt-use" (*iṇaparibhoga*); it is use after having taken a loan, because there is no purification of the offering for the recipient.
“Viya” means “like. Therefore, with the words “of one who is virtuous,” etc., he refers back to the very meaning already stated by way of its causal nature. The connection is:
having removed the robe from the body, it should be reviewed before each use—at dawn, during the morning meal, and during the last watch of the night.
For one unable to do so [at every instance], it should be reviewed four times or three times a day according to the specific times mentioned above.
It should be reviewed either twice or just once. If dawn breaks, it stands in the same position as the "use of borrowed goods.
[One reflects: "The robe I used yesterday was only for warding off the cold...
[and so on] ...for the purpose of covering the private parts. The alms-food I consumed yesterday was not for amusement," and so forth.
If it is said that one should not perform a review of past enjoyment, that must be investigated. Regarding the lodging as well, [this applies] with every enjoyment and with every entry.
"The state of being a condition for mindfulness" (satipaccayatā) means that mindfulness is a condition for receiving and for enjoyment;
this is appropriate because mindfulness serves as a condition for the reviewing [of those acts]. One should receive [the requisites] only after having reviewed them.
The meaning is "it should be consumed. For this very reason, he said, "having established mindfulness," and so forth.
Even though this is so—meaning, even though although reflection is appropriate in both instances—even though this is so. Others, however, say:

"Sati paccayatā" means that mindfulness is the state of being a condition for the consumption of medicine; the meaning is "when there is a condition. "Even though this is so" means "even when the condition exists. That is merely their own opinion.
For in this way, virtue dependent on requisites is purified by means of reflection, not merely by the existence of the requisites themselves.
Having thus shown the purification of virtue dependent on requisites, he said, "Purification is indeed fourfold," and so forth, in order to show all forms of purification in that same context.
In this regard, it is called *suddhi* (purification) because one is purified by means of it; according to the nature of the phenomenon (*yathādhammaṃ*).
Purification by confession (*desanā-suddhi*) means purity through confession. Here, even emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*) should be understood as being included within confession itself.

For those offenses whose roots have been severed, however, confession consists simply in the acknowledgment of non-recurrence. Purity through restraint (*saṃvara-suddhi*) is restraint distinguished by its resolution.
Purity through search (*pariyeṭṭhi-suddhi*) is the very search for the requisite conditions in a lawful and righteous manner.
In all four conditions, purity is simply the reviewing according to the method already stated; thus it is "purity through reviewing" (*paccavekkhaṇa-suddhi*).

This, first of all, is the summary method regarding the purities. Regarding those [terms] containing the word "purity," however: that which has teaching as its purity is "purity of teaching" (*desanā-suddhi*).

The same method applies to the remaining ones as well. The word "purity" (*suddhi*) itself follows the method already explained. The word "thus" (*evaṃ*) is said with reference to the classification of restraint. "Having abandoned" (*pahāya*)—
"Having avoided," means "not having done.
It is a *dāya* in the sense of being something to be given; those who take that are *dāyādā* (heirs).
Because there is no use whatsoever of things not permitted, and because use is possible only of those things permitted, these requisites are to be used by the bhikkhus [only] from the Blessed One.
The *Dhammadāyādasutta* (The Discourse on the Heirs of the Dhamma), which proceeds thus: “Bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things.
I have compassion for you, thinking: ‘How may my disciples be heirs of the Dhamma, not heirs of material things?’”—this sutta is the proof for this meaning here.
For those who have not yet abandoned lust, there is no state of mastery over the enjoyment of requisites due to their being under the sway of craving;
because of the absence of that [craving], for those who have abandoned lust, there is mastery therein, since they can enjoy them according to their own preference.
For in that way, they enjoy the requisites by viewing even the repulsive as non-repulsive, the non-repulsive as repulsive, or by avoiding both and maintaining an attitude of equanimity.
And they fulfill the wishes of the donors. Therefore it was said: "For, having transcended the servitude of craving, they enjoy [these things] as masters.
"Of all" refers to both the noble ones (ariyas) and worldlings (puthujjanas). How do these enjoyments come to pass for worldlings?

By way of figurative usage (*upacāra*). For when even an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), established in the practice of effacement (*sallekha*) and having abandoned greed for requisites, makes use of things here and there with an unattached mind, that use is like the use of a master.
However, for one possessed of virtue (*sīlavat*), use made after reflection is like the use of an heir, fulfilling the wishes of the donors.
By way of non-violation. For it has been said: "Or rather, it is included as an enjoyment of an inheritance.
There is no need to speak of the enjoyment by a virtuous worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*), because he is included among those in training (*sekkha*). The *Sekkhāsutta* is the proof for this meaning.
Therefore, he said: "Even one who is virtuous," and so forth. Regarding the word "adversary" (*paccanīka*): just as a debtor [is led] to whatever place he desires by his own will...
Just as one who is bound by debt does not obtain the freedom to go, so too one who is engaged in the enjoyment of debt does not obtain the means to escape from the world.
Because it is the opposite of that, the enjoyment of one who possesses virtue is called "debt-free enjoyment" (*āṇaṇyaparibhoga*); thus he says, "or debt-free enjoyment.
By this, he shows that, in the primary sense, this is a distinct type of enjoyment, separate from the four [other] types of enjoyment. "By this training... [is said].
Regarding the training known as virtue (*sīla*): "One who performs what is to be done" means one who practices in accordance with their promise, acting appropriately and suitably.
Now, in order to clarify that very quality of performing what is to be done by means of a scriptural passage, it is said:

"And this has also been stated," and so forth. Therein, "dwelling" (*vihāra*) refers to a residence. "Bedding and seating" (*sayanāsana*) refers to couches and the like. By both terms, the lodging itself is expressed. "Water" (*āpa*)...
Water. "Washing away the dust and dirt from the outer robe" means the cleansing of the dust and impurities adhering to the *saṅghāṭi*.

"Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Sugata" means having heard the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One regarding robes and other requisites, according to the method beginning with: "Reflecting wisely, he uses the robe for protection against cold," and so forth. "The disciple of supreme wisdom, having reflected, shall use [them]"—this refers to one who, having reflected, employs them.
Having reckoned the fourfold requisite— namely, the almsfood spoken of as “alms,” the lodging-place spoken of by the words “vihāra” and so forth,
the requisite for the sick indicated by way of the water for quenching thirst and fever, and the robes such as the outer cloak—
and having reflected upon them in the manner beginning with, “only for the maintenance of this body,” etc.
A disciple of the Blessed One of supreme wisdom—whether a trainee (*sekha*) or an ordinary person (*puthujjana*)—would be able to attend upon [the Teacher].
And because that disciple of excellent wisdom attends with discernment, therefore, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, it remains so.
"At the proper time" means at the time for the Noble Ones' meal. "Having obtained" means having received. "From another" means from a donor other than oneself.
"Anuggahā" means out of compassion. "Mattaṃ so jaññā" means he should know the proper measure; "satataṃ sabbakālaṃ upaṭṭhito" means one who is constantly established in mindfulness.
"Yathā ālepanarūhane" means as in the healing of a wound by the application of medicinal ointment;
the construction is "he should know the measure. "Āhare" means he should take [food]. Alternatively, the reading is "āhareyyāhāraṃ. "Yāpanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of sustaining life.
"For the maintenance of the body. "Uninfatuated" means not infatuated by the infatuation of craving (*taṇhāmucchā*), having not fallen into the greed of craving.
Because he mentions the name of his own maternal uncle, the Elder Saṅgharakkhita, [he is called] the novice Saṅgharakkhita, the nephew.
"Rice-gruel" means rice-food. "Well-cooled" means very cool. "The unrestrained" is said with reference to a lack of reflection (*apaccavekkhaṇa*).
"Sabbāsavaparikkhīṇo" means one whose all taints (āsava) are completely destroyed.
20. First, the commentary on the five precepts:
"Pariyantāni" means those which have limits; those for whom the training rules (sikkhāpada) are limited are called "pariyantasikkhāpadā."

Of those training rules which have a limit. "Of those who are ordained" means: excluding the noble worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*), those in training (*sekha*), and those beyond training (*asekha*), it refers to other ordained ones.
For a general designation also stands for a specific instance. "Engaged in wholesome states" means:
engaged and devoted to the practice of insight (*vipassanā*). "One whose limit, supreme boundary, or ultimate limit is the states of those in training" is thus *sekkhapariyanto*.

From the point of discerning name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), or from the undertaking of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) up to the stage of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*), the continuity of wholesome states that has proceeded thus far stands reaching as far as the qualities of the trainee (*sekkhadhamma*); this is the limit of the trainee (*sekkhapariyanta*).

Alternatively, the three mundane trainings (*sikkhā*) which are to be practiced and which constitute the lower boundary of the qualities of the trainee are the "limit of the trainee"; it is within that limit of the trainee.

"Those who fulfill" means those who complete the training without omitting anything. "Those who are regardless of body and life" means those who, for the sake of attaining higher distinctions, have no regard for their own bodies or lives.
For that very reason, "those who have renounced life" means those who have sacrificed their lives for the sake of fulfilling their virtue (*sīla*).
Virtue that possesses purity because it is not clung to by the defilement of views is "virtue of purity through non-clinging. [It is so called] because of the total absence of defilements...
Virtue possessing purity through subsiding is "virtue of purity by subsiding" (*paṭippassaddhipārisuddhisīla*).

Because the virtue of those who are not fully ordained, of those beyond training (*asekha*), of those in training (*sekha*), and of noble worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) is indeed limitless due to its great majesty and power, he said:
"Because it is limited by way of enumeration. [It is so called] because of the restraint of body and speech.

"By way of training" refers to the training of restraint (*saṃvara-vinaya*). "Shown by way of a summary" means they are shown there and there according to the method of detailed exposition taught by the Teacher, following the enumeration already mentioned.
"Training" refers to the training known as virtue (*sīla*). "In the restraint of the discipline" means in the *Vinaya Piṭaka*.
One should connect this by bringing back what was stated previously: that the virtue of those fully ordained (*upasampanna*) is limited by way of its enumeration.
For whatever training in virtue (sīla) is to be practiced by one who is fully ordained, it must be done there without exception and in its entirety.

"The state of undertaking" means the actual presence of the undertaking. Regarding "gain...": the non-transgression of virtue for the sake of gain and so forth is the state of not seeing a limit [to such pursuits].
One should sacrifice wealth for the sake of a superior limb when oppressed by highwaymen, thieves, and the like;

one should sacrifice a limb while protecting one’s life at a time of being bitten by a snake and so forth; and a person should sacrifice everything—limb, wealth, and even life—while recollecting the Dhamma, as did the Great Bodhisatta Sutasoma and others.
Therefore it was said: "Not abandoning this recollection of the True Person. [This applies] to the distress of hunger.

"Even though there was a danger to life. "Without transgressing the training rule" means that although ownerless mango fruits had fallen on the ground nearby, he did not consume them because there was no recipient to receive them; thus, he did not transgress the training rule regarding receiving.
"Because of his being virtuous" means for the sake of his state of virtue, or [it refers to] such carrying on the shoulder and so forth for you, who are virtuous.
The intention is that it performs its function because of its nature (*kāraṇa*). "Like a well-washed gem of birth" means like a gem of noble origin that has been thoroughly washed upon four stones.
"Like [the cases of] the Elder Saṅgharakkhita, the nephew of the Great Saṅgharakkhita, and the Elder Saṅgharakkhita" means like the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita and his nephew, the Elder Saṅgharakkhita.
"And why have we come here?"—the intention is that the great multitude will feel remorse.
"With a finger snap" means by snapping the fingers. "Through lack of mindfulness" means through a lapse of mindfulness.
"Done out of ignorance" means done having offended through ignorance; the meaning is, done without knowing [the consequences].

“Even if he is of little learning” means that he is devoid of the study of the discourses, verses, and so forth. “Unsettled in the virtues” means that he is not properly established even in the virtues such as restraint according to the Pātimokkha.

“His learning does not succeed” means that for this person who lacks virtue, his learning brings about neither success in existence for himself nor for others in any state. [As it is said: “This person is an individual of bad character.”
Indeed, those who desire training do not approach him. Furthermore, in the phrase "even though he is learned," the word *ce* is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*).
"Praised" means that he is indeed praised.
By the mention of being "unmistaken through lust," he expresses the absence of clinging through craving (*taṇhāparāmāsa*). "Of such a kind" means unmistaken through lust.
"Having pierced" means having struck. "I shall persuade him" means I shall win him over; the intention is that he will release me after a short time.
"I am repelled" means I feel disgust. "I am ashamed" means I feel shame.
"Sunk in mud" means sinking down or being smeared. "I shall die together with my virtue" means without destroying my virtue.
"I shall die together with him; I will never abandon him now. The intention is: "For as long as there is grasping at existence (*bhavādāna*), there might be a separation from virtue;
therefore, I will not grasp at existence itself. "Comprehending the disease" means:
having grasped feeling—which is the disease—by way of feeling, and having likewise grasped the remaining immaterial phenomena and material phenomena, he practices insight (*vipassanā*).
“Is being afflicted” means undergoing transformation while the body is in a state of change. “Is parched” means it dries up on all sides. What is it like?
It is like a flower—meaning, for example, a *sirīsa* or similar flower placed in dust that has been heated by the sun’s rays.
“Unpleasant” means disagreeable and loathsome. “Designated as pleasant” means [designated] as “pleasant” by fools.

Thus it was praised. Regarding the phrase "one who does not see the knowable form": for one who does not see things as they truly are, for the ignorant person, it is praised as "knowable" (*jañña*). "Dhiratthu maṃ" means "fie on this!";

due to its connection with the word *dhi*, the accusative case is used in all instances, meaning "let there be a curse upon this putrid body. "Duggandhiyaṃ" means "foul-smelling," that which possesses a foul odor.
Wherein—in this aforementioned putrid body—beings (*pajā*) who are heedless due to the cause of lust fall into negligence.

They "neglect the path to rebirth in a happy state" (*sugatūpapatti*); the intended meaning is that they neglect even the path to rebirth in a happy state, which is virtue (*sīla*), let alone the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth.
Only those disciples whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) should be called "Arahants"; as for others, however, [the term refers to] Paccekabuddhas.
Because it includes the qualification "Perfectly Enlightened One," he says, "of the Arhats and so forth.
"Through the subsiding of all distress" means through the subsiding of the distress of all defilements (*kilesa*).
Commentary on the Second Set of Five Precepts.

Regarding the phrase "of killing living beings, etc.," by the word "etc. (ādi), one should understand the inclusion of everything from taking what is not given up to the defilements to be abandoned by the highest path (agga-magga).
Regarding the phrase "abandoning, etc.," by the word "etc.," the four [factors] beginning with abstinence (veramaṇi) are included.

In some manuscripts, it is written as "by way of abandoning" (pahānavasena); that is a scribal error. For the abandoning of killing living beings is virtue (sīla) when preceded by moral shame (hirī), moral dread (ottappa), compassion (karuṇā), non-greed (alobha), and so forth.
That arising of a wholesome state of consciousness by which the taking of life is abandoned is virtue (*sīla*) in the sense of steadfastness (*sīlana*).
Likewise, abstention from the taking of life (*virati*), desisting from it (*veramaṇī*), is virtue. The volition that is the opposite of the taking of life is virtue.
The restraint of the taking of life—the closing of the door of entry—is restraint (*saṃvara*), which is virtue. [Of] the taking of life...

Non-transgression is *sīla*. This same method applies to the phrases "of taking what is not given," and so forth. However, the abandoning of covetousness and the rest should be understood by way of non-covetousness and so on.
Abstinence (*veramaṇī*) is volition; that which is associated with it includes the restraint, the non-transgression, and the states headed by those [factors].
Having thus shown the morality of abandoning and the others by way of the ten courses of wholesome action, [the text now proceeds] to the eight [precepts] together with their means.

In order to demonstrate those [states] by way of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*), and the noble paths (*ariyamagga*), the passage beginning with “by renunciation” (*nekkhammena*) is commenced.
Therein, “by renunciation” means by an arising of wholesome consciousness (*kusalacittuppāda*) dominated by non-greed (*alobha*).
For here, wholesome states (*dhamma*) that are the opposites of sensual desire (*kāma*) are intended by the term “renunciation. Therefore he said: “of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*)...”
“Abandoning is virtue,” and so forth. Therein, the virtues of abandoning and the others are to be understood in the manner already explained above;

we shall speak only of their specific distinctions. “By non-ill will” means by loving-kindness (*mettā*). “By perception of light” means by the manifestation of the perception of light through mental attention that has made [the object] clear.
“By non-distraction” means by concentration (*samādhi*). “By the definition of phenomena” means by the determination of wholesome and other phenomena as they truly are.
They also say it is by means of the discernment of mind-and-body together with its conditions.

Thus, having shown the virtue of abandoning and the other factors by way of the preliminary practice— which serves as the means for attaining the first jhāna, as described in the passage beginning, "Having abandoned covetousness for the world"— [the text now treats] those [factors] together with their means.
The phrase beginning with "by means of knowledge" (*ñāṇena*) is stated in order to show [the development] by way of the eight attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) and so forth.

For when delusion (*moha*), which acts as an obstacle to the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the overcoming of doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇa*), is removed, the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*) and the others are accomplished for one who stands firm in full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*).

Likewise, they are accomplished through gladness (*pāmojja*), which is the cause of delight in the meditative absorptions (*jhānasamāpatti*), once lack of delight (*anabhirati*) has been dispelled therein.
"The attainment of the jhānas and so forth" refers to the means for dispelling discontent and shattering ignorance through meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and insight (*vipassanā*), as stated:

"By knowledge, ignorance; by gladness, discontent. However, this presentation in reverse order should be understood as intended to show that ignorance—which has the nature of an hindrance—is included even among the hindrances mentioned previously.

Regarding such passages as, “By means of the first jhāna, [one is freed] from the hindrances,” how can these jhānas have the nature of virtue (*sīla*), or how can there be the occurrence of abstinence (*virati*) therein?
For these jhānas proceed by way of the mind’s undertaking (*cittasamādāna*) on the part of one whose bodily action and so forth are already thoroughly purified;
they do not proceed by way of purifying bodily action and so forth like limited wholesome states (*parittakusala*), nor are they the factors of the path or the fruit.

Is it by way of the cutting off and the subsiding of misconduct and wrong livelihood? This is true. In the sublime states (*mahaggata-dhamma*), in the primary sense (*nippariyāyena*), there is no meaning of "steadying" (*sīlana*);
how then could there be the meaning of "abstaining" (*viramaṇa*)? However, it should be understood that this was stated in a figurative sense (*pariyāyena*).
What, then, is that figurative sense? It is that to the same extent that the sublime wholesome states abandon their opposites, to that same extent...
Therefore, they are "on this side" (*orata*). And because they do not allow the mind to ascend [into unwholesome states], they are said to be "restrained" (*saṃvuta*).

Furthermore, because there is no transgression at the door of the mind characterized by obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) in these cases, they are called "non-transgressors" (*avītikkama*); however, the volition (*cetanā*) is associated with that [state].
This matter will be explained further below. By taking it in this way, even the statement regarding the abandoning of applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth becomes consistent.
For it is not tenable that virtue (*sīla*) in its primary sense is the abandoner of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*),
nor are unwholesome thoughts (*akusalavitakka*) and so forth intended here. Although the abandoning of suffering occurs precisely in the access to the first jhāna,

and the abandoning of pleasure occurs in the access to the fourth jhāna, it is said with reference to their "superlative abandoning" that "by the fourth jhāna there is the abandoning of pleasure and pain."
“Abandoning. Regarding what should be said concerning “the attainment of the base of infinite space,” etc., that will follow in the discussion on the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
Contemplation of the impermanent as “impermanent” is the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).

This is the name for insight (*vipassanā*) that proceeds by grasping the impermanence of phenomena belonging to the three planes. “Of the perception of permanence” means: [the view] that “conditioned phenomena are permanent and eternal.”
When wrong perception has arisen in this way, by the mention of "perception" (*saññā*), the inclusion of both views and consciousness should also be understood.
This same method applies to those that follow. "Contemplation of disenchantment" (*nibbidānupassanā*) means contemplation occurring in the mode of becoming disenchanted with formations (*saṅkhāra*).
"Delight" (*nandi*) refers to craving accompanied by rapture. "Contemplation of fading away" (*virāgānupassanā*) means [contemplation] occurring in the mode of fading away.
"Of lust": of lust for formations. "By contemplation of cessation": by the contemplation of the cessation of formations.
Or, contemplation in such a way that formations simply cease and do not arise again in the future as a new existence—that is contemplation of cessation.
For this very reason it is said: "By contemplation of cessation, one causes [lust] to cease; it does not arise."

For this [insight] has reached its full strength through the desire for deliverance. Contemplation that occurs in the mode of relinquishing formations is the "contemplation of relinquishment" (*paṭinissaggānupassanā*).
For this is the reflective discernment and the settling [of the mind]. "Of grasping" means of the seizing by way of permanence and so forth.
"The perception of compactness" (*ghanasaññā*) is the grasping at unity by way of continuity, collection, function, and object; it is of that perception of compactness. "Of accumulation" means...
Of volitional formation (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*). Transformation (*vipariṇāma*) is the attainment of specific states, such as aging, by the formations (*saṅkhārā*).

Of the perception of stability (*dhuvasaññā*): that is, of the grasping after solidity. Of the sign (*nimitta*): because the formations possess a semblance of a concrete entity through their density as an aggregate and so forth, and through their delimitation of their own respective functions.
Of aspiration (*paṇidhi*): of aspiration consisting of lust and so forth; the meaning is: of being inclined toward the formations by way of craving (*taṇhā*). Of misapprehension (*abhinivesa*):...

Regarding "view of self" (*attānudiṭṭhi*): insight into phenomena through higher wisdom (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*) is the investigation of all phenomena belonging to the three planes by way of impermanence, suffering, and so forth. Regarding "clinging to the grasping of the essence":

this refers to the perversion of perceiving an essence in what is essenceless. "Knowledge and vision according to reality" (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*) is simply the contemplations of impermanence and so forth once they have reached a state of stability;
some say it is the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbayañāṇa*), while others say it is the vision of mentality-materiality together with its conditions (*sappaccayanāmarūpadassana*).
The adherence that [the world] has arisen by way of the creation of a Lord (issarakutta) and so forth is adherence through delusion (*sammohābhinivesa*).

Some say it is adherence to annihilationism (*uccheda*) or eternalism (*sassata*). Others say that falling into doubt, proceeding in the manner of “Did I exist in the past? and so forth, is adherence through delusion.
Grasping at conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as a refuge or a shelter is adherence through attachment (*ālayābhinivesa*), as in: “Delighting in attachment, rejoicing in attachment.”

According to the verbal definition, *ālaya* is craving (*taṇhā*). Others maintain that it is precisely that [craving] which, by way of its occurrence through the process of adhering to the eye and so forth, as well as to forms and so forth, is called "adherence to the substrate" (*ālayābhinivesa*).
The knowledge that occurs in the form, “These formations, being thus established, are to be relinquished,” is the contemplation of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*).
Non-reflection (*appaṭisaṅkhā*) consists of unwholesome states dominated by delusion, which stand as the opposites of reflection.

Nirvana is called "the turning away" (*vivaṭṭa*) because it is free from the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). The occurrence of contemplation characterized by being inclined toward that [Nirvana] is "contemplation of the turning away" (*vivaṭṭānupassanā*);

this consists of both equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and knowledge of conformity (*anulomañāṇa*). "Adherence through bondage" (*saññogābhiniveso*) is the fixation upon formations by way of being bound to them.
"Co-existent with views" means both co-existent with views by way of simultaneous arising and co-existent with views by way of being abandoned together.
"Gross" is said in reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths; otherwise, even those to be abandoned by seeing would be grosser than those to be abandoned by the second path.
"Subtle" means having become minute; this is said in reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the lower paths. "All defilements."
Of all remaining defilements. For defilements already abandoned by the first path and so forth are not abandoned again.
In such passages as "They lead to non-remorse of the mind," restraint has the purpose of non-remorse.
Because of the statement, "Ānanda, wholesome virtues have non-remorse as their purpose," they exist for the purpose of the mind's non-remorse. Non-remorse...
For the sake of gladness: because of the statement, "Gladness arises for one who attends wisely," they lead to gladness.
Gladness leads to rapture: because of the statement, "Rapture arises for one who is glad," they lead to rapture. Rapture leads to tranquility:
because of the statement, "The body of one whose mind is rapturous becomes tranquil," they lead to tranquility. Tranquility leads to happiness.
Because of the statement, “One whose body is tranquil experiences happiness,” they lead to mental joy (*somanassa*).

Furthermore, in the phrase, “For the sake of happiness, one experiences happiness,” what is called “happiness” here is actually mental joy. Regarding the phrase “by way of cultivation”: it is by way of the cultivation of concentration.
For when non-sensual happiness is established, concentration is indeed established as well, according to the statement, “The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.”
Therefore, the meaning is that they lead to the cultivation, proficiency, and strength of concentration.
"For development" means for the increase of that very concentration. "For frequent practice" means for repeated performance.
"For adornment" means they lead to the adornment consisting in the production of the faculty of faith and so forth, which serve as the ornaments of that very concentration. "For equipment" means...
They conduce to the equipment for that very concentration, for the sake of accomplishing the requisites of concentration such as non-remorse.

For here the word *parikkhāra* (requisite) has the sense of a *sambhāra* (requisite/support). As in the passage, "And these requisites of life which must be procured by one who has gone forth," the term *sambhāra* should be understood as a condition (*paccaya*). And although this word *parikkhāra*—

In such passages as “The chariot has virtue as its equipment,” the sense is that of an ornament. In such passages as “It is well-fortified with the seven fortifications of a city,” the sense spoken of is that of an accessory.
But here, since ornament and accessory have been mentioned separately, it is said that the sense is that of a constituent part (*sambhāra*).

“For the sake of the accessory” means by way of being the fundamental cause itself, through the accomplishment of specific qualities such as mindfulness and energy which serve as the accessories to concentration.

They lead to the perfection of the retinue. Regarding "fulfillment": they lead to the fulfillment of concentration by means of achieving mastery and by establishing it as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for insight (*vipassanā*), thereby accomplishing its state of completeness.
Having thus shown concentration that is complete in all aspects and rooted in perfectly pure virtue (*sīla*), [the text now says] "one who is concentrated..."
Because of the statement, “He understands and sees; knowing and seeing according to reality as it is, he becomes disenchanted; being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate;

through dispassion, he is liberated,” the phrase beginning with “for the sake of absolute disenchantment” was spoken in order to show the purpose, which is the states rooted in virtue that have concentration as their proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).
For when disenchantment is shown, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*), which serves as its proximate cause, is thereby shown as well.
[This] exists because, in its absence, disenchantment (*nibbidā*) cannot be established. Disenchantment and the other [stages] have already been analyzed according to their meaning.
Here, however, "knowledge and vision in accordance with reality" (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*) is intended to mean the seeing of name-and-form together with its conditions.
Thus, it should be understood that the purpose of virtue (*sīla*) has been shown here, culminating in the great Nirvana, the Deathless.
Now, in order to show the meaning of virtue (*sīla*) with respect to abandoning (*pahāna*) and the other [aspects], the passage beginning with “And here” is commenced.

In that context, “abandoning” refers to the non-arising and cessation [of defilements]; thus, with reference to its nature as an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*), it is said: “There is no such thing as a ‘dharma’ called abandoning.
How, however, its status as a dharma is possible has already been explained below. For in this way, its status as virtue (*sīla*) [is established].
It is well joined. "The abandoning of this or that" refers to the specific abandonings mentioned as "the abandoning of killing living beings" and "the abandoning of taking what is not given.
"Of this or that wholesome state" means: the abandoning of killing living beings is [the basis] for wholesome states such as loving-kindness;
the abandoning of taking what is not given is [the basis] for wholesome states such as generosity—and so on for each respective case.
Of that wholesome state (*kusaladhamma*). "In the sense of being a foundation" means by way of its nature as a foundation. For when that [wholesome state] exists, abandoning occurs;

when it does not exist, it does not occur. Considering that it thus receives the designation "foundation," in whichever continuum there are [tendencies such as] killing living beings and so forth, those are the causes for its shaking;
therefore, the abandoning of them is "concentration" (*samādhāna*) by way of producing the absence of shaking.
Thus it has been said. The same should be stated regarding the remaining abandonments as well. "Establishment" means stabilization or restraint.
"The other four" refers to the four factors beginning with abstinence; the intention is that, unlike abandonment, these are merely conventional designations.
"From this or that" means from each respective instance of killing living beings and so forth. "Of this or that" refers to the act of restraining oneself from killing living beings and so forth.
"By way of this or that restraint" means by way of the volition associated with both.
"By way of the volition associated with the abstentions and the factors of restraint" means by way of the volition conjoined with the *veramaṇīs* (abstentions) and the phenomena of restraint.

"Of one who does not transgress this or that" refers to the presence of mental activity in a person or a collection of phenomena who does not transgress this or that—such as killing and so forth—with reference to the actual occurrence of the mind.
[They] have been stated. Therefore, the intention is that they are obtained even in a single moment.
Regarding the commentary on the defilement and purification of virtue (sīla):
it is called "defilement" (saṃkileso) because one is defiled by it. As to what that is, he says: "The state of being broken and so forth is the defilement of virtue."

"Vodāna" (cleansing) means that by which one is cleansed or purified; it refers to the state of being unbroken and so forth. In the phrase "gain, fame, etc.," the word "etc. includes relatives, limbs, life, and so on.

Regarding the statement "at the beginning, at the end, or in the middle of the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*)," this is said according to the sequence of their recitation in the Canon (*pāḷi*);
for there is no other fixed order for these classes of offenses. "Broken" (*khaṇḍa*) means possessing a break.
"Or torn. The same method applies here for "perforated" as well. "Like a garment with its edges cut" means like a cloth whose hem or fringe has been cut.
"In this way" means by the manner that is now being described. "By way of sexual union" means by the attainment of a state of similarity through the obsession of lust.
"Of pairs" means of sexual union; it is a bond. "Sexual union" (*methunasaṃyoga*) is a conjunction by way of sexual intercourse.
But here, "sexual union" (*methunasaṃyoga*) means that which is like sexual union; [it is] by way of that. "Here" (*idha*) means in this world. "A certain one" (*ekacco*) means one person.

"Whether a recluse or a brahmin" (*samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā*) means either a recluse by virtue of mere renunciation, or a brahmin by virtue of mere birth. "The attainment of the couple" (*dvayaṃdvayasamāpattiṃ*)—
"By twos, by twos" means one should enter [into union] with two each time; "sexual intercourse" is the meaning. "He does not indeed enter into it" is the grammatical connection.
"Anointing" is rubbing in [ointment]; "massaging" is kneading. "Relishes" means he endures it.
"Takes delight in that" means he finds pleasure in that anointing and so forth. "Desires" means he wishes for it. "Satisfaction" means contentment. "This too, indeed..."—here [the context continues].
"This" refers to what has been stated above—receiving [sexual pleasure] and so forth—which is spoken of as a single unit by way of its various constituent parts, such as the state of being broken.
The word *pi* (also/even) has the sense of conjunction, referring to what is about to be said. The word *kho* (indeed) has the sense of emphasis. This is what is meant:

even though there is no actual "pairing of two by two" for one who merely claims to be a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), there is still this receiving of the woman’s rubbing, bathing, massaging, and so forth.
This too is "broken," "perforated," "mottled," and "blemished" because it brings about the state of being broken and so forth for that holy life (*brahmacariya*).
Thus, by falling into such states as being broken, he leads an impure holy life, not a pure one;
he is fettered by the bond of sexual intercourse, not unfettered. Consequently, he is not [freed] from birth and the rest.
Showing that it is "complete liberation," he said, "This is called... and so forth.
*Sañjagghati* means she laughs with a loud laugh due to the influence of the defilements (*kilesa*). *Saṃkīḷati* means she plays by way of physical contact.
*Saṃkelāyati* means she dwells completely cherishing womenfolk. *Cakkhunā* means with her own eye. *Cakkhuṃ*... [means] the eye.
"The eye of a woman. "He gazes upon" means he approaches and gazes, that is, he looks at her.
"Beyond a wall" means beyond a wall (*kuṭṭa*). Likewise for "beyond a rampart" (*pākāra*). They say that a wall made of clay is a *kuṭṭa*, while one made of bricks is a *pākāra*.
Alternatively, any wall measuring one and a half *ratana*s in height is a *kuṭṭa*; anything greater than a wall in size is a *pākāra*.
"Assa" means of one who has made the profession of being a celibate practitioner (*brahmacārī*). "Pubbe" means prior to the undertaking of the vow.
"Kāmaguṇehi" means by means of the strands of sensual pleasure. "Samappitaṃ" means well-endowed, joined together. "Samaṅgībhūtaṃ" means possessed of.

"Paricārayamānaṃ" means sporting about, or being attended upon. "Paṇidhāya" means having made an aspiration. In the phrases beginning with "sīlena," it refers to the undertaking of restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth.
Virtue (*sīla*) is so called by way of non-transgression. Vow (*vata*) is also virtue; however, that which is undertaken as a difficult practice is specifically termed a vow.

Alternatively, virtue has the characteristic of abstaining from whatever is considered improper. A vow is the specific performance of duties—such as eating only at certain times—for one who has undertaken such a commitment.
In every sense, difficult practice is austerity (*tapas*). Abstinence from sexual intercourse is the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

"Sabbaso" means "without remainder" or "of all. "Abhedenā" means "without transgression. The construction is: "He is comprised [by this] through the non-arising of evil qualities and the arising of virtues by another [means].
In that context, anger (*kodha*) has the characteristic of being provoked to wrath.

Resentment (*upanāha*) has the characteristic of persistent ill-will. Sycophancy (*makkha*) has the characteristic of smearing over the virtues of others. Prevarication (*paḷāsa*) has the characteristic of grasping at both sides...
Palāsa (malice). Envy has the characteristic of being jealous of the success of others. Avarice has the characteristic of concealing one's own success.
Deceit has the characteristic of hiding existing faults. Guile has the characteristic of fabricating non-existent virtues. Stiffness has the characteristic of rigidity of mind.
Aggression has the characteristic of seeking preeminence in action. Pride has the characteristic of loftiness.
Excessive conceit has the characteristic of upraising; intoxication has the characteristic of exhilaration; negligence has the characteristic of the mind’s non-abandonment [of unwholesome states].
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), greed, delusion, distorted attention, and others are included.
Now, in order to make clearer the very meaning stated by the words "But the state of being unbroken, etc.," he says "For those which... and so on.

In this context, "unimpaired" means unafflicted. Making them into a state of freedom by releasing them from the servitude of craving through their being a necessary condition for turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).
It is said, "because they are praised by the wise," because the ignorant are immeasurable [in number].

Alternatively, their purpose is the leading toward concentration (*samādhi-saṃvattana*); or, they are called "leading to concentration" because they are applied to the leading toward concentration. Through rain, there is the success of crops.
Just as the perfection of virtue (sīlasampadā) arises through the removal of its opposite, and that occurs by seeing the fault therein, he said: "by seeing the danger in the failure of virtue.
Because those who act with circumspection regard their purpose as weighty, right practice occurs only when the qualities [of virtue] have been seen;
thus it was said: "and by seeing the benefit in the perfection of virtue."
In this context, the disadvantage of the failure of virtue (sīlavipatti) should be understood as the opposite of the benefits of the perfection of virtue (sīlasampadā) shown below;
since that is easy to understand, it is not elaborated upon here. To show it by other means, the phrase "Moreover" (apica) is introduced.
In this regard, just as the perfection of virtue is the cause for beings being pleasing, so too the failure of virtue is the cause for being unpleasing.
He said: “The immoral one... [up to] ...of gods and humans. He is not to be instructed because he is to be loathed. “Suffering” means one in whom suffering has arisen.
“Remorseful” means one who feels regret, thinking, “Alas, I have not done what is good,” and so forth.
“Ugly” means devoid of the beauty of virtues and the beauty of the body. “Of him” means of the immoral one. Contact with those associated with him is painful; contact brings about suffering.
"Of this" means of contact with suffering. It is "of little value" because it lacks both quality and power.
"Like a cesspool of ordure many years old" means like a pit of accumulated filth that has been built up over a multitude of years. "Difficult to clean" means impossible to purify.
"A funeral torch" refers to a firebrand cast away after the cremation of a corpse. "Excluded from both" means excluded from the state of a recluse and from the enjoyments of a householder.
And he has fallen away. One who has enmity toward all, or one for whom all are enemies, is a "sabbaverī";

such a person is a "sabbaveriko. He does not deserve communal living; thus, he is "asaṃvāsāraho" (one unworthy of communion). Regarding "in the True Dhamma," this refers to both the True Dhamma of practice (*paṭipatti-saddhamma*) and the True Dhamma of realization (*paṭivedha-saddhamma*).
The meaning stated briefly as "because of sharing in suffering as described in the Discourse on the Mass of Fire" is now explained in detail:
The passage beginning with “For those who are immoral” (*dussīlānañhi*) was commenced in order to demonstrate this.

Those whose minds are intoxicated by the gratification of the pleasure derived from enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*), as well as the pleasure of being honored and venerated by others, are “those whose minds are intoxicated by the five [sensual pleasures]...,” and so forth; for them.
That which has the aforementioned gratification of pleasure as its condition is “conditioned by that” (*tappaccaya*). This is to be connected with the word “suffering” (*dukkha*).
"Behold"—does it mean "behold," or does it mean "behold indeed"? "Great" means vast. "Mass of fire" means a collection of flames.
"Blazing" means set ablaze. "Flaming on all sides" means burning all around, emitting sparks.
"Become a single mass of light" means possessing radiance, having become a unified emergence of light through flames rising up from every side. What is that?
"Maññatha" means: he asks for the sake of obtaining consent, asking, "What do you think of this matter now being spoken by me?
"Āliṅgetvā" means having embraced. "Upanisīdeyya" means she would sit down close to him by that very act of embracing.
To clarify the purpose for which the Teacher introduced here the embracing of a mass of fire and the embracing of a maiden, he said, "I announce," and so forth.
In this context, "I announce" means I address you. "You" refers to yourselves. "I inform" means I awaken you to it. "Of one who is immoral" means of one devoid of virtue, lacking in moral conduct.
"Of evil character" means, precisely because of that immorality, one whose disposition is base and whose nature is inferior.
"Of impure and suspicious conduct" means being impure due to the lack of purity in physical conduct and so forth, and being suspicious because of that.

One whose conduct must be guarded: for a person of bad character, upon seeing anything inappropriate, becomes an object of suspicion for others, thinking, "This must have been done by such-and-such a person";

or, seeing monks consulting together on some business, he suspects even himself, thinking, "Could it be that they are consulting because they know of an action committed by me? Thus, his conduct must be guarded against such suspicions.
"Of one whose conduct is concealed" means of one whose conduct ought to be concealed because it is shameful.

"Of one who is not an ascetic" (assamaṇassa) means of one who is not a true ascetic; that is, of one who falsely claims to be an ascetic by declaring "I too am an ascetic" during the taking of voting sticks and other such occasions.

"Of one who does not lead the holy life" (abrahmacārissa) means of one who does not practice celibacy; that is, of one who falsely claims to be a practitioner of the holy life by declaring "I too am a practitioner of the holy life" during the Uposatha and other such occasions.

Of one who has professed himself a celibate student (*brahmacārin*). Of one who is "rotten within" because he has entered into internal corruption through impure conduct and a failure in virtue (*sīla*).
Of one who is "lustful" because he is drenched by the constant pouring of defilements such as passion through the six sense-doors.

Of one who is "born of filth" because he is covered with the refuse of passion and the like, and because he must be discarded by those possessed of virtue. [The phrase] "by way of a lowly simile, being like a mass of fire" refers to this.
This is the meaning. Therefore the Blessed One said: "This alone is his boon. The connection is: having shown suffering, the Blessed One shows suffering.
"With a hair-rope" means with a rope made of hair; for that is indeed rougher. "He should rub" means by way of rubbing.
*Ghaṃseyya*: "She should rub. *Teladhotāya*: "With one washed with oil," meaning sharpened with oil. *Paccorasmiṃ*: "Upon her breast," meaning facing the breast;
the intended sense is "in the middle of the breast. *Ayosaṅkunā*: "With an iron hook," meaning with a pair of tongs.
*Pheṇuddehakaṃ*: "Scooping up foam," meaning having repeatedly raised up foam.

Because its fruit is a bitter suffering that is even more intense than the suffering of embracing a mass of fire, it is called "having a bitter fruit more painful than the suffering of embracing a mass of fire.

For one who does not abandon sensual pleasure—a person of broken virtue and immoral conduct—how could there be happiness for him? The intention is that there is none at all. "Sādana" means consenting to; "yaṃ" refers to the consenting to the act of joining the palms in salutation.
"Of one lacking virtue" means of one who is immoral. "Wounded" means afflicted by the ruin of virtue. "Mutilated" means mutilated by the cutting away of the roots of wholesome merit;
the intended meaning is that his qualities have been excavated from his body. "From all fears" means from all fears such as self-reproach and so forth.
"By all [forms of] bliss" refers to all blisses of attainment, beginning with access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*).

"By being the opposite of the manner described above" means by way of the antithesis to the modes described under the failure of virtue (*sīlavipatti*), such as "he is pleasing to gods and humans," and so forth.
"The fragrance of the body of a virtuous bhikkhu brings joy even to the gods"—here, the verse beginning with "The fragrance of the seers who have long been consecrated...
should be cited in full. "Unassailed" (*avighātī*) means unopposed. [This refers to] the afflictions such as killing, imprisonment, and so on.
The taints pertaining to the present life are calamities. Immorality is indeed the root of sufferings in future lives. "Beyond the limit" means absolute;
it is absolutely peaceful because it is forever peaceful due to the absence of distress consisting of the fever of the defilements.
"Having become afraid" means having become terrified through the fear born of knowledge (*ñāṇutrāsa*). "Should be purified" means should be cleansed.
The commentary on the Description of Virtue is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the first chapter. 2.
Commentary on the Description of the Ascetic Practices (Dhutaṅga).
22. One who has few desires is *appiccha*; that is, one who is free from grasping for requisites. The state of being such is *appicchatā*, meaning a disposition characterized by non-greed (*alobha*).

*Santuṭṭhi* is contentment; *santuṭṭhitā* is simply the state of being contented (*santuṭṭhi*), which is satisfaction with what one already possesses or with whatever various requisites have been obtained without seeking anything else. [The phrase] "by means of contentment and so forth" refers to this.
Or, the letter *ta* functions as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). Alternatively, the reading is “santuṭṭhiādīhi.

“Those qualities” refers to those qualities such as fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) which serve as the causes for the purification of virtue (*sīlavodāna*). “To bring to completion” means to make them fully accomplished.

For when they have merely been acquired through the purification of virtue, they become even more perfected by means of the ascetic practices (*dhutadhamma*). “The undertaking of the ascetic practices” refers to the factors that shake off the defilements.
The proper undertaking of the causes for dispelling [defilements]. "Thus" means that being so, when the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) have been undertaken; "of this" refers to the practitioner.

"Effacement" (*sallekha*) is the proper scraping away, cutting off, and thinning out of the defilements. "Seclusion" (*paviveka*) is the state of having the body withdrawn from society, which serves as the means for mental seclusion.
"Diminution" (*apacaya*) is the reduction of defilements through such practice.

They diminish [defilements] and do not accumulate them; such is the way of practice. The exertion of energy (*vīriyārambha*) is the state of having initiated energy by means of the non-arising of unarisen evil states and so forth.
Being easy to support (*subharatā*) is the state of being easily maintained and nourished by attendants, established through the aforementioned quality of fewness of desires and so on.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes having few duties, a simple livelihood, and other such qualities.
One’s virtue (*sīla*), exactly as it was undertaken, will become thoroughly purified by the distancing of opposing states.
The practices (*vata*) and the ascetic qualities (*dhutadhamma*) will be accomplished, perfected, or brought to fruition—
that steadfast contentment with robes, almsfood, and lodgings, which belongs to the ancient Noble Ones such as the Buddhas.
They exist as a continuous lineage; with reference to the state of being established therein, he says: "having been established in the three ancient noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa).

One for whom cultivation (bhāvanā) is a delight (ārāma) in the sense that it is to be resorted to is a "delighter in cultivation" (bhāvanārāma); the state of being such is "delight in cultivation" (bhāvanārāmatā), which is the state of being devotedly engaged in the cultivation of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
The connection is: "because he will become one worthy of attainment."

Gains, honors, and so forth are called "worldly bait" (*lokāmisa*) because they are to be grasped by craving and because they are included within the world. The "conformable practice" (*anulomapaṭipadā*) is the cultivation of insight (*vipassanābhāvanā*), so called because it conforms to the attainment of Nibbāna.

"In meaning" (*atthato*) means according to the etymological definition of the words. "By way of classification" (*pabhedato*) means by way of division. "By way of dissolution" (*bhedato*) means by way of destruction. "Of the ascetic practices, etc.

(*dhutādīnaṃ*) refers to the ascetic practices (*dhuta*), the proclaimer of ascetic practices (*dhutavāda*), the ascetic qualities (*dhutadhamma*), and the factors of asceticism (*dhutaṅga*). "By way of summary and detail" (*samāsabyāsatō*) means by way of concise and extensive treatment.

23. *Rathikā* means a street. In the phrase *saṅkārakūṭādīnaṃ*, the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). By the sense of "rising up" (*abbhuggata*), that is, by the sense of being elevated (*ussita*).

He says, "like a rag from a dust-heap, [it is] a rag-robe," because the word *kūla* has the meaning of a heap or accumulation (*samussaya*), as in the expression "the bank of a river" (*nadiyā kūlaṃ*) and so forth.
Since the syllable *ku* signifies contempt (*kuccha*) and the syllable *ula* signifies going (*gati*), he says, "it goes toward a state of contempt."
It is said [thus]. Or, it is called *paṃsukūla* because it is as despicable as dust (*paṃsu*), or because it moves about (*ulati*) like dust.
The wearing of *paṃsukūla* is *paṃsukūla* through the elision of the middle term; one whose habit (*sīla*) is that is a *paṃsukūlika*, just as one is called an *āpūpika* (a cake-seller).

It is called a *kāraṇa* (cause) because it goes (*aṅgati*) toward the state of being a cause with respect to its own fruit; by means of which a person is designated a "wearer of rag-robes" (*paṃsukūlika*).
It is said: that phenomenon (dhamma) consisting of the volition of undertaking is a factor for one who wears rag-robes; thus it is called a "rag-robe-wearer's factor" (*paṃsukūlikaṅga*).

Therefore he said, "of the rag-robe-wearer," and so forth. "Of that" refers to the undertaking. It is an "undertaking" (*samādāna*) because by means of this one undertakes; it is volition (*cetanā*). By this same method:
just as wearing rag-robes is "rag-robe" (*paṃsukūla*), one whose habit is that is a "rag-robe-wearer" (*paṃsukūlika*), and its factor is [the undertaking].

The volition of undertaking [the practice] is called the "refuse-rag-wearer’s factor" (*paṃsukūlikaṅga*). In the same way, according to this method of explaining the meaning of words, wearing the three robes is the "three-robes" (*ticīvara*);
one whose habit is that is a "three-robed one" (*tecīvarika*); and the volition of undertaking that [practice] is to be understood as the "three-robed factor" (*tecīvarikaṅga*).
The designation "three robes" applies only to the three robes beginning with the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*), and not to the itch-covering cloth, the rainy-season robe, and so forth.
Showing them according to their form, he said: "consisting of the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), and the inner robe (antaravāsaka).
"Alms-food" (piṇḍapāta) refers to the alms-food characterized by the falling of morsels given by others into the bowl;

one who gathers this is a "beggar for alms" (piṇḍapātiko), just as there are those who live on *bādara* fruits or those who live on millet (*sāmākiko*). A "beggar for alms" is simply one whose food is alms-food, just as...
"Bhaddo" means auspicious (*bhaddaka*). "Breaking apart" (*avakhaṇḍana*) means severing; it is the non-occurrence [of an action] without interruption.

By way of its negation, "non-breaking apart" (*anavakhaṇḍana*) means non-severing, that is, occurrence without interruption. "Together with the stepping" (*saha apadānena*) means together with non-breaking apart.

The term "with stepping" (*sapadāna*) is used to show that "stepping" (*pada*) functions as an adverbial modifier of the action, and furthermore, to indicate the locus where that non-breaking apart occurs.
"It is said that they consume it without breaking [the meal] up," so it is stated.

"In one sitting" means in a single session of sitting, uninterrupted by any other posture. Regarding the phrase "alms-food in a bowl," here the specific instance (*vatthubheda*) is intended, not the general category (*sāmañña*).
And showing that the particle *eva* is indicated by elision (*luttaniddiṭṭha*), he says: "only in a single bowl."

Showing that this is an explanatory exposition (niddesa) formed by eliding the latter member of the compound, he said: "having applied the designation 'alms-bowl and alms-food' to the taking of alms in the bowl.
This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well.
"After the meal" (pacchābhattaṃ) means precisely the food obtained after the invitation (pavāraṇā). This is because the particle *khalu* expresses the sense of negation (*paṭisedha*).
Taking the negative particle (*na*) as having the same meaning as that [term], he said, "not one who eats after the meal.

The domain of the training rule is prohibited by the training rule itself; that which is not its domain is precisely the domain of the undertaking. Therefore, he said, "of one for whom eating leftover food has been prohibited by way of such an undertaking.
Dwelling in the open air is *abbhokāsa*. Dwelling in a charnel ground is *susāna*.
The entire passage beginning with "he would have that virtue" (taṃ sīlaṃ assa) should be stated; thus he says, "the same method applies.
"As spread" (yathāsanthataṃ) means as it was originally spread out, just as it was first indicated.
For he accepts it without rejecting it by saying, "This is full of bugs and emits a foul odor," and so forth. Therefore he says, "This is for you," etc. "Lying down" (sayanaṃ) refers to reclining.
"By each respective undertaking" means by each respective undertaking of such factors as the refuse-rag-wearer's practice (*paṃsukūlikaṅga*);

"because of having shaken off the defilements" means because of having destroyed the defilements; the meaning is that, by way of those factors, evil states such as craving and clinging have been abandoned.
Those very things by which there is the shaking off of defilements are intended here as the "factors of the ascetic monk" (*dhuta-aṅga*), and no others.

“Whatever [vows] there may be, or by another, for one who has shaken off [defilements] (dhuta)” — this meaning is thus established in substance. By the phrase “knowledge is their factor,” he clarifies that knowledge preceded their undertaking.
“By way of practice” means by way of the right practice of virtue (sīla) and so forth.
It is called an “undertaking” (samādāna) because one undertakes by means of it; it is the volition (cetanā) occurring by way of undertaking. These have that as their characteristic.
These are the characteristics of volition as undertaking.
And this is also stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Because it is the most effective factor in the act of undertaking, the associated states are shown by way of its instrumentality.”
The volition of undertaking is the grasping; because it is rooted in that, the volition of maintaining is also indeed a *dhutaṅga*.
Greed (*loluppa*) is the conduct of craving (*taṇhācāra*) in the sense of the violent plundering of wholesome things, whether by oneself or through another;

since their function is to destroy that greed, they have the function of destroying greed. For this very reason, they stand forth by way of being free from greed, or they cause that freedom from greed to stand forth.

They have the manifestation of being free from greed and delusion. They have the noble Dhamma as their proximate cause (*padatthāna*), meaning they have the true Dhamma such as pure virtue (*sīla*) and so forth as their proximate cause.

The statement "they must be undertaken only in the presence of the Blessed One" is said for the purpose of ensuring there is no interruption in between, just as one who has made a promise in the presence of a king must absolutely not deceive his dependents regarding that matter. [This applies] in the presence of others...
The same principle applies to undertaking [the training] as well. "Of one belonging to a single collection" means belonging to one of the five collections, such as the *Dīghanikāya* and so forth.

"Of a commentator-master" means of one for whom the lineage of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) alone is particularly well-mastered. "In this case" refers to when the undertaking has been successfully established by oneself.
Regarding the story of the elder brother's desire for the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*): it is said that this elder was a perpetual sitter (*nesajjika*).
No one knew of this. Then one day, seeing him sitting on the back of his bed at night by the flash of lightning, the other asked, "Venerable sir, why do you remain in a sitting posture?
The Elder, out of a desire for the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) of fewness of wishes, lay down immediately and afterwards undertook the practice; such is the account as it has come down.
1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Refuse-Rag-Wearer’s Practice (Paṃsukūlikaṅga) 24.

Regarding the phrase "a robe given by a householder": it should be understood that here, even though they are ascetics, monks are included within the category of "householders" by virtue of being recipients of gifts.
A "householder’s robe" may be one that has been set aside with the thought, "A renunciant will take this."
However, the inclusion of the word "giving" (*dāna*) is not for the purpose of excluding such things as "garments given by householders. Regarding the phrase "by one or another":
first, let it be that something is undertaken (*samādinna*) by means of a statement of undertaking; but how can it be so by means of a statement of prohibition?
Because it is implied by the sense (*atthato*). Just as when it is said, "Devadatta does not eat during the day," it follows by implication that "he eats at night."
It follows as a matter of course that for him there is no maintenance of the body without food;

likewise here, when the monk has rejected a robe-gift from a householder, the acceptance of other robes follows as a matter of course, for there is no maintenance within the Dispensation without a robe.

This is the method of practice regarding the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice (*paṃsukūlika-aṅga*), according to the rule beginning with "one who has undertaken the ascetic virtue" (*samādinnadhutaṅgena*). [A robe] obtained in a charnel ground...
“From a charnel ground. Since that [cloth] has fallen there because it was discarded by someone, it is therefore called “fallen in a charnel ground.
The same should be understood for [the cloth] from a shop as well. The Tālaveḷimagga is a certain street in Mahāgāma; some say it was in Anurādhapura.
It is called *ḍaḍḍhappadesa* because a portion of it was burnt; [this refers to] a cloth. On the road.
They say that what has been dropped for many days may be taken up. Others say it is when it has been dropped for two or three days.
"Having waited a little" means having let some time pass. Even if it has been blown away by the wind, because it is like something dropped through the owners' forgetfulness, it is said:
"It is permissible to take it if one does not see the owners. Therefore, it should be taken after waiting a short while.

That which is given with the thought, "We give it to the Saṅgha," and that which is obtained by way of begging for cloth—starting from the time it is obtained—it is said, "that is not *paṃsukūla*," in order to remove the doubt as to whether or not it might be "an ascetic's robe" (*samaṇacīvara*).
For it is not included among any of the twenty-three sources of origin (*uppattiṭṭhāna*). Now, by this same occasion, regarding that which is given to a monk...

Regarding "rag-robe that has reached the [proper] characteristics" (*lakkhaṇapatta-paṃsukūla*), the passage beginning with "even in the case of what is given to a monk" (*bhikkhudattiyepi*) was stated in order to show the distinction between the superior and the inferior types thereof.

In that context, "given after having been assigned" means that when those giving to the Saṅgha or a group (*gaṇa*) assign a robe according to the seniority of the rains-residence (*vassaga*) and give it to the monks;
"lodging-robe" (*senāsanacīvara*) refers to a robe [obtained] after having had a lodging constructed, thinking, "In this lodging..."
“Let them enjoy it during the spring,” [he said regarding] the robe-cloth that had been given.

That is not a *paṃsukūla* (rag-robe) because it lacks the status of a *paṃsukūla* for the reasons previously stated, and because it was given after having been formally accepted (*gāhetvā*). Therefore he said:
