“A *paṃsukūla* is only that which is given without having been formally accepted. In that case as well—that is, even regarding what is given by a monk without having been formally accepted—the monk who gives the robe-cloth...

Because there is respect and reverence in both cases—both in the receiving of what has been obtained and in the giving—and because these are absent in the case of what is given by a monk (*bhikkhudattiya*), the purity of one side, the purity of both sides, and the lack of deficiency [of the gift] occur. To show this meaning, it was said: "That which by the donors...
and so forth; the intention is that it is "given by the ascetic" after having been placed at the base of his feet. Of whom...

"Of anyone" (*kassaci*) means of any one among those such as the *ukkaṭṭha* (strict) and others. "By choice" (*ruciyā*) means by inclination. "By approval" (*khantiyā*) means by the approval arising from contemplation (*nijjhānakkhanti*).

"The existence of a practice corresponding to the dependence" (*nissayānurūpapaṭipattisabbhāvo*) means the presence of a practice that conforms to whichever of the four dependencies (*nissaya*)—as stated by the teacher immediately after the full ordination—one has promised for oneself. "Absence of the suffering of guarding" (*ārakkhadukkhābhāvo*)...
The absence of suffering regarding the protection of robes is due to the fact that rag-robe-wearing (*paṃsukūlacīvara*) is not an object of greed.
The absence of craving for enjoyment is due to its specifically coarse nature. "Inspiring confidence" (*pāsādikatā*) means being a cause for inspiring faith in others.

The accomplishment of the fruits of fewness of wishes and so forth is because the maintenance of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) must be brought about by those very qualities, such as fewness of wishes. Regarding the ascetic qualities (*dhutadhamma*):
"Taking it up and practicing it" is said to mean "for the sake of accomplishing right practice further on"; thus it is called "the intensification of right practice.
"For the destruction of Māra’s army" means for the striking down and the dispersal of Māra and his host.
One who is restrained and self-controlled in body, speech, and mind is a *yati*, a monk. That rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*) which was worn by the Honored One of the World—
"Who would not wear it?"—the construction is: "Since the rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*) was worn by the World-Honored One (*lokagaru*), who would not wear it?
This is because the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* possess an absolute state of mutual connection.

"They recall their promise" means they recall the promise given in the presence of the Saṅgha headed by the preceptor (*ācariya*) in the ordination hall (*upasampadamāḷa*), saying, "Yes, Venerable Sir."
Thus ends the commentary on the discourse concerning the practice of wearing rag-robes (paṃsukūlikaṅga). 2.

Commentary on the Discourse Concerning the Practice of Wearing Only Three Robes (tecīvarikaṅga): 25. "A fourth robe" means a fourth robe suitable for use as an undergarment or an upper garment; this is the intended meaning, [referring] to the shoulder-cloth (aṃsakāsāva).

Because it is not to be rejected. Regarding the phrase "by way of a particular expression," what is to be said there has already been stated according to the method explained above. The word *yāva* (as long as) should be connected to each of the following:
"as long as he is not able," "as long as he does not obtain," and "as long as it does not succeed. "Does not succeed" means it is not accomplished.
"There is no fault in the condition being set aside" refers to the fault of defilement regarding the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) of non-storing of provisions.
There is none. "Nearby" means in a place close to the robe. At the time of dyeing, the *kāsāya* being used is the dyeing *kāsāya*.
A "spread that remains where it is" (*tatraṭṭhaka-paccattharaṇa*) is one belonging to oneself or another, which has been determined as a spread for a lodging.
"The shoulder *kāsāya* is a requisite cloth; thus it is a spread, the shoulder *kāsāya*."
"It is said in the Commentary that even these two [robes], though kept as extra robes (*atirekacīvara*), do not cause a breach of the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*).

However, it is not permitted to keep them; because they are only authorized at the time of dyeing, for one who observes the practice of wearing only three robes (*tecīvarika*), they are not permitted by way of constant use.
"Shoulder-cloth" (*aṃsakāsāva*) means the saffron-colored cloth that should be placed upon the shoulder. "By way of body-protection" (*kāyaparihārikena*)...
"Merely by protecting the body from the perils of wind, heat, and so forth. "Having taken up" means having indeed accepted [the requisites].

"Little undertaking" means having few duties. "By using what is allowable in moderation" refers to the fact that although many robes are permitted—such as sitting cloths and various accessory garments—one remains content with the mere three robes.
"Together with bowl and sandals" means possessing a bowl and sandals; like a bird, one possesses wings.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the practice of wearing only three robes.
3. Commentary on the Section Concerning the Practice of Eating Only Almsfood (Piṇḍapātikaṅga). 26.
Regarding the phrase "extra acquisitions": this refers to acquisitions other than the food obtained through alms-gathering as described by the expression, "subsisting on the food of alms."
"Extra gain" means such things as a meal for the Saṅgha (*saṅghabhatta*). A meal to be given to the entire Saṅgha is a *saṅghabhatta*.
A meal to be given after designating a few specific bhikkhus is an *uddesabhatta*. A meal to be given on one day of a fortnight is a *pakkhika* (fortnightly meal).
A meal to be given on every observance day (*uposatha*) is an *uposathika*. On the first day of the lunar half-month...
"Meal to be given on the first day of the lunar fortnight" (pāṭipadika-bhatta). "Meal to be given for the sake of a monastery" (vihāra-bhatta).
"Meal to be given by setting it aside specifically at the head household" (dhura-bhatta). "Meal to be given by rotation by village residents and others" (vāraka-bhatta). By the word "etc.
in the phrase "‘Take the meal for the Saṅgha,’ etc.," one includes meals designated for specific purposes (uddesa-bhatta) and so forth. To partake of...
"It is allowable" because it is stated as part of the sequence of alms-food (bhikkhā-pariyāya). It refers to non-material tokens associated with medicine and so forth;

they also say these are "except for what is to be consumed at the proper time. "Even cooked food prepared in the monastery": when lay devotees prepare food right there in the monastery by cooking it themselves, thinking, "We shall give it to all the venerable ones," that is allowable even for those who subsist on alms-food (piṇḍapātika). "Having brought [it]" means...
Having taken the bowl and brought it from the house. "He sat down on that day" means he sat down by accepting [the invitation] from those who said, "Venerable sir, do not wander for alms;
let alms-food be brought right here to the monastery. "The happiness of dwelling in Seṭṭhi-vihāra" means the happiness of living independent of others.
"The Noble Lineage" refers to a discourse on the Dhamma connected with the *Ariyavaṃsa Sutta*. "The flavor of the Dhamma" means...
It has the flavor of joy and so forth associated with the Dhamma.
By relying on the strength of one's legs, it crushes laziness through the pursuit of almsfood.

Through the method described in the verse beginning, "Just as a bee [goes to a flower]," it possesses a pure livelihood by way of seeking food. It belongs constantly to one who enters among the houses.
The fulfillment of the practice of the training rules (*sekhiyadhamma*) consists in the proper performance of such acts as going with well-covered [body].

Through moderation in receiving alms and by not living in close association with householders, one is not supported by others. By taking only a very small amount of alms from each family, one performs an act of assistance to others.
By remaining steadfast in this final livelihood, pride is abandoned. For it has been said: "This is the end..."

"Monks, this is the foremost among ways of livelihood, namely, the alms-gathering life," and so forth. Because one sustains oneself with mixed alms-food, there is the prevention of craving for flavors.
Because one does not accept invitations, there is non-offensiveness regarding the training rules concerning eating in groups and so on.
Because it proceeds unimpededly, it is "four-directional" (cātuddisa) in the sense of wandering in all four directions. Thus, "one's livelihood is purified."
His livelihood is purified. "Self-supporting" (*attabharassa*) means one who supports oneself through requisites that are easily obtained and free from blame regarding the self.
For that very reason, because of living alone, he does not nourish others such as co-residents; thus he is "not nourishing others.
By both these phrases, it is meant that he wanders about with a robe that merely serves the body and alms-food that merely serves the belly.
It demonstrates a life of fewness of wishes, being easy to support, supreme contentment, and serenity. Regarding the phrase "even the gods envy such a one":

for such a person—who is exceedingly tranquil due to the extreme tranquility of their bodily, verbal, and mental actions, and who is endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection—the gods, such as Sakka and others, [envy] the alms-collecting bhikkhu who is ever-mindful.
Even the gods envy and long for him; they show respect, generating great esteem for his virtues such as moral discipline, let alone human beings.
"If he is not dependent on gain, honor, and fame" means that he does not desire them.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the alms-food-eater’s practice (*piṇḍapātikaṅga*).
4. Explanation of the Section on the Practice of Begging from Door to Door (Sapadānacārikaṅga) 27.
"By this" means by the practice of begging from door to door. "At an earlier time" means at the very early part of the day.

"An unpleasant place" refers to a location that is difficult to enter due to dangers and other such obstacles. "In front" means in front of one who is walking along the street, even before having entered the house.
"The place where the bowl was dropped" refers to the spot where the bowl was dropped at the door of Sakka’s house, where he stood having manifested himself as a weaver in the weavers’ street.
On that day, the one who practices the alms-round of the highest limit (ukkhaṭṭha-piṇḍapātika) does not sit waiting for alms;
therefore, it conforms to that practice. Because there is no fixed habit of visiting any particular family, there is an absence of familiarity.
Being constantly like a newcomer among families; being like the moon due to a mind that is unattached everywhere and a gentle disposition;
the abandoning of stinginess therein through the absence of a possessive mind toward families; equal compassion because of the lack of partiality in one’s desire for their welfare;
and the dangers associated with householders, such as being entangled in socializing with families. "Not delighting in invitations" refers to [the refusal of] formal invitations.

By not accepting invitations. "By bringing [food]" means by the bringing of alms-food. "Wandering at will" means wandering according to one's own preference. Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the practice of wandering from house to house in succession (*sapadānacārika*).
5. Commentary on the Section Concerning the Practice of Eating at a Single Sitting (*ekāsanika*).
28. “Eating at various seats” means eating at many seats; the meaning is the consumption of food while sitting in separate sessions rather than eating while remaining in a single session.
“Suitable” means appropriate or not to be disregarded. “It is proper to perform the duties” means it is fitting to perform the duties.
What is called a “duty” (vatta) is simply that which must be done for those who occupy a position of respect. In this regard:
However, in order to show the method of practice, he stated the Elder’s teaching beginning with, “One should guard either the seat or the food,” and so forth.
Its meaning is as follows: one should guard the seat of a bhikkhu who eats at a single sitting;
that is to say, one must not rise until the conclusion of the meal, for fear of breaking the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*). Or, one should guard the food, for fear of breaking the ascetic practice.
The meaning is that one must rise while the food is still unbegun, before one begins to eat.

Since these two conditions are absent here, the intention is that the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) of performing the duties (*vattakaraṇa*) is not maintained. Therefore he said, "And this," and so forth.
By the phrase "only for the purpose of medicine," [it is implied] that even ghee and the like are [permissible] only by way of their use as medicine.

This shows that they are fit [to eat]. "Freedom from illness" (*appābādhatā*) means health. "Freedom from affliction" (*appātaṅkatā*) means a life free from hardship and the absence of bodily suffering.
"Lightness" (*lahuṭṭhāna*) refers to the body's agility in movement. "Strength" (*bala*) refers to physical strength. "Comfortable dwelling" (*phāsuvihāra*) means a state of ease.
All of this is a phrase intended to preclude the physical disturbances that arise as a consequence of eating too much. "Ailments" (*rujā*) refers to diseases.
"Not merely for the sake of work" means that he does not neglect his own practice of yoga before or after the meal;
the intention is that this is because he is not preoccupied with eating frequently and because he is free from illness.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the one-sessioner’s practice.
6. Explanation of the Discussion on the Alms-Bowl Practice (Pattapiṇḍikaṅga) 29.
It is permissible to eat without finding it repulsive; the intention is that there may even be no grasping at what has been eaten as repulsive.
One should take only a moderate amount; thus, having taken much while thinking, "I am taking only one bowlful," [one would be at fault].
It should not be abandoned. "Dispelling craving for various flavors" means the dispelling of craving for food consisting of various flavors.
One who has desire for this or that various flavor found in various dishes is called *atriccha*; the state of being such is *atricchatā*, and the abandonment of that *atricchatā* [is the goal].
[The phrase] "seeing only the purpose in food" refers to the absence of greed for unmixed, various flavors.
By not doing so, one merely shows the purpose for which food was permitted by the Teacher.
For one who takes various condiments from separate vessels, there may be distracted eating due to the mental preoccupation with each respective spot;

however, this is not the case for one who perceives everything as contained within a single bowl. Thus it is said, "eating without distraction. "With eyes cast down" refers to the mindfulness regarding the bowl.
"With eyes cast downwards. "Should partake" means: should be able to partake. Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the practice of eating from the alms-bowl (*pattapiṇḍika-aṅga*).
7. Commentary on the section concerning the practice of not eating after the meal time (*khalupacchābhattika-aṅga*).
30. "Atirittabhojana" (leftover food) refers to that food which has been brought to one who is eating; it is called leftover food because of the refusal of that [food].
One should not eat it again after having had it made permissible (*kappiya*), because this ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) has that very thing as its object.
Therefore he said: "This is its procedure. "In whatever food" means in whatever food being eaten. That very same...
He eats, not anything else. An offense due to eating what is not left over is an "anatirittabhojana-offense";

being far from that is non-transgression. Gluttony (*odarikatta*) is the state of being voracious (*ghasmarabhāva*), the filling of the belly; the absence of that is because one sustains oneself even with a single morsel.
Non-storing of worldly things (*nirāmisasannidhitā*) is because one does not eat what has been stored. Furthermore, it is by way of seeking through the act of seeking.

It does not lead to weariness. The production of the growth of qualities such as contentment through those things that promote self-effacement is "the production of the growth of qualities such as contentment.
This refers to the practice of eating only after the meal has been prepared.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the practice of eating only after the meal.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Forest-Dweller’s Practice (Āraññikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā) 31.

Regarding the statement, “Having abandoned a dwelling within a village, one should cause the dawn to rise in the forest,” the passage beginning with “therein, together with its precincts” is commenced in order to show the nature of both the village and the forest. Therein, because it is included within the village...

Regarding the "lodging within the vicinity of a village" (*gāmantasenāsana*), it is stated that "the village itself is the lodging within the vicinity of a village. The connection is that even any caravan is called a "village.

"Indakhīla" refers to the threshold stones. "Of that" refers to the range of a clod-throw. The definition of the forest according to the Vinaya method is found in the *Pārājika* on taking what is not given.
For therein, in the complete inclusion of the places from which theft may occur, it says: "from a village or from a forest."

To show that these two are distinct and unmixed, it is said: “except for the village and its precincts,” and so forth. For in common worldly usage, the precincts of a village are considered part of the village itself.
However, from the perspective of ultimate analysis (*nippariyāya*), a place separated from a village is indeed forest;
thus, in the Abhidhamma it is said: “Having gone out beyond the threshold post of the village, all this is forest. This is according to the method of the Suttantas.
In the *Āraññaka-sikkhāpada*, the phrase "at least five hundred bow-lengths" is stated with reference to a forest-dwelling (*āraññika*) bhikkhu.
For he is not described in the Vinaya discourse as "a forest-dweller because of living in the forest" in the sutta that says, "one who dwells in the forest, in a remote lodging.
And since this is an exegesis of the sutta, here in all cases the explanation of the sutta alone is the authority. Therefore, it is only what is found there [in the sutta] that applies.
Showing that the characteristics must be grasped, he stated the method of measuring with the words, "With that teacher’s bow set up," and so forth.
For it is for this very reason that the method of the Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā alone is stated here as the authority.
"From here and there along the path" means he blocks the small paths here and there. "By one purified by the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)" means by one intent on purifying the ascetic practices.

Regarding the time limit as it has been defined: for one who is strenuous (*ukkaṭṭha*), there are three seasons; for one who is moderate (*majjhima*), two; for one who is gentle (*muduka*), one season.

Even in that case, the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) is not broken because of the presence of the resolve (*saussāhattā*). It is said that the ascetic practice is broken by the slackening of the mind with the thought, "I shall go after lying down.
By attending to the perception of the forest (*araññasaññaṃ manasikaronto*), one thinks: "I shall dwell in a secluded abode."
"Physical seclusion should be made as beneficial as it has been obtained"—because of the presence of such attention, it is said: "He is capable...
[and so on] ...to guard [it]. The mind of this forest-dweller is not distracted because [sense objects] do not come within its range.
He becomes free from fear through familiarity with seclusion. He abandons attachment to life precisely by dwelling in the forest, which is full of many perils, due to the fear of death.
“By keeping at a distance”: because of the absence of contact with people, he relishes and experiences the flavor of the bliss of seclusion (*paviveka*). “Gratifying” means pleasing.

Because the forest-dweller’s practice is like a vehicle by virtue of its being the foundation for seclusion through practicing according to the instructions, it is said that he has “the remaining ascetic qualities as his weapons”;
the meaning is that he has the remaining ascetic virtues (*dhuta-dhamma*) as his weapons.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the forest-dweller’s practice (*āraññika-aṅga*).
9. Commentary on the section concerning the tree-root dweller’s practice (*rukkhamūlika-aṅga*):
32. “A roofed place” (*channa*) means covered with tiles, thatch, and so forth; the meaning is a dwelling (*āvasatha*). A “boundary-tree” (*sīmantarikarukkha*)...
There was a tree standing on the boundary between the kingdoms of two kings. For there, the military forces of those kings would approach and engage in intermittent battles;
likewise, bandits and highwaymen would gather there and would not allow the bhikkhu to sit in peace.
As for the cetiya-tree, it was a tree highly esteemed by people as being "presided over by deities," and thus it was approached by those who had come to worship it.
It is not secluded from people. A "sapwood tree" (niyyāsa-rukkha) refers to trees such as the *sajja* tree. A "bats' tree" (vagguli-rukkha) is one frequented by bats.
Trees at the boundary of a village and the like are fraught with dangers and offer little opportunity for seclusion; thus he said, "having avoided these trees.
"Falling leaves" (paṇṇasaṭa) refers to leaves fallen from a tree. One should sit in a concealed place for the sake of being a "tree-root dweller" (*rukkhamūlika*).
For the purpose of concealment. Dwelling in a roofed structure may also be for the sake of listening to the Dhamma and so forth.
Therefore it was said: "as soon as dawn has been known to have arisen.
"By seeing the frequent change in the leaves of trees" means by the constant change in the leaves of trees, or in the trees themselves.
By seeing its momentary dissolution. "Of stinginess regarding lodgings and delight in work" means of the states of being stingy about one's residence and taking pleasure in new construction.
"By deities" means by tree-deities; for they too dwell in trees, residing in celestial mansions situated within trees. "This tree as well" refers to co-residency.
"Praised" means commended by such phrases as "even though it is small. "The lodging at the foot of a tree..."
"Depending on [this], one goes forth"—thus it is called "dependence. [The leaves] are green when young, blue-black in their middle stage, and pale-yellow when old.
They fall due to the process of withering. Seeing them in this way, one directly dispels and abandons the perception of permanence regarding the young leaves;
the perception of impermanence becomes firmly established for him. This is because the Blessed One’s birth, enlightenment, turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, and final passing away—
Since they were born at the very roots of trees, it is therefore said: "The inheritance of the Buddhas is the root of a tree.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the practice of dwelling at the root of a tree.
10. Commentary on the Section Concerning the Practice of Dwelling in the Open Air.
33. When it is said, "I reject the foot of a tree," the covered place is not thereby rejected; therefore, it is said, "I reject both the covered place and the foot of a tree.
For the undertaking of a dhutaṅga succeeds only through the total rejection of its opposite, and not otherwise.
By the phrase "for the sake of hearing the Dhamma," [it is implied that] even by one who is preaching the Dhamma...
On days such as the Uposatha, it is permissible for one who has been requested by others to enter a hut for the purpose of protecting their minds while they listen;
however, after preaching the Dhamma, he should depart into the open air. The same rule applies to one who dwells at the foot of a tree (*rukkhamūlika*).
"For the sake of the Uposatha" means for the performance of the Uposatha ritual. "Reciting" means giving the recitation to others. "Causing to recite" means...

By one who is receiving the recitation himself: "A *sāla* tree standing in the middle of the road" means a *sāla* tree that must be entered directly without leaving the road, as is the case in the island of Sīhaḷa.

It is not permissible to go with speed because it is improper; the intention is that one should wait until the end of the rains before departing, for as long as that, there is no breach of the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*).
"Inside a tree" means at the foot of the tree. "A mountain region" refers to a place on a mountain similar to a mountain cave (*pabbhāra*).
"With an uncovered boundary" means that the boundary above has not been made by way of a roof, so that rainwater does not enter within;
however, if rainwater enters within a mountain cave, it is considered merely an open space (*abbhokāsa*), and therefore one may enter there.
It is permissible. A "branch-pavilion" (sākhāmaṇḍapa) is a pavilion with a sparse roof made of tree branches. A "stool-cloth" (pīṭhapaṭa) is a coarse, stiff garment.

The intention is that the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is broken at the moment of entering [the village], except in cases such as those mentioned regarding mountain slopes and so forth. "Having known" means:
having entered and sat down under a covered tree root for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma or other such reasons, [he thinks] "now the dawn is rising."

Having understood this: even at the foot of a tree, there may still be some degree of comfort in dwelling; thus, there might be the obstacle of a dwelling (*āvāsa-palibodha*) preceded by attachment there.
However, it is not the case that the benefit of severing the obstacle of a dwelling is stated here only in relation to the open air (*abbhokāsa*).

"Appropriateness for the praise" means being suitable for the state of non-attachment (*anālaya-bhāva*) in accordance with the praise expressed as "homeless" (*aniketa*). "Freedom from attachment" (*nissaṅgata*).
Non-attachment there arises precisely from the absence of possession of a dwelling place.
He is "four-faceted" (*cātuddisa*) because he lacks such reflections as, "There is no place to live in this direction; therefore, it is not possible to go there.
He is "like a deer" (*migabhūta*) because, through the absence of possession, he has become like a deer. "Dependent" (*sita*) means supported. "Experiences" (*vindati*) means obtains.
Thus ends the commentary on the discourse regarding the practice of dwelling in the open air. 11.

Commentary on the Discourse Regarding the Practice of Dwelling in a Cemetery. 34. "Not a cemetery" means a non-cemetery. The particle *na* has a negative sense here; it refers to a place of residence devoid of the characteristics of a cemetery.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Not there" means that one should not dwell even in a place merely designated as a "charnel ground" (*susāna*).
For the defining characteristic of a charnel ground is not established by name alone. Therefore he said, "For not," and so forth. However, from the time the body has been cremated... [etc] ...

it is indeed a charnel ground because it has attained the status of a charnel ground by the mere fact of having been a place where a corpse lay. For a place where a corpse lies is called a "charnel ground."
In order to show that one who dwells in a charnel ground (sosānika) must be one of few duties and light livelihood, it was said: "But by one dwelling there... and so forth.
"Heavy" means difficult to maintain. To demonstrate that very quality of being difficult to maintain, it was said: "Therefore... and so forth.
In that context, "for the sake of warding off dangers that have arisen" refers to the fact that "a charnel ground is indeed a place frequented by humans in secret."
Thieves—both those who have committed the crime and those who have not—may come there;
if, upon seeing the owners of the goods among the thieves, they abandon the goods near the monk and flee, people might seize the monk, thinking, "He is a thief," and beat him.
Therefore, in the monastery, one should inform the senior elder of the Saṅgha or the royal official appointed by the king in the alms-village of one's status as a cemetery-dweller.
Having made it known that there is no such danger or any other peril, one should dwell heedfully.

To show that even when walking, if the cremation ground is not directly in front of one, one should still cast one's gaze upon it for the sake of generating a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), it is said: "looking at the cremation ground with a sidelong glance."
One should go by a path not usually traveled in order to keep one’s status as a charnel-ground dweller from being revealed. Regarding the "object":
even during the day, one should define the object in that cemetery, noting things such as, "This is an anthill; this is a tree; this is a stump," and so on.
"Terrifying" refers to anthills and the like that produce fear. One should not wander near [such things] with anything such as a clod of earth or a stone.
They should be struck. "Sesame flour" refers to sesame pulp. "Meat-mixed rice" means rice mixed with meat.
By the word "etc. in "molasses etc.," one includes solid cakes such as sesame balls and the like.
"One should not enter a household" means that because the household has been perfumed by the smoke of spirits and because it is haunted by *pisācas*, one must not enter its interior. Daily...
“*Chavaḍāho* (corpse-burning) means *dhuvaḍāho* (constant burning). For those who have died, going there to weep every day is *dhuvarodanaṃ* (constant weeping).

‘In the manner stated’ means in the manner stated [in the commentary]: ‘from the time it has been cremated onwards. Because it was desired that ‘it is permissible to withdraw during the last watch of the night,’ the reciters of the Aṅguttara Nikāya say: ‘on a day when one has not gone to the charnel ground.’”
By constantly visiting the charnel ground and observing the cemetery, one attains mindfulness of death; from that very practice, one dwells in heedfulness.
Therein, by seeing the discarded corpse of the dead, one masters the sign of foulness; from that very practice, sensual lust is dispelled.
By frequently observing the impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome nature of the body, one constantly perceives the true character of the physical body.

From the acquisition of mindfulness of death, there arises an abundance of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). By seeing those afflicted by disease, those worn out by old age, and the dead, one abandons the intoxication of health, youth, and life.
Through the overcoming of both small and great fears, there comes the endurance of terrors and alarms.
For one who is stirred with urgency, appropriate exertion (*yoniso padhāna*) becomes possible; thus [it leads to] non-human beings...
The state of being difficult to honor. "Even when fallen asleep" means even while dreaming; this is the intended meaning.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the charnel-ground dweller (sosānikaṅga).
12. Commentary on the section concerning the one who uses whatever seat is provided (yathāsanthatikaṅga).
35. Regarding the taking of lodgings: having caused others to rise up, taking [the lodging] oneself; weighing it out by thinking, "This is beautiful, this is not beautiful";
and looking [around]—these constitute greed for lodgings (*senāsanaloluppa*). It should be said that one "should be satisfied" (*tuṭṭhabba*) means one ought to be contented.

Because of being at the edge of the monastery, or because it is far away, or because it is too close to places where many people gather and so forth, one is not permitted to ask; even by asking, for him...
Because of the defilement of the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*). "To look" means to gaze with a sense of greed (*loluppa*).

"If it does not please him" means that if, for one who dwells wherever he is assigned (*yathāsanthatika*), that lodging as it was received does not please him due to its lack of comfort—provided there is no illness—and if, in the absence of soft bedding, he abandons what was received to take another lodging, that is greed (*loluppa*). For one of medium [capacity]...
Going to see [the sick person] is the highest form of inquiry. When all have been made to rise, there is no need for further speech.

By not making even those who require attendance rise, one demonstrates a desire for the welfare of one’s fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*). Through that, there is conformity with abiding in compassion (*karuṇā-vihāra*).

By not making distinctions between the beautiful and the ugly, there is the relinquishing of conceptualizations regarding the inferior and the superior. By that, there is conformity with the characteristic of being "such-like" (*tādi-lakkhaṇa*).
From this very fact comes the abandoning of attachment and aversion. "Closing the door" refers to not providing an opening [for further needs].

"Content with whatever bedding is available" means a state of delighting in the lodging exactly as it is taken up and exactly as it is assigned. Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the practice of being content with whatever bedding is available.
13. Explanation of the Discussion on the Practice of Always Sitting (Nesajjikanga) 36.

"Reclining" (seyya) refers to the reclining posture as its defining characteristic. By the very negation of that [reclining], beds, mattresses, and so forth—which serve that purpose—are already excluded.
Furthermore, by the term "one who always sits" (nesajjiko), lying down is prohibited, and by means of sitting...

Because the meaning intended here is "one whose nature is to dwell thus," only lying down (*seyyā*) is the counterpart in this context, not the others, since they are not undesirable [here] and are impossible [to practice]. For it is a posture belonging to the side of laziness (*kosajja*) that is intended here as the counterpart, not the others.
Moreover, it is not possible to maintain oneself or to engage in such practice by sitting alone, without standing and walking.
The bed is its opposite. Therefore he said, “But by that,” and so forth. One should not walk about;
rather, one should remain seated all night, thinking, “I am a sitter. For a body supported by a different posture is capable of sustained attention (*manasikāra*).
It is “five-limbed” because it consists of these five parts: four legs and a back-rest. By means of the four supports...

Others say that the "five-limbed" posture includes the use of a back-rest. To refute the misconception that there is no difference between one who dwells in the sitting posture (*nesajjika*)—resting as he pleases on both sides and on his back—and one who does not so dwell, the Elder Abhaya was cited [as an example], for it is said:
"The elder, having become a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), attained final Nibbāna."
"Upacchedana" (cutting off) means that by which something is cut off; thus, it should be understood as the state of being the most effective instrument for cutting off the bond.
Sitting is suitable for application to all meditation subjects because it belongs to the side of neither laxity nor agitation. For that very reason, it possesses a graceful posture.
It is conducive to the exertion of energy and appropriate for the yoking of balanced energy. Precisely for that reason, it is conducive to right practice.
*Anubrūhanatā* means strengthening. *Paṇidhāya* means having set aside. *Tanuṃ* refers to the upper part of the body. *Vikampeti* means to move;
the intended meaning is that one causes frustration of one's wishes. *Vataṃ* refers to the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*).
Thus ends the commentary on the discussion of the practice of sitting (nesajjikaṅga).
Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discussion of the Dhutaṅgas: 37.

With respect to those in training (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana), the dhutaṅgas may be wholesome (kusala); with respect to those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), they may be indeterminate (abyākata).

In this regard, those in training and worldlings undertake the dhutaṅgas for the purpose of fulfilling their practice, while those whose taints are destroyed undertake them for the purpose of dwelling in comfort.
They avoid [this]. The statement "even unwholesome [action] is a *dhutaṅga*" intends that there is the practice of a *dhutaṅga* even with an unwholesome mind.

That is not correct; for that unwholesome mind by which one who has gone forth becomes a forest-dweller (*āraññika*) does not constitute a *dhutaṅga*. Why? Because it lacks the defining characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*).
For that which belongs to a person who has shaken off (*dhuta*) the defilements (*kilesa*) by shaking them off—[is what constitutes a *dhutaṅga*].

The status of being a factor (*aṅga*) belongs either to knowledge (*ñāṇa*) or to volition (*cetanā*), and that is not possible among unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*). Therefore, let those who merely dwell in the forest and so forth be called "forest-dwellers" (*āraññika*) and the like for that reason alone;
however, they do not possess the "factors of the forest-dweller" (*āraññikaṅga*) and so on. To show this point, it was said: "We [do not]," etc.
Therein, "these" refers to the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). This was stated previously in the exposition of the etymological meaning (*vacanatthaniddesa*). Not...
Nor does anything unwholesome become called "dhuta" (shaken off) in the sense of shaking off the defilements; this is the intended meaning.
By the first alternative of meaning, it is shown that for a bhikkhu whose limbs are these undertakings, there is no such thing as an "unwholesome dhutaṅga.
Nor does it shake off any unwholesome thing; that is, it does not shake off any evil at all because it lacks an opposite.

If those undertakings were called *dhutaṅgas* by treating that unwholesome knowledge as a factor (*aṅga*) like [the other factors], then by this second alternative interpretation he shows that "there is no unwholesome *dhutaṅga*.
The phrase beginning with "nor is it unwholesome" is the application according to the third alternative interpretation.
The passage beginning with "Therefore" is the conclusion of the very meaning already stated.
This was said with reference to the inhabitants of the Abhayagiri monastery. For they claim that what is called a *dhutaṅga* (ascetic practice) is merely a designation (*paññatti*).
If that were so, since it would not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), there could be neither the meaning of "shaking off" the defilements (*kilesa*) nor the necessity of undertaking them;
thus, their statement contradicts the Canon (*pāḷi*). To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "excluded from the triad of the wholesome" (*kusalattikavinimutta*) was stated.
Therefore, since these faults are difficult to avoid on the side of the "provisional designation" (paññatti), the meaning is that their statement should not be accepted;

rather, the method already explained regarding the side of "volition" (cetanā) alone should be accepted. Since these ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) are included within the first and third categories of the triad of the wholesome (kusalattika), they may be associated with pleasant feeling, or they may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

They may be subject to ripening (*vipākadhammadhammā*), they may be neither ripening nor subject to ripening (*nevavipākanavipākadhammadhammā*), they may be not-clung-to-yet-favorable-to-clinging (*anupādinnupādāniyā*), and they may be undefiled-yet-favorable-to-defilement (*asaṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikā*);
in this way, their inclusion under the remaining sets of three and pairs of terms should be clarified as appropriate.
Granted that every Arahant has shaken off the defilements, yet here [the term *dhuta*] refers to one who has shaken off the defilements by means of practicing the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
One who stands firm, having exhausted the taints (*khīṇāsava*), is intended here as "a person whose defilements have been shaken off" (*dhutakileso puggalo*).

Likewise, in an absolute sense (*nippariyāyena*), the entire Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is the Dhamma that shakes off defilements, especially the Supreme Path (*aggamagga*); but in a figurative sense (*pariyāyena*), it refers to insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*) and so forth.

At its lower limit, it should be understood as the knowledge associated with the volition of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). Having thus shown what is shaken off, the teaching on shaking off (*dhutavāda*) must now be shown.

Since the practitioner of ascetic practices (dhutavāda) is twofold—just as there is one who is "ascetic" (dhuta) by way of the division of ascetic practices, so too there is one who is a "practitioner of ascetic practices" by way of the division of those who profess them—it follows that a tetrad is possible here through these two and their negation. To demonstrate this, it is said:

"There is one who is ascetic," and so forth. *Tayidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is "this [is] that. Regarding the phrase "those called ascetic qualities" (*dhutadhammā nāma*): [it refers to] those things which are the opposites of the cultivation of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).

They are called "ascetic qualities" (*dhutadhammā*) because they are factors that assist the volition of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga-cetanā*), which has acquired the name "ascetic" (*dhuta*) due to its occurrence by way of shaking off evil states.

Because they proceed by way of non-greed for requisites—whether those requisites have been obtained or not—both fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and contentment (*santuṭṭhitā*) are in essence non-greed (*alobha*). [They counteract] the defilements such as greediness (*lolatā*), which are caused by craving for requisites and the like.
Through writing correctly, through cutting [defilements], through the various types of socializing with groups and the like, through association, and through the separation of the mind,
both effacement (*sallekhatā*) and seclusion (*pavivekatā*) follow after these two states— namely, non-greed (*alobha*) and non-delusion (*amoha*)— and are included within them and comprised by them,
because they are specific modes of activity for both of those. By means of these wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), there exists...

"This is the purpose" (*idamatthitā*) refers to that knowledge by which one who has gone forth, having established himself in such things as the refuse-rag-wearer's practice (*paṃsukūlikaṅga*), should act accordingly;
it is that knowledge by which one both undertakes and maintains the ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*) as instructed. Therefore he said: "This-purpose-ness is indeed knowledge.
Regarding "in the cases of objects to be rejected": this refers to householders' robes and so forth, [which are to be avoided] by means of those respective ascetic practices.
Regarding the objects to be rejected: "Lobha" means craving. "Tesveva vā" means precisely upon those objects of rejection.

"Ādīnavapaṭicchādakaṃ" means that which conceals the disadvantages (ādīnava), such as the suffering of guarding [possessions], dependence on others for one's livelihood, fear of thieves, and so forth.

"Anuññātānaṃ" refers to things such as comfortable bedding and coverings that have been permitted by the Teacher for use free from desire and lust. "Paṭisevanamukhena" means by way of their utilization.
"By way of enjoyment" means by way of that deception. "By way of extreme effacement" means by way of the practice of extreme effacement;
the meaning is by way of rejecting even those observances that are considered superior.

He said, "Lust supported by the making of things subtle does not find a footing in the practice that is painful," because: *dukkhāpaṭipadañca*... [and the practice that is painful]... [the rest of the passage follows].

“Dependent on effacement, lust is stilled. Effacement belongs to one who is clearly comprehending; since delusion does not find a footing when there is mindfulness and clear comprehension, it arises from heedfulness.
Thus it is said: “Dependent on effacement, delusion is abandoned by the heedful.
“In this context” means among these ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas). “Therein” means in the forest and at the foot of trees.
"Head-limbs" (*sīsaṅgāni*) means limbs that are like a head; the meaning is that they are "principal limbs" because they are easy to grasp and because no one else can stand between them.
"Unconfused limbs" (*asambhinnaṅgāni*) means they are free from confusion with anything else; what is meant is that they are distinct limbs.
The meditation subject increases for one of lustful temperament, for one of deluded temperament, and also for one of hateful temperament.

The intention is: "for one who practices that particular ascetic practice (dhutaṅga). The meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) declines for one who, due to being delicate, cannot endure the austere practice.
It increases indeed for one of the nature of a Great Man; this is the intention. The meditation subject does not increase for one who lacks the necessary support (upanissaya).
For even a single ascetic practice, in the sense of shaking off the defilements (kilesa), is of the same nature as volition (cetanā).
Therefore he said, "volition of undertaking.

Having stated that there are "forty-two" by way of the individuals who undertake and maintain even the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), [the author] now shows that the maintenance of all thirteen is possible for monks simultaneously: "If..."
The passage beginning with “hī” and so forth has been stated. Therein, it is said: “One is able to enjoy all the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas) simultaneously.
How does one dwelling in the open air possess the tree-root-dweller practice (rukkhamūlikaṅga)?

Because of the statement, “I reject a roofed place; I undertake the tree-root-dweller practice,” the ascetic practice is broken as soon as dawn rises while one is in a roofed place, not when one is in the open air.

Therefore, due to the absence of that cause for division, this [practice] is also conducive to health. Likewise, it should be understood as the "as-it-is-laid-out" factor (*yathāsaṃthataṅga*) because of the absence of greed for lodgings.

The "forest-dweller" factor (*āraññikaṅga*) is prohibited by the training rule regarding leaving the community; the "later-food-refuser" factor (*khalupacchābhattikaṅga*) is prohibited by the training rule against eating food that has not been made "leftover" (*anatiritta-bhojana*).
For when a nun has been invited to eat, one may eat what is made "leftover" (*atiritta*) [only after she has finished].

It is not obtained. The undertaking of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) is for the sake of abandoning greed regarding allowable things (*kappiya*), not regarding unallowable things, because the latter are already prohibited by the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). There are eight [robes] for a bhikkhunī;

this is because the five [robes], including the *saṃkaccika* and the *cīvara*, are included within the category of the three robes (*ticīvara*). "As stated" means as stated for the bhikkhus in the thirteen [ascetic practices].
Because there is no formal legal act (*vinayakamma*) for the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the three robes, the factor of possessing the three robes (*tecīvarika-aṅga*) is excluded for novices;

thus, there are twelve [factors] for them. Regarding the "seven" mentioned for nuns: among the eight factors stated for them, one is omitted because there is no formal legal act for the determination of the three robes; thus, there are seven.
Indeed, by carrying forward the phrase "excluding the factor of possessing the three robes," it is said: "seven for trainees (*sikkhamānā*) and female novices (*sāmaṇerī*)."
It has been said. "Suitable" means appropriate for the state of a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
The commentary on the description of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the second chapter.
3. Explanation of the Description of Taking up a Meditation Subject (Kammaṭṭhānaggahaṇaniddesavaṇṇanā) 38.
"By means of fewness of wishes, etc. means by means of fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, reduction [of defilements], the arousal of energy, and so forth.
"Purified" means thoroughly cleansed and free from defilements. "In this virtue" refers to the fourfold purification of virtue as already described. "'Develop the mind'"—[this is the instruction].
It is with reference to this very teaching that he says, "because it was taught too concisely. "What is concentration? is a question regarding its essential nature (*sarūpa-pucchā*).

"In what sense is it called 'concentration'? means: by what meaning is it designated as "concentration"? What referent object (*abhidheyyattha*) does the word "concentration" depend upon in order to function?
"Of how many kinds? is a question regarding its classification (*pabheda-pucchā*).

“‘What is concentration?’—while this is indeed a question regarding its essential nature, for those who possess distinctions, the manifestation of that essential nature occurs precisely by way of showing the divisions;
therefore, the divisions must first be shown in their entirety. And in order to show that there is a disadvantage in not seeing them, it was said:
‘Concentration is of many kinds,’ and so forth. In that context, ‘of many kinds’ means manifold according to the categories of wholesome (*kusala*) and so on. ‘Of various types’ means...”
It is of various kinds, such as through diversity in object, mental attention, desire, aspiration, resolution, exertion, perception, and so forth.
"He would not accomplish" means that the cultivation of mundane concentration is intended here as the subject matter, and he would not accomplish that.

For when concentration is extracted from the jhānas, liberations, and so on, and an analysis is made according to its available divisions in the *Jhānavibhaṅga* and other such texts— *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the partial nature of the input.*
The entire classification of concentration that has been introduced here would have to be explained.
And if that were so, there would be no room at all for the explanation of the method of developing mundane concentration (*lokīyasamādhi*), which is what is intended here.

Furthermore, [if it were explained], its ninefold division according to the status of the Brahmā’s Retinue (*brahmapārisajja*) and so forth—by way of its occurrence (*pavatti*) distinguished by the lower and other grades of the threefold and fourfold jhānas, and by the fifth jhāna—would be omitted.
The classification of existence (bhava) results in ten or eleven types, beginning with the Vehapphala realm.

If one were to state this specific analysis of its occurrence after having determined it as "this is that," it would lead to confusion, just as if one were to speak of something outside its proper scope.
Therefore he said: "And it would lead further to confusion. "Wholesome one-pointedness of mind" means one-pointedness of mind that is wholesome, characterized by the ripening of blameless happiness.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is the fixing and the steady holding together of mind and mental factors as if they were being gathered by way of non-distraction.

For concentration has non-distraction as its characteristic and gathering together as its function. Alternatively, concentration is the fixing and steady holding together by way of right non-distraction; for concentration has non-distraction as its characteristic and the destruction of distraction as its function.
And this [concentration] is the cause for the stability of the mind upon a single object.
Therefore, he said, "It is called 'steadying'. For it has been defined as "the stability, the steadiness, the firm standing of the mind.
And here, the mention of grasping a single object is for the purpose of showing the state of continuity in concentration.
For its commentary illustrates this by the example of a lamp's steadiness. "By its power" means by its strength; "by its conditionality" means...
The meaning is as follows: "Unwavering" (*avikkhipamānā*) means not wavering, but rather becoming tranquil; for concentration (*samādhi*) has tranquility as its manifestation.
By this, he shows that it is the opposite of wavering. "Undispersed" (*avippakiṇṇā*) means not scattered. By this, he shows its characteristic of non-diffusion.
It is "non-wavering" (*avikkhepa*) because it does not itself waver, or because associated states do not waver by means of it; that is its characteristic.

"Of this" refers to that which has non-distraction as its characteristic. Its function is the destruction of distraction, or it succeeds in that way; thus, its function is the destruction of distraction.
It stands firm by way of being unshakable by restlessness, or it presents itself to its associated states; thus, its manifestation is unshakability.
"Bliss" should be understood as spiritual bliss (*nirāmisa-sukha*).
39. Non-distraction (*avikkhepa*) is the unique intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of concentration; since no further differentiation of it can be found, it is said:

"First, it is of one kind by way of the characteristic of non-distraction. Initial application (*vitakka*) is absorption (*appanā*) because it occurs as if placing the associated states upon the object.
For it is defined as "absorption" (*appanā*) and "application" (*byappanā*). By virtue of its being the primary door to that [concentration]...
However, in all sublime (*mahaggata*) and unsurpassed (*anuttara*) states of jhāna, the term "absorption" (*appanā*) is used as a conventional designation in the Commentaries.

Likewise, the term "access" (*upacāra*) is used for limited (*paritta*) jhāna, which serves as the stage where that absorption does not arise; this is like the common usage of terms such as "village access" (*gāmūpacāra*) for the vicinity of villages and so forth.
Thus he said: "It is twofold by way of access and absorption. But here, it should be understood by way of concentration (*samādhi*). In the sense of breaking down and crumbling away...
The "world" (loka) is said to be the round of existence (vaṭṭa). Because it is included within that, it is "mundane" (lokiya), meaning it is known therein.
Because it is not included within that, it is "supramundane" (lokuttara), meaning it is superior to the world or has transcended it.
Although mundane concentration is indeed included here by virtue of being something to be developed, both are taken together in order to distinguish the other from them.
“It is said to be twofold by way of the mundane and the supramundane. Regarding “by way of being with rapture and without rapture”:

it is *sappītiko* because it occurs together with rapture (*pīti*), that is, it is associated with rapture. It is *nippītiko* because there is no rapture in it, that is, it is dissociated from rapture.
It is by way of these two. It has attained the state of arising simultaneously with pleasure, etc., thus it is *sukhasahagato*, meaning associated with pleasure.

This is the meaning. The same method applies to that which is accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata*). Here, "equanimity" is intended as neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkha-m-asukha-vedanā*);
for it looks upon (*upekkhati*) the occurrence in the mode of pleasure and pain because it is established in a neutral mode.

By the term "accompanied by pleasure," both that which is with rapture (*sappītika*) and a portion of that which is without rapture (*nippītika*) are included; however, by the term "accompanied by equanimity," only a portion of that which is without rapture is included.
This is the distinction between these terms.

It is "inferior" (hīna) because it is inferior to the middling and superior [states] in terms of its intrinsic nature (sabhāva), its conditions (paccaya), and its fruit (phala), or because it is devoid of their qualities.
It is "superior" (paṇīta) because it has been brought to a state of excellence by its own conditions. That which exists between both of these is "middling" (majjhima).

By way of association, that which proceeds together with *vitakka* (initial application) is "with *vitakka*" (*savitakka*); that which proceeds together with *vicāra* (sustained application) is "with *vicāra*" (*savicāra*). That which is both with *vitakka* and with *vicāra* is "with *vitakka* and with *vicāra*" (*savitakkasavicāra*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the states "without *vitakka* but with *vicāra* only" (*avitakkavicāramatta*) and "without *vitakka* and without *vicāra*" (*avitakkāvicāra*) are included.
Among these, it is "without *vitakka*" because there is an absence of association with *vitakka* beyond the stage of *vicāra*, yet it is "with *vicāra* only."

And thus it is "without applied thought and having only sustained thought. Alternatively, the word *matta* has the sense of excluding a specific quality. For concentration accompanied by both applied and sustained thought (*savitakkasavicāra*) is "with sustained thought" because of its sustained thought which is distinguished by applied thought;

this [concentration], however, has only sustained thought, being devoid of the specific quality designated as "applied thought," and is therefore "without applied thought and having only sustained thought.
Or else, because applied thought has been abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), this is "having only sustained thought" due to the absence of applied thought.

The term "without applied thought" (*avitakka*) was stated to qualify the phrase "mere sustained thought" (*vicāramatta*), in order to show that there is no other associated state of one's own apart from sustained thought. That which is devoid of both is "without applied thought and without sustained thought" (*avitakkāvicāra*). "By way of being accompanied by rapture, etc.

means by way of being accompanied by rapture, accompanied by pleasure, and accompanied by equanimity. Whatever needs to be said here regarding this has been explained in the "Dyad on Accompanied by Pleasure" (*sukhasahagataduka*).
It is exactly as previously stated. It is "limited" (paritta) because it is broken on all sides by its opposites.
Alternatively, "limited" is said to mean "insignificant"; this [state] is also "limited" because it possesses little power, like something small.

It has attained greatness through the suppression of defilements, through its vast fruit, and through its long continuity; or else, it is "great" because it has gone forth—that is, proceeded—by means of great and sublime factors such as zeal (chanda).
It is "lofty" (*mahaggata*). It is "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) because, by way of making it its object, there are no factors that can limit it, or because it is the opposite of such factors.

It is called "practice" (*paṭipadā*) because one practices jhāna by means of it; thus, it refers to the preliminary development (*pubbabhāga-bhāvanā*). That which has a painful and difficult practice is "of painful practice" (*dukkhā-paṭipada*).
Because it is distinguished from ordinary wisdom, the wisdom of development that brings about absorption (*appanā*) is called "direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*).

"Slow direct knowledge" (*dandhābhiñño*) means one for whom the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) are sluggish and dull. "The painful way of practice and slow direct knowledge" (*dukkhāpaṭipadādandhābhiñño*) refers to concentration; it is stated thus by way of beginning with that [the first jhāna].
"By way of the factors of the four jhānas" means by way of being the constituent parts of the four jhānas, and this is also stated by way of the fourfold method.
"By way of the partaking of decline and so forth" means by way of the category of decline and so on.
The commentary on the single factor of concentration (*samādhiekakaduka*):
"Of the six subjects of recollection" means of the six meditation subjects consisting of the recollection of the Buddha and so forth.
"By way of these" means by way of these ten meditation subjects. By the phrase "one-pointedness in the preliminary stage," [the author] excludes absorption (*appanā*).
The inclusion of the various acts of adverting that act as contributory conditions should also be understood, not merely that of a single act of adverting.

In the phrase "of the absorption-concentrations" (*appanāsamādhīnaṃ*), the genitive case is used to express a relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary, as in the expression "the purpose of a man.
To show that the concentration is not limited, it is said: "of the first jhāna," and so forth. "Preparation" (*parikamma*) refers to the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*).

“In the three planes” means in the planes of sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial existence. Because it is the concentration of wholesome consciousness that is intended, it is said to be “associated with the noble path.
The statement “it may be with rapture, or it may be without rapture” is an indefinite expression;

by virtue of its commonality with access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*), for all jhānas as well, access concentration in the cognitive process of multiple advertances (*nānā-āvajjana-vīthi*) may be with rapture or without rapture. In the cognitive process of a single advertance (*ekāvajjana-vīthi*), [it is always with rapture].

However, from the beginning, the access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) for the two-fold and three-fold jhānas is accompanied by zest (*sappītika*), whereas for the others it is without zest (*nippītika*).

This is because a consciousness associated with a dissimilar feeling lacks the status of being a condition through repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*), and because there is no shifting of feelings within a single cognitive process (*ekavīthi*).

Regarding the statement "it may be accompanied by pleasure (*sukha-sahagata*), it may be accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata*)," the meaning here should also be understood according to the method already stated. In that context, however, the phrase "of the two-fold and three-fold jhānas" [is used].
It has been stated; here, however, it should be said:
"of the threefold and fourfold jhānas.

The commentary on the triad of concentration: "Merely obtained" means simply attained, not practiced or cultivated repeatedly. For that [concentration] is inferior due to its state of extreme weakness.
"Not well cultivated" means it has not been brought to a state of extreme proficiency. "Well cultivated" means it has been thoroughly developed and properly brought to a state of proficiency;
therefore he said, "attained to mastery. Furthermore, their inferiority and so forth should be understood by way of the inferiority and so forth of desire and the other factors.
For indeed, that which proceeds by way of a desire for the fruit of sublime merit is inferior, whereas that which proceeds for the sake of accomplishing mundane direct knowledge (*abhiññā*)...

That which is practiced for the sake of one's own welfare and the attainment of worldly success is inferior; that which is practiced solely with an intention free from greed is middling; and that which is practiced for the welfare of others is superior.
Alternatively, that which is practiced with an inclination toward the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is inferior; that which is practiced with an inclination toward seclusion (*viveka*) is middling.

That which is set in motion with a medium inclination is the middling; that which is set in motion with an inclination toward turning away (vivaṭṭa) for the sake of establishing the supramundane is the sublime.
"Together with access concentration" means together with the access concentration of all the jhānas.
"Seeing the danger in mere initial application (vitakka)" means seeing, while initial application itself appears as coarse, that "this is a state that causes agitation of the mind."
Having seen the danger and having reflected upon sustained thought (vicāra) from the perspective of peace, he therefore said, “not seeing [the danger] in sustained thought.
“With reference to that” means with reference to that very concentration thus attained. This second phrase, “concentration without applied thought and with only sustained thought,” was stated.
“In three” means in the first three.

"In those very same" means in those very systems of fourfold and fivefold [jhanas]. "In the third and fourth" should be construed as: in the third of the fourfold system, and in the fourth of the fivefold system.
"At the end" means in the final jhana in both systems. "In the fourth or fifth, respectively" refers to the sequence.
"Accompanied by rapture and pleasure"—here too, the meaning should be understood according to the method already explained below.
And here, although concentration accompanied by rapture is also accompanied by pleasure,

the Teacher’s teaching of the threefold rapture should be understood as being for the purpose of showing the three terms without confusion and for the purpose of showing the distinction between pleasure with rapture and pleasure without rapture;
thus, "concentration accompanied by pleasure" is taken here specifically in terms of pleasure that is free from rapture.
“In the plane of access” means in the arising of consciousness associated with access concentration.

For the arising of consciousness is called a “plane” (*bhūmi*) because it is the ground for the arising of co-nascent states, as in such expressions as “in the plane of pleasure in the sense-sphere” (*kāmāvacara*).
Concentration is limited because it belongs to the sense-sphere state.
Commentary on the Tetrad of Concentrations:
The first application is the initial fixing of the mind upon the meditation subject—such as "earth, earth," and so forth—for one who has begun the development.
The access concentration of each respective jhāna is that which has become stable through the subsiding of the hindrances, applied thought, sustained thought, attachment, and so forth.

Regarding the fine-material-sphere jhāna: they say that by the phrase "up to absorption" (yāva appanā), it appears as though the state of direct knowledge (abhiññā) is being attributed solely to the wisdom of the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga-paññā).
However, the wisdom of absorption (appanā-paññā) is indeed direct knowledge itself.

For to the same extent that there is slowness or swiftness in the wisdom of the preliminary stage, there is likewise [slowness or swiftness] in the wisdom of absorption. Regarding the phrase "by way of grasping the manifestation" (samudācāra-gahaṇatāya): of the manifestation...
The meaning is: by way of grasping, and because of the abundance of its occurrence. "Unpleasant cultivation" means arduous development. By the word "etc.
in the phrase "the severing of impediments, etc.," it includes the methods of cultivation, the non-neglecting [of duties], and so forth.

"One who cultivates what is unsuitable" refers to the painful path of practice due to having cultivated what is unsuitable prior to attaining access concentration; subsequently, it is due to cultivating what is unsuitable.
The direct knowledge is sluggish. The method is the same here for one who "practices what is suitable.
"In the prior stage" means prior to the attainment of access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*). "In the subsequent stage" means after that. Regarding "for him it is mixed":

for one who practiced what was unsuitable in the prior stage but practices what is suitable in the subsequent stage, the way of practice is painful with swift direct knowledge; for the other, it is pleasant.
The direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is sluggish. Thus, by way of the combination of the first and fourth [factors], the meaning is that the second and third are [the path].
For one who has not removed the obstacles, the practice is painful because of the presence of hindrances; for the other, it is pleasant.
For one whose skill in absorption (*appanā*) has not been perfected, the direct knowledge is sluggish due to the lack of clarity of knowledge; due to its clarity, the direct knowledge is swift.
"By way of craving and ignorance" means by way of the overcoming and non-overcoming of craving and ignorance.
"By way of the application of serenity and insight" means by way of the application—both that which is lacking and that which possesses—serenity and insight.
Because craving is the direct opposite of concentration, it is an obstacle to the path of serenity; thus he said: "For one overcome by craving, the practice is painful."
And its "overpowering" (abhibhava) should be understood as referring to craving (taṇhā), because it is not overcome by other defilements due to its predominance;
likewise, ignorance (avijjā) is the direct opposite of wisdom (paññā), and thus the sluggishness of higher knowledge (dandhābhiññatā) is said to belong to one who is overcome by it.

"One who has not performed the preliminary task" (akatādhikāra) means one who has not cultivated familiarity in another existence, such that even with a slight application of effort, one might recite a text fluently after having mastered it.
The words of Suppavāsā have already emerged [from her mouth]; thus, for one who has practiced previously, meditation succeeds with little difficulty.

Therefore it is said: "It is easy for one who has performed the preliminary service (*adhikāra*). This preliminary service—both unperformed and performed—is described in the context of the path based on serenity (*samatha*), because that path has concentration (*samādhi*) as its primary factor.
When based on insight (*vipassanā*), it is described in the context of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), because that has knowledge (*ñāṇa*) as its primary factor.
"By way of absorption. "By way of defilements and faculties" means by way of sharp and dull defilements and faculties. Therefore he said, "of one with sharp defilements," and so forth.
Therein, the defilements are sensual desire and the rest; the faculties are faith and the rest.
Since the practice and direct knowledge described above are expressed in terms of persons, this exposition of the Dhamma is also presented by way of a person-centered approach.
To show this, the passage beginning with “the person who” was stated. “Unskilled” means not well-cultivated, not brought to mastery. Therefore he said:
“he is unable to become a condition for higher jhāna. “This is limited” means that this concentration is limited due to its lack of power.
“Not extended” means not increased by even a finger’s breadth or two fingers’ breadth in the object as it has appeared.
For they say that even an increase of the measure of a single finger is indeed immeasurable.
Having stated "proficient and well-developed," [the author] says "capable of becoming a condition for higher jhāna" in order to show that just as concentration, though proficient,
is merely limited and not immeasurable if it is unable to become a condition for higher jhāna, so too is knowledge for the sake of the higher knowledge (*ñāṇuttara*) attained in a single sitting.

Regarding "by way of producing higher jhānas": even though it is well-developed, it is called "immeasurable" precisely because of the accomplishment of its function as a well-developed state, which consists in being a condition for higher jhānas.

Others, however, say that even if it is not a condition for higher jhānas—provided it is well-developed, proficient, and has attained mastery—it is still "immeasurable," because those factors such as lust that act as limits are very far removed.
They say: "Because of the mixture with the characteristics already stated":
that which is unskilled and unable to become a condition for a higher jhāna, and which occurs with an expanded object, is limited (paritta) with respect to its immeasurable object (appamāṇārammaṇa).
But that which is skilled and able to become a condition for a higher jhāna, and which occurs with an unexpanded object, is immeasurable (appamāṇa).

"Having a limited object" (*parittārammaṇo*): in this way, the "mixed method" (*vomitakkanayo*), which includes the second and third jhānas by way of their mixed characteristics, should be understood as applying to the characteristics stated for the first and fourth jhānas.
"Beyond that" (*tato*): beyond that first jhāna. "With fading away from rapture" (*virattapītikaṃ*): either having transcended rapture or being disgusted with rapture.
Or: a part (*avayava*) is called a limb (*aṅga*) of a whole (*samudāya*), as in the cases of "army-limb" (*senaṅga*) and "chariot-limb" (*rathaṅga*). Therefore, he said:
"the four concentrations that have become limbs of the four jhānas.
It "partakes of decline," thus it is "conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgiya*); or, it has a portion of decline, thus it is "conducive to decline," meaning it belongs to the category of falling away.
Meaning: Because it does not relinquish its attachment due to regard for the *ālaya*, it partakes of stability; thus it is "partaking of stability" (*ṭhitibhāgiya*).

Because it partakes of distinction, it is "partaking of distinction" (*visesabhāgiya*). "By way of the manifestation of opposites" means by way of the occurrence of the respective opposites of each jhāna, such as the hindrances, applied thought, and sustained thought.
"By way of conformity to that" means by way of mindfulness that is in accordance with that. "By way of steadying" means by way of stabilization.

"By way of being a foundation. Regarding this, the *Sammohavinodanī* states: "But that [foundation] is either wrong mindfulness consisting in the relishing of that [state], or wrong mindfulness consisting in the aggregates associated with the relishing of that.

In this context, because one who possesses longing is unable to produce further distinction above that state, it is also appropriate to call it "mindfulness of avoiding this or that" for one whose longing has not yet disappeared. And having established it thus...

The alternative expression, “either through mindfulness or through attachment,” is also appropriate. “By way of the attainment of distinction” means by way of being a condition for the attainment of distinction;
or, that by which one attains distinction is the “attainment of distinction,” and [it is] by way of that.

“By way of the manifestation of perception and attention accompanied by disenchantment” means by way of perception associated with the knowledge of disenchantment, which is preceded by the vision of danger.

And [it is so] by way of the occurrence of mental application (*ābhoga*). "Conducive to penetration" (*nibbedhabhāgiyā*) means that it leads to insight (*vipassanā*) which is on the side of piercing through the truths; this is the meaning.

"Accompanied by sensual desire" (*kāmasahagatā*) means having sensual objects as its focal point, or being intermingled with perceptions of sensual desire. "Accompanied by non-initial application" (*avitakkasahagatā*)—how indeed...
"May there be for me a jhāna without applied thought"—thus it has "without applied thought" as its object and "without applied thought" as its domain.
Granted that this reading beginning with "of the first jhāna" and so forth has come down by way of wisdom (*paññā*), nevertheless, concentration (*samādhi*) is also included here;
thus, in order to show the purposefulness of the example, [it says]: "And the concentration associated with that wisdom..."
The meaning is that it was stated thus by way of those four [types of concentration].
Since the concentration consisting in development (bhāvanāmayo samādhi) is intended here, access one-pointedness is called "concentration belonging to the sense sphere" (kāmāvacaro samādhi).
"Making desire the dominant influence" means making desire the dominant influence [with the thought]: "If one who possesses desire attains concentration, the same happens for me."
"Having made desire (chanda) the yoke, the foremost, and the precursor. "He attains concentration":

thus, whatever concentration one attains in this way is called *chandasamādhi*; the meaning is "concentration dominated by desire. In the same way, *vīriyasamādhi* and the others are to be understood.
"In the fourfold division" refers to the exposition of the divisions of concentration according to the tetrad. Elsewhere, it is [distinguished] by way of association with *vicāra*.

Even though applied thought (*vitakka*), which occurs simultaneously [with sustained thought], has been separated out in the fivefold method within the second jhāna, it has not yet been fully separated;

therefore, in order to show the transcendence of sustained thought (*vicāra*) together with that very [applied thought], it is said: "The third [jhāna] by the transcendence of applied and sustained thought.
The construction is: "the second jhāna" as stated in the fourfold division, having been split into two parts. [This is said] by way of the five jhāna factors.
The fivefold nature of concentration should be understood by way of its being a constituent factor of the five jhānas.

40. "In the *Vibhaṅga*" refers to the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga*. For there, in the passage beginning with "the defilement and purification of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments," it is said:
"defilement," and so forth. Therein, "states conducive to decline" refers to the first jhāna and the others when they are not yet proficient.
The non-intrusion of sensual desire and so forth into the perceptions and mental attentions of one who has emerged [from concentration] is the "dhamma conducive to distinction.

This means that for those who have emerged from the first jhāna and so forth with which they are proficient, there is the non-intrusion of the second jhāna and so forth into their perceptions and mental attentions. Therefore he said, "one who has attained the first jhāna," and so on. The meaning of this is: for those who have attained the first jhāna while it is not yet proficient...
Then, having emerged from that [attainment], perception and attention associated with sensual desire arise and operate by way of the object;
they incite and prick [the mind]. Through the influence of those perceptions and attentions that have leaped into sensual desires, that wisdom of the first jhāna declines.
Therefore, it is "wisdom partaking of decline. "Accompanied by non-thinking" means the second jhāna is peaceful.
For one who attends to it as excellent, the [jhāna factors] accompanied by non-applied thought (avitakka) proceed by way of the object;
they urge and incite one who has emerged from the familiar first jhāna for the sake of attaining the second jhāna.
Through the influence of those perceptions and acts of attention that have leaped into the second jhāna, there arises the second jhāna, which is a distinction of wisdom over the first jhāna.
