Wisdom that partakes of distinction is so called by virtue of its being the proximate cause [of concentration]. It is the concentration associated with that wisdom which is intended here.

"By this method" means that according to the procedure explained for the first jhāna, the factors conducive to decline and the factors conducive to distinction should likewise be understood in relation to the second jhāna and those that follow.
Commentary on the Ten Hindrances.

41. "Associated with the Noble Path" (ariyamaggasampayutta): By the inclusion of the supramundane, the immeasurable, and the non-included, concentration associated with the Noble Path is described as being unique when compared to mundane states;
by the inclusion of [states] such as those accompanied by joy (sappītika), it is described as being shared.

It is "developed" because it is associated with perception (saññā). "That" refers to the concentration of the Noble Path. We do not say that it is "separate" (visaṃ) in the sense of being distinct from the development of wisdom (paññābhāvanā).
It is called a *palibodha* because it hinders, obstructs, and does not allow the development of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to proceed;

the letter *ra* having been changed to *la*, the meaning is "an obstacle" (*paripantha*). "Having severed" means having blocked by means of attaining absorption (*samāpatti*) or by grasping [the object], that is, having made it free from obstacles (*apalibodha*).

It is called an *āvāsa* because they dwell (*āvasanti*) there. It is called a *pariveṇa* because it is seen as being enclosed (*paricchedavasena*) by a fence (*veṇi*). It refers to the various dwelling places of the bhikkhus within a monastery (*vihāra*).
This is that very *āvāsa*. Regarding the phrase "in new construction work and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes other causes for the further development of the *āvāsa*.
By the phrase "by reason of [the site] being endowed with shade and water, where alms-food is easily obtained," and so on.
By reason of. "One who has expectations" means one who is attached.
"Therein" means in that absence of obstacles. "The eastern Khandarājī" refers to the location of a forest range situated between mountain ridges in the eastern direction.
By the word "named," he shows that this is the conventional designation for that region. "Only brought back" means...

This shows that he would depart from the monastery only after having settled everything at all times. "The place for depositing the relics" refers to the location where the bodily relics—consisting of the waist-band, the Dhamma-cloth, the bathing-garment, the bone-ornaments, and the bodily relics themselves—are enshrined.
This [instruction] is for one whose mind is unattached, such as this Elder.
By this, an exhortation is given: "A monk must be of such a nature in his dwelling. In the following passages as well...
The same principle applies to the [types of] robes (*vatthu*).
"Family" (*kula*) refers, by the mention of "family," to the people of that family, just as the mention of a "village" refers to the inhabitants of that village.

By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "the family of supporters" (*upaṭṭhākakulam-pi*), he shows that this applies even more so to the family of kinsmen (*ñātikula*). "For the purpose of recitation" (*uddesatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of having [the text] recited; that is, having had the text recited.
The meaning is "to be recited. "Right here" means in this very place; the meaning is "in whatever monastery.
"That monastery" refers to that Koraṇḍaka Monastery.
"Has entered" means he has entered for the rains retreat. "Always" means from the time he arrived, and specifically from the day of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) onwards.
"At all times" means day after day. "Lamenting" means lamenting in various ways by means of uttering various cries of woe.
"The entire course of events" refers to the boy's whole life story, beginning from the time he was seen there until the conclusion of their subsequent meeting.
*Kāyasakkhin*: having made one a direct witness by saying, "See this! *Rathavinītapaṭipadā*:

the path of purification consisting of the seven stages, as set forth in the *Rathavinīta Sutta*, preceded by an exposition of the ten bases of discourse and elucidated through the similes of the chariot-driver. *Nālakapaṭipadā*:
the path taught by the Teacher to the Elder Nālaka, beginning with the words, "I shall explain to you the state of sagehood (*moneyya*). *Tuvaṭakapaṭipadā*: the path of Tuvaṭaka.
The path taught by the Blessed One beginning with the words, “The root of conceptual proliferation,” is as follows:
therein, in due order—“The sage, having entered a village, should not wander hastily among the families;
having ceased conversation while seeking alms, he should not utter discursive speech.”
“One should not be attached to the village, nor should one flatter people out of a desire for gain.

Such passages concerning the discourse on supreme fewness of wishes have been handed down. It is an indicator of contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation; it clarifies contentment regarding the four requisites, such as robes and so forth, and the state of finding joy in the cultivation of meditation.
“Lābha” means that which is obtained. Therefore he said, “the four requisites. “Mahāparivāra” means having a vast retinue. “Piṇḍapātaṃ”...
Giving thus, they give by making the robes, alms-bowls, and so forth of the Buddha their requisites; likewise also in the giving of robes and other items.
"Alms-food-eaters who are luxurious" means those who, while being alms-food-eaters, are luxurious regarding the four requisites.

"They speak" means they speak on the previous day according to what they have heard during the time of wandering for alms. "Constantly busy" means occupied with the task of attending to lay followers and others.
“Of that” means of the group. “That” refers to the impediment of the group. “In this way” means that even the seeking of one who speaks for the group should be desired as something light;
thus he said, “without going beyond a yojana. “One’s own duty” refers to the ascetic practice (samaṇadhamma).

Regarding “what has been done and what has not been done,” one must apply oneself with diligence by way of knowing both the duties performed and those left undone. “What has been done and what has not been done” [refers to this].
Whether small or large, they are performed, as in the expression "fruit after fruit. If much remains, that is the connection.
"Bearers of the burden" refers to those who direct the affairs of the Saṅgha. Regarding "one seeking ordination":
it is said that in the island of Sri Lanka, the ordination of young men of good family is like a marriage ceremony; therefore—

It is not possible to let that determined day pass by. By concluding with the words, "If, failing to obtain it, he is unable to endure [the delay]," the cutting off of obstacles (*palibodhupaccheda*) has been stated;
however, by way of contrast (*byatirekato*), the following meaning is shown through inclusion:
"If, failing to obtain it, he is able to endure [the delay], then having entered the forest, the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) must be performed."
The cutting off of obstacles (palibodhupaccheda) should be understood. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

"In that way" means just as a preceptor who is ill must be attended to for as long as life lasts, so too has the pupil who was ordained been ordained by his own recitation of the ritual formula (kammavācā).

"Any illness whatsoever" refers to either a primary disease or a secondary one that has arisen in oneself. "In the beginningless" (anamatagge) means in that which is endless and without a starting point (anādimati).
By the word "book" (*gantha*), it is said that here the obstruction of books (*ganthapalibodha*) is intended; thus he says, "the carrying of the scriptures. "By means of recitation, etc.
refers to recitation, memorization, mastery, questioning, and so forth. "For the other" means for one who is not occupied [with study].
For one who stands having relinquished the burden of books, even though the book continues to exist, the book is not an obstruction for him. Just as in various instances...
It is not that the Elder has come, nor is it that he has entirely abandoned the study of the texts. The *Majjhima-paṇṇāsaka* is coming;

because of the similarity between the passages of the Suttas and the sections [of the commentary], there is a risk of confusion. "I shall not look again"—the meaning is that having taken up the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he sets aside the burden of the textual studies.
"By the village-dwelling elders" means by those residing in Anurādhapura. "Without having assisted" means without having taken hold [of them] or cultivated familiarity with them there.
"In the assembly of the five Nikāyas" refers to a circle of those trained in the five Nikāyas, beginning with the Dīgha Āgama.
"I shall recite" means I shall explain. "The golden drum" means the most excellent drum. "From which teachers did he learn? means from which teachers?
The intention is: by what is the *uggaha* (learning) transformed? "The path of the teachers" (*ācariyamagga*) means the method of discourse of the teachers.

"Of one's own teachers" (*attano ācariyānaṃ*) means of those teachers who are suitable for one to speak with. "Possessing the entire *pariyatti*" (*sabbapariyattiko*) means that all the teachings of the Three Baskets (*tipiṭaka*) are contained within this;
thus, it means "one who has mastered the Three Baskets. Sitting on a seat, he then descended from it to the ground.
"Having sat down on a mat. "Of one who has gone" means of one who has gone by way of the practice of the path and has seen the Truths.
"Having put on the robe" means having put on the robe in a circular manner (*parimaṇḍala*) for the purpose of showing respect to the teacher.
"Upright" because of the absence of deceit. "A thoroughbred" (*ājānīya*) because of knowing what is the proper cause and what is not.

“Of ordinary people” means existing among ordinary people (*puthujjana*). They are difficult to maintain because they are beset by many dangers; for this reason, a child lying on its back and young crops are cited as examples.
This is an impediment to insight (*vipassanā*) for one whose vehicle is serenity (*samatha*), but not for one whose vehicle is insight.
For generally, one who has attained the jhānas is one whose vehicle is serenity, owing to the bliss of insight. “By the other” means by one who seeks serenity.
The remaining nine impediments.
42. Commentary on the One Assigned a Meditation Subject:
A "kammaṭṭhānika" is one who is engaged with a meditation subject, practicing cultivation. By that person who is a kammaṭṭhānika.
“Having delimited” means having delimited it thus: “all the bhikkhus in this monastery.
[This refers to] the bhikkhus who are co-residents. “He generates a gentle mind” means he generates gentleness of mind toward himself;

and this purpose of generating mental softness toward co-residents is to be illustrated by the Discourse on the Benefits of Loving-kindness, which proceeds in the manner beginning with, “He becomes dear to human beings,” and so forth. He is one whose conduct is not shirking.
It occurs in right practice. This applies even to divine objects, let alone others.
In every respect and in all that is to be done by a recluse, or in the entire application to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), one must strive according to one's previous habituation.
"Application to yoga" (*yogānuyoga*) is the engagement in the cultivation of yoga; that itself is the "work" (*kamma*) in the sense of being what is to be done. Of that work of application to yoga—
*Ṭhānaṃ* means the cause of accomplishment.

"Because it must be constantly maintained" means that, unlike a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) used for all purposes, it should not be practiced only occasionally, but must be cultivated at all times because it is to be maintained continuously.
"Endowed with such qualities as these" refers to qualities such as being beloved and so forth.

It is accomplished. For one who has a virtuous friend is accomplished in faith, accomplished in virtue, accomplished in learning, accomplished in generosity, accomplished in energy, accomplished in mindfulness, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom.

Therein, through the perfection of faith, he has conviction in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata and in the fruit of kamma; by that means, [he directs it] toward beings as the cause for supreme perfect enlightenment.
He does not abandon what is beneficial and desired. Through perfection in virtue, he becomes dear, respected, and esteemed by beings;

he is one who exhorts, censures evil, speaks with propriety, and is patient with reproach. Through perfection in learning, he becomes a speaker of profound discourses connected with truth, dependent origination, and so forth.
Through perfection in generosity, he becomes one of few wishes, contented, and secluded.
Unassociated with worldly society, he is one who has initiated energy through the perfection of vigor in the practice for his own welfare and the welfare of others;
he is one whose mindfulness is established through the perfection of mindfulness; he is undistracted and concentrated in mind through the perfection of concentration;
and through the perfection of wisdom, he understands things without error. Examining the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states by means of mindfulness, he [discerns them] by means of wisdom.
Having understood, as they truly are, the welfare and non-welfare of beings, he becomes one-pointed in mind toward that through concentration;
then, by means of energy, he restrains beings from what is harmful and enjoins them to what is beneficial. Therefore it was said: "endowed with qualities such as being beloved... and an enjoiner.
To show that this spiritual friend has reached the highest excellence, the passage beginning with "my" was spoken. [This refers to] the state of being a benefactor.
Of the practice of yoga (*yogakamma*). He reveals himself by demonstrating the fruitfulness of his own practice, for the purpose of exhortation and encouragement;
the intention is that he does not speak merely for the sake of preserving the lineage. "One such as this" means one who is amiable and learned.

"A bearer of the thread" (*tantidhara*) means a bearer of the Suttas, unshakable therein by anyone. "A protector of the lineage" (*vaṃsānurakkhaka*) refers to the lineage of those awakened after the Buddha.
Anurakkhaka (guardian): One who maintains the lineage (*paveṇipālaka*) is a protector of the lineage, that is, of the tradition received from the teachers.
Ācariyamati (one whose mind is fixed on the teacher’s thought): One who is intent upon the teacher’s thought because he does not overstep it.
*Na attanomati* (not one who expresses his own opinion): He does not proclaim or speak according to his own opinion; the meaning is that he does not speak having adopted his own personal view.

The passage beginning with “Those previously mentioned, such as those whose taints are destroyed,” is commenced for the purpose of showing that, among various types of those whose taints are destroyed, one who is well-versed in the scriptures (*bahussuta*) is superior in the giving of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

In this context, “those previously mentioned, such as those whose taints are destroyed” refers to those whose taints are destroyed and so forth, mentioned in the passage beginning with “Whatever meditation subject he wishes to take up.
“Because of the purification of learning (*uggaha*) and inquiry (*paripucchā*): here, “learning” is a name given to that which is to be learned.

Because it has been specially refined by means of a commentary on the meaning— which bears the designation "Paripucchā" (Inquiry) due to its being an inquiry for the sake of that [meditation subject] and for the sake of the Pāḷi text that assists the meditation subject—
and because it has been grasped by making it free from thicket and free from tangle; and because one has observed the suttas and the reasons here and there among all five Nikāyas.
Having thoroughly observed both the scriptural passages appropriate to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and the reasoning that follows from those scriptures;

"having applied what is suitable and what is unsuitable" means having applied the reasoning—by way of seeking out the logic—as to whether it is beneficial or not beneficial for the person to whom the meditation subject is being explained;
or alternatively, it means having properly taken it up and established it in the heart. "Showing the great path."
Having established the great path as the method for the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he shows it.

"In all places" means in various monasteries. "By one performing the duties of conduct" means by fulfilling each respective duty as appropriate—namely, the duty for a visitor at the time of entering, and the duty for a departing traveler at the time of leaving. "All the oil for requisites" means...
Oil that should be kept for the sake of all parts [of the body] or for the sake of all monks. “I set aside” means to authorize its storage. The connection is:
“that which was prescribed as the proper conduct. The construction is: “even with what has been released one evening.
The reason for coming must be announced. “A suitable time” means a period when the body and mind are fit.
Commentary on the *Cariyā*: 43.
The term *rāgacaritā* refers to the movement or activity of passion (*rāga*) due to its being predominant within one's mental continuum;

it should be understood as being like the latent tendencies toward eternalism and so forth. The same applies to *dosacaritā* and the others. Their association should be understood by way of their suitability for conjunction, just as in the following [examples].

“Conduct characterized by lust and delusion,” “conduct characterized by hatred and delusion,” and so forth. A combination (*saṇnipāta*) occurs by way of being included within a single continuum (*ekasantati*), such as “conduct characterized by lust and hatred,” “conduct characterized by lust, hatred, and delusion,” and so forth.
It is with reference to these very cases that it is said, “there are another four.

“In the same way” means that just as with lust and the others, so too with faith and the rest, there is conduct characterized by faith and wisdom (*saddhā-buddhi-caritā*) by way of their association and combination.

The course of thought associated with faith (*saddhā-vitakka-cariyā*), the course of thought associated with wisdom (*buddhi-vitakka-cariyā*), and the course of thought associated with both faith and wisdom (*saddhā-buddhi-vitakka-cariyā*).

These are another four. Thus [they are classified] by way of association (*saṃsagga*) and combination (*sannipāta*). "Association" means being joined together or mixed, such as "the course of thought associated with lustful faith" (*rāga-saddhā-cariyā*), "the course of thought associated with hateful faith" (*dosa-saddhā-cariyā*), and so forth.
"Many" refers to sixty-three, or even more than that; however, these should be understood without confusion.
It has been shown in detail in the *Saṃyutta-sutta-ṭīkā*, and thus it should be understood according to the method explained there.

By the term “nature” (*pakati*), he shows that when there is no cultivation of the opposite quality, it is the inherent disposition (*sabhāva*) of a particular temperament within the continuum in various instances.
“Predominance” (*ussannatā*) is the superiority of lust and so forth over other states; hence, when the conditions for a lustful temperament and so on come together, lust and the others [arise].
They are powerful and frequently recur. "By way of these" means that by way of the six root-practices, there are exactly six types of persons.
Otherwise, there might be many types of persons; and if that were the case, the intended meaning would not be established—this is the intention.
Faith becomes powerful because, in a mental continuum saturated with lust, there necessarily arises a state of superiority in a phenomenon that conforms to it.
Therefore, he said: "Because it is a quality proximate to lust. The meaning is that it shares the same nature through the seeking of affection and the act of relinquishing.
For a similar thing is considered "proximate" even if it is distant; thus, the term "proximate" is used here to define the characteristic of similarity. In this regard:
In the case of faith, it is a state of non-turbidity and lack of coarseness due to clarity and affection; whereas in the case of lust, it is due to the coloring of passion.
In the case of faith, it is a seeking characterized by resolution and inclination toward that [object]; whereas in the case of lust, it is through the act of craving.

In the case of faith, it is a non-relinquishing characterized by conviction and plunging into [the object]; whereas in the case of lust, it is through attachment. Thus, even though they have different intrinsic natures...

Just as there is a commonality among those [states] by virtue of their shared characteristics such as being unclouded, so too there is a commonality among the individuals who possess them; thus it is said:
"One of faithful temperament is similar to one of lustful temperament.
Wisdom becomes powerful in a continuum where hatred is suppressed, because it is possible for a state of excellence to necessarily arise in accordance with that [wisdom].
Therefore he said, "Because it is a quality proximate to hatred. The meaning is that it shares a common nature with hatred through its non-adherence, seeking, and avoidance.
In this context, the non-adherence of wisdom to its object consists in its dissociation from it by way of understanding its true nature;
whereas for hatred, it consists in its state of being afflicted. The seeking by wisdom is the investigation of faults as they truly are; [the seeking] of hatred is...
The desire to remove faults; the avoidance by means of wisdom through such methods as disenchantment and so forth, which is the dread of knowledge;

and the discarding of hatred by way of its bringing about harm—thus, although these have different intrinsic natures, they share a commonality in their non-adherence and so on. Just as there is a similarity between them, so too there is a similarity between the persons who possess those qualities.
Therefore, it is said: "One of an intellectual temperament is similar to one of a hating temperament."

“Thoughts that create obstacles” refers to wrong thoughts and wrong intentions that arise because, in a mental continuum saturated with delusion (*moha*), there is generally the presence of the occurrence of states conducive to it.
Therefore he said, “because they have a characteristic proximate to delusion,” meaning they share a similar nature through their instability and flickering quality.
In this context, the instability of thought (*vitakka*) is...
Because of its expansive nature through the process of conceptualization (*parikappa*), and because of its confusion due to the state of delusion (*moha*).
Likewise, thought (*vitakka*) is flickering due to its rapid reflection and its instability through the movement of its own factors; and delusion is flickering due to its lack of depth.

Thus, just as these [mental states] have a commonality (*sabhāgatā*) despite their differing intrinsic natures (*bhinnasabhāva*) by virtue of their shared characteristics such as non-stability, so too does this apply to the persons (*puggala*) who possess them. Thus he said.
“The thought-temperament (vitakkacarita) is similar to the delusion-temperament (mohacarita).
Craving (*taṇhā*) is indeed nothing other than lust (*rāga*) by its very nature; therefore, the meaning is that there is no temperament of craving apart from the temperament of lust.
“Associated with that” means associated with that lust; the intention is that it is never dissociated from it, as is the case with hatred (*dosa*) and the rest. “Both of those” refers to...
"The two types of craving and conceit. "Does not transcend" means that it does not pass beyond them by way of its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) nor by way of association (*sampayoga*).
Now, although delusion (*moha*) exists here together with greed and hatred by way of association, it possesses a distinct temperament (*cariyā*) due to its own predominance;
this is true not only of delusion, but likewise of faith, wisdom, and thought. Thus, by way of greed...
Even though there is a concomitance with the mind, it would be logical for there to be a separate manifestation (*cariyā*) for conceit (*māna*);

nevertheless, just as with underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), the specific meaning of "manifestation" for these [defilements] such as lust and so forth belongs exclusively to lust and the rest themselves, and thus there is no separate manifestation for conceit.

For this reason, manifestation is said to be "nature" (*pakati*), and nature is "intrinsic character" (*sabhāva*). By this very principle, the absence of a separate manifestation for views (*diṭṭhi*) is also established.

It should be understood as "praised. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated, "because they have delusion as their source," and so forth, in order to show that the conduct of views (*diṭṭhicariyā*) is indeed included within the conduct of delusion (*mohacariyā*).
In that context, the word "and" (*ca*) conjoins association; that is, "because they have delusion as their source" and "because they are associated with delusion."
44. "What is suitable? means what kind of suitability regarding lodgings and so forth. "Formerly practiced" means that which was performed in previous births.
"Some" refers to the Elder Upatissa; for it was stated thus in the *Vimuttimagga*.
"It is said that formerly..."—the particle *kira* here indicates a lack of approval. "Desirable application" means agreeable activity. "Abounding in wholesome karma" means for the most part.

One who performs beautiful deeds. Not all are of a lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*), because even those who are not greedy may have performed many beautiful deeds through desirable applications in the past, and because it is possible for them to be reborn here after falling from a heavenly realm (*sagga*).

By this, he shows the following point: in the absence of a fixed necessity of past causes, their greediness does not arise merely from the aforementioned reasons, and the practice of lust is caused by the state of being greedy.

The construction is as follows: those who have been reborn here from hell and other realms after performing many acts such as cutting and so forth are not all exclusively of the temperament of hatred or delusion.

Here too, because the aforementioned causes for being prone to anger and being deluded are non-conclusive (*anaikantika*), one should understand that the state of having a temperament of hatred or delusion is also not certain.
If the determination of the predominance of the elements is based on their measure, [then...]
That [distinction] does not exist; rather, it exists by way of capacity (*sāmatthiya*). To show that even this is not found as an absolute certainty, he said:

"In the very manner already stated, there is no fixed rule regarding the predominance (*ussada*). In this context, "in the very manner already stated" means precisely according to the method described starting with the words, "But of two elements...

and so forth. Regarding "the fixed rule of defilement" (*dosaniyama*), one becomes a person of a lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*) due to the predominance of phlegm (*semha*) and other such humors; thus, it is by way of the defilements (*dosa*).

Regarding the restriction of temperament (*cariyā-niyama*), after stating that "one with an excess of phlegm (*semha*) is of lustful temperament (*rāga-carita*)," it is further stated that "one with an excess of phlegm is of deluded temperament (*moha-carita*);

and after stating that "one with an excess of wind (*vāta*) is of deluded temperament," it is further stated that "one with an excess of wind is of lustful temperament. Because of this, such a restrictive statement is indeed internally contradictory.
As for the term "indefinite statement" (*aparicchinna-vacana*), it refers to that which has not been delimited by the wisdom (*paññā*) that functions as a delimiter.
The meaning is: "a statement that has been uttered," i.e., a statement that has not yet been investigated.

"In the description of the preponderant factor" means in the discourse on kamma-result (vipāka) where the preponderant factor has been taken up. "By the law of the prior cause" means by the law of causes such as greed and so forth that operated in a previous existence.
And "law" (niyāma) refers to the specific, inherent nature of those very same factors, such as greed and so forth, consisting of the act of being greedy and so on.
It should be understood as follows: "Lobhussadā" means those for whom greed (*lobha*) is predominant; that is, those with excessive greed, meaning those in whom greed is preponderant.
Regarding the phrase "and [those] predominant in non-delusion (*amohussadā*)," the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*).

By this, it includes without exception all the fourteen divisions that are intended—namely, those consisting of each of the states such as being predominant in greed, both individually and in combination—within the very six types already mentioned.
Because they are included within it. And here, the state of being prone to greed (*lobhussadatā*) and so forth, which have become the fruit, should be understood.
Now, in order to show the individual classification of these—such as being prone to greed—in terms of their distinct and mixed nature, the passage beginning with "For one who...
is commenced. "At the moment of accumulating karma" means at the time of performing the deed. "Greed is strong" means that greed [is predominant] in relation to that [action].
It is superior in terms of its capacity due to the completeness of its conditions. "Greed is weak" means that its opposite, non-greed, is feeble.
But how can these two—greed and non-greed—which are direct opposites of one another—occur at the same moment?
This should not be viewed as occurring at the same moment; rather, the moment of attachment belongs exclusively to the side of accumulation.
Thus it was said. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well. "To exhaust" means he is unable to overcome it.

For that non-greed (alobha) which is associated with the volition occurring through such qualities as being unattached in giving—thinking, for instance, "It is not possible to give something so beautiful, so vast, or so precious"—is truly unable to exhaust greed (lobha).
Because of the non-arising of hatred and delusion, and because of obtaining such corresponding conditions, non-hatred and non-delusion are powerful.
Therefore, it refers back to the very reason already stated: that greed, hatred, and delusion are weak, while non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are strong.
"He" refers to the person possessing those qualities. "By that kamma" means by that wholesome kamma which possesses greed and so forth as its decisive support (*upanissaya*).
“Of pleasant virtue” means he is gentle. He states that same meaning by way of a synonym as “free from anger. “In the same manner as before” means:

according to the method previously stated, dull non-greed and non-hatred are unable to overcome greed and hatred, whereas powerful non-delusion is able to overcome delusion; thus it should be applied accordingly in each respective section.

The meaning of the extension [of the terms] should be understood as follows: "Corrupt" (*duṭṭha*) means prone to anger; "foul" (*daṇḍha*) means dull-witted; "virtuous" (*sīlaka*) means of pleasant character.

In this context, there are seven permutations on the side of the unwholesome according to the predominance of greed and so forth: three single factors, three pairs, and one triad—namely, by way of greed alone, by way of hatred, delusion, and greed, by way of hatred and delusion, by way of greed and hatred, by way of greed and delusion, and by way of greed, hatred, and delusion. Likewise...
Regarding the side of the wholesome (*kusalapakkha*), fourteen instances are obtained by way of the predominance of non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth.

Among these, by the inclusion of the third, second, and first instances of the wholesome side—expressed as "non-greed, hatred, and delusion," "non-greed, non-hatred, and delusion," and "non-greed, hatred, and delusion are powerful"—the instances of the predominance of hatred (*dosa*), the predominance of delusion (*moha*), and the predominance of both hatred and delusion are already included.
Likewise, on the side of the unwholesome (*akusalapakkha*), [there are] greed, non-hatred, and delusion...

By means of the third, second, and first sections—which arrive with the statements "greed, hatred, and delusion," "greed, non-hatred, and delusion," and "greed is powerful"—the sections characterized by an abundance of non-hatred, an abundance of non-delusion, and an abundance of both non-hatred and non-delusion are included.
Thus, having subsumed three sections each within the unwholesome and wholesome sides, eight sections are shown.
Furthermore, forty-nine other sections should be shown according to the combination of both [sides], such as the sections characterized by an abundance of greed and non-greed, and so forth.

They were not shown precisely because they cannot be obtained [simultaneously]. For it is not possible within a single continuum, without passing through another state, for both "greed to be strong" and "non-greed to be present," and so forth;
rather, their relative strength or weakness is determined either by way of their opposites or by way of their co-nascent factors.
In that regard, first, greed is not overcome by non-greed by way of its opposite.
Likewise, hatred and delusion are weak in relation to non-hatred and non-delusion.

However, non-greed and the others possess strength by virtue of their co-nascent states, because they prevail over greed and the rest, and because they function by prevailing over those of their own kind.
Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "Greed is strong and non-greed is weak; non-hatred and non-delusion are strong, while hatred and delusion are weak."
And this state of their weak strength is to be understood from their prior supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) and from the way their underlying tendencies (*āsaya*) have been cultivated.

He who was called "greedy" (*luddha*) in the exposition of the predominance [of temperaments] is to be understood here, in the investigation of conduct (*carita*), as "one of greedy temperament" (*rāgacarita*).
Those called "hateful" (*duṭṭha*) and "dull" (*dandha*) are, respectively, those of hateful temperament (*dosacarita*) and deluded temperament (*mohacarita*).
"Paññavā" means one who possesses wisdom in an eminent degree. This is why he is called "one of intellectual temperament" even though faith and applied thought are present.
Since the strength of non-greed and non-hatred does not occur without the support of faith, it is said:
"Those of faithful temperament are characterized by non-greed and non-hatred due to their nature of clarity."

And since this method has been stated generally, the phrase "or as" and so forth was spoken in order to show that even in the case of those whose temperament is characterized by wisdom (*buddhicarita*) and the like, it occurs through the very necessity of previously produced causes. Therein, "by the retinue of non-delusion" means by that which is surrounded by non-delusion;

the meaning is: by wisdom conditioned [by it] both through decisive support (*upanissaya*) and through association (*sampayoga*). The same method applies to the remaining three phrases as well. By greed and so forth...
"By way of a mixed retinue": here the meaning is "by way of a mixed retinue consisting of greed, delusion, and so forth, which are not mutually contradictory.
And this non-contradiction should be understood as occurring through their simultaneous occurrence (*yugaggāha*) rather than through their non-arising.

For instance, the lineages (*gotta*) of the faith-follower (*saddhānusārī*) and the Dhamma-follower (*dhammānusārī*) are indeed distinct in nature even from one another. Furthermore, a mixed course of conduct must be accepted as a matter of necessity, according to the determination of past causes.

Because of the accomplishment of conduct. And likewise, the description of the predominance [of certain factors] has been set forth according to what is appropriate, because of their being conditions for the result of greed, non-greed, and so forth.
Therefore, it was said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*:
"In the case of one who possesses a fortunate rebirth and is associated with knowledge, through which eight causes does rebirth occur?"
At the moment of impulsion (*javana*) of wholesome kamma, three wholesome roots are co-nascent conditions for the volition born at that moment;

therefore, it is said that formations have wholesome roots as their condition. At the moment of attachment (*nikanti*), two unwholesome roots are co-nascent conditions for the volition born at that moment; therefore, it is said that [formations] also have unwholesome roots as their condition.
“Volitional formations (saṅkhārā). At the moment of rebirth-linking, the three roots are indeterminate; at that moment, they act as conascence conditions for the volition born therein.
Therefore it is said: ‘Consciousness has name-and-form as its condition, and name-and-form has consciousness as its condition,’ and so forth.
Furthermore, according to the law of prior causes, the clarity of wisdom found in one possessing three roots is not the same as that found in one possessing two roots.”
And just as there is discernment (*nepakka*) regarding what ought to be done for one possessing two roots, there is none for one who is rootless.
Thus, it should be concluded that persons characterized by an excess of greed and so forth are those of a lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*) and so on.
To show the aforementioned point by way of conclusion, the passage beginning with “Thus, regarding greed and so forth” was stated.

45. *Tatra* means in that statement of the question. *Naya* means the method of knowing. Although the meaning was stated by way of reference to persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), it is made known through the door of the Dhamma;

therefore, he spoke by way of reference to the Dhamma, saying, "one should discern the modes of conduct" (*cariyāyo vibhāvaye*). *Pakatigamanena* means by way of natural movement, that is, by way of movement according to one's own nature.
*Cāturiyena* means by way of cleverness, that is, by way of gracefulness. *Ukkuṭikaṃ* means with the middle [of the body] not touching [the ground].
“As if digging” means as if digging the ground.
“Dragging along” means that at the time of setting down the foot, he sets it down as if dragging it; therefore his step is dragged along, pulled backward.
“Completely agitated” means thoroughly churned up. “As if trembling” means as if shrinking back; some say “as if terrified. “Suddenly pressed down” means...

It was suddenly and completely crushed by his forefoot and his heel. "Of one whose covering is removed" (*vivaṭṭacchadassa*) means of one whose covering has been stripped away, of one who has abandoned the defilements (*pahīnakilesassa*).
"This is such a footprint"—this he says upon seeing the footprint of the Blessed One.
"Inspiring confidence" (*pāsādika*) means bringing about faith. "Sweet in appearance" (*madhurākāra*) means having a desirable form. "Stiff in appearance" (*thaddhākāra*) means having a rigid form.
*Ataramāno*: not hurrying; the meaning is "slowly. *Samodhāya*: having properly composed [the body], without distraction. *Nipajjitvā*:
having lain down—that is, having reclined in a bed characterized by the stretching out of the body—he sleeps or slumbers.
*Pakkhittakāyo*: with the body cast down, the body fallen suddenly as if against its will. *Dussaṇṭhānaṃ*: an ill-formed posture, a deformed arrangement.
"With scattered limbs" means with his various limbs and members cast here and there.
"Turning over" means having turned over. "Churning up" means throwing the sand and debris into disorder.
"One who acts skillfully, sweetly, evenly, and carefully" means one whose habit is to act with great dexterity, beautifully, without unevenness, and with deliberate application.
"Gāḷhathaddhavisamakārī" means one who is habitually firm, unyielding, and uneven in his actions. "Aparicchinnaṃ" means not limited; "apariniṭṭhitaṃ" means not finished.

"Mukhapūrakaṃ" means filling the mouth, that is, eating a large amount. "Arasapaṭisaṃvedī" means one who does not experience the taste. "Bhājane chaḍḍento" means throwing rice-grains into the food-bowl. "Mukhaṃ makkhento" means smearing the outside of the mouth.

"Kilantarūpo viya" means as if having reached a state of exhaustion due to his inability to endure [the food]. "Aññāṇupekkhāya" means by equanimity that is characterized by ignorance. Some say it means by equanimity reckoned as ignorance.
Among these, *māyā* is characterized by the concealment of existing faults; *sāṭheyya* is characterized by the manifestation of non-existent virtues;
*māna* is characterized by haughtiness; *pāpicchatā* is characterized by a lack of moderation in receiving [offerings] under the guise of being esteemed for non-existent virtues;
and *mahicchatā* is characterized by a lack of moderation in receiving [offerings] under the guise of being esteemed for existing virtues.

Non-contentment has the characteristic of not being satisfied with any gain whatsoever. In the sense of piercing, it is a "horn"; the defilement-horn consists of what is known as coquetry, vanity, and urbanity.
Restlessness is the greed and agitation that occurs by way of adorning one's own body and requisites such as robes.
By the phrase "and so forth" (*evamādayo*), words such as shamelessness, lack of moral dread, conceit, and negligence are included.
Resentment (*upanāha*) has the characteristic of nursing a grievance. Slander (*makkha*) has the characteristic of smearing over the virtues of others.

Denial (*paḷāsa*) has the characteristic of grasping with both hands, as if biting off and removing the virtues of another. Envy (*issā*) has the characteristic of being jealous of the success of others.

Avarice (*macchariya*) has the characteristic of concealing one's own success. Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of such factors as difficult speech (*dovacassatā*) and association with evil friends (*pāpamittatā*) should be understood.
Stiffness is sluggishness. Drowsiness is the exhaustion of lethargy. Restlessness is the lack of tranquility of the mind.

Remorse is regret. Doubt is uncertainty. Dogmatic adherence is the stubborn grasping of things through improper attention. It is the difficulty of disentangling and the difficulty of relinquishing a false grasp as it has been taken up.
Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of forgetfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and so forth, should be understood.

"Relinquishing what has been approached" means having abandoned what has been approached; it is a relinquishment free from attachment. One should understand that the unwholesome aggregates function in the same way as illusions and the like, while the wholesome aggregates function in the same way as the noble ones' desire to see [the Truth] and so forth.

The "objects inspiring confidence" refers to the Three Jewels. The "objects inspiring spiritual urgency" are birth and the other [stages of suffering]. "Devotion to the wholesome" refers to the cultivation of wholesome states.
"Reflecting on duties during the night" means contemplating one's tasks, thinking, "I shall do this and that."
“Smoking at night”: this refers to the failure to act during the day on those very thoughts that were thus reflected upon. “Blazing by day”:
this refers to the casting of the mind onto various objects here and there, running hither and thither. For this reason it was said:
“This mind formerly wandered on its wanderings, wherever it wished, wherever it desired, as it pleased,” and “his mind runs about.”

Since the observation of the occurrence of phenomena (*dhammappavatti*) and so forth is not mentioned in either the Canon (*pāḷi*) or the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it could not be stated [otherwise];
therefore, it was said "in every way. For the intention is that even if something is not mentioned here and there, it nonetheless exists.

Having stated, "It should not be understood as essential," he spoke the passage beginning with "For one of lustful temperament" (*rāgacaritassa hi*) in order to show the reason for that. Regarding the term "dwelling in heedfulness" (*appamādavihārin*): therein—
By practicing while setting aside one's own disposition, one acts with diligence. The postures and so forth have distinct characteristics;
thus, walking and other activities are performed either with grace or without grace, slowly or suddenly. "They do not arise" means they are not appropriate.
"It should be known by asking" means it should be understood by inquiring about the manifestation of phenomena and so forth.
46. *Sappāyaṃ* means beneficial; it means that which destroys the defilements (*kilesa*). *Adhotavedikaṃ* means having a railing or enclosure that is not purified.

*Bhūmaṭṭhakaṃ* means built right upon the surface of the ground, lacking an upper floor. An *akatapabbhāra* is the lower part of a mountain slope that slants toward one side, where the work of constructing walls or leveling the ground has not been done.
*Jatukābharitaṃ* means filled with lacquered materials [placed] face-downward...
It was filled with small bats hanging from their mouths. "Oluggavilugga" means broken and shattered. "Ujjaṅgala" means parched, coarse, and grey, devoid of shade and water.
"Sāsaṅka" means dangerous due to the fear of lions, tigers, and other such beasts. "Durūpa" means ugly. "Dubbaṇṇa" means having an unattractive color or an ill-formed shape.
"Jālapūva" refers to a cake made in the form of a net. "Sāṇi" [refers to a cloth screen].
"Like a rough touch" means like the touch of a coarse surface, such as a sandal-wood plank; it refers to a painful contact.
"Difficult to maintain" is due to its heavy weight and because it must be mended from time to time. "Struck by the handle and the knot" means its beauty is marred by the handle and the knot.

This is suitable for one of a lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*); the intention is that in this way, the manifestation of his defilements (*kilesasamudācāra*) does not occur. The same method applies to the others as well.
"Facing the directions" means facing toward the directions; the intention is that it faces toward open space. "A great kasiṇa" means a large kasiṇa disk.
Whatever remains to be said regarding lodgings and so forth for one of deluded temperament is exactly the same as what was said for one of hating temperament.

It becomes a condition for the wandering of discursive thought, just as in the case of the Venerable Meghiya Thera. "In a mountain cleft" means in a mountain cave. "Small" means about the size of a water-pot.
The word "section" (*pariccheda*) should be applied respectively as: the section on classification, the section on the causal basis, the section on discernment, and the section on suitability.
"Discernment" (*vibhāvanā*) refers to the discernment of knowing [the temperament] by such means as "this person is of lustful temperament" and so forth.
It is stated that [this] is not yet in accordance with the temperament because it was mentioned only incidentally in connection with certain kasiṇas and objects of recollection.
"The meditation subject has been revealed in every aspect.
[End of] the Commentary on the Forty Meditation Subjects. 47.
Regarding "the exposition of the reckoned": this refers to those subjects that have been enumerated by way of the number "forty" and thus designated as "reckoned."
From the point of exposition: by way of bringing about access and absorption, as in, "Of these, so many bring about access concentration, and so many bring about absorption concentration";
by way of the classification of jhānas, as in, "So many consist of a single jhāna, so many consist of two, three, or four jhānas, and so many consist of all [four] jhānas";
and by way of transcendence, as in, "In these there is transcendence of factors, and in these there is transcendence of the object."
"By way of increase and non-increase" means: "This much here should be increased; this much should not be increased. "By way of object" means:

by way of the classification of objects according to whether they are the signs of phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) or are not so described, and according to whether they are moving or unmoving. "By way of plane" means: by way of the classification of planes such as the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth.
"By way of apprehension" means: by way of the classification of apprehension through views and so forth. "By way of condition" means...

Because the formless states and others serve as conditions according to their respective suitability. "Conducive to temperament" means being suitable for temperaments such as those dominated by lust (*rāga-carita*).

"Meditation subjects" (*kammaṭṭhāna*) means bases for the occurrence of the work of yoga (*yoga-kamma*) by way of being objects of focus. "Possessing the four jhānas" means possessing the fourfold fine-material-sphere jhānas;
the meaning is that they are the objects of those jhānas. This is stated according to the fourfold method. Regarding the phrase "those possessing three or four jhānas":
In the case of the first three jhānas among the divine abodes (brahmavihāras), and the four jhānas among the mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) and the kasiṇas;
"in the rest" refers to the remaining twenty-one meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna).
A beginner, having seen the bodily form of a being with the divine eye, can discern that being's mind by means of the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa).
Because he is able [to do so] and not the other, the pervasion of the kasiṇa becomes a condition for the knowledge of penetration of minds. Therefore it is said:
"He is capable of knowing the mind with his own mind as the mind of another being.

Because it is delimited by its location—that is, because it is delimited by the location where it resides—and likewise because proficiency in learning has been accomplished, it exists only in a delimited manner.
They remain as they are; therefore, there is no increase therein—this is the intended meaning.

However, showing that no benefit whatsoever arises even if someone were to increase them, he says, "And because of the absence of any advantage. With the words "But among those," etc., he explains that very absence of advantage.
For when they are increased, only a heap of corpses increases; yet even when not increased, there is the suppression of sensual lust.

It indeed exists; therefore, there is an absence of benefit [in that regard]. "Vibhūta" means clearly manifest due to its vastness as an object (*vipulārammaṇatāya*); the meaning is that it is fully evident through its state of having an immeasurable object (*appamāṇārammaṇabhāvena*) because the sign has been expanded (*vaḍḍhitanimittatāya*).
"Kevalaṃ" means entirely and without remainder. The expression "this earth" is stated by way of the mode of appearance (*upaṭṭhānākārena*), not...
The meaning is "by the expansion of the sign. "Possession" (lābhitā) means possessing it pre-eminently;
the sense is that he has attained mastery in its highest degree.

For the Elder, by virtue of having reached supreme mastery, could enter that very jhāna—whether sitting or standing—just as if he were driving a horse within a circus ring. Thus, the sign was expanded by him all around.
It appeared as if [it were] so. Therefore it was said:
“In all directions,” and so forth. “Vuttā” means stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. “Mahante” means extensive.
For when one does not fix the sign on a single part—such as a depression or a raised area—but grasps it by way of encompassing the entire body, that [sign] becomes extensive. In the extensive...
"Or in the body. "In a small portion" is to be construed as: he takes the sign in one part of the body; or, in a small or minute body such as that of a child.
"This" refers to the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*). "Disadvantage" refers to the disadvantage stated as: "Only a heap of foulness increases, and there is no benefit whatsoever."
The phrase beginning with “Why? is stated in order to explain from a logical standpoint the point briefly mentioned—that the remaining [signs] also should not be increased.
Although the sign appears in the form of a lump of cotton or similar objects, it is said that “only a mass of wind increases,” because it is dependent upon a collection of winds.
It is “delimited by its location” by way of the locations such as the tip of the nose or the mouth.
"With its delimitation. Just as in the expansion of the air-kasiṇa, there is no special quality here; it is merely the expansion of the wind itself.
Thus he says, "because of its disadvantageous nature. "Of these" refers to the divine abodes (brahmavihāras). "The sign" means the object.
"And there is no need for that" means that there is no purpose whatsoever in that expansion of the sevenfold [wind] as there is in the expansion of the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.
“By way of embracing” means by way of embracing the object of meditation that was previously unembraced, not by way of increasing the sign (*nimitta*).
Therefore he said: “by means of a single dwelling, two dwellings, and so forth,” etc. “In this” refers to the development of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra-bhāvanā*).

“That which” refers to the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) which this practitioner [perceives]. Here, the arising of access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) occurs precisely through the breaking down of boundaries, not through the arising of the [counterpart] sign.

If this is so, one might ask: "How can the jhāna have limited (paritta) and other types of objects? To this he says: "The state of having limited or immeasurable (appamāṇa) objects here is also by way of inclusion.
The meaning is that loving-kindness (mettā) and the like, which proceed after including only a few beings, have limited objects;
those which include many have immeasurable objects. The construction is: "Space is not to be expanded because it is merely the removal of the kasiṇa."
Or he will say what must be connected with that. It is possible to extend only a conceptual object as an objective support, not any other;
thus he said, "for it is not possible to extend a dhamma that possesses intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

The fact that the formless attainments have limited or measureless objects should be understood from their occurrence in the space remaining after a limited kasiṇa has been removed, and in the space remaining after a vast kasiṇa has been removed. The rest...
The ten meditation subjects beginning with the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*). "Signlessness" (*animittatta*) means the absence of a counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*).
"Having the counterpart sign as their object" means having objects that have become counterpart signs. The remaining eighteen.
The remaining six are the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*), and the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*); these are the remaining ones.
Six: *Vipubbaka* (the festering) because of its state of oozing; *lohitaka* (the bloody) because of its state of trickling blood;
*puḷuvaka* (the worm-infested) because of the wriggling of worms—a moving object is thus described.

Furthermore, because the manner of movement of sunlight and so forth that has entered through window openings and the like is perceived, even the object consisting of a circle of light is described as a moving object. "In the preliminary stage" (*pubbabhāge*)...
"At the preliminary stage of the arising of the counterpart sign. "Completely still" means peaceful and motionless.

"Among the gods" refers to the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara); for there, because of the absence of unwholesome things, repulsive things, and [craving for] food. Because of the absence of in-breaths and out-breaths in the Brahma-world, it is said, "and mindfulness of breathing.
"By what is seen" means by a visible object acting as a cause. "To be grasped" means to be acquired; that is, the learning-signs (uggaha-nimitta) which are to be produced.
This is the meaning. Therefore he said, “In the preliminary stage,” and so forth. “Of that” means of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati).
Because it must be grasped by way of perceiving the color of the ripening sugarcane and so on in their leaves, it is said, “the air-kasina by what is seen and touched.
“They are not to be grasped by a beginner” means they are not to be grasped by a beginner; [this refers to] not [grasping them] by way of the commencement of meditation.
The lower three divine abidings (brahmavihāras) should be established;
for it is impossible to accomplish them without first attaining the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere within the kasiṇas.

Regarding the phrase "among these meditation subjects" (kammaṭṭhānesu), it should be understood that by the term "meditation subject," the appropriate objects and jhānas are included. "For the sake of dwelling in happiness" means for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra).
“Eleven meditation subjects are favorable”: this is stated by way of direct opposition. The same applies to the rest.
For he will say, “And all this,” and so forth. They are favorable because they serve as the means for suppressing lust. The construction is: “eight are favorable.
The same applies to the rest. “One”—this refers to the recollections; it means “one among the recollections.”
It does not depend on whether one is of deluded temperament (*moha-carita*) or discursive temperament (*vitakka-carita*), because nothing else would be as suitable for them.
The statement, "The first six recollections are for one of faithful temperament (*saddhā-carita*)," is said by way of extreme suitability.

Since there is no distinction to be grasped such that these are the direct opposite for this [temperament] while being extremely suitable for that, they are suitable for all temperaments. "Limited" (*paritta*)...
"Of limited size" means the measure of a small bowl; "immeasurable" means a size greater than that.
Alternatively, "limited" refers to the measure of a fine, small bowl, while "immeasurable" refers to a larger size encompassed as a meditation object (*kasiṇa*) such as a threshing-floor circle.
"Four things" refers to the four things to be attended to. "Higher" refers to perfection in virtue (*sīlasampadā*) and the quality of having good friends (*kalyāṇamittatā*).
Hearing the Dhamma that is conducive [to progress], energy, and wisdom—after being established in these five qualities, one proceeds further.
"Foulness" refers to the practice of the development of foulness through engagement with the eleven subjects of meditation on foulness (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*).

"Loving-kindness" refers to the development of loving-kindness meditation as it occurs either without specific limitation or with specific limitation. "Mindfulness of breathing" refers to the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing based on the sixteen bases.
“For the cutting off of applied thought” means for the purpose of severing wrong thoughts.
“Perception of impermanence” refers to the contemplation of impermanence that occurs as follows: “All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
“For the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am’” means for the total eradication of the ninefold conceit that arises as “I am. For here, four qualities must be developed for each [of these].

They were taught for the sake of one person’s fourfold temperament, not because Rāhula himself possessed all four. By this it is understood that “all meditation subjects indeed suppress all unwholesome states and nourish all wholesome states.
The seven meditation subjects were taught for one specific individual; the intention is not that the Venerable Rāhula possessed every type of temperament.
“Merely by the words”: this refers to the mere statement that “this particular meditation subject is suitable for a person of such-and-such a temperament.
“The intention”: this is the underlying purpose of those words; it has already been clarified by the passage beginning with “All this,” and so forth.
“A virtuous friend of the kind described” refers to one who is “dear and venerable,” etc. “His own bowl and robe himself”...
Having approached in the manner described by the words beginning with "having taken," only joy arises [in him] thinking:
"This body of mine, which is subject to so many dangers, has been surrendered by me to the very place [of its origin]. Therefore he said, "Just as," and so forth.
"One who is not to be threatened" means one who is not to be intimidated or restrained. And this state of being unthreatenable is due to his difficult-to-correct nature (*dovacassatā*).
Or it may be due to a lack of affection for the teacher; to show both of these, the phrase "difficult to speak to" and so forth is stated.

For one who, when being rebuked by the teacher, displays anger, hatred, and resentment, or one who departs thinking, "What is the use of living in his presence?"—both of these types are not to be rebuked.
"In accordance with the Dhamma" means by way of the Dhamma of exhortation and instruction.

"Deeply bound" (*gūḷhaṃ ganthanti*) means they are bound by the "book of meditation subjects" (*kammaṭṭhānagantha*), which is profound and associated with emptiness (*suññatā*), together with the truths, dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), and so forth.
"For your benefit" (*tumhākamatthāyāti*) is said when someone says, "There is some benefit for you in falling down a precipice a hundred fathoms deep.
"Rubbing" (*ghaṃsento*) refers to when someone says, "There is some benefit for you in being ground up by human dung," and one proceeds to rub oneself.
"I would be able to exhaust my entire personal existence. When someone says, "By stopping your inhalation and exhalation,
do you have some purpose such as the pacification of your illness?", all three monks have, by way of expressing their devotion to the Teacher,
demonstrated the very undertaking of energy.
49. Although the mind may have been active elsewhere, that place where it comes to rest is its *āsaya* (abode), just as one speaks of a "deer's abode.

*Ajjhāsaya* is simply another term for *āsaya*. It is twofold: corrupted (*vipanna*) and perfected (*sampanna*). Among these, the corrupted is based on wrong adherence to eternalism and other such views. The perfected is twofold:

based on the round of existence (*vaṭṭanissita*) and based on the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭanissita*). Of these, the inclination based on the turning away from the round is referred to as "by means of a perfected inclination" (*sampannajjhāsayena*).
This is what is intended here. Now, in order to show this by way of analysis, it is said: "by way of non-greed and so forth," and so on.
Therein, "in six ways" means by way of the six modes beginning with non-greed. "One whose inclination is perfected" (sampannajjhāsaya):

one whose inclination (ajjhāsaya) is perfected through the accomplishment of the perfections of virtue and so forth belonging to the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga), and by way of being the decisive support (upanissaya) for those that are supramundane (lokuttara); thus, he is "one whose inclination is perfected."
By that [means]. For non-greed and the others are of great benefit to beings—especially to the practitioner—because they dispel manifold faults and bring about manifold virtues.
Thus, non-greed and the others function as the opposites of the stain of stinginess and so forth. For it has been said: "Non-greed is the opposite of the stain of stinginess;
non-hatred is the opposite of the stain of immorality; non-delusion is the opposite regarding wholesome states."
Regarding non-cultivation: herein, non-greed is the cause for giving, non-hatred is the cause for virtue, and non-delusion is the cause for cultivation.

Among these, by means of non-greed one takes what is not excessive, because a greedy person takes excessively; by means of non-hatred one takes what is not deficient, because a hateful person takes deficiently;
and by means of non-delusion one takes what is not perverted, because a deluded person takes perversely.
“Herein, by means of non-greed (*alobha*), one who perceives a fault as it actually exists as a fault engages with that fault; for one who is greedy conceals a fault.
By means of non-hatred (*adosa*), one who perceives a virtue as it actually exists as a virtue engages with that virtue; for one who is hateful defiles a virtue.
By means of non-delusion (*amoha*), one who perceives the true nature of things as it actually is as the true nature of things engages with the true nature of things.”
It proceeds thus: for one who is deluded, the real is grasped as "unreal," and the unreal is grasped as "real.
Through non-greed (*alobha*), the suffering of separation from the beloved does not arise, because a greedy person possesses what is dear and cannot endure separation from that which is dear.

Through non-hatred (*adosa*), the suffering of association with the disliked does not arise, because a hateful person possesses what is disliked and cannot endure association with that which is disliked.

Furthermore, through non-delusion (*amoha*), there is no suffering from not obtaining what one desires; for in one who is undeluded, there is the presence of such reflections as, "How could that possibly be obtained here?
In this context, through non-greed (*alobha*), the suffering of birth does not occur, because non-greed is the antidote to craving (*taṇhā*) and the suffering of birth is rooted in craving.
Through non-hatred (*adosa*), the suffering of aging does not occur, because aging arises quickly in one whose hatred is sharp.
Through non-delusion (*amoha*), there is no suffering at death; for death in a state of delusion is suffering, and that does not occur for one who is undeluded.
Through non-greed (*alobha*) householders [attain] it, through non-delusion those who have gone forth, and through non-hatred (*adosa*), however, all attain pleasant companionship.
Furthermore, specifically through non-greed, rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*) does not occur; for, as a general rule, beings [are driven] by craving.
They are reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*); and non-greed (*alobha*) is the antidote to craving (*taṇhā*). Through non-hatred (*adosa*), there is no rebirth in hell;
for through hatred, by way of a fierce nature, one is reborn in a hell that resembles hatred; and non-hatred is the antidote to hatred.
Through non-delusion (*amoha*), there is no arising in the animal womb (*tiracchānayoni*); for through delusion, one is reborn in the animal womb, which is perpetually bewildered.
They arise; and non-delusion (*amoha*) is the opposite of delusion (*moha*). Among these, non-greed (*alobha*) prevents the approaching [of objects] by way of lust (*rāga*);
non-hatred (*adosa*) prevents the departing [from beings] by way of hatred (*dosa*); and non-delusion prevents the state of lack of neutrality by way of delusion.

"By means of these three as well, in their respective order, there are these three: the perception of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saññā*), the perception of non-ill-will (*abyāpāda-saññā*), and the perception of non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā-saññā*)."

There are these three perceptions: the perception of foulness, the perception of the measureless, and the perception of elements. Furthermore, by means of non-greed there is the avoidance of the extreme of devotion to sensual pleasures;
by means of non-hatred, the avoidance of the extreme of devotion to self-mortification;
and by means of non-delusion, the practice of the middle way. Likewise, by means of non-greed, there is the avoidance of the bodily tie of covetousness.
There is the breaking up [of the bonds]: through non-hatred, the bond of ill-will is broken; through non-delusion, the remaining two bonds are broken.
Furthermore, the first two foundations of mindfulness succeed through the power of the first two [factors], and the latter two succeed through the power of the last one alone.
"In this context, non-greed is the condition for health; for one who is not greedy does not indulge even in unwholesome things that are tempting."

By means of that, one becomes free from disease. Non-hatred is the cause of youthfulness; for one who is not corrupted by the fire of hatred—which brings about wrinkles and grey hair—remains youthful for a long time.
Non-delusion is the cause of longevity; for one who is undeluded, having understood what is beneficial and what is harmful, avoids the harmful and pursues the beneficial, thereby becomes long-lived.
“In this context, non-greed (*alobha*) is the condition for the attainment of wealth, because through generosity one acquires wealth;
non-hatred (*adosa*) is the condition for the attainment of friends, because through loving-kindness (*mettā*) one acquires friends and does not lose them;

and non-delusion (*amoha*) is the condition for the attainment of self, for it is the undeluded person who, by doing only what is beneficial for themselves, perfects the self. Furthermore, non-greed is a condition for the divine abode (*dibbavihāra*), as is non-hatred.”
Non-delusion is the noble abiding for the divine abiding.
Herein, through non-greed one is extinguished regarding one’s own side—the beings and formations—because with their destruction there is an absence of suffering caused by attachment;
through non-hatred regarding the other side, because for one who is not hating there is an absence of the perception of enmity even toward enemies.
Through non-delusion, because one who is undeluded toward neutral parties lacks all forms of attachment.
"Through non-greed, there is the vision of impermanence; for one who is greedy, through the hope for enjoyment, does not see even impermanent formations as impermanent.
Through non-hatred, there is the vision of suffering; for one whose disposition is non-hatred has abandoned the grasping for objects of resentment."
One sees formations themselves as suffering. Through non-delusion comes the vision of non-self;
for one who is undeluded and skilled in grasping things as they truly are awakens to the five aggregates—which lack a leader—as being without a leader.

And just as the vision of impermanence and so forth arise through these [three roots], so too do these [roots] arise through the vision of impermanence and so forth. For through the vision of impermanence, non-greed arises; through the vision of suffering...

Non-hatred [arises] through the vision of non-self, and non-delusion through the vision of non-self. For who, indeed, having correctly understood that "this is impermanent," would generate a longing for its sake?
Or, knowing conditioned phenomena to be "suffering," would one generate yet another extremely sharp pain of anger?
And having awakened to the emptiness of self, how could one fall back into delusion?

Therefore it was said: “One whose inclination (ajjhāsaya) is perfected—meaning that his inclination is perfected by way of accomplishing the precept-perfection and so forth belonging to the preliminary stage, and by way of being the decisive support (upanissaya) for those that are supramundane—is one ‘of perfected inclination. Hence he said:
“In this way, one attains one of the three types of enlightenment.”

Now, in order to clarify their underlying dispositions (*ajjhāsaya*) by means of the canonical text itself, the passage beginning with "as it was said" (*yathāha*) was spoken. Therein, "six" (*cha*) is the delimitation by number;
"dispositions" (*ajjhāsayā*) is the indication of the delimited phenomena. By taking both together, the meaning is: "the sixfold dispositions.
"Bodhisattvas" (*bodhisatta*) refers to beings who awaken, or those who are fixed, attached, or intent upon awakening (*bodhi*) by virtue of their destined nature.

The meaning is: "inclined toward that" and "tending toward that. "They conduce to the ripening of enlightenment" means they serve for the maturation of the enlightenment to be attained by oneself, in accordance with one's initial aspiration.
"With a disposition of non-greed" means a disposition that proceeds by way of non-greed;
first, thinking, "How indeed may we be entirely and at all times free from greed? and in the middle, likewise by way of non-greed.
And subsequently, they proceed according to the inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) toward that very [non-greed] itself.

"Seeing the danger in greed" means seeing the disadvantage in every way regarding greed, which has the characteristic of coveting. This is a demonstration of the manner in which that inclination is expanded in part.
For one who sees the danger in greed and the benefit in non-greed, the inclination toward non-greed increases; and this—
In this context, the method for seeing the danger and the benefit has already been explained. The meaning in the remaining phrases should also be understood according to this same method.
However, there is this distinction: here, “renunciation” (*nekkhamma*) refers to going forth (*pabbajjā*).

“Seclusion” (*paviveka*) consists of seclusion by way of its own nature (*tadaṅga-viveka*), seclusion by suppression (*vikkhambhana-viveka*), bodily seclusion (*kāya-viveka*), and mental seclusion (*citta-viveka*). “Escape” (*nissaraṇa*) is *nibbāna*. “In all states of existence and destinies” (*sabbabhavagatīsu*)...
"In all states of existence and in all destinations. "By being intent upon that" means:

by one who is intent upon that for which the practice of development is undertaken and for which the going-forth is undertaken. For this very reason, he said: "by one intent upon concentration," and so forth.
50. If, when asked, "What is your habitual practice? he should say, "I do not know," [the teacher should ask], "Which qualities are most frequent for you?"
He should be asked: "What do you practice?"—whether it be the foul (asubha), a basis for recollection (anussatiṭṭhāna), or something else.
"What brings you ease when you attend to it?"—this means that there is happiness through one-pointedness of mind.
"The mind inclines toward it"—this means it inclines by way of natural delight. By the word "etcetera" (evamādīhi), the inclusion of postures (iriyāpatha) and so forth is intended.
It should be understood that even these three are not invariably deceptive for everyone. For it has been stated that one’s actual practice (*samudācāra*) must be questioned.
One should be told: "Devote yourself for a few days to such-and-such and such-and-such methods of attention (*manasikāra*.
And regarding the phrase "of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) normally studied," this refers to the recitation (*sajjhāya*) of whichever meditation subject the person intends to take up.
This was said with reference to one who has already practiced it by way of attention (*manasikāra*) or through prior familiarity. "One or two sessions" means one or two warm seats.
Having had him recite the study (*sajjhāya*)—that is, having had him learn it in the teacher's own presence—it should be given;
the intention is that this applies if he wishes to go elsewhere. Therefore he said, "for one living nearby. It should be explained at every moment of his arrival.
The intention is "having heard the account.
"Earth-kasiṇa" refers to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of the earth-kasiṇa. "Of what has been done" means of the kasiṇa that has been prepared.

"That and that aspect" refers to the words, the meaning of the words, the intention, the similes, and so forth, as they are spoken by the teacher regarding the meditation subject, according to one's own knowledge.
"Each respective aspect" refers to whatever is called a "sign. "Having bound it" means having brought it near and made it as if tied fast;
the meaning is that one should place it in the heart and ensure it is not forgotten.

Thus, by means of well-established mindfulness, having grasped the sign, and by listening attentively through clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) regarding that [object], "that" refers to what has been described above.
"Depending on what has been well grasped. "Of the other" means of one who does not grasp it in that way. "In every aspect" is said because no mode whatsoever remains there ungrasped.
The commentary on the description of the taking up of meditation subjects is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the third chapter.
4. Commentary on the Description of the Earth Kasiṇa. 51.

"It is comfortable" means that through the acquisition of favorable conditions for the dwelling and so forth, there is comfort of attention (*manasikāra*) and suitability for meditation (*bhāvanā*). "While purifying" means...
By purifying through the cutting away of those various knotty places. "Without becoming weary" means with an unwearied body;
for the intention is that if there is bodily fatigue, it might become an obstacle to the attention directed toward the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

"A knotty place" refers to a place that has become like a knot because it is difficult to penetrate, both in terms of its literal meaning and its intended sense. "Having cut" means according to reality.
The intention is: having cut through by means of elucidating the meaning and the underlying purpose, and having made it manifest and clearly revealed.
"Suvisuddhaṃ" means thoroughly purified; the sense is that it is free from tangles and devoid of roots.
*Ananurūpavihāravaṇṇanā* (Commentary on the Unfit Abodes)
52. "By one or another" means even by one, let alone by many; this is the intended meaning. "Greatness" (*mahattam*) refers to the state of being great.
The same applies to the remaining terms. "Soṇḍī" means having a trunk (or a mouth). The same applies to terms such as "paṇṇa" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "to be done here," it is said that "the duty" (*vatta*) intended here refers to tasks such as those performed in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree. "When it is finished" means by the giving [of water] to those who have entered and entered repeatedly.
"Completely worn out": even in a dilapidated dwelling where the monks say, "Venerable sir, practice the duty of a recluse as you please;
we shall look after it," it is permissible to dwell in such a place—this principle also applies, but it has not been stated here because it follows the previously mentioned method.
