"In a great road-dwelling" means in a dwelling near a main road. "Dye-vessels, wooden troughs, and so forth" refers to dyeing vessels.
Wood for dyeing, wooden troughs, the place for boiling dye, washing boards, and so forth.
"Gatherers of greens" refers to women who gather greens. They say that "discordant sounds" refers to the sound of singing associated with the strands of sensual pleasure;
however, even the mere sound of women is itself a discordant sound. "Therein" means in the monastery at Pupphavanta. "Just like that" means...
“Having taken his meditation subject there,” and so forth; the kind of danger described regarding the monastery where he informs others is exactly the same [as before].
However, it should be said: “Gathering women were plucking flowers. This is the distinction here.

“Desirable” means that because of the esteem in which he was held by those living there, he was to be longed for through such acts as approaching him. Therefore he said, “regarded as a shelter. “Dakkhiṇāgiri” refers to what they call Dakkhiṇāgiri in the Magadha region.

The objects of perception (*ārammaṇa*) are both desirable and undesirable. It is for the purpose of showing those that are undesirable that it is said, “rubbing against [the pots],” and so forth. Trees suitable for timber and building materials are called “timber-trees.
As for the monastery (*vihāra*): a threshing floor (*khala*) is a place for processing grain. Cows are kept penned there [thinking], “They might eat the crops.
A water-distribution turn (*udakavāra*) is the turn for providing water to the crops in the fields. “This too” refers to the monastery belonging to the Mahāsaṅghika community.

Though being restrained by the monk who was practicing meditation (*kammaṭṭhānika*), the people of the king—those living near oceans, seas, and rivers, as well as those near river ports (*udakapaṭṭana*) which serve as gateways for great cities, and those near land ports (*thalapaṭṭana*) such as forest entrances—became displeased.
The intention is that because of this, he did not have a comfortable stay there. [The phrase] "thinking" refers to the king’s men.

“By wandering about” means by moving hither and thither. “At the precipice” means standing at the edge of a precipice, he sang, thinking, “I will cause whoever comes here by the sound of my song to fall into the abyss and devour them.
“Having seized him with speed” means having come quickly and seized him on the shoulder, saying, “Where are you going?

“In which” means in whichever monastery, or in the vicinity of a monastery where it is not possible to find a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitta*); there, in that monastery, that lack [of a friend] is a great fault—this is the construction.
*Paṇṭhanī*: that which is led onto a path (*paṇṭhe*) and has proceeded there is *paṇṭhanī*; it is a dwelling dependent on a path. *Taṃ paṇṭhaniṃ*: that [dwelling] which is a *paṇṭhanī*. *Soṇḍī*:
a dwelling accompanied by a tavern (*soṇḍī*) is *soṇḍī*; *taṃ soṇḍiṃ*: that [dwelling] which is a *soṇḍī*. Likewise in the cases of *paṇṇa* and so forth.

It is called *nagara* (city) when dependent on a city, through the elision of the latter member of the compound, just as "Bhīmasena" is called "Bhīma. *Dārunā*: by means of that which is dependent on a forest (*dāru*).
"Together with. "Unsuitable" (*visabhāga*) means that which is inhabited by those who are unsuitable, or the dwelling place of those who are unsuitable; such a monastery is "unsuitable.
Together with that unsuitable [place]. "Dependent on the border and dependent on the boundary, and unsuitable" refers to what is unsuitable regarding the border and the boundary.
"Where even a friend cannot be found"—this is expressed in the neuter gender because it refers to the word "place" (*ṭhāna*) in all instances.
"Thus having understood" means: having discerned that "these are unsuitable for meditation.
53. Description of the Suitable Abode:
"This is what is called suitable" means this abode is indeed suitable for meditation. "Not too far" refers to [the distance] from the place of alms-gathering.
It is not too far because it is within half a *gāvuta* from the place where sheep are kept.
It is not too near because, by the latter measurement, it is five hundred bow-lengths (*dhanus*) from the grazing ground.
And because it is neither too far nor too near, and because the path to and from the grazing ground is free from dangers and the like, it is "well-suited for coming and going."
By day it is "uncongested" (*appākiṇṇa*) because of the absence of a great crowd of people;
for this word *appa* has the sense of "absence," as in such terms as *appiccha* ("of few desires"). By night it is "quiet" (*appasadda*) because of the absence of the sound of people's chatter.

At all times it is "without noise" (*appanigghosa*) because of the absence of the clamor of crowds gathering. "Without difficulty" (*appakasirena*) means without hardship, that is, with ease. [This refers to] the qualities of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
They are *theras* because they have attained a state of stability. They are *bahussutas* (learned) because they have heard much—the discourses (*sutta*), verses (*geyya*), and so forth.

They are *āgatāgamā* (those who have mastered the tradition) because the *āgama*—that is, the Dhamma consisting of the scriptures—has come to them through the act of committing it to memory and by having properly received it from the presence of their teachers.
They are *dhammadharā* (bearers of the Dhamma) because of their retention of the Dhamma known as the Suttas and the Abhidhamma; and [they are *vinayadharā*] because of their retention of the Vinaya.
They are holders of the Vinaya. They are holders of the Mātikā because they retain the matrices (mātikā) of those very same Dhamma and Vinaya.

Therein, they inquire by means of inquiry into the Dhamma; they question, investigate, examine, and scrutinize by means of inquiry into the meaning. "Venerable sir, what is this? What is the meaning of this?"—this is the demonstration of the manner of inquiry and questioning. And that which is undisclosed...
They clarify the meaning of the text from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*) by showing parallel passages from other parts of the canon.
They elucidate what has not been made clear through the exposition of logical reasoning (*yutti*).

And regarding those points in the text that constitute knots because they serve as causes for the arising of doubt concerning matters that provoke uncertainty, they dispel that doubt by providing a decision according to reality. In this context, "not too far..."
"Not too near, yet convenient for coming and going"—this is one factor; "not crowded by day, with little noise and little clamor at night"—this is one;
"free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping things"—this is one;
"for one dwelling in that lodging... [and] the requisites"—this is one; "in that lodging... [and so forth].
“The elders... dispel their doubts”—thus is one [factor]. In this way, five factors are to be understood.
Regarding the commentary on the minor obstacles (khuddakapalibodha):

the purpose for cutting off the minor obstacles will follow later. Alternatively, strengthening work may be done by providing door-bolts, ventilation-slits, plastering, and so forth; or sewing work may be performed when threads are broken and so on.
The Explanation of the Method of Cultivation (Bhāvanāvidhānavaṇṇanā):

"By way of all meditation subjects" means by way of all forty kinds of meditation subjects that are being demonstrated in successive order. "Having returned from almsround" means having turned back from the consumption of almsfood.
"Having finished eating the alms-food" means having removed the bowl from his hand. "Having dispelled the drowsiness caused by the meal" means having removed the fatigue resulting from eating;
for as soon as food has entered the stomach, there generally arises some degree of physical fatigue due to that foreign substance, and he has calmed that down.
For if that fatigue were not calmed, [he would be hindered] by bodily exhaustion.
“He would not attain one-pointedness of mind”: “Secluded” means secluded from people.
“Sitting comfortably” means sitting comfortably by having folded his legs crosswise and set his body erect.

“For this has been said” refers to what is called here the grasping of the sign of the earth by means of the passage beginning with “or when it has been prepared,” for this has been stated in the ancient commentary (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
Now, showing that commentary and the canonical text (pāḷi), he said: "One who is learning the earth-kasiṇa," and so forth. Herein, this is the summary of the meaning:
"One who is learning the earth-kasiṇa" means one who takes up and adopts the earth-kasiṇa by way of its status as the acquired sign (uggahanimitta);
the meaning is that one is producing the earth-kasiṇa which has become the acquired sign. And here, "producing" refers to the production of such a sign.
The "establishing" is to be understood as follows: "On the earth" refers to the earth-circle, which will be described in detail later.

"He takes the sign" means that there, by means of the knowledge of meditation (bhāvanā-ñāṇa), he takes the sign of the earth—which will be described in detail—as one takes the sign of a face in a mirror with the eye.
Although it is said "on the earth," the neuter designation is used in view of the circle (maṇḍala). "Made" refers to the method that will be described later.
The meaning is "conditioned" (*abhisaṅkhata*). The word *vā* has the sense of indefiniteness. "Unconditioned" (*akatā*) refers to natural earth-spheres such as threshing floors and the like.
"Finite" (*sāntaka*) means precisely "having an end," that is, "having a limit"; for this statement is restrictive.
Indeed, it is said "not infinite" (*no anantake*) in order to show what is excluded by that [term]. "With a boundary" (*sakoṭiya*) and so forth are also synonyms for that very same thing.
Regarding the phrases "the size of a ladle" (*suppamatta*) and so forth, it is intended that the ladles (*suppa*) and saucers (*sarāva*) are of equal measure. However, some say:
"The size of a saucer (*sarāvamatta*) is one cubit and four finger-breadths; the size of a ladle (*suppamatta*) is a measure greater than that.
According to this, the artificial kasiṇa disk is the size of a saucer at its lower limit and the size of a ladle at its upper limit, but not smaller than that.

It is said, "In order to include the measurement of a *suppa* or a *sarāva* for the purpose of grasping the distinction of limited [kasiṇas]," because even if it is increased by only the measure of a finger's breadth when the object is present before one,
it is still called "immeasurable. However, some say that the kasiṇa disk should be made even the size of a parasol.
"He makes that sign well-grasped" means that the practitioner makes that earth-disk a well-grasped sign.
When, having opened his eyes and looked, he grasps the sign there, and then, upon closing his eyes and reflecting,
it appears to him just as it did at the moment he opened his eyes and looked, then it is said to be "well-grasped."
Then, having established mindfulness well upon this object, observing it again and again with a mind that does not stray outward, one is said to "retain what has been well-retained.

Furthermore, repeatedly bringing to mind and attending to what has thus been retained, and engaging in frequent repetition and development directed toward that very same object, one is said to "define what has been well-defined. Upon that object...
When that object known as the earth-kasiṇa has been properly established through such means as correct grasping and so forth, one "binds the mind" to it;
that is, having brought one's own mind into access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), one binds it and turns it away from other objects.
The passage beginning with "Surely by this... and so forth is a demonstration of the perception of benefits (ānisaṃsa).

Now, desiring to clarify the method of cultivation along with an exposition of the meaning of the commentary passage as it has been shown, he first shows the grasping of the sign (*nimitta*) when it has not yet been produced, saying:
"In that regard, by means of which [sign] even in a past existence... and so forth. Herein, "in that regard" (*tattha*) means in that commentary passage.
"The fourfold and fivefold jhānas" refers to them according to the fourfold and fivefold systems.
"Meritorious" means possessing merit consisting of mental development (*bhāvanāmaya*). "Endowed with a decisive support" means being possessed of such a decisive support (*upanissaya*).
"In a threshing floor" refers to a place for processing grain that is circular in shape. "Only the size of that place" means only the extent of the area looked upon.
"Without violating" means without failing, according to the very method prescribed.

"By way of the division into blue, yellow, red, and white" means by way of the individual combination of clays of blue and other colors, both separately and together. "In the flow of the Ganges" means in the current of the Ganges.
It is said that on the island of Siṃhala there is a river named Rāvaṇagaṅgā; at the place where its current cut away the bank, the clay is the color of dawn (ruddy).

With reference to this, it was said: “like the clay carried by the Ganges, having the color of dawn. “Having the color of dawn” means having the appearance of dawn, or having the hue of the radiance of dawn.
Having thus shown the defects of the kasiṇa, he now says “And yet,” etc., in order to show the remaining modes such as the making of the kasiṇa.
It has been stated. “Portable” means that which is fit to be carried about by taking up what is to be gathered together.
“Remaining in its place” means that which stays exactly where it was placed. “Of the stated measure” means the measure stated as “the size of a ladle or the size of a shallow bowl.
“Circular” means having a round shape. “At the time of preparation” means at the time of meditation for the purpose of grasping the sign (*nimitta*). “This very same” [refers to the aforementioned].
Whatever is four finger-breadths wide—that very measure is intended when it is said, "the size of a spoon or the size of a shallow bowl.
For a spoon is not too large, and a shallow bowl is large enough to serve as a lid for a jar; thus, they are of equal measure.
(56) "Therefore" means because it was stated for the purpose of defining the limit. "The limit of the measure stated thus" means the measure as it has been described.
Having made a boundary four fingerbreadths wide, or having made a boundary for the *kasiṇa*-mandala of the aforementioned measurement by means of a dissimilar color;
"tree-paint" refers to tree-paint such as red sandalwood, which produces a dissimilar color to that of the dawn-hue.
Therefore, it is said that one should not take that. However, natural tree-paint...
"Like the movement of a stone on a palm" means having made it like the surface of a drum by eliminating uneven places.

"Farther than that," etc., refers to seeing the disadvantage in a location other than the aforementioned spot or in a chair. "Defects of the kasiṇa" refers here to the hands, feet, and so forth as defects of the kasiṇa.
"In the manner already stated" refers to: "in a place two and a half cubits away, on a chair with legs a span and four finger-breadths high."
And this is according to the method already stated. As for the danger in sensual pleasures (*kāmesu ādīnava*): "These sensual pleasures are like a skeleton in the sense of being devoid of sustenance;
they are like a grass torch in the sense of burning up; they are like a pit of embers in the sense of great heat; they are like a dream in the sense of appearing only briefly;
they are like borrowed goods in the sense of being temporary; they are like the fruit of a tree in the sense of crushing all one's limbs and members."
“Swords and knives are like them in the sense of cutting; spears and stakes are like them in the sense of piercing; the heads of snakes are like them in the sense of being terrifying,” and so forth;
and likewise, “Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair”;
and further, “This sensual pleasure is fraught with many dangers, full of anxiety, full of fear, defiled, like the enjoyment of filth, base, vulgar, and worldly.”

Having reflected upon the danger and fault in sensual objects and the defilements of sensuality through many modes and aspects, such as [the words] "it is un-Ariyan" and "it is not conducive to welfare";
and regarding "renunciation from sensuality" (*kāmanissaraṇa*), [this refers to] that which is the renunciation of sensual pleasures, or that which has emerged from them;

and regarding "renunciation" (*nekkhamma*), [this refers to] the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) which, by serving as the foundation for the supreme path, are the means for transcending all suffering. With a desire thus born...

With desire having arisen—having generated rapture and gladness directed toward the Triple Gem by recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha thus: “The Blessed One is indeed a Perfectly Enlightened One because he teaches the Dhamma without error;
the Dhamma is well-expounded because it leads exclusively to liberation; the Saṅgha has practiced well because they practice according to the instructions”—[one should cultivate] renunciation.

"One proceeds by means of this" is the meaning of *nekkhamma-paṭipadā* (the way of renunciation); it is the cause for the attainment of jhāna together with its access, of insight (*vipassanā*), of the path (*magga*), and of Nibbāna.
However, since previously only the first jhāna was called "renunciation," all remaining factors of renunciation are also included. As it has been said:
“Going forth, the first jhāna, nibbāna, and insight;
all wholesome states as well are called ‘renunciation. Regarding the flavor of the bliss of seclusion:
this refers to the flavor of the bliss born of seclusion of mind and so forth. Thus, by these five phrases—
It should be understood that the meaning of the phrases beginning with “seeing the benefits” has been shown.

“In an even manner” means by a mode of observation that is balanced, avoiding both excessive opening of the eyes and excessive dimness of vision—that is, by a mode of observation characterized as neither too wide-open nor too dim.
“Grasping the sign” means grasping with the mind the sign apprehended by the eye in the earth-kasiṇa. “Should be developed” means [the meditation] proceeding in such a way.
The grasping of the sign should be expanded, cultivated, and practiced frequently.
The eye becomes fatigued as if one were contemplating a form that is too subtle or too brilliant. It becomes overly vivid due to the non-manifestation of its own intrinsic nature;
and thus it may present itself either by way of color or by way of characteristic. Therefore—
It is said: "Therefore, the sign does not arise for him. It is as unclear as a form seen by one who squints with his eyes closed.
And the mind becomes sluggish due to its feeble activity in seeing, because it has fallen into indolence.
Therefore he said: "In this way too, the sign does not arise. It is like one looking at the reflection of a face on the surface of a mirror. Just as... [on] the surface of a mirror...
Just as a man looking at the reflection of his own face does not open his eyes too wide, nor too narrow;
he does not contemplate the color of the mirror’s surface, nor does he attend to its characteristics;
rather, looking with an even gaze, he sees only the reflection of his own face—exactly so, this person also looks upon the earth-kasiṇa with an even gaze.
He is simply intent on grasping the sign; therefore it is said, “in an even manner,” and so forth.

“The color should not be reviewed” means that the dawn-colored appearance which is there in that earth-kasiṇa should not be thought about. However, it is impossible to prevent its being grasped by eye-consciousness.
For this very reason, instead of saying here “it should not be looked at,” the term “reviewing” (paccavekkhaṇa) is used.
"One should not attend to the characteristic" means that the characteristic of hardness belonging to the earth element therein should not be attended to.
Although it was said "without abandoning the color" because it must be grasped after seeing it, one should not direct attention here by way of the color;
rather, showing that the color should be treated according to its support, he said, "making it the same color as its support. By the support...

The meaning is that this color, being based on a common appearance, should be brought to the same destination as that earth and attended to as "earth" together with the color itself. Regarding "conventional designations by way of prominence":
this refers to the worldly convention of "earth" applied to the composite earth, which arises from the predominance—that is, the superior state—of the earth element.
Having fixed the mind upon that designated phenomenon (paṇṇatti-dhamma), one should attend to it as "earth, earth.
If the mind is to be placed on the mere designation according to worldly convention, then earth might also be attended to by way of its synonyms;
saying "let it be, what is the harm? he states "mahī, medinī," and so forth. In this context, "yamicchati" means...

Whatever name one wishes to utter should be spoken; however, that name which is conducive to one's perception (*saññā*) should be spoken—that is, the name which, by virtue of the perception previously grasped therein by the yogin, comes to him through its abundance or its familiarity.
And as for "should be spoken," in the first act of attention, there may even be an utterance of speech for some.
This was stated because it *does* occur, or with reference to what ought to be said by the teacher. Or rather, why say more?
To show that manifest appearance alone is the authority here, he said, "Furthermore," and so forth. "Having opened the eyes at one time and closed them at another" means:
having opened the eyes for a short while and looked at the circle of the earth by way of grasping the sign (*nimitta*), and then again for a short while...
Having closed one's eyes for a moment, one should direct the mind toward it. One should again attend to it in the same manner in which it was perceived when looking at it. 57.
"It comes into the range" means it enters the sphere of the mind-door impulsion consciousnesses. Of that learning sign (*uggahanimitta*).
One should not sit in that place. Why? If, even when the learning-sign has arisen, one continues to develop it while looking at the circle of earth, the counterpart sign will not arise.
Furthermore, it is impossible to look [at the earth] from such a close proximity. Therefore it was said:
"having entered one's own dwelling place," and so forth. Single-soled sandals are taken up for the purpose of ensuring silence.
The taking up of a walking stick is for the purpose of warding off dangers. The connection is: "If it is lost, then it must be developed by means of this.
"By some unsuitable cause" refers to any one of the unsuitable factors that will be explained.
"Taking the sign" means having grasped the learning-sign (*uggahanimitta*) exactly as it appeared. "It should be attended to" means the sign should be brought to mind (*āvajjitabba*).

The meaning is: the underlying intention (*adhippāya*), or the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) that should be properly and repeatedly brought forward. "Struck by reasoning" (*takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ*) means:

it is struck by right thought (*sammāsaṅkappa*)—which is associated with the mind of development (*bhāvanācitta*) and bears the names "reasoning" (*takka*) and "applied thought" (*vitakka*) because of its nature as reasoning and its nature as reasoning with distinction—and which functions through the activities of striking and pounding as it proceeds again and again; thus the meditation subject is struck.
It must be "struck about" (pariyāhata); the meaning is that one should frequently exercise attention accompanied by thought that has reached its full strength.
"Doing thus" means doing so as to strike the meditation subject with reasoning and with thought.
"For one who practices thus" means for one who applies himself in such a way that the development brings about successive excellence. "By gradual stages" means by the sequence of development.
When the faculties beginning with faith (saddhā) proceed in a state that is very clear and sharp, then— due to the distancing of states such as lack of faith (assaddhiya)—

the factors of absorption belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), such as applied thought (vitakka) and the rest, become numerous and manifest, having gained support from the seven powers (bala) which have attained an especially high degree of strength.
For this very reason, the hindrances such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda), which are their direct opposites, [are suppressed].
Together with the evil states associated with them, they become far removed;
and with the arising of the counterpart sign, access concentration arises directed toward that [object]. Therefore it was said: "They suppress the hindrances," and so forth.
In this context, "they settle down" means they settle properly; the meaning is that they are pacified.
"Of this" refers to the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*). Finger-marks, footprints, handprints, and so forth are defects of the kasiṇa.
By means of the similes of the mirror-disk and others, he shows that the counterpart sign is far more pure and subtle than the learning sign (*uggaha-nimitta*).
Furthermore, that counterpart sign possesses neither color nor shape, because it lacks the nature of a separate ultimate reality (*paramattha-sabhāva*). "Such as this" [refers to it].

“Possessing color and shape. “Struck by the three characteristics” means either entered into the triad of characteristics such as arising (*uppāda*), etc., or marked by the triad of characteristics such as impermanence (*anicca*), etc.
If this [object] does not possess such color and so forth, how can it serve as the object of jhāna? To this he says, “For it is only...,” and so on.

“Produced by perception” means produced by the perception of meditation (*bhāvanā-saññā*), or merely arisen from the perception of meditation. For that which lacks intrinsic nature (*asabhāva*) cannot [arise] from anything.
There is an origin [for this]. Therefore he said, "merely the mode of appearance.
(58) The intention is that they are merely suppressed and settled, but no effort should be made for that purpose.
When it is said, "by access concentration," it follows by implication that the other kind of concentration also exists; therefore, in order to show that as well:
“Concentration is indeed twofold,” and so forth, begins the exposition.

“In two ways” means by these two causes: the distancing of the factors opposed to the states of jhāna, and the attainment of stability. Now, in order to show those causes by way of their stages, it is said:
“On the level of access (upacārabhūmi),” and so on. “On the level of access” means at the stage of access. Even though at that time...
The jhāna factors do not arise as more intense or having reached a sublime state;
rather, the mind becomes concentrated by the suppression of those states that are their opposites. Therefore he said: "By the abandoning of the hindrances, the mind becomes concentrated.
"In the stage of acquisition" means at the time of attaining the jhāna; for at that time, the jhāna factors have entered into absorption (appanā).
The mind becomes concentrated through its arising. Therefore he said, "by the manifestation of the factors. The connection is: "the mind becomes concentrated.
"Not of firm birth" means not having attained firmness, that is to say, not having reached the power of cultivation. "Mind" refers to the jhāna-consciousness.
"It remains for the whole night and for the whole day" is said with reference to the time of attainment. [This occurs] on the level of access concentration (upacāra-bhūmi).

Thinking that the development of the sign (*nimitta*) is appropriate, it is said: “having developed the sign. “Loss of what has been gained” means the loss of the access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*) already attained.

While the sign does not perish, the concentration that takes it as its object remains unlost; however, when the sign perishes due to a lack of protection, even the concentration already attained perishes, because its existence is dependent upon that sign. Therefore, he says: “In guarding,” and so forth.
59. Regarding the commentary on "it becomes stable":
after stating that it becomes stable, in order to show how it becomes stable, it is said, "mindfulness is established and the mind becomes concentrated.
For, having made mindfulness well-established upon whatever sign has been obtained there, [one proceeds].

For one who finds one-pointedness, it becomes firm and well-guarded. Furthermore, by the mention of mindfulness (*sati*), clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) is included here, and by the mention of concentration (*samādhi*), energy (*vīriya*) is also included, because they are not mutually exclusive. "Therein" means in those dwellings.
"Three each" means having stayed for three days at a time, according to the rule of staying in each dwelling place that was previously unoccupied.
The statement "to the north or to the south" is intended to prevent facing the sun during going and coming. "A thousand bow-lengths" is one and a half *kosa*.
Regarding the phrase "the thirty-two kinds of worldly talk," this refers to talk about kings and so forth;

for although these are not mentioned by their specific names in the text, they are included under the term "talk" (*iti-sadda*) alongside talk of forests, mountains, rivers, and islands, because heaven and liberation are beyond the scope of such worldly discourse.
“Thirty-two kinds of frivolous talk” have been mentioned. Regarding “based on the ten bases of talk”:

the bases for talk such as that on fewness of desires are these—fewness of desires, contentment, seclusion, non-association, arousal of energy, virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—and speech based upon these is suitable.

"Not one who talks irrelevantly" (*natiracchānakathiko*) means he is not one who engages in irrelevant talk; the intention is that he speaks only talk connected with a legitimate meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), which is contrary to irrelevant talk.
"Endowed with qualities such as virtue" (*sīlādiguṇasampanno*) means endowed with qualities such as virtue, concentration, and so forth.
For one who is himself established in the meditation subject of concentration, or has reached the further shore of the meditation subject of concentration, is suitable for this practitioner.
Therefore he said, "Depending on which," and so forth. "Abounding in bodily rigidity" means being intent upon the warming and nourishing of the body.

With reference to this, it was said: "Having eaten as much as he desires until his belly is full, he dwells devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness."
Food generally comes to the use of beings primarily through its sweet and sour tastes, as is seen in the case of curd and similar items.
However, pungent and other such tastes serve merely as stimulants; therefore, it is said:
"For some, the sweet is suitable; for some, the sour is suitable."
"In whichever posture as a basis," meaning while that posture is occurring, or "in whichever posture for one who is proceeding.

"Abundant cultivation of the sign" means: for one who is abundant in cultivation toward the sign—that is, for one who frequently cultivates the attention of meditation directed toward the counterpart sign as its object;
or, for one who is abundant in cultivation by way of cultivating the range of the sign. For it is by this [cultivation] that for one who is developing...
Through the cultivation of development (*bhāvanā*), the cultivation of the objective field (*gocara*) must also be intended. 60.
Commentary on the Tenfold Skill in Absorption (*appanā-kosalla*): There is no absorption. That tenfold method by which one becomes skilled in absorption is "skill in absorption."

Or it is the knowledge produced by that [purification]. Regarding "by making the basis clear": the connection is that skill in absorption (appanā) must be sought because it makes the bases (vatthu) clear.
The same applies to the remaining [purifications]. 61.
For the body is the locus for the occurrence of consciousness and mental factors; and the robes and so forth are dependent upon it.
And here, these are intended by the term "bases" (*vatthūni*). Their "clearing" (*visada-bhāva-karaṇa*) is the act of making them such that they bring happiness to the mind.
Therefore it is said: "of the internal and external," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "or the body":
the word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of "and"; [it means] the body is afflicted by sweat and grime, or by some other function of impurity.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Regarding the phrase "or a lodging" (*senāsanaṃ vā*), by the word "or," the inclusion of alms-bowls and so forth should be understood. One might ask: "Is this method not already included under the cutting off of minor impediments (*khuddakapalibodhupaccheda*)?
Why then is it stated again? It is true that it is included, but that was at the time of beginning the development of meditation (*bhāvanā*).

Here, however, for one who has commenced the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), having stood in access concentration (*upacārajjhāna*), [it is stated] for the sake of the preparatory period for absorption (*appanāparivāsa*).
The practice in that manner when a period of time has passed since the spring [of the path] is said for the sake of skill in absorption (*appanā-kosalla*).

Whether the object is not yet present or has become the object: how do those [objects] become the domain for one devoted to meditation? This is stated by way of the mental states (*cittuppāda*) that arise from time to time;
for those mental states lead to a lack of purity in one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) among the mind and mental factors (*citta-cetasika*). Regarding the mind and mental factors...
Regarding those things that serve as conditions such as the support (nissaya), etc.: the word "also" (pi) in the phrase "knowledge also" (ñāṇampīti) serves to include [other factors].
By this it is shown: "It is not only that object itself which is impure; rather, when that [object] is impure, knowledge also becomes impure.

Furthermore, the impurity of the states associated with that [knowledge] is established even without being explicitly stated. And the separate mention of knowledge is because it is of great assistance for absorption (appanā). Likewise...
For jhāna has been explained by way of knowledge as being "of slow direct-knowledge" and "of quick direct-knowledge.
Since that which is supported and the support itself are both called simply "the support," he said, "supported by the lamp, the stand, and the oil.
He stated, "by means of impure knowledge," and so forth, in order to show that when knowledge is not purified, the development of concentration is just as weak as the development of insight.
In this context, "meditation subject" refers to the meditation subject for serenity (*samatha*). Growth (*vuḍḍhi*) should be understood as the manifestation of the factors [of jhāna];
increase (*virūḷhi*) as the presence of the qualities; and abundance (*vepulla*) as the attainment of mastery in every respect. As for "the bright side," it is the white quarter [of the moon];
its meaning should be understood by reversing what was stated [for the dark side].
62. "Making them equal" means, in terms of function, making them neither deficient nor excessive.

Due to the more prominent state of the function of resolve (*adhimokkha*) toward an object of faith according to the conditions, and due to the lack of clarity in wisdom (*paññā*) and the laxity of energy (*vīriya*) and the other faculties, the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) becomes strong.
Therefore he said, "the others are weak. "From that" means from that [state] of the faculty of faith.

Because of its powerful nature and because other [mental factors] are weak. "Exertion" (*paggaha*) is the grasping and providing of support for the associated states, not allowing them to fall into the side of laziness.
It should be connected as follows: "It is unable to perform the function of exertion.
"Establishment" (*upaṭṭhāna*) is the act of approaching and remaining with the object, or the non-relinquishing of it; it is the opposite of distraction.
Non-distraction is that by which [the mind] associated with it becomes undistracted.

It is unable to perform the function of seeing—that is, to see the true nature of the object as it really is, just as the eye sees forms—because it is overwhelmed by the powerful faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
For among co-nascent phenomena (*sahajātadhamma*) that arise together while exercising their respective lordly functions (*indaṭṭha*), [one may be suppressed by another].

The accomplishment of the goal occurs solely through the state of having a single flavor (ekarasatā), and not otherwise. Therefore, the phrase "tasmā" (therefore) refers back to that very point by way of its causal relationship.
"Taṃ" (that) refers to the faculty of faith (saddhindriya). "By means of reflecting on the intrinsic nature of phenomena" (dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena) means:

for one in whom the faculty of faith has become powerful due to the exceptional occurrence of resolute conviction (adhimuccana) regarding the sublime qualities—such as loftiness—of the object to be believed, there arises [insight] from the analysis of conditions, the conditionally arisen, and so forth.

By investigating things as they truly are. For when things are grasped according to their intrinsic nature and essential flavor by way of this principle of the fixed nature of phenomena (*dhammatā*), there is no expansive resolve (*adhimokkha*);
this is because the activity of wisdom (*paññā*) is predominant through the thorough understanding that "this is the intrinsic nature of these phenomena.
Indeed, among the factors that bear the burden [of the path], just as there is a state of weakness in wisdom when faith is powerful, [so it is here].
Thus, when wisdom is strong, faith becomes weak. Therefore it is said: "It should be diminished by reflecting on the specific nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).

Likewise, regarding "by non-attention": this means not engaging in the cultivation of meditation in the manner that causes the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) to become strong for one who is devoted to cultivation. Here, [the faculty of faith] is twofold.
The state of being strong [occurs] either through a specific condition of one's own that exceeds its function, or because the functions of energy (*vīriya*) and the other faculties are weak.
Therein, in the first alternative, the method for weakening is shown;

however, in the second alternative, just as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) becomes strong for one who attends [to it] due to the weakness of the functions of energy and the others, so too, by not attending [to them], the functions of energy and the others [become weak].
By means of attention that brings about a state of proficiency, one should cause the faculty of faith to become of a single flavor with those [other faculties] and thus eliminate [its deficiency].
By this method, the procedure for eliminating [deficiencies] in the remaining faculties should also be understood.
Regarding the case of the Elder Vakkali: for that venerable one, having performed his duties through devotion to faith, was intent upon beholding the physical body (rūpakāya) of the Teacher.
While he was dwelling thus, the Teacher admonished him with the words, “Vakkali, what is the use of seeing this foul body?
He who sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me,” and so forth;
yet even though he was directed toward a meditation subject, failing to apply himself to it, he was dismissed and climbed to a precipice to cast himself down. Then the Teacher—
Sitting there as he was, emitting a radiance and revealing himself,
he said: “A bhikkhu who abounds in gladness, having faith in the Buddha’s teaching,
shall attain the state of peace, the bliss that is the subsiding of all conditioned formations.”
Having spoken this verse, he said, "Come, Vakkali. Being sprinkled by him as if with the Deathless itself, Vakkali became joyful and elated and began to practice insight (vipassanā).
However, because his faith was so powerful, he did not enter the path of insight.
Knowing this, the Blessed One, establishing him in the balance of the faculties, purified the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and gave it to him. He [then] by the Teacher...
By means of the method of giving, he intensified his insight and attained Arahatship through the successive stages of the Path. Therefore it is said:
"The story of the Elder Vakkali is an illustration in this regard.

"The distinction of other duties" refers to specific duties such as attending upon [the teacher] and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "tranquility and so forth," the enlightenment factors of concentration and equanimity are included.

The inclusion [of these factors] should be understood. Regarding "should be diminished": just as the state of strength of the faculty of faith is diminished by reflecting on the specific nature (*dhammasabhāva*) of phenomena, so too the intensity of the faculty of energy is diminished by the cultivation of tranquility (*passaddhi*) and the rest, because that [tranquility] belongs to the side of concentration (*samādhipakkhiya*).

For it is that [cultivation of tranquility], protecting the intensity of the faculty of concentration from falling into indolence, [is what constitutes] the cultivation of energy and the other [faculties].
Just as it guards against falling into restlessness by ensuring the preponderance of the faculty of energy, it causes [the hindrance] to be entirely abandoned.
Therefore it is said: "It is to be abandoned through the cultivation of tranquility and the other factors.
The story of the Elder Soṇa refers to the case of the delicate Elder Soṇa; for that venerable one was in the presence of the Teacher...
Having taken up his meditation subject and dwelling in the Sītavana forest, he resolved:
"My body is delicate, and it is not possible to attain happiness merely through ease; even by wearying the body, the duty of a recluse must be performed.

Thus, devoting himself solely to standing and walking, he applied himself to striving, remaining equanimous toward the pain even as blisters arose on the soles of his feet, maintaining his resolve firmly.
While exerting effort, he was unable to produce any distinction because his energy was over-exerted.

The Teacher went there, instructed him with the parable of the lute, and having shown the method for applying balanced energy and purified his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), He departed for Vulture Peak.
The Elder, too, by applying balanced energy according to the method given by the Teacher, brought his insight (*vipassanā*) to its peak.
He was established in arahantship. Therefore it is said: "The story of the Elder Soṇa should be shown.

"In the remaining ones as well" means in the case of the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. "Of each one" means of each individual faculty; this should be understood as a general statement.
Thus, having shown the balance [of the faculties] by way of the reduction of the excessive strength of each of the five faculties, [the text continues:]
Now, in order to show those for whom equality—specifically, unequally, individually, and equally—is required therein, it was said:
"But specifically... and so forth. "Therein" means among these five faculties. "Equality" refers to the state of faith and wisdom being neither deficient nor excessive in relation to one another;
likewise for concentration and energy. For just as faith and wisdom [are to be balanced] separately...
In particular, it is precisely desirable that those factors which have become the primary constituents of the yoke do not overstep one another in their function,
since absorption (appanā) is accomplished through their state of balanced equilibrium; thus, when there is a state of equal flavor between concentration and energy—
which belong respectively to the sides of sloth and agitation— due to their mutual support, the associated states avoid falling into either of the two extremes.
Absorption (appanā) succeeds only when [the conditions are right].
The passage beginning with “One who has strong faith” is stated by way of illustration. Its meaning is as follows:

one who possesses strong faith but lacks clear knowledge is “faith-placed” (muddhappasanna), not “one whose faith is rooted in penetration” (aveccappasanna). For such a person, in the absence of a factual basis...
He finds faith just like the disciples of the sectarians. He sides with the Kerāṭika faction, that is, he resorts to the side of deceit.

Running ahead with a wisdom devoid of faith, deceived by pseudo-reasons, he imagines such things as: "Merit consisting in giving arises even by the mere arising of the thought, without the relinquishing of the object to be given. Being thus, his mind is parched, scorched, and withered.
He does not accept the words of the wise and does not follow their counsel. Therefore it was said:
"Like a disease arising from medicine, he becomes incurable.

And just as here the mutual absence of faith and wisdom does not bring about welfare but brings about harm, so too here the mutual absence of concentration and energy does not bring about non-distraction but brings about distraction.
This is how it should be understood. The intention is that one overcomes laziness (*kosajja*), and because of that, one does not reach absorption (*appanā*).
The same principle applies here to the statement "one overcomes restlessness" (*uddhacca*). "Both of those" refers to the pair of faith and wisdom, as well as the pair of concentration and energy.
"It should be made equal" means it should be made of equal flavor (*samarasa*).
“Of one whose work is concentration” means of one whose meditation subject is serenity (*samatha*). “Thus” means this being so; the sense is: when faith is powerful in them.

“Having faith” means not considering how jhāna can arise merely by attending to “earth, earth,” but rather having faith and generating faith, thinking: “Surely the method taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One will succeed.”
"Okappento" means resolving by way of conviction as if entering into the object, leaping forward into it.
Strong one-pointedness is required because meditation (jhāna) has concentration as its primary factor.

"Of both" refers to concentration and wisdom; since for one whose task is concentration, a preponderance of concentration is also desired, he says "even by way of evenness," meaning by way of balance.
The meaning is as follows. "Absorption" (appanā) here refers to the absorption intended in this context.

For he speaks with apprehension, saying, "It indeed occurs," whereas for them, supramundane absorption is desired precisely through the balancing of those two. As it is said: "He develops serenity and insight coupled together.
If the equality of faith and wisdom, as well as concentration and energy, is desired specifically, why then does he mention mindfulness? He says: [to balance] mindfulness.
"But mindfulness must be strong in all cases. "In all cases" refers to the five faculties belonging to the sides of lethargy and agitation.
Taking those on the side of agitation, he says, "faith, energy, and wisdom.
One should also understand that it can be taken otherwise; for it is said, "by concentration on the side of laziness," and not "by tranquility, concentration, and equanimity."
That is mindfulness (*sati*). It is "universal" (*sabbatthika*) because it is appointed to all royal duties—that is, it is required everywhere for that purpose.
This is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "It is universal because it is appointed everywhere;

or, it is 'to be sought' (*atthiyā*) by means of the inclusion of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) belonging to both the side of sloth and the side of agitation; thus, being 'to be sought' everywhere, it is universal. "Mind" (*citta*) refers to wholesome consciousness (*kusalacitta*).

For when that [mindfulness] exists, it is a refuge and a resort for one who has not yet attained, for the sake of attaining what has not been attained, and for the sake of realizing what has not been realized.
Therefore he said: "It is manifested as protection," and so forth. 63.
"Of the sign of one-pointedness of mind" means of the sign of one-pointedness of mind, and of that which is termed one-pointedness of mind.
Regarding the sign (*nimitta*): for by observing the state of concentration of the mind and guarding the sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*), one guards the kasiṇa-sign.

Therefore, by the word "etcetera" in the phrase "of the earth-kasiṇa, etc.," it should be understood that not only the counterpart-sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) is included, but the sign of serenity as well. "That" refers to skill in guarding. Here, in this discourse on skill in absorption (*appanā*).
“Skill in signs” is what is intended here; the intention is that skill in the means and in development is already established.
64. By the phrase “excessive laxity of energy, etc.,” the word “etc. includes the opposites of gladdening and a sense of urgency.

“Lethargic” means contracted, fallen on the side of indolence. “Mind” refers to the mind engaged in development. [The factors beginning with] the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor, etc. [are to be understood].
Regarding the phrase "he develops," the word "three" should be brought forward and connected here.
As for how they are to be developed, he will explain that himself.
"Limited" means small. "Desiring to kindle" means desiring to light. "He should provide water and wind" means [water] mixed with water.
One should bring it under control through the wind-element. "Inopportune" (akāla) means not the right time, or an unsuitable time.

It is called *bodhi* because one awakens by means of it—referring to enlightenment (*bodhi*) defined as the assembly of factors such as mindfulness—or because one who possesses it awakens; thus, it is a factor (*aṅga*) for the practitioner (*yogin*) of awakening, hence a "factor of awakening" (*bojjhaṅga*).
A "perfectly awakened factor" (*sambojjhaṅga*) is a praised or beautiful factor of awakening. Tranquility (*passaddhi*) itself is characterized by the subsiding of the agitation of body and mind.

The enlightenment factor of tranquility (*passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga*), [and] of that enlightenment factor of tranquility. This same method applies to the enlightenment factors of concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth.
However, this is the distinction: first, the etymological meanings and characteristics of concentration have already been explained above.

It is called equanimity (*upekkhā*) because it looks on (*ikkhati*) with approach (*upa*). In terms of its actual meaning, this equanimity as an enlightenment factor here is precisely the equanimity of specific neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
It is to be understood. *Dusamuṭṭhāpayanti*: that which is impossible to arouse or produce. *Dhammavicayo*: the investigation (*vicaya*) of phenomena (*dhamma*), or among phenomena;
the meaning is "wisdom" (*paññā*). *Vīriya*: the state of one who is heroic (*vīra*), or his action, or that which is to be impelled (*īretabba*) or set in motion according to method;
it means "exertion" (*ussāha*). *Pīti*: that which refreshes the body and satisfies the mind.
"Whatever is one's own" means according to each individual; "one's own" is the meaning. "By way of nutriment" means by way of condition.
"Development" (bhāvanā) means production and increase. "Wholesome and unwholesome": in the sense of being produced through skill (*kosalla*), they are wholesome;
their opposites are unwholesome. Those that are unwholesome are blameworthy (*sāvajja*); those that are wholesome are blameless (*anavajja*). The unwholesome are inferior; the others are superior.
Alternatively, even wholesome states initiated with inferior zeal and so forth are inferior, while the others are sublime.

"Black" means dark, because they cause the mind to lose its luminosity; "white" means bright, because they cause the mind to become luminous. Or, they are black because they are the cause for rebirth in a black lineage, and white because they are the cause for rebirth in a white lineage.
These very same states are "with counterparts. For the black states are direct opposites [of the white].

The bright are counterparts to the dark; likewise, the dark are counterparts to the bright. Alternatively, "dark-and-bright-counterparts" refers to those that are both dark and bright and possess counterparts.
For pleasant feeling has painful feeling as its counterpart, and painful feeling has pleasant feeling as its counterpart.
"Of the unarisen" means of that which has not yet come into being. "For the arising" means for the purpose of producing it.
"Of what has arisen" means of what has been produced. "For further increase" means for repeated occurrence.
"For expansion" means for vastness. "For development" means for growth. "For fulfillment" means for the purpose of complete perfection.
"Therein" refers to the passage shown beginning with "There are, monks. "By way of penetration into the specific and general characteristics" means...
"Attention occurring in the course of an experience" refers to the arising of a javana consciousness that has occurred by way of penetrating, on one hand, the individual characteristics—

such as the grasping [of an object] as a single whole, which has a blameless and pleasant result, etc., and the touching [of it], etc.— and, on the other hand, the general characteristics such as impermanence, etc.
It does so by way of understanding those respective individual characteristics and so forth of the wholesome states and others exactly as they are.

For it is precisely because of its state of non-erroneous attention that it is called "wise attention" (*yonisomanasikāra*). Since it has that as its objective range, even the act of adverting (*āvajjanā*) is included therein.
It should be understood that even the characteristic of being subject to transformation (*ruppana-lakkhaṇa*), and so forth, is here subsumed under the general characteristic itself.
The energy that proceeds by way of the initial undertaking of wholesome activity is called a "constituent element" (*dhātu*) because its intrinsic nature is steadfastness (*dhiti*).
He said: "The 'element of initiative' (ārambhadhātu) is called the first energy.
Because energy that has gained practice reaches a state of power and disperses its opposites, he said: "Because it has emerged from indolence, it is stronger than that.
It becomes capable of dispersing even the most excessive opposing states, having reached a state of being sharp, sharper, and so forth; thus it was said: "Supreme..."
"Because it ascends to a higher state, it is even stronger than that. It is called *ṭhāniyā* because one stands (*tiṭṭhati*) or proceeds (*pavattati*) therein;

thus, "factors conducive to the joy factor of enlightenment" (*pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyā*) means those things which are conducive to the joy factor of enlightenment. Alternatively, *ṭhāniya* means that which should be established;
thus, "those in which the joy factor of enlightenment is established" means those associated with the joy factor of enlightenment as they proceed from one stage to another.
[These are] mental states (dhammas). However, since among those [mental states] joy alone is the specific cause for the joy enlightenment factor (pītisambojjhaṅga), it is therefore said:
"This is the name for joy itself. "Productive attention" means the kind of attention that, when one attends in such a way, the unarisen joy enlightenment factor arises and the arisen one increases.

"Being inquisitive" (*paripucchakatā*) means the state of questioning after having thoroughly investigated. For instance, it refers to one who, having mastered the five collections of the scriptures (*pañca-nikāya*) and attended upon a teacher, questions him regarding their respective meanings;

or alternatively, it refers to one who, having thoroughly investigated [the texts] together with the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), asks about each point that constitutes a knot (*gaṇṭhi-ṭṭhāna*) therein, saying: "Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?"
"The enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena arises.
The purification of the basis and the balancing of the faculties have already been explained both in brief and in detail.

However, there they were presented as leading to concentration, whereas here they are presented as leading to wisdom. For to the same extent that they lead to concentration, to that same extent they lead to wisdom.
Because knowledge is the manifestation of concentration; for it is said: "One who is concentrated understands things as they truly are.

Avoidance of persons of poor wisdom means keeping at a distance and abandoning those dull-witted, deluded individuals who are like crows that eat the food set out or dogs that eat the meat left behind.
Cultivation of persons possessed of wisdom means [associating with] those who have performed service through wisdom.
Approaching from time to time virtuous noble ones (ariya) who are skilled in the truths, dependent origination, and so forth, or those of great wisdom engaged in the practice of insight;
and reflecting upon the conduct of profound knowledge— that is, reflecting on the aggregates, bases, elements, and so forth, which are to be traversed by profound knowledges,
or on the discourses associated with emptiness that illuminate the truths, the modes of conditions, and so forth.
Reviewing. "Devotedness to that" means devotedness to wisdom; the meaning is being inclined toward, sloping toward, and leaning toward wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "the states of loss and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes birth and other forms of suffering rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the past, suffering rooted in the cycle of existence in the future, and in the present, suffering rooted in the search for nutriment. Of the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane, which depends upon energy...
Realization itself is the benefit; its nature of seeing [the truth] depends upon energy... [as previously shown].
Because it is the path leading to Nibbāna, the road of travel, that which is to be traversed, and that which is to be practiced—including its preliminary stages—it is called "the way" (*paṭipadā*).

It is called "honoring the alms-food" because it makes the gift of those who give the requisites bear great fruit, thereby acknowledging the service rendered to oneself by the donors of the requisites.
The honoring of the alms-round (*piṇḍa*) is by way of making right practice a state of great fruitfulness. "Otherwise" refers to material worship.

"Avoiding indolent persons" means avoiding those who are lazy, who do not know even the mere name of meditation, who are preoccupied with physical strength, who eat as much as they desire, who devote themselves to the pleasures of sleep and so forth, and who engage in frivolous talk.

The avoidance of persons from afar; the cultivation of association with persons who have aroused energy—meaning, approaching from time to time those persons who possess firm exertion by way of undertaking development according to the passage beginning, "By means of walking and sitting during the day";
and the reviewing of the right exertions—meaning, the power of the fourfold right exertion.

Reflective contemplation (*paccavekkhaṇatā*). Inclination toward that (*tadadhimuttatā*) means: inclination toward that energy-enlightenment factor (*vīriya-sambojjhaṅga*), being bent, inclined, and leaning toward it in all postures.

And herein, the removal of sloth and torpor, the avoidance of persons who are indolent, the cultivation of persons who have initiated energy, and inclination toward that [energy] function by way of dispelling the opposing factors and providing the necessary conditions;
while the reflection on the fear of the states of woe and so forth function by way of encouragement.
They should be seen as factors that give rise to the enlightenment factor of energy.
By the absence of serene confidence and affection toward the Buddha and others, persons are to be understood as "rough" individuals, whose hearts are as hard as husks;

conversely, by the opposite of that, they are to be known as "smooth" individuals. Those discourses that elucidate the virtues of the Buddha and others, such as the *Sampasādanīya Sutta*, are the "inspiring suttantas."
"By these modes" means by the modes such as the penetration of the specific and general characteristics of the wholesome and so forth as they have been described,
as well as by the modes such as thorough inquiry. "These states" refers to these states, namely, wise attention toward the wholesome and so forth,
as well as knowledge of the meaning of the Dhamma and so forth.
65. "By means of over-exerted energy, etc. means by means of energy that is excessively applied, and so forth. By the word "etc.," it includes agitation, joy, and the like.
"Agitated" means not calmed due to the weakness of concentration and other factors. "Difficult to settle" means impossible to pacify or to bring into composure.

"Having observed that mode" means: having observed and reflected upon that mode of the mental factors associated with consciousness—namely, the mode of serenity (*passaddhi*), the mode of concentration (*samādhi*), and the mode of equanimity (*ajjhupekkhitā*)—in whatever way these qualities of serenity and so forth previously arose at their respective times as appropriate for this practitioner. In all three [meditations]...
"In the passages" means in the three statements that have come down beginning with, "Bhikkhus, there is bodily tranquility," or in the three components of the Dhamma revealed by them.
Since serenity itself, when grasped after having observed the mode of being as it has been concentrated, is the sign of serenity, he said:
"And 'the sign of serenity' is a designation for serenity itself. Regarding "on various objects":
That which has various peaks (*agga*) due to its wandering is *byagga*; it is distraction.

For it is said that its essence is instability and its manifestation is wavering. Because it lacks one-pointedness, it is the opposite of non-distraction (*abyagga*), which is concentration (*samādhi*).

It should be stated as before that this itself is the "sign" (*nimitta*). Therefore he said: "And in the sense of non-distraction, that very [concentration] is a designation for the 'sign of non-distraction'."

Having understood the condition of the body, excellent food consumed in moderation becomes a condition for tranquility by giving rise to bodily lightness and so forth; likewise, when a favorable climate and a favorable posture are utilized, and physical effort is applied, it is said:
"the practice of consuming excellent food," and so on. [This is stated] because of the absence of imbalance in effort and the like.
Persons whose body and mind are agitated are persons who are restless. By the reverse of what has been stated, persons whose bodies are tranquilized are to be understood.
"Lacking relish" means devoid of the delight in cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

For when cultivation has entered the proper course and proceeds with successive stages of distinction, it brings to the mind the relish of tranquility and the happiness of peace; in the absence of that, the mind is without relish.
It exists. "By way of faith and a sense of urgency" means by way of faith and by way of a sense of urgency.
"Gladdening" means the act of gladdening thoroughly; it is the satisfying of the mind through cultivation that produces confidence preceded by a sense of urgency.

"Of that which proceeds rightly" means proceeding correctly—both evenly and with distinction—by being free from sluggishness and agitation, and by following the path of the course of serenity (*samatha*).
Of the consciousness that has proceeded in meditation. Equanimity (*ajjhupekkhanatā*) is non-engagement in exertion, restraint, or encouragement.
Reviewing the jhānas and liberations (*jhānavimokkhapaccavekkhaṇatā*) means: the first and subsequent jhānas are themselves liberations by virtue of being well-liberated from opposing states;
their cultivation is thus, their attainment is thus, their resolution is thus, and their emergence is thus.
"Thus is defilement, thus is purification"—this is contemplation of each [factor] individually.
Equanimity toward beings means the attitude of neutrality and impartial observation toward beings, whether they are objects of affection or consist of householders and those gone forth.
Equanimity toward formations means the attitude of neutrality toward internal things such as the eye and so on, and toward external things such as the alms-bowl and robes.
Equanimity. The act of claiming as "mine" the seven formations, the act of cherishing the seven formations.
"By these modes" means by these aforementioned modes, such as the observation of the state of tranquility in body and mind, and by modes such as the practice of suitable nutriment.
"These phenomena" refers to these phenomena beginning with tranquility.
"66. Due to the weakness of the application of wisdom (*paññā*)," means due to the scarcity of the activity of wisdom.

For just as generosity and virtue have non-greed (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adosa*) as their primary factors, so too does development (*bhāvanā*) have non-delusion (*amoha*) as its primary factor, especially when it leads to absorption (*appanā*). In that regard, when wisdom is not strong, then development does not produce delight in the mind, just as unprepared food does not please a man; therefore—

That [mind] becomes disinterested. And when cultivation does not bring about successive excellence due to practicing incorrectly, then the mind becomes disinterested because of the non-attainment of the bliss of tranquility.
Referring to both of these, it says: "Due to the dullness of wisdom and application," and so forth. "It" refers to the mind.
Birth, aging, sickness, and death occur respectively in the happy destinies and the miserable destinies; therefore, it is something other than those.
The suffering of the woeful states (apāya-dukkha) should be understood as being caused by the fivefold bondages, hunger, thirst, and mutual affliction.

Since all of that is already included as pertaining to the present existence of those respective beings, the sufferings rooted in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa-mūlaka-dukkha) for past and future times are taken separately. Furthermore, regarding those beings who subsist on nutriment, therein...

It should be understood that the eighth ground for spiritual urgency (*saṃvegavatthu*) is said to be the suffering of livelihood, which is not shared with others, experienced by those who subsist on the fruits of their own exertion.
Regarding the terms "unsluggish" (*alīna*) and so forth: it is "unsluggish" because of the absence of excessive states belonging to the side of indolence.
It is "not over-exhilarated" due to the absence of excessive states belonging to the side of restlessness.

It is "not dissatisfied" due to the perfection of application of wisdom and the attainment of the bliss of tranquility. Because of this very [absence of dissatisfaction], it proceeds evenly toward the object with successive stages of increasing excellence, having entered the path of serenity (*samatha*).
Therein, through non-laxity there is exertion (*paggaha*), through non-over-exhilaration there is restraint (*niggaha*), and through non-dissatisfaction...
It does not engage in the activity of self-exaltation. For it should be understood as follows: because of its state of being neither sluggish nor agitated, it proceeds evenly toward the object;

because of its lack of relish, it has entered the path of serenity (*samatha*). Alternatively, it is "neither sluggish" due to proceeding evenly, and "not agitated" due to having entered the path of serenity;
it is "without relish" due to having entered the path of serenity.

"The practice of renunciation" refers to the practice of meditative absorption (jhāna). "Devotion to concentration" means being diligently engaged in the production of concentration and the attainment of jhāna.

Since that [devotion] occurs by making concentration one's primary value and proceeding with a tendency, inclination, and leaning toward it, the phrase "valuing concentration," and so forth, was stated.
67. When the sign has been acquired, for one who accomplishes it in this way, there is skill regarding absorption; the connection is that “this absorption proceeds.
“It” refers to absorption. Regarding the word “having abandoned” (*hitvā*), the particle *hi* has the sense of a reason.
Because that state does not exist, therefore one should observe the mode of mental activity—the mode of occurrence of the development-mind by way of sluggishness, agitation, and so forth.
While examining [the mind], one should apply the evenness of energy itself to the very same flavor (samarasatā) of energy and concentration.
To the question, "How, then, should one apply them?", he says: "Even slightly," and so forth. Therein, *līna* means the state of being sluggish;
the meaning is "contracted. *Yanta* means "going"; the intention is that one should indeed exert [energy] for the sake of equilibrium. Therefore, he said: "Having restrained over-exertion..."
"One should cause it to proceed evenly. But how does one cause it to proceed evenly? He says: "As dust," and so forth.

"Yathā" (as): just as the activity of bees and others among the dust and so on has been correctly described in the Commentary by way of a simile, even so, having freed [the mind] from states of lethargy and restlessness, one should direct the mind toward the sign by means of applying equanimity of energy (*vīriyasamatā*).
The meaning is: "one should bring the mind of meditation face-to-face with the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*).
68. Commentary on the Instruction for Bringing [the Mind] Face-to-Face with the Sign:

Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tatra*), it refers to those two verses beginning with "In the dust," etc. "Illumination of the Meaning" (*atthadīpanā*) is the elucidation of the meaning of the simile and the thing illustrated by the simile.
"Ache" means unskilled. "Pakkhandati" means having begun to run forward. At the very moment of blooming, the flower possesses the essence of its pollen;
afterwards, it falls away due to wind and other factors, or becomes sapless.

Therefore, he said, "When the dust has subsided, one reaches [the goal]," meaning that the dust is cleared away upon turning back. "Puppharāsiṃ" refers to a heap of flowers clinging to the branches of trees.
“Among the pupils of the surgeon” means among the pupils of the master surgeon. “Placed in a water-tub” means placed in a water-vessel.
“Surgical work” refers to surgical procedures such as venesection and the like. “Even to touch a lotus leaf” is the connection [of the sentence].
“Equally” means not with a heavy or slow application as in the previous cases, but with an application of equal measure. “Therein” means...
"On a lotus leaf. "One with a purified craft" means one whose craft is thoroughly cleansed and perfected.
"Spider's thread" means a silken thread. "The pilot" is the helmsman of the ship. "The deck" refers to the framework of the ship made of reeds and the like.
"Filling the tube without spilling oil" means filling a small tube with oil contained in a saucer or similar vessel without letting any of it spill.

It fills the oil-tube. "In the same way" means: just as those previously mentioned—the honey-bee, the porcupine, the apprentice, the sawyer, and the oil-presser—exert their effort with speed, even so, the monk who exerts intense energy thinking, "I shall quickly reach absorption," and he who, like the honey-bee and the others mentioned in the middle, does not exert such energy—both of these, by virtue of the balance of their energy (vīriya-samatā), [attain it].

They are unable to reach absorption (*appanā*). However, that balanced application (*samappayoga*)—likened to bees and so forth mentioned at the end—is able to reach absorption because it is the application of evenness in energy (*vīriyasamatāyoga*); this is how the connection with the similes should be understood.
Therefore it was said: "A certain monk," and so forth. The intention is that the mind of development (*bhāvanācitta*) has become sluggish (*līna*).
Commentary on the First Jhāna (Paṭhamajjhānakathāvaṇṇanā) 69. "In this way" means by the manner already described.

For that yogi who, by means of yoking together the balance of energy, directs the mind of development—which has entered the path—toward the sign of the counterpart (paṭibhāga-nimitta) by fixing it thereon, [it will succeed]. "It will succeed" means...
"It will succeed" means "it will arise. "By way of application" means by way of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). "The remaining ones" refers to the remaining three or four.
"By way of ordinary minds" means by way of ordinary sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) minds. "Strong... [etc.

...one-pointednesses" [are so called] because they have attained a more acute nature through the power of cultivation. "Because of being preliminary" means because of their preparatory nature (*paṭisaṅkhārakatā*). "If, because of proximity..."
He says, "or because of moving in proximity," [meaning] that the designation "access" (upacāra) might apply only to the lineage stage (gotrabhū).

For even one who is not extremely close, if he moves within a short distance, is called one who moves in proximity. They are called "accesses" (upacārāni) because they move having approached absorption (appanā).

"Prior to this" refers to the preliminary stages (parikamma) in the cognitive process involving various adverting moments. "In these" refers to those designated as preliminary, access, and conformity (anuloma).
"Sabbantima" refers to the third or the fourth [jhāna]. "From the overcoming of the limited category" (*parittagottābhibhavanato*) means from the overcoming of the limited category.

For "category" (*gotta*) is so called because it goes along; the designation (*abhidhāna*) occurring as "limited" (*paritta*) protects both the understanding (*buddhi*) and the object, because they share a single-pointed objective range. Just as understanding [is protected] by the object which has become its referent...

Just as [an action] does not proceed without [its object], so too the designation does not proceed without that which constitutes its referent. Therefore, it is said that "it protects" (tāyati) those [referents]; that is, it guards them.

Furthermore, this should be understood as the unique form of sense-sphere phenomena (kāmāvacara-dhamma), which is devoid of the sublime and the supramundane, and serves as the objective domain for craving for sense-pleasures (kāmatanha).
The meaning should also be understood in this same manner regarding the sublime lineage (mahaggata-gotta). "From cultivation" (bhāvanato) means from production.

Since, in a general sense, all [terms] are synonyms for all [states], the first method is one that includes what has already been included; thus he said, "by way of including what was not previously included," and so forth.
With the intention that the preliminary work (*parikamma*) consists specifically of the various acts of adverting (*āvajjana*), it was stated, "or else the first access," and so forth.
The fourth is the absorption consciousness (*appanā-citta*); or else, according to the method explained previously, the fifth is the absorption consciousness, if it is the fourth.
The meaning is that one becomes a "change-of-lineage" person (*gotrabhū*). Regarding the phrase "or the fifth," the word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of non-fixity.

To show by what reason this non-fixity occurs, it is said: "And that is according to whether the direct knowledge is swift or sluggish. In this context, for one with swift direct knowledge, the mind enters the fourth [jhāna];
for one with sluggish direct knowledge, it enters the fifth. But why does it enter the fourth or the fifth?
"Not beyond that" means he says, "Beyond that, the impulsion falls.
The intention is that from the fifth onward, the sixth and seventh impulsions are as if falling because their momentum is exhausted.
Just as the first impulsion, having not yet acquired repetition, does not produce the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) due to its weakness, so too [the subsequent ones]... having acquired repetition...
However, because it has become strong, it produces either the second or the third *gotrabhū*;
thus, because it has become strong through the power of repeated practice (*laddhāsevanatā*), it enters upon the sixth and even the seventh—this is the Elder’s intention. Therefore he said:

“Therefore, absorption (*appanā*) occurs in the sixth and in the seventh. “That” refers to the Elder’s statement. [It is not accepted] because it is not supported by the suttas, the suttas’ concordant teachings, or the teachers’ doctrines.

It is stated as “only one’s own opinion. However, the Sutta passage “preceding wholesome states” is not a reason for the strength of the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*), because that is not invariably so.
For instance, even without having attained repetition, the first volition is to be experienced in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*);
whereas from the second volition up to the sixth, having attained repetition, they are to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparāpariyavedanīya*).
The passage beginning with “Only in the fourth and fifth” is stated for the purpose of concluding the aforementioned meaning by way of demonstrating its logical consistency.

In that regard, if the sixth and seventh impulsions are called “fallen” because their impetus is exhausted, how can the volition of the seventh impulsion be both to-be-experienced-in-rebirth and an immediate (ānantariya) deed?
This distinction is due to the attainment of strength through the acquisition of the condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya).
Why is this? Because of the distinction in the stages of the action. For the stage of action is threefold, by way of its beginning, middle, and end.

And therein, it should be understood that at the stage of the conclusion, volition possesses the state of being "to-be-experienced upon rebirth" (upapajjavedanīya) and so forth due to its nature as a "concluding volition" (sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā), and not because of its strength.
[This applies] to the stream of result (vipāka-santāna) which serves as the immediate condition (anantara-paccaya) for rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
