And they say it is because it has been so conditioned by way of being an immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*).
Therefore, for the sixth and seventh [stages], because they are facing a precipice, their exhaustion of momentum cannot be prevented. For it is said: "Just as a man," and so forth.
Furthermore, that is absorption (*appanā*). "Limitation of duration" means limitation of time. And that here occurs in seven places.
In some cases it is said that [the full duration] does not exist because of the immeasurability of the thought-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*), and in others because the moments are extremely brief.
For here the complete course of the impulsion (*javana*) is not obtained. Therefore he said: "Herein, the fruit immediately following the path," and so forth.

"In the remaining places" refers to the first absorption (*paṭhamappanā*), mundane direct knowledge (*lokikābhiññā*), the moment of the path (*maggakkhaṇa*), and the moment of the fruit for one emerging from cessation (*nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa phalakkhaṇa*).
In these four places.

"By this much" means by this sequence of development (*bhāvanā*), this practitioner of yoga (*yogāvacara*) enters and dwells in the first jhāna. And for one dwelling thus, the connection is that he has attained that very same first jhāna based on the earth-kasiṇa (*pathavīkasiṇa*).
70. "Therein" means in that recitation of the jhānas. "Having secluded oneself" means having become separate. Therefore he said: "having become apart, having withdrawn."
The meaning is: "having withdrawn by way of abandoning. Regarding the phrase "quite secluded from sensual desires" (*vivicceva kāmehi*):

here, by the word "secluded" (*vivicca*), the mere absence of sensual desires at the moment of jhāna is stated. However, by the word "quite secluded" (*vivicceva*), the fact that jhāna is the opposite of sensual desire is indicated through the demonstration that sensual desires must be definitively separated from;
furthermore, it shows that seclusion from sensual desire is the means for attaining jhāna.
In order to demonstrate this meaning—that [the first jhāna] has been shown—the passage beginning with “the first jhāna” was stated;
then, to make that same meaning more evident, the passage beginning with “how” was spoken.

By the phrase “like the light of a lamp when there is darkness,” he shows that just as the darkness of night is overcome by the absence of a lamp’s light, so too is the realm of sensual desire overcome within the continuum of beings by the absence of jhāna.

The word "only" (*eva*) is a restrictive term applied specifically to the preceding phrase. However, it should not be understood as "only by means of sensual pleasures," because no such restriction has been made.
It is called "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) because one escapes from or goes forth by means of it, or because it exists therein.
What is it that goes forth? It is sensual pleasures; the escape from those sensual pleasures—that is, their abandonment—is "the escape from them. From what [does one escape]? From that. How?
However, since the suppression [of defilements] is the same [in all cases], one might raise the objection: "This is the escape from sensual desires alone, not from ill-will and so forth.
To clear this away through both reasoning and scripture, the passage beginning with "the sense-sphere element" (kāmadhātu) was stated.

Therein, "by transcending the sense-sphere element" means because this is the path for transcending the entire existence of the sense-sphere (kāmabhava). By this, he states that this jhāna constitutes the full understanding (pariññā) of sensual desire.
"By way of being the opposite of sensual lust" means because it is the adversary of the defilement of sensual desire (kilesakāma), which will be analyzed below.
By this, he shows that just as loving-kindness is the opposite of ill-will and compassion is the opposite of cruelty, so too this jhāna is the direct antidote to sensual lust.
Thus, by its own occurrence and the occurrence of its result, its intrinsic nature is such that it turns away from sensual lust and from the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu).
This jhāna is specifically the escape from sensual pleasures (kāmā) alone. Since this point is already established by the text, he says “as it has been said,” and so forth.
Granted, the restrictive particle was already employed in the preceding phrase to illustrate this meaning;

however, the words “even in the subsequent phrase” and so forth were stated to show that the particle must likewise be understood in the subsequent phrase as well, because the sense is possible there too. From this...

From sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). This is the fixed rule. By the term "in common" (*sādhāraṇavacana*), it means by way of an undifferentiated expression. "Separation through its own nature, suppression, eradication, tranquillization, and escape" refers to separation through its own nature (*tadaṅgaviveka*) and so forth.

"Separation of mind, body, and substrate" refers to separation of mind (*cittaviveka*) and so forth. Only these three are to be understood here in this discourse on *jhāna*, because separation through eradication (*samucchedaviveka*) and the others are impossible in this context.

It is explained in the *Mahāniddesa*. For there, after first stating, "In brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures: sensual pleasures as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasures as defilements (*kilesakāma*)," the sensual pleasures as objects are then defined by the passage beginning, "In that regard, what are sensual pleasures as objects? Agreeable forms... agreeable tangibles," and so forth.
Furthermore, they should be understood as "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) because they are desired (*kāmīyanti*). "Right there" means in that very explanation (*niddesa*).
"In the *Vibhaṅga*": in the *Jhāna-vibhaṅga*. Weak greed that proceeds by way of aspiration is "desire" (*chanda*) in the sense of longing;
stronger than that is "lust" (*rāga*) in the sense of coloring; even stronger than that is "intense lust," which is "desire-and-lust" (*chandarāga*).

It is called "intention" (*saṅkappa*) because one intends the signs and secondary characteristics by means of it; it is the greed proceeding in that manner, and stronger than that is "lust" in the sense of coloring.
That which proceeds by way of mere intention is even stronger than that; it is called "intentional lust" (*saṅkapparāga*).

This distinction is to be understood as being due to the mode of occurrence of a single state of greed (*lobha*), and also due to the difference in its stages, just as [one says] "a calf," "a tamed ox," or "a draft-ox.
These are the defilement-desires (*kilesakāma*). They are called *kāma* because they desire, or because one desires by means of them.

"Evaṃ hi sati" means: when there is thus an inclusion of both kinds of desire. "Vatthukāmehipi" means that the sense of "even by way of objects of sensual pleasure (*vatthukāma*)" is also appropriate;
thus, the particle *pi* has the sense of adding another meaning that is logically consistent, not the sense of adding the defilements of sensual pleasure (*kilesakāma*).
Why? Because in this context, seclusion from the defilements of sensual pleasure is already established by the second phrase.

Because it has been stated thus. "By that" means by the seclusion from sensual objects (*vatthu-kāma*); thus, bodily seclusion (*kāya-viveka*) is expressed, as this illustrates seclusion from the possession of children, wife, and so forth.

"By the former" means by bodily seclusion. "In this" refers to these two phrases: "quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states," or to the two kinds of seclusion distinguished from this [context].
Even though the word "unwholesome" (*akusala*) refers to the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesa-kāma*),...
Alternatively, all unwholesome states may be included; however, since seclusion from the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*) has been stated in every respect, he says:

"Because of the statement of seclusion from the defilements of sensual desire in the second [phrase]. And "by the second" means by the seclusion of mind (*cittaviveka*). "Of these" refers to the two aforementioned phrases;
this is the genitive case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). It is the abandoning of the basis for the defilements such as craving (*taṇhā*).
The abandoning of the basis for defilement: "Lustfulness" means the arising of craving for various objects such as forms and so forth;
its cause should be understood as sense-desires themselves (*vatthukāmā*). "Foolishness" is ignorance (*avijjā*), or thinking ill-thought thoughts and the like;

its cause is improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), or all unwholesome states (*akusala-dhammā*) are the cause. Furthermore, even the cause for attaining the strands of sensual pleasure involves impure practices such as killing living beings and so forth.

By means of detachment from that [object], purification of the application is manifested. Through the cleansing of the defilement of craving and through the strengthening of the support for turning away (*vivaṭṭa*), there is the purification of the underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) and the nourishing of the latent tendency (*āsaya*).
"In sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) is the locative case used in the sense of selection.

"Of many kinds" means it is manifoldly divided by way of the taint of sensual pleasure (*kāmāsava*), the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*), and so forth, as well as by way of craving for form (*rūpa-taṇhā*) and the rest.
"Kāmacchando yeva" means that desire is of the very nature of sensual pleasure; the intention is that it is neither the desire for action nor wholesome desire.
It is mentioned separately because it is an adversary to jhāna—that is, by virtue of being its opposite and its cause.
It is taken separately in its own form rather than being included under the general category of unwholesome states. If "sensual desire" (kilesakāma) alone were intended in the first phrase...
Having asked, "Since it has been stated [in the singular], how can there be a plural form?", he says, "Because of its many divisions," and so forth.

This refers to other factors as well, such as views, conceit, lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), and lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), as well as the contact (*phassa*) and other mental states associated with them.

The "higher jhāna-factors" (*upari-jhānaṅga*) are those jhāna-factors that will be discussed further on; they are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*) because they are stated to be the opposites of their respective adversaries, thereby demonstrating their state of being the counter-agents to those adversaries.
For the hindrances are the opposites of the jhāna factors because they obstruct their occurrence.

Concentration is the antidote to sensual desire because it is the direct opposite of the longing for passion, and because it steadies the mind that is wandering about, being enticed by various objects.
Joy is the antidote to ill will because it shares in the same security of well-being as gladness.
Applied thought (*vitakka*) is the antidote to sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), because it functions with expansion by way of wise intention (*yoniso saṅkappana*).
Pleasure (*sukha*) is the antidote to restlessness and remorse (*uddhaccakukkucca*), which are by nature lack of tranquility and burning heat, because pleasure is by nature tranquil and cool.
Sustained thought (*vicāra*) is the antidote to doubt (*vicikicchā*), because it has a nature resembling wisdom (*paññā*) by way of its continuous investigation of the object.
The *Peṭaka* is the commentary on the Piṭakas taught by the Elder Mahākaccāyana; [it refers to] within that *Peṭaka*.

Regarding "the object consisting of the distinctions of the five strands of sensual pleasure": this refers to the specific objects of the five strands of sensual pleasure, such as visible forms and so forth. Regarding "objects consisting of the distinctions of the bases for resentment (*āghātavatthu*) and so forth":

by the expression "seclusion from ill-will" (*byāpādaviveka*), there is the mention of hatred (*dosa*) which has as its object the distinctions of the bases for resentment, such as "he has done me harm," and so forth.

By the term "seclusion" (*viveka*), the suppression (*vikkhambhana*) of delusion (*moha*)—which has as its objects such things as suffering and the past limit—is described as being concealed by sloth, torpor, and so forth, which are predominant in that delusion. And this [seclusion] suppresses sensual lust, ill-will, and the sloth-torpor etc.
associated with them, because it has the nature of being the opposite of all unwholesome states. By virtue of that nature, it abandons all unwholesome states among all wholesome states.
Whether it exists or not, it possesses the very nature of suppressing sensual desire and so forth;
because it has that nature, he said—without making a distinction—that "seclusion by suppression" is stated for the hindrances, the unwholesome roots, and the rest.

(71) Since there is no exercise of mastery over intrinsic phenomena as they proceed according to their respective conditions, [this is] for the purpose of precluding the state of having mastery over them.

“Vitakka is the act of thinking (vitakkana),” it is said. Since this "act of thinking" is the imagining of an object in the form, "The object is such-and-such," he says, "it is called 'weighing' (ūhana).

Because the mind, through the power of vitakka, becomes as if it has fully ascended upon the object, it is therefore described as having the characteristic of directing the mind toward the object (ārammaṇābhiniropana).
For just as someone [might approach] a royal favorite or a relative to that [favorite]...
Just as one might ascend to or enter the royal palace by relying on a friend, so too does consciousness ascend to an object by relying on applied thought (*vitakka*).
If this is so, how does consciousness that is without applied thought (*avitakka*) ascend to an object? It is precisely through the power of applied thought.
For just as that same man, through familiarity, enters the royal palace without apprehension even without [the friend], so too, through familiarity...

Even without applied thought (*vitakka*), a mind without applied thought (*avitakka*) mounts upon its object. By "through familiarity" is meant through the familiarity consisting in the cultivation of applied thought as it occurs within the mental continuum.
For, by virtue of applied thought occurring frequently within the continuum, the mind’s mounting upon the object becomes long-practiced;
therefore, at times it proceeds there even without applied thought. This is just as in the case of [insight] accompanied by knowledge (*ñāṇasahita*).
Just as something that was previously familiar through the practice of contemplation may at times proceed by way of contemplation even when devoid of knowledge;

or just as something that proceeded accompanied by defilements may, though entirely free from defilements, proceed by virtue of the latent tendencies of those defilements due to past habituation—so too should this be understood.
Striking (*āghāta*) is the act of striking (*āhana*) directed toward (*abhi*) [the object] from the outset (*ādito*). From all sides (*parito*),...

“Striking” (*āhanana*) or “striking repeatedly” (*pariyāhanana*) means turning it over and striking it. It should be understood as the occurrence [of the mind] as if one were striking [an object], thinking, “Form is form,” or “Earth is earth.
“Bringing” (*ānayana*) means leading the mind toward the object, or drawing it back to it.

*Anusañcaraṇaṃ* means wandering along or revolving around. This specific distinction should be understood as becoming manifest within the mental continuum (*santāna*) precisely because it is obtained within that very continuum.
The same principle applies to the others as well. *Anumajjanaṃ* is the mind’s stroking of the object;
the meaning is "rubbing all around. For it is said that sustained application (*vicāra*) is "like a hand that rubs all around" or "like a hand that moves about."

And it has been stated [thus]. "Therein" means in the object (*ārammaṇe*). The application (*anuyojana*) to co-nascent states should be understood by way of the very same "rubbing" (*anumajjana*), which is the reckoning of sustained examination (*anuvicāraṇa*) upon the object.
"Continuous binding" (*anuppabandhana*) is the occurrence of the mind upon the object as if uninterrupted.
For that reason, it is defined as "the state of connecting" (*anusandhānatā*). And for that very reason, it is described as "like the resonance of a bell" and "like revolving."

"In some places" means in the first jhāna and in limited states of consciousness. It is gross in the sense of being coarse compared to sustained application (*vicāra*), and it is the precursor to that very sustained application.

Thus, applied thought (*vitakka*) is like the striking of a gong, which is the precursor to its resonance. For just as the striking of the gong is the initial impact, so too is applied thought the initial directing of the mind toward the object in the sense of placing it before it.
Applied thought (*vitakka*) is the mind’s initial application. Here, by the term "impact," it should be understood that the sound produced by the impact is included.
"Diffuse" means connected with vibration and accompanied by movement, like a wandering about for the purpose of testing whether there is any danger.
It occurs through continuous succession, either in access concentration (*upacāra*) or in absorption (*appanā*).
In the continuity of the process. For therein, applied thought (*vitakka*) proceeds as if it were entering into the object after becoming steady, not at the very first moment of impact.
It becomes manifest: this specific mode of directed application (*abhinīropanākāra*) of applied thought is manifest in the first jhāna because of its grossness;
due to the absence of that [grossness], in the second jhāna of the fivefold system, [sustained thought] (*vicāra*) [is manifest].
The specific mode of reflection becomes manifest.
A "hair-cleanser" (*vālaṇḍupaka*) is a pad made of wool or similar materials. The "hand for pressing" (*uppīḷanahattha*) is the hand used for pressing the mass;
it is the hand that moves back and forth over that very [mass]. A "circle" (*maṇḍala*) refers to some circular mark or line on a bronze vessel or the like.

While performing [the meditation]. Just as a tree—which, though non-existent apart from its constituent parts such as flowers, fruits, and branches—is conventionally designated as "having flowers" or "having fruit"—so too, although jhāna is non-existent apart from its factors such as applied thought (vitakka) and so on, it is conventionally designated as "with applied thought and sustained thought" (savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ).
To show this, the phrase "like a tree," etc., was stated. [This concludes the section] on the cultivation of jhāna by way of the individual (puggala).
Because they must be taught, the jhānas are indicated by way of a person through the passage beginning, "Here, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures...

Although the teaching in the Vibhaṅga is presented by way of a person, the meaning therein in the Vibhaṅga should be understood exactly as it is stated here by way of phenomena (dhamma), such as "by this thought-conception," and so forth; for in the ultimate sense...

The intention is that there is no person (puggala) whatsoever. The meaning... [etc. ...should be understood by way of showing that one possessing jhāna possesses applied and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra), and because it is stated that jhāna itself is "with applied and sustained thought" (savitakka-savicāra). Or rather, the meaning here should be understood in this way:
"from seclusion" (vivekā) means "seclusions acting as causes," having in mind the fact that the word *viveka* functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*). "In seclusion" (viveke)...

[It expresses] either the sense of the agent (*kattu-sādhana*) or the sense of the object (*kamma-sādhana*). For by the word "secluded" (*vivitto*), both modes of expression are indeed included: that which is devoid of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and that which is separated from them.

72. "It refreshes" (*pīṇayati*) means it satisfies or increases. "Characterized by gratification" (*sampiyāyana-lakkhaṇā*) means characterized by complete contentment. "Having refreshment as its function" (*pīṇana-rasā*)...
The function of intensifying is its essence. The function of pervading means that it suffuses the body with sublime forms. *Udaggatā* (elation) is the state of being uplifted.
The minor [type] is merely a slight thrill of the hair that, once broken, does not arise again;
the momentary [type] arises frequently. Pervasion is superior to elation because of its immobility and its long duration. [This occurs at] the temple courtyard (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*).
"Having gone" means having gone to the courtyard of the shrine (*cetiyāṅgaṇa*) in the Puṇṇavallika Monastery.
"By way of an object seen in the natural state" means by way of an object previously apprehended at the Mahācetiya. "A painted ball" is a ball made in various forms.
"In dependence" (*upanissaye*) means in the vicinity, or in that which serves as the support for that monastery; the meaning is "in its range of activity."
*Gharājire* means in the courtyard of the house. A shrine built on a mountain peak is called an "air-shrine" (*ākāsacetiya*).

*Gahitanimitteneva* means by means of the wholesome object (*kusalanimitta*) grasped for the purpose of worshipping the shrine and listening to the Dhamma—namely, the thought beginning with "Blessed indeed are these [beings]" which serves as the cause—or alternatively, it refers to the mind proceeding in the manner described, having taken that object as its basis.
Together with the mind that has grasped that very sign, they "leap forward" (pakkhandanti), meaning they have entered [into it].
They "permeate" (anuparipphuṭanti), meaning they are pervaded from all sides and in every way; the sense is that they have completely suffused it.
By means of serenity, they take up the embryo (the seed); by means of ripening, they reach maturity.
Only the joy associated with absorption (appanā) fulfills absorption concentration (appanāsamādhi).

That which fulfills momentary concentration (khaṇikasamādhi) and that which fulfills access concentration (upacārasamādhi) are much further removed from absorption concentration; therefore, not mentioning those two, he said:

"Among them, that which [is associated] with absorption concentration," and so forth. "Having come to association with concentration" means having previously been associated with access concentration and subsequently increasing in stages.
It has attained association with absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*).
73. It is called "pleasure" (*sukha*) because it pleases; the meaning is that it causes the states associated with itself to obtain satisfaction.
This designation as an agent is obtained figuratively for the purpose of excluding any agent other than the dhamma; but in the primary sense, however—
Since it is obtained as a noun of action (*bhāvasādhana*), it is stated as "pleasure (*sukha*) is the act of being pleased.

Because its intrinsic nature is desirable, it causes the person possessing it, or the associated mental states, to settle within itself; thus it is called *sāta* (with the substitution of the letter *t* for the letter *d*).
They call *sāta* "sweet. That which has *sāta* as its characteristic is "having *sāta* as its characteristic" (*sātalakkhaṇa*). It is the nourishment of the associated mental states.
Fostering (*saṃvaḍḍhana*): the successive grasping [of the object] without discarding it as if it were suffering, nor regarding it with equanimity as if it were neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
or, assistance (*anuggaha*) is its helpfulness. In some instances, such as the first jhāna and so forth.

"Satisfaction at acquisition" (*paṭilābhatuṭṭhi*) means satisfaction arising by way of acquisition. "Experiencing the flavor of what has been acquired" (*paṭiladdharasānubhavana*) refers to the flavor of the object that has been acquired.
"Experiencing" shows the distinction between joy (*pīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*) by way of their intrinsic natures.
"Where there is joy, there is pleasure" expresses the absolute conjunction of joy with pleasure, as in the case of applied thought (*vitakka*) with the other [factors].
"Where there is pleasure, there is not necessarily joy" expresses the non-absolute conjunction of pleasure with joy, as in the case of sustained thought (*vicāra*) with applied thought. By this...
This shows the distinction between rapture and pleasure through their association with the finite and the infinite. "Kantāra" means that which causes one to cross over (*kaṃ tārenti ettha*);
it is a waterless desert. "Vananta" means the forest itself. "At each respective time" refers to: at the time of obtaining a desirable object;
at the time of experiencing the flavor of what has been obtained; at the time of hearing or seeing the forest's shade and so forth; and at the time of entering and enjoying them.
"By way of manifestation" means by way of the clear appearance of rapture and pleasure in their respective order.
Regarding the phrase "rapture and pleasure born of seclusion," in the first sense, "born of seclusion" refers to the jhāna.

From the word "rapture and pleasure," and because of the specific meaning of the suffix *atthi*, the letter *a* should be understood here as meaning "of this jhāna" or "in this jhāna. In the second [sense]...

It is precisely rapture and pleasure born of seclusion (*vivekaja-pītisukha*). The compound *vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ* is a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (compound with a different referent), and the elision of the case-ending in the individual designation has been made.
Alternatively, if the elision were not applied, the reading would be *vivekajapītisukhaṃ*; this is the distinction.
Regarding the word *upasampajja*, here the prefixes *upa-* and *saṃ-* are meaningless, as in the cases of words such as *upalabbhati* (“is found”) and *saṃbhuñjati* (“eats together”).
Having stated "having approached" and so forth in order to show this, it was further said "having ordained" and so forth to demonstrate their purposefulness;
therefore, the meaning is "having reached" or "having accomplished. *Iriyanti* means activity (*kiriya*). *Vutti* and the others are synonyms for that very thing.
For "preservation" (*pālanā*) is the protection of one posture by means of other postures when one posture is being disturbed.
Commentary on "Abandoned of Five Factors," etc. (74):
That from which five factors have been abandoned by way of suppression is "abandoned of five factors" (*pañcaṅgavippahīna*).
Here, the word *vippahīna* should be understood as having the same grammatical function as the word *āhita* in the compound *agyāhito*; [it is a past participle] with respect to the five [factors].
"Abandoned by the factors" means abandoned by the five factors. [An objection: "Are not other unwholesome states also abandoned by this jhāna?
Then why is it said to be 'abandoned by the five factors' specifically? To this he says, "Even though... and so forth.

Since even for one who has attained jhāna, at times when they are not actually possessing the jhāna, there is the occurrence of greed and other mental states that are opposed to jhāna, he specifies "at the moment of jhāna."
It has been said. "They are abandoned" means they disappear; the meaning is that they do not proceed.

"Upon a single object" means upon an object that is of a single nature by way of the earth-kasiṇa and so forth, or upon an object that produces singleness, which is known as one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*). "That" refers to that mind which was enticed by various objects.
"For the abandoning of the sense-sphere" means for the abandoning—that is, the transcending—of the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*) which is crowded with various objects.
It does not enter upon the path of meditation (*jhāna*). "Without interval" means uninterrupted by distraction; the sense is that it is continuous. "Unworkable" means unfit for work;
the sense is that it is unsuitable for the task of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). "Overcome by restlessness and remorse" means overpowered by restlessness and remorse.
It "wanders about" because of instability—that is, because of a lack of steadiness (*avaṭṭhāna*) or concentration (*samādhāna*).
The meaning is "due to non-existence. "Afflicted by doubt" means it is afflicted by doubt that arises because of the absence of superior investigation, such as:
"Is the Blessed One truly a perfectly enlightened Buddha, or is he not?"; through mental attention such as "earth, earth," and so forth;
and through doubt such as: "Might there be jhāna, or might there not? It does not ascend because it is a sign of non-attainment.
"Specifically, because they create obstacles to jhāna" means that, by being the direct adversaries of concentration and the other factors, they create an impediment to the attainment of jhāna.
"By those" refers to applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), which serve as conditions for the attainment of jhāna.

"For one who has accomplished the application for non-distraction" means for one who has thus produced the practice of cultivation for the sake of such composure. "The possibility of the perfection of mental application."
It arises from the successful application of the practice of meditation as previously described. *Pīti* is gladdening; it is a warming [of the mind] by way of meditation.

The connection is that it brings about the nourishment and growth of the mind by way of meditation. *Taṃ* refers to the mind. *Sasesasampayuttadhammaṃ* means together with the remaining associated states, such as contact (*phassa*) and so forth.
The connection is that it "places" (*ādhiyati*) [the mind] evenly (*samaṃ*) and rightly (*sammā*). This is by way of the equilibrium of the faculties (*indriyasamatā*).

"Equally" means equally with respect to opposing states (*paṭipakkhadhamma*). The meaning is that it "places [the mind] rightly" by being free from both laxity (*līna*) and agitation (*uddhacca*) during the state of distance [from those opposites].

For one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), by its function of concentrating, causes the mind and its associated mental factors to follow after itself, thereby making them exceptionally concentrated at the moment of absorption (*jhāna*).
"By way of arising" means by way of arising according to conditions. Among these...

Meditative absorption (*jhāna*) is said to have arisen with respect to applied thought (*vitakka*) and the other factors precisely because of the conventional designation of "absorption" applied to them. Therefore, he says "Therefore," and so forth.
Furthermore, by means of the simile beginning with "Just as," he makes that same point even more clear.
"From the natural mind" means from the ordinary sense-sphere mind (*kāmāvacara-citta*). "By the very lucid" means by the well-purified, that is, by the more acute.
The meaning is as follows: "Containing all" (*sabbāvanta*) means containing all constituent parts; the meaning is "without remainder. "Untouched" (*apphuṭa*) means not contacted.
It is said that one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*), occurring by way of absorption (*appanā*), is as if it pervades the object on all sides because it touches the objects.
But why is this one-pointedness of mind included here when it was not included in the standard recitation of the jhānas?
With reference to *anuyoga* (the subsequent application), it was stated: "Therein, one-pointedness of mind," and so forth. "Therein" means among those jhāna factors.
"Not specified" means not specified by way of its own specific form (*sarūpato*), but rather included by the general mention of "jhāna.

"Because it was stated thus" means because it was stated by its own specific form; the connection is that "one-pointedness of mind is itself a factor. "By which intention" refers to [the intention] regarding applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth.

The summary was made by way of the intention to explain it, in order to illuminate the dhamma occurring together [with it], beginning with the words "accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ*).
That very intention was made manifest by the Blessed One in the *Vibhaṅga* when he pointed it out as "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittekaggatā*).
Therefore, one should not think that this [one-pointedness] is not included in the exposition of the jhānas.
Commentary on the Threefold Goodness (Tividhakalyāṇa): 75.

“By way of beginning, middle, and end” means by way of the beginning, middle, and end of the jhāna. “By way of characteristic” means by way of their state of being characterized within the absorption (appanā) itself.
“Therein” refers to that exposition of the characteristics of goodness. “Purity of the way” (paṭipadā-visuddhi) refers to that which one enters into, namely, the jhāna.

This is the way of practice (*paṭipadā*), the method of development (*bhāvanā-naya*) belonging to the prior stage, culminating in the lineage-determining state (*gotrabhū*). Purification (*visuddhi*) is cleansing from obstacles;
purification of the way of practice is "purification-of-way-practice" (*paṭipadā-visuddhi*). Since this is obtained at the moment of the arising of jhāna, it is therefore said:
"Purification-of-way-practice comes first. "The intensifying of equanimity" refers to [the factors] such as that which is to be purified.

“Development through equanimity” (upekkhānubrūhanā) refers to the fulfillment of the function of the neutral equanimity included within the jhāna by means of its non-existence [when other factors are present].
This, moreover, is specifically obtained at the moment of the jhāna’s stability (ṭhiti). Therefore it is said: “Development through equanimity in the middle.
“Encouragement” (sampahaṃsanā) refers to the fulfillment of the function of knowledge that accomplishes the non-overstepping of those factors and so forth.
Purification. Since that [purification] becomes evident at the concluding moment of the jhāna, it is therefore said: "Encouragement is the conclusion.

These three characteristics—namely, the mode of the mind’s purification from obstacles, the mode of proceeding toward the middle sign of serenity (samatha), and the mode of leaping into that [sign]—are the three characteristics of the jhāna from the beginning.

At the moment of arising, these possess the characteristics of reaching absorption (*appanā*), because there is no attainment of absorption without those modes, and if absorption is absent, those [characteristics] are likewise absent. It is "good in the beginning" because it is a path of purification.

It is "endowed with the three characteristics" because it is possessed of the characteristics already mentioned, and because its characteristics are perfected. In this same manner, the application of the characteristics of the middle and the end should be understood.

That by which meditation (*jhāna*) is brought about is "equipment" (*sambhāra*), namely, the preliminary work consisting of various acts of adverting. Together with this equipment is "with-equipment" (*sasambhāra*);
that itself is "possessing-equipment" (*sasambhārika*). "Access" (*upacāra*) refers to the access of a single act of adverting.

Since the function beginning with exertion (*paggaha*) has already been accomplished through cultivation prior to that, the equanimity established there in the access of a single act of adverting is [present] at the moment of absorption (*jhāna*).
It is said that "intensification" (paribrūhitā) is absorption (*appanā*); thus it is stated: "Absorption is called the intensification of equanimity.
Regarding the state of mental exhilaration and satisfaction based on the jhāna already attained, which occurs by way of reviewing, it is said:
"Gladdening is called reviewing. "Some" refers to the inhabitants of Abhayagiri; for they [explain] the purification of the path (*paṭipadāvisuddhi*) and so forth in this manner.
They describe it thus, but that is incorrect. For if that were so, it would mean describing the qualities of *jhāna* by means of the factors of *jhāna*;
indeed, one stage of existence (*bhūmi*) does not fall within another stage of existence. Furthermore, to show that this contradicts the Canon, the passage beginning with “Because, however...
was stated. Therein, “the mind has attained unity” refers to the state of the faculties having a single flavor (*ekarasa*).
"Attained to unity" (*ekattagata*) means that, through the reaching of the summit of one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), it has attained a state of oneness corresponding to that;

it refers to the consciousness accompanied by its associated factors that has reached absorption (*appanā*). Its very progression toward purification of the path (*paṭipadāvisuddhi*) and so forth is stated immediately thereafter. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means:
because the purification of the path and so forth are stated in the Canon as occurring in the very same moment of the absorption-consciousness, therefore [it is said] "by way of the approach."

By way of the arrival of the preliminary work (*parikamma*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "not overstepping, etc.," it includes the unification of the faculties, the application of energy appropriate thereto, and repeated practice.

"Of the purifier" means of that which cleanses thoroughly and brings about luminosity. Furthermore, in this context, the accomplishment of the function of knowledge should be understood as precisely the establishment of the state of not overstepping and so forth.
"In that or that occasion" means in the cognitive process of absorption (*appanā-vīthi*), which consists of four or five moments of consciousness.

"The mind becomes purified from that obstacle": although this is stated generally as if it were applicable to all stages of the approach, the purification of absorption is indeed superior to the purification of the preliminary work (*parikamma*).
Therefore he said, "Because of its purity," and so forth. "Having become free from hindrances."

The meaning is: having become secluded from that obscuration by which, when enveloped, the mind was previously unable to proceed toward the intermediate sign of serenity (*samatha*), and having suppressed it;
it is "intermediate" because it does not fall into either of the two extremes known as laxity and agitation; and it is "serenity" (*samatha*) because it especially pacifies opposing states.
Because it is the cause of the specific types of happiness for the yogi, it is also the sign; thus, it is the intermediate sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*). Therefore, he said:

"It is precisely the absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) proceeding evenly. Furthermore, "the preceding consciousness immediately following that" refers to the preceding consciousness which serves as the condition of contiguity (*anantarapaccaya*) for that absorption consciousness;
the meaning is "the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhū-citta*). "By way of the transformation of a single continuity (*ekasantati-pariṇāmanā-nyāya*)" means...

Just as one says, "that very same milk has turned into curd," so too, despite the distinction between the limited and the sublime states, and the distinction between the condition and the conditioned state, [the mind] is understood through the principle of unity by way of the process of transformation within a single continuity (*santati*).

"Suchness" (*tathattā*) means the state of being thus, the state of being concentrated by way of absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*). "Because of practicing in this way" means because of practicing according to the manner described.

For at the very moment when one enters into suchness—the intermediate sign of serenity—at that same moment, by way of approaching suchness through absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*) and attaining a state of composure, one is said to "launch into" it.

"In the preceding consciousness" means in the consciousness preceding the absorption consciousness, namely, the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhucitta*). "Producing the mode that is present" means...

It is that which brings to completion the modes of purification from obstacles, the intermediate state, and the launching into serenity (samatha) existing within that consciousness; the meaning is that it is produced in those very modes.

For it is those same modes, being produced at the moment of jhāna through specific conditions, which receive the designation "purification of the way" (*paṭipadāvisuddhi*) as they bring about that particular excellence of jhāna.

[The terms] are stated as if [they were separate]. "At the very moment of arising" means at the very time of its own acquisition. If this is so, how are those modes produced? He says: "By way of arrival.
"Of that" refers to the mind. In the Pāḷi, [the statement] "He looks on with equanimity at the purified mind" is expressed by way of reference to a person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna).

He said, "not performing any activity. And since the attainment of suchness through the practice of serenity (*samatha*) is here precisely the attainment of the state of serenity itself, he said, "by the attainment of the state of serenity.

For one who has abandoned contact with the defilements (*kilesa*) and is established in unity—referring to one who previously practiced, thinking, "How indeed might I abandon contact with the defilements?"—now, by means of the practice of serenity...
Because of its abandonment, the jhāna-consciousness is established in unity through the absence of the company of defilements.

When the jhāna-consciousness has reached growth by means of purification from obstacles and by leaping forward into the practice of middle-level serenity (samatha), equanimity toward the middle (tatramajjhattupekkhā)—having found its opportunity—proceeds by way of even distribution among the associated factors, as if it were strengthening them; thus he said: "by equanimity toward the middle."
“The strengthening of equanimity is to be understood by way of its function.
As for the phrase “these factors that are yoked together,” this is the connection. “Therein” means in that jhāna-consciousness.

They are called “yoked together” (yuganaddha) because they perform their functions by way of not overstepping one another, as if bound together in a yoke. “By the essence of liberation” means by the function of liberating.
Or, [it is so called] because of the perfection of liberation. This one is the yogi. "He causes to proceed" means he sets it in motion.

"Of that" refers to the jhāna-consciousness. "At that moment" means at the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*); for when the moment of arising has passed, it is from the moment of presence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) onwards that what is called "repetition" (*āsevanā*) occurs.
"Those modes" refers to the modes of occurrence of the phenomena therein, such as their not overstepping one another. Repetition, too...
For this is simply the mode of occurrence of those states that function as conditions through repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*).

Regarding "defilement and purification" (*saṃkilesa-vodāna*): non-performance due to the lack of equal flavor (*samarasatā*) between concentration and wisdom is defilement in cultivation; performance is purification.

The same applies to the remaining pairs. Thus, regarding these defilements and purifications, one should first [recognize] their respective disadvantage (*ādīnava*), fault (*dosa*), advantage (*ānisansa*), and quality (*guṇa*) by means of the knowledge of the miracle (*pāṭihāriya-ñāṇa*).

Having seen how they do not overstep one another and so forth, because they have been gladdened by development and purified by that very knowledge—since purification here is what constitutes gladdening—he shows, by way of a conclusion, what was stated at the beginning of the commentary on the characteristics: "Therefore it was said: 'The manner in which... should be understood.'"
Regarding the phrase, “Because knowledge becomes clear by means of equanimity,” what is the connection? This is stated in response to the objection:

“Why is it said that encouragement (*sampahaṃsanā*) alone is the conclusion, and not the intensification of equanimity (*upekkhānubrūhanā*)? To this, it is said: “In that regard, because knowledge becomes clear by means of equanimity.
Here, “in that regard” (*tattha*) refers to that mind of development (*bhāvanācitta*). “Knowledge becomes clear by means of equanimity” means:
At the time of absorption (*appanā*), because the meditation proceeds with evenness and because the opposing factors have been abandoned, no effort such as exertion needs to be made;
thus, there is only equanimity (*ajjhupekkhanā*). It is with reference to this that it is said: "Equanimity regarding the mind at the proper time;
one looks on with equanimity at the purified mind," and so forth. Furthermore, this equanimity arises through the fulfillment of the function of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
Because the function of absorption (*appanā*) is specifically a means for knowledge, there is an inference of the cause from the effect.
Since knowledge becomes manifest by way of equanimity (*upekkhā*), the connection is that encouragement (*sampahaṃsanā*), which constitutes the function of knowledge, is stated to be the conclusion.
Now, in order to support the aforementioned meaning with the canonical text (*pāḷi*), the words beginning with "As it has been said" (*yathāha*) were spoken. Thus-grasped...

"Mind" (*citta*) means that the mind of cultivation is exerted by way of frequent practice of those states conducive to the enlightenment factor of energy, so that it does not fall into the side of indolence.

"He looks on with complete equanimity" means that even while exerting, he looks on with care because the exertion is joined with the balancing of energy for the sake of concentration; this is the equanimity of middle-state neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).

It gains the opportunity. Furthermore, that equanimity—by way of its function as equanimity and by way of the functional wisdom (pārihāriya-paññā) previously active—is a predominance of the function of absorption-wisdom (appanā-paññā);
thus it is said: "By way of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) becomes predominant.

Precisely because of its predominance, even while one is maintaining equanimity, the absorption-consciousness [remains] from the defilements headed by the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), which possess various intrinsic natures.
It is liberated. By way of liberation, by way of the process of being liberated. "By way of wisdom" means by way of the functional wisdom that had previously arisen.
"Because of being liberated" means precisely because of being liberated from various defilements.

Those states—faith and the rest, specifically faith, wisdom, energy, and concentration—become single-flavored and perform a common function. Thus, this development of the faculties, in the sense of their having a single flavor, reaches its fulfillment.
"Operation of knowledge" is what is meant by the statement: "Encouragement, which consists in the function of knowledge, is the conclusion.

Thus, when the fourfold encouragement is accomplished through the state of the faculty of wisdom being exceptionally resolute—by means of the threefold intensification of equanimity following the threefold purification of the path—the ten modes [of encouragement] should be understood as belonging to the jhāna itself by way of the function of knowledge; this is the equanimity of arrival.
“By way of numerical sequence” means: by way of numerical sequence, or simply because of being first in numerical sequence; this is the meaning.
By this, he indicates the order of the teaching. With the phrase “first arisen is ‘first,’” he indicates the order of practice, for “arisen” here has the sense of “attained.
However, with the phrase “first to be attained is ‘first,’” [he indicates the order of the path].
Because it is rejected in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as not having a single characteristic (*ekantalakkhaṇa*), it is not included here.

Regarding the two kinds of jhāna—namely, jhāna that contemplates the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and jhāna that contemplates characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*)—the phrase "from contemplating the object" (*ārammaṇūpanijjhānato*) is stated specifically to show the type of jhāna intended here.
This is because one contemplates each respective object, known as the earth-kasiṇa, just as one contemplates a visible form with the eye.
"By burning up the adverse states" means by incinerating the adverse states such as the hindrances, that is, by abandoning them through suppression.

"In the sense of being complete" means in the sense of making the entire [earth] the object; for, whether the portion of earth or the earth-circle has been prepared or not prepared according to the method mentioned below, it is grasped as a delimited whole, and thus its entirety constitutes the object, for a mere part of it does not serve as the object.
It is made. Because it depends upon the earth-kasiṇa, the sign is called the "earth-kasiṇa," just as one says, "the beds are shouting.
Because it accompanies that [sign], the jhāna is called the "earth-kasiṇa," just as one says, "the spears are moving.
This concludes the commentary on the achievement of long-term stability.
76. One who pierces a hair with an arrow while it is fixed at its mark is called a "hair-piercer" (*vālavedhī*).
Here, however, one who pierces the filament of a hair divided into many parts is intended by the term "hair-piercer. By that hair-piercer; by the cook (*sūda*), that is, the kitchen-steward.
To explain the meaning stated briefly as "the modes (*ākāra*) should be discerned," the passage beginning with "for just as" (*yathā hi*) was spoken.
In this context, "very skillful" means extremely clever. "Archers" refers to bowmen. "Work" means that which is suitable.
"Of the steps taken" means of the steps occurring by way of taking a step at the time of piercing. "The form" means the form assumed by the bow, the bowstring, and the arrow.
"Should grasp" means he should examine. The word "etc. in "suitability of food, etc. includes other unmentioned modes as well.
It should be seen. By this, the grasping of the signs for the development of the seasons and so forth is also stated.

"In that" means in that nascent concentration (*taruṇasamādhi*). "Master" means the owner; the meaning is one who supports with food, wages, and so forth. "Attending upon" means feeding him. The construction is:
having observed the manner in which he eats according to his preference, one offers it to him. This practitioner as well, at the moment of attainment...
"Food and so forth as the sign" (*ākāra*) refers to the modes (*ākāra*) present in food and other requisites that accomplish one's purpose at the time when jhāna was previously attained.
"Having grasped" means having encompassed and observed them. "Again and again into absorption" refers to the state of absorption whenever concentration has lapsed.
"A wise man through familiarity with the science of cooking" means he is skilled therein due to his clear knowledge. By means of the application of quick-wittedness appropriate to the occasion...
“Skilled. “By various ingredients” means by various substances; the meaning is “by various flavors. Therefore he said, “with sour-topped [sauces],” and so forth.
“With soups” means with condiments (*byañjana*). “With sour-topped” means with sour portions, or those which, being of a sour flavor, have become the primary part;

that is, mixed with the four kinds of sour [sauces] and so on. This same method applies to the bitter-topped and others as well. “With crunchy things” means mixed with the shoots of vātiṅgaṇa and the like.
“Sign” (nimitta) means the mode [of appearance], specifically the mode of eating according to one’s preference. “Grasps” (uggaṇhāti) means he takes hold of it again and again, or he attends to it;
or, for the sake of this curry, he stretches out his hand. “Of offerings” (abhihārānaṃ) means of presents that are to be brought forward, or of offerings of worship.
“He grasps the sign” means: “In this way my mind was concentrated.”
He grasps the sign and observes it.
"Of obstacles to concentration" means of those things that have become obstacles to concentration. "Of states" refers to the states of the hindrances, such as sensual desire and so forth.
"Because of being well-purified" means because of being thoroughly purified, that is, because they have been properly abandoned by way of suppression.

The meaning is as follows. By the phrase “by reflecting on the danger of sensual desire, etc.,” the word “etc. includes such things as reflection on the contemplation of the unattractive (*asubha*) and reflection on the benefits of renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
For by seeing the virtue of renunciation, the danger in sensual desire—which acts as an obstruction to it—becomes especially evident.
“Bodily corruption” (*kāyaduṭṭhulla*) means bodily distress or restlessness of the body. By that [term], the cause for the agitation of body and mind is indicated.

He did not speak of the purification of the hindrance of ill-will (*byāpādanīvaraṇa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "attention to the element of initiative and so forth," the inclusion of the factors conducive to the enlightenment factor of energy (*vīriyasambojjhaṅga*) and of the perception of light (*ālokasaññā*), etc., should be understood.

By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "attention to the sign of serenity and so forth," the inclusion of those phenomena that are the proximate causes for the enlightenment factor of concentration (*samādhisambojjhaṅga*) should be understood.
Furthermore, by the term "obstacles to concentration," doubt (*vicikicchā*) and its proximate causes, as well as intoxication, conceit, and so forth, are included.
And having in mind this [point], he said: "They cause to dwell" means they cause [the mind] to dwell in the hollow of the dwelling-place.
"Well-purified" means perfectly purified by the absence of anything to be clung to. Here it is asked:

"But surely, having already reflected on the danger of sensual desires and so forth, and having entered upon the path of serenity (samatha), the hindrances were suppressed by jhāna at the very moment of access; then why is there again the reflection on the danger of sensual desires and so forth?"
"Was it already included?"—Yes, that is true. However, it was mentioned again for the sake of superior abandonment, so that the jhāna might endure for a long time.
As for "restlessness and torpor," it is stated thus because remorse is included by virtue of its association with them, and lethargy is likewise included due to its being of the same class.
"He went to the edge of the pure [grove]" means he went to a park whose boundaries were perfectly pure and whose corners and limits were entirely cleansed.
There he delights; he should delight in that jhāna, and even for a portion of the day he would remain possessed of jhāna.
"For the sake of the expansion of the development of the mind" means for the sake of the vastness of the development of concentration.
For just as the sign arises by way of development, so too its increase occurs by way of development alone. Therefore, by means of one finger-breadth and so forth...
For one who increases the sign by repeated cultivation, the meditation (jhāna) also reaches growth, development, and abundance.

Therefore it is said: “And for the sake of the abundance of mental development, the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) should be increased as it has been obtained. “Of that” means of the counterpart sign.
Commentary on the Method of Increasing the Sign (Nimittavaḍḍhananaya-vaṇṇanā): 77.
*Tatra* is a locative case used in the sense of possession (*sāmī-attha*), meaning "of that. *Avaḍḍhetvā*:
just as a potter, when making a bowl from clay, first increases the size of the bowl without yet defining its boundaries, so too by way of increasing the bowl [of the sign].

The "increasing of the cake" refers to increasing the quantity of a cake without exceeding the original size of the cloth. The "increasing of the meal" refers to adding more food on top of the existing meal.
The "increasing of the cloth" refers to dyeing and so forth a cloth that has already been soaked. The word *yoga* (practice/application) should be applied to each term individually.
One should not increase [the object] without defining its limits; for the development of meditation proceeds only within defined boundaries. Likewise...
For it is said: "The finite, not the infinite. *Haṃsapotakā* means young swift swans.

*Ukkūlaṃ* is a raised place; *vikūlaṃ* is a low place. A difficult passage made by the current of a river is a river-ford (*nadīviduggaṃ*). A mountain region situated in an uneven manner is a mountain-unevenness (*pabbatavisamaṃ*).
They appear as gross because of the abundance of reflective contemplation (*paccavekkhaṇā*), due to their state of being manifest (*vibhūta*); they appear as weak...
They attend [to him] because he is one who does not commit an offense due to his state of being proficient and strong. "By striving further" means by ascending further in meditation;
the meaning is: for the attainment of the second jhāna.
"Mountain-dwelling" means one who frequents mountains. "Not knowing the field" means not knowing the proper range (agocara). Of the obstacles to concentration...
He is foolish because he has not mastered purification. He is incompetent due to the lack of proficiency and skill in attaining mastery over jhāna.

He is ignorant of the field because he does not understand that jhāna serves as the proximate cause for the higher stages. He is unskilled in every respect due to the absence of proficiency in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

Alternatively, he is foolish because he has not cultivated the sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*); he is incompetent because he has not developed it; and [he is unskilled] because he has not practiced it repeatedly.

"Akhettaññū" (one who knows no field). It should be connected thus: "unwholesome because of not being rightly resolved. "Fallen from both sides" means fallen from both meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).
For he, due to lack of proficiency and lack of firm establishment, has fallen away from the two absorptions despite his effort, owing to destruction and incapacity.
"One who has practiced mastery" means one who has cultivated mastery.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Five Masteries (Pañcavasīkathāvaṇṇanā): 78. Regarding the phrase "mastery" (*vasī*): because it is a designation of a verbal root (*dhātu*), it is intended as a designation of an action;

thus he says "masteries" (*vasiyo*), meaning "occurrences according to one's wish. Mastery over advertence (*āvajjana*)—or mastery by way of advertence—is "advertence-mastery. [The purpose is] to advert to the jhāna.
“Wherever there is a desire” means wherever one wishes. “Whenever” means at whatever time; “in whichever jhāna-factor” means whichever one desires.
“As far as there is a desire” means for as long as one wishes; the letter *da* serves to facilitate the euphonic junction (*sandhi*) of the words.

Furthermore, the word “yāvā” is stated with reference to the occurrence [of the mind] in such a way as if it were continuous through many series of impulsion moments (*javana-vāra*), and not merely a single one.
For he is one whose moments of consciousness are delimited. Regarding the absence of sluggishness in adverting:

according to the method already stated, whenever he adverts to any jhāna factor whatsoever in any place, there is no sluggishness, protractedness, or delay in the occurrence of the adverting of the mind at the desired time. Such is mastery in adverting.
The meaning is that it is called "accomplished" (*siddhā*). "The rest" refers to the mastery of emergence, resolution, reviewing, and the finality.
Since jhāna consists of a collection of factors, one who wishes to accomplish mastery of adverting within jhāna must advert to the jhāna factors in their proper sequence;
thus he said, "for one who adverts first to initial application" (*vitakka*). Although here only adverting itself is intended.
Because what is intended is mastery over adverting, once adverting has arisen, there must be impulsions (javana).
And since the directing of the mind is intent upon adverting, those impulsions have as their object only the jhāna factors that were adverted to;
they are only a few and not complete. Thus it is said: "Four or five impulsions, having only applied thought (vitakka) as their object, impel."
It should be understood that there are four [turnings] for one with sharp faculties and five for one whose faculties are not overly sharp.

"Uninterrupted" means uninterrupted by heterogeneous states. "But this," however, refers to the aforementioned mastery over adverting consisting of four impulsion-moments, separated by two life-continuum (bhavaṅga) moments;
or it refers to others such as the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) and so forth. "At such a time" means at the time when, having repeatedly arisen, one produces mastery over adverting more swiftly.
And that [attainment] is indeed brief and of limited duration, not possessing such long-lasting continuity as the Teacher’s Great Twin Miracle.
For it is said to be uncommon to disciples. Right attainment, right practice, and right entering into jhāna together with its associated factors through realization is the possession of jhāna.

"Quickness" here refers to the capacity for swift attainment: the ability to enter [jhāna] immediately after the desire to attain it, following the interruption of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) by two successive moments of the life-continuum and the subsequent arising of the advertence (*āvajjana*).
This mastery of attainment, having reached its pinnacle, is found in the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma; with reference to this, it was said: "I, indeed..."

“Aggivessana, at the conclusion of that very discourse, right there upon that same initial object of concentration, I steadied my mind within, settled it, made it one-pointed, and concentrated it, by means of which I have dwelt for all time.
Indeed, there is nothing swifter than this mastery of attainment. On a night of moonlight, with hair recently shorn...
While the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling in the Kapotakandara cave, a yakkha struck him on the head with a blow capable of splitting even a massive mountain peak;
here, his attainment of meditative absorption (samāpatti) must be illustrated. For it will be said:
“At that time, when he was struck, the Elder entered into absorption. However, in the Pāḷi [it says]: “a certain concentration...”
It is said, "having entered [meditative attainment], he sat. However, these elders say, "The blow was struck by him at the very moment of emerging from that attainment.
"For the duration of a finger-snap" means for a moment as brief as the snapping of a finger. "To establish" means like a bridge across a river with a swift current.
The power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-vasī*) is the capacity to establish the aforementioned moment of jhāna without allowing the flood to flow with its usual force.
Alternatively, it is called "resolution" because it is an establishing that overcomes [the flow], like a firm determination. Mastery therein is the mastery of resolution.

Likewise, the power of emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-vasī*) is the ability to emerge quickly from that very state—possessing the jhāna for a brief moment, such as the duration of a finger-snap or ten finger-snaps.
The capacity to emerge from jhāna after having offered [the oblation]. Here, "emergence from jhāna" refers specifically to the arising of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*).

And in this context, just as the capacity for resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-vasī*)—by means of prior preparation—is the ability to resolve, thinking, "I shall maintain this jhāna for exactly this many moments," so too is the capacity to emerge from jhāna by means of emerging, thinking, "Having been possessed of this jhāna for exactly this many moments, I shall emerge from it."

The mastery of emergence (*vuṭṭhānavaśī*) should be understood as the capacity to emerge by means of prior preparation, thinking, “I shall emerge,” which is what is called “skill in emerging from attainment. “For the purpose of showing both of these” means for the purpose of showing mastery over resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and mastery over emergence.
“Therein” means in that created mountain, in its opening. Although it is indeed only a single supernormal consciousness (*abhiññācitta*) by which—

It should be understood that while one might create a mountain, what is demonstrated here is the lighter establishment and emergence of the meditative absorption (jhāna) that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā).
Otherwise, we would be subject to reproach, [as if to say]: "How is it that so many possessors of psychic power (iddhimantā) were unable to protect even a single attendant from Garuḷa?"

"Immediately following the adverting [consciousness]" means that those impulsion consciousnesses which have occurred subsequent to the adverting of the jhāna factors— such as initial application (vitakka) and so forth— in order to achieve mastery over adverting,
are the reviewing consciousnesses of those [factors]. To the same extent that mastery over adverting is established,
it should be understood that mastery over reviewing is likewise established.
Commentary on the Second Jhāna (79):

Because it is the first to abandon the hindrances, [the factors] are the immediate adversaries of those hindrances. "Coarse" means that even though it is extensive, it is easily broken like soft wood;
thus he said, "because of its grossness, the limbs are weak. "Having attended to it as peaceful" means...
One attends to it as "peaceful" because its factors are not gross like those of the first jhāna, and because it possesses peaceful states.

For although the states such as rapture and pleasure that exist in the second jhāna are indeed present in the first jhāna as well, they are more peaceful and more sublime than those [of the first]. "Inclination" (*nikanti*) means inclining toward; it means longing for.
*Attha*: meaning. *Pariyādāya*: having exhausted. In the phrase "four or five," the word *vā* (or) is indicated by elision (*luttaniddiṭṭha*).
"Possessing the second jhāna" means that this [consciousness] has the second jhāna. "Of the very same kind as stated" means they are of the very same kind as those stated in the first jhāna;
the meaning is that they are named "preliminary" (*parikamma*) and so forth.
80. "Calm" (*vūpasama*) means the cause of calm; and here, "calm" is intended in the sense of abandoning, specifically the abandoning of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
As for "surpassing," this refers in meaning to their non-arising at the moment of the second jhāna; thus he says, "by surpassing," and so forth.
But which applied thoughts and sustained thoughts are intended here as being calmed? Are they those belonging to the first jhāna, or rather those belonging to the second jhāna?

Now, what is the meaning here? If it refers to those belonging to the first jhāna, there is no subsiding for them; for the first jhāna is never devoid of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
If, on the other hand, it refers to those belonging to the second jhāna, even so there is no subsiding at all, because they are entirely absent from that state.
To this it is said: [it refers to] those applied thoughts and sustained thoughts by which the first jhāna is characterized as gross.

The meaning that "the attainment of the second jhāna occurs through the surmounting of those [factors], and not through the surmounting of contact and so forth which are not gross by nature" is illustrated by the phrase "with the stilling of applied and sustained thought.
Therefore, an objection such as, "Is the stilling of applied and sustained thought intended here as belonging to the first jhāna, or rather to the second jhāna? finds no place.

Because what is intended by "subsiding" (*vūpasama*) is the establishment of the state of non-arising for those specific defilements whose dangers have been seen at the moment of each respective jhāna.
It is only applied thought (*vitakka*) and the other factors that, having become jhāna-factors, are made to do so; it is not the contact (*phassa*) and other factors associated with them.

Therefore, the mention of the subsiding and so forth of applied thought and the others alone is logically consistent. However, because the factors associated with them [the jhāna-factors] are also—just like applied thought and the others—[subject to the same process...]
By this [statement], the perception of danger in the form of "this is gross" (*oḷārika*) is shown as it appears in the Sutta;

therefore, although the subsiding (*vūpasama*) of applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth, along with their concomitants, should be stated without distinction, the fact that only the subsiding of applied thought and so forth is mentioned constitutes a superfluous statement (*adhikavacana*).
Considering that this indicates another meaning, it is shown in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that it reveals a certain specific distinction: "of the gross..."
The phrase beginning with “panā” is included here; it should be understood that the passage beginning with “by which initial application and sustained application” is what is stated here.

This same method applies to the phrases beginning with “and with the fading away of rapture. Therefore, the statements regarding the surmounting of initial application, sustained application, rapture, and pleasure are indicators of the attainment of the second jhāna and so forth, by means of surmounting each increasingly gross factor.
Consequently, the statement regarding the surmounting of initial application and sustained application—which constitutes a portion of those [statements]—is also an indicator of that [attainment].

It has been stated. For even though [the factors] such as the "surmounting of applied thought and sustained thought" stand separately, since they are grasped collectively by the mind through their commonality as descriptions of the factors to be abandoned, the expression "the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought" should be understood as referring to a single part of that whole.

And this meaning is expressed according to the method of characterizing a whole by means of a part. Alternatively, it is expressed by the very expression "the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought."

By stating that "having transcended that," the words "fading away of rapture" (*pītivirāga*) and so forth—which indicate the attainment of the second [jhāna]—are shown to indicate the attainment of the third and subsequent jhānas through the transcending of rapture and the rest;
thus, their indicative nature regarding those [attainments] is stated.

What is intended here is one's own internal state (*niyakajjhatta*), not the internal-internal (*ajjhattajjhatta*) and so forth. He states the reason for this with the words, "In the *Vibhaṅga*, however," and so on.
The intention is that, just as cloth is blue due to its connection with the color blue (*nīlavaṇṇa*), so too cloth is blue due to its connection with blueness (*nīlayoga*).

By means of that serenity (*sampasādana*) with which it is connected, the jhāna is "serene" (*sampasādana*). When that [jhāna] is shown, there is no contradiction in the fact that the application of that term to the jhāna—due to its connection with it—is demonstrated precisely by the grammatical construction of a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa-niddesa*) in the phrase "serene jhāna.
As for the question "How [is it] in the state of singleness (*ekodibhāve*)?", [it is] in singleness (*ekodimhi*).

If it is argued that by the very use of a coordinate designation (*samānādhikaraṇaniddesa*)— namely, "jhāna which is a state of singleness" (*ekodibhāva*)— the fact that jhāna increases singleness is already stated,
then it would follow that after extracting the word "state of singleness," one should not provide a separate description of singleness;
thus, it is logical that the term *ekodibhāva* itself, just like the term *sampasādana*, occurs in the sense of concentration within jhāna.

And regarding this alternative interpretation of the meaning: in the position [of the commentary] that says "it clarifies the mind" (*cetaso sampasādayati*), the genitive case in "of the mind" (*cetaso*) is used in the sense of the accusative.

In the former [position], namely the one stated as "jhāna is clarification because it is associated with clarification," the genitive case in "of the mind" (*cetaso*) is used in the sense of a relationship.
Even the "best" person in the world is called "one" (eka) in such expressions as, "I shall do this for you alone for one day.

Furthermore, the word *eka* is seen to have the sense of "without a companion" in such passages as, "He was conquered by the small ones alone (ekākībhi). Thus, he said, "being alone, that is, without a companion.
Granted, faith and the other factors are indeed conditions for associated states both in a common and a specific sense.

But as for concentration (samādhi), it shows that at the moment of jhāna it is an especially predominant condition by exercising the function of a lord (indaṭṭha) over the associated states characterized by non-distraction; thus he says: "the associated states... [etc. ...a designation.
The two qualifying terms, "tranquillity" (sampasādana) and "singleness of mind" (cetaso ekodibhāva), are used according to the desire to express the excellence of the jhāna.
[This] has been grasped. In order to show this distinction—that this excellence which is obtained in this jhāna is not so obtained in the first jhāna—it is said, "But is it not," and so forth.

Even though the turbidity of the defilements has departed due to the abandoning of the hindrances, the mental states (dhammas) that proceed by way of striking and beating at the object, and by way of rubbing and pressing upon it, [cause] the associated [states]...
As if causing some agitation, they do not remain settled; thus it is said: "not well-purified due to the agitation of applied and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra-kkhobha).
Small waves are ripples (vīci); large ones are billows (taraṅga).

Even when there is equality of the faculties and equality of energy, because of that very agitation and the absence of serene confidence (sampasāda), concentration (samādhi) is also not clearly manifest.
Like a fish in shallow water; the aforementioned agitation itself is the impediment.

"By what has been stated thus" means by that faith through which serenity (*sampasādana*) is said, and by that one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) through which unification (*ekodibhāva*) is said—namely, the jhāna.
It is stated by way of specifically analyzing the mode of occurrence of those very [qualities] through such terms as "believing" (*saddahanā*), and so forth. By that...
This commentary on the meaning, which proceeds thus: "It is called *sampasādana* because it is associated with confidence (*sampasādana*) or because it is confidence itself;
and it is called *jhāna* of unification (*ekodibhāva*) because one develops [the mind] as unified (*ekodiṃ bhāvetī*)," is not contradictory when considered according to the reading of the *Vibhaṅga*.
As to how there is no contradiction, that has already been stated.
81. *Santā* means gone to cessation (*nirodha*) in a state of equanimity (*sama*). *Samitā* means brought to equanimity and ceased through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
*Vūpasantā* means, for that very reason, thoroughly calmed. *Atthaṅgatā* means gone to destruction (*attha*), which is to say, to ruin (*vināsa*).
*Abbhatthaṅgatā* is stated by prefixing a prefix (*upasagga*) to the word. *Appitā* means made to go to destruction. *Sositā* [refers to] the continuity (*santāna*) known as the process of existence.

"By means of non-existence" means having gone to a state of exhaustion and dryness. "The state of being brought to an end" (*byantikatā*) means the state of being free from the ender (*vigatantakatā*).
This is the meaning: because they have been abandoned through cultivation, there is an absence of applied thought and sustained thought (*vitakkavicārānaṃ abhāvo*).

Having accepted the point stated by the challenger and in order to resolve it, he said, "In this way, this established meaning is indeed so," and then stated, "But this is not [the case]," and so forth. Therein:

"Etanti" refers to this statement: "With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought. "Tadatthadīpakan" means that it illuminates its meaning, which consists simply in the absence of applied and sustained thought. Herein, the meaning is as follows:

by the very statement "with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought," which illuminates the cause for internal confidence and one-pointedness of mind—thereby showing the means for attaining the second jhāna and so forth—and which illuminates the cause for the state of being without applied and sustained thought.

If the absence of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) has already been illuminated, what is the purpose of further stating "without applied thought and sustained thought" (*avitakka-avicāra*)? It is not so, because it was not yet fully illuminated. For by the statement regarding the subsiding (*vūpasama*) of applied and sustained thought, their non-occurrence has not yet been expressed.

Indeed, the subsiding of these two consists in the abandoning of craving (*taṇhā*) for applied and sustained thought; and as for those who effect the abandoning of craving for mental formations (*saṅkhāra*), in them—

For even when craving has been abandoned in the paths and their fruits, the occurrence of formations still persists; likewise, in this case as well, the association with applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) might not have been ruled out for the second jhāna, whose craving for applied and sustained thought has been suppressed.
Therefore, in order to rule that out, and to show that their subsiding consists precisely in the transcendence of the desire to advert and so forth, it is said:
"without applied thought, without sustained thought" (*avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ*).
It has been stated. "The first" means the first jhāna.

It is indeed appropriate to say that "the second" refers to when the second [jhāna] arises. However, its applied thought and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*) are not like those of the first jhāna;
for while the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are abandoned at the moment of access concentration (*upacāra-khaṇa*) for the first jhāna, they are not so for this second jhāna.
