At the moment of access (upacāra), initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra) are not abandoned because their intrinsic nature is not defiled, and because access development is incapable of abandoning them.
Even though craving for them is abandoned by that [access], it is not so specifically;
for the specific abandonment of craving therein occurs only at the moment of absorption (appanā). Therefore it was said: "Only at the moment of absorption," and so forth.

The state of being a factor of abandoning should also be understood as referring specifically to the abandonment of the hindrances by means of the first jhāna, just as it is for the first jhāna itself.
Therefore—meaning because this jhāna consists of only three factors—therefore. "That" refers to the statement in the *Vibhaṅga*.

Serenity is an accessory (*parikkhāra*) of the jhāna, like a white woolen rug is an accessory of a chariot; it is not a factor of the jhāna itself. Thus he said, "in order to show the jhāna together with its accessories."
Commentary on the Third Jhāna (82).

"Exhilarated" (*uppilāvita*): While this is indeed the mode of occurrence of joy accompanied by craving in one who has not abandoned affection for possessions and does not see their danger, here it is the joy of the second jhāna that is intended. Nevertheless, when all joy has entirely...
It is said that she too would follow one who is not dispassionate. Alternatively, it is called *uppilāvita* because it is like being agitated.
It should be understood that this was stated in order to demonstrate the danger therein more clearly.
83. Dispassion (*virāga*) is the fading away of lust. That fading away, however, is either a loathing by way of disenchantment, or the abandoning of the lust bound up with that [object].
In order to show both of these, he said: "either disgust with the kind of rapture already described, or its transcendence.
"Of the kind already described" means of the kind described by the passage beginning, "Whatever rapture there is therein... "Sampiṇḍana" means conjunction;
"magga" means the means. "Tadadhigamāya" means for the attainment of the third path.
84. "By way of arising" means by way of being well-composed and appropriate.
Since even the equanimity of jhāna occurs having made itself inwardly well-composed, he says, "he sees evenly. "Clear" means distinct due to the departure of defilement.
"Vast" means great, having attained a state of preeminence through its exalted nature. "Firm" means having attained a state of stability through the disappearance of rapture.

It is the nature of complete purity, the nature of one whose taints are destroyed, and the state of being free from defilement. Among beings, it is the mode of viewing with equanimity based on the perception of beings as the owners of their own karma; it is the mode of neutrality, which is the divine abiding of equanimity (*brahmavihārupekkhā*).
The term "of co-nascent states" (*sahajātadhammānaṃ*) is used in the genitive case for the purpose of specification (*niddhāraṇe*).

Because there is an absence of active intervention in the exertion, restraint, or encouragement of associated states—due to the lack of depression, agitation, or dissatisfaction when the cultivation has entered its proper course through even progression—it is [equanimity] among those associated states.
Equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*) consists in the mode of neutrality.
Regarding the term "sign of equanimity" (*upekkhānimitta*): here, energy that is neutral—free from falling into the sides of lethargy or agitation—is "equanimity.
Precisely that [energy] is the "sign of equanimity" because it serves as the sign for such energy that should be practiced by assuming that very mode.

It is called equanimity (*upekkhā*) because it looks on with indifference (*upekkhati*) at the time of being fully engaged in development; thus, energy itself as equanimity is "energy-equanimity" (*vīriyupekkhā*).

It is the wisdom that consists in the reflective discernment and steady establishment [of the mind] for the purpose of attaining the first jhāna regarding the hindrances... up to ... for the purpose of attaining the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception regarding the perception of the base of nothingness;
this is the knowledge in the equanimities about formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāsu ñāṇaṃ*), as it has been handed down.

These eight arise by way of concentration: for the sake of attaining the path of stream-entry—arising, occurrence, sign, accumulation, rebirth-linking, destiny, generation, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and despair;
for the sake of attaining the fruition of stream-entry—arising, occurrence... [and so on] ...the path of arahantship.

Reflecting upon arising, occurrence, sign, accumulation, rebirth-linking, destiny, generation, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and despair for the sake of attainment— [and so on]... for the sake of the attainment of the fruit of arahantship, for the sake of the attainment of the dwelling in emptiness, and for the sake of the attainment of the dwelling in the signless.
“Wisdom as composure is knowledge regarding equanimity towards formations”—thus it is said. These ten [kinds of knowledge] arise by way of insight (vipassanā).

And herein, having reflected upon and examined the hindrances, applied thought, sustained thought, and so forth—which have been suppressed by the first jhāna and the others—as they truly are, one stands with a state of decisive resolution; this is “composure through reflection on the hindrances and so forth.”

Because it has seen their danger, insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) maintains equanimity toward both grasping and generating them; thus, regarding grasping, it is equanimity in the sense of being neutral.
In this context, "arising" refers to the production here of the aggregates through the condition of past karma.

"Occurrence" refers to the continued functioning of what has arisen in that manner. "Sign" refers to everything comprised within the formations of the three planes, because they present themselves as signs.
“Accumulation” (āyūhana) refers to karma that serves as the cause for rebirth-linking in the future. “Rebirth-linking” (paṭisandhi) refers to arising in the future.

“Destination” (gati) refers to the specific realm of existence where that rebirth-linking occurs. “Generation” (nibbatti) refers to the manifestation of the aggregates. “Arising” (upapatti) refers to the occurrence of the resultant state, as expressed in the phrase “of one who has attained [a meditative absorption] or of one who has arisen [in a new existence]”.
“Birth” (jāti) refers to aging and the other [characteristics of the life-process].
[It refers to] birth conditioned by becoming, which serves as the condition. Aging, sickness, death, and so forth are indeed evident.
And here, only the five beginning with arising are mentioned by way of being the objects of the knowledge of equanimity toward formations; the rest are synonyms for them.

For this pair—“origination” (*nibbatti*) and “birth” (*jāti*)—is a synonym for both arising and rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*); while “destiny” (*gati*) and “reappearance” (*upapatti*) [are synonyms for becoming].
It should be understood that these two pertain to the process [of existence], while aging and so forth pertain to the sign.

There are ten kinds of equanimity regarding formations: four which serve as the cause for the arising of the path by way of the desireless liberation; likewise four for the attainment of fruition; and two by way of the dwelling in emptiness and the dwelling in the signless.
Insight-wisdom proceeds. "That which exists" refers to the three characteristics, such as impermanence, which are apprehended.
"That which has come to be" refers to the pentad of aggregates, which have come to be because they are produced by conditions.

"He abandons that" means that, by abandoning perceptions of permanence and so forth through the contemplation of impermanence and the rest, he correctly sees their danger and thereby abandons the desire and lust associated with them.
He abandons; he abandons by means of practice such that there is no grasping in the future.
Being thus, he attains equanimity therein. "Investigating" refers even to comprehension by way of impermanence and so forth.
It is "evenly directed" because it is the cause for the equal functioning of the associated states. [It is freed] from all adversaries, such as the hindrances, applied thought, and sustained thought.

Because of their liberation, they are purified of all opposition. Because of their subsiding, even in the subsiding of opposition, they are characterized by non-activity (*abyāpāra*), proceeding by way of non-activity, or having attained a state of non-activity.
If they are one in meaning, how is there this distinction? To this he says, "By this and that," and so forth. "Therefore" means because, although [they are one] in intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*)...
However, since those specific conditions by which this distinction of states exists do not occur together as one, there is no non-distinction between them, nor do they occur simultaneously;
therefore [it is said]: "Wherein six-factored equanimity," and so forth. "Oneness" (*ekībhāva*) means unity.
Even though there is a commonality in the state of neutrality (*majjhattābhāva*), it is nevertheless distinguished by the difference in its objects. For this purpose...
Having intended this, it was said: "It is divided into two according to its function. To show this in detail, he said, "For just as... and so forth.

This is equanimity regarding insight (*vipassanupekkhā*). It is with reference to this that it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Whatever exists, whatever has come to be—that he abandons; he attains equanimity.
Therein, "whatever exists, whatever has come to be" refers to the five aggregates, which [he abandons] by means of the knowledge of the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatāñāṇa*).

He abandons [them]. Just as in the investigation of all characteristics by one who has already mastered the three characteristics he has seen, so too in the investigation of the characteristic of formations—which is a reality whose three characteristics have been seen—he attains equanimity.

Because the characteristics of impermanence and so forth of formations have been well-seen, when equanimity in the form of insight-equanimity (vipassanupekkhā), which is a state of neutrality, is established through that investigation, then for those [formations] whose dangers have thus been seen—
Even in the apprehension of those [objects], equanimity is indeed established, because the underlying tendency (ajjhāsaya) is entirely inclined toward the dissolution of formations (visaṅkhāra).
"Having non-exertion as its essence" means that even toward that sublime pleasure, its function is to counteract inclination.
"Manifesting as non-activity" means that even when the perfection of pleasure is attained, it stands present without being occupied with that pleasure, [remaining] associated [with the mind].

The meaning is that it establishes non-activity toward that object. It is "unmanifest" because it is overwhelmed by applied thought (*vitakka*) and other factors which bring about agitation and elation in the associated states.
In that case, its function is the state of equanimity (*tatramajjhattatā*); due to the absence of those [agitating factors], it is manifest here.
The complete commentary on the meaning of the phrase “and he dwells equanimous” is finished. 85.

Regarding the word “mindful” (*sato*), he states that it is formed as a noun denoting the agent (*kattusādhanam*): “he is mindful” means he remembers; “clearly comprehending” (*sampajāno*) means he understands correctly.
It has the characteristic of remembering (*saraṇa*), reflecting upon, and being present; thus it is "characterized by remembering. Non-forgetfulness is the opposite of forgetfulness;
its function is that non-forgetfulness; thus it is "of the function of non-forgetfulness. It stands ready by way of guarding against defilements, or it establishes protection [against them];
thus it is "manifested as protection. Non-confusion is the correct understanding [of an object].
Or, non-delusion (*asammoha*) is the opposite of delusion. "Investigation" (*tīraṇa*) is the act of crossing over to the further shore. "Discernment" (*pavicaya*) is inquiry (*vīmaṃsā*).
Granted that, relative to access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*) and so forth, even the first and second jhānas are subtle;
however, this is stated to be "gross" in relation to the higher jhānas. And that grossness should be understood by way of its possession of coarse factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*). Some...
And they say, “because of the abundance of mental factors. The intention is that the progress there in those jhānas is easy.
The function of mindfulness and clear comprehension is not manifest there because there is no need to say, “This particular thing is being done with difficulty.
Although this meaning—that it is subtle due to the abandoning of gross factors—can certainly apply to the second jhāna as well, nevertheless...

Since joy and happiness generally occur in a state of non-separation, the activity of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*) is here especially predominant due to the subtlety resulting from the abandoning of the gross factor known as joy; thus it is said, "of a man," and so forth.
"He might again approach joy" means that the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) could become one partaking of decline, and he might actually fall back into the second absorption itself.
This is the meaning. Therefore he said: “It may be associated with rapture (pīti) alone. He said this with reference to the bliss of the third jhāna, thinking, “And this is exceedingly sweet bliss.
Its extreme sweetness is to be understood precisely through the absence of rapture, whose nature is exhilaration and buoyancy. “This” refers to the two terms:
“mindful (sato)” and “clearly comprehending (sampajāno).”
Therefore, in order to demonstrate this meaning: because that meditator would experience the pleasure associated with the mental body (*nāmakāya*);
or rather, "that" refers to that aforementioned pleasure associated with the mental body.
By means of the exceedingly refined matter produced from that—that is, arisen from that—of that meditator...

Because the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is pervaded. Due to the pervasion of that form-body, even when one has emerged from meditative absorption (*jhāna*), being still possessed of that absorption, one experiences bodily happiness (*kāyika-sukha*).

Therefore, the construction is as follows: "He experiences happiness with the body" was said in order to show this meaning, which consists in the experience of both mental and bodily happiness. This, then, is the summary of the meaning here.

It is said that one possessing jhāna experiences mental happiness through the mental body (*nāmakāya*), and physical happiness through the arising of material form that is the cause of physical happiness.
"Pervaded" (*phuṭatta*) means "pervadedness" (*byāpitatta*).
For just as pleasure arises when a body pervaded by water is touched by such non-adverse contacts as wind, so too does it arise for one whose body is pervaded by these [factors].
Another method: regarding the objection to the phrase "he experiences pleasure with the body"—namely, how there can be an experience of pleasure without mental application (*ābhoga*)—it says:
"Even though... nevertheless. Because his pleasure is associated with the mental body (*nāmakāya*), the construction is:
"he experiences pleasure with the body. Now, [the text explains] the experience of pleasure even with mental application:
In order to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “yaṃ vā taṃ” was stated.
(86) “Yaṃ” is a particle used in the sense of a reason; its meaning is “yasmā” (because). Therefore he said, “yaṃjhānahetū” (on account of which jhāna).

With the intention that the words beginning with “ācikkhanti” (they declare) have the sense of praising, he said, “the intention is ‘they praise’. “Kinti” is a question regarding the manner of praising.
In other instances, full awareness (*sampajañña*) is included by the very mention of mindfulness (*sati*);

however, since only mindfulness is mentioned here in the text, it is stated simply as "mindful" (*satimā*) because of the presence of such established mindfulness, or because "fully aware" (*sampajāno*) was already stated previously.
Furthermore, at the moment of jhāna, only mental pleasure is obtained; therefore, it is said, "he experiences pleasure with the body of mind."
“Third”: this refers to the sequence of enumeration; from this point forward, there is no difference from the discourses on the second and third jhānas, and the distinction has already been stated.
**Commentary on the Discourse on the Fourth Jhāna:** 87.
Now, in order to show the specific excellence of its production, he says, “But this is the distinction,” and then begins with the words, “Because...”.

There is no condition by way of repetition-condition (*āsevanapaccaya*), because in an undesirable state there is an absence of the repetition-condition for what is included within the subsequent moments.
[The consciousness] arising with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is characterized by an excessive lack of cultivation of the fading away of pleasure (*sukhavirāga*).
By "those," he refers to the impulsion-moments (*javana*) within the cognitive process of absorption (*appanāvīthi*).
88. Because it was stated [previously] as "even before," in response to the objection—"But when does their abandonment occur?"—it is said: "At the moment of the access (upacāra) of the four jhānas.
This is to be understood as the connection [of the sentence]. The "sequence of abandonment" (pahānakkama) refers to the chronological order of the arising of the factors that effect the abandonment.
When that sequence is being stated, one must say: "Suffering, mental grief, pleasure, and mental joy."
It may be so. Why is the statement different from this? He says: "In the *Indriyavibhaṅga*," and so forth. Now, why is cessation mentioned only in relation to the jhānas? This is the connection.
And where does it say "the arisen faculty of pain"? It means the faculty of pain arisen through its own conditions. Where?
And because it ceases without remainder, he asks for the locus of cessation. Therefore, in the question "Where?
and in the answer "There," the locative case should be understood as expressing the reason (*hetu*).

For it is said that "the faculty of suffering ceases without remainder" because its non-arising is due to the power of jhāna. Excessive cessation is thorough abandoning; it is pacification by means of the direct opposite.
"By means of various adverting" means by an adverting that is distinct from the adverting for the path of absorption (*appanāvīthi*), or by multiple instances of adverting.

For in the path of absorption, the access concentration (*upacāra*) involves a single instance of adverting, whereas the other [the path of absorption] involves multiple instances of adverting because it occurs many times.

"Fatigue arising from sitting in an uneven position" refers to the affliction caused by an uneven seat. "By the pervading of rapture" means because rapture has the function of pervading, [referring to] those things originated by rapture.
Or rather, it is said because [the mind] pervades the body with more sublime forms. Therefore he said: "The entire body becomes suffused with pleasure.

As for the phrase "even with the condition of applied thought and sustained thought," the word *pi* (even/also) is used out of place; it should be brought back and connected with the word "abandoned" (*pahīnassa*), thus:
"even though the faculty of mental grief has been abandoned. This faculty of mental grief arises.

The connection [is as follows]: From the statement, “As I was reflecting and examining for too long, my body grew weary and my mind became distressed,” it should be understood that weariness of body and mind has initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained examination (*vicāra*) as their conditions.

This should be connected by supplying the words, “When there is the presence of initial application and sustained examination, the faculty of mental grief arises. In this context, “there may be its arising” means that its arising occurs therein.
The arising of that displeasure (*domanassa*) might occur in the vicinity of the second jhāna.
And here, by one who says, "there might be its arising therein," it is shown that even for those who have attained jhāna, there is the arising of displeasure.
By this, he indicates that hatred (*dosa*), like greed (*lobha*), exists as something whose intrinsic nature is not an hindrance (*anīvaraṇa*).

For mental grief does not arise without hatred. Nor should a contradiction with the *Paṭṭhāna-pāḷi* be considered here, because what is shown there is the mental grief that occurs taking as its object a jhāna that has been lost, since it is impossible for mental grief to arise taking as its object a jhāna that has not been lost.
For those who have attained jhāna, mental grief does not arise at all.
Nor can it be said that [it does not arise] because it has arisen even for one who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*).

Some say, "He had not yet abandoned the jhāna," but that is incorrect, because hatred (*dosa*), whose intrinsic nature is the absence of hindrances (*anīvaraṇa*), is non-existent [in such a state]. If it were possible [for it to arise], it would also arise in beings of the fine-material and immaterial realms;
however, it does not arise there. For it is said: "In the formless realm, the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor arises dependent upon the hindrance of sensual desire."
In such passages as "the hindrance of restlessness and the hindrance of ignorance," the hindrances of ill-will and worry are not mentioned.

Nor is this a matter of them not being hindrances; for even sensual desire and the others, though they are not [inherently] hindrances, are designated by the term "hindrance" because they resemble hindrances.
As for what was said—"because it arises even in one who has attained the eight meditative attainments"—it is as follows:
This too is not a reason, because one falls away from jhāna through the arising of even slight displeasure (*domanassa*).
However, it should be understood that when one has fallen away due to a minor condition, those of similar character restore it to its original state with little difficulty.
The statement, "There might be its arising therein," is a hypothetical expression intended to show that displeasure has not been abandoned at the moment of access concentration (*upacāra*).

For it has been said: "But not even within the access concentration. However, if mental distress (*domanassa*) were to arise at that time, it should be understood that even the first jhāna would have been lost for him.
Although the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) has been abandoned, it is described as being "near" because, like rapture (*pīti*), it is not far away.
Even though the factor of abandonment has been abandoned during the process of various adverting, it remains [as a factor] by way of its opposite.
Showing the meaning of the phrase "because it is unimpeded, it might arise again and again," he said,
"having reached absorption," and so forth. Because such repetition is desirable, they say that just as two or three moments of impulsion prior to the path-moment proceed as similar contemplations,
so too here, two or three moments of impulsion prior to the absorption-moment proceed accompanied by equanimity.

"Collected" (*samāhaṭā*) means brought together; the sense is that they are stated by being grouped together. They are "subtle" (*sukhumā*) because, like pleasure and pain, they are not gross due to their lack of manifestness.

For that very reason, they are "difficult to discern" (*duviññeyyā*) because their intrinsic nature must be inferred. "Of one who is corrupt" (*duṭṭhassa*) means of one whose application [of the mind] is corrupt;
the sense is "of one who is difficult to tame. The intention is that it is possible to cause this [corruption] to be grasped by means of the method of exclusion (*aññāpohanana*).
“By the liberation of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant”: this should be understood as the fourth jhāna itself.

“For the purpose of showing the conditions” means for the purpose of showing the conditions that serve as the means for its attainment. Therefore he said: “For the abandoning of pain and so forth are its conditions.
And here, by the phrase “the abandoning of pain and so forth,” the first jhāna and the others are intended in a figurative sense.
“Abandoned” is said because of the complete destruction of the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*). “These” refers to feelings such as pleasure and so forth.
Mental joy (*somanassa*) is a condition for lust (*rāga*); for it has been said: “Friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust lies latent within pleasant feeling.
Mental grief (*domanassa*) is a condition for hatred (*dosa*); and this too has been said: “Friend Visākha, [the underlying tendency to aversion lies latent within painful feeling]...”
“The underlying tendency to aversion lies latent in feeling. By the “striking down of pleasure and so forth” means by the abandoning of pleasure and so forth.
Of that jhāna. “Not suffering” (adukkhaṃ) means free from suffering; it is devoid of suffering. Because there is no suffering therein, it is therefore said:
“by the absence of suffering. The same method applies here for “not pleasure” (asukhaṃ). “By this” refers to the statement that is the negation of both suffering and pleasure.
“Being the opposite” is stated here because this third feeling is to be attained by means of the transcendence of suffering and so forth;
it is not because of being a direct antithesis like wholesome and unwholesome states.

It has the characteristic of an object that is neutral, being the reverse of the desirable and undesirable, or it has the characteristic of experiencing in a neutral manner that which is the reverse of the desirable and undesirable. It has the characteristic of experiencing what is the reverse of the desirable and undesirable in a neutral way.
For that very reason, they have the flavor of equanimity (*majjhatta-rasa*). They are "of non-manifest appearance" (*avibhūta-paccupaṭṭhāna*);

unlike pleasure and pain, they do not have a manifest mode of appearance, but rather appear in a non-manifest mode to be inferred through them, like the track of a deer on a stone slab. "Cessation of pleasure" (*sukhanirodha*) here refers to the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) of the fourth jhāna;
since this [equanimity] has that as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), it is called "having the cessation of pleasure as its proximate cause."

89. Regarding the phrase “purity of mindfulness through equanimity,” he says, “the purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity,” explaining that this is a compound word formed by eliding the latter member of the first term (*uttarapadalopa*).

When equanimity—which is purified of all opposing states and remains unoccupied even when dealing with those opposites—is present in the fourth jhāna, mindfulness becomes perfectly pure, just as wisdom is highly refined during the act of gladdening.
And it is "very clear," as he says: "Whatever purity that mindfulness has, it is produced by equanimity (upekkhā), not by anything else.
If "equanimity" here is intended to mean "neutrality" (tatramajjhattatā), then how is it that mindfulness itself is called "purified"?
To this he says: "Not only... and so forth.

In this way, with reference to the inquiry as to why this [fourth jhāna] alone is called "purity of mindfulness through equanimity" (*upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi*), the passage beginning with "In that regard, although...

was stated. Therein, although the state of neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā*) exists in the three lower jhānas, there is no purity because it is overcome by its opposites and lacks the necessary supporting conditions; the same applies to the mental factors associated with it.
In order to demonstrate this meaning—that "purity here [arises] from the absence of that"—the passage beginning with "But just as...
was stated by way of a simile. "Overpowered by the sun's radiance" means because it is being overwhelmed by the sun's light.
Like a crescent moon at dawn, even at night it possesses a gentle nature; and since a crescent moon shines only on a night similar [to its own], it belongs to that [category].
Showing that they are "concordant" (sabhāgā), he said: "for a night that is concordant by way of its pleasantness or by way of being beneficial to oneself.
The phrase "in a single cognitive process" (ekavīthiyaṃ) is stated because of the absolute absence of joy (somanassa) therein, not because of its absolute presence in the preceding moments.
Just as applied thought (vitakka) and the other factors are abandoned only at the moment of the second jhāna and beyond, so it is not for these [preceding moments].
This was stated in order to show that it is not the case in the first two sections of the single path.
"In the fourfold jhāna" means in the set of four jhānas produced by way of the fourfold method. Explanation of the Discussion on the Fivefold Jhāna.
90. *Tattha* means in the first jhāna. *As in the second jhāna of the fourfold method* means as in the second jhāna associated with the fourfold method.

*Dividing that into two ways* means dividing the second [jhāna] of the fourfold method into two ways—namely, "without initial application, with sustained application only" and "without initial application, without sustained application"—and [applying them] as the second and third [jhānas] in the fivefold method.
The intended meaning is that this exists in the Abhidhamma. However, the fivefold method (*pañcakanaya*) is not taken up in its explicit form within the Suttantas.

But why is the division into these two methods taken up here? Because in the Abhidhamma, the meditations (*jhāna*) are taught by way of these two methods. And why are they taught in that manner there?
Due to the inclinations of the individuals (*puggalajjhāsaya*) and due to the elegance of the teaching (*desanāvilāsa*). [This was said] regarding the assembly of devas who had gathered together.
It is said that for those to whom, in the first jhāna as thus taught, only applied thought (vitakka) appeared coarse while the others appeared peaceful,
the four-factored jhāna without applied thought and with only sustained thought (vicāramatta) was taught according to their inclination.
For those to whom sustained thought, rapture (pīti), or pleasure (sukha) appeared coarse while the others appeared peaceful, [the respective higher jhānas were taught] for each of them.
The third and subsequent jhānas were taught by way of the inclinations [of those to be trained]. This, first of all, is the inclination of the individual (puggalajjhāsayo).
However, because the Blessed One has thoroughly penetrated that element of phenomena (dhammadhātu), he has attained mastery in the elegance of teaching;
therefore, due to the greatness of his knowledge, being highly skilled in teaching, he [teaches] according to his own preference by way of whichever factor is applicable.
He concludes the teaching by way of the fourfold method and the fivefold method.
Therein, he taught the first jhāna as five-factored, the second as four-factored, the third as three-factored, the fourth as two-factored, and the fifth jhāna likewise as two-factored;
this is the elegance of the teaching. And here, the second jhāna in the fivefold method [is the same as] in the fourfold method...

It is analyzed by being categorized as belonging to the second jhāna: "At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, entering and dwelling in the second jhāna, which is without applied thought, with sustained thought only, born of concentration, and accompanied by rapture and pleasure. Why?

Because it shares the same fruit as the second jhāna, in that its result is the abode of beings who possess a unity of body and diversity of perception; [this is so] because of its difference from the concentration of the first jhāna.
And because it has already arisen. For the first jhāna alone is described as "secluded from sensual desires and from unwholesome states";
since those [factors] are absent here, it cannot be said that it is "quite secluded from sensual desires and secluded from unwholesome states," nor can it be called "born of seclusion.

Furthermore, in the Suttanta teachings, according to the fivefold method, the second and third jhānas are subsumed under the second jhāna alone, due to the subsiding of applied thought (vitakka) and the subsiding of sustained thought (vicāra).

Because of the absence of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). And by establishing it thus, it is proven that the fivefold method (*pañcakanaya*) is indeed found even in the Suttanta teachings. [Objection:
But surely the four jhānas alone are analyzed in the Suttanta; therefore, the fivefold method is not found there. [Reply:

No, because the fivefold method is found through the designation of the three kinds of concentration (*samādhi*), beginning with "concentration with applied and sustained thought" (*savitakkasavicāro samādhi*).
However, since the fivefold method is explained by taking it as dependent upon the fourfold method, the fivefold method must also be extracted from the Suttanta teaching.

For in the phrase "with the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā*), it is possible to speak of "applied thought and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicārānaṃ*) as referring to applied thought alone, sustained thought alone, or both applied and sustained thought together.
Likewise, this applies to the term "without applied thought and without sustained thought" (*avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ*), whether taken separately or together.

By means of investigation (*vicāra*) there is "without initial application" (*avitakka*) through the abandoning of initial application; and by means of investigation together with, or even without, initial application, there is "without sustained application" (*avicāra*) through the abandoning of sustained application.

Thus, it can be subsumed under three categories: "without initial application," "without sustained application," and "both without initial application and without sustained application. Furthermore, the term "second" refers to that which is free from initial application, as well as that which is free from both initial and sustained application;
it is called "second" because it is to be attained following the teaching that has come down through the proper method.
Because, even though it is devoid of *vicāra* alone, it possesses the same quality attained through the abandonment of both [vitakka and vicāra].

And having established this, in the exposition of the fivefold method (*pañcakanaya-niddesa*), regarding the second [jhāna], although *vitakka* has subsided, it is not "perfectly subsided" because its companion, *vicāra*, has not yet subsided.

Thus, by showing that the subsiding of those two is equivalent to the subsiding of *vicāra* alone—as if they were both absent—and by showing the equality of the remaining factors, [it says]: "Of *vitakka* and *vicāra*..."

"With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is born of concentration, and possesses rapture and happiness free from directed thought and evaluation"—
thus, in the fourfold method, the third [jhāna] is explained as being indistinguishable from the second.
It is "without directed thought" (avitakka) both because it lacks its companion [vicāra] and because of the abandonment of directed thought in another way.
Because it is equal in its possession of the joy and happiness born of concentration (*samādhija-pītisukha*), it is described as "the second" due to having common characteristics.

For even that which consists of investigation alone (*vicāramatta*), being devoid of the pair of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*), is called "without applied thought" (*avitakka*)—just as in the passage: "At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, one dwells having attained the second jhāna, which is without applied thought, with investigation alone, born of concentration, and accompanied by joy and happiness."

"Born of concentration, rapture and pleasure" is thus analyzed. Alternatively, within the first jhāna, having transcended one of the two concomitants—vitakka and vicāra—and seeing that the second [vicāra] as well is likewise faulty, for one who transcends both together, the third [jhāna] is mentioned according to the fivefold method because it is to be attained thirdly.
Its status as "second," however, is due to its occurring immediately after the first.

And it arises. But why is the fivefold method not analyzed here in its own form? Because of the inclinations of those to be trained. For the teaching of the Suttas is a teaching given according to what is appropriate [to the listeners].
The commentary on the description of the earth-kasiṇa is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourth chapter.
5. Commentary on the Description of the Remaining Kasiṇas;
Commentary on the Discussion of the Water Kasiṇa.
91. Since even an extension (*atidesa*) of a meaning already explained in detail remains within the context of that detailed exposition itself, he says: "There is a detailed discussion.
"The water-kasina" (*āpokasiṇa*) refers either to the jhāna of the water-kasina or to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) of the water-kasina.
"Everything should be detailed" means it should be detailed according to the method stated for the earth-kasina meditation subject. "Even this much" refers to the phrase: "Whether made or unmade..."
Without saying even this much—that "all should be detailed"—it is said: "A reservoir filled with salt water from the ocean is a 'salt-pool.
It is stated that it was 'taken up in a clean cloth' in order to avoid mixing with colors such as blue and so forth.
'Another' means that which has reached the ground. 'Of such a kind' means of the same nature as rainwater from the sky. Therefore he said: "clear."

"Untroubled" (*anāvila*) is connected with the word "water. Regarding what should be said about such passages as "the color is not to be reviewed," that has already been stated in the discussion on the earth-kasiṇa (*pathavīkasiṇa*).
However, the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) here should be understood as the characteristic of trickling.

"In the same manner as stated" means in the very same manner as stated in the development of the earth-kasiṇa. Here, the defects of the kasiṇa consist of waves, bubbles, and so forth, as well as being mixed with froth. "He" refers to the practitioner (*yogāvacara*). "Of it" refers to the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*).
Commentary on the Fire Kasiṇa (Tejokasiṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 92.
"Glossy" means possessing moisture. "Hard wood" means not softwood. Glossy hardwood is specified for the purpose of ensuring that the flame persists for a long time.
"Having made it into small pieces" means having cut it into sections. "Having kindled it" means...
"Having kindled": in a mass of flames occurring without gaps. "Like falling": like something that is actually falling.

"For one who grasps it when unmade": for one who, according to the method already stated, grasps the sign in the mere fire-element itself, without having fashioned it, just as the kasiṇa-disk appears.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Air Kasiṇa.
93. Regarding the phrase *vuttañhetam*: here the word *hi* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*), meaning "because" (*yasmā*).
Its connection is with the word "therefore" (*tasmā*). *Ucchaggaṃ* means the tip of sugarcanes as they stand in the sugar-cane field.
*Eritaṃ* means moved by the wind. *Sameritaṃ* means moved in every way. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) refers to what was stated thus: "He characterizes the air-kasiṇa... [etc.]..."
In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), therefore: "standing with level tops" means standing with level tops by way of the leaves above.
Regarding the phrase "a bamboo or a tree," here too it should be connected by supplying the words: "a bamboo with dense foliage or a tree with dense foliage standing with level tops.
Because hair that is one finger-breadth or more in measure is short in nature, and because longer [hair] hangs down.
Because the impact of the wind is not perceived when it enters through sparse openings, the measurement of four finger-breadths is taken, and the term "dense" is also employed.

"Striking at this spot" means having established mindfulness; that is, by way of perceiving the manner in which the stalks of sugarcane and so forth move, one establishes mindfulness upon those aggregates of wind that strike them.
In that context, "having established mindfulness" refers to that specific region of the body.
Having established mindfulness by way of grasping the mode of impact in the mass of air as it occurs through the process of striking, [the text says] "resembling a ball of heat.
By this, it shows that, like the previous kasiṇa, this sign also lacks a physical basis (*saṃviggahata*).

By the word "motionless," it shows that its specific distinction from the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*) is precisely its state of being motionless; this applies to the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*) as well.
The resemblance to a smoke-wisp is thus made clear.
94. The description of the blue kasiṇa:
[it may be] like a line of collyrium, a circle, and so forth, or from a color-element; likewise, it may be like a grove of garlands covered with dense, blooming blue-colored flowers.
A flowering shrub. "By the other" means by one who has not performed the preparatory duties (*akatādhikāra*). By the mention of *girikaṇṇikā*, he refers to the blue *girikaṇṇikā*.
A *karaṇḍapaṭala* is the lid of a casket. "With petals alone" means having removed the filaments and stalks of the blue lotuses and so forth, [filling it] with the petals alone.
"It should be filled" means taking a cloth of blue color and binding it together like a bundle.
Just as it appears when there is a blue circle, so too should the *caṅkoṭaka* or the lid of the casket be filled.
Or it may be on the rim of the mouth; that is, it should be fastened to the rim of the mouth of that *caṅkoṭaka* or the lid of the casket.
A "jeweled palm-leaf fan" (*maṇitālavaṇṭa*) is a palm-leaf fan made of sapphire (*indanīlamaṇi*).
Commentary on the Yellow Kasiṇa (Pītakasiṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 95.
Regarding the yellow kasiṇa: "A garland-grove" refers to a grove of *ikkaṭa* and other such flowering shrubs. "Mineral" refers to either yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) or realgar (*manosilā*).

"With *pattaṅga* flowers" means with the flowers of a certain species of shrub named *pattaṅga*, which has yellow-colored blossoms. "Worship of the seat" refers to [the offering] at the courtyard of the cetiya.
The worship of the seat has been described. Regarding the phrase "kaṇikāra flowers, etc.," the word "etc. (ādi) should be understood as including *ākulika*, *kiṅkirāta* flowers, and so forth.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Red Kasiṇa (96):
"Red gems" refers to rubies (*lohitaṅgamaṇi*), etc. "Red minerals" refers to types of red chalk (*geruka*) and vermilion (*hiṅgulika*), etc.
Commentary on the White Kasiṇa: 97.
Regarding the white kasiṇa, "garland-pattern" refers to a garland-pattern such as the *nandiyāvatta* and others. "Mineral substance" refers to lime, oyster-shell, chalk, and so forth.
Commentary on the Light Kasiṇa:

98. "Being unable to do so" means: being unable to produce the sign in that manner because the circle of light (obhāsa-maṇḍala) does not persist for long, just as the production of the sign by means of sunlight and so forth was previously described.
Because the light emerging from the mouth of the pot is large, it is said, "having closed the mouth of the pot. "The surface of the wall" means...
"Facing the wall": "resembling a circle of light arisen [on it]" means resembling a natural circle of light that has arisen on walls and such surfaces.

"Dense and serene, like a mass of light": the meaning is that if there is a light which, like the fathom-wide radiance of the Blessed One, is both thick and serene, and exists as a mass, it is similar to that.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Space-Kasiṇa Limited by a Boundary (99).
“It remains just like a hole”: the meaning is that it appears as the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*) in the same shape as that hole which was delimited by the boundaries of the wall and so forth;
it is similar to that. “Even when being increased, it does not increase”: this refers to the learning sign.
This was said to demonstrate its non-increase. For indeed, even when the learning-sign (*uggahanimitta*) is being increased, it does not actually increase at all.
And even though there may be a desire to increase it, such increase is impossible because the meditation (*bhāvanā*) is too weak. For the increase of the sign occurs by way of meditation.
However, regarding the counterpart-sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*), once it has arisen, meditation is firm; therefore, it is said that "when being increased, it increases."

Although in the Pāḷi only eight kasiṇas—beginning with the earth-kasiṇa—are mentioned by name as the objects of the fine-material jhānas, the teaching was given with the underlying intention that the light-kasiṇa is included within the white-kasiṇa, and the limited-space-kasiṇa is included within the space-kasiṇa;
thus it was said: "These ten kasiṇas which the Ten-Powered One spoke. This is also a supplementary discussion.
"Should be understood" means that, unlike before, one should understand not only the specific meaning restricted to each respective kasiṇa in its uncommon aspect,
but also the miscellaneous discourse (pakiṇṇakakathā) which proceeds by taking up various scattered meanings there and there in both their uncommon and common aspects.
Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discourse (Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā) 100.
Regarding the phrase "the state of being primary" (*ādibhāvo*): here, by the word *ādi*, one includes the creation and so forth of any material object belonging to the earth element.
Regarding the phrase "or the arrangement of standing, sitting, and so forth": here too, the words "in the air or in water" should be brought forward and connected.
"By way of the limited and the measureless" means without touching upon colors such as blue and so forth, but solely by way of the limited and the measureless.
"And so forth"—by the word "and so forth," one includes such things as the emission of streams of water from the body.
"The capacity to burn whatever he wishes" refers to [the power] to burn many cotton bolls, heartwood of teak, and so on, all together.
When things have become a mass and remain so, there is the capacity to burn whatever one desires. Here, by the word "etc.
(*ādi*), the dispelling of darkness and so forth are included.
"Going by way of the movement of wind" (*vāyugatigamana*) means going with extreme speed. Here, by the word "etc.," reaching whatever other destination one desires and so forth are included.

"Gold" refers to the resolve and the determination of its golden state, such as in the case of the Venerable Pilindavaccha regarding the grass hut, the Pāsāda palace, and so forth. "In the manner stated" means by way of the beautiful and the ugly.

In the case of the color-kasinas (*vaṇṇakasiṇa*), it should be understood that the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the manifestation of blue light and other such qualities in their respective places. "Earth, mountains, and so forth"—here too, the word "and so forth" should be understood to include the oceans and the like.
"All ten kasinas" means they all obtain this classification; that is, they reach this specific distinction of expansion and so on.

“One person” means a certain individual. “Perceives” means he perceives by means of the wisdom of meditation (*bhāvanā-paññā*). By the word “etcetera,” the textual passage beginning with “the water-kasiṇa” is included.
Having brought forward the words from the text, “One person perceives the earth-kasiṇa directed toward the upper surface of the sky,” they should be connected [to the present context].

And that is by way of expansion. Therefore he said: “For one person expands the kasiṇa only upwards. This should also be applied to the phrases beginning with “directed toward the lower surface of the earth,” and so forth.

The same method applies here. Because it was previously stated with reference to those who expand [the kasiṇa] without regard for a specific purpose, he now says, "For this or that reason, he extends it thus," meaning he expands the kasiṇa.
To the question "In what way?", he says, "Just as one desiring to see forms with the divine eye [extends] light. If he desires to see forms above...
If one wishes to see forms above, one extends the light upwards; if one wishes to see forms below, one extends the light downwards;
if one wishes to see forms all around, one extends the light all around. Such is the meaning of "this is the *kasiṇa*.

"Of each" means of each one among the earth-*kasiṇa* and the others. "For the purpose of not lapsing into the state of being something else" means for the purpose of demonstrating that it does not lapse into the state of being any other *kasiṇa*.

It is not something other than earth and so forth. For where it stands upon water, there is no earth together with its constituent parts. "Another confusion of the kasiṇa" means a commingling with the water-kasiṇa and the others. "In all places" means in all the remaining kasiṇas, such as the water-kasiṇa.
Because it does not occupy only one part but is grasped as a measure of pervasion without remainder, the pervasion is immeasurable. For that very reason, they receive the designation "kasiṇa."
And so he said, beginning with "Therein" (*tañhi*), and so forth. In that context, "pervading with the mind" means making the object of focus by means of the mind of meditation (*bhāvanā-citta*).
For the mind of meditation attends to the entire *kasiṇa*—whether limited or vast—in a single moment; it does not attend to only a portion.
(101) "Those possessing actions of immediate retribution" refers to those endowed with any one of the five actions that bring immediate result.

"Those with fixed wrong view" means those endowed with any one of the three types of wrong view—namely, the view of no cause, the view of non-action, or the view of nihilism—that is fixed. "Hermaphrodites and eunuchs" refers to both hermaphrodites and eunuchs.
Granted, because they possess rebirth-linking consciousness without roots (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*), they are endowed with the obstruction of karmic result (*vipākāvaraṇa*); nevertheless...
Because their defilements are sharp, they are said to be "possessed of the obscuration of defilements. Regarding the phrase "those with rebirth-linking based on no-root or two-roots":

this refers to those with rebirth-linking based on no-root and those with rebirth-linking based on two-roots. For even those with rebirth-linking based on two roots lack penetration of the Noble Path and the attainment of jhāna;
therefore, they too are indeed possessed of the obscuration of kamma-result.
"In the practice that is not contrary" means in the practice conformable to the Path, in insight (vipassanā) which conforms to the Truths.
Regarding "those lacking desire," it is stated in the *Sammohavinodanī* that they are "devoid of the desire of the wish-to-do";

however, even that should be understood as being said with reference specifically to the desire of the wish-to-do for the sake of attaining Nibbāna. This applies even to humans of Uttarakuru, Māra, and so forth.
They have entered as it were into a state of lack of desire because they are devoid of the desire for Nibbāna.
"Lacking in wisdom" means being deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-paññā*).

For it is stated in the *Sammohavinodanī*: "Even one whose life-continuum is complete in wisdom, if that life-continuum does not serve as a basis for the supramundane, is likewise lacking in wisdom. Indeed, while that life-continuum is occurring...
When supramundane [consciousness] arises within that continuity, it is called its "foundation" (pādaka).
"In wholesome states" means in blameless states or in states that have a pleasant result. "To descend" means to attain. "Only in the kasiṇa" means only in the kasiṇa meditation subject.
"Of these" refers to those possessed of the obstruction of karma and so forth. "Therefore" [means...].
Because these obstacles to fruition and so forth thus bring about what is harmful and are causes of misfortune, therefore—
here, it should be understood that only three obstacles are mentioned because the others are remediable or belong to the category of obstacles to karma (*kammantarāya*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "relying on a true person, and so forth," one includes appropriate wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and the like.

"Faith" (saddhā) refers to faith in the results of kamma and faith in the Triple Gem. "Zeal" (chanda) refers to wholesome zeal characterized by an intense desire to act in the practice of meditation. "Wisdom" (paññā) refers to functional wisdom (pārihāriya-paññā).
"Having increased" (vaḍḍhetvā) means having fully cultivated it in such a way that meditation succeeds.
As for those points not analyzed here in terms of meaning, they have not been analyzed because they are easy to understand and because the method has already been stated below.
The commentary on the description of the remaining kasiṇas is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifth chapter.
6. Commentary on the Description of the Meditation Subject of Foulness (Asubha-kammaṭṭhāna).
Commentary on the Terms *Uddhumātaka*, etc. (102):
“In the case of the unperceiving foul” is stated by way of showing the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of the bloated corpse and the rest.
Therefore, it should be regarded as a mere statement of fact; for it is not that the perceiving foul is not a subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Likewise...

For he will say: "Not only my own body," and so forth. *Uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā* means after the exhaustion of life, beyond death. *Samuggatena* means having arisen. *Uddhumātattā* means because of being bloated, puffed up, and swollen.
He uses the syllable *ka* to extend the word, saying *uddhumātakaṃ* (the bloated), because there is no difference in meaning, just as [in the case of] *sukhaṃ* and *sukhakaṃ*.

“Yellowish, reddish. By way of repulsiveness means by way of being disgusting. To show that the syllable *ka* is used here in the sense of contempt—as in the expression “an evil report has spread”—it is said: “The bloated is called *uddhumātaka* because it is contemptible (*kucchitaṃ uddhumātaṃ*), or because it is bloated (*uddhumātaṃ*).
“Of such a kind” means of such a kind as described by the words “like a bellows filled with air,” and so forth.
*Vinīla* refers to what is disintegrated by other [elements] and mixed, or blue-black; it is blue-black because it has undergone a transformation from its previous color.
By "in the places where it is disintegrated" is meant by crows, *kaṅka*-birds, and so forth. "Flowing pus" means oozing pus; the meaning is that the pus is trickling here and there.

"Spread open" means uncovered or opened up. "Cast away" means discarded; having been torn from the mass of the body by dogs, jackals, and so forth through devouring, it is cast away here and there. "Variously cast" means scattered.
"By the previous method" means by the method stated previously in the passage beginning with "variously scattered.

"Having struck with a weapon" means having been struck by enemies with weapons such as swords or scimitars. "By the stated method" means by the method stated previously in the passage beginning with "by another hand.
He said "full of worms" because it is a mass of maggots (*puḷavaka*) where swarms of worms are oozing out from within.

The bloated corpse and so forth are the unattractive things discarded in raw charnel grounds and similar places. "Depending on" means relying upon them, taking them as the object. "Of the signs" refers to the learning sign (*uggaha-nimitta*) and the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*). "These very names" refers specifically to the names of the bloated corpse and the rest. Commentary on the Bloated Corpse Meditation Subject (103):

"By one desiring to develop" means by one desiring to produce [the meditation subject]. "By him" means by the teacher. "His" refers to the practitioner (*yogin*). "For the sake of the sign of the unattractive" means...
It is for the purpose of grasping the sign of foulness, or for the purpose of the learning sign within the foul.
"The method of going" means the procedure of going; it is the procedure by which one should go.
He says, "ending with the method of absorption," referring to the procedure of practice already described for the earth-kasiṇa, starting from the time the learning sign arises.
104. “At that very moment” means at the very instant of hearing. It is like one who enters a full river and so forth by leaping in with a lack of a ford.
“At the edge of a field” means at the boundary of a field. “A disagreeable form” refers to the disagreeable physical matter of a field-guardian or similar being.
“A body” refers to a bloated corpse. “Recently deceased” means not long dead, one who has not yet reached the state of being bloated.
"Takkayati" means he reflects; having considered it weighty, he does not disregard it.

Regarding "forms, sounds, and so forth": here this refers to the forms of non-human beings, the sounds and so forth of lions, tigers, and the like, or the forms, sounds, and so forth of non-human beings themselves.
Likewise, for lions, tigers, and so forth, the application should be made as appropriate. "Of one who is overcome by an undesirable object."
"Overwhelmed and overwhelmed by" means overcome and submerged by undesirable objects such as terrifying things.
"Does not settle down" means it does not remain in its natural seat due to the state of being scorched; the meaning is that it must be cast out.

"Another" refers to a disease other than those mentioned above, occurring either through non-human beings or otherwise. "He" refers to the senior monk of the Saṅgha, a bhikkhu of well-known reputation.

Or: he to whom it has been reported by him. "Those who have committed the deed" (*katākammā*) means those who have performed the act of theft. "Those who have not committed the deed" (*akatākammā*) means those desiring to perform the act of theft;
however, here it is those who have committed the deed that are intended. Therefore, "those" refers to the thieves who have committed the deed.
"Together with the stolen goods" (*sahoḍḍham*) means together with the property being taken after having stolen it—that is the meaning. "The sacrificer" (*yajamāno*) means one performing a sacrifice.
The master of the sacrifice, having generated joy and gladness [thinking], "Surely by this practice I shall be liberated from aging and death.
Having thus explained the procedure for going in part, he now says, "By the method stated in the commentaries," etc., in order to show it according to the manner handed down in the Aṭṭhakathās.
Therein, "learning" (uggaṇhanto) means for the sake of learning. This word "one" (eko)— [End of fragment]
The meaning is "without a companion," not "having no other [qualities] such as beauty" (*aññādi*); thus it is said "without a second" (*adutiya*).

Just as the determination [of a word] from the perspective of phoneme (*vaṇṇa*) and so forth must necessarily be accepted as combined because of its universal applicability, it is not so with respect to euphonic combination (*sandhi*) and the like;

in order to demonstrate this, the particle *pi* is employed in the six instances beginning with "even from the perspective of the phoneme" (*vaṇṇato pi*) to signify inclusion. Furthermore, [the passage begins] "one, without a second," and so forth.
This was said with reference to the yogi who, having grasped the sign, returns to his dwelling place.

"Belonging to that very category" means belonging to that same side, namely, accompanied by attention to the sign of foulness (*aśubha-nimitta*). "He prepares a seat" means he arranges a place to sit.
Furthermore, what he will later say—"on a patch of ground facing the direction of the sign of foulness"—also refers to this very same point.
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). For nothing is accomplished by the mere fact of facing a direction.
"Observing the signs all around" means the careful examination of signs such as stones and so forth all around the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*).

"For the sake of non-delusion" means for the purpose of removing the delusion that arises when the sign of apprehension (*uggaha-nimitta*) has appeared. "In eleven ways" refers to the modes beginning with color (*vaṇṇa*).
"In eleven ways": the purpose of binding is the purpose of binding the mind to the object of foulness (asubha).
"The purpose of introducing it into the cognitive process" means the purpose of correctly introducing it into the sequence of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna-vīthi).
The connection is: "the basis for meritorious action is attained."
106. Therefore: because the apprehension of the sign of foulness is the means for attaining the first jhāna, which is the proximate cause for the Noble Path;
or because it is said, "One who apprehends the sign of foulness goes alone, without a companion";
therefore [he went]. "For the purpose of instructing his own mind" means by means of observing the true nature of the body and by generating a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) within himself.

For the purpose of making the mind compliant, for the purpose of making it amenable. Alternatively, there is the reading *cittasaññatatthāya*, which means for the purpose of restraining and taming the mind that is unrestrained due to the defilements, and not for the sake of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

"By way of the meditation subject as the head" means with the meditation subject acting as the head—that is, making it the foremost limb, the primary cause. "The root meditation subject" (*mūlakammaṭṭhāna*)...
The all-pervading meditation subject, such as the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), which is by its very nature something one should attend to from time to time.
Without relinquishing that [subject], thinking, “I am going under the heading of a meditation subject,” he said: “By attending to that very thing.
“By accomplishing the state of being well-established” means by accomplishing the state of being thoroughly established in the primary meditation subject.
For this being so, it is called "unconfused. When the mind does not operate upon external, manifold objects but operates only upon the meditation subject, it is said to be "not gone outward.
And when it is in such a state, the functions of the physical sense-faculties are rendered inactive;
thus he says: "The six, with the mind as the sixth... must not go..."

"The door should be observed" means that one should ascertain the door by noting which direction among the eastern directions and so forth this door is in the monastery, and thinking, "From there, I have gone out through such-and-such a door" as it was observed in that direction.
"After that" means after the observation of the door. "The place of the sign" refers to the object of meditation on the foul (*asubhanimitta*).
The place for taking [food]. "Should cause to discard food" means one should cause vomiting. "A place with thorns" means a place possessing thorns. 107.
Regarding the statement "the directions should be determined," the passage beginning with "In one [case]" and so forth was spoken in order to explain the meaning stated in brief.
"Appears" means it presents itself. "Fit for work" means capable of being worked upon through meditation (*bhāvanā*). "Of one who is oppressed" means of one who is afflicted.
"It runs about" means it wanders among various objects. "Moving away" means moving straight away from the wind.
He said, "Fear arises when [the corpse] is very near," because for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), a dead body generally appears as something fearful. "Nearby" means close to the feet.
That place where one can look at it easily while standing is the comfortable spot for looking at it.
108. *Samanta* means all around. Again, *samanta* means neighboring or nearby.
*Kacchaka* refers to the black *kacchaka* tree; some also call it a *pilakkha*. *Kapītana* is the *pippali* tree. *Sindī* is the small date palm.
*Karamanda* and the others are well known. *Sāma* is the *sāma* creeper. *Kāḷavallī* is a species of creeper that is black in color and leafless. *Pūtilatā* is the rotten creeper.
The *jīvanavallī*, which is called "galocī. 109.
That making of a sign and so forth is included and contained within the very making of signs such as stones, etc., as already described here.
"He makes it with a sign" means he makes it together with a sign; he makes it, that is, he defines it, together with a sign such as a stone, etc., [using] the foul (*asubha*).
Alternatively, one who combines the sign of foulness and the sign of a stone or similar object together in one place and defines it is said to "make it with its sign.
For this compound is formed with the word *saha* (together) indicating simultaneity, just as in the expression "give [it] with the wheel" (*sacakkaṃ dehī*).
This making of the sign occurs through repeated observation, not just once; thus he says:
“By defining it again and again, one makes it with its sign. “Two” refers to the two signs of the foul (asubha-nimitta): the stone and the [corpse].
Having combined, having gathered, and having brought them together into one. “With an object” means: he makes the stone, etc., share the same object as the foul object;
or he makes it with an object; or he makes both objects as if they were a single object, bringing them together.
The meaning is that by observing one thing after another, such as a stone and so forth, he takes both of these—the stone and the sign of foulness—as his object.

"One's own" (*attaniyo*) means belonging to oneself. "Wound" (*vaṇitaṃ*) means a sore. "By its own nature and essence" means by its own characteristic, namely the state of being bloated, and by its own function, namely the production of disgust in others; it is the very nature [that is meant].
Or, it is called "the essence" (rasa) because it is produced in that way.
110. Regarding the sign to be grasped in six ways: first, the sign of the bloated foulness (uddhumātaka-asubha-nimitta) should be grasped in six modes, such as color and so forth.
Some say it is "sevenfold," including the dimensions of the corpse, such as long or short.

That [explanation] is not found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Regarding the phrase "by way of gender" (*liṅgato*): here, "gender" (*liṅga*) refers to age-gender (*vayo-liṅga*), and not to the physical marks of female or male such as breasts, beard, and so forth;
this is shown by the statement "or female gender," etc. The connection is: "this body of a being who has come to stay.
It is precisely by way of the shape of a bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*), and not by way of its natural shape. By this—
This shows that if there were any part therein that had reached the state of being bloated, it should not be included.
This determination of shape is by way of gross components, not by way of subtle components; thus, only the nine kinds of shape, beginning with the shape of the head, are taken.
"In this direction" means: the construction is that one is situated in this eastern, southern, western, or northern direction, or in an intermediate direction (*anudisā*).
"In this very place, the hands" means: it should be determined that "the hands of this physical body are situated in this particular spot of ground"—this is the construction.
"Below by the sole of the foot," and so forth, is said according to this definition: that which is below the navel is "below," and that which is above it is "above.
The delimitation of the hand is to be grasped as below by the tip of the fingers, above by the joint of the shoulder-peak, and across by the limit of the skin.
This same method applies to the delimitations of the foot and so on. Or, however much space—
"Grasps": if one is unable to grasp the entire body by delimiting it as a whole, then a particular part of it is bloated.
To whatever extent one grasps that bodily region with knowledge according to its bloated state, it is exactly that much, precisely as it has been delimited.
"This is such-and-such": this refers to the hand and so forth; it is "such," meaning of such a form. "Bloated" is to be delimited according to its true nature.
When the body is in a dissimilar state, the meditation subject as an object—the aspect of repulsiveness—does not appear or manifest;
rather, it would appear as beautiful. Therefore he said: “It is a condition for agitation alone,” meaning it becomes a sign for the agitation of the defilements.
“Even when burst open” means even when it has reached the state of being bloated, or even when the body is completely putrefied.
Or rather, this is the meaning. This meaning is to be illustrated by the cases explained in the first *pārājika* rule. 111.

"One who has cultivated the meditation subject" means one who has gained proficiency in the meditation subject of foulness (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*). One who, by means of the ascetic practices such as the cemetery-dweller's practice (*sosānika-aṅga*), has fulfilled the ascetic virtues (*dhutaṅga*).

One who, by means of the analysis of the four elements (*catudhātu-vavatthāna*), has thoroughly rubbed and examined the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*). By means of knowledge according to their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*)...
One who has discerned conditioned phenomena; one who has defined name-and-form by means of discerning conditions;
one whose perception of a "being" has been removed by the power of the contemplation of emptiness through the intensification of insight that takes specific characteristics as its object;

one who has fulfilled the duties of a recluse by bringing the purification of knowledge and vision of the way of insight to completion; and, for that very reason, one whose latent tendencies have been perfumed by the fulfillment of wholesome tendencies and wholesome cultivation.

He is one who has cultivated cultivation. He possesses the seed because he has the wholesome seeds that are the necessary conditions for turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*). He is supreme in knowledge due to the ripeness of his knowledge.
He has few defilements because he has thinned out the defilements through the practice already described. "Only in whatever place it is looked upon" means:
only in whatever specific place the foulness (*asubha*)—such as a bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*) and so forth—is observed; such is the distinction of time.

The meaning is that there is no need to consider a particular portion of the foul (asubha). "If it does not appear thus" means if the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) does not appear in the manner described for the specific type of person mentioned above.
"In this sixfold way" means in the sixfold manner according to the aspects such as color (vaṇṇa) and so forth, as already stated. Furthermore, the word "also" (pi) has the sense of inclusion; by it—
This summarizes the method for grasping the sign, not its fivefold nature; for previously, the grasping of the sign was prescribed as sixfold.
Having stated "with one hundred and eighty joints" in order to show that all those joints still exist even then, [it is said] "in the bloated":
this is to show that those which are generally no longer discernible due to the state of being bloated must nevertheless be defined. In the bloated...
The passage beginning with “panā” has been stated. Therein, “three joints of the right hand” refers to the three joints of the right hand by way of the shoulder, elbow, and wrist.
Likewise for the joints of the left hand. By way of the hip, knee, and ankle, there are three joints of the right foot;
likewise for the joints of the left foot. “One joint of the waist” refers to [the joint] together with the waist.
He speaks with reference to the joints of the spinal vertebrae.

"The space between the hands" refers to the interval or opening between the right hand and the right side, and between the left hand and the left side. "The space between the feet" is the middle point between both feet.
"The space between the belly" is the middle of the abdomen designated as the region of the navel, or the interior of the belly. "The space between the ears" [is the interval between them].
“The ear-holes. The word *iti* has the sense of “beginning with”; by it, the inclusion of the nostril-holes and so forth should be understood.
To show that an opening is indeed found even by way of the eyes and the mouth, the passage beginning with “of the eyes too” was stated. “On all sides”:
if, while one is thus defining the bloated corpse starting from the joints and so forth, the sign (nimitta) appears, that is well.
"Then, it should be defined all around"—this was said in order to show the method of definition.

Therein, "having directed knowledge" means having adverted to the entire body and, with respect to that state of bloatedness accompanied by its repulsive aspect, having set forth the knowledge of meditation continuously.
"Whatever place," however, refers to this: [the text continues: "But when..."
For one who is directing his knowledge [toward it], that part of the body which has become bloated appears in the form of a bloated corpse by way of its state of being bloated.
This refers to the upper part of the body, ending at the abdomen.
[End of] the commentary on the exposition of the analysis.
113. *Vinicchayakathā* means a commentary on the meaning together with a detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*).

"By way of apprehending the sign as previously described" means by way of apprehending the sign of the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*) in the manner already stated, such as by its color and so forth, or by its joints and so forth.
"The sign must be well-apprehended" means that the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*) should be correctly grasped in such a way that the learning-sign (*uggahanimitta*) becomes manifest.
Now, pointing out that very manner of grasping the sign thoroughly, he said, "Having made mindfulness well-established," and so forth.

Therein, "by doing this again and again" means: having developed a sense of urgency, thinking, "By this practice I shall be liberated from aging and death," and having properly established both mindfulness and clear comprehension, one first adverts to the bloated foulness.
Thus, by repeatedly directing the mind toward that object, one must "carefully examine" and "define" it;
that is, one must attentively observe it with mindfulness and determine it with wisdom.
For mindfulness is defined as "retention," and here retention means observation. Wisdom is defined as "investigation," and here investigation—
"Ascertainment" (*nicchaya*): Alternatively, "to be scrutinized" means it should be characterized by wisdom preceded by mindfulness.
For there is never such a thing as wisdom devoid of mindfulness. "To be defined" means it should be determined by mindfulness preceded by wisdom.
For here, mindfulness accompanied by wisdom is intended, not that which is devoid of it. Even looking [at objects] by way of a sidelong glance or a squint is [included].
"It exists" means "having opened [the eyes] and looked"; by this, he shows that the looking must be quite distinct.
"Doing so again and again" means doing repeatedly many times in the manner described—the opening of the eyes and looking, and the closing of the eyes and adverting—alternately.
"The learning sign" (uggahanimitta) refers to the sign acquired from the bloated corpse.
“Suggahitaṃ” means well-grasped. It is grasped in such a way that it does not perish and is not forgotten.
“Ekasadisaṃ” means identical. For this word *eka* has the sense of “identical,” as in:
“In the Noble Discipline or in the Discipline of the True Persons—these are the same, identical, synonymous, equal, equivalent, of the same kind, or similar.”
"At the time of coming" means at the time of coming from the monastery toward the charnel ground.

By the phrase "in the manner already stated," he demonstrates by way of reference (*atidesa*) that the meaning has been shown, and then presents it explicitly in its own form with the words "by himself alone," and so forth. Therein, "that same meditation subject" refers to the bloated (*uddhumātaka*) meditation subject.
Some say it is the "root meditation subject," but that is incorrect; for it is the sign (*nimitta*) that has appeared [which is meant].
Abandoning the meditation subject and attending to something other than the meditation subject is like a king abandoning his kingdom and going abroad.
"Having returned" means having come back to one's own dwelling place.
"At an improper time" means at an unsuitable time such as the twilight hour. "Repulsive" means ugly. "A terrifying object" means...

A terrifying object resembling a *vetāla* (a corpse-demon). "With a distracted mind" means that, like a timid man who has fallen into mental agitation upon seeing a *pisāca* or similar spirit, his mind becomes deranged.
"Like one insane" means that some person becomes like one possessed by a *yakkha*.

"One who has fallen away from jhāna" means one who has slipped away from meditative absorption, just as there are those who have fallen away from virtue or fallen away from spells (*manta*). "Having steadied himself" means by means of the pacification of the minor taints (*parittāsava*) that have arisen.
"Being motionless" means having become free from trembling. "Mindfulness well-established," and so forth, shows the method for steadying oneself.
There is no such thing as a dead body rising up and following one, unless there is the application of a corresponding spell (*mantappayoga*).

Even that [spell] succeeds only when the form has not yet decomposed and has not reached the state of being bloated (*uddhumātaka*), etc.; likewise with the seizing by a deity (*devatādhiggaha*), it does not happen in such a case.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Born of perception" (*saññājoti*) means born of the perception consisting in the conceptualization of meditation (*bhāvanā-parikappa-saññā*). For that very reason, it is "the arising of perception," originating from mere perception.
"Having dispelled those" means having dispelled and pacified, by the method described, the fear arisen in the mind-stream due to the appearance of the sign (*nimitta*).
Having generated laughter, rapture, and joy [with the thought]: "Now your exertion has become fruitful."
