"Cittaṃ sañcarāpetabbaṃ" means that the mind of meditation should be set in motion, it should be brought to mind, and it should be attended to.
"Nimittaggāhaṃ" means the grasping of the sign; that is, the learning-sign (uggahanimitta). "Sampādento" means accomplishing or bringing to completion.
"Kammaṭṭhānaṃ upanibandhatī" means he ties the meditation subject fast by fixing the meditation upon the aforementioned sign. This is the work of yoga (yogakammaṃ).
For it is intended as a "subject of meditation" (*kammaṭṭhāna*) because it serves as the cause for the specific types of happiness of the yogi;
or else, because it is the locus for the occurrence of the work of yoga, the sign as it appears is the subject of meditation.
One binds that [sign] to the mind of development (*bhāvanācitta*). With reference to that binding of it, the mind must be made to move about. In this way, one "attains distinction."
Showing that it has been so stated, he says, "For him," and so forth. Therein, "for him" refers to the yogi, or to that unattractive bloated corpse.
"While moving the mind" means while causing the meditative consciousness to proceed from one point to another; the meaning is: while repeatedly attending to the learning-sign (*uggahanimitta*).

115. Having stated that the meaning of the phrase “for the purpose of entering the path” is “for the purpose of entering the path of the meditation subject,” he says “If, however,” etc., in order to show in detail that path of the meditation subject and the method for entering it.
Therein, “on which day? means on which day of the fortnight; is it the second, the third, and so forth?
Or "one or another"—this is the meaning. It is not permissible to go away in silence, for the purpose of avoiding any change of heart in those who are questioning.
For the practice of the Dispensation is for the sake of inspiring confidence in those without it, and for increasing the faith of those who already possess it.
"It perishes" means it is no longer seen; the meaning is that it does not appear. By the phrase "hospitality should be extended to the guest," the duty toward a guest is indicated.
Because it was shown only in part, the term "guest" is mentioned again so that the remaining duties may be understood as being fully included under the heading of "guest duties.

Regarding the phrase "gamika-vatta, etc.," the word "etc. (ādi) should be understood as including the resident’s duty of thanksgiving, the alms-collector’s duty of thanksgiving, the forest-dweller’s duty, the duty regarding lodgings, the duty regarding the restroom, and so forth.
For the "Great Duties" (mahā-vatta) that appear in the Khandhaka section are referred to here as "Khandhaka duties."

[The duties] have been stated. However, those to be practiced at the time of performing a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure) and so forth, as well as during the period of probation (*pārivāsika*) and so forth, are not intended here because they are impossible for this monk.
Or, "the sign disappears" means that the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*) situated in a charnel ground disappears through the passing away of the state of being bloated (*uddhumātaka*).
Therefore, he said "bloated," and so forth. "Therefore" means by that.
The meaning is: "for this reason," that is, because this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is difficult to obtain. The connection is: "having sat down, it should be reviewed.
Just as when going to grasp the sign, so too when returning after grasping the sign, there should be a reviewing of the direction and other details exactly as they were observed;

this is for the purpose of maintaining [the sign] without interruption until the sign's disappearance, by means of the activity already set in motion. For when there is mindfulness, its continuous maintenance occurs.

When he has entered the monastery and is seated, the mode of appearance of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should stand out clearly, like the state of concentration of the mind when grasping the sign of serenity (samathanimitta). Therefore it was said: "For him, in this way... he enters upon the path.
Because the sign stands out clearly through its mode of appearance as previously described, it is by that very same mode of appearance—
Mental attention directed toward the meditation subject enters the path of development. 116.
What is called a "swollen corpse" is exceedingly impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, repulsive, hideous, and terrifying.
For one who applies himself to the development of meditation upon such an object, and for whom the preliminary work has been thus established and stabilized—
The phrase beginning with "one who sees the benefits" is stated to show that the intention of the yogi succeeds.
"In this way" means precisely in the manner described—that is, by one who sees the benefits.

"He should guard it" means he should guard that jewel-treasure as if it were his own life, thinking, "Surely I shall live happily through this. The passage beginning with "one whose meditation subject consists of the four elements," etc., refers to them.

This is the demonstration of the ease with which meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) are obtained. In this context, one who has the four elements as their meditation subject (*catudhātukammaṭṭhānika*) is either engaged in that meditation subject on the four elements, or is devoted to it, or is maintaining the meditation subject on the four elements.
"The others" refers to those remaining subjects mentioned previously, such as the recollections (*anussati*), the divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), and so forth.
"That sign" (*taṃ nimittaṃ*) refers to the acquired learning-sign (*uggahanimitta*) as it was obtained. "It should be guarded" (*rakkhitabbaṃ*).
Having stated the method of protection, the words beginning with "rattiṭṭhāne" were spoken in order to show it again. 117.
That by which something is made different is a "differentiator" (nānākaraṇa), meaning a distinction.

It appears as something loathsome and terrifying because of the lack of refinement in one's attention and because the object is not tranquil. By way of its opposite, it is the "counterpart sign" (paṭibhāganimitta).
It should be connected [to the previous context] by bringing in the phrase: “it appears like a person with thick limbs and members.

“Externally” means outside of what is internal to the range of one’s own domain. “By non-attention to sensual pleasures” means that because the perception of sensual pleasure has been driven far away by the power of the meditation on the foul (asubhabhāvanā), there is simply an absence of attention directed toward the strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa). Alternatively, “non-attention” refers to the cause that is the opposite of attention.

For that perception of the unattractive (*asubhasaññā*), which is the opposite of the perception of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*) by virtue of which beings attend to sensual pleasures, is the non-attention to sensual pleasures;
this is the meaning of "its sign" (*tannimitta*). Therefore he said: "Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is abandoned by way of suppression.
For concentration that has attained strength together with the perception of the unattractive, which has the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*) as its object—
As it arises, it suppresses sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*); since resentment rooted in attachment is suppressed once its primary cause is suppressed, it is said:
"attachment... is abandoned. For ill-will (*vyāpāda*) can never arise in one whose attachment has been abandoned.
Indeed, the joy (*pīti*) accompanied by the aforementioned perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*), while proceeding with exceptional intensity, [suppresses it].
It proceeds by suppressing ill will. Likewise, "by the arousal of energy" means by the exertion of energy through attention to the meditation subject in such a way that access concentration arises.
For when one exerts energy, right intention arises—suppressing sloth and torpor just as wrong intention suppresses right intention—due to its expansive nature.
Remorse (*vippaṭisāra*) is subsequent regret; its opposite, non-remorse (*avippaṭisāra*), is the state of the mind being quenched due to the absence of distress and feverish agitation.
Virtue (*sīla*) is the condition for that non-remorse.

The joy, tranquility, happiness, and so forth, which are conjoined with it and supported by it as its decisive dependence, are peaceful by nature and by cause. By devoting oneself to these, one [abandons] that which is unpeaceful by nature.
"Restlessness and remorse are abandoned," he said; thus, "restlessness and remorse are abandoned by means of devotion to those states that produce non-remorse.

For when meditation brings about successive stages of distinction, the particular happiness that is obtained arises precisely as it suppresses restlessness and remorse, which are by nature unpacified. "Of one who has attained distinction" means...

Of the specific attainment already realized. "Because of being directly perceived" means that for the practitioner who is engaged in the practice, because it is directly perceived, [there is confidence] in the Teacher who teaches the practice, thinking:
"Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, who teaches such right practice.
"In the practice" means in the practice of jhāna being undertaken. "In the fruit of the practice" means in that which is to be accomplished by means of it.
Regarding the mundane and supramundane fruits: doubt is abandoned by the power of investigation, which is gained through the investigation into the nature of phenomena (dhammānvaya-vicāra).

Thus, the five hindrances are abandoned; in this way, at the very moment the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) is acquired, the five hindrances such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda) are suppressed by means of concentration and the other factors produced by the power of the preceding development (bhāvanā).
They are abandoned. For the abandonment of that which is to be abandoned is not possible without its opposite;
and concentration and the other factors are the opposites of sensual desire and the rest. As it is said in the *Peṭaka*: "Concentration is the opposite of sensual desire," and so forth.
And for this very reason, the factors of jhāna are presented by way of illustrating their abandonment, stating: "By these, there is the abandonment of those hindrances."
To show this according to its specific form, the passage beginning with “And in that very same” was stated.

Therein, “and in that very same” refers to that very sign—the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta)—which, as it were, breaks through the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) as it appeared, and which has become concealed from it.
“Of the mind” means of the consciousness associated with itself. “Characterized by directing” means characterized by fixing [the mind].
The meaning is "the nature of absorption. "Reflecting on the sign" (nimittānumajjana) is the continued investigation of the counterpart sign.
For its function of reflecting consists in proceeding by way of investigating the object, like a bee circling repeatedly over a lotus.
It is called "attainment of distinction" because it is precisely a distinction that is to be attained; and that attainment of distinction has been acquired.
...and so on, up to the village. Because of that, with that as the cause, there is rapture (*pīti*) conditioned by the attainment of specific distinctions.

"Of one whose mind has rapture" means of one whose consciousness is accompanied by rapture. "From the arising of tranquility" means from the convergence of bodily and mental tranquility (*passaddhi*).
For it is said: "The body of one whose mind has rapture becomes tranquil. Happiness conditioned by tranquility, having tranquility as its sign, is "one whose body is tranquil."
Because of the statement, “he experiences pleasure,” one-pointedness has pleasure as its sign and pleasure as its condition. For it is said: “The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
Thus, the jhāna factors become manifest; in this way, these factors beginning with applied thought (vitakka) arise upon that very same sign.
“Becoming a reflection of the first jhāna” means becoming a concealed likeness of the first jhāna.
At that very moment, simultaneously with the acquisition of the counterpart sign, access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*) is also produced;
the intention is that it is not merely the abandoning of the hindrances.
[This concludes] the commentary on the meditation subjects beginning with the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*).
118. Regarding the meditation subjects beginning with the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*): "The characteristic has been stated" refers to that characteristic of grasping the sign which was stated.

"In the same manner as stated" means in the very manner stated for the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*). "Together with the exposition and the intention" means together with the exposition and the intention (*savinicchayādhippāya*).
The connection is that all that characteristic is to be understood.
“Of variegated color” means that it is for the most part white in color. “By way of prominence” means by way of whichever color is predominant among the red, white, and blue colors.
“Seated” means being entirely steady by virtue of its immobility.
“In a forest infested by robbers” means in a wilderness overrun by thieves. “Where” means at which execution ground. “At the place where men have been executed.”

In a place where a person has been cut in half. "Even though fallen in various directions" means that although the body has been severed into two parts and fallen separately in different directions. "By a single adverting" means by a single act of attention (*ekasamannāhāra*).
"It comes into range" means it comes into range all at once. "One gains confidence" means one would approach it without disgust, just like a cremator of corpses.
He said, "One should bring [the body] near with a wooden staff or a stick... because loathing is established precisely in not touching it with one's own hand.

Making an interval of one finger-breadth is for the purpose of making manifest the state of being cut asunder. "Should be brought near" means it should be led near. "Just like what has been gnawed" means just like a bloated corpse (aśubha) that has been gnawed.

"An interval of a finger-breadth" refers to various scattered limbs and members of the body, each separated by an interval of a finger-breadth. "Or having made [it so]" means either with a wooden staff, or with a stick, or having done it oneself.

"Of those who have received blows" (*laddhappahārānaṃ*)—the connection is with "from the mouth" (*mukhato*). "From the mouth" means from the opening of the wounds and so forth. "At the time when it is trickling" (*paggharamānakāle*) means at the time when the blood is flowing.

The construction is: "The bloody [meditation subject] is obtained. "That" refers to the worm-infested corpse (*puḷavaka*). "In them" (*tesu*) refers to the bodies of dogs and so forth. The connection is: "The skeleton" (*aṭṭhikaṃ*)—that is, the skeleton as an object of meditation—is described in various ways. "Precisely by the previous method" (*purimanayeneva*) means by the very same method previously stated regarding the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*).
119. "That skeleton": it does not appear as its own intrinsic nature; the meaning is that it does not appear by way of its repulsiveness.
Therefore he said, "There is a breaking up of the white-kasiṇa. Regarding the skeleton, one cannot discern characteristics such as the first stage of life and so forth;
thus it is said here, "'Sex' refers to the hands and so on. However, the chain of bones... this...

It would indeed be possible to define [the parts] according to their stages of life, such as: "this belongs to one who is young," "this belongs to one established in youth," and "this belongs to one who has reached maturity through the growth of limbs";
however, it should be understood that because they are not all-encompassing, they are not included here.

Even though definition by way of joints is obtainable in the case of a skeleton, it is not obtainable in the case of a single bone; therefore, this is for the purpose of showing its indefinite nature.
Having transcended sensual desire, it is said: “By way of the concave and convex parts of each respective bone,” and so forth.

Therein, the “concave part” refers to the depressed region of the bone; the “convex part” refers to the elevated region. “By way of the joined and unjoined parts” means by way of the places where the bones are not bound together by sinews and those where they are so bound, respectively.
“By way of the thoroughly defiled and slightly defiled parts” refers to the manner in which these various regions are interconnected.
"By way of the spaces between" means by way of the mutual spaces and by way of the hollows.
"In all places" means in the entire skeleton, or in every single bone.
"120. Herein" means in this foulness of bones. "It should be observed according to what is applicable" refers to the grasping of the sign.
Wherever it is applicable, that should be characterized there by way of grasping the sign (*nimitta*) for the purpose of learning it.
"Entirely" means without remainder, with all parts complete. "It succeeds" by way of the manifestation of the sign. "Among those" refers to the skeletons of bone-chains.
This was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "That" refers to the statement, "exactly the same. "Applicable to one skeleton"—this is...

It is said thus because, unlike in the case of the livid corpse and so forth, where a distinction between the two signs is obtained according to their respective differences in color, their completeness or incompleteness, their having cavities or being without cavities, and their being moving or non-moving—such [distinctions] do not apply here;
however, it is not because there is an absolute absence of all distinction. For this very reason he says, "And even in a single bone," and so forth. Therein, "by the loathsome" means:
Because its skeletal form is well-manifested, it is "by way of its very nature as bone" and thus "ugly. It is "terrifying" because it brings fear to ordinary beings precisely for that reason.

It is "arousing joy and gladness" because it appears with a smooth and polished quality, and because it gives rise to joy (*pīti*) and gladness (*somanassa*) due to its particular excellence in meditation; for this very reason, he says, "because it brings access concentration (*upacāra*)."

"In this place" means in the location where the learning-sign (*uggaha-nimitta*) and the counterpart-sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) were described. "Or by providing an opening" means that instead of stopping at the mere statement,

"When the state of repulsiveness itself is seen, it is called a sign," he immediately thereafter provides an opening for the aforementioned classification of signs by means of the words beginning with, "The sign here is twofold," etc., thus analyzing the learning-sign and the counterpart-sign.

"Having given" has already been explained. "Free from conceptualization" (*nibbikappa*) means free from the conceptualization that thinks "it is beautiful"; the meaning is that it is simply "the foul" (*asubha*).
"Having investigated" means having investigated by way of [the formula] beginning with "Is it appropriate for one bone?
and so forth. "Of the Elder Mahātissa" refers to the Elder Mahātissa who dwelt at Cetiyapabbata. "Examples" refers to [the perception] through the mere sight of a tooth-bone.

In this meditation subject on bones (*aṭṭhika-kammaṭṭhāna*), the appearance of the entire body of that woman as a collection of bones and so forth are examples illustrating the distinction between the learning-sign (*uggaha-nimitta*) and the counterpart-sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*).

"Possessing beautiful qualities" means having qualities that are perfectly pure due to the abandonment of the defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*). "With a thousand eyes" means...

By Sahassakkha, the lord of the gods. For he is called "Sahassakkha" (Thousand-eyed) because he is endowed with the eye of wisdom capable of discerning a thousand locations while remaining on a single seat.
"Thutakitti" refers to one whose fame and renown have been praised by such verses as, "The wise one who is self-controlled in every way."
Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discourse (Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā) 121.

He says, "Because of the state of lust being well-suppressed," with reference to its having been abandoned by way of its direct opposite. "The classification of the foul" refers to the divisions of the foul, such as the bloated corpse and so forth.
"By way of the body’s attainment of its own specific nature" means by way of the body’s arrival at its own inherent characteristic.
For the body, when perishing, perishes precisely by way of reaching its own inherent nature, like a demon who remains in another form until he reaches his true nature.
"By way of the classification of the lustful temperament" means by way of the division of the lustful temperament.

If this classification of the foul is stated by way of the body’s attainment of its own inherent nature, how is it that there is a ninefold classification in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta and other texts? That [ninefold classification] is by way of its essence (*sarasato*).
That was stated by way of reaching the natural state; this one, however, is also by way of another's effort.

Furthermore, among the ten kinds of foulness brought here, only some have been taken up, and the skeleton has been analyzed in five ways. Moreover, those [previous ones] were by way of insight (vipassanā), while these are by way of serenity (samatha);
thus, this distinction is evident.

Now, although the mere sight of these [corpses] is generally suitable for those of a lustful temperament because of their commonality in being unattractive (asubha), the phrase "and by way of the different types of lustful temperaments" was stated;
to demonstrate this in detail, the passage beginning with "specifically" (visesato) was spoken.
For even a body that is well-proportioned becomes ill-proportioned through the state of bloatedness (uddhumātaka); thus, regarding the bloated corpse...
"It explains the failure of shape" means he said, "because it demonstrates the failure of the body's shape.

One who is attached to the perfection of shape is "one who lusts after shape"; [this teaching] is suitable because it serves as a means for suppressing that lust for shape. "The body itself is the wound on the body" (kāyavaṇa);
[it refers to] that which is bound to, or dependent upon, it. "Because it demonstrates the state of being hollow" means because of the hollow...
Because it reveals the existence of cavities. "Those who delight in the density of the body" means those possessing lust arising in dependence upon the firmness of the limbs and members of the body.

"Because it reveals its dismemberment" means that it is suitable for those who delight in the grace of the limbs and members, as it reveals the scattering [of the body] here and there by dogs, jackals, and so forth. It is said that for such people whose forms are unstable...
"What is the playful grace of the limbs? [is asked] because of the arising of dispassion. "By way of manifesting the breaking up and alteration of the composite" means:

the breaking up (*bhedo*) of the composite—that is, the state of being well-connected (*susambandhatā*)—of the limbs and sub-limbs, which is itself the alteration (*vikāro*), is the "alteration through the breaking up of the composite" (*saṅghātabhedavikāro*);

it is by way of manifesting that. "The state of being repulsive due to being smeared with blood" (*lohitamakkhitapaṭikkūlabhāvo*) means that having become smeared with blood, there is a state of repulsiveness.
Because of its exposition. "Those who lust after 'mine'" means those in whom the lust arising from the thought "this is mine" has occurred.
"Those who lust after the excellence of teeth" means those whose nature it is to take delight in the excellence of teeth.
But why, in this context, does only the first jhāna arise regarding the bloated corpse and so forth, and not the second and subsequent ones? To this question:
Having taken this into consideration, he said, “But because,” and so forth.

“With water that is not settled” means with water that does not remain still on all sides due to its flowing nature—that is, water that is not stagnant. “By the power of the oar” means by the power of the oar-handle.
“Because of the weakness of the object” means that the weakness of the object consists in its inability to establish the mind within itself by way of its repulsiveness. Regarding the repulsive...
For the mind is not able to proceed toward an object by its own inherent power;
rather, it is while being directed by *vitakka*, which has the characteristic of directing, that the mind attains one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*).
Thus, the second and subsequent jhānas—which are devoid of *vitakka*—do not find a firm footing there without *vitakka*. Therefore he said: "By the power of *vitakka* alone," and so forth.

"If the second and subsequent jhānas do not occur with regard to objects such as a bloated corpse because of their repulsiveness, then, that being the case, even the first jhāna should not arise there.
For it is not logical that joy and mental happiness could possibly exist there"—anticipating this objection, he says:
"And even though this is repulsive," and so forth. In that context, [the factors] include the perception of benefits, the removal of the hindrances, and the pacification of the fever of illness.
The similes of the discarded flower, the emetic, and the purgative should be applied in their respective order.
Having stated "And this tenfold [consciousness]," etc., in order to show that although it is established as tenfold by the aforementioned reasons,
it is actually of only one kind by way of its intrinsic nature (sabhāva), he explains that this intrinsic nature is indeed found among conscious beings just as it is among insentient things.
Therefore, showing that even in this case cultivation succeeds for one who possesses wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), he said: "This [body] by means of this characteristic," and so forth.
"In this" means in this living body. "By way of adornment" means by way of decoration preceded by grooming.
"It is not perceived by ordinary people" is the intended meaning. [It is a heap of more than one hundred and eight bones, including the teeth and jawbones.]
Together with them, yet excluding them, he will speak of "three hundred bones" in the context of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*).
"Full of holes and crevices" means possessing small and minute apertures. "A vessel filled with fat" means a container brimming with fat.
"Constantly oozing and trickling" means flowing out from above and below at all times. "Diverse" means manifold. "With various cloths" means with cloths of various colors.
By means of garments. Because it causes one to be ashamed and because it destroys modesty through shame, it is called *hirikopina*, the path for excrement and urine.
*Yāthāvasarasam* means the true nature as it actually is. For "essence" (*rasa*) is that which is tasted or known according to its actual state;
thus, it is the true nature. *Ratim* means delight or preference. *Attasineharāgarattā* means those who are stained by the passion known as self-attachment. *Vihaññamānena* means being distressed.
"By one who meets with frustration through not obtaining what is desired.
*Kiṃsuka* refers to the *pālibhaddaka* tree; some say it is the *palāsa*, while others say it is the *simbalī*. "Excessively greedy" means having an exceedingly fickle or covetous nature.

"This" (*adaṃ*) refers to this [body]. "That" (*naṃ*) refers to a constituent part of the body such as the hair. "Infatuated" (*mucchitā*) means deluded, or [possessed] by the craving that causes fainting (*mucchāpāpikā taṇhā*).
"By way of this, they fell into a swoon. "Its true nature" means its state of repulsiveness.
"Like a heap of refuse" means equal to a place for excrement and urine, or equal to a cesspool.

"By those who have become eyes" means by those who have attained the eye, that is, those who have acquired the eye of wisdom, or by those who have become the eyes of the world. "Covered with raw skin" means enveloped in raw skin.
"By one of a nature capable [of attaining]" means by one who is capable of attaining superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
"In whatever part of the body" or "in whichever particular portion of the body.

"Having grasped the sign" means having grasped the sign by way of thoroughly observing the aspect of foulness, so that the learning-sign (*uggahanimitta*) arises; thus, having grasped the sign by way of learning it, [one obtains] the learning-sign.

The meaning is "having produced. "The meditation subject should be brought to absorption" means that by one who practices with the learning sign as it was obtained, having produced the counterpart sign and established himself in access concentration, he should bring the foulness meditation subject to absorption by intensifying that very meditation.
For when one has attained absorption and is established in the first jhāna, he [should continue] with that same...
Having made *jhāna* the foundation and having begun insight (*vipassanā*), by comprehending conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), he exhausts all taints (*āsava*) before long.
The commentary on the exposition of the meditation subject of foulness (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*) is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the sixth chapter.
7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Recollections (Cha-anussati-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) 1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 123.

"Immediately after the foul" means immediately after the meditation subject of the foul (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna). "Among the recollections" means among the meditation subjects of the recollections (anussati-kammaṭṭhāna).
In order to show the meaning of the phrase “*anu anu sati anussatī*,” it was stated, “because it arises again and again.
Then, to show that the word *sati* does not denote a different meaning here through its connection with the prefix *anu*, it was said, “*sati* itself is *anussati*.
Therefore, this prefix *anu* is not meaningless—as the prefix *upa* is in words such as “*upalabbhati*”—nor does it mean “perceiving” (*sañjānana*).
In passages such as "understanding" (*pajānana*), he shows that [the prefix *pa-*] indicates a difference in meaning, just like the word *saṃ* and others.
By the phrase "because it occurs in the very place where it ought to occur," the suitability of the recollection to that which is to be recollected is stated;
thus, in order to show the suitability of the one who practices it, it is said, "suitable for a clansman" (*kulaputtassa anurūpā*), or for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith.
"Suitability" (anurūpatā) occurs precisely because it is suitable to the place where one should proceed; thus, suitability is stated for the practitioner alone, not for both.
"Suitable" (anurūpa) means "fitting" (yutta). "Of the Buddha" (buddha) refers to those qualities on account of which the Blessed One is designated as "Buddha";
taking those qualities together as a whole, it is so stated. Therefore he said: "having the qualities of a Buddha as its object..."
“This is a designation for mindfulness. “Having taken up” means having made it an object.
“The Dhamma” refers to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma together with the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti). But will not Nibbāna be mentioned separately as a meditation subject?
Although he will indeed mention it, here it is included in the text together with the paths and fruits because they share the common characteristic of being the Dhamma.
The inclusion of this [recollection of the Dhamma] should also be understood as occurring within the meditation subject of the recollection of the Dhamma;
however, because it is distinguished from the paths and fruits by way of its being unconditioned, deathless, and so forth, it has been treated as a separate meditation subject.
As for the three other recollections, such as the recollection of virtue and the rest, their treatment as separate meditation subjects is for the sake of the practitioner’s own...
This is because virtue, generosity, faith, and so forth must be grasped by way of being objects for recollection (*anussati-ṭṭhāna*).

"Gone to the material body" means occurring by way of making one's own physical body composed of the four great elements (*karaja-kāya*) the object. "In the body" means in the body which has become the objective field.
"Having the sign of the parts as its object" means having the repulsive sign among the parts, such as hair and so forth, as its object. Regarding the preceding [passages] from here...
The inclusion of the term "sign" (*nimitta*) is for the purpose of showing that while there is no arising of a sign among the seven recollections (*anussati*), here there is one.

The same applies to the phrase "having the sign of the in-breaths and out-breaths as its object. "Peace" (*upasama*) means the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*); the meaning is Nibbāna.
124. "Verified confidence" (*aveccappasāda*) is the confidence that has arisen after having known the qualities of the Buddha as they truly are through the Noble Path.

"By one who has attained confidence, or by one similar to him, who is unshakable and immovable by the winds of speculative views (diṭṭhigata), and who is endowed with such qualities—for such a person the cultivation of the recollection of the Buddha succeeds, but not for another.

'In a suitable lodging' means in a lodging endowed with the five factors and free from the eighteen faults as previously described. 'Having gone into seclusion' means having gone to a private place; by this, he shows physical seclusion (kāyaviveka)."

"By seclusion" means by one who has secluded himself from various objects; having turned away from external manifold objects, he has settled into the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*)—this is the meaning of "with a well-composed mind. "Thus" refers to the method as it has come down in this scripture.
"That Blessed One": here, "he" refers to the one who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and shattered all defilements, attained the unsurpassed...

He who has fully awakened to perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), the god beyond gods, the Brahmā beyond Brahmās, the Lord of the World, whose fame and renown as "Bhagavā" have spread throughout the world including the devas due to reasons such as his great fortune—this is he. "Bhagavā" is the naming of the Teacher’s title.
For it is said: "This name 'Bhagavā' was not given by his mother," and so forth. But further on...

"Bhagavā" is a praise of his qualities. Showing that the Buddha-qualities are to be recollected by joining the word "itipi" to each of the nine titles beginning with "Arahan," he said: "Thus 'Arahan'... pe... thus 'Bhagavā,' he recollects.
In expressions such as "Thus this is real, thus this is true," the word *iti* has the sense of making something proximate or evident.
The word *pi* has the sense of "conjunction" (*sampiṇḍana*). By it, their multiplicity is indicated.
And showing that these causes for discerning qualities must be brought face-to-face with the mind by one who is developing them, he said: "It means 'by this and that cause. 125.
Distance (*dūratā*), like proximity (*āsannatā*), is spoken of in successive stages; thus, it refers to the state of being far removed to the ultimate degree.
In order to show this, he said, "very far away" (*suvidūravidūre*); the meaning is that they are distant precisely by way of being well-distant.

Furthermore, showing that their distance from defilement (*kilesa*) is due to those defilements having been abandoned in every respect, he said, "because the defilements have been shattered by the Path.
Considering the objection that "are these not indeed abandoned for other *khīṇāsavas* as well?", he stated, "together with their latent tendencies" (*savāsanānaṃ*).
Indeed, apart from the Blessed One, no others are able to abandon the defilements along with their underlying tendencies (*vāsanā*);
by this, it is shown that the Blessed One’s state of *arahantship* is not shared with others. But what is this so-called "underlying tendency"?

It is a specific capacity residing within the defilements, which serves as the cause for a mode of activity similar to that of one whose defilements have been abandoned acting like one whose defilements have not been abandoned; [this refers to] the Venerable...
It is like the case of Pilindavaccha’s being addressed with the term “outcaste. But how is it that when “far from” (*ārakā*) is stated, this meaning “from the defilements” (*kilesehi*) is obtained?
Because a general indication is fixed upon a specific instance, and because a specific qualification must be applied by one who seeks that specific qualification.
Here, such scriptural passages as “Far from him are evil, unwholesome states” should be cited as examples.
In this context, the vowel *ā* in the word *āraka* is shortened to *a*, and the consonant *k* is changed to *h*;
by applying the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), the formation of the term should be understood as “*arahanto*.

To facilitate the grasping of this very meaning, he spoke the verse beginning with “He is therefore called *āraka*,” which is composed in metrical form. Therein, one whose nature is to possess is “possessing” (*samaṅgī*); the absence of possessing is “non-possessing” (*asamaṅgitā*), which is non-endowment (*asamannāgama*) and non-coexistence (*asahavuttitā*).

126. Because the defilements (kilesa) themselves are the enemies due to their harmful conduct, they are called "defilement-enemies" (kilesārayo). Although it should be said, “An arahant is so called because he has slain his enemies (ari),” it is stated as “arahant” according to the rules of etymological derivation (niruttinaya).
127. The connection is with the phrase “this wheel of saṃsāra. Like the hub of a chariot wheel, that which constitutes its fundamental component is situated both within and without;
this pair consisting of ignorance (avijjā), existence (bhava), and craving (taṇhā) is described as “having ignorance, existence, and craving for its hub” (avijjābhavataṇhāmayanābhī).
The spokes, which are connected to the hub and the rim, are like ignorance, craving, and aging-and-death, being related to the results that are the conditions [for rebirth].
Thus it is said: "the spokes consisting of the formative forces of merit and so forth.
In this context, aging-and-death is manifest as the limit of existence within each respective becoming; making that the place of the rim, he says: "the rim of aging-and-death."

And just as the axle is the primary cause for the turning of a chariot wheel, so too is the origination of the taints (*āsava-samudaya*) the primary cause for the turning of the wheel of saṃsāra; thus it is said:

"having pierced with the axle consisting of the origination of the taints. The taints themselves are the "origination of the taints" because they are the cause of ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest, as it is said:

"From the origination of the taints comes the origination of ignorance. [The result] consists of the various types of resultant matter (*vipāka-kaṭattā-rūpa*) and so forth, such as sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) and the rest.
The three realms of existence themselves are the chariot; [it is] "in that chariot of the three realms of existence.

It is "thoroughly yoked" (*samāyojita*) because it has been yoked from the very beginning together with its own conditions, or yoked in every respect from the start. Because it proceeds throughout time that is devoid of a beginning, it is said to be "proceeding from beginningless time" (*anādikālappavatta*).
"And the succession of the aggregates, And of the elements and the sense-bases..."
“The continuity being uninterrupted is called ‘saṃsāra’”—thus, the saṃsāra spoken of in this way is indeed the wheel of saṃsāra (*saṃsāracakka*). “By him” means by the Blessed One.

“At the seat of enlightenment” (*bodhimaṇḍe*) means at the place or time when the state of being the essence (*maṇḍa-bhāva*) of the knowledge termed “enlightenment” was attained. “With the feet of energy” refers to [the factors] among those belonging to the side of defilement and purification.
By means of his own feet, which are called "energy" (viriya) and function in two ways through the acts of suppressing and laying down.
On the earth of virtue (sīlapathavi): virtue itself is the earth in the sense of being a foundation; on that [earth]. Having stood: having established himself by way of accomplishment.
With the hand of faith (saddhāhatthena): because it is the means for grasping the blameless Dhamma, faith itself is the hand; with that.
"Destroying karma" (*kammakkhayakara*) means that which brings about the destruction of all karma, including its divisions such as bodily action (*kāyakamma*). "The axe of knowledge" (*ñāṇapharasa*):
having taken up the axe of the knowledge of the Path, well-sharpened upon the whetstone of concentration (*samādhi*). 128.

Thus, regarding the phrase "because the spokes have been destroyed," having understood that "wheel" (*cakkam*) refers to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which is like a wheel, in the context of the destruction of the spokes mentioned there—

Having thus explained it by way of the eightfold arrangement, now, in order to show it again by way of the teaching on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), the passage beginning with "Or else" (*atha vā*) was stated.
Therein, "the beginningless round of saṃsāra" (*anamataggaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭaṃ*) refers to the wheel of saṃsāra whose beginning is not known—that is, its limit is unperceived.
The remaining ten factors, from volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) up to birth (*jāti*), are the spokes. How so? From the hub of ignorance (*avijjā*), which is the root.
Showing that it is connected at its end with aging and death by way of the sequence, he said: "Because ignorance is its root and because aging and death are its limit.
Regarding "in suffering and so forth," this refers to suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Therein, ignorance regarding suffering is included within it and because it conceals it;
regarding the remaining [truths], it is included only by way of concealment. And here, "suffering" refers to the Noble Truth of Suffering.

"Intended" means that, having divided [existence] into three types—namely, existence in the sense-sphere (*kāma-bhava*) and so forth—and likewise showing the ignorance (*avijjā*) that conceals them, as well as the formations (*saṅkhāra*) and other factors in the three existences according to their respective conditions such as ignorance, he said:

"In the sense-sphere existence there is ignorance," and so on. Therein, "ignorance in the sense-sphere existence" refers to the ignorance that conceals the danger (*ādīnava*) in the sense-sphere existence. [The same applies to] the fine-material existence (*rūpa-bhava*) and the immaterial existence (*arūpa-bhava*).
The same method applies here to the term "ignorance" (avijjā) as well. Regarding the phrase "of volitional formations in the sensual existence" (kāmabhave saṅkhārānaṃ):

it means of those volitional formations included within the sensual plane; or, of those volitional formations that are to be produced in the sensual existence—the meaning is "of those volitional formations that bring about rebirth in the sensual existence.

It "is a condition" means that, first of all, for meritorious volitional formations, it is a condition both by way of object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and decisive support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya).

Thus, it is a condition in two ways: for co-nascent unwholesome formations (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), it is a condition by way of being co-nascent and so forth; for those that are not co-nascent, it is a condition by way of being immediate, contiguous, and so forth;
but for those that are not immediate, it is a condition by way of object (*ārammaṇa*) and also by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
"For formations in the formless realm" means for the imperturbable formations (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*). It is a condition solely by way of decisive support.
If this matter were explained here in detail, it would become excessively prolix; and since it will be dealt with by itself later on, we do not elaborate upon it now.
"Of three bases" refers to the eye, ear, and mind bases. "Of one base" refers to the mind base. By this—

By this method, the classification of contact and the other factors should also be understood. In each respective instance, "that craving" refers to the craving arising in those various spheres such as the sense-desire realm (*kāma-bhava*) and so forth, categorized as craving for forms (*rūpa-taṇhā*) and so on.
Since the discussion beginning with craving has been presented too concisely, it is now shown by analyzing and expanding upon both clinging (*upādāna*) and becoming (*bhava*).
The passage beginning with “How? has been stated. Therein, by the phrase “I shall enjoy sensual pleasures,” he speaks of the occurrence of craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatanha*).
Likewise, this is shown by such phrases as “I shall experience the excellence of heaven.

Since that craving, when occurring through the mode of intense grasping, becomes what is called clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), it is therefore said: “conditioned by clinging to sense-pleasures. “In the same way” means:
It is precisely with the condition of clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).
"Attainment in the Brahma-world" means attainment in the world of form-Brahmas (*rūpībrahmaloka*).

Since it is stated that "all phenomena belonging to the three planes are sensual pleasures (*kāma*) in the sense of being desirable," even craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) is considered to be simply clinging to sensual pleasures; thus, it is said: "Loving-kindness [arises] precisely with the condition of clinging to sensual pleasures."
"...he develops," and so forth, is what was stated. Regarding the phrase "in the cases rooted in the remaining types of clinging as well," the construction here is as follows:

someone here adopts the nihilistic view, thinking, "There is no other world. Following that, one should apply the method already explained, beginning with: "On account of the clinging to views, he engages in misconduct by way of body," and so on.
Another adopts the annihilationist view, thinking, "In such-and-such a state of prosperity, the self is annihilated."
"He grasps [the sign]; he practices good conduct with the body for rebirth there"—this and all else should be construed according to the method already stated.
Another, thinking "the self, being material and mind-made, is annihilated," develops the path for rebirth in the form realm (*rūpa*).

All regarding the fulfillment of that development should be understood according to the method already stated. Another, thinking "having arisen in the formless existence (*arūpabhava*), the self is annihilated,"...
One develops the path for rebirth in the formless realm. Regarding "the fulfillment of development," everything should be understood according to the method already explained.

It should be seen that by these very [terms], the application based on the root of the clinging to a self (attavādupādāna) has also been commented upon. In this way, the application should also be understood by way of the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life (diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda).
Another [person], misapprehending [the path] as "purification is through virtue" or "this is a path of purification where there is no path of purification,"...
"By means of clinging to rules and observances, one engages in misconduct with the body," and so forth— all this should be applied according to the method already stated.
Now, that which was shown by the expositor of the wheel of saṃsāra— namely, "in the sensual existence, ignorance is the condition for volitional formations in the sensual existence," and so on—
demonstrates the state of being a condition for ignorance and the rest, as well as the state of being conditionally arisen for volitional formations and the rest.
Bringing forward that very *Paṭisambhidāmagga* text as a conclusion, he said, "Thus this... and so forth.

Therein, just as volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) are produced by causes, so too ignorance (*avijjā*) has causes such as the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*); thus he said, "Both of these are arisen from causes.
Regarding "the discernment of conditions," this refers to the conditions for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), namely ignorance and the rest.
"In the grasping after having delimited" (*paricchijja gahaṇe*): the locative case is used because it is something to be accomplished.

"Wisdom" (*paññā*) is the thorough knowledge characterized by the purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*). "Knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) is the comprehension of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
And this knowledge of the stability of phenomena proceeds by way of overcoming the stain of doubt throughout the three time periods; therefore, [it is said]: "The past time as well," and so forth.
It has been stated. "By this same method" means by the method stated regarding ignorance (*avijjā*) in the passage beginning, "Ignorance is the cause.
All the terms should be expanded in detail according to the formula: "Volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) are the cause; consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is arisen from a cause," and so forth.
It is a "summary" (*saṅkhepa*) because ignorance and the rest, as well as consciousness and the rest, are summarized herein; that is, the cause and the result. Thus, "cause and result."
It is called a "concordance" (*saṅkhepa*) because it is condensed; these are ignorance and the rest, as well as consciousness and the rest.
It should be understood that the singular number is used by virtue of their commonality as being "concords. Furthermore, those concords are fourfold when divided by time:
as cause in the past, result in the present, cause in the present, and result in the future. Therefore he said: "And herein, the former concord..."
"Past time," and so forth. Alternatively, the word *saṅkhepa* (abbreviation) is a designation for a part; thus, the past causal portion is the first abbreviation.

This same method applies to the remaining [divisions] as well. Craving (*taṇhā*), clinging (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are already included because they share the common nature of defilement (*kilesa*) and karma (*kamma*), and because without them, ignorance (*avijjā*) and formations (*saṅkhāra*) would fail to perform their respective functions. Karma and craving are its (the past life's) cooperative causes.
Having performed [the sacrifice], it is the "kamma-process" (kammavaṭṭa) in the sense of revolving.
Because the states of consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling, along with birth, aging, and dissolution, are stated as "birth, aging, and death," he said:
"Because consciousness and the others are indicated by way of the designation 'birth, aging, and death. These are consciousness and the rest.

The future round of fruition (*vipākavaṭṭa*) is included because future states arising from present causes are grasped therein. "Those" refers to ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest. "As modes" (*ākārato*):

although not stated by their specific forms (*sarūpato*), they are scattered within those respective groupings; they are called "modes" (*ākārā*) because they are made manifest through the inclusion of ignorance, volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), and so forth.
Alternatively, "modes" are the ways (*pakāra*) of past causes and so on; thus, "as modes. They are of twenty kinds.
[This occurs] through the division of the five past causes and so forth.

Between formations (*saṅkhāra*) and consciousness (*viññāṇa*), there is one "link" (*sandhi*); because of the state of the fruit proceeding without interruption from the cause, this is one link consisting of the connection between cause and fruit.

Likewise, there is one between existences (*bhava*) and births (*jāti*). Furthermore, between feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*taṇhā*), [there is one link], because of the state of the cause proceeding without interruption from the fruit.

The single *sandhi* (connection) consists in the relationship between cause and fruit. For even a phenomenon that has become a fruit serves as a condition for another phenomenon whose intrinsic nature is that of a cause.
The word "iti" is a reference to the manner just described. Therefore he said, "the fourfold compendium," and so forth. "In all aspects" refers to those [aspects] mentioned here.
And in all the modes found in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga* not explicitly mentioned [here], as well as in the *Anantanaya*, the *Samantapaṭṭhāna*, and so forth.
"He knows" means he understands. "He sees" means he sees directly with the eye of knowledge that consists of vision.
"He cognizes" and "he penetrates" are synonyms for those same acts. "That" refers to that knowing. "In the sense of being known" means...
In the sense of knowing according to their true nature. "In the sense of understanding" means in the sense of penetrating [them] by way of their modes, such as impermanence and so forth.

Now, in order to show the purpose for which this wheel of existence (bhavacakra) has been introduced here, the words beginning with "by this" are stated. Therein, "those phenomena" refers to those phenomena beginning with ignorance.
"Having known them as they really are" means by means of the great thunderbolt-like knowledge (mahāvajirañāṇa) according to their actual state.
"Having known. The construction is: "Becoming disenchanted, becoming detached through powerful insight, and being liberated by means of the Noble Paths, he struck down Māra.
In this context, when the Blessed One becomes detached and is liberated, that is what is meant by "striking down Māra.
Subsequently, however, referring to the moment of his full enlightenment, it is said: "He struck him down, he struck him down utterly, he destroyed him."
129. When the insentient Wheel-Treasure (cakkaratana) of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti) has appeared, the world offers worship right there;

elsewhere, special forms of worship are discontinued. How much more so when a Perfectly Enlightened One (sammāsambuddha) has appeared? Demonstrating this, he said, "When the Tathāgata has appeared," and so forth.
What need is there to mention other special forms of worship? [This refers to] those other than what was mentioned above, performed by those who are not of great power.
What need is there to speak of his being worthy of even the most sublime and distinguished honors performed by gods and humans?
"Appropriate to the goal" (*atthānurūpa*) means suitable for the goal of *arahatta* (worthiness), that is, consistent with its meaning.
"Out of fear of ill-repute" (*asilokabhayena*) means out of fear of disrepute. They commit evil in secret, thinking, "Let no one know of it. This...

The Blessed One never performs the causes of evil because they have been thoroughly abandoned right at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). There is another method: he is an *arahant* because he is "far away" (*āraka*);
the meaning is precisely that he is at a great distance. But from what is he so far removed?

From those who have not developed the body, have not developed virtue, have not developed the mind, and have not developed wisdom; and for that very reason, because their lust, hatred, and delusion are unabandoned, [he is far] from the noble Dhamma.
They are unskilled in the noble Dhamma, undisciplined in the noble Dhamma, lacking vision of the noble Dhamma, not practicing it, and practicing wrongly;
for they are very far removed from it. Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, even if a bhikkhu were to follow closely behind me, holding onto the hem of my outer robe..."

While placing foot after foot [on the path], he is one who is covetous for sensual pleasures, with intense passion, with a mind of ill will, with corrupt intentions, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and with unrestrained faculties. Then he is far from me, and I am far from him.
Why is that? Because, monks, that bhikkhu does not see the Dhamma.
“Not seeing the Dhamma, one does not see me.

For even if the persons mentioned above were to remain in the presence of the Teacher day and night, they could not for that reason alone be called “in the presence of the Teacher,” nor could the Teacher be said to be in their presence. Thus, because he is far away from such unworthy persons, he is the Arahant.
“Those men of inferior aspirations do not practice rightly;”
“The Blessed One is far from those; therefore, he is considered an Arahant.
Likewise, “far” (āraka) means an Arahant; the meaning is “from being near. But from what is there nearness?

From those who have cultivated the body, cultivated virtue, cultivated the mind, and cultivated wisdom—it is precisely from them that [the Blessed One is near], for they have abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion through the Noble Dhamma.
They are experts in the noble Dhamma, well-trained in the noble Dhamma, seers of the noble Dhamma, and practitioners of the right way, because they are in close proximity to it.
And this was said by the Blessed One:
"Monks, even if a monk were to dwell a hundred yojanas away from me, yet he is one who is free from covetousness for sensual pleasures..."

"One who is not intensely passionate, whose mind is without malice, whose intentions are not corrupt, who is established in mindfulness, clearly comprehending, concentrated, one-pointed in mind, and with senses restrained—he is indeed close to me, and I am close to him. Why is that?
Because, monks, that bhikkhu sees the Dhamma; seeing the Dhamma, he sees me."

For such individuals may be a thousand yojanas away from the Teacher, yet they cannot be said to be "far from the Teacher" by that much; likewise, the Teacher is not far from them. Thus, because he is neither distant nor near to true persons (sappurisa), he is an Arahant.
To those who practice rightly and are intent on the well-guided path, the Victor is neither distant nor near;
therefore, too, the Conqueror is an Arahant.
These evil states, such as lust and the rest, which arise within a particular continuum, bring about harm both in this present life and in future lives.
They are the absolute and direct adversaries of the path leading to Nibbāna;
therefore, they must be shunned from afar by the virtuous who are practicing correctly to fulfill their own welfare and the welfare of others.

Those things which must be relinquished and abandoned are called *rāga*. And since these were entirely abandoned and utterly eradicated by the Blessed One at the very foot of the Bodhi tree through the Noble Path—just as it is said:

"Brahmin, lust has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, hatred and delusion have been abandoned; all evil unwholesome states have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future"—[he is thus called Arahant].

Therefore, although it should be called *arahā* because evil is entirely absent from him (*etassa rahā*), by substituting the vowel *a* for the long *o* along with its nasalization (*sānusāra*), it is stated as "Arahant.
Evil qualities are indeed called "evil" (*rahā*) because they are to be abandoned by the virtuous;
because the Blessed One has utterly abandoned them, he is considered an Arahant.
By those who are Arahants with taints destroyed— having fully understood the aggregates in every way, abandoned the defilements, developed the path, and realized cessation—
and by those who are trainees (*sekha*) whose minds have not yet reached their goal but dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage,
and by those individuals whose application is pure, whose disposition is virtuous, and who are endowed with qualities such as faith, virtue, and learning.
He is not to be separated from nor abandoned by those [disciples], and because he is so for the Blessed One, he is *arahant*.

For likewise, noble persons (*ariya-puggala*), because they have made the Dhamma of the Teacher directly manifest in this very life, are never separated from the Teacher’s Dhamma-body. As the Venerable Piṅgiya said:
“I see him with my mind as if with my eye...”
Day and night, O Brahmin, being heedful,
I spend the night paying homage;
by that alone, I consider myself never separated from him.
“Faith, rapture, mind, and mindfulness—
these do not depart from the teaching of Gotama;
in whichever direction the one of vast wisdom goes,”
"I am led by him alone.
And for that very reason, they do not point to any other teacher. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should point to another teacher—such a case does not exist."
Even virtuous worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) are for the most part possessed of unshakable faith in the Teacher.
Thus, because he is never separated from these distinguished persons who have practiced well, and because they do not abandon him, there are no "seizers" (*raha*)—those who would forsake him;
or, there is no "secrecy" (*raho*) regarding his being forsaken by the virtuous. Therefore, he is *arahant*.
“Those noble ones who have realized the true Dhamma and whose range is pure—the Lord is not separated from them;
therefore he is considered ‘Arahant. Here, *raha* means wandering;
for the Blessed One, [the state of being] *arahanta* refers to his freedom from the wandering through various states of existence within *saṃsāra*.

There is no going by means of the Noble Path that causes the exhaustion of karma, because at the very foot of the Bodhi tree, the entire cycle of karma along with its constituent factors has been utterly destroyed. As it is said:
"By which [path] one is reborn as a deity, or becomes a gandhabba, or a bird..."
"Those taints by which one might go to the state of a *yakkha* or fall back into the human state—
those taints of mine are exhausted, shattered,
and rendered baseless. Thus, because there is no going into solitude nor rebirth in the various realms of existence for him, he is also called an *arhat*.
Or, he for whom wandering in secret within saṃsāra does not exist in any way whatsoever—having abandoned birth and death, the Worthy One (Arahant) is considered the Well-Gone One (Sugata).
Or, the Blessed One is "Worthy" (Arahant) because of his being praiseworthy; for etymologists explain the word *arahant* as meaning praise.
And the Blessed One’s state of being praiseworthy is unique, not shared by others; it is attained through qualities that correspond to reality and is well-established in the world with its devas.

For in this way, he is peerless, equal to the unequaled, matchless, incomparable, and without a rival—being unequalled in unsurpassed virtue, unsurpassed concentration, unsurpassed wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation. Thus, having analyzed him according to each of these qualities...
Even when being spoken of by wise men, by devas, by Brahmas, or even by the Blessed One himself, it is impossible to reach its conclusion.
Thus, because he is praiseworthy, the Blessed One is an Arhat.
There is no one equal to him in virtues within the world, including the devas.
Therefore, because he is worthy of being seen, he is the Worthy One (Arahaṃ), the supreme among bipeds.
Thus, in every respect:
“He is far removed from those of dull intellect, And far removed from those who possess understanding;”

“Because he has completely abandoned the taints (āsava), because he is free from the stains (mala) of the knowable, and because there is an absence of taints regarding states of existence (bhava), the Victor is praised as an Arahant.
“Samma” means non-perverted (aviparīta). “Sāma” means by himself. For here, in the word “Sambuddho,” the prefix “sam-” signifies “by himself.”
This should be understood as the elucidator of this meaning. "Of all phenomena" means of all knowable phenomena without exception.
But how is the awakening to all phenomena obtained here? Because there is no mention of a partial portion.
For when there is no mention of a specific part, the fact that what is to be grasped is without limitation is understood, just as in the expression, "The initiated one does not give. And thus...
One should understand that the derivation of the word *buddha* applies to the agent alone, regardless of the specific object, because there is no desire to express the object (the karma).

For here, from the standpoint of the word itself, only this much is obtained: “Because he has awakened rightly and by himself (*sammā sāmaṃ buddhattā*), he is the Perfectly Awakened One (*sammāsambuddho*)”;

however, the phrase “of all phenomena (*sabbadhammānan*)” is stated having taken what is obtained from the standpoint of the meaning. Indeed, an act of awakening cannot be logically tenable if it lacks an object.

Now, in order to analyze and demonstrate the scope of that [knowledge] which was stated generally as "all phenomena" (*sabbadhamme*), it is said: "the phenomena to be directly known" (*abhiññeyye dhamme*), and so forth.
Therein, "to be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) means to be known by means of distinguished knowledge (*abhivisiṭṭha-ñāṇa*). But what are they? They are the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths.

"He is a Buddha because of the state of being one who has directly known" (*abhiññeyyato buddho*) means he awakened (*bujjhi*) to the state of being those things to be directly known. In the prior phase...

The meaning is that he "knew" by means of insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) at the moment of attainment, by means of path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*) at the subsequent moment, and later by means of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*), and so forth.
This same method applies to what follows as well. "Phenomena to be fully understood" refers to the Noble Truth of Suffering. "To be abandoned" refers to the side of the origin [of suffering].
"To be realized" is said with reference to Nibbāna. As for the use of the plural form, it includes [the truths] such as those with a residue remaining (*sopādisesa*).
This enumeration is made by taking the distinction established through a particular method (*pariyāya*)—namely, that these are the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths.
For it will be said later: "The eye is the truth of suffering," and so forth. Furthermore, an enumeration is performed on the basis of phenomena whose specific meanings have not yet been determined.
For by means of an enumeration, only the mere existence of the phenomena being enumerated is stated, but not [their specific characteristics].
"Distinction" (*paricchedo*) is expressed by means of an indefinite plural number, as in "states without conditions" (*appaccayā dhammā*) or "unconditioned states" (*asaṅkhatā dhammā*).

Alternatively, in the phrase "to be realized" (*sacchikātabbe*), the inclusion of both the fruits and the liberations is intended, rather than referring to Nibbāna alone; thus, the plural designation was employed.
Likewise, in the phrase "and so to be developed" (*evaṃ ca bhāvetabbe*), the inclusion of the meditative absorptions (*jhānāni*) should also be understood.
Regarding the phrase "and that which is to be developed" (*bhāvetabbañca*) in this verse, the word *ca* (and) has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*avuttasamuccaya*).

By means of it, the inclusion of "that which is to be realized" (*sacchikātabba*) should be understood. Therefore, the meaning is: "I am a Buddha"—because the Four Truths have been awakened to by me, and there is no object of knowledge (*ñeyya*) whatsoever apart from the Truths, I am a Buddha with respect to the entire object of knowledge; that is, I have fully known it (*abbhaññāsiṃ*).

132. Thus, having explained the matter generally by way of the Truths, the passage beginning with “Moreover” is commenced in order to demonstrate it by analyzing it further through the Truths themselves, in relation to the doors and objects, as well as the mental states occurring at the doors, such as the aggregates and so forth.

Therein, “by way of being the root cause” means that although there are other causes such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest, [craving] is the root-cause even for those. For craving is the cause of karma...
It is the primary cause for the diversity of suffering because it is the cause for the variety of states of consciousness and because it leads to the acquisition of various associations.
"Originator" means that which produces. "Prior craving" refers to the craving established in previous existences. "Of both" refers to the eye and its origination.
"Non-occurrence" is the cause for non-occurrence. "Understanding of cessation" is by way of the clear realization through direct knowledge (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*).
“Through the penetration of cessation. By “extracting each term individually” means by the extraction of each individual category, such as “the eye, the origin of the eye,” and so forth.

Since craving also possesses the state of being fully understood (pariññeyya) and because it is included within the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), it is stated that “there are six groups of craving, beginning with craving for form,” in order to show its inclusion within the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca).
"Kasiṇas" means kasiṇa-jhānas. "The thirty-two aspects" refers to the thirty-two parts as well as the jhānas that have them as their objects.

"The nine existences" refers to the nine existences: the three beginning with sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), the three beginning with perception-existence (saññībhava), and the three beginning with single-aggregate existence (ekavokārabhava).
"The four jhānas" refers to the four fine-material-sphere jhānas, without specifying their particular objects.

Or rather, this is a reference to the jhānas born of kamma-result (*vipākajjhāna*). And here, it should be understood that for wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), the craving that serves as their decisive support (*upanissaya*) is the preceding craving that gives rise to them.
For functional states (*kiriyadhamma*), however, it is where they serve as the cause for that particular personal existence (*attabhāva*).
"Anubuddha" means awakened in accordance with the dhammas to be awakened to. "Tena" means therefore; because [he is so] by way of commonality.
And specifically, he is called "Buddha" because he has awakened to all phenomena by extracting them one by one; therefore it was said. To the question "How so?", he replied:
"Because of his having fully and personally awakened to all phenomena. The meaning is that he himself has perfectly and directly awakened to the entirety of what is to be known in all its aspects.
By this, [the quality of] his capacity to awaken to all phenomena in every aspect, without depending on the instruction of another, is shown.
The attainment of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), which is designated as unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) because its functioning is bound to his own wish, has been demonstrated.
But is not unobstructed knowledge different from omniscient knowledge? Otherwise, the statement that "the six unique knowledges are the Buddha-knowledges" would be contradicted.
It is not contradicted; for it is intended to show that [omniscience] is unique among others by way of the distinction between its objective sphere and its mode of occurrence.

Because this single knowledge is described in two ways. For that very same knowledge is called "omniscience" (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) because its object is the entire range of conditioned and unconditioned conventional phenomena without exception;
and because it moves without attachment due to the absence of any obstruction therein, it is called "unobstructed knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*).
As it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "It is omniscient knowledge because it knows all the conditioned and the unconditioned without remainder."
"In that regard, there is no obstruction; thus it is 'unobstructed knowledge,'" and so forth. Therefore, there is no difference between them in meaning, and this must certainly be accepted as such.
Otherwise, it would follow that omniscience and unobstructed knowledge are identical and that they do not have all phenomena as their object.
For there is not even the slightest obstruction to the Blessed One’s knowledge, [which is] unobstructed knowledge.

Furthermore, if it were not the case that all phenomena serve as its object, then in those places where it does not occur, there would be no state of non-obstruction due to the presence of an obstruction.
Alternatively, let there be another kind of "unobstructed knowledge" distinct from the knowledge of omniscience;

however, in this context, by virtue of its unimpeded operation everywhere, the term "unobstructed knowledge" refers specifically to the knowledge of omniscience itself. And through the attainment of that—
The Blessed One is called "the All-Knowing," "the All-Wise," and "the Perfectly Enlightened One" not merely because of his single act of awakening to all phenomena.

Thus it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "This designation 'Buddha' is a realization-based appellation attained by the Blessed Buddhas at the foot of the Bodhi tree simultaneously with the acquisition of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). This is through the attainment of the knowledge capable of awakening to all phenomena.
For indeed, there was in the Blessed One’s continuum the capacity to penetrate all phenomena without exception.
Here it may be asked: when this knowledge arises, does it arise all at once regarding its entire object, or rather gradually?

What follows from this? If, first of all, it arises all at once regarding its entire object, then [it would have to grasp] those things divided by the distinctions of past, future, present, internal, external, and so forth...
If conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) and the conventionally designated unconditioned phenomena (*asaṅkhata-sammuti-dhammā*) were to appear together as one,

there would be no distinct comprehension of them, like looking at a cloth from a distance; and if that were the case, then for those practicing insight (*vipassanā*) with the thought "all phenomena are non-self," all phenomena would be objects of the Blessed One’s knowledge in an undifferentiated form, just as they appear through the aspect of non-self.

They fall into [the error of asserting that] they exist. As for those who say: "The Buddha's knowledge at all times functions with respect to the fixed characteristics (*ṭhitalakkhaṇa*) of all knowable phenomena, being free from conceptual construction;

therefore, he is called 'all-knowing' (*sabbavidū*); and by taking it this way, the statement, 'The Naga is concentrated while walking, and concentrated even while standing,' is well-said"—even for them, the aforementioned faults do not cease.
Furthermore, because past and future conventional phenomena lack the characteristic of stability as their object, the Blessed One’s knowledge would have only a partial range.
Therefore, it is not tenable that his knowledge occurs all at once.
If, on the other hand, his knowledge occurs gradually throughout the entire range of objects, even that is not tenable; for [knowledge] does not [arise] by way of genus, plane, nature, and so forth.
When the objects of knowledge— which are divided into many categories according to direction, location, time, and so forth— are apprehended in succession,

their complete and exhaustive penetration becomes possible, because the objects of knowledge are limitless. However, those who maintain that "the Blessed One is omniscient because he does not deceive regarding the meaning,
having made one portion of the objects of knowledge directly perceptible, having resolved that 'the rest is also thus,' and having established it"— [hold this view].
And that knowledge is not inferential because it is free from doubt; for they say that in the world, inferential knowledge is bound up with doubt.

But even their view is not tenable, because if everything were beyond direct perception, it would be impossible to determine—by making one part of the knowable directly perceived and resolving that "the rest is likewise"—that the object is non-deceptive.
For that which remains is not directly perceived (*paccakkha*).
If even that were directly perceived, its status as "the remainder" would not exist—is this so? All of this is without reason. Why?
Because it is an investigation into what is not an object [of such perception]. For it was said by the Blessed One: "The domain of the Buddhas, monks, is inconceivable."
"It should not be thought about. Whoever should think about it would partake of madness and frustration. This, however, is the conclusion here:

whatever the Blessed One wishes to know—whether in its entirety or in part—knowledge regarding that proceeds directly through its unimpeded operation, and there is constant composure due to the absence of distraction. Regarding that which he wishes to know...
Furthermore, if everything were outside the range of his [cognition], his activity would not be dependent upon his desire; yet that dependence must be admitted absolutely, because of the statement:
"All phenomena are dependent upon the advertence, dependent upon the desire, dependent upon the attention, and dependent upon the arising of the mind of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
This applies even to objects past and future for the Blessed One.
Knowledge is indeed direct perception (*paccakkha*) because it is devoid of inference, scripture, reasoning, or conceptual grasping.

But is it not the case that, according to this position, when one desires to know everything, the Blessed One’s knowledge would have to proceed all at once toward its entire object in an undifferentiated form; thus, would you not fail to avoid the aforementioned fault? No, for that...
Because it has been purified. For that domain of the Buddhas is indeed purified and inconceivable.
Otherwise, if its mode of operation were identical to the knowledge of ordinary people, the inconceivability of the knowledge of the Blessed Buddhas would not exist.
Therefore, although that [knowledge] has all phenomena as its object, it proceeds by making those phenomena well-defined as if they were the object of a single phenomenon; this is what is meant here.
It is inconceivable. For this has been said: "As far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge; as far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable.
Knowledge is limited by the knowable, and the knowable is limited by knowledge.

Thus, because he has perfectly and personally awakened to all phenomena—whether taken together, separately, all at once, or in succession, according to his wish—he is the Perfectly Self-Awakened One (Sammāsambuddha).
