He said, "Pervading the three worlds," because he has attained qualities exactly as they are. He is exceedingly pure precisely because of having attained such qualities.
He is complete in every aspect through his perfection of all primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).

The splendor of all his limbs and members (*sabbaṅgapaccaṅgasirī*) is the beauty of each and every part of his body. By such statements as "Having crossed over, he shall ferry others across," whatever was desired by this Lord of the World—
By way of aspiration through mind and speech, it is that which was wished for by way of aspiration through the body. "In the same way" means exactly in accordance with that aspiration.
"Exertion" refers to the application characterized as right effort, which has reached the state of the perfection of energy and is included within the Noble Path.

"By way of divisions" means by way of the various classifications connected with all the triplets and pairs of terms. By the word "etc. in the phrase "dependent origination, etc.," [the remaining factors are implied].
It should be understood that not only the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth found in the Vibhaṅga-pāḷi are included here;

rather, the aggregates (saṅgaha) and so forth, the liberations through occasion (samaya-vimutta) and so forth, the establishing (ṭhapana) and so forth, and the triple foundations (tika-paṭṭhāna) and so forth are also included.

Regarding the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca), its sense of oppression is the harming of the being who possesses it and the making of it non-expansive. Its sense of being conditioned (saṅkhata) is [the state of] having arisen together through conditions.

The sense of being made (katabhāva) is the state of being tormented and scorched by the various forms of suffering, such as the suffering of suffering (dukkhadukkhatā). The sense of change (vipariṇāma) is twofold:

the state of being subject to transformation through aging and through death. The sense of accumulation (āyūhana) regarding origination is the gathering together of suffering by way of its production.
The sense of source (nidāna) is the act of originating [suffering] as if pointing it out, saying, "This is that suffering."
The sense of conjunction is the binding together with the suffering of saṃsāra. The sense of impediment is the obstruction to the attainment of the Path.
The sense of escape from cessation is its state of being escaped from all acquisitions because its intrinsic nature is the relinquishing of them, or because it is the cause for escaping from them.
The sense of seclusion is the dissociation from all conditioned formations. The sense of the unconditioned is the state of not being conditioned by any condition whatsoever.
The meaning of "deathless" (*amata*) is the absence of death due to its permanent nature, or else it is the state of being the cause for the absence of death for sentient beings.

The meaning of "escape" (*niyyāna*) for the Path is the act of going forth from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). The meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) is the state of bringing about the attainment of Nibbāna. The meaning of "seeing" (*dassana*) is the realization of Nibbāna, which is extremely subtle.
The meaning of "predominance" (*ādhipateyya*) is the exercise of sovereignty by the associated mental factors over the vision of the Four Noble Truths.
Or rather, it is the state of being a dominant object (ārammaṇādhipatibhāva) [that is meant], specifically because of the expression "dominant by way of the Path" (maggādhipati).

For even though jhāna and the other factors possess the status of being dominant objects, instead of saying "states dominant by way of jhāna" and so forth, it is said simply "states dominant by way of the Path.
Therefore, it is understood that "there is a distinction in the Path's status as a dominant object. And these [factors] such as oppression (pīḷana), etc.,...
These are called the sixteen aspects. But why, when other aspects such as disease, tumors, and so forth exist here, are only these taken up for contemplation?

It is because they are distinguished by their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*) and because they reveal the vision of the other truths (*saccantara*). This matter will be made clear later in the discussion on the Truths (*saccakathā*) itself.

The "divine abodes" (*dibbavihāra*) are the fine-material-sphere jhānas that have the kasiṇas and other objects as their basis. The jhānas of loving-kindness and the rest are the "sublime abodes" (*brahmavihāra*).

The attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is a noble abiding (*ariyavihāra*). Physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) is the state of being solitary by way of having withdrawn the body from sensual pleasures.

Mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*) is the state of the mind being secluded from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth by means of the first jhāna and the rest. Seclusion from the substrata (*upadhiviveka*) is Nibbāna.

"Others" refers to mundane higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the like. Wandering through the realms of existence by way of defilements and volitional formations—that is, with craving as the predominant factor—is what is meant by "craving-consisting" (*taṇhāsaṅkhāta*).
"Going. "Vanta" means that which has been vomited forth by way of the mouth of the Noble Path, discarded so as never to be swallowed again.
He says, "As... pe... a girdle," showing that the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) is so called according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*).

Another method: he is *bhagavā* because he possesses fortune (*bhāga*); he is *bhagavā* because he has nurtured (*bhatava*); he is *bhagavā* because he desires portions (*bhāge vanī*); he is *bhagavā* because he has resorted to the fortunate states (*bhage vanī*); he is *bhagavā* because he has conquered (*bhattava*); he is *bhagavā* because he has vomited out the fortunate states (*bhage vamī*). He is *bhagavā* because he has vomited out the portions (*bhāge vamī*).
The Blessed One has attained the portions, he has conquered fortune, and he has won the victory; he vomits out fortune as well as portions—thus the Conqueror is called "Bhagavā.
In this regard, how is he "Bhagavā" by virtue of having attained the portions? Those aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue and the rest, which are portions of qualities, are not shared by anyone else.
Incomparable qualities are found in the Tathāgata. For indeed, his virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
his moral shame and dread of blame; his faith and energy; his mindfulness and clear comprehension; his purification of virtue and purification of view;
his serenity and insight; the three roots of the wholesome; the three types of good conduct; and the three kinds of right thought—all these exist in him.
Three perceptions of blamelessness, three elements, four foundations of mindfulness,
four right endeavors, four bases of psychic power, four noble paths, four noble fruits, four analytical knowledges,
four types of knowledge delimiting the four modes of birth, four noble lineages, four grounds of self-confidence, and five factors of exertion.
The five-factored right concentration, the five-knowledge right concentration, the five faculties, the five powers,
the five elements leading to emergence, the five knowledges of the bases of liberation, the five perceptions that ripen liberation,
the six bases of recollection, the six forms of reverence, the six elements leading to emergence, the six constant abidings, and the six...
The unsurpassed states, the six perceptions conducive to penetration, the six direct knowledges, the six unique knowledges, the seven qualities that prevent decline,
the seven noble qualities, the seven noble treasures, the seven factors of enlightenment, the seven qualities of a true person,
the seven bases for the wearing away [of defilements], the seven perceptions, and the teaching on the seven types of persons worthy of offerings.
The teaching on the seven stations of consciousness; the teaching on the seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed; the teaching on the eight causes for the attainment of wisdom;
the eight rightnesses; the eight transcendences of worldly conditions; the eight bases for exertion; the teaching on the eight inopportune moments;
the eight thoughts of a great person; the teaching on the eight bases of mastery; the eight liberations; and the nine [qualities] rooted in wise attention.
the [nine] states, the nine factors of striving for complete purification, the teaching on the nine abodes of beings, the nine ways of removing resentment,
the nine perceptions, the nine diversities, the nine successive dwellings, the ten states that are grounds for being a protector,
the ten bases of totality, the ten courses of wholesome action, the ten rightnesses, the ten noble abodes, and the ten qualities of one beyond training.
The powers of a Tathāgata, the eleven benefits of loving-kindness, the twelve aspects of the Wheel of Dhamma,
the thirteen ascetic qualities, the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha, the fifteen factors that ripen liberation, the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing,
the sixteen things that burn away the future, the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, and the nineteen knowledges of review.

There are forty-four bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*), fifty knowledges of arising and passing away (*udayabbayañāṇa*), more than fifty wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), seventy-seven bases of knowledge,

the great diamond-like knowledge (*mahāvajirañāṇa*) that traverses twenty-four million meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the knowledges of teaching through the investigation and review of the *Paṭṭhāna* with its infinite methods,
and likewise the knowledges that discern the inclinations and other traits of infinite beings in infinite world-systems; such are these.
Infinite and immeasurable divisions, qualities, and portions of qualities exist and are found that are not shared with others and are unsurpassed.

Therefore, because he possesses these aforementioned divisions, qualities, and portions, although he should be called "Bhāgavā" (the possessor of portions), by shortening the vowel *ā* to *a*, he is called "Bhagavā.
Thus, first of all, he is "Bhagavā" in the sense of being a possessor of portions.
Because all the portions of qualities, beginning with virtue, exist without exception in the Sugata, he is therefore called "Bhagavā.

How is he "Bhagavā" in the sense of one who has broken? Those [qualities] which were attained by those who exerted themselves for the welfare of the entire world, beginning with human birth—these eight...

Having synthesized the teachings, the ten perfections— namely, the perfection of giving, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity— which must be fulfilled by Great Beings (mahābodhisattvas) through their great resolutions toward perfect enlightenment;
as well as the ten secondary perfections (upapāramīs), the ten ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramīs), making thirty perfections in total, beginning with giving and the rest.
The four bases of sympathy; the four foundations beginning with truth;
the five great renunciations—namely, the renunciation of oneself, of one’s eyes, of wealth, of a kingdom, and of wife and children;

and such things as previous application, previous conduct, the proclamation of the Dhamma, conduct for the benefit of kinsmen, conduct for the benefit of the world, and conduct for the benefit of Buddhahood—or, in brief, all of these.
The qualities that constitute the equipment of merit and the equipment of knowledge, which are the factors that produce a Buddha, from the time of the Great Resolve onwards,
for four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons, do not become conducive to decline, conducive to defilement, or conducive to stagnation; rather,
they become exclusively conducive to ever-increasing distinction, thus being practiced with care and continuity.
Because he has possessed and accumulated [all qualities] without remainder, one should say "bhatavā";
however, by way of etymological method (*niruttinaya*), the letter *t* is changed to *g*, and thus he is called "Bhagavā.

Alternatively, "bhatavā" means that he bore (*bhari*) and accumulated (*sambhari*) those very same aforementioned qualities that constitute a Buddha, in the manner already described; thus, having borne them, he is "Bhagavā."
The Protector has fulfilled all the requisites for Perfect Enlightenment, beginning with the perfection of giving;
therefore, he is also considered "Bhagavā" (the Blessed One).
How does he "possess a portion"? Those portions consisting of the meditative attainments that are utilized daily, numbering twenty-four million billion—[he possesses these].

He constantly, for all time, frequented, cultivated, and repeatedly practiced the forest for the sake of the welfare of the world without remainder, and for the sake of his own dwelling in happiness in this very life;
thus he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because he "possessed" (*bhaji*) the forest.

Alternatively, among the things to be directly known—such as the wholesome factors, etc., and the aggregates, etc.—there are those fourfold portions of direct realization (*abhisamaya-bhāga*), categorized briefly by way of full understanding (*pariññā*) and so forth.
In detail, however, there are numerous portions to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*), such as: "The eye is to be fully understood... [and so on] ...aging-and-death is to be fully understood";
portions to be abandoned (*pahātabba*), such as: "The origin of the eye is to be abandoned... [and so on] ...the origin of aging-and-death is to be abandoned";
and portions to be realized (*sacchikātabba*), such as: "The cessation of the eye... [and so on] ...the cessation of aging-and-death is to be realized."

By such expressions as “the practice leading to the cessation of the eye,” and so forth, and “the four foundations of mindfulness,” and so forth, there are various classifications of phenomena (*dhamma*) that are to be cultivated;

he shunned all those [unwholesome] parts and, according to what was appropriate, practiced them through the cultivation of their respective spheres of activity (*gocara*) and through repeated practice (*sevana*).
Thus, because he shunned the parts (*bhāga*), he is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*). Alternatively, regarding these aggregates of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*) beginning with virtue (*sīla*)...

The portions of qualities, the shares of qualities, which are common to his disciples—he, with great compassion, made a prayer for the forest [of the world], thinking, "How might I establish these in the mental continua of those to be trained?
And that prayer of his brought about the fruit exactly as intended.
Thus, because he prayed for a share, he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā).

Because the Tathāgata has partaken in and aspired for the portion of qualities consisting of the knowable and the attainments for the welfare of beings, he is therefore called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*).
How does one "win" (*vanī*) these qualities (*bhaga*)? Briefly stated, by those who have performed merit and are endowed with skillful means according to their respective wealth...
They are called *bhaga* because they are to be enjoyed (*bhajīyanti*), namely, mundane and supramundane attainments.
Regarding these, first, while the Tathāgata was still a bodhisatta prior to his full enlightenment, he frequented and cultivated (*bhaji sevi*) those things that had reached the highest excellence;

established therein, he brought to maturity the qualities of a Buddha by fully acquiring all the factors that constitute a Buddha. However, having become a Buddha, he [enjoyed] those [qualities] which are endowed with blameless happiness.

He frequented and cultivated the forest even in its supramundane sense, which is not shared by others. In detail, however, he frequented and cultivated the forest of "blessings" (*bhaga*) that are manifold and not shared by others—whether in terms of the sovereignty of a regional king, the prosperity of a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*), the attainment of divine kingship, and so forth;

or in terms of superhuman qualities such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), liberations (*vimokkha*), concentrations (*samādhi*), attainments (*samāpatti*), knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*), the development of the path (*magga-bhāvanā*), and the realization of the fruits (*phala-sacchikiriyā*). Thus, because he frequented the forest of blessings, he is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*).
Whatever prosperities there are in the world, and those many supramundane ones—the Sambuddha has enjoyed them all;
for that reason also he is considered the Blessed One (Bhagavā).
How is he "possessed of devotion" (bhattavā)? He is "possessed of devotion" because he has many devoted followers who are firm in their devotion. Thus is the Tathāgata.
Indeed, because he possesses immeasurable and incomparable qualities of power such as great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), he is the supreme among all beings;

because of his unsurpassed perfection of application—which is preceded by the avoidance of all harm for all beings and intent solely upon providing their welfare and happiness in its entirety—he is of ultimate benefit to the world including gods and humans;

and because his physical body is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*), the eighty minor characteristics (*anubyañjana*), the fathom-wide radiance (*vyāmappabhā*), and other unique, extraordinary qualities not shared by others.

Because he is endowed with a vast and perfectly pure sound of praise—extending throughout the three worlds and proceeding in the manner of "Thus indeed is that Blessed One," etc.—which arises from the realization of his qualities as they truly are;
because he is firmly established in such supreme perfections as fewness of wishes and contentment;
and because he possesses extraordinary and distinguished qualities such as the ten powers and the four grounds of self-confidence.
“Measuring by form, he is confident in form; measuring by sound, he is confident in sound; measuring by the coarse, he is confident in the coarse;

measuring by the Dhamma, he is confident in the Dhamma. Thus, because he is pleasing in every way within this world-system characterized by these four measures, and because he is a source of respect, esteem, and reverence for immeasurable beings—both gods and humans—he is called Samantapāsādika (the All-Pleasing).

It is a ground for supreme love and affection. Those who are established in his instruction and endowed with verified confidence (aveccappasāda) cannot be led away from that affection by anyone—whether by a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, or Brahmā.
For even at the sacrifice of their own lives, they do not abandon their confidence in him.
Or it is because of his state of firm devotion to that [teacher]. For this very reason it was said:
"The wise man who is grateful and mindful of what has been done for him is one who possesses virtuous friends and is firmly devoted."
“Just as, monks, the great ocean is stable in its nature and does not overstep its shore,
even so, monks, whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives.

Thus he is called *Bhattava* (the One Honored) by the Blessed One, according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), by eliding one *ta*-sound and changing the other to a *ga*-sound.
Because many have placed their trust in the Teacher who is endowed with an excellence of qualities and who seeks the welfare of the world, he is therefore called "Bhagavā.
How does he vomit forth blessings (*bhaga*)? Because even while he was a Bodhisatta in former births, the Tathāgata [fulfilled] the perfections (*pāramī*).

Filling [the perfections], he vomited forth glory, sovereignty, and fame known as "splendor," and cast them away without regard, like a globule of spittle. For instance, during his time as Prince Somanassa,
Prince Hatthipāla, the Wise One of Ayoghara, the Wise One of Mūgapakkha, Cūḷasutasoma, and so forth,
by way of fulfilling the perfection of renunciation, even while possessing a divine kingship—
There is no limit to those who have renounced their very selves for the sake of royal glory. Even in his final existence, having renounced the sovereignty over the four continents—
which was as if it were the lordship of the deva-worlds— and having cast aside the splendor of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin),
which was supported by the excellence of a cakravartin and radiant with the seven treasures, regarding even such fame as if it were mere grass, he went forth into homelessness without attachment.

Because he has fully awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), he is therefore called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because he has vomited out (*vamīti*) these fortunes (*bhage*) beginning with glory (*siri*). Alternatively, "fortunes" (*bhagā*) refers to the constellations (*bhāni*);

those which proceed and revolve together with them are the fortunes—the splendors based on the specific features of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), such as Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, and the Himavat—which endure for the duration of an eon (*kappa*).
The Blessed One has also vomited these out by transcending the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*) where they reside, through the abandonment of desire and lust (*chandarāga*) bound to them.
"He has abandoned" (*pajahī*): thus too, he vomits out the *bhagas*, therefore he is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*).
Because the Sugata, the Blessed One, has abandoned the glory of a wheel-turning monarch, as well as fame, sovereignty, happiness, and the worldly mind, for that reason he is the Blessed One.
In what sense does the Blessed One vomit up a portion? "Portions" (bhāgā) refers to the constituent parts of phenomena possessing intrinsic nature;
these are manifold, categorized by way of aggregates, bases, and elements, and within those, further by way of form, feeling, and so forth, as well as by way of the past and so on.
And the Blessed One, having utterly severed all proliferation (papañca), all bondages (yoga), all ties (gantha), and all fetters (saṃyojana), while attaining the deathless element (amata-dhātu)...
Having vomited it up, he cast it away without looking back and did not vomit it up again. For in this way, he has entirely abandoned earth, water, fire, and air;
the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects;
eye-consciousness … pe … mind-consciousness; eye-contact … pe … mind-contact; and so forth.
“Feeling born of eye-contact... [and so on] ...feeling born of mind-contact;
perception born of eye-contact... [and so on] ...perception born of mind-contact; volition born of eye-contact... [and so on] ...volition born of mind-contact;

craving for forms... [and so on] ...craving for mental phenomena; thought concerning forms... [and so on] ...thought concerning mental phenomena; examination concerning forms... [and so on] ...examination concerning mental phenomena,” and so forth.

Furthermore, by way of analyzing phenomena according to their categories, he vomited up all divisions of phenomena without exception; he disgorged them and cast them away with a relinquishment free from longing.
For it has been said:
"Ānanda, that which has been abandoned, vomited up, released, relinquished, and discarded—that the Tathāgata would ever take back again: such a possibility does not exist."
"Thus he vomited out even a portion," said the Blessed One.

Or alternatively, "he vomited out a portion" means that by means of the noble path-knowledge, he vomited up, disgorged, cast aside without regard for, and abandoned all phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome, blameworthy or blameless, inferior or superior, dark or bright—which are counterparts to one another;
and he taught the Dhamma to others so that they might become likewise. And this has also been said:

“Monks, even phenomena (*dhammā*) are to be abandoned, how much more so non-phenomena (*adhammā*). Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma as a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping,” and so forth.
Thus he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because he has vomited out (cast aside) all things.
The various classifications of phenomena—such as the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—were [taught] by the Great Sage.
Since black and white have been vomited out, even more so is the Blessed One considered dead.
Therefore it was said:
"The Blessed One (Bhagavā) has partaken of (bhata-vā) the portions (bhāge), and he has conquered (vani) fortune (bhage)."
“He has attained (bhage) and likewise he has vomited out (vami) the portion (bhāge); thus the Blessed One, the Victor, is called ‘Bhagavā’.

And here, since the qualities of a Buddha are twofold in brief—consisting of the attainment of one’s own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others—and among these, the attainment of one’s own welfare is twofold, being divided into the perfection of abandonment and the perfection of knowledge; [and] of the perfection of power, etc.,...

Because it is invariably concomitant with that [compassion], it is included within it. The practice for the welfare of others is twofold, distinguished by its application (*payoga*) and its disposition (*āsaya*).
Therein, in terms of application, it is the teaching of the Dhamma that leads out of all suffering to one whose mind is indifferent to gain, honor, and so forth;

in terms of disposition, it is the constant desire for the welfare of others even toward those who are hostile, as well as the practice for the welfare of others such as waiting for the time when their wisdom has reached maturity, and so on—even through the acceptance of material gifts and the like.

The practice for the welfare of others (*atthacariyā*) is indeed the pursuit of the benefit of others. Therefore, it should be understood that the inclusion of terms such as "Arahant" and so forth in the Canon is by way of elucidating these two aspects.
Therein, by the term "Arahant," the Blessed One’s perfection of his own welfare is elucidated by way of the perfection of abandonment (*pahānasampadā*).
By these two phrases, “Sammāsambuddho” and “Lokavidū,” [the Buddha’s excellence] is shown by way of the perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇasampadā*).

But is it not the case that even by the phrase “Lokavidū,” the state of being a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddhatā*) is made manifest? True, it is made manifest; however, there is a distinction:

by the phrase “Sammāsambuddho,” the power of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is made manifest, whereas by the phrase “Lokavidū,” [the power of] the knowledge of underlying tendencies and latent dispositions (*āsayānusayañāṇa*), and so forth, is also [made manifest].
"The majesty has been manifested. By the phrase "endowed with true knowledge and conduct" (*vijjācaraṇasampanno*), all of the Blessed One’s attainment of his own welfare is manifested.
By the term "Well-Gone" (*sugato*), however, both the Blessed One’s attainment of his own welfare and his practice for the welfare of others are manifested from the very beginning of his realization.
[And by the phrase] "the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans..."

By these words, the Blessed One’s practice for the benefit of others is elucidated. By the term “Buddha,” both the Blessed One’s attainment of his own welfare and his practice for the benefit of others are elucidated.
And by doing so, after stating “Sammāsambuddho” (Perfectly Enlightened One), the word “Buddho” is justified.
For this very reason, it was said: “He awakened himself and awakened other beings as well,” and so forth. “Bhagavā” (the Blessed One) [is explained as follows].
And by this [passage] as well, beginning from his full attainment, all the Blessed One’s success in his own welfare and his practice for the welfare of others have been elucidated.
There is another method: briefly, the qualities of a Buddha are threefold, according to cause, fruit, and assistance to beings.

Among these, the qualities of a Buddha by way of the perfection of the fruit are expressed by the words: “The Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, perfected in knowledge and conduct, the Knower of the World.”
“Vibhāvitā. By these [epithets], “The unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans,” the qualities of a Buddha are manifested by way of his assistance to sentient beings.
By the term “Buddha,” the qualities of a Buddha are manifested by way of the fruit and by way of his assistance to sentient beings.
Furthermore, by these two phrases, “The Sugata, the Blessed One,” the qualities of a Buddha are manifested by way of both cause and fruit, as well as his assistance to sentient beings.
"It should be understood as 'fully developed.
(145) "Of him" means of the yogi who has the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) as his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

"In this way" means by the manner described in the passage beginning with "In this regard, this is the method. "At that time" means at the time of recollecting the qualities of the Buddha. "Overwhelmed by lust" means by lust...

A mind possessed by, that is, accompanied by lusts that have reached the state of obsession, is said to be "obsessed" (pariyuṭṭhita) by them—just as a forest is [said to be] by robbers—because it serves as the locus for their obsession; thus, the meaning is "one whose lust is obsessed.
Alternatively, it should be understood that the obsession of lust itself is metaphorically attributed to the mind associated with it. In this...

"By passion for one's own side": the meaning is "by passion as the cause. "It has indeed become straight" means that it has been made straight because bodily crookedness and so forth have already been removed, because of the absence of deceit and other factors that cause the mind to be unstraight, or because of the absence of the obsession of passion and so forth, it is free from depression and elation.
Alternatively, "it has indeed become straight" refers to the removal of dullness and agitation due to the mental state having entered the path of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
It has attained straightness through the practice of the sign of middling tranquility. "Taking the Tathāgata as the object" means making the qualities of the Tathāgata the focal point.
"Iccassa" means *iti assa* (thus for him). The connection is: "contemplating the Buddha-qualities in the manner previously stated, namely, 'That Blessed One is indeed an Arahant,' and so forth.
"In this way" refers to the method described by the passage beginning with "not at that time," and so on. "Inclined toward the Buddha-qualities" [is the meaning].

“Inclined toward the qualities of the Buddha. By the phrase “thoughts and examinations proceed,” it is shown that the meditation subject consisting of the Buddha’s qualities is struck by thought, assailed by thought, and repeatedly polished by it.
“Rapture arises”: through the process of development, a powerful rapture arises that brings about access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*). For one whose mind is filled with rapture...

Of the mind accompanied by the kind of rapture (pīti) already described. "Dissipation of bodily and mental distress" refers to the subtle states of defilement associated with restlessness, which are the opposites of bodily and mental tranquility (passaddhi). "They subside" means they settle down.
"Gradually, in a single moment" means when the meditation (bhāvanā) having the qualities of the Buddha as its object proceeds, bringing about ever-increasing distinction.
At that time, the hindrances are indeed suppressed, the defilements have subsided, and the faculties such as faith become very clear.
Due to proficiency in cultivation, initial application and sustained application perform their functions with exceptional skill;
powerful rapture arises, and from rapture as its proximate cause, tranquility is born in an especially distinguished manner. For one whose body is tranquil...
Happiness, having its proximate cause in concentration, proceeds in a more stable manner;

the mind, nourished by happiness, becomes properly concentrated upon the meditation subject. Thus, in due course, during the preliminary stage, applied thought and the other factors proceed in a progressively clearer and more refined state, through the practice of middling serenity and the development of the faculties.
The factors of jhāna arise in a single moment, having become most intense through their state of being of a single flavor. It was with reference to this that the Blessed One said:
“Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust... [and so on] ...the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
But why, in this case, does the jhāna not reach absorption (appanā)? To this he says: “Because of the profundity of the Buddha’s qualities,” and so forth.
For when the object is profound, the development of serenity finds no firm footing, like a ship fallen into deep water.

By the term "profundity," the nature of phenomena (*sabhāvadhammatā*) is also included. For it is the phenomenon as intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) that is profound, not the designation (*paññatti*).
But is it not the case that the phenomenon as intrinsic nature is apprehended by means of its corresponding designation? True, it is so apprehended.
In the preliminary stage, however, as development increases, the mind transcends the conceptual description (paññatti) and comes to rest upon the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) itself.
But is it not the case that absorption (appanā) is achieved even with respect to phenomena of intrinsic nature in certain instances, such as the second formless jhāna and others?
True, it is achieved; yet that occurs only when the object is of a single mode. This [present case], however, is of various modes—showing this, [the author says]:
He said, "Because of being intent on recollecting various kinds of qualities. But even so, one might ask:

why does it not happen here that, just as for one who directs attention to various parts such as the head-hairs and so forth, the development culminates in absorption (appanā) with respect to only a single part?
This is an unequal comparison. For in that case, although there is a multiplicity of parts, [the mind settles upon one].

In that [previous] case, meditation proceeds in only a single mode because one grasps only the aspect of repulsiveness; here, however, it proceeds in various modes because the qualities are of various kinds.

This meditation cannot remain fixed upon only a single quality, because through the power of meditation the Buddha’s qualities appear directly before one, and thus faith becomes powerful. For this very reason, it is said: "by way of resolution."
If it is a meditation that has reached the stage of mere figurative designation (*upacāra*), how can it be called "recollection of the Buddha"? To this he says, "This, however," and so forth.
One becomes full of reverence and deference because the Teacher’s body of qualities stands directly before one.

Precisely for that reason, there is an abundance of faith—a greatness of faith resembling the confidence born of penetration (*aveccappasāda*). This occurs by way of recollecting the qualities of the Buddha.
Because it proceeds by way of meditation, there is an abundance of mindfulness. Because of their supreme profundity and their manifold variety, there is an abundance of wisdom.
And because they are a field of sublime merit, one attains an abundance of merit.

One becomes full of rapture and gladness, because recollection of the Buddha is a basis for the enlightenment factor of rapture. One overcomes fear and terror through the object of the Buddha’s qualities.
Because mindfulness overcomes fear and terror. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Recall the Fully Enlightened One; then no fear shall be yours.
One is capable of enduring suffering because, through the recollection of the Buddha, bodily pain is turned away like water from a lotus leaf.
"Perception of living together" means the perception of co-residence. [This refers to] the mind on the plane of Buddhahood.
It is called "namati" because the greatness of the Buddha’s qualities appears directly before one.
Because the qualities of the Buddha constantly revolve within the mind through the cultivation of the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), it is said: "as if seeing the Teacher face to face.
"Not penetrating further" means not penetrating the Truths by making that [recollection] a firm basis for what lies beyond this cultivation.
“Having a happy destination as one’s ultimate goal” means having a happy state in the future life.
“Diligence” means non-negligence, that is, careful and devoted application. “One should do” means one should perform. “The wise one” means one of beautiful wisdom.
“Thus of great power” means by way of being capable of suppressing the hindrances and so forth, as described above, through such causes as the state of reverence toward the Teacher.
[She was] endowed with great capability. 2.
Commentary on the Recollection of the Dhamma (Dhammānussati-kathāvaṇṇanā): 146.

Regarding "recollection of the Dhamma" (*dhammānussati*), since both the literal meaning and the meaning in terms of its intrinsic nature have already been stated at the outset, we shall not address them here.
In order to demonstrate the method of cultivation itself, the passage beginning with “One who wishes to cultivate the recollection of the Dhamma (dhammānussati) as well... has been commenced.
But why is it not stated here—as it was in the case of the recollection of the Buddha—that one must be “endowed with verified confidence (aveccappasāda)”?
Is it not true that these six recollections were taught in this sequence for the sake of noble disciples (ariyasāvaka)? This is indeed true; however, [the reason is as follows:]...

Although [the attainment of these qualities] occurs even for worldlings who possess virtues such as pure morality, the phrase "endowed with unwavering confidence" is not mentioned here in order to show that [for them] they are achieved with difficulty;

however, for noble disciples, they are achieved easily. Nevertheless, because it has come down in the Canon, it should be understood as having been stated in the exposition of the recollection of the Buddha. Furthermore, this investigation will indeed follow later.
147. Regarding the phrase "the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyattidhamma) as well": by the word "as well" (pi), the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttaradhamma) is included.

Regarding the words "in the others," this refers to the terms such as "visible here and now" (sanditthika). The specification "the supramundane Dhamma" is stated with reference to the literal meaning of "visible here and now" and so forth;

however, in a figurative sense (pariyāyato), these qualities are indeed possible even in the Dhamma of the scriptures. For it is said that the Dhamma of the scriptures [is to be realized] by one who has heard much...

It is "visible here and now" (*sanditthika*) because it is to be seen for oneself—by means of the highest tradition (*āgata-āgama*), endowed with supreme mindfulness and discernment, and possessed of wisdom—starting from its excellence at the beginning. If it is asked: "Is it not obtained without attending upon a teacher? [The answer is no.

Even though the supramundane Dhamma is common to all, it is accomplished only through reliance on a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*); likewise is it with the Teacher’s demonstration. "Visible here and now..."

The meaning "He conquers" (*jayati*), however, is obtained in its primary sense (*nippariyāyato*) as the crushing of the heretics; it is obtained in a secondary sense (*pariyāyato*) as the conquest of the defilements, because [the teaching] serves as a successive cause for that conquest.

The meaning "It deserves to be seen face-to-face" (*sanditṭhaṃ arahati*) is also certainly obtainable, because it proceeds with the aim of the total abandoning of all phenomena of defilement and the full cultivation of phenomena of purification. And this meaning—“Those who... [is established].
“You, Gotamī, should know the Dhamma thus: ‘These things lead to passion, not to dispassion;
they lead to bondage, not to liberation; they lead to clinging, not to non-clinging. You should categorically conclude, Gotamī:
‘This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher’s instruction. [And: “Monks, even those things that are called ‘Dhammas’...”
It should be clarified by such scriptural passages as, “Even dhammas are to be abandoned, how much more so non-dhammas.

It is “timeless” (akālika) because it is a means for immediate realization. It is “inviting one to come and see” (ehipassika) because it deserves the method of saying, “Come and see,” due to its existing presence and purity.
For that very reason, there is either the directing of one’s own mind toward it by those seeking to cross over the suffering of saṃsāra, or the directing of the mind toward it.

It is called "worthy" (*opanayika*) because it leads one to the goal. Standing at the head of the bases of liberation (*vimuttāyatana*), those who, through familiarity, rightly obtain the knowledge of the meaning (*atthaveda*) and the knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhammaveda*) should realize it for themselves by means of wisdom (*viññūhi*).
Thus, attention is indeed appropriate even when including the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*) within such terms as "visible here and now" (*sanditthika*).
The verse on Sāti. "Samantabhadrakatā" means being beautiful in all its aspects. "Dhammassa" refers to the Dhamma of the Dispensation.

Although, in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a "whole" (samudāya) apart from its constituent parts (avayava), yet when those parts are viewed in the form of a whole, they receive the conventional designation "verse" (gāthā).
Having treated that [designation] as if it were distinct from them, the expression "of it" (tassa) is employed.
Having established this, he says, "It is 'good in the beginning' by the first foot," and so forth.
The term "having a single connection" (*ekānusandhika*) is stated with reference to that which has a single connection through its sequence of links, as it does not have too many divisions;

for in the other case, the portions of the beginning, middle, and end are obtained precisely through the division of the dhamma to be taught. "By the introduction" (*nidānena*) means by way of the characteristics of the indication of time, place, teacher, assembly, and so forth.
By means of the *nidāna* (introduction) and the conclusion—namely, by the words beginning with "This was said," or by the conclusion of the meaning as it has been stated:
"Thus, that which was spoken, this was spoken in dependence upon that.
Since this discourse is specifically a commentary on the Sutta Piṭaka, the quality of the Dhamma being "good in the beginning" and so forth is established by way of the Sutta Piṭaka.

Having shown this, he now says "because it possesses a cause and an origin" (*sanidānasauppattikattā*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate that same [Buddha-word] by way of the Sutta Piṭaka and the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Therein, "because it possesses a cause and an origin" means because of having a cause through the aforementioned cause (*nidāna*), and because of having an origin (*aṭṭhuppatti*).

"In accordance with those to be trained" (*veneyyānaṃ anurūpato*) refers to the proclamation of training rules (*sikkhāpada*) and the teaching of the Dhamma, by way of the specific nature of each respective training rule.

"By way of being made known" means by way of proceeding in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*). "Of the meaning" refers to the meaning of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth that is being taught.

"Because it is endowed with reasons and examples" is because of the inclusion of reasons and similes in various places, such as the passage beginning, "It is just as if, monks... (*Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave*).

Having thus shown that the Dhamma of the scriptures is beautiful in its beginning, middle, and end by way of the Sutta and Vinaya, he now says "the whole of it" and so forth to show this by taking the three Piṭakas together. Therein, the "Dhamma of the Dispensation" is as follows:
"To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome, and to purify one’s own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas."

The Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*) is the elucidator of the Teacher’s instruction thus spoken. It is "good in the beginning" by virtue of moral discipline (*sīla*), because the Dispensation has moral discipline as its root.
It is "good in the middle" through serenity (*samatha*) and the other [qualities], because these constitute the middle stage of the Dispensation’s perfection.
It is "good in the end" by virtue of Nibbāna, because once that is attained, there is nothing further to be done. This is what is called "right practice in the Dispensation."
"Wisdom arises, and for that, virtue and concentration are the roots"—thus he said, "It is good in the beginning by virtue of virtue and concentration.
But since wisdom is twofold—by way of initial awakening and by way of penetration—he, including both of these, said, "It is good in the middle by way of insight and the path.
Its accomplishment is the fruit; its function is the realization of Nibbāna; beyond that...
Showing that there is nothing further to be done, he said: "It is beautiful in its conclusion by way of the fruit and Nibbāna.

Alternatively, by the mention of "fruit," he refers to Nibbāna with residue remaining (saupādisesa-nibbāna), and by the other term [Nibbāna], he refers to the other [Nibbāna without residue]; since both of these constitute the culmination of the excellence of the Dispensation, he said: "It is beautiful in its conclusion by way of the fruit and Nibbāna."
The Buddha’s state of being well-awakened is his perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambuddhatā*); because it is the source [of the Dhamma], the teaching is "good in the beginning.

Complete purification through the total abandonment of defilements, as well as the fulfillment of the Dhamma’s excellent nature (*sudhammatā*), constitutes its "goodness in the middle," because that is the very essence of the Dhamma.
Practice according to the Teacher’s instructions is the Saṅgha’s "good practice"; because of this, the teaching is "good in the end," for it is by means of this that the Dispensation [endures].

Because it is well-established in the world. "That" refers to the Dhamma of the Dispensation. "For the sake of its suchness" means for the sake of its being as it was taught by the Blessed One, for its state of being thus (*tathatā*).

That [awakening] is threefold—namely, perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), independent enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*), and disciple-enlightenment (*sāvakabodhi*)—because there is no attainment of Nibbāna other than these. Among those, because it is the preeminent state in all qualities, [it is called the supreme].
Furthermore, the first enlightenment is said to be "good in the beginning" because it is the root of the other two enlightenments;

the second is "good in the middle" because it stands in the midst of its qualities; and the third is "good in the end" because it is the culmination of both those [first two] and because it is the finality of the Dhamma of the Dispensation.

This is the Dhamma of the Dispensation. "By way of suppressing the hindrances" means that for one standing at the head of the bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana) and listening to the true Dhamma, the suppression of the hindrances becomes possible. For this has been said:

"In whatever way, friends, the Teacher or a certain venerable fellow-celibate teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, in that very way he gains therein a sense of the meaning (atthaveda) and a sense of the Dhamma (dhammaveda)."
“Bhikkhus, at whatever time a noble disciple listens to the Dhamma with an attentive ear, at that time his five hindrances are abandoned,” and so forth.
“Because it brings about the bliss of serenity and insight” means because it accomplishes both the bliss of serenity (*samatha*) and the bliss of insight (*vipassanā*). And this has been said:

“Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion,” and so forth.
Likewise:
"From whatever point one comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one gains rapture and gladness; that is the deathless for those who understand."
“And there is superhuman delight for one who clearly sees the Dhamma rightly.
Thus, “practicing accordingly” means practicing in such a way that it brings about the bliss of serenity and insight, or as instructed by the Teacher;
this is the Dhamma of the Dispensation. “Because it brings about the state of neutrality” refers to [equanimity] toward the desirable and so forth by way of the sixfold equanimity.

Because it brings about a state of being untainted by the worldly conditions (lokadhamma) such as gain and loss, this Blessed One, while teaching the Dhamma that is excellent in three ways according to the method already described, reveals both the holy life of the Dispensation (sāsanabrahmacariya) and the holy life of the Path (maggabrahmacariya). The construction is as follows:

that [holy life] is "possessed of meaning" (sāttha) through its perfection of meaning (atthasampatti), and "possessed of phrasing" (sabyañjana) through its perfection of phrasing (byañjanasampatti), each in accordance with its respective nature.
In this context, the three trainings without distinction and the entire doctrine of the discourses (tantidhamma) constitute the holy life of the Dispensation (sāsanabrahmacariya).
With reference to this, it was said: "Venerable sir, for which Buddhas, Blessed Ones, was the holy life not long-lasting?
and so forth. The Noble Path, comprised within the three trainings which are the essence of all trainings, is the holy life of the Path (maggabrahmacariya).
It is with reference to this that it was said: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done.

“According to what is appropriate” means according to what is fitting. For the holy life of the Dispensation, which comprises the three trainings, is “possessed of meaning” (sāttha) by virtue of its attainment of purpose.

There is nothing further to be said regarding the holy life of the Path. “By virtue of its attainment of purpose” means by way of its perfected state of purpose; for here the word *saha* has the sense of “attainment.”
The other, however, is "with meaning" (sāttha) and "with phrasing" (sabyañjana) in the sense already stated.

As for those who explain here by distinguishing them, saying that "that which has the nature of speech is 'with meaning,' and that which has the nature of the meaning is 'with phrasing,'" that is not correct;
for there exists no such division within the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma). For sound and meaning, being as if inseparable in form, function [in unison].
They proceed [together]. For they acknowledge that these possess a worldly, mixed nature.

Or, even if there is a distinction, if in the phrase "with the phrasing" (*sabyañjana*) a coordinate conjunction (*tulyayoga*) is intended—as in expressions such as "the father came with his son"—then, in that case, the teaching that emphasizes the meaning, namely, "Bhikkhus, be those who rely on the meaning, not those who rely on the phrasing," would be contradicted. Alternatively, it may refer to mere existence.
In cases such as "salomako sapakkhako," the excellence of the phrasing (*byañjanasampatti*) might not have been intended;
therefore, the meaning should be understood according to the method explained in the Aṭṭhakathā.

Regarding the phrase "sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ" (possessing the meaning and possessing the phrasing), in order to demonstrate the meaning even by way of the *Netti* method, it says: "saṅkāsana... pe... sabyañjanaṃ."

It has been said. In that regard, although in the *Netti* the phrases of the letter were first enumerated—beginning with "syllable" (*akkhara*) and "phrase" (*pada*)—because the grasping of the meaning of the letter occurs by way of the letter, yet here, because it is stated in the *Pāḷi* as "endowed with meaning, endowed with letter" (*sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ*), the phrases of the meaning themselves are shown first;
thus, "proclaiming and manifesting" (*saṅkāsanapakāsanā*) and so forth was said. Therein:
In brief, *saṅkāsana* means making clear or illuminating, as in such passages as: “A monk who conceives is bound by Māra; one who does not conceive is freed.
For by that much has that bhikkhu penetrated [the truth]. Hence he said, “It is understood, Blessed One,” and so forth.
First, *kāsana* means making manifest. For this prefix (*pa-*) is used in the sense of an initial action, as in “he makes known” (*paññapeti*) or “he establishes” (*paṭṭhapeti*).
...as it were. These two terms are stated with reference to those of sharp faculties (tikkhindriya), because they function as a summary (uddesa).

For one of sharp faculties practices the meaning already stated in brief at the very outset. A detailed explanation of what was stated in brief, and a restatement of what was said once, constitute exposition (vivaraṇa) and analysis (vibhajana).
Just as, for example, "wholesome states" (kusalā dhammā) is stated once in brief—

And there is the restatement of the meaning already stated, by way of detailed exposition and analysis, beginning with: "Which phenomena are wholesome? At whatever time there is wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere...

These two phrases refer to those of medium faculties, because they constitute a formal exposition (*niddesa*). There is a further expression that is more extensive for what has been briefly explained (*vivaṭa*), and for what has been analyzed (*vibhatta*), it is by way of various modes.
Informing [others] consists of gladdening the minds of those to be trained, as well as making clear and establishing [the meaning].

For example, regarding the meaning already disclosed and analyzed in such passages as "there is contact," there is the act of making it clear and establishing it through such statements as: "What, at that time, is contact?
It is that which at that time is contact, the contacting, the thorough contacting. These two terms are intended with respect to those of dull faculties.

Because it is a state of re-explanation (*paṭiniddesa*). There is also a reading: “Because of establishing, setting forth, disclosing, analyzing, making plain, clarifying, and the conjunction of meaning and words.
But how did this alternative reading arise? It is said: the first reading follows the method found in the *Netti-pāḷi*; for therein it says: “Making known, clarifying... [and so on].
“Exposition, analysis, making clear, and description of action—
by these six terms,
the meaning and the action are demonstrated.”

And in the *Desanāhārayojanā*, this same meaning is presented through the passage beginning with "proclaiming (*saṅkāsanā*) and revealing (*pakāsanā*). However, the latter [set of terms] is based merely on the phrasing found in the Sutta according to the method:
"He makes known (*paññapeti*), establishes (*paṭṭhapeti*), discloses (*vivarati*), analyzes (*vibhajati*), clarifies (*uttānīkaroti*), and says, 'Behold!
Thus, there is a difference between these two readings only in their wording, not in their meaning.
For thus, in brief, these terms— “first making known (ñāpana), making understood (paññāpana), and first establishing (ṭhapana), setting forth (paṭṭhapana)”—
are not different in meaning from the terms “making manifest (saṅkāsanā)” and “making clear (pakāsanā). And that which was stated as the sixth term in the first recension—
“making known by way of classification (pakārato ñāpana)” as “making understood”— is, in the second recension, [equivalent to] the term “making clear,” without distinction.

Having established [the term] as "explanation" (*kāsana*) by way of the letter *pa* (*pakārato*), it is because both the proclamation (*ñāpana*) and the explanation (*kāsana*) are non-different due to their nature of illuminating the meaning (*atthāvabhāsana-sabhāvatā*).

Furthermore, the satisfaction of the minds of all those to be trained (*veneyya*) and the sharpening of the intellect (*buddhi-nisāna*) arise when the true nature of things is illuminated according to reality.

Thus, because the meaning of the teaching (*pariyatti-attha*) consists of the aforementioned six types of meaning-words (*atthapada*), the Dispensation (*sāsana*) is "possessed of meaning" (*sāttha*) through its conjunction with these six types of meaning-words.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the perfection of the description of the forms of syllables, words, and phonemes": here, at the time of pronunciation, a *vaṇṇa* (sound) that has not yet completed a word is a *akkhara* (syllable).
Some say: "A single-syllable word is a *akkhara*, like the *ā*-phoneme and others in expressions such as ‘ā evaṃ kira taṃ’. Others say:
"It is called a *akkhara* because it is articulated (*akkharana*) by means of the mind through the speech of pure articulators. [This refers to] that which ends in a case-ending.
It is a *pada* because it makes known the meaning. It is an *abyañjana* (phrase) because it clarifies the meaning expressed by the *pada* when stated in brief;

it is a sentence (*vākya*). For they say: "A sentence is a verbal form connected with indeclinables, cases, and adjectives. The mode (*ākāra*) is the classification of sentences according to their types.

Etymological derivation (*nirutti*) is the analysis of words as expressed through that mode. Exposition (*niddesa*) is the detailed expansion of that etymological derivation through exhaustive instruction.
It is "with phrasing" (*sabyañjana*) because of the perfection, that is, the excellence, of these syllables and other phrases.
In this regard, its connection with the words of meaning and its perfection of phrasing is as follows:

it makes known by means of syllables, it reveals by means of phrases, it discloses by means of phrasing, it analyzes by means of modes, it clarifies by means of etymologies, and [it explains] by means of definitions.
He makes it known; thus, having opened it up through syllables, he guides the one who gains knowledge through what is condensed (*ugghaṭitaññū*) by means of phrases.

Having expanded it through phonemes, he guides the one who gains knowledge through expansion (*vipañcitaññū*) by means of modes. Having led it through etymologies, he guides the one who is to be guided (*neyya*) by means of explanations.

And so, this Dhamma, when being condensed, guides the one who gains knowledge through what is condensed; when being expanded, it guides the one who gains knowledge through expansion; when being led...

It is to be led [to understanding]. In this regard, the summary is the beginning, the exposition is the middle, and the guidance is the end. Thus, taught in three ways across the three times, it dispels the three defects, brings about the three qualities, and disciplines the three kinds of those to be trained. In this way too, this Dhamma is "good in three ways" (tividhakalyāṇa);
through the perfection of both meaning and phrasing, it should be understood as "possessing meaning and possessing phrasing," and as "complete and pure."

Regarding "depth of meaning" and so forth: "meaning" (*attha*) refers to the meaning of the textual tradition (*tanti*). "Dhamma" refers to the textual tradition itself. "Penetration" (*paṭivedha*) is the realization of the textual tradition and the meaning of the textual tradition exactly as they are.
"Teaching" (*desanā*) is the teaching of the textual tradition as it has been determined by the mind.
Now, these aforementioned factors—beginning with meaning—are difficult for those of dull intellect to fathom and provide no foothold, just as the great ocean is for fish and other creatures.
Therefore, it is profound. Alternatively, "meaning" (attha) refers to cause and fruit; "Dhamma" refers to the cause;

and "teaching" (desanā) refers to designation (paññatti), which is the verbal expression of phenomena (dhamma) according to their nature, or the exposition by way of direct order, reverse order, summary, detailed explanation, and so forth. "Penetration" (paṭivedha) is clear realization (abhisamaya);
it is the awakening to phenomena in accordance with their meaning, to meanings in accordance with the phenomena, and to designations in accordance with the path of designation.
The true nature, characterized as their specific defining mark (*salakkhaṇa*), is that which must be penetrated regarding those various phenomena.

Furthermore, these meanings and so forth are "profound" because they are difficult to fathom and provide no foothold for those of poor wisdom who have not accumulated the equipment of merit—just as the great ocean is for crocodiles. This is because penetration into them is also dependent upon the meaning.
It is said, "It possesses the meaning through its profundity of purpose and its profundity of penetration," because it illuminates the qualities of the meaning.
It is said, "It possesses the phrasing through its profundity of doctrine and its profundity of teaching," because it illuminates the excellence of the phrasing of those teachings of the Dhamma,
since they are dependent upon that phrasing.
Knowledge that has reached the analysis of meanings is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).

Knowledge that has reached the analysis of the analytical knowledges of meaning, phenomena, and language is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*). Because this latter analytical knowledge also has meaning as its object, it is said:

"It is 'with meaning' because it is the object of the analytical knowledges of meaning and perspicuity," for in the absence of the perfection of meaning, those [other qualities] would not exist. "Phenomenon" (*dhamma*) refers to the doctrine (*tanti*). "Language" (*nirutti*) refers to the words of the doctrine.

Having extracted the statement: therein, the knowledges that have reached differentiation are called the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and the analytical knowledge of language (*dhammanirutti-paṭisambhidā*).

Thus he said, "It is 'with phrasing' because it is the objective domain of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and language; for if there were no perfection of phrasing, those [knowledges] would not exist.
Regarding the phrase "inspiring confidence in discerning people," here the word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Because for discerning people who are seeking what is wholesome...

It brings confidence; therefore, it is "possessing meaning" (*sāttha*). That it is "endowed with meaning" is an inference from the fruit to the cause, like [inferring] rain upstream from the swelling of a river.
Its quality of possessing meaning, however, is to be understood through its being perceivable by the wise, and that is to be known from its state of being supremely profound, subtle, and delicate.
For this has been said: "Profound, hard to see," and so forth. It is "pleasing to worldly people" because it possesses the [proper] phonemes (*byañjana*).
Because it inspires confidence in worldly people, it is "with the letter" (*sabyañjana*). For worldly people are satisfied by the excellence of the letter;

here too, there is an inference of the cause from the fruit. Its possession of the letter, moreover, is due to its trustworthiness, which should be understood through its state of being "good in the beginning" and so forth.

Alternatively, because it is to be experienced by the wise, he speaks of its perfection of meaning (*atthasampannatā*) as the basis for wisdom (*paññā*), saying it is "with the meaning" (*sāttha*). From that...
It inspires confidence in those who investigate. "Possessing phrasing" means it possesses phrasing because it is a basis for faith;

therefore, it inspires confidence in worldly people—this is how the meaning should be understood here. "Possessing meaning" means it is endowed with meaning because its intention is unfathomable and boundless;
otherwise, that [meaning] would be absent. "Possessing phrasing" means [it has] clear words.
It is "endowed with phrasing" because of its clarity of expression, since it renders even the most profound meaning easily understood by those to be trained.
All of this should be seen as a classification of the first two meanings; for it has been explained as such in various places.
Likewise, there is no inclusion here of an alternative (vikappa) or a conjunction (samuccaya). "Of that which is to be brought near" means of that which is to be inserted.
Because there is no absence of the meaning of purification when it has not been stated. "By way of being entirely complete" means by way of completeness in all its parts.
"Of that which is to be removed" refers to the phenomena of defilement (*saṃkilesadhamma*).

"By way of practice" means by way of right practice, such as the purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*), for the sake of that [purification]. "By way of proficiency in attainment" means through the penetration of the Truths (*saccapaṭivedha*).

It is "possessing the meaning" (*sāttha*) because of the presence of systematic mastery over realization (*adhigama-veyyattiya*); that is, because it is not empty or purposeless like the *Kapilavatthu* [Sutta] and others, but is endowed with meaning.
"By means of the teaching" (*pariyattiya*) refers to familiarity with the Dhamma as taught.

"Through proficiency in the tradition" (*āgama-byattito*) means because of the presence of systematic mastery of erudition (*bāhusacca*), such that one does not produce confusion, unlike one who merely makes a study of poorly expounded doctrines.
"With the phrasing" (*sabyañjana*): for when there is perfection of phrasing, there is proficiency in the scriptures (*āgama*).

"Endowed with the five aggregates of Dhamma beginning with virtue" (*sīlādipañcadhammakkhandhayutta*): because it is not devoid of the five categories of Dhamma beginning with virtue. "Entirely perfect" (*kevalaparipuṇṇa*): completely full and filled without remainder.
"Free from defilements" (*nirupakkilesa*): because of the absence of defilements such as wrong view and conceit. "For the purpose of crossing over" (*nittharaṇatthāya*):...
For the sake of escape from the suffering of saṃsāra. "Indifference to worldly gain" means not being dependent on any form of support for craving.

Having thus elucidated the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma by way of the Teacher’s first two grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), he now demonstrates it also by way of the latter two grounds of self-confidence: "Because of the absence of perversion regarding the goal..."
Having stated, "It is well-expounded because it has been well explained," he spoke the passage beginning with "Just as... in order to clarify that meaning by way of contrast (*vyatirekamukhena*).

Therein, "it does not undergo perversion" means that because those factors—namely, the factors described as "obstructive"—lack the quality of being obstructive to their own results and so forth, they lack, as an absolute certainty, the status of being causes for rebirth in the woeful states. [This is] because of the absence of the quality of leading to liberation (*niyyānikattābhāvato*).

Because they lack the state of being "not made of that" (*atammayatā*) and because they do not lead out from *saṃsāra*, those things described as leading out—such as certain types of other-worldly activity, the knowledge of another person, and so forth—are indeed the opposite, since they lack the quality of leading out from that [saṃsāra]. "By that" means by way of falling into a perversion of the meaning.
"Those" refers to the followers of other sects (*aññatitthiyā*). "Because of not transcending such a state" refers to the fivefold nature of obstacles, such as obstacles to karma and so forth.
Because the state of being a means of deliverance for the factors of the Noble Path never deviates;
and because it is declared to be the practice conforming to Nibbāna— that is, the correct practice together with its preliminary stages,
which serves as the means for escaping all conditioned formations, in accordance with the Nibbāna that is to be attained and is free from all the conditioned.

The construction [of the compound] is as follows: "Conforming to the practice" (*paṭipadānurūpassa*) means conforming to that kind of practice which, being the means for deliverance from all suffering, cannot be touched by defilements even by the mere act of making it an object of focus.

"Well-laid out" (*supaññattā*) means well and correctly established by way of its state of abandoning wrong view and so forth, consisting of the various factors such as right view, and comprised within the three aggregates beginning with virtue (*sīla*).
It "converges" (*saṃsandati*) because it is purified of the stains of the defilements; it "accords" (*sameti*).

Having thus shown the well-expounded nature of the Path and Nibbāna through their mutual suitability in terms of being the practice and that which is to be practiced, [the text] now says, "And herein, the Noble Path...
and so forth, in order to show the well-expounded nature of each of the three supramundane states individually. Therein, the "two extremes" refers to eternalism and annihilationism.
The two extremes are distinguished as follows: devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires and to self-mortification; lethargy and agitation; and settling and exerting.

"Not approaching" means not having approached, or by reason of not having approached. "With defilements fully stilled" means with defilements thoroughly pacified, and with faults completely abandoned through the abandoning that consists in full subsiding.
"By way of the intrinsic nature of eternalism, etc. means "eternal..."
“Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is the Deathless, the Refuge, and the Shelter,” and so forth, by way of describing the state of eternalism and other views in various suttas. 148.
By the phrase, “It must be seen for oneself by a noble person who has brought about the absence of lust and the other defilements,” it is [taught] by means of the Noble Path.

"Passing away has been realized by me; birth is destroyed; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no more of this state of being"—thus it is to be seen by oneself, not by relying on another. This is "visible here and now" (*sanditṭhika*). Being visible here and now is precisely what is meant by "visible here and now.

By means of that very instrument of reviewing-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), each noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*)—having abandoned the need to go by the faith of others, by the trusting of others, or by being led by another, and having abandoned the state of being made known [by another]—[realizes it]. A praiseworthy view is "visible here and now" (*sanditṭhi*).
Just as with the enlightenment factor, the Noble Path conquers defilements by means of the clear vision associated with itself;

the Noble Fruit does so by means of that same clear vision which has become its own cause; and Nibbāna conquers defilements by means of the clear vision which has become its own object through being made the focal point—this is the construction of the meaning.

The dhamma of the path is so called by way of the clear comprehension through cultivation (*bhāvanābhisamaya*). The dhamma of Nibbāna is so called by way of the clear comprehension through realization (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*).

As for the lower fruit as well, because it serves as a condition for insight and so forth, and because it acts as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the subsequent attainment of the path, it may, in a figurative sense (*pariyāyato*), be said to "ward off the fear of the round [of existence] while being seen."

149. "There is no time for it" means that there is no time to be awaited for its fruition. For while there is a time to be awaited for the giving of the fruit of mundane wholesome kamma—such as "in the next life," "in a subsequent existence," and so forth—there is no such time for this [supramundane kamma].
That is the meaning. Therefore he said, "not after five days," and so on. "Pakaṭṭho" means distant. Because its time for the giving of fruit is distant, it is called "kālika."

It yields fruit at another time. Therefore he said, "in the giving of its own fruit. "Brought" means presented. "This" refers to the word "timeless" (*akālika*). 150. "Instruction" (*vidhi*) means a method;

it refers to the verbal expression of an instruction proceeding in such a manner as "Come, see! "Because of its existence" means because it is apprehended from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*).
"Because of its purity" means because it is completely purified by being free from the stains of the defilements (*kilesa*). Even that which is unpleasant...
"Sometimes, because of a specific purpose, it might need to be shown by way of explaining its true nature; therefore, in order to show that this [other method] is absent, he says:

'by way of explaining its pleasantness. (151) "That which is to be brought near is *opaneya*; since it is precisely that which is to be brought near (*opaneya*) that is intended as the meaning of the term *opanayika*," so it is said.
He said: “It is ‘to be brought near’ (opanayika), thus it is ‘leading on’ (opanayyika). Because bringing near refers to the arising [of the mind] in the mind, he said:

“This applies to the conditioned supramundane state. However, if “bringing near to the mind” is intended in the sense of bringing the state that has become the object into the state of being an object, then it would also apply to the unconditioned:
“It is ‘leading on’ because it deserves to be brought near, which is to say, made into an object.”
“Embracing” (*allīyana*) means touching. The intended meaning is that it leads the noble person (*ariyapuggala*) toward *nibbāna*.

(152) “By the wise” (*viññūhi*) means by those who know; the sense is “by those who have penetrated the Truths. Since they are, without exception, those who understand through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and so forth, he says “by those such as the *ugghaṭitaññū*.
Regarding the term “individually” (*paccattan*), [it is explained] as “in relation to oneself” (*pati attanī*), according to its locative sense.

"The meaning must be grasped," he said; thus he spoke "within oneself, within oneself. It was stated that "it should be understood"; as to how it should be understood, he said "It has been developed by me," and so forth.
Therein, having shown by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) the meaning expressed by the word "personally" (*paccattaṃ*) through the word "by me" (*me*), he further spoke "for not...
and so forth in order to show it by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); this is indeed easy to understand. "By the wise" (*viññūhi*).
Showing that this is an inclusive restriction (*antogadhāvadhāraṇa*), he said, "But this is not within the sphere of fools.
Having thus demonstrated the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma through its excellence in being good in the beginning and so forth— by way of a mutually corresponding teaching—
he now said, "Moreover," etc., showing that each subsequent term is a statement of the reason for each preceding one.

In this context, "visible here and now" (*sandiṭṭhika*) means that because this Dhamma is to be seen by oneself in the manner described, it destroys the defilements through direct vision and is worthy of being demonstrated;
therefore, it is well-expounded, since those qualities are absent in the poorly-expounded teachings of the sectarians (*tīrthika*).
Following this method, the meaning should be understood accordingly for the remaining terms as well.
153. Regarding the passage beginning with "Tasseva," whatever is to be said should be understood according to the method already explained in the *Buddhānussati* (Recollection of the Buddha).
3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Recollection of the Saṅgha (Saṅghānussatikathāvaṇṇanā) 154.

The qualities of the Noble Saṅgha: Because they are far removed (*ārakatta*) from defilements, because they do not proceed in what is not the goal (*anaya*), and because they proceed in what is the goal (*aya*), [the Saṅgha is praised] by the world including the devas...
And because it is worthy of being sought after by the world as a "refuge," that Saṅgha is noble; or else, the Saṅgha of the noble ones is the "Ariya-saṅgha," and [the verse refers to] its qualities.
155. One who has practiced the right way of practice is called "one who has practiced well.

That way of practice of the Noble Path, by making the opposing states subject to non-retrogression and thereby abandoning them, is itself of a nature not to retrogress, due to the absence of any further purpose [to achieve].
And because it is entirely in conformity with Nibbāna, which is to be realized, it is for that very reason non-opposing and in accordance with the Dhamma.
To show that the Noble Saṅgha is called "well-practiced" (suppaṭipanna) because they have practiced that [path], the phrase "well-practiced," and so forth, is stated.
Therein, by the term "the practice of non-retrogression," he shows the straight practice. As for "repeatedly returning":

For when that [wrong practice] exists, there is no straight practice (*ujuppaṭipatti*). By the phrase “the practice in conformity, the practice not contrary,” it indicates the practice according to the method (*ñāyappaṭipatti*), because that [practice] conforms to and is not contrary to Nibbāna, which is what is to be practiced, and because it is done by way of the method.

By the phrase “the practice in accordance with the Dhamma” (*dhammānudhammapaṭipadā*), it indicates the practice of proper conduct (*sāmīcippaṭipatti*), because it demonstrates the state of being suitable.
By this, the first term is an exposition of the manifold elaboration (*papañca*).
This shows that the other three terms [refer to the disciples]. Therefore he said, "But because... and so forth.

Since the accomplishment of what is to be done occurs through practicing according to the instruction, listening that brings about the state of an Ariya is called "attentive listening" (*sakkacca-savana*);
thus it is said, "They listen attentively, therefore they are *sāvakā* (disciples). Consequently, only the Ariyas are [true] disciples in the primary sense of the Teacher.
He shows that they are called "disciples" (sāvakā) because of their commonality in virtue and view—that is, by virtue of their shared state of noble virtue (ariya-sīla) and noble view (ariya-diṭṭhi).
