For the virtue and views of the Noble Ones are indistinguishable from one another, like gold that has been melted down, because they have entered upon the Path.
Therefore, wherever they may be situated, they remain united. Thus he said: "He has attained the state of being a Saṅgha."

It is *uju* (straight) because it has completely cut off evil qualities such as deceit and hypocrisy. For that very reason, it is *avaṅka* (without crookedness) due to the absence of the curvature of a cow’s urine.
It is *akuṭila* (not tortuous) due to the absence of the curvature of the moon’s crescent. It is *ajimha* (not bent) due to the absence of the curvature of a plow’s tip.

Alternatively, it is *uju* by virtue of its being *avaṅka* and so forth. It is *ariya* (noble) in the sense of being utterly pure. It is *ñāya* because, through its state of being unerring (*apaṇṇaka*), one goes toward or reaches Nibbāna; or else, Nibbāna is "known" or penetrated by means of it.

It is the *ñāya* (the method). Because it is suitable for the escape from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*), because it is appropriate, it has acquired the designation and common name of *sāmīci*, *opāyikā*, and *sammāpaṭipatti* (right practice).
By being endowed with that [practice], they are "well-practiced" (*suppaṭipanna*), considering them as "practicing rightly" (*sammā paṭipajjanti*).
For this word *paṭipanna* has a present sense, just as in the phrase "for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry."
"Practicing" refers to the practice of the path and right conduct as previously described regarding the past. By means of both types of general designation—

either through the method of "single remainder" (*ekasesa-naya*), where the group of those taken up as "well-practiced and well-practiced" is called "the one who practices well," or through a collective expression—
the text shows that the term "one who practices well" is used to denote the assembly of those so designated.

Having thus explained the meaning of the other terms by way of defining the meaning of the first term, the words beginning with “Furthermore” (apicā) are now spoken in order to show the unmixed meaning of all four terms.
Therein, “as instructed” (yathānusiṭṭhaṃ) means as instructed by the Teacher; the sense is:
in accordance with the instruction. “The unfailing path of practice” (apaṇṇakapaṭipadaṃ) means the path of practice that does not fail.
The meaning is "the practice of blamelessness. And here, it should be connected thus: "because he has entered upon the unerring practice in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya.
[An objection is raised: "If it were connected with the first word, the second word would not need to be stated;
and if it were connected with the second word, would not the first word likewise not need to be stated? [The reply is: No, for that first...
Because of being looked after. Furthermore, that [practice] is the "unerring path" (apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā) for the disciples;
in order to show that it is a practice according to the instructions, it should be stated as "because of practicing according to the instructions.
Or rather, both are stated because they establish the state of having practiced well in both respects. For indeed, by means of the word *pi* ("also"), he conjoins both.

Because one falls into the two extremes due to the crookedness of the defilements, it is said: “By abandoning that entirely, the right practice—which abandons the crookedness of body and so forth—is the straight practice,” thus: “By the middle way... he is one who has entered upon the straight practice.
“Method” (ñāya) refers to a practice that has reached its proper application, as well as Nibbāna;

for because of the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena, it must indeed be practiced even while disregarding a burning garment or head. Thus it is said: “Method is called Nibbāna. This is stated by way of the act of extinguishing.

And here it should be understood that Nibbāna is what is spoken of; or else, the meaning should be seen as follows: it is called "Ñāya" (the Way) because it is known, penetrated, and realized by means of path-knowledge and so forth.
They are "worthy of respectful service" (*sāmīcikammārahā*) because they deserve respectful acts such as the offering of hospitality performed by others through appreciation of their virtues.

156. Regarding the phrase *yadidam*, since it is a particle (*nipāta*) that includes internal distinctions of gender and number, its meaning is stated according to those distinctions as *yā imāni* (“which are these”).
*Evam* is a particle in the sense of manner; the meaning is “in this manner. By this, the other three pairs are shown;
thus he says, “In this way there are four pairs of persons. *Etam* refers to this [phrase] “persons who are individuals” (*purisapuggalā*).
This is a word stated in the plural number. "Purisā" means men, and "puggalā" means persons; thus, "purisapuggalā" means men who are persons.

In this context, the meaning should be understood as follows: by the term "purisā," the nominative case is grasped, while by the term "puggalā," the accusative case is also grasped through the commonality of the term "sattā" (beings).
Of what kind are the four conditions? They are those that are to be brought and offered, according to the context.

This meaning is clear. Alternatively, the word *dātabbaṃ* (to be given) is a term in the singular; it should be transformed according to the sense of the agent (*sāmivasena*) by referring to the phrase "of the four requisites" (*catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ*).
Otherwise, there might be the designation "offering" (*āhuna*) for just any four requisites whatsoever.
Or, one who is worthy of an offering (*āhuna*) is "one worthy of offerings" (*āhuneyya*). Or, it is an offering even to Sakka and others—that is, that which is being given even by Sakka and others.

Generosity. "Where what is offered bears great fruit": this is the doctrine of those brahmins that when an offering—such as curd and so forth—is made into the *āvahanīya* fire, it yields more exalted fruit than when offered into the *āhuneyya*, *gahapataggi*, or *dakkhiṇeyya* fires.
"Offered" (*huta*) means given. "In another school" (*nikāyantare*) refers to the school of the Sabbatthivādins. "Excluding these sixteen hundred" (*ṭhapetvā te soḷasa satāni*):
the intention is that having set aside those dear and agreeable kinsmen and friends, one does not give to them. This...
"Eso" (this). "And it is seen within the interval between one Buddha" means it is seen when one interval between Buddhas has passed.

By the word "ca" (and), it is shown that sometimes it is seen even after an incalculable number of eons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*) have passed. "Uninterrupted" (*abbokiṇṇa*) means unmixed with opposing factors; this is an adverbial modifier.
The qualities that produce what is dear and agreeable are virtue (*sīla*) and so forth; these are well-established in the Noble Saṅgha.
This is the intended meaning here: relatives and friends, being separated, soon meet again, and their affection and fondness for one another is unstable;
but it is not so with the Noble Saṅgha. Therefore, the Saṅgha alone is worthy of hospitality. "One who does first service" means one who performs the foremost deed.
"In every way" means by means of respect, reverence, esteem, and so forth, as well as by performing the act of giving with diligence toward the object to be given.
And in every respect. This term *pāhavanīya* is called *pāhuneyyo* by way of synonymy.
It is called *dakkhiṇā* because by means of it sentient beings are seen to increase with the intended attainments.

It is worthy of the *dakkhiṇā* because it causes such a state [of increase] to come about; just as something is said to be "purified" through the acquisition of a noble and exceedingly vast wealth, so too is the *dakkhiṇā*.
"By way of having abundant fruit" is what is meant by the statement: "It purifies by producing great fruit.
It is "to be honored with joined palms" (añjalikaraṇīya) because here those seeking merit should perform the añjali-gesture.
Although it is called "unsurpassed" (anuttara) in the Canon, it is "unsurpassed" because there is nothing superior to it.
Showing that there is nothing equal to it, he said, "incomparable" (*asadisa*). It protects (*tāyati*) or guards (*rakkhati*) the seed sown or planted by making it yield great fruit;

or else, it is a "field" (*khettam*) because seeds are scattered (*khipanti*) or sown (*vapati*) therein—referring to fields such as rice paddies—and like a field, it is a "field," namely a "field of merit" (*puññakkhetta*).
The remainder should be understood according to the method explained in the *Buddhānussati* (Recollection of the Buddha).
4. Commentary on the Recollection of Virtue (Sīlānussati-kathāvaṇṇanā) 158.
“O, may my virtues be unbroken! O, may they be flawless!”—in this way, the construction should be applied everywhere.
*Aho vata* is a particle used for expressing esteem. Therefore, he said: “by way of the qualities of being unbroken, etc. This means by way of the attainment of such states as being unbroken.
The meaning is as follows: Even when another’s virtues are recollected, they serve merely as a basis for loving-kindness (*mettā*) by bringing about a state of endearment and mental agreeableness;

they do not constitute an independent meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Therefore, it says, “one’s own virtues should be recollected. The same method applies to generosity (*cāga*) and the rest. “Of whom” refers to those virtues and so forth.
“In successive undertaking” means according to the order of undertaking; “in simultaneous undertaking” means according to the order of enumeration.
The beginning and end of the virtues (sīla) should be understood. "Like a garment with its border cut" refers to the edge of a cloth or a garment with its hem cut;
this is a dissimilar example. The remaining examples are to be understood in the same way. "A garment with its border pierced" means a garment pierced through by penetration.
"Like a cow with a discordant color" is the connection [to the preceding]. They are devoid of blemishes.
Or they are unblemished. Likewise, they are untarnished. The sevenfold bond of sexual intercourse has already been mentioned above in the discussion on virtue (*sīla*).
By the phrase "with anger, enmity, and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes malice, domineering, envy, avarice, guile, deceit, pride, and arrogance.

These very virtues of virtue are characterized by being unbroken and so on. The liberation from the slavery of craving regarding virtue is the bringing about of its state as a necessary condition for the turning away from suffering (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).

For that very reason, the person endowed with them is called "one who is masterful, self-governing, and independent. Therefore it was said: "By means of creating the state of independence, they are 'independent.

Because this [practice] is not clung to by craving or views—such as "by this virtue may I become a god or some other kind of deity, and there may I be permanent, stable, and eternal," or "purity comes through virtue"—it is, among those virtues...
"Fault" (*dosa*) means that which is grasped or defamed by seeing any one of the four failures (*vipatti*).
"Conducive to concentration" (*samādhisaṃvattanika*) refers to those things whose purpose is to lead to concentration.
"Respectful toward the training" (*sikkhāya sagāravo*) means having an especially high regard for the training because of having undertaken it based on the wealth of virtue (*sīladhana*).

He is respectful and deferential. "Conducting himself in conformity" means conducting himself in conformity with those endowed with virtue, or conducting himself in conformity with that very training.
For one who is devoid of reverence for the training is said to conduct himself in non-conformity with it, because of his opposition to it.
Just as he has no flaw in himself toward others, so too he extends a welcome with the gifts of Dhamma and material goods.
Hospitality. Because of his reverence for the training, he is heedful therein.

Since fears such as the fear of self-reproach, the fear of reproach by others, the fear of punishment, and the fear of an unhappy rebirth have been cast far away from him, it is said: "free from the fear of self-reproach and so forth.
The rest is easily understood.
5. Explanation of the Discourse on the Recollection of Generosity (Cāgānussatikathāvaṇṇanā) 160. “By nature” means by one’s own inherent disposition.

“One who is intent upon generosity” means one who is constantly engaged in the relinquishing of things to be given, being inclined toward it, leaning toward it, and devoted to it. “One for whom giving and sharing are constantly practiced” means one in whom the acts of giving and sharing occur perpetually.
By that [term]. Here too, the word “by nature” (*pakatiyā*) should be brought in and connected. That which is given when prepared for another is *dāna* (giving).
That which one shares from what is to be consumed by oneself is *saṃvibhāga* (sharing). “From now on” means starting from this point;
“from today onwards” means beginning with this very day. “I will not eat without having given” is the undertaking of giving (*dānasamādāna*).

"Having done that. "On that day" means on the day of beginning the meditation. "Having grasped the sign therein" means having grasped the sign by way of observing the mode of occurrence of the volition of relinquishment in that act of giving. "By way of the quality of being free from the stain of stinginess and so forth":

that from which the stains and stinginess have departed is "free from the stain of stinginess" (*vigatamalamacchera*), which is generosity (*cāga*); the state of that is "the quality of being free from the stain of stinginess" (*vigatamalamaccheratā*).
By way of the excellence of such qualities, attainments, or benefits.
They follow the Dhamma of the virtuous—that is, they follow, step by step, enter into, or do not deviate from—the lineage of the Dhamma of the noble Bodhisattas.
These are the gains for the donor: longevity, beauty, happiness, strength, eloquence, and so forth.
And such qualities as being beloved have been praised and extolled by the Blessed One. Regarding the phrase "humanity (*manussattaṃ vā*"), the word *vā* has the sense of an unstated alternative;
by it, the inclusion of such factors as the acuity of the faculties, the state of being the owner of one's kamma, and wisdom should be understood.
"By the stain of stinginess (*maccheramalenā*)" means by the stain known as stinginess. Alternatively, "stinginess and stain" is *maccheramalaṃ*.
"By that stinginess and by the stain of greed, etc. is the meaning. "By way of being born" means by way of being produced through their respective kamma.
"Of dark states" refers to evil states that are entirely black, such as greed and so forth. "Because of its absence" means because of its abandonment.

"With a mind from which the stain of stinginess has departed" is an instrumental expression used in the sense of a characteristic (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). "Of a stream-enterer" means of one who dwells in a house.
"While being a stream-enterer": "A dwelling based upon" means a dwelling that must be inhabited by relying [on others];
the meaning is a meditation subject for daily practice. "Having overcome": having overcome the defilements such as lust that arise in others who dwell in the household.
One who gives anything while still being full of longing does not possess "freely-bestowing generosity," but this one is not like that; thus he is called "one of freely-bestowing generosity."
It has been said. "One who gives with confidence" (*vissaṭṭhacāgo*) means one who relinquishes without expectation.
Just as a person who is full of violence toward living beings is called "blood-handed" (*lohitapāṇī*), so too a person who is full of giving is called "pure-handed" (*payatapāṇī*);
showing this, he said, "Always having his hands washed for the sake of giving. In that context, "always" (*sadā*) means constantly or frequently. "Relinquishment" (*pariccāgo*)...
"Relinquishment of the object to be given" is understood from the context. "Whatever object to be given" refers to whatever gift others, who are supplicants, [seek].

"Application to begging" (*yācanayoga*) means being fit to be begged by others; the sense is that one is fit for being asked by others. "Devoted to sacrifice" (*yājena yutto*) means devoted to giving, because of constant relinquishment.
"In both" means delighted and fond of the aforementioned giving and sharing.

161. Just as the development of the recollection of virtue (*sīlānussati*) succeeds for a person of pure virtue who recollects their own virtue by way of its qualities such as being unbroken, so too it is shown that the development succeeds for a person of pure and noble relinquishment (*pariccāga*) who recollects their own relinquishment as being indeed undefiled, by way of its qualities such as being free from the stain of avarice (*macchariya*).
Thus begins the passage: “By way of the quality of being free from the stain of avarice,” and so forth.
What has been said is exactly as stated.
*Bhiyyoso* means "furthermore. *Mattāya* means "of measure" or "of magnitude"; the sense is "by a great measure" or "by an abundant extent.

*Cāgādhimutto* means "intent upon relinquishment," being inclined, leaning, and tending toward it; for that very reason, one whose underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) is characterized by non-greed (*alobha*) [is not attached] to anything whatsoever.
"Unattached in mind": there is a relinquishing toward recipients by way of loving-kindness; thus, this is the practice conforming to and corresponding with loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*).
"Confident": one who is fearless due to his own virtues, not shrinking back from anything, but dwelling having overcome all obstacles. The rest is easily understood.
6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Recollection of Deities (Devatānussati) 162.
“By way of the noble path” means by way of the attainment of the noble path. “Accompanied by” means having arisen properly from that point onward.
For even though the mundane faith and other qualities present in the mental continuum of the noble ones are of such a kind, they are never like those [supramundane qualities] found in the noble ones.
The faith and other qualities of worldlings (*puthujjana*). They shine, thus they are "gods" (*devā*). Those for whom there are four great kings are the Four Great Kings;
those very ones are the Cātumahārājikās. Thirty-three [gods] together with those who performed meritorious deeds were reborn there;

thus, the place associated with them is called Tāvatiṃsa, and the gods dwelling there are also called Tāvatiṃsas because of that association. They have departed from suffering, thus they are "departed" (*yātā*).
The Yāmas. They are called Tusita because they have gone to (itā) the joy (pīti) of contentment. They are called Nimmānarati because they delight (rati) in the creation (nimmāne) of enjoyments.
They are called Paranimmitavasavatti because they exercise mastery (vasaṃ vattenti) over enjoyments created by others. The "Brahmakāya" is the body or assembly of Brahmas;
they are called Brahmakāyika because they exist there due to being included within that [assembly]. "Beyond that" means beyond those Brahmakāyikas.
He speaks with reference to those above, such as the Parittābha deities and others. "Having placed the deities in the position of witnesses" means:

"Those deities who, possessing such faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom as they came by way of the path, having passed away from here, were reborn there; may I too possess such faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom."
One should recollect one's own qualities, such as faith and so forth, as if placing a deity in the position of a witness and then invoking that witness, thinking, "And this is found.
If it is asked, "If both sets of qualities are to be recollected thus according to the Sutta, how is that?"—bearing this inquiry in mind, he says, "But in the Sutta...
and so on. Therein, although it was stated as "both one's own and those deities," [the two are mentioned].

Although it is stated in the Sutta as if it were of equal weight, nevertheless, that statement beginning with “the faith and virtue of the deities” should be connected by bringing forward the subsequent word “stated” (*vuttaṃ*) to mean that it “should be placed in the position of a witness.
As for the purpose of placing it in the position of a witness, he says: “for the purpose of demonstrating that the deities possess qualities identical to one’s own faith and so forth.”
"It should be understood. But why is the meaning taken in this way, rather than taking the meaning according to the literal expression in the Sutta?
To this he says: "For in the Aṭṭhakathā," and so forth. 163.
"Therefore" means because, in the Aṭṭhakathā, having placed the deities in the position of witnesses, [the Buddha] recalled his own virtues.

It was stated [by the commentator] with firm resolve; for just as in the case of the recollections of virtue (*sīla*) and generosity (*cāga*), here too it is appropriate that the recollection of one’s own qualities is the sign for the arising of jhāna.

Therefore: "In the prior stage" means at the commencement of the development (*bhāvanā*). "In the subsequent stage" means at the time of development, in such a way that access-concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) succeeds for one who is developing it.
If only one's own qualities are to be recollected here, how is this the "recollection of deities" (*devatānussati*)?
He said: "By way of recollecting the qualities of the deities, such as their faith and other virtues.

This shows that this meditation is called "recollection of deities" (devatānussati) because it is a mental construction based on similarity to them, and not because it is a direct recollection of the deities themselves or of their qualities.
Alternatively, the designation "recollection of deities" is applied to this practice by taking as its basis the recollection of the deities' qualities that occurred during the preliminary stage.
[This] should be understood. For he will say: "In the preliminary stage, by way of the mind proceeding with reference to a deity. The rest is indeed easy to understand.
Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discussion (Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā) 164.
"Of these" means of these six recollections, beginning with the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*). "In the detailed teaching" means...
In this teaching that proceeds by way of detailed exposition, he speaks with reference to the Mahānāma Sutta.

"The meaning of 'Bhagavā' and so forth" refers to the meaning of the words beginning with "Bhagavā. Or, "knowledge of the meaning" (*atthaveda*) refers to the satisfaction (*tuṭṭhi*) that arises dependent upon cause and fruit;
"knowledge of the Dhamma" (*dhammaveda*) refers to the satisfaction that arises dependent upon the cause. For one who recollects, "He is an Arahant because of being far removed (*ārakattā*),"...

For that which consists in the Blessed One’s being remote from defilements (*kilesa*) is the cause (*hetu*). And here, the cause intended is one that makes known (*ñāpaka*), not one that produces (*kāraka*) or one that brings about (*sampāpaka*).

The state of worthiness (*arahattattha*) understood by means of that [cause] is the fruit (*phala*). By this method, the distinction between cause and fruit should be understood in the remaining phrases as well.
In the case of the recollections of the Dhamma (*dhammānussati*) and so forth, it is likewise stated: "because of its excellence in the beginning, middle, and end," and so on.
Furthermore, because that is the right practice (*sammāpaṭipadā*), a statement of the reason has indeed been made here and there by such phrases as "because of this.

"Connected with the Dhamma" (*dhammūpasaṃhita*) means endowed with the qualities consisting of the aforementioned causes and the fruits of those causes. "Qualities" (*guṇe*) refers to one's own qualities.
165. "They succeed only for noble disciples" (*ariyasāvakānaṃ eva ijjhanti*) is an emphasis on the latter term, meaning they succeed exclusively for noble disciples.
The mention of "should be seen" and "determination" is for the purpose of showing that these [attainments] are easily accomplished. Therefore he said, "For them," and so forth.
They do not succeed in every respect for ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*). For he will say later, "Even though this is so," and so forth.
If this is so, why is the term "noble disciple" (*ariyasāvaka*) used in many suttas such as the Mahānāma-sutta? Because of them...
"By dwelling frequently," say the teachers.
"Departed" (*nikkhanta*) means gone out, emerged, or escaped. "Released" (*mutta*) means let go. "Risen above" (*vuṭṭhita*) means departed.
All this is said with reference specifically to suppression (*vikkhambhana*). "From craving" (*gedhamhā*) means from an impediment. "This too" refers to the recollection of the Buddha.
He says that access concentration has been attained. "Making it the object" means making it a condition, making it the foundation; such is the meaning.
"They become purified" means they reach ultimate purification.

"In the confinement" refers to the narrowness and oppression of the household life due to the defilements of craving and so forth. "The attainment of space" refers to the supramundane state (*lokuttara-dhamma*).
The "occasion for what is to be attained" refers to the state that must be realized through attainment. The "recollections" (*anussati*) themselves are the "bases of recollection" (*anussatiṭṭhāna*).

"Purifying phenomena" (*visuddhidhamma*) means those whose intrinsic nature is to be purified, or those capable of being purified. "By way of the state of being a phenomenon capable of ultimate purification" means by way of the capacity for ultimate purification, which is *nibbāna*.
"By means of application" (*upakkama*) means by means of the practice (*payoga*). "Cleansing" (*pariyodapana*) means purification (*visodhana*).
"Even though this is so": although in many suttas such as the Mahānāma Sutta, the six recollections are taught specifically with reference to the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*).
"By whose power": by the strength of that clarity of mind (*cittappasāda*). "Having obtained joy":
having generated joy directed toward the Buddha by way of oral tradition (*anussava*).
The commentary on the exposition of the recollections (cha-anussati) is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the seventh chapter.
8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Recollection Meditation Subjects (anussati-kammaṭṭhāna).
Commentary on the Discourse on Mindfulness of Death (Maraṇassatikathāvaṇṇanā) 167.
“It” refers to the recollection of the deities (*devatānussati*). For that is proximate and immediate, as it is taught last among the six recollections.
It is stated [to follow] immediately because it was taught right after that. Mindfulness of death is *maraṇassati*.
In order to show death first, it was said: “Therein, death,” and so forth.

Granted that here the dissolution of the aggregates—since it is stated that “aging-and-death is comprised by two aggregates”—should be called death as the destruction of the aggregates at the moment of passing away;
nevertheless, it presents itself specifically to those practicing meditation (kammaṭṭhānika) by way of the destruction of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya).
“It is the cutting off of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya),” it is said. For this very reason, it is stated in the Niddesa: “The casting off of the body is the cutting off of the life-faculty.

In that context, “of what is comprised within a single existence” means of what is delimited by a single birth. “Cutting off of the life-faculty” is the severance of the continuity of the life-faculty, its disappearance due to the exhaustion of the lifespan and so forth. This is “death by total eradication” (samucchedamaraṇa).
Death as the total annihilation of the continuum of an Arahant;
death as the momentary dissolution of conditioned phenomena, which is reckoned as the cessation of the moment of occurrence delimited by arising and passing away;
and momentary death, which is the death occurring at that very moment within the aforementioned momentary existence.

The conventional designation "tree" and so forth is based upon the continuity of the aggregates; even while that continuity is not yet severed, the usage of the term "dead" in dependence upon the disappearance of greenness and such is "conventional death.

That is not what is intended here. The intention is that this conventional death—whether as total eradication (*samuccheda*) or momentary (*khaṇika*)—is not intended here in the recollection of death (*maraṇānussati*), because it is not common, because it does not present itself [to the mind], and because it is not a basis for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
[It is] intended as the object of mindfulness. Death at the time when life-span and the other [factors] are exhausted is "death at the proper time" (*kālamaraṇa*).

Death when those [factors] have not yet been exhausted is "untimely death" (*akālamaraṇa*). The statement, "Death at the proper time occurs through the exhaustion of merit," is said with reference to a fortunate existence (*sampattibhava*) according to its specific context;
however, with reference to an unfortunate existence (*vipattibhava*), it should be stated that it occurs "through the exhaustion of demerit."
"By the excellence of the conditions that produce the continuity of life" means by the excellence of the conditions such as nutriment, which cause the stream of life to proceed.

"Because the ripening result has been given" means because the ripening result to be bestowed in accordance with its own fruit has already been bestowed. "Due to the absence of excellence in realm, time, nutriment, and so forth" refers to the absence of excellence in realm, such as that of the devas;
excellence in time, such as that of those in the first aeon; and [excellence in place], such as Uttarakuru and so forth.
And by the absence of the perfection of food. By the word "etc. (ādi), temperature, semen, blood, and so forth are included.
Regarding the phrase "like people of the present day," the word "like" (viya) is placed in an inappropriate position;

the construction is: "by way of the exhaustion of a lifespan of only about a hundred years for people of the present day. For in this way, the inclusion of even the maximum lifespan in the future is accomplished.
In the past, however, due to the perfection of the time, food, and other conditions—just as with the perfection of one’s destiny—one’s lifespan was even measured in many thousands of years.
It should be understood that this distinction is stated with reference to the present intermediate aeon (*antarakappa*).
Regarding the phrase "Kalābu-rāja and others," the word "others" (*ādi*) should be understood as including Nanda the Yakṣa, Nanda the Brahmin youth, and so forth. That...

"All" refers to every kind of death that has been described as "timely death and untimely death," which is further divided into "death through the exhaustion of merit, death through the exhaustion of the life-span, death through the exhaustion of both, and death by violence.
"By way of method" means by means of a skillful means (*upāya*). "Attention" (*manasikāra*) means attention having death as its object. By whatever method this attention [is applied]...
This [practice] should be carried out; in order to show it by way of its opposite, the text says, "for one who carries it out unmethodically," and so forth.
Therein, "carrying it out unmethodically" means recollecting death without having established mindfulness, a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), and knowledge through improper means.
All of this—namely, the arising of sorrow and joy, the non-arising of spiritual urgency, and the state of agitation—is...

And their arising occurs respectively for one who dwells in mindfulness, spiritual urgency, and knowledge. For one who remembers the words of the wise, "Death is the absolute certainty for the born," and thereby becomes filled with spiritual urgency and possesses clear comprehension, there is no room at all for sorrow and the like caused by the death of loved ones and so forth.
Therefore, because [these states arise] for one who applies improper attention...

These are the faults; therefore [it is said]. "In this and that" means in the forest, the cemetery, and so forth. "Beings who have been killed or died" refers to beings killed by thieves and others, and those who have died naturally.
"Those who have previously seen prosperity" means those for whom prosperity has been seen before;
[the phrase] "of those who have previously seen prosperity. "Having applied" means having established [the mind]. "Of some" refers to one of keen faculties and superior knowledge.
169. "From its standing as an executioner" means because it stands present at every moment like an executioner, being ever near.
"From the failure of success" means because the success of life fails just as the successes of health and so forth fail.
"From the bringing [of death] upon oneself" means by showing the death of others, one brings death upon oneself. "From the body’s being shared with many" refers to the physical frame...
Because it is common to many; because of the weakness of the life-force, that is, because of the frailty of life; because of signlessness, that is, because death lacks any fixed sign;
because of the limitation of duration, that is, because time is delimited; and because of the brevity of the moment, that is, because the moment of life is short-lived.
Regarding the phrase "because it presents itself like an executioner" (*vadhakapaccupaṭṭhānato*), he indicates that the word *viya* (like) is here expressed by elision (*luttaniddiṭṭho*).
Having stated, "Because it presents itself like an executioner," he says "For just as... and so forth, in order to explain that very meaning.

In that context, "carrying out" (*cārayamāno*) means summoning [the victim] while making the gesture of striking. "Presented" (*paccupaṭṭhito*) means having approached and standing right nearby. [This refers to] aging and death (*jarāmaraṇaṃ*).

They are born having already taken [the burden], for just as a mushroom cluster emerging from the ground is never free from soil, so too beings being born are never free from aging and death; this is the extent of the simile.
While a mushroom cluster might perhaps at some time or place be free from soil, beings, however, are by no means free from aging and death.

Having first shown momentary death by way of a simile with the words "they do not exist," the passage beginning with "for thus" (*tathā hi*) was stated in order to show the kind of death intended here.
Alternatively, it was said with reference to the following objection: "If these beings are born only after having already taken up aging and death, then they must die immediately upon being born.
[The phrase] "because of inevitable death" (*avassaṃ maraṇato*) means because death is unavoidable.

Or, because death is inevitably present. "Mountain-born" means come from a mountain. "Carrying away what is carried" means having the habit of excessively sweeping away grass, leaves, and so forth that have fallen into its current.
"It flows indeed" means it flows; "it moves indeed" means it continues by way of its current and does not stand still.
“Yamekarattiṃ” means on which single night; it should be understood as the accusative case used in the sense of the locative, or as expressing immediate connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
“Paṭhamaṃ” means at the very first moment, at the instant of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). “Gabbhe” means in the mother’s womb. “Māṇavo” refers to a sentient being (*satta*).
The mention of “night” is because, for the most part, beings take rebirth-linking during the night. “Abbhuṭṭhito” means one from whom the clouds have risen (i.e., one who has emerged).
The intention is that he has arisen as if facing death, or by way of being directed toward it. "He goes" means that the youth goes;
from the very first moment, he simply proceeds. "Going thus, he does not turn back" means that while going in this manner, he does not turn back even for a single moment;
rather, he approaches nothing other than death itself.
"Kunnadīnaṃ" refers to small streams falling from mountains. "Pāto āporasānugatabandhānaṃ" means that because the binding fibers had become moist and loosened during the night—
having been permeated internally by the moisture of the day due to the sun's heat on the previous day—
their binding was followed by the presence of water (āporasa) at dawn.
"Passing away" means they transcend [it]. "Is obstructed" means it ceases. "Water itself" is *odakaṃ*, or else it is a flood of water (*udakoghaṃ*).
Because days and nights pass away, therefore life is obstructed. Because life is obstructed, therefore the lifespan of mortals is exhausted.
"From falling" means from the danger of falling for those who stand on a tree while performing work.
[This refers to those] desiring to employ [them], or those who have already entered below. "The sign of rising" (*uggamananimitta*) means with respect to the act of rising.
The intention is: "Mother, do not prevent me from going forth.

To show that while some enemy in the guise of a friend might not strike even when living together with one in search of a vulnerability, this one strikes with absolute certainty, it was said: "Because he came along at birth" (*sahajātiyā āgatato*), and further stated: "And because he takes away life" (*jīvitaharaṇato*).

170. *Nanti* means prosperity. *Sukhī* means one who possesses happiness through divine-like enjoyments and sovereignty. *Dehabandhena* means by means of the physical body. *Asoko* refers to King Asoka the Great. *Sokamāgato* means having come to a state where one ought to grieve.
*Ārogyaṃ* and *yobbanānaṃ* (health and youth) are brought forward as examples for the fact that life ends in sickness and old age, and that existence ends in death;

or they are brought forward by way of being conditions [for such states]. *Loko eva lokasannivāso*, just as in the case of the "abodes of beings" (*sattāvāsā*), because it is a place where one must dwell.
Or it refers to the multitude of beings, the inhabitants of the world. "Followed" means pursued, like by an enemy. "Permeated" means entered, like by a gadfly.
"Overwhelmed" means overspread, like by elephants in rut. "Assailed" means struck down, like by spirits.
"Rocky" means made of stone, not made of earth and so forth. "Vast" means great, measuring many yojanas in length and breadth. "The sky..."
"Having struck" (*āhacca*) means having struck against the sky because of its vastness, and having pervaded all directions.

"They would wander about" (*anupariyeyyuṃ*) means they would move along. "Crushing" (*nippothenta*) means making that which has been struck by them into powder and fragments. "Overpowering" (*adhivattanti*) means surpassing.
[This refers to] being esteemed among the khattiyas and others as superior in lineage, beauty, virtue, learning, or in faith and so forth.
She avoids no one at all. Thinking, "He is inferior because of those very [qualities]," she does not avoid anyone among the *suddas* and other castes;
rather, she crushes and tramples everything. To show that methods such as sticks and the like are simply out of place there, it is said:
"In that place, there is no ground for elephants," and so forth. In that context, "by means of a battle of spells" (*mantayuddhena*) refers to that which is prescribed in the *Atharvaveda*.
"By the employment of counsel and battle. "By wealth" means by the giving of wealth. The word *vā* has the sense of an unmentioned alternative;
by it, one includes both [conciliation] and sowing dissension (*bheda*) personally. 171. "Bringing oneself together with others who have died" means: "Those too, indeed, have died."
"And how much more so for one like me?"—this is said because he brings about his own death.

"Greatness of glory" means greatness of retinue and greatness of wealth. "Greatness of merit" means the state of possessing great merit. "Greatness of fortitude" means the greatness of the power of energy.
Yudhiṭṭhila was the son of Dhamma. Cānura was killed by Baladeva after they had engaged in a wrestling match.

"Along with his powers" means together with his own supernormal powers (iddhi), the majesty of which was witnessed in such events as the shaking of the Vejayanta Palace and the taming of Nanda and Upananda; he entered the jaws of Death.
"They do not equal a sixteenth part" means they do not equal even a sixteenth portion of those sixteen. This is what is meant:
having divided the wisdom of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta into sixteen parts, one of those parts [is not equal to all the others].
"Except for the Perfectly Enlightened One, the wisdom of other beings does not equal even a single fraction— counted as one part— of what has been obtained by him.
He said, "By the power of knowledge and energy," because the eradication of the entire side of defilement occurs through the method of one who has initiated energy.
For when right view and right effort are accomplished, the Noble Eightfold Path is indeed accomplished.
Being like the horn of a rhinoceros by virtue of their solitary state; having realized the unshakable [Dhamma] by themselves without the voice of another, they are "Self-Become" (sayambhu).
Just as there is no mutual clashing between golden bracelets on one's hand, nor any attachment to the bamboo stalk at any point—[so too is their solitude].
"Having come upon such various signs and causes as these. "Investigating" means examining the processes of occurrence and cessation.

"Great seers" (mahesi) in the sense of seeking the great aggregates of virtue and so forth. "By the mere dwelling in solitary wandering" means by the state of living alone, not by virtue and the like.
"Those for whom the rhinoceros deer's horn is their simile," or "those whose simile is the rhinoceros deer's horn."
They are like the tips of sword-horns.

He whose wondrous and marvelous physical body is variegated by the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—such as well-placed feet—and adorned with the eighty minor characteristics (anuvyañjana), such as copper-colored nails and long nails, is one "whose physical body [is endowed with] the eighty... and so forth.

Because all defilements have been abandoned along with their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), he possesses the jewel-like qualities of the aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth, which are purified in every aspect;
thus, he is one whose "Dhamma-body" (*dhammakāya*) is enriched by these qualities. This is the meaning of "Sabbākāra... dhammakāyo. "At that very moment" (*ṭhānaso*) means at that precise instant.

"Of such great majesty" (*mahānubhāva*) refers to the Buddha’s vast and immeasurable majesty as it is perceived through both the aforementioned perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the perfection of the Dhamma-body. "Not having come under his power" means not having approached [him] by way of submission; this is the intended sense.
"Death is common to this," thus it is "death-common" (*maraṇasāmañña*); the state of that is "death-commonality" (*maraṇasāmaññatā*), by which [it is so called]. 172.
"Of swarms of worms" means of groups of worms, or of those belonging to the species of worms. "Live" means they reach old age. "Passed away" means having gone beyond.
"Following after" means pursuing. "That would be an obstacle for me"—that which has been described as such.
It is not merely the passing away; rather, having obtained this extremely rare opportunity, there might be an obstacle to my attention directed toward the Teacher’s instruction.
"Byāpajjeyya" means it would go to ruin. "Sword-winds" (satthakavātā) are the winds that, like a sword, cut through the limbs and members at the time of death, severing the joints and bonds.

173. *Abalaṃ* means "lacking strength. *Dubbalam* is a synonym for that same thing. For this prefix *du-* has the sense of "absence," as in such cases as "immoral" (*dussīla*) or "unwise" (*duppañña*).
This refers to vitality (*āyu*). It is simply the equal movement of inhalation and exhalation—the entering and exiting back and forth.
When the breath from the nostrils that has gone outside enters within, or when what has entered does not go out, [that is it].
It is stated as if there were only one entry and exit; this should be understood by way of the commonality of being the air of the nose.
Due to its intensity, it is designated by its extreme proximity and so forth. For the absence of that [intensity] is the evenness of the postures (*iriyāpatha*).
The failure of the body overcome by excessive cold should be illustrated by the time of snowfall in countries such as Mahiṃsara. For there, beings [are afflicted] by the cold.

With their bodies shattered, they reach the end of their life-span. The failure resulting from being overwhelmed by excessive heat should be illustrated by the example of a woman who died after stepping on a basket heated by the sun in a desert wilderness, as well as the upper garment placed thereon and her child.
The even state of the great elements is the absence of agitation. [This occurs] through the non-agitation of the earth element and the others.
The transformation of the body will be discussed later in the section on the meditation subject of the elements (*dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna*).
"At the proper time" means at the time suitable for eating, that is, when one is overcome by hunger. 174.
"Due to lack of definition" means due to the absence of a definition by way of time and so forth. And here, "definition" means delimitation.
It is intended [here] as a determination by way of non-confusion and as a definitive conclusion; thus he says, "due to the absence of delimitation.
"Na nāyare" means they are not known.

Regarding the phrase "from this point onward" (*ito paraṃ*), here "onward" (*paraṃ*) means another time, that is, a subsequent time. By this, the inclusion of even the most recent time is established.
[It] exists. Here, by "supreme" (*paramā*), it is intended that [it lasts] for only a short time (*orakāla*).

Beyond that, because there is no further life for sentient beings, one cannot say "due to the absence of a fixed duration" (*vavatthānābhāvato*). In the cases of "the *abbuda* stage," "the *pesi* stage," and so forth, the word "time" (*kāla*) should be applied individually as "at the time of the *abbuda*" and "at the time of the *pesi*.
Here, "time" (*kālo*) refers to periods such as the morning (*pubbaṇha*) and so on. Therefore, he said: "Even in the morning..."
"‘Hī’ and so forth. The connection is: ‘one must fall right here with this very body. ‘In many ways’ means: those born in a city [fall] in a village;
those born in a village [fall] in a city; those born in a forest [fall] in a district; those born in a district [fall] in a forest, and so on—in these various ways.
‘Having passed away from here’ means having passed away from this state of existence. ‘Here’ means in this state of existence. ‘Like an ox yoked to a machine’: as for example—"
Just as a draft ox does not overstep the cart to which it is yoked, so too the world [does not exceed] the five destinies; this is the extent of the simile.
(175) "Or only a little more" means that living for only a short time—such as ten or twenty years beyond a hundred years—without reaching a second century, is what is meant by "living little.
"One who must go" refers to the *gandhabba* in the sense of its arising [in the womb].
“Samparāya” means the world beyond.

“Hīḷeyya” means he would despise or fail to honor it. “Taṃ” refers to life. “Suporiso” means a good person, one possessed of wisdom. “Careyya” means he should practice good conduct. Thus he said: “As if with his head on fire. By means of the seven similes—
“Just as, brahmin, a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass quickly vanishes when the sun rises;
it does not last long. Or a bubble on water. Or a line drawn with a stick on water. Or a mountain stream that flows far, swift-moving, carrying away all that it meets.
Or as a strong man might gather a lump of spittle on the tip of his tongue and spit it out without difficulty.”
A strip of meat thrown into an iron cauldron heated all day long vanishes instantly;
it does not remain for long. A cow condemned to death, being led to the slaughterhouse, is at every step she lifts her foot close to slaughter, close to death.
Even so, brahmin, the life of humans is short and comparable to the cow’s life at the slaughterhouse.
"This life is light, full of suffering, and full of despair; this must be understood through wisdom.
What is wholesome must be done, the holy life must be lived, for there is no escaping death for one who is born.
Thus it is adorned by these seven similes thus brought forward.
"Night and day" means one night and day. "The Blessed One’s teaching" refers to the Teacher’s instruction which brings about the penetration of the Noble Path.
"Much indeed would have been done by me" means that much indeed for my own benefit—the duty of one who has gone forth—would have been accomplished by me.
"In that interval" means at that moment, for that duration of time. "Even a single alms-meal" means for even a single day.
Almsfood sufficient for maintenance. "Slowly" means sluggishly or after a long time. "Untrustworthy" means not to be relied upon. 176.
The conventional designation "living beings" exists only as long as the mind persists; moreover, the moment of the mind is exceedingly brief due to its state of rapid transformation.
As the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single other thing that undergoes such rapid transformation."

"Such is this mind. Therefore, showing that the life of beings is swift and brief because it lasts for only a single moment of consciousness (cittakkhaṇa), he said "from the ultimate standpoint" (paramatthato) and so forth.

Therein, by the phrase "from the ultimate standpoint," he indicates that the occurrence of the life of beings—which was stated in such passages as "he who lives long lives for a hundred years"—is according to conventional usage (vohāra), because its object is a continuous succession (pabandha).
He rejects that [position]. By the phrase "too narrow," [he refers to the simile]:
"Bhikkhus, suppose there were four archers of firm strength, well-trained, skilled of hand, and practiced, standing in the four directions.
Then a man might come and say: 'I shall [shoot] these... [who are] well-trained, skilled of hand, and practiced, standing in the four directions.'"
‘I shall take it from the place where it stands, though not firmly fixed in the earth, and bring it here.
And, monks, the speed of that man was swifter than the speed of the moon and the sun;
and, monks, the speed of that man was swifter than the speed of the moon and the sun, and even swifter than the speed of those deities who attend upon the moon and the sun.

“They run ahead; the speed of those deities is such that the life-formations (āyu-saṅkhārā) exhaust even more quickly than that”—thus [the opponent] rejects even what was stated as a protective charm (paritta).

For in that case, even from the collision of the sharp edges of the hooves of the gods who delight in running, as they dash headlong against one another in upward and downward succession, the material life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) is exceedingly fragile.
That moment has been described, yet it is exceedingly more minute than even that; there is no simile for it. For this very reason, it was said:
"Bhikkhus, to such an extent is it difficult to find a simile for how quickly the mind turns.
"The moment of life" means the moment of living. It lasts only as long as the occurrence of a single state of consciousness; by the mere occurrence of a single state of consciousness, beings [exist].
Because, in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), the moment of living is delimited. Now, illustrating that meaning by means of a simile, he said, "Just as if," and so forth.
Therein, "occurring" (*pavattamāna*) means existing. "Consisting of a single moment of consciousness" (*ekacittakkhaṇika*) means having the duration of only a single moment of consciousness.

"When that consciousness has just ceased" (*tasmiṃ citte niruddhamatte*): regarding that moment of consciousness which is currently occurring and by virtue of which one is called "living," in that [moment]...
As soon as the cessation and dissolution of the mind have occurred, the being who possessed it is said to be "ceased" or "dead.

To clarify this very point by means of the canonical text (pāḷi), the passage beginning with "as it has been said" was stated. By this, he shows that in all three times, what is called the "life" of beings in the ultimate sense (paramattha) occurs solely by way of moments of consciousness (cittakkhaṇa).
"Life" means the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "Pleasure and pain" means pleasant and painful feelings (*vedanā*).

For equanimity (*upekkhā*) is also included within pleasure and pain, because it consists of the states of the desirable and the undesirable. "The personal existence" (*attabhāva*) refers to the remaining phenomena, excluding life, feeling, and consciousness.
"Entirely" means unmixed with itself, or by way of permanence. "Associated with a single state of consciousness" means with each individual consciousness.
“Together. In the manner already stated, because it lasts for only a single moment of consciousness, the extremely brief moment of life and so forth passes quickly.
Those that have ceased for one who is dying—that is, for a being undergoing death—should be described as “ceased” subsequent to the moment of death (*cuti*).

"Those aggregates which, for one who is staying here"—that is, those aggregates which, while staying and persisting here during the course of existence, have ceased through reaching dissolution—all of them are alike; all of them are exactly the same. How so?

They have "gone," meaning they have departed without re-linking, due to the absence of a subsequent re-linking even if they were to return. For just as the aggregates at the moment of death do not return, [so too do these].
Thus, the aggregates (khandhas) existed even prior to that; therefore, the intended meaning is that the life of sentient beings lasts for only a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*).
One who has not been born by means of what has not arisen—that is, one who has not been born by means of a non-arisen consciousness—is called "unborn" (*ajāta*).
One lives by means of a present, functioning consciousness; such a one is called "living. When consciousness ceases, the world is dead; this refers to the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*).
Just as with all such states of consciousness, when that particular consciousness reaches dissolution,

this world is said to have "died" in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) because that which has ceased does not undergo rebirth. Even so, there exists a conventional designation (*paññatti*) based on the ultimate reality,
which serves as the objective referent for the occurrence of expressions such as "Tissa lives" or "Phussa lives," depending upon that respective consciousness which continues to persist.
This is a designation for a continuity; herein, it is ultimate in the sense of being a conventional reality. For they say: "Name and clan do not decay. (177) "In one way or another":
the mind is the mind that has the meditation subject as its object. "It receives repetition" means it receives the repetition of development;
having abandoned external distraction, by way of unification, it takes death itself as its object.

It occurs. Therefore he said: "Mindfulness, having death as its object, becomes established. Since the dissolution of phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāva) follows the very course of those phenomena possessing intrinsic nature, he said:
"But because the object possesses intrinsic nature. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, aging-and-death is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen," and so forth.
"Because it is provocative" means because it generates a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding the great primary elements.
When death is recollected as something involving great transformation, it brings about an ever-increasing agitation;
thus, the mind of meditation is unable to settle there. If it does not reach absorption because it is a phenomenon characterized by its own nature (sabhāvadhamma), one might ask:
"How then [do] supramundane jhāna and certain formless jhānas [attain absorption]? To this he says: "But supramundane jhāna," and so forth.

"By way of the sequence of the development of purification" means: through the power of the lower purification, there is the development of the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*) which has attained excellence, as well as absorption (*appanā*) characterized by resolution for dissociation—consisting of disenchantment with and dispassion toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
It is by way of such a sequence of the development of purification that supramundane jhāna [arises], wherein there is the disappearance of those evil states that constitute its opposites.

It reaches absorption itself. Therein, there is merely the surmounting of the object; thus, unlike other meditation subjects that take specific intrinsic-nature phenomena (*sabhāvadhamma*) as their objects, there is no need for an effort of the mind toward concentration.
Rather, with a mind already concentrated, only the surmounting of the object needs to be performed through development.
Therefore, even with respect to an intrinsic-nature phenomenon, the formless jhāna attains absorption.
He is constantly heedful because of his abundance of a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*); from that very state, he attains the perception of non-delight in all states of existence.
He abandons attachment to life by seeing that death is inevitable. He censures evil because of his attainment of the perception of impermanence;

for that very reason, he possesses an abundance of non-storing and is free from the stain of stinginess. "In accordance with that" means in accordance with the cultivation of the perception of impermanence.

"Unpracticed in regard to death" means those who have not cultivated the recollection of death (*maraṇānussati*). One dies fearless and undeluded precisely because the perception of death is well-established through that practice.
Commentary on the Discourse on Mindfulness Directed to the Body (Kāyagatāsati): 178.
"The arising of Buddhas" (*buddhuppāda*) refers to the place where Buddhas arise; it is the time of the Buddhas' appearance. Therefore, [the phrase] "except at... [is used].
"Excepting that" means at another time. "Never before occurred" (*apavattapubba*) means it had not happened previously;
for that very reason, it was outside the scope of all other teachers. But did not the Teacher Sunetta and others, as well as various ascetics and wanderers, know the body to be "impure"?
For instance, it was said by the ascetic Sumedha while he was feeling disgust for the body: [The text continues with the verse: *“Asubhānupassī viharanto...”* etc.
“Let me now cast aside this putrid body, filled with various kinds of filth,
and go forth without longing and without desire for it”— and so forth.
Granted that Bodhisattvas and other ascetics and the like know the body to be “impure” (aśubha) by way of its being a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

But they do not know it. Therefore it is said: “Except upon the arising of a Buddha,” and so forth. It leads to spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) because it makes known the true nature of the body as it really is.

It is for the sake of welfare (*atthāya*) in the sense of welfare pertaining to the present life and so on. It is for the sake of security from bondage (*yogakkhemāya*) in the sense of being secure from the four bonds (*yoga*).
It is for the sake of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajaññāya*) in the sense of non-separation from mindfulness in all circumstances and of the sevenfold clear comprehension.
"For the attainment of knowledge and vision" means for the realization of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).

"For the realization of the fruits of true knowledge and liberation" refers to the three true knowledges (*tisso vijjā*), the mind's inclination toward *nibbāna*, and the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*);

it is for the purpose of making these directly manifest. Mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) is so called because it is the cause for attaining the deathless *nibbāna*, and because it is accompanied by a pleasant happiness that resembles the deathless.
It is called "the deathless. "They enjoy" means they make use of it by entering into the meditative absorptions (jhānas).
"Lost" refers to the Victor. "Missed" means failed to be attained. "Attained" means accomplished or brought to fruition.
The connection is: having praised that meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body in many ways throughout various discourses, it is now pointed out.

But where is it demonstrated? In the *Kāyagatāsati Sutta*. For there this teaching comes down, beginning with: "In what way, monks, has the development of mindfulness directed to the body been developed? Herein, this is the summary of the meaning:

Monks, in what manner has the development of mindfulness directed to the body been developed, and in what manner has it been practiced repeatedly so that, through the production of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) on breathing and so forth, it becomes of great fruit?

Is it not because of this that there is great benefit in the successful accomplishment of those various qualities pertaining to true knowledge (*vijjā*), those things to be realized through direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), and such qualities as the endurance of boredom and delight?

Thus ends the section on "Breathing" (*ānāpāna*), which is the limit for the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-kammaṭṭhāna*). This same method applies to the remaining subjects as well.

Although access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) may be achieved by means of the meditation subject of "attention to elements" (*dhātu-manasikāra*), the stage of comprehension (*sammasana-vāra*) is not possible therein.
The section on the attention to elements (*dhātumanasikāra*) is also stated to have been "spoken by way of insight (*vipassanā*). It is said that "these nine charnel ground contemplations...

were spoken" because this teaching has come down in various places as being presented for the purpose of discerning the danger in the body through such qualities as its impurity and impermanence, with the words: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from such a fate."
"Here, among the bloated and so forth" means among these various types of corpses mentioned in the *Sivathika* [Cemetery Sutta].
"By way of mindfulness of breathing" means by way of the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).
Showing that the section on brain matter—which is taken up above as "feces and brain matter"—is included here in the text under the very category of bone-marrow, he says: "Brain matter..."
“Having grasped it by means of the marrow,” he said. “Here” means in this exposition of recollection (*anussati*). The construction is as follows:

mindfulness that has gone to the body, or mindfulness within the body, is “mindfulness directed to the body” (*kāyagatāsati*); by way of this term for mindfulness, this meditation subject consisting of the thirty-two aspects is intended.
(179) “Consisting of the four great elements” means dependent upon the four great elements. “A putrid body” means a body that has become rotten, a body of extreme foul odor.
With reference to the body in its state of standing or walking, or to its parts, it is said that "upward from the soles of the feet" refers to the very lowest part, the soles of the feet.
Regarding the phrase "across, bounded by the skin": one might ask, "Is there not a lack of being bounded by skin in the case of the head-hairs, body-hairs, and nails, as well as the skin itself?
Although this is true, [the definition applies] because of the predominance of what is bounded by skin.
"It is said that the body has skin as its boundary. By this statement, "having skin as its limit" (*tacapariyanto*) means that the skin, which constitutes a portion of the body, is indeed included;

and since the hair and so forth, which are attached to it and whose roots have entered into it, are likewise limited by the skin, it should be understood that the entire collection of the thirty-two aspects is called the body with skin as its limit.
"It exists" (*atthi*) is stated by way of a verbal inversion, or it is a particle (*nipāta*). Therefore, its form remains the same across all three tenses.

Hence he said, "they are found" (*saṃvijjanti*). Showing that even when etymologists explain the word *kāya* as meaning "body," it must be understood here specifically as a collection of impurities, he said, "because it is a heap of impurities" (*asucisañcayato*), and then further demonstrated its derivation through the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*) with the words, "of the contemptible... and so forth.
It has been stated. Therein, "because it is the source" means because it is the place of origin. It was said, "full of various kinds.
To show what those kinds are—by which the various kinds of impurity are said to be present—the text says, "hair of the head, hair of the body," and so forth.
Explaining this meaning, he said: "These thirty-two aspects, beginning with hair."
For the meanings of *ā* and *pa* are one and the same. Thus, regarding "connection":
in all the sections beginning with "In this body there are nails," the connection should be understood through the three phrases beginning with "In this body.
"Parito" means across or on all sides, because the skin is found even at the soles of the feet and the roots of the hair. "Sucibhāvaṃ" means the existence of purity, or simply purity itself.

180. The sevenfold method by which one becomes skilled in learning (*uggaha*) is called "skill in learning," or the knowledge produced thereby. The same method applies to skill in attention (*manasikāra*).

"While reciting" means while actually performing the recitation. It is said that as they were reciting for four months, examining the sections through the very process of recitation, the thirty-two aspects (*dvattiṃsākāra*) became increasingly clear to them in their proper sequence, and the perception of repulsiveness (*paṭikkūlasaññā*) [arose].
They remained; having entered jhāna upon that sign and having developed insight (vipassanā) based on that jhāna, they penetrated the path of seeing.
Therefore it is said: "While reciting, they became stream-enterers.
"Having delimited" means having made a delimitation by way of the fivefold skin and so forth. Because of the predominance of the earth element—

At the end of the section on brain matter, he speaks of the placement of the string. Here, having recited the forward-order meditation (*anuloma-sajjhāya*) for the fivefold group beginning with the kidneys—namely, flesh, sinew, bone, marrow, and kidney;

then kidney, marrow, bone, sinew, and flesh; and finally skin, teeth, nails, body hair, and head hair—the backward-order meditation (*paṭiloma-sajjhāya*) follows in connection with the preceding sections.

Thus it was said. In the *Sammohavinodanī*, the recitation for five or six days is mentioned separately as "five or six days," whereas here it is mentioned as "five or six days" together with the preceding [periods].

This should be understood as being stated by way of showing the beginning and the end. For even in the case of recitation in forward and reverse order, the reverse recitation is the last; or rather, this too should be understood as another variety of recitation.
"Hand-finger-row" refers to a row of fingers.
"Recitation by mind" refers to mental reflection; that which is called "mental muttering" (*mānasa-jappana*), or alternatively, "reciting properly" (*sammā-ajjhāya*) is *sajjhāya*, meaning "thinking.
[The text continues: "By means of prolonged and thorough practice, it becomes proficient..."
For one who applies the mind and attends to the sequence of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna-tanti), from the beginning until the end, it appears continuously without being obstructed anywhere;
and by following that, the meaning of it also becomes more distinct and is perceived.
Thus he said: "Recitation by word... is a condition for penetration. This refers to the penetration of the characteristics (lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha).
Regarding the penetration of the characteristic of foulness:
for some, the analysis of the parts proceeds by way of perceiving color; for some, by way of perceiving shape;
for some, by way of perceiving the distinction of directions; and for some, by way of perceiving the location where they are situated.
Showing that the observation of color and so forth by way of completely delimiting each part is said to bring about skill in learning, he says:
"The color of the head-hairs and so forth must be defined," and so on.
A "part" (bhāga) is a portion (sabhāga); the delimitation by means of such portions is "delimitation by portions" (sabhāgapariccheda), [defined] by the lower, upper, and lateral boundaries.

The meaning is that there is a delimitation by means of the hair, the intervals between the parts, and so forth. "By way of non-mixture" means by way of not being mixed with the intervals between the parts;
for here, "dissimilar" (visabhāga) is intended in the sense of being of a different category (asabhāga), not in the sense of having a contradictory nature.
And this meaning is obtained from the words "hair" and so forth themselves, because a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meanings of other words.
When "hair" (kesā) is mentioned, the meaning understood is "there are no non-hairs" (akesā). But what are those non-hairs? They are body hair (lomā) and so forth;
for they are excluded by the very mention of the equipment [of the head], just as in the case of a jar and other objects.
It is spoken of specifically in terms of repulsiveness, because it is not included under the general category of the analysis of elements (dhātuvibhāga). Therein, separately...

Because the meditation subject of the elements (*dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna*) has been explained, there is the Analysis of Elements (*dhātu-vibhaṅga*), the *Pakkusāti-sutta*, and the text of the Analysis of Elements within the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*.
With reference to that person for whom the hair and so forth appear by way of color, the jhānas having the color-kasina as their object are analyzed among the hair and so forth.
"Having known, it should be declared"—this is the purpose for which it was stated.
To demonstrate that, it was said: “Therein, by way of the elements,” and so forth. “Here” means in this section on the attention to repulsiveness (*paṭikkūlamanasikāra*).
For, having taken the section on the attention to repulsiveness from the *Kāyagatāsati Sutta*, the development of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) is explained here. 181.
“Not skipping over” means that one should not attend [to the parts] by skipping even one; how much less by skipping two or more.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). The connection is as follows: "One who attends to [the object] intermittently does not accomplish cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and does not reach the penetration of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha*).
Regarding "entering and departing," this refers to the paths that are to be practiced and relinquished; one must proceed only after having asked [for instruction].

Because one has not clearly discerned the points that are to be grasped and let go of. "The meditation subject reaches its conclusion" means that from the beginning until the end, there is merely mental attention (*manasikāra*); this is the intended meaning.
However, it remains unmanifest because the aspect of repulsiveness has not been properly discerned. For that very reason, it does not bring about any distinction.
The meditation subject does not reach its conclusion because, even for one who attends to all the sections in their proper sequence, they appear only as manifest objects.

For one who attends to them with an excessive degree of repulsiveness, the meditation subject might reach its conclusion; however, for this person, who attends to them very slowly, there is only the appearance of the object as manifest.
There is none; how could there be a configuration of repulsiveness? Therefore he said: "It is not a condition for the attainment of distinction.

Regarding "external diverse objects": here, even the hair and so forth that would otherwise be apprehended as beautiful and so on—once one has set aside the contemplation of foulness (asubhānupassanā) directed toward hair and so forth by way of the thought "the impure is repulsive"—should be understood as "nothing but external diverse objects."
For visible forms and so forth, by virtue of their diverse nature as blue and so on, are called "diverse objects" (*puthuttārammaṇa*); the meaning is "various objects.
Distraction (*vikkhepa*) is a dissimilar tossing about of the mind, a lack of concentration.
That must be warded off by one who, having made mindfulness well-established, carefully attends to the meditation subject. "Is lost" means it diminishes; "is destroyed" means it perishes.
This designation—beginning with "head-hairs, body-hairs," and so forth—is in accordance with worldly convention. "Designation" (*paññatti*) means a designation based upon eight [physical] phenomena.
"Having transcended" that designation of head-hairs and so forth means having transcended it by means of the meditation on repulsiveness, having stripped it away.
Because that [designation] has been stripped away, when each respective part appears as repulsive, the mind [perceives] it as "repulsive."
It should be set aside. Now, illustrating that meaning by means of a simile, he says, "Just as," and so forth. Herein, this is the correlation of the simile:
the practitioner is like the people; the body parts are like the well; the designation of hair and so forth is like the sign of the palm leaves and so on.

Just as people [use] a well for bathing, drinking, and so forth, so too, in the preliminary stage of the practitioner, [there is the use of the body] by way of the designation "hair, body-hair," and so on.

Mental attention (*manasikāra*). Just as people perform their business at a well without needing a signpost because they pass by it frequently, so too for the practitioner, through the power of mental attention, the mind is established upon the state of repulsiveness itself after transcending the conventional designation (*paññatti*); this is the application to meditation.
In the preliminary stage... [as before] ...it becomes manifest: for one who applies himself to meditation by means of the formula beginning with "head-hairs, body-hairs," etc.
The repulsiveness of the body parts becomes evident in the preliminary stage together with the very designation of the head-hairs and so forth.

"Then" means later, at the time when [the meditation] has entered the path through cultivation. "The mind should be fixed on repulsiveness alone" means that the mind of cultivation should be made to proceed toward the repulsive aspect of the body parts alone.
"Gradual relinquishing" (*anupubbamuñcana*) means relinquishing little by little as it does not remain present; the meaning is that it is relinquished as each [moment] fails to persist.
But how does this non-persistence come about? To this he says, "For a beginner," and so forth.

"It stands having reached only the final limit" means that, according to the sequence of the discourse, the attention directed toward the meditation subject proceeds from the beginning until it reaches its conclusion.

This was said because, for him, mental attention proceeds by merely touching upon each respective section, like a mental recitation, rather than by way of discerning their specific characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
But when he attends to them with thorough investigation by way of discerning their specific characteristics, then some appear clearly while others do not. In that regard:
Showing the method of practice, he said, "Then for him," and so forth. Therein, first the work of attention (*manasikāra*) must be performed.
For how long? Until both [images] have appeared, and even of those two, until one appears more clearly.
"Rising right at the place where the call was made" means, as before, by means of the call made while remaining in a squatting position (*ukkuṭika*), gradually...

The meaning is: having fallen upon all the palm trees and repeatedly rising up, having come from the edge of the palms to the first palm, and then rising up with shouts of joy made here and there at each respective spot.
"Two alms-meals" means alms obtained from two houses.
"From absorption" means that there are absorptions (appanā) in respect of the thirty-two aspects.
In investigating whether these occur individually in each constituent part (koṭṭhāsa) or otherwise, he says "from the absorption-constituents" (appanā-koṭṭhāsato), meaning from each constituent part.
Therefore he says, "In the hair, etc. and so forth.
*Adhicittaṃ* means the mind of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
*Anuyuttena* means by one who is devotedly engaged; the meaning is "by one who is cultivating it. *Kālena kālaṃ* means from time to time.

The *samādhinimitta* is concentration itself—the mode of being concentrated that has been clearly characterized. *Manasikātabbaṃ* means it should be attended to in the mind; it should be brought forth.

The meaning is as follows: "The object" (*ārammaṇa*) refers to the cause of concentration or the sign of concentration; the meaning is that it should be brought to mind (*āvajjitabba*). The same method applies to the sign of exertion (*paggaha-nimitta*) and the sign of equanimity (*upekkhā-nimitta*).

The phrase "there is a possibility" (*ṭhānam atthi*) is an elliptical expression. The meaning is: "There is a possibility—that is, a cause—for that cultivation of the mind to lead to indolence. Or else, [it means] that the mind which is attending to that [object] might lead to indolence.
"Would lead to [this]" means there is a possibility or a reason for this; such is the meaning. "Supple" means made pliant by being well-developed;
the meaning is that it has attained mastery. Precisely because of its suppleness, it is "workable," capable of action, and fit for action.
"Luminous" means purified through the removal of defilements; the meaning is "brightly cleansed. And "not fragile" means by way of having attained a state of workability.
Nor is it capable of being employed like gold from a pure mine, which has the nature of not breaking apart. Therefore he said:
"It is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
