"He binds the crucible" means he prepares the furnace. "He smears" means he ignites and kindles it. "And that" refers to that which is reckoned as a variety of jewelry.
It experiences, attains, and accomplishes the purpose or utility for that goldsmith; or, the goldsmith experiences and reaches the purpose of that gold.

Regarding "direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*): it refers to the direct knowledge of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) and so forth, which is to be realized through the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power, such as the experiencing of those very powers.
[It is] of that which is to be realized. One who has direct experience is a witness (*sakkhi*). The state of being capable of being a witness is "witness-capacity" (*sakkhibhabbatā*);
what is meant is "the state of becoming a witness. Or alternatively, one who is both a witness and capable is a "capable witness" (*sakkhibhabbo*).

For he is capable of the various kinds of supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) and so forth, and he is a witness therein; thus he is a "capable witness. His state is "witness-capacity," and he attains that.
"When the appropriate basis exists" means when the respective causes, such as the prior cause, exist.

"The state of coolness" refers to *nibbāna*, or the subsiding of the distress of the defilements. "He restrains" means he restrains the excited mind by way of protecting it from falling into restlessness.
"He exerts" means he exerts the sluggish mind by way of protecting it from falling into indolence.
He exerts. "He gladdens" means he satisfies with wisdom, or inspires, the mind that is proceeding evenly in its course.
Or, when the mind is devoid of zest and does not leap forward into meditation, then, having reflected upon the grounds for spiritual urgency such as birth and so forth, he gladdens and inspires it.
"He looks on with equanimity" refers to when the mind is no longer sluggish.
When it has entered the path of development quite correctly and is free from agitation, then— without performing any function such as exertion,
restraint, or encouragement— the mind becomes one of equanimity, looking on with impartiality like a charioteer when the pair of horses are proceeding evenly.
"Inclined toward the sublime" means being intent upon, leaning toward, and tending toward the sublime and supreme paths and fruits.
"Having well grasped" means having thoroughly mastered by means of learning, etc., the method known as proficiency in learning as previously described.
"Having well defined" means having correctly investigated by way of observation the method known as proficiency in attention.
"Distinction" refers to the distinction in development that occurs later than before. "Again and again" [refers to]...
"Having turned over" means having turned it over repeatedly by means of speech and the mind, thereby bringing the manual of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to a state of proficiency.

"A knotted place" (*gaṇṭhiṭṭhāna*): just as a part of a tree that is difficult to split, or a dense thicket in a forest, is called a "knotted place," so too is that part of the manual of the meditation subject which is difficult to penetrate in meaning and is dense.
And that area is called the "knot-place. Having cut it with the axe of knowledge obtained through thorough inquiry and so forth;
"the sign" refers to the sign of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna-nimitta*), namely the aspect of foulness (*asubhākāra*).

To show that even plucking [hair] is blameless for such a purpose, it is said "having plucked it. "In the place where it was cut" means in the shaven area. It is indeed permissible when one's intention is directed toward renunciation (*nissaraṇajjhāsaya*).

"By way of looking": by way of the predominance of those that have not yet sprouted or those that have already sprouted. Having seen [the skin], the sign should be grasped because the pentad of skins is suitable for seeing;
in the case of the others, the sign should be grasped after hearing and after knowing.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Definition of the Parts.
182. *Addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā* means having the color of a fresh *ariṭṭha* fruit. *Kaṇṇacūḷikā* refers to the upper part of the earlobe.
"Delimited from one another horizontally"—how so? Because two hairs do not exist together [in the same space].
*Āsaya* means support; the meaning is "condition."
184. *Asambhinnakāḷakā*: black hairs that are unmixed with any other color; that is, black hairs not intermingled with others. 185.

Because they resemble leaves, the nails themselves are called "nail-leaves" (*nakhapattāni*). It is said that the nails are "separately defined" because they are mutually delimited across [the fingers], referring to their distinct demarcation. To demonstrate this very point, it is said: "Two nails do not exist together.
186. *Dantapāḷiyā*: by the row of teeth. *Yānakaupatthambhinī*: a supporting pole at the front of a cart. The bone that serves as the support for the teeth is the jaw-bone (*hanukaṭṭhi*).
187. *Saṅkaḍḍhiyamānā* means being gathered together. A *kosakāraka-kosa* is a small bundle or pouch, which is also called a "silk-cotton fruit" (*koseyya-phala*).
A *puṭabandha-upāhana* is a sandal that covers the entire back of the foot.
An *ānisada* is the seat-base. A *tūṇira* is a quiver. A *galakañcuka* is a neck-guard. A *kīṭakulāvaka* is a hut for wild beasts.
Regarding the phrase "in forward and reverse order": here, the descent along the back of the arm starting from the shoulder region is the forward order;
the ascent along the front of the arm starting from the wrist is the reverse order.
"In that same manner" means in the forward and reverse order according to the method described for the right hand. "Even the subtle" refers to [the skin] other than the coarse skin already mentioned.
"Subtle": among the parts such as the inner skin of the mouth, that which is difficult to discern because it is delimited by the outer skin is called "subtle.
For that becomes manifest to one who, in the manner described, sees by opening the skin with knowledge.
Here, since even the flesh belongs to the category of the skin, it is said that "the skin is delimited above by space."
188. *Nisadapota* is a stone statue. *Uddhanakoṭi* is the edge of a hearth made from a lump of clay.

*Tālaguḷapaṭala* refers to the film removed after drying, having smeared the viscous juice of ripe palm fruit onto palm-leaf strips and other materials. *Sukhuma* means finer than the aforementioned flesh.
[This applies] to those who are thin throughout their entire body, as opposed to those with thick flesh on the heels and so forth.
Because it is mostly covered by flesh, it is said: "delimited from side to side by one another. 189.
A net-like covering is a "net-armor" (*jālakañcuka*). By virtue of their distinct, established nature, the sinews are delimited from side to side by one another.
190. Because the teeth have been mentioned separately, it is said: "excluding the thirty-two bones of the teeth. There is one knee-bone (*jaṇṇukaṭṭhi*).
The mention of "one thigh bone" (ekaṃ ūruṭṭhī) includes the word "one" because it is intended to apply to each individual foot.

Thus, regarding the phrase "just three [hundred]," it should be understood that by means of the word "just" (*matta*), the words indicate that the ankle bones and so forth, though not explicitly mentioned here, are also included.
By doing so, this statement—"a collection of more than three hundred and eighty bones"—is fully justified.
"Playing marbles" refers to playing with marbles bound together by a string and struck against one another.

"The bow-staff" refers to the small bows used for play by children. In that context, the phrase "the place where the shin-bone is established" means the place where it enters and remains fixed within the knee-bone;
this is the intended meaning. By that, the place established by the thigh-bone is [the place] of the hip-bone.
That is like a large *puṇṇāga* fruit with its tip cut off.
A furnace produced by a potter is a "potter's furnace. A headband made of lead is a leaden strip placed there after being wrapped around [the head].
The balls inserted into the grooves and placed therein, by which means they spin the thread—that is the *takkamhi*.
“Carving” (*vaṭṭanā*) means the act of carving; a series of carvings is a “carving-series.
“Bamboo-cylinder-sections” refers to pieces of split bamboo stalks cut into circular shapes. An “avalekhana-spatula” is a spatula for scraping sugarcane.
(192) “Delineated by the portion of the kidney” means delineated by a portion bounded by the edge of the kidney. This same principle applies to similar cases that follow.
193. *Yaṃ nissāya* means depending on that blood; even the support of a support is called simply "support.
For the designation of a cause is applied even to the cause of a cause, as in the expression, "The village was burned by thieves.

Alternatively, it is said "depending on which" because within that group of material phenomena (*rūpakalāpa*) where the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) resides, that [base] also remains having become of the same nature as the blood.
194. *Paṇḍukadhātu* means the yellow nature. 195.
*Pariyonahana-maṃsa* means the flesh that covers [the stomach]. 196.

*Udarajivhā-maṃsa* means the flesh shaped like a tongue located on the upper side of the belly. Having said "blue," he stated that what is called blue consists of many elements by saying "the color of the *nigguṇḍī* flower."

197. *Papphāsamaṃsaṃ* (lung-flesh) is the flesh that hangs down exactly where it is located and turns slightly. *Nirasaṃ* means having a low flavor. *Nirojaṃ* means lusterless, or devoid of nutritive essence (*ojā*).

198. *Obhagga* means standing bent over. *Sakkharasudhāvaṇṇaṃ* means having the color of lime made from oyster shells. There is also a reading, *setasakkharasudhāvaṇṇaṃ*, which means having the color of white gravel and the color of lime.
199. The places where the intestines are coiled up and remain are the "intestinal coils" (*antabhogaṭṭhānāni*). That which serves as their binding is...
Showing that it is called *antaguṇa*, he said: “*Antaguṇa* means a binding at the places where the intestines (*anta-bhoga*) are located.

For those performing work such as digging with a spade or using an axe, [it is used] by binding together the intestines so they do not slip out; like what? Like the cords of a machine for the wooden planks of the machine.
To the question, “What is situated there? he said: “A foot-wiper... is situated. And here, the former [term] refers to the binding.
The second [example] should be understood as an illustration of the mode of location (*ṭhānākāra*).

200. "Eaten" (*asita*) refers to boiled rice and so forth that has been consumed. "Drunk" (*pīta*) refers to beverages and so forth that have been swallowed by way of drinking. "Chewed" (*khāyita*) refers to things such as flour, roots, fruits, and snacks that have been masticated. "Tasted" (*sāyita*) refers to things such as mangoes, honey, and molasses that have been relished.

"Wherein" (*yattha*) means in which stomach (*udara*). "That" (*yaṃ*) refers back to the stomach itself. The connection is: "wherein the drinks, food, and so forth, having fallen, remain. "A dog’s vomit" (*suvānavamathu*) is the vomit of a dog. "Distinction" (*viveka*) means separation.

201. "Between the base of the navel and the root of the spinal vertebrae" means, by way of the anterior portion, below the region of the navel; by way of the posterior portion, in the middle of the lower spinal vertebrae.
The intended meaning is that the location is like the hollow of a bamboo tube.
202. "Accumulated" (*samohita*) means piled up. 204. A rotten chicken egg is one that has reached a state of putrefaction. "Uddeka" is the upward-moving wind alone, without bile or other humors.
205. *Ācāma* is sour gruel made from the water used for rinsing rice.

206. Regarding "moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs": here it should be understood that the liver moistens by filling its lower portion, while the others moisten by trickling down little by little over them.
207. A seasonal change is caused by factors such as hot clouds. A cluster of lotus roots (*bhisā*) and the like that has been cut unevenly drips water unevenly.
In the same way, the term "unevenly cut" (*visamacchinna*) is used to show that sweat flows out irregularly from the pores of the hair and other openings of the body— above, below, and across.

(208) "Uneven food" (*visamāhāra*) refers to food that is unsuitable for the state of the body as it exists at that time, such as food that is excessively pungent, too hot, or otherwise discordant with the body's condition.
Alternatively, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, it is stated simply as "dissimilar nutriment" (*visabhāgāhāra*) because the elements occurring at that time are dissimilar. (209) "At the time of bathing":
this is said for the purpose of showing the occurrence of moisture on top of the water. "Having the shape of spreading, wandering drops of moisture":
that is, having the shape of drops of moisture that have spread out and are wandering about. Dissimilarity of temperature (*utu-visabhāga*) is externally originated.
"Dissimilarity of elements" (*dhātu-visabhāga*) means arising from within. "Those locations" (*te padesā*) refers to those locations such as the palm of the hand and so forth. 210.

"Something" (*kiñci*) refers to any one of the nutritive bases (*āhāra-vatthu*), such as the taste of heat and so on. "Of them" (*nesam*) refers to sentient beings. "The heart becomes distressed" (*hadayaṃ āgilāyati*): depending on dissimilar food and so forth, the region of the heart becomes agitated (*vivattati*).

211. "Curd-water" (*dadhi-mutta*) is the liquid that drips from curd. "Having flowed down" (*gaḷitvā*) means having trickled. "Having descended through the opening at the top of the palate" (*tālumatthaka-vivarena otaritvā*): having come from the opening at the top [of the head] and descended by way of the opening at the top of the palate.
212. Like oil for the nave and axle-heads of a cart, it performs the function of lubricating the joints of the bones.
"Creaking" means they make the sound "kaṭa kaṭā"; this is a description of their resonance.
"They suffer" means they become afflicted, having experienced pain.
213. Having burned it down to its roots and foundations, and having let the ashes drain away, what remains is the liquid extract; this is *māsakhāra*.
A cesspool (*candanikā*) is a place for discarding used water, fetal waste, filth, and so forth. A "mouthless jar" (*ravaṇaghaṭa*) is one that naturally has no opening at the front.
To show that which has not even a needle-point's worth of an opening for water to enter, [the text says] "in a mouthless jar."
It has been said. "Āyūhana" means striving. 214.
The passage beginning with "Evañhi" (for thus) is the conclusion of the practice of proficiency in learning as previously described.
Now, having also taken up the practice of proficiency in attention as previously described by way of conclusion, and having brought the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to its culmination—
The passage beginning with “by way of successive order” (*anupubbato*) was commenced in order to demonstrate this.

Therein, “at the conclusion of the surmounting of the designation” means at the end of the development that proceeds by way of surmounting the designation of head-hairs and so forth. “As if it were not before and after” means as if it were all together. In the phrase “head-hairs,” the word “iti” has the sense of “beginning” or the sense of “manner”;
thus the meaning is “in this manner, beginning with these. “Those phenomena” refers to those determined by way of color and so forth.
The constituent parts appear in their repulsive aspect.
"Externally too" means even outside of one's own continuum; that is, in the bodies of other continua. "He applies attention" means he directs his attention toward the aforementioned repulsiveness.
"As this is, so is that. Thus it is with all the constituent parts.
"When they have become manifest" means that, just as in one's own body, so too in the bodies of others, all parts beginning with head-hairs appear clearly through their repulsive nature;
this is the meaning. Herein, this specific excellence of the meditator’s development is shown to be similar to the expansion of the kasiṇas.
By the word "etc. in the phrase "gradual relinquishing, etc.," the application of balanced energy as elucidated by the method of the Suttas is included.
When one repeatedly applies attention according to the method described— directing the mind frequently toward the parts of one’s own body,
such as the head-hairs and so forth, thinking “repulsive, repulsive”— then the faculties beginning with faith, having attained serenity, become clear and active. At that time,
through the distancing of states such as lack of faith, [the practitioner] possesses the seven true qualities (saddhamma) which have attained an especially high degree of strength.
Having obtained support, the jhāna factors such as applied thought (vitakka) and the rest become more prominent and manifest.

Because they are the direct opposites of those factors, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), along with the evil states associated with them, are suppressed. Through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), the mind becomes concentrated;
by cultivating, developing, and repeatedly practicing that very sign, one attains absorption (appanā).
Therefore it was said: “Absorption (appanā) arises in due sequence. “In all aspects” means in five ways, by way of color and so forth. “That” refers to absorption.

But if this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is accomplished through the first jhāna, like the meditation subjects consisting of the unperceivable impurities, then why is it called “mindfulness directed to the body” (kāyagatāsati)?
To answer this, he says: “Thus, by way of the first jhāna,” and so forth. Regarding the various colors, shapes, and so on:
He said, "Because it succeeds through the power of mindfulness," because the function of mindfulness as it occurs regarding the thirty-two parts is preeminent here.
It endures and overcomes (*sahati abhibhavati*) aversion toward secluded lodgings and superior wholesome states, as well as attachment to the strands of sensual pleasure;

thus it is "enduring both aversion and attachment" (*aratiratisaha*), since dissatisfaction has been abandoned by reflecting on the true nature of the body. Likewise, by means of the cultivation of the parts...
Because self-attachment has been completely exhausted, he endures fear and terror, and he is by nature one who tolerates cold and other such conditions.
For it is through self-attachment that a person experiences fear and terror, as well as the inability to tolerate suffering.
However, for one devoted to this meditation on the parts of the body, there is not only the first jhāna, but there is also higher penetration.
In order to show that [the object] exists, the words beginning with "of the head-hairs, etc. were spoken.

Regarding the commentary on the discourse on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati): the connection is that the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing was thus praised and then explained. Therein—

Since the meaning of the section of questions beginning with "How is it developed? has been elucidated, the meaning of the section of praises is also necessarily elucidated because there is no difference between them;
therefore, skipping that [section], he begins with "And how is it developed? and so forth.
For therein, the absence of praise from this point onward and the statement "This too, moreover" constitute the distinction. Among those two, in order to show the absence of praise:
It is said, "Having thus praised. And the purpose of that praise there was to inspire enthusiasm by generating delight.
For having heard that, the monks—thinking, "The Blessed One praises this concentration in many ways;
indeed, this concentration is peaceful, sublime, refreshing, a blissful dwelling, and it causes evil states to vanish on the spot"—developed a sense of delight.
Having become inspired, they think that one should diligently apply oneself to and practice [this].

Regarding the phrase "This too," the Blessed One—by the power of his teaching—described his own realization of concentration (*samādhi*), which had become manifest to him, saying: "Not only those [meditations] taught by me as the bathing-ghats for entering the great lake of Nibbāna, such as the kasiṇa-jhānas and the foulness-jhānas, but this too."
The meaning should be understood through the connection [of the words] as follows: "He spoke thus by way of summary, making it near and evident even to those monks.
"Consisting of sixteen bases" means sixteen points by way of four tetrads within the four contemplations (*anupassanā*).

"Complete in all aspects" refers to the meaning of the word, the summarized meaning, the simile, the objection, the resolution, the purpose, and so forth, according to the text of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna-pāḷi*).
"Complete in all aspects" means the complete and detailed exposition of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "How?
is a phrase that clarifies the manner of the question; and here, the questioning occurs because there is no other possibility than the desire to explain.
And that [desire] functions by way of touching upon all the specific modes that have been introduced in the subsequent teaching.
Showing this meaning, he said: “How... [etc. ...the inquiry out of a desire to explain.
Here too, the phrase “concentration through mindfulness of breathing” (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*) should be brought forward and connected.

In that context, “how” is an inquiry out of a desire to explain in detail, in various ways, the cultivation of concentration through mindfulness of breathing. “Concentration through mindfulness of breathing has been cultivated” is the demonstration of the state as it was thus asked about.
The phrase "the same method applies" (eseva nayo) extends this point by way of analogy.

Furthermore, to show that his states of peace and so forth are also included simply by mentioning those [qualities] which are accomplished through the frequent cultivation of meditation, it is said: "How does it, when frequently cultivated...? ...it becomes tranquil;
here too, the same method applies."

Furthermore, Udāyi, in such passages as, “I have proclaimed to my disciples the way of practice, by practicing which my disciples develop the four foundations of mindfulness,” development (*bhāvanā*) is said in the sense of producing and increasing.
Therefore, showing the meaning according to both of these, he said: “‘Developed’ means produced or increased. In this context, *bhāva* refers to existence (*vijjamānatā*).
"Developed as 'gone from here'" means that it has been produced and merely acquired. "Arisen," however, means that it has gained practice;
"developed" means it has been brought to a state of proficiency; "increased" is the meaning.

"By mindfulness that grasps inhalation and exhalation" means by mindfulness that discerns and grasps the inhalations and exhalations along with their specific qualities such as long and short, which occurs taking those [breaths] as its object and serving as its condition.

This is the meaning. For in the first sense, the state of concentration being a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and so forth for mindfulness is stated because of the mention of its association (*sampayutta*);

but in the second sense, it is also its state as a decisive support (*upanissaya*). For mindfulness accompanied by access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) is a decisive support for absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*).
"Well-practiced" means practiced extensively; by this, he expresses the attainment of mastery over the stages beginning with adverting (*āvajjana*).
For that which has been brought to mastery occurs again and again because it can be entered at any desired moment;

therefore it is said, "repeatedly performed. Just as in such passages as "Right here, monks, is the ascetic" and "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures," the word *eva* (only/just) stated in the first clause is understood to apply to the second and subsequent clauses as well, so it is here too.

He said: "The restriction (niyama) is to be understood by means of the word 'only' (eva) in both places. In order to show the benefit obtained through the restriction of both terms, he stated "For this... and so forth.

"The meditation subject of the foul" (asubhakammaṭṭhāna) refers to jhāna having the foul as its object (asubhārammaṇa). For that [jhāna] exists as the practice of yoga regarding the foul objects, and for the yogin...
And because it is the cause of specific types of happiness, it is called the "foulness meditation subject" (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*).
By the word "exclusive," the object is excluded. "By way of penetration" means by way of the penetration of jhāna.
For jhāna, when succeeding through a particular mode of development, proceeds only by penetrating its own objective field; it is penetrated according to its true nature.
And thus it is called "penetration" (*paṭivedha*). "Because of having a gross object" means because of having a loathsome object.
"Because of having a repulsive object" means because of having an object that should be felt with disgust. "By way of method" means by way of a reason or by another figurative expression.
"Because of the continuity of the object" is said with reference to the extreme subtlety of the object reached through successive stages of discernment; for when...
A state that occurs with respect to a peaceful object itself becomes peaceful as well. Therefore, it is said: "peaceful, stilled, extinguished";

the meaning is that all feverish distress has been extinguished. The peace of those states which take that [object] as their focus should be illustrated by means of the reviews (paccavekkhaṇā) that have supramundane states as their objects, due to the peacefulness of the object.

It has no "sprinkling" (secanam) that brings about a state of agitation; thus it is *asecanaka*. Because it is *asecanaka*, it is *anāsittaka* (unsprinkled). Because it is *anāsittaka*, it is *abbokiṇṇa* (uninterrupted), unmixed with preliminary exercises (*parikamma*) and so forth.
For that very reason, it is *pāṭiyekka* (distinct), separate, and unique. It is *āveṇika* (exclusive), not shared [with anything else].
All of this was stated to show the state of peace (*santabhāva*) by way of its own intrinsic nature (*sarasa*). Or, the preliminary exercise is for the sake of the sign of the state of peace.
"Preparatory work" (*parikamma*) refers to everything from the preparation of the *kasiṇa* up to the arising of the sign; the intention here is that such [work] does not exist in this case.
For at that time, because the meditation subject lacks flavor, it would be non-existent and unexalted.

Or rather, the construction is: "There is no peace here even by way of access" (*upacāra*). Just as at the moment of access, through the disappearance of the hindrances and the manifestation of the factors, for others...
It is continuous, but not so for this [person]. However, this one is endowed with the beginning... [and so on] ...and is sublime; such is the construction.

"Some" refers to those dwelling in the Uttaravihāra monastery. "Unsprinkled" (anāsittaka) means not sprinkled with a condiment. Therefore he said, "rich in essence" (ojavanta); the meaning is "resembling that which is rich in essence.
"Sweet" (madhura) means desirable, leading to the attainment of mental pleasure by way of the third and fourth jhānas.
Or rather, it should be understood that because equanimity (*upekkhā*) is a state of peace and leads to a happy destination, this applies to all [beings].

However, the attainment of bodily pleasure should be seen as resulting from the body being touched by the sublime matter produced by meditative absorption (*jhāna*); and this occurs specifically at the time of emerging from that absorption.

In this interpretation, the locative case in the phrase "at every moment of absorption" (*appitappitakkhaṇe*) should be understood as expressing a causal sense. Regarding the term "unobstructed" (*avikkhambhite*):

"By means of jhāna": [this refers to] that which has not been removed and not abandoned from one's own continuum. "Born of unskillfulness (*akosalla*)," here *akosalla* is said to be ignorance (*avijjā*);
[the defilements] are born from that, for all evil states are preceded by ignorance. "In an instant (*khaṇena eva*)" means in the very moment of its own occurrence.
"He makes them disappear (*antaradhāpeti*)," here "making disappear" means destruction; and since it is the jhāna that is intended here as the agent, [it is the jhāna that effects this].
He says "he suppresses" because there is the abandoning of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*). "He pacifies" means he pacifies specifically.
Since specific pacification is indeed thorough pacification, he says "he thoroughly pacifies.
But is it not the case that other types of concentration also cause the opposing states to disappear and pacify them at the very moment of their own occurrence?

Now, why is this very concentration described with such specific distinction? It is because, starting from the preliminary stage, there is the actual presence of the subsiding of various types of applied thought (*vitakka*).
For it has been said: "Mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) should be developed for the cutting off of applied thought.

Moreover, this is a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) for one of sharp wisdom and pre-eminent knowledge; and for one of pre-eminent knowledge, the abandoning of the defilements (*kilesa*) is far more excellent than that of others. Just as...
[This is] for one who has attained [the goal] through view compared to those resolved through faith. Therefore, with reference to this distinction, it is said:

"It makes them disappear and pacifies them instantly. Alternatively, because when the sign appears, the manifestation of the limbs [of the body] occurs in that very moment, this very concentration is called "it makes them disappear and pacifies them instantly," just as [one might say of] a great unseasonal cloud.
As soon as it rises and the rain falls, the dust and mud on the earth are instantly stilled. Therefore he said:

"Just as, monks, a great unseasonable cloud has arisen," and so forth. For one belonging to the Dispensation (sāsana), the development of jhāna is for the most part conducive to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya);
thus he said, "because it is conducive to penetration. However, for Buddhas, it is invariably conducive to penetration alone.
For it is by developing this very meditation subject that all Fully Enlightened Ones attain supreme enlightenment.
This concentration, which serves as the foundation for the Noble Path, gradually increases until it effectively becomes the Noble Path itself;
thus it is said: "gradually reaching the growth of the Noble Path."
But this meaning is correctly applicable by way of the contemplations of fading away (*virāga*), cessation (*nirodha*), and relinquishment (*paṭinissagga*).

In order to facilitate easy comprehension, he presents the meaning stated above—which was explained by way of conceptual proliferation (*papañca*)—by summarizing it, saying: "But here is the concise meaning. What is meant is that this is the "combined meaning" (*piṇḍattha*).

218. "In those places with the characteristics thus stated" means in those places whose characteristics have been stated according to the method of the Abhidhamma and the method of the Suttanta.

"Near a tree" refers to the vicinity of a tree as described thus: "As far as the shadow spreads all around at midday, or as far as leaves fall in a windless place—this much is called 'the root of a tree'. "The remaining seven kinds of lodgings" [refers to the rest].

"Displaying. *Ūrubaddhāsana* (the cross-legged posture) is sitting by way of binding the thighs below.

And in order to show this, the words beginning with "eighteen" were spoken. "They do not bend" means they do not incline.

*Parī* has the sense of encompassing (*pariggaha*), as in the word *pariṇāyikā* (“guide”) and others. It has the sense of departure (*niyyāna*), in the sense of going forth from the opposite side. Therefore, *pariggahita-niyyānaṃ* means:
having established mindfulness that is in every way grasped without confusion and abandoned of confusion; [this is] supreme—
The meaning is: "having established mindfulness and clear comprehension.

219. "Mindful" means endowed with mindfulness; the meaning is that he breathes in only while being mindful, and there is no occurrence of breathing devoid of mindfulness. Regarding the phrase "mindfully breathing out," here too [the word] "only" applies to "mindfully breathing out."

"By that mindfulness and that knowledge" refers to the mindfulness as previously described and the knowledge as previously described.
And by means of knowledge. This is what is meant: for one whose mind is undistracted, mindfulness is indeed established toward that long inhalation when it is understood without confusion;

Through that mindfulness and clear comprehension dependent upon it, the practitioner endowed with them is "one who acts with mindfulness" (*satokārī*).
"It is called [the mindfulness of breathing]": "By way of the inhalation while contemplating relinquishment" means having become one who contemplates relinquishment, by way of the inhalation.

According to the method of the Vinaya, it refers to the instruction that has arisen within.
In-breathing (*assāsa*) is the movement of air entering within; out-breathing (*passāsa*) is the movement of air exiting outward.

However, according to the method of the Suttas, even when it has exited outward, it is called in-breathing because it enters within, and even when it has arisen within, it is called out-breathing because it exits outward. And this is precisely the method [taught]:
"For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breath, the body—even with a mind distracted internally—" [is calmed].
“Both the body and the mind become agitated, perturbed, and restless,” and, “For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the out-breath,
because the mind has gone into external distraction, both the body and the mind become agitated, perturbed, and restless.”
This accords with the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
They say that the first breath is called inhalation (*assāsa*) because it occurs according to the sequence of its occurrence: first, the internal wind goes out.
"It is extinguished by striking the palate" means it ceases after striking the palate. For it is said that one who has just been born [does so].
“A young child throws it up. The phrase “Thus, first of all,” and so forth, is the conclusion of the meaning as previously stated.
Some say: “The intention [of the phrase] ‘Thus, first of all’ is that one should understand that ‘inspiration’ is the out-breath according to this sequence of occurrence.
“By way of extent” means by way of temporal duration (*kāla-addhāna*). For this word *addhāna* denotes both time and space.

Having shown there the measurement of space by way of illustration, the passage beginning with "Just as" (*yathā hi*) was stated in order to clarify the long and short duration of the in-breaths and out-breaths by way of the measurement of time.
Therein, "measurement of space" (*okāsaddhāna*) means the distance that constitutes the space. "Pervading" (*pharitvā*) means having extended [the breath] over it.
"Even in fine particles" (*cuṇṇavicuṇṇāpi*) refers to their state as many distinct clusters. "A long distance" (*dīghaṃ addhānaṃ*) means a long region. Therefore...
They are called "long" because they proceed slowly and have a long continuity.

In this context, it should be understood that the length or shortness of the inhalations and exhalations in the bodies of elephants and so forth, as well as in the bodies of dogs and so forth, is stated solely by way of the duration of time (*kāla-addhāna*), distinguished by the extent of space (*desa-addhāna*).
[The texts state: "Having filled [the body] slowly, they exit slowly," and "having filled [it] quickly, [they exit] quickly."
And because of the statement, “...emerging. Regarding the phrase “among humans”: even among human bodies of equal proportions.
“Breathing long” means causing a long succession of inhalations to proceed;
the same method applies here for “breathing out. The construction is: like dogs, hares, and so forth, they breathe in and breathe out short [breaths]. But this—
The long and short inhalation and exhalation should be understood as the natural physical characteristic of those beings. "Of them" means of those beings.
"They" refers to the inhalations and exhalations. "A short duration" means a small amount of time.

"In nine ways" refers to [the case] of one who is devoted to the development [of meditation] but has not yet attained any distinction between what precedes and what follows, [practicing] merely by way of duration.
The three modes mentioned at the beginning refer to three types of persons: one who clearly observes the in-breath, another the out-breath, and another both.

However, some say that the expression "breathing in and breathing out" is stated as a single unit in order to show the uninterrupted occurrence of the meditation. This is according to inclination (*chanda*).
As before, there are three [ways], and likewise by way of gladness; thus, by these nine modes.

Although only three modes are obtained for a single person here, nevertheless, because they have been included in the Canon (pāḷi) for all [persons] according to the thread [of the teaching], and because the preliminary work (parikamma) must be performed by way of them, it says: "In this case, this bhikkhu [proceeds] by nine modes."
It has been said. "Understanding thus" means understanding in-breaths and out-breaths in the manner already described, applying attention to them.
"In one aspect" means by one of the four aspects beginning with long in-breaths, or by one of the three [remaining] among the nine. For he will say accordingly:
“Long and short inhalation, and likewise exhalation—these four colors proceed right at the tip of the bhikkhu’s nose.

Since this meditation consists of the contemplation of the body as inhalation and exhalation, it is said: “The development of the foundation of mindfulness through the contemplation of the body succeeds.”
Now, in order to show those nine modes and the method of development according to the text itself, the passage beginning with “As it is said” is commenced.
Therein, “How does he understand? is asked out of a desire to explain the method of understanding.

“A long in-breath” refers to the long in-breath possessing the characteristics already mentioned. “In what is reckoned as a duration” means in that which has come to be designated by the term “duration,” namely, the long [breath].

"At the proper time" means they dig for a long duration. Alternatively, the word *saṅkhāta* has the sense of "division," as in expressions such as "that which is reckoned as theft" (*theyyasaṅkhāta*).
Therefore, "reckoned as a journey" (*addhānasaṅkhātā*) means in the divisions of the journey; that is, in the portions of the region.

"Zeal arises" means that because one has gained a sense of satisfaction through the practice—which brings about successive improvements from before to after—there arises therein a particularly strong desire to act, characterized by the wish to do so.

Wholesome desire arises. "By way of desire" means for one who is devoted to meditation with distinction by virtue of such arisen desire, and for whom the meditation subject reaches growth and expansion.
"Subtler than that" means subtler than the previously mentioned occurrence of desire.
For, through the power of meditation, because the distress and feverishness of the body have been stilled, [the body becomes more subtle].
The in-breaths and out-breaths proceed having become more subtle.

"Gladness arises" means that, due to the subtler state of the in-breaths and out-breaths, the extreme peacefulness of the object, and the fact that the meditation subject has entered its proper course, a joy accompanied by the developing consciousness—an infantile joy and so forth—arises. "The mind turns away" means:

Some say that when the in-breaths and out-breaths eventually fail to appear because they have reached an extremely subtle state, the mind turns away from them as they have entered a stage where they must be investigated.

However, it is through the power of meditation (*bhāvanā*) that, when the in-breaths and out-breaths have reached a subtler state and their counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) has arisen therein, the mind turns away from the natural in-breaths and out-breaths. Equanimity (*upekkhā*) becomes established.

When the concentration characterized by the distinction between access and absorption has arisen regarding that counterpart sign, there is equanimity because of the absence of further effort for the sake of producing the jhāna.
Furthermore, this equanimity should be understood as "equanimity as specific neutrality" (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
"By these nine aspects" means occurring by way of these nine modes as previously stated. Long inhalations and exhalations...
"Body" (*kāya*) refers to the long-form inhalations and exhalations; even when they are broken into minute particles, they are called "body" in the sense of being an aggregate.

Here, the sign that arises dependent upon the inhalations and exhalations is also spoken of by the same designation, "inhalations and exhalations. "Establishment" (*upaṭṭhāna*) is mindfulness (*sati*);
it is called "establishment" because it stands having approached the object. "Contemplation" (*anupassanā*) is knowledge (*ñāṇa*), [referring to] the sign by way of serenity (*samatha*).

Contemplation (*anupassanā*) is the knowledge that consists in the contemplation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), having defined—in accordance with insight (*vipassanā*)—the in-breaths and out-breaths together with their physical basis as "form" (*rūpa*), and the mind and its associated mental states as "name" (*arūpa*);

it is the awakening to things as they truly are therein. "The body is the establishment" (*kāyo upaṭṭhānaṃ*): that body approaches [as the object] by way of being made the objective support (*ārammaṇakaraṇa*).
It is called "establishment" (*upaṭṭhāna*) because mindfulness (*sati*) stands firm therein.

And here, by the phrase "the body is the establishment," the other bodies are also included, since the aforementioned mode of comprehension (*sammasanacāra*) is also intended here. It is not that the body itself is mindfulness;
rather, mindfulness is both the establishment and the mindfulness itself, in the sense of remembering and in the sense of standing firm. By means of that...
“With mindfulness” means with the mindfulness already described. “With that knowledge” means with the very knowledge already described.

“That body” means both that body of in-breaths and out-breaths, and the material body which is its support. “Contemplates” means he contemplates repeatedly with both the knowledge associated with jhāna and the knowledge of insight (vipassanā).
Therefore it is called the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body.
By means of that contemplation upon the body as described, this is called "the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body.

This is what is meant: that which is the contemplation of the very body—both in the aforementioned body of inhalation and exhalation and in the "karma-born" body that serves as its support—is like the contemplation of water in a mirage that is not water; it does not [grasp] the true nature of impermanence and so forth.

Contemplation of the body consists not in contemplating its state as permanent and so forth, but rather in contemplating it precisely as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul, as appropriate to each case.

Alternatively, because there is nothing whatsoever in the body to be grasped as "I," "mine," "woman," or "man," contemplation that does not perceive such things, but contemplates the mere body itself, is "contemplation of the body" (*kāyānupassanā*). By means of that contemplation of the body...

Mindfulness itself, when associated [with other mental factors], is the establishment; thus, the development and increase of that is the "development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body.
This method refers by extension to the procedure stated in the passage beginning with "by way of nine aspects" and so forth, using the term "short" (*rassa*).

"In this" (*ettha*) means in this method of the Pāli text as it has been shown, which begins with "How, breathing in long... and so on. "Here" (*idha*) means in this method of the Pāli text as it has come down under the heading of the "short" (*rassa*) phrase.
The practitioner of yoga (*yogāvacara*) approaches. "By way of duration" means by way of a long period of time. "By way of brevity" means by way of a short period of time.
"By these modes" means by these nine modes. "Such as that" refers to both the long and the short. "The four colors" means the four modes, and those are precisely the long and so forth.

In the phrase "or on the tip of the nose, O Bhikkhu," it is stated as "on the tip of the nose" using the short vowel for the sake of metrical convenience; the word "or" (*vā*) [indicates an alternative].
The meaning of *aniyata* (indefinite) is that by it the upper lip is included.
220. *Sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī*: one whose nature is to feel and know each and every part of the entire body correctly;
or one who possesses a correct individual experience of that [body] part by part; or one who [experiences] it correctly part by part.

The meaning is "he understands. Although the inclusion of the word "all" (*sabba*) in each instance establishes the complete exhaustion of the body beginning with inhalation, the prefix *paṭi-* is employed to demonstrate that there is a distinct perception of every single part of it, owing to its nature as a composite of many aggregates.
Furthermore, the prefix *saṃ-* is employed to demonstrate the state of performing the practice with thorough attention (*sakkacca-kārī*); such is the meaning.
He spoke the words beginning with "of the whole" in order to show that, although the inhalation and exhalation are the same for the practitioner regarding the method of practice,
one must nevertheless practice each one with full care; thus, even though the meaning is identical,
he provides a separate commentary on the meaning of each of the two phrases, "of the whole," and so forth, in order to illuminate that very point.
It should be understood that "katā" means making manifest; "making manifest" (*pākaṭaṃ karonto*) means making clear (*vibhūtaṃ karonto*), the sense being "making it entirely distinct.
Showing that making manifest, which is the act of discerning, occurs through knowledge alone by way of the non-confusion regarding those [breaths] and their proceeding, he said:
"making them thus known," and so forth. In that context, "therefore" (*tasmā*) means because the in-breaths and out-breaths [are known] only by a consciousness associated with knowledge.

He causes [the breath] to proceed, not with a dissociated mind; therefore, one who is thus disposed is said by the Buddhas and others to "train himself: 'I shall breathe in and breathe out experiencing the whole body.
The phrase *cuṇṇavicuṇṇavisaṭe* means "dispersed in a state of being finely powdered" due to its manifold constituent parts.
The beginning becomes manifest through mindfulness and by the power of knowledge, as well as through the influence of previous mental formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*).
"Because it occurs. "One should become like that" means one should become similar to the fourth type of person;
the intention is that, having established mindfulness and knowledge, one should direct the mind associated with knowledge in all three instances—let alone in the case of mindfulness.
"In this way" means by means of the very manner already described, namely, through the experience of the whole body. "Exerts" means strives. "Strives" means...
The meaning is that he exerts effort and applies attention. "Of one who has become such" means of one who is developing mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).
"Restraint" refers to mindfulness, or alternatively, to energy. "By that mindfulness" means by that mindfulness which occurs directed toward the in-breaths and out-breaths.
"By that attention" means together with that attention of development which is preceded by mindfulness regarding that [breathing].
The intention is as follows: "He cultivates" means that when the "three trainings" are mentioned, he cultivates the states of superior virtue (*adhikusaladhamma*).
Here, it is this cultivation of them that is intended by the term "training.
"In the former method" refers to the previous method of development; the meaning is "in the first two bases. Even there, indeed—
The arising of knowledge is indeed obtainable because there exists the awakening to the actual long and short states of the in-breaths and out-breaths;
nevertheless, since that [knowledge] consists merely in grasping them as they occur, it is not difficult, and thus the use of the present tense was employed therein.
But this [present practice] is difficult, resembling a man walking on the edge of a razor’s blade; therefore, one must apply oneself here with exceptional effort.

In order to illustrate that one must be conditioned by past volitional formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*), and to show the meaning of the application [of the formula] to the future time, the passage beginning with “Therein, because...

was stated. In that context, by the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “in the arising of knowledge and so forth,” the subsiding of the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*), the experiencing of rapture (*pīti*), and so on are included.
However, some here say that it includes the undertaking of the restraints (*saṃvara*).

"Body formation" refers to inhalation and exhalation. For although it is mind-originated, it is called "body formation" because its activity is dependent upon the physical body (karaja-kāya) and is thus formed by that body.
However, as for the "body formation" mentioned in the passage beginning "body formation, speech formation," this body formation has the characteristic of volition (*cetanā*);
even though it may arise through other doors [of sense], it is so named because it generally functions through the body-door.
And because it is characterized by the bodily door through its frequent occurrence, that [type of breathing] is not intended here.
In the phrases beginning with "calming" (*passambhento*), each subsequent term is an explanatory gloss for the preceding one;
therefore, "calming" (*passambhana*) means "tranquillizing" (*vūpasamana*), and that refers to the gross bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) which would otherwise arise if such application were absent.
It should be understood as the non-arising [of defilements] through the perfection of the method (*payoga*). "Therein" refers to the passage: "calming the gross bodily formation.

"At a time when it is not yet taken hold of" means at a time when the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) has not been commenced; for that very reason, it is also a time when neither body nor mind have been taken hold of.

For by the words, "he sits down, having folded his legs crosswise and set his body erect," there is the taking hold of the body; and by "facing the front... [the taking hold of the mind is indicated].
By the phrase "having established mindfulness," the grasping of the mind is stated. For this very reason, he said: "Both the body and the mind are grasped.
"Body" refers to the body composed of the four great elements (*karaja-kāya*). "With fever" means with burning distress;
and that state of theirs being "with fever" is inseparable from their coarseness, as if by their heaviness, which is why he said "coarse. "More powerful" means strong and thick. "Calmed" (santā).
"They are" means that first the mind, having become one-pointed through the absence of external distraction, becomes calm and tranquil as it proceeds while grasping the meditation subject;
consequently, the material phenomena originating from it attain lightness, malleability, and wieldiness, and the remaining thirty-two types of corporeal continuity conform to that state.
Thus, when the mind and body are proceeding in a state of tranquility, those [phenomena] dependent upon them—
Inhalation and exhalation proceed by gradually becoming more and more subtle until they reach their most refined state.
Therefore it was said: "But when his body... and so forth.
*Ābhoga* is application; it is the initial mental advertence, "I am tranquilizing. *Samannāhāra* is the repeated, correct bringing [of the mind] toward [the object].
Attention (*āvajjanā*) is the repeated occurrence of advertence toward that very object. Mental application (*manasikāra*) is the attending to that same object, its placing in the mind.
Investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) is reflective examination.

"Agitated" (*sāraddha*) means with agitation (*sadaratha*) and with feverish excitement (*sapariḷāha*). "Excessive" (*adhimatta*) means powerful and gross. [The word *sāraddha* is used here] by way of a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
It has been stated. For "bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) is what is intended here. Or else, this is an adverbial qualification of the action, meaning "it proceeds in an excessive manner.
The same principle applies here to the term "subtle" (*sukhuma*). Regarding the phrase "in the body," one should supply the words "and in the mind" (*citte ca*) and connect them.
221. The preliminary work (*parikamma*) for the second jhāna, which consists of different moments of advertence (*nānāvajjana*), is performed after emerging from the first jhāna.

Having regarded it as having its opposite far removed, just like the first jhāna, the bodily formation originating from that [second jhāna] is described as being "gross" in both the first jhāna and the access to the second jhāna;
this same method applies to the other two accesses as well.
Alternatively, for one who is practicing to attain the second jhāna and so forth, and who is wearying through the mode of practice that is painful and so on—

The grossness of the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) should be understood in the access stages of the second jhāna and beyond, due to the wavering of the mind's activity caused by physical fatigue, mental affliction, and so forth, as well as by the agitation of applied thought (*vitakka*) and the rest.
"Exceedingly subtle" means that the bodily formation found elsewhere becomes more subtle than even what has been transcended in the fourth jhāna. This is its state of subtlety.
In that state, nothing exists; how, then, could there be grossness, since there is no occurrence? Therefore it is said:

"He reaches the very non-occurrence. Referring to the time of entering successive attainments once he has gained [the ability], or referring to the attainment of all jhānas in a single sitting, the Majjhimabhāṇakas maintain that even in the access (upacāra) to each successively higher jhāna from each lower jhāna, [this occurs].
They desire something more subtle. For therein, there may arise a progressive distinction and tranquility among the jhānas accompanied by access (sopacāra);

or rather, this was said with reference to the single advertence (ekāvajjana) as the access. Thus, because their objects are different, the non-contradiction of this statement with the doctrine stated previously is established. "Of all" refers to both types. Because...

All of them, according to the method already stated, desire tranquility alone. The statement, "The bodily formation that occurred when [the breath] was unattended subsides when it is attended," is said because of the continuity of the stream;
for it is not the case that those same gross in-breaths and so forth become subtle. The manner of their subsiding has already been explained below.
"Subtle in the discernment of the great primary elements" is said with reference to the application of insight by way of the four elements.

It is subtle in the discernment of all material form because it becomes increasingly refined through successive stages of meditation. For this very reason, he says: "It is subtle in the discernment of both the material and the immaterial.
"Insight having the characteristics as its object" refers to the comprehension of groups (*kalāpasammasana*). This is because it leads to the contemplation of disenchantment.
From that point on, insight (vipassanā) is strong; prior to that, it is weak.

"By the method stated previously" means that by the method stated in the way of serenity (samatha)—beginning with "at the time of non-apprehension"—the subsiding should also be applied to the way of insight (vipassanā), according to the passage beginning: "The bodily formation that occurred during non-apprehension subsides upon the apprehension of the great primary elements. This is what is meant.
"Assā" refers to this phrase, "calming the bodily formation. "By means of interrogation and clarification" means by means of questions and their resolutions.

"In this way" means in the manner that will now be stated. "How?"—having asked this out of a desire to explain how it is, and in what manner, the calming of the bodily formation and the training of the yogin occur, as expressed in the passage: "Calming... [etc. ...he trains."

The passage beginning with “Which are the bodily formations? is commenced in order to show the bodily formations by way of their essential nature, by way of the gross and the subtle, by way of their subsiding, and by way of their application and relinquishment.
Therein, “bodily” (*kāyika*) means existing in the material body (*rūpakāya*). “Connected with the body” (*kāyapaṭibaddha*) means dependent upon the body.
They exist when the body exists and do not exist when it does not; for that very reason, although they are not originated from the body itself, they are [associated] with the body.
They are called "bodily formations" (*kāyasaṅkhārā*) because they are being formed. "Calming" means calming them down, starting from the coarsest of the coarse.
The remaining two phrases are synonyms for that same term. For one who causes the coarse bodily formation—which has an unappeased nature—to settle is said to be "calming";
one who brings about its non-arising and cessation is said to be "stopping"; and one who leads it to a state of perfect peace is said to be "appeasing."

"By such kinds" means by those of such a nature. "Bodily formations" refers to gross bodily formations. "Bending forward" (*ānamanā*) is the bending of the body toward [the object] by way of being directed toward it.
"Bending aside" (*vinamanā*) is the bending as one looks from side to side. "Bending all around" (*sannamanā*) is the bending completely or thoroughly.
"Bending backward" (*paṇamanā*) is the bending toward the rear. "Quivering" (*iñjanā*) and the others are synonyms for "bending forward" and the rest, used in their most intense forms.
Or, "moving forward" refers to actions such as bending; "sluggish" refers to actions such as trembling.
"Calming the bodily formations" means calming those coarse bodily formations that serve as the cause for such actions as bending.
For when they are calmed, the bending and so forth are likewise calmed.
"Peaceful and subtle": by means of such bodily formations as cause the body not to tremble, there is no bending and so forth;
thus, due to the absence of distress, it is peaceful, and due to its lack of grossness, it is subtle.
He speaks by treating "tranquilizing the bodily formations" as a single general term. Alternatively, previously [he spoke of] the bodily formations that were increasingly gross.
While calming them, he gradually produces states that are more and more subtle than the causes for the body’s lack of movement;

having calmed even those, it is with reference to that bodily formation which he calms—having reached the ultimate limit of extreme subtlety—that it is said: “calming the peaceful, subtle bodily formation.”
The phrase beginning with "iti" is the statement of the opponent (codaka). Therein, "iti" is a particle used in the sense of manner. "Kira" indicates a lack of conviction;

the meaning is "if this were so. This is the intended sense here: if, in the manner stated, one calms even the most subtle bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*). "Evaṃ sante" means "this being so," that is, when the mode described by you is applicable. "Vātūpaladdhiyā" means...

Regarding the perception of the wind: the word *ca* has the sense of conjunction. The meaning is that there is no production, generation, or occurrence of a mind that takes the wind of inhalation and so forth as its object; rather, those [breaths] are to be tranquillized by it.
Furthermore, "the development of inhalation and exhalation" means that after one has stilled the coarse inhalations and exhalations through development, there is the production of their subtle forms.
Nor does it occur for both [of these], because they must be pacified by that [insight].
Regarding "mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānassati*): there is no occurrence of mindfulness having inhalation and exhalation as its object, because of the absence of inhalation and exhalation.

For that very reason, there is also no development—that is, no production—of the concentration associated with mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*). Indeed, conditioned phenomena possessing an object can never arise without an object.

"And not that" (*na ca naṃ*): here, *naṃ* is merely a particle. The construction is as follows: "The wise, the possessors of wisdom, neither enter into that aforementioned attainment, nor do they emerge from it.
Thus, the accuser accuses with the intention that the complete non-existence [of the attainment] is its subsiding.
“Puna” (again) and so forth refers to the response to the aforementioned challenge.
In this context, “kira” is a particle used in the sense of “yadi” (if). Thus, “iti kira sikkhati” means “if he trains in the manner stated by me.
“Evaṃ sante” means when there is such tranquillity. “Pabhāvanā hoti” means that even though the gross bodily formations are stilled, [there is still further development].

"But the subtle [breaths] certainly exist"—the intention is that by means of the gradual attainment of the state of supreme subtlety, the arising of the sign (*nimitta*) succeeds, and thus the development of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) and the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*) is indeed accomplished.
"In what way?"—how should that aforementioned method be regarded? There is something which, when correctly applied for that purpose, [leads to success].
The intended meaning is "a simile. Now, in order to show the simile, the passage beginning with "seyyathāpi" (just as) was spoken.

In that context, "seyyathāpi" is a particle used in the sense of a comparison. "Kaṃse" means in a bronze vessel. "Nimittaṃ" means of the sign; the meaning is "of the mode of occurrence of those sounds.
This accusative case is used here in the sense of the genitive. "Suggahitattā" means because of being well-grasped. "Sumanasikatattā" means...
Because it was well-established in the mind. "Well-attended to" (*sūpadhāritattā*) means because it was properly attended to and clearly discerned.
"Subtle sounds" refers to reverberations (*anurava*), those which are faint; for here the particle *ka* has the sense of "small.

"Even by having subtle sound as its sign and object" (*sukhumasaddanimittārammaṇatāpīti*): the subtle sound itself is the sign, thus it is "the sign of subtle sound"; even by having that as its object. What is meant?
Granted that even those very subtle sounds have ceased by then, nevertheless, because the sign of the sound was well grasped,
the mind continues to proceed by taking as its object the sign of an even more subtle sound. For from the beginning,
as he examines with an undistracted mind the sign of each successive sound that has ceased, eventually, at the conclusion, even the sign of an exceedingly subtle sound becomes the object.
Having done so, the mind continues to proceed. The mind does not fall into distraction because of the presence of concentration upon that sign as it has appeared.
"While it is thus," and so forth, is stated by way of a conclusion to the very meaning already explained. In that regard, of whichever sutta-passage...
The meaning has been stated together with the exhortations and clarifications;

having extracted that, the following beginning with "calm" (*passambhaya*) was spoken in order to show the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) by way of their classification. All of that is clear because it follows the method already explained. 222.
"For a beginner, by way of the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhāna*) refers to the meditation subject of serenity (*samatha*). [Regarding] insight (*vipassanā*):
The meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), however, is indeed found in the other tetrads as well. "Therein" means in the first tetrad.
"Five-jointed" means having five sections; that is the meaning of "fivefold.
"Learning the meditation subject" means learning the manual of the meditation subject. "Inquiry into its meaning" refers to the inquiry concerning the meditation subject.
Inquiry. Alternatively, "learning" (*uggaha*) is the acquisition of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) both from the text and its meaning.

Within that, "inquiry" (*paripucchā*) is the questioning to resolve doubts. "The appearance of the meditation subject" refers to the appearance of the sign (*nimitta*); it is the discernment by one devoted to such development, thinking, "In this way the sign appears here. Likewise, there is the "attainment" (*appanā*) of the meditation subject.
“Thus he enters into jhāna. Regarding the characteristic of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*):

it is the perfection of the stage of “fixing” (*ṭhapanā*) after having promoted the development by means of counting, following, and touching; or else, it is the reaching of the summit by means of discernment (*sallakkhaṇā*) and so forth.
Thus, it is the discernment of the intrinsic nature of the meditation subject. Therefore he said: “the grasping of the intrinsic nature of the meditation subject is what is meant.”
He does not weary himself because he learns the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) by stages.

For that very reason, he does not trouble his teacher, since he brings the matter of the Dhamma to its culmination through development (bhāvanā). Therefore, "for that" means for the sake of not wearying oneself and not troubling the teacher.

"Little by little" means in small portions. It is called "learning" (uggaha) because it is to be learned; it refers to the entire procedure of the meditation subject, and not merely what was previously [studied].
"Merely what has been learned from the recitation": *ācariyuggaha* is learning from a teacher; "from that. "Even a single word" (*ekapadam-pi*) means even a single portion.
223. "Following after" (*anuvahanā*) refers to the continuous proceeding of mindfulness by way of following after the in-breaths and out-breaths.
"Touching" (*phusanā*) refers to one who, having withdrawn the counting while counting the in-breaths and out-breaths, follows them with mindfulness.
Just as there is absorption, so too for one who places the mind [on the object], there is the touching of those [sensations] at the location such as the tip of the nose.

However, since there is no separate act of attention by way of touching as there is by way of counting and so forth—because counting and so forth must be performed precisely at the place touched—it is shown here that "touching" is mentioned to demonstrate this, stating: "Touching is the place touched."
He said: "Fixing" (*ṭhapanā*) means establishing (*samādhāna*). For that is indeed the correct fixing and placing of the mind upon the object.
Thus, concentration (*samādhi*) is defined as "the steadiness and stability of the mind. But since absorption (*appanā*) has concentration as its primary factor, he said: "Fixing is absorption.
Insight (*vipassanā*) is so called because it observes impermanence and the other characteristics; it proceeds from [that observation].
The path is called "turning away" (vivaṭṭanā) because it turns away from signs and because it turns away [from defilements].
Complete purity (pārisuddhi) is the fruit, because it is the state of the subsiding of all defilements. "Of those" refers to turning away and complete purity.
"Reviewing" (paṭipassanā) means seeing or looking at each thing individually; therefore he said "reviewing" (paccavekkhaṇā).
“Breaking up” means breaking up by way of counting, such as one, three, five, and so forth. He says this with reference to the method of counting.
It is dependent on counting, not dependent on the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). The phrase “Has it reached the peak?
is said with reference to one who is attending to it for a longer duration through counting. For he, relying merely on the non-distraction thus obtained, [thinks] in this way...
One might think: "Taking that which appears in the in-breath and out-breath.
This was said with reference to one for whom only one of the two appears first among the in-breaths and out-breaths;
however, for one to whom both appear, both should be taken and counted. By the phrase "that which appears," it is meant whichever of the two winds in the nostrils is more manifest.
It should be understood that this meaning—that "whatever presents itself must be grasped"—is also illustrated here.
By the reduplicated expression "as it occurs, as it occurs," he shows the continuous characterization of the in-breaths and out-breaths.
"Thus" means having characterized them in the manner described. They become manifest because, by means of counting, there is no outward distraction.
The turning of the crossbar; that place where they set it down is the crossbar-pillar (*paligha-thambha*).
"For three nights" is the accusative case used to express continuous duration (*accanta-saṃyoga*). "By the former method" means by the rapid counting, that is, by the cowherd’s method of counting.
"One, two, three, four, five" is the demonstration of the procedure for counting. Therefore, in the cases of "eight," and so forth, one begins from the very first.
The numbers eight and so forth must be reached individually; one must simply count very quickly.

As for the reason why this is so, he shows the cause and the illustration with the words, “For when bound to counting,” and so on. In that context, *aritta* is that by which one navigates, namely, the rudder-pole.
*Arittūpatthambhana* is the stabilization by means of the rudder; it is by way of that [stabilization].
In the ultimate sense, uninterrupted occurrence refers only to the act of placing [the mind]; thus he said, "as if occurring uninterruptedly.
One is said to "insert the mind within" by attending to the air entering within. The same method applies to the drawing out of the mind externally.
"Struck by the wind" refers to one who attends excessively to the air that has gone inside, [and is consequently] struck by the wind.
That place becomes as if struck by a blow and as if filled with fat; it appears in that way.
When one exhales, leaving behind the space touched [by the breath], yet when exhaling in such a manner, the mind runs after various objects by way of investigating the course of the wind;
thus he said, "the mind is distracted by a multiplicity of objects."

This much constitutes this category of in-breaths and out-breaths. 224. "Following" means the successive proceeding or following along by means of mindfulness through making the in-breaths and out-breaths—both as they occur and as they have occurred—the object [of attention].
For this very reason, it is said: "And that is not by way of following the beginning, middle, and end."
The navel and so forth are mentioned first because they arise there initially. Here, the consideration of "first" is by way of initial arising, not merely by way of arising.
For indeed, those [sensations] arise everywhere from the navel up to the tip of the nose.
And wherever they arise, right there they break up, because there is no going of phenomena. However, according to conditions...
The designation "going" (gati) refers to arising in another location. "The heart is the middle" means that the area near the heart, specifically its upper portion, is the middle.
"The tip of the nose is the end" means that the place of the nose is the end, because it serves as the limit for the designation "in-breath and out-breath.
For they are described as "mind-originated," yet mind-originated phenomena do not exist externally [to the body].
There is a possibility [of this]. Therefore he said: "The tip of the nose and so forth for the incoming breath.
However, it should be understood that the method of describing both entering and exiting is stated by way of similarity [to one of them]. "Fallen into distraction" means having reached distraction;

the sense is that it is scattered and unconcentrated (*asamāhita*). "Of the agitated" means of the state of being restless (*sadaratha*). "Of the wavering" means of the fluctuation of the attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

“With a distracted mind”: this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), or as a characteristic of a state thus attained (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇa*). “Agitated” (*sāraddha*) means restless. “Shaken” (*iñjita*) means subject to shaking or movement; likewise for “quivering” (*phandita*).
“By way of beginning, middle, and end” is to be connected with “should not be brought to mind by way of following after the beginning, middle, and end.
“By one who brings it to mind through following after it, and by way of touching and by way of establishing, [one should bring it to mind]... [End of fragment].
In order to explain the intention behind the statement "it should be done," he said, "as if by way of counting and following," and so forth.

In that context, "there is no separate attention" means that there is no attention to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) either solely by way of touching or solely by way of fixing, respectively, without counting and following. [Objection: But is it not the case that without touching...?
Is there no attention even by way of counting, without touching, just as in the case of fixing?
Even if there is not, counting must nevertheless be grasped as the primary factor because it serves as the root for the attention to the meditation subject;
likewise, following must be grasped as the primary factor for fixing, because fixing is impossible without it. Therefore, even though there is touching, there is no state of non-interruption.

Taking only counting and continuous following as primary by way of their fundamental nature, he says, "For there is no separate attention by way of touching and fixing, as there is by way of counting and continuous following," in order to show the absence of those other factors.
If this is so, why are they mentioned separately in the summary? He replies, "Only at the place where it has been touched," and so forth. Therein:
“Counting only at the place where [the breath] has touched”: by this, he shows that touching is a factor of counting.
Therefore he said, “He brings it to mind by means of both counting and touching. “Right there” means right at the place where it has touched.
“Following them with mindfulness” means following the sequence of counting and binding them with mindfulness.
The meaning is: "He investigates them continuously right within the touched area.
"Placing the mind by means of absorption" (appanāvasena) means placing and concentrating the mind upon the sign as it has appeared, in such a way that absorption occurs.

Regarding the phrases beginning with "and by means of following," the construction is: "It is said that he attends [to the object] by means of following, by means of touching, and by means of placing."

The meaning of "Svāyam attho" (this is the meaning) is as follows: it refers to that which was stated as "counting only at each point touched, withdrawing the counting right there, and following those [objects] with mindfulness.
That which does not measure or decide absolutely is "near to measuring" (*māna*); this is a comparison, just as one says, "a *gavaya* is like a cow."
225. *Paṅguḷo* means one who is lame, a cripple. *Dolā* means a swing. *Kīḷatan-ti* means of those playing.
*Mātāputtānan-ti* means of his own wife and son. *Ubho koṭiyo* means both ends: the front end for one coming toward it, and the rear end for one going away.
*Majjhan-ti* means the middle of the swing-board itself. *Upanibandhanathambho viyā* means like a support pillar.
Standing at the tip of the nose or the sign of the mouth, near its base. How standing? By means of mindfulness.
For when the practitioner establishes mindfulness well there, he is said to be "standing" there, because the whole may be designated by way of its constituent parts.
"At the sign" means at the sign of the tip of the nose and so forth. "Sitting by means of mindfulness" means by way of mindfulness.
While sitting: "For mindfulness is there," etc., should be stated as in the case of standing. "There" means in each place touched [by the body]. 226.
"Them" refers to the people both inside and outside the city; their "gathering" has come into his hands. 227.
"From the beginning" means starting from the point where the meaning of the simile is shown. In the verse, "the sign" (nimitta) refers to the sign for anchoring [the mind].
"An object for a single consciousness" means it is not an object for one consciousness; the sense is that they do not become objects.
"And for one who does not know the three things" refers to one who does not find these three things—namely, the sign (*nimitta*), the in-breath, and the out-breath—by way of making them objects.

The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of distinction. "Development" (*bhāvanā*) refers to the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*). "Is not obtained" (*nupalabbhati*)...
"It is not apprehended, it is not accomplished"—this is the meaning of the verse of the objection; the second verse, however, which is the response, is indeed easy to understand.

To explain their meaning, there is the inquiry arising from a desire to speak. Regarding the passage beginning with "These three things," this is the exposition of the meaning together with the grammatical construction of the words:
how can these three things—the sign and so forth—be the object of a single consciousness?
They do not exist; nevertheless, these three factors are not unknown. How are they not unknown?
For if they were unknown, how could the mind avoid falling into distraction?
