And how could exertion—the energy that brings about the accomplishment of development—be made manifest? [Only when known] does it truly bring about concentration that suppresses the hindrances.
How does the yogi accomplish the practice known as the application of cultivation, and how does he attain successive distinctions, both mundane and supramundane?
Now, in order to establish this matter by means of the simile of the saw, it is said, "Just as," and so forth. Due to the unevenness of the ground...
If the tree were unsteady, the act of cutting would not be easy; that being the case, the movement of the saw’s teeth would be difficult to discern.
Therefore, he said, "on a level patch of ground. "With a saw" means with a small, coarse-toothed blade. For this reason, he said, "a man.
"Of the saw-teeth that have been touched" refers to the state of those saw-teeth that have repeatedly come into contact. Thus, it is precisely at the places touched by those saw-teeth...
This shows the establishment of mindfulness in a person. Therefore he said: "He does not attend to the teeth of the saw as they come together or go apart.
When the saw is being pulled toward oneself, the teeth moving in the direction of the person are called "come";
when it is being pushed away from him, those moving away from him are called "gone. And yet, the teeth of the saw are not unknown at all, whether coming or going.
Because mindfulness is established, there is no contact with the place where [the saw] should cut for those [saw-teeth] moving forward and backward;
this is due to the absence of "saw-teeth" (kakacadanta). "Exertion" (*padhāna*) refers to the effort of cutting the tree. "Application" (*payoga*) refers to the act of cutting that very tree.
"Distinction" (*visesa*) refers to the production of various states, as well as the specific purpose to be accomplished thereby.
The correlation of the similes begins with "Just as a tree," and so forth. It is called *upanibandhanā* (binding) mindfulness because by means of it the mind is bound to the object;
its sign (*nimitta*) for the observation of the in-breaths and out-breaths is the *upanibandhanā-nimitta*, namely, either the tip of the nose or the sign at the mouth.
"In the same way" means just as that man, while cutting the tree with a saw, [observes] the movement of the saw’s teeth... [as they come and go].

Just as one who does not direct the mind toward the teeth of a saw, by establishing mindfulness precisely where they touch, comes to know the teeth of the saw as they move back and forth, and accomplishes his purpose without missing a single thread, so it is here.
Regarding "at the tip of the nose" or "the sign of the mouth": for one with a long nose, it is the tip of the nose; for another, it is the mouth—that by which the teeth are covered or concealed.
"The sign of the face" refers to the upper lip, which has received that name.

"This is the striving" means that by means of which exertion of energy the body and mind of the practitioner who has initiated energy become wieldy, capable of the work of development, and fit for the work of development;
this energy is called "striving," [here] the cause is expressed by means of its fruit.
It shows that the defilements are abandoned; "the defilements are abandoned" means that the hindrances, which constitute the defilements of the mind, are abandoned by way of suppression.
"Thoughts are stilled" means that for that very reason, wrong thoughts such as sensual thoughts and so forth come to rest;
or else, having shown the attainment of the first jhāna through the abandoning of the hindrances, it indicates the stilling of thought by this designation.

He speaks of the attainment of the second jhāna and the others. "This is the application" means that this engagement with the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), which serves as the cause for the attainment of the jhānas, is the application.
"The fetters are abandoned" means that even the ten fetters are abandoned by way of their total eradication through the sequence of the paths.
"The underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are exhausted" means that likewise the seven underlying tendencies are rendered subject to non-arising.

They become entirely and without remainder vanished even down to their mere dissolution. And here, the abandoning of the fetters (saṃyojana) occurs precisely through the cessation of the underlying tendencies (anusaya);
and it is for the purpose of showing that once the fetters are abandoned, not even a trace of the underlying tendencies will remain, that it is said:
"The fetters are abandoned, the underlying tendencies are brought to an end. This is the distinction. By means of this concentration, in due course...
The meaning is that the abandonment of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, which are being attained, constitute the specific excellence of this concentration. "Of whom" means by whom.
"Successively" means in gradual order. "Cultivated" means thoroughly practiced. Herein, the summary meaning is as follows:
just as mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) was taught by the Blessed Buddha, even so, by whatever method—such as the discernment of long and short [breaths]—it has been cultivated.

Gradually accumulated, well-developed, and thereby fulfilled—fully perfected through the completion of the sixteen bases—that bhikkhu illuminates this world of his own aggregates and so forth with the radiance of wisdom. How?
Like the moon released from clouds; like the moon, the king of stars, freed from the defilement of clouds.
"Here" (*idha*) refers to the simile of the saw. "His" (*assa*) refers to the meditator (*yogī*). Alternatively, "here" (*idha*) means in this place;

"his" (*assa*) refers to the saw which serves as the simile. Just as that man had no concern (*amanasikāra*) regarding the coming and going [of the saw], so too the sole purpose here is merely the lack of concern regarding the coming and going of the inhalations and exhalations.

228. "The sign" refers to the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*). Regarding the phrase "adorned with the remaining jhāna factors," they say it means adorned with the remaining jhāna factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth;
however, strictly speaking, one should say "sustained thought (*vicāra*) and so forth," because applied thought lacks the state of absorption (*appanā*).

For that [applied thought] is defined in the Canon as "absorption and directed application" (*appanā byappanā*); or else, because of its association with that [state], the jhāna itself is called "absorption."

In the terminology of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), among the factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*), concentration (*samādhi*) is the predominant factor. Therefore, showing that this is "absorption" (*appanā*), he said:
"The fixing (*ṭhapanā*), known as absorption, which is adorned by the remaining factors of absorption, also succeeds.

However, in the passage beginning with "But for some, from the time of attention by way of counting," the text [in the original source] has been omitted up to the point: "...reaches a state like leaping over [the stages]."
For a certain person whose body is agitated, it bends by hanging down from the belt and so forth.
It "twists" means it makes a sound. It forms folds at the joints of the limbs, such as the knees;
it becomes wrinkled here and there. Why? Because a body that is agitated becomes heavy; therefore, together with the subsiding of bodily distress—

The cessation of gross inhalation and exhalation, while occurring during the process of attainment (*sijjhamāno*), is described as if it were the means of proving that [attainment] by way of contrast (*byatirekamukhena*).
"By way of the cessation of gross inhalation and exhalation" refers to the proof of that meaning through positive concomitance (*anvayavasena*).

In this context, when bodily agitation has subsided, there is a state of lightness, malleability, and wieldiness in the material phenomena born of mind; and by virtue of that, even the remaining material phenomena of the continuity of consciousness possess lightness and so forth.
Thus, here it is intended as the lightness of the body. Since this [lightness] does not exist without the mind’s state of lightness and so forth, it is said: “The body and the mind become light.

The passage beginning with “When the gross in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased,” etc., has been introduced to show the method of investigating the bodily formation that has reached the stage of being analyzed, following the manner already explained below.

229. "Manifested higher and higher" means they become increasingly clear through the power of meditation (*bhāvanā*). "By way of location" means by way of the natural place of contact, or the place previously determined by oneself through the act of contacting.

In order to clarify the matter—which is being examined both by way of location, as in "Where is it not found?", and by way of person, as in "In whom is it not found?"—the passage beginning with "Within the mother’s womb" is stated. Therein, just as for one submerged in water...
In a person whose space has ceased, inhalation and exhalation do not occur; likewise within the mother’s womb.

Just as in the case of the dead due to the absence of the consciousness that originates them, so it is for those who have become unconscious, those overcome by fainting, or those born among the non-percipient beings, as well as for those who have attained the attainment of cessation. However, in the case of those who have attained the fourth jhāna, [it is] solely by way of the natural law (*dhammatā*).
There is no arising of these [breaths] for those [beings], nor likewise for those possessing existence in the fine-material or immaterial realms. Some, however, state the reason:

"Because of the attainment of subtlety through successive stages, for one who has entered the fourth jhāna, and because of the subtlety of both material phenomena and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) in the fine-material realm, there are none for those possessing existence in the fine-material realm.
The intended meaning is that those breaths do indeed exist when sought out, apart from the seven aforementioned locations.
Because there is no place where inhalation and exhalation do not arise. "By way of the natural point of contact" means by way of the place touched in its natural state.
"The sign should be established" means that a firmer perception should be maintained through mindfulness so that mindfulness may proceed easily in those various places;
for mindfulness has firm perception as its proximate cause. "This very [sign]" refers to this very [sign] for one to whom it does not yet appear.
The method of establishing [the mindfulness] is precisely by way of extracting a thorn from the bodily formation. "Purpose" (*atthavasam*) means the cause;

for "purpose" (*attha*) is the fruit, and that by which it occurs is the "purpose-condition" (*atthavasa*). "Of one with muddled mindfulness" (*muṭṭhassatissa*) means of one whose mindfulness is destroyed.
"Of one lacking clear comprehension" (*asampajānassa*) means of one devoid of clear comprehension, when the inhalations and exhalations do not appear in sequence as he is developing [the practice].
The intention is that he is devoid of mindfulness and wisdom capable of investigating and determining "these are those" and of understanding them correctly.
230. This is another meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "Heavy" means burdensome. Its heaviness is due to the fact that its cultivation is extremely difficult;
thus he says, "heavy cultivation. Because it attains a state of being progressively more peaceful and subtle, it is "powerful, clear, and courageous."

Having said, "And mindfulness and wisdom must be sought," he spoke the passage beginning with "For just as... in order to show that even for the accomplishment of a subtle matter, one must be subtle oneself.
Now, showing the method for seeking the in-breaths and out-breaths when they do not appear, he said, "But by those...
and so forth. In this context, "at the gateway to the range" (gocaramukhe) means facing toward the range.
“Word by word” means following each word in succession. “Having practiced” means having taken up the range of activity. “In that very place” means in the place designated as the sign for anchoring.

“Having joined” means having joined it through mental attention (*manasikāra*). Or, the phrase “having bound it with the rein of mindfulness” expresses the same meaning as “having joined it in that very place.
For in the case of the object of comparison, separate locations for binding and joining are not found.

231. "The sign" (*nimitta*) refers either to the learning sign (*uggaha-nimitta*) or the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*). Both are mentioned here together. For the three similes beginning with the tuft of cotton are applicable to the learning sign, while the rest apply to both.
"Some" (*ekacce*) refers to certain teachers. "Like the form of a star" means like the radiant form of a star. The similes of the jewel-bead and so forth are appropriate for the counterpart sign.
But how is it that this single meditation subject appears in many forms? To this he says: "And furthermore, this... and so on.
"Suttanta" means a single discourse (*sutta*). It is said to be "like a great mountain river" with reference to its uninterrupted flow due to its state of being well-mastered and its vast scope.

It is said to be "like a single forest grove" because a discourse endowed with excellence of both meaning and phrasing is auspicious on all sides, like a forest thicket that is delightful in every part and in full bloom. Therefore he said:

The Blessed One said: “Just as when the tops of forest thickets are in full bloom. He said, “...like a tree with cool shade,” meaning that this sutta—which possesses various connections, various appendices, diverse skillful methods, and many kinds of meditation subjects—should be diligently lived by those who seek it.
“Because of the diversity of perceptions” means because of the manifold nature of the perceptions occurring prior to the manifestation of the sign (*nimitta*).
"These three things" refers to these three phenomena: the in-breath, the out-breath, and the sign (*nimitta*).
"There are not" means that, by way of being a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), they do not exist [as such] and are not found when one attends to them.

"Nor even access" means that it does not even reach access concentration (*upacāra*), let alone absorption (*appanā*); this is the intended meaning. However, the side of those for whom [the breaths] do exist should be understood according to the method already explained.
Now, in order to support the meaning just stated, the verse beginning with “The sign” (*nimitta*), which appears in the *Kakacūpama Sutta*, is cited here.
232. “In the sign”: in the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) as previously described. “It occurs thus”: it occurs only for one who is devoted to meditation.
Therefore, he should be told: “Reflect upon it again and again in this way. “He might fall into complacency”: [thinking] “The sign is indeed...”
"It is difficult to produce [this], yet this has been obtained; well then, I shall now produce a distinction whenever it may be.
Thus he might fall into despondency. "He would despair" means he would fall into dejection, thinking:
"Even after devoting myself to meditation for so long a time, not even a sign has arisen; I am surely incapable of reaching distinction."
When it is said, "This is the sign for one who has practiced with the thought, 'By this practice I shall be freed from aging and death,'" the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya say:
"How could there be an offense of shrinking back? One should rather exert even greater effort;
thus should this sign... be described. This is by means of fixing the developing mind precisely upon the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) in the manner already described.
"From this point on" means starting from the arising of the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*).

Regarding what was previously stated—"he attends to it by way of pursuing, by way of touching, and by way of fixing"—here, having set aside pursuing and touching, there is development by way of fixing;
thus, the meaning is that it should be developed solely by way of fixing.
"This is the meaning spoken by the ancients" refers to the verse beginning with "In the sign. Therein, "in the sign" means in the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*).
"Placing the mind" means placing the mind of meditation; the sense is that one attends to it by way of fixing it.
"Various forms" refers to the various forms mentioned as "the four colors. This singular number is used because of the commonality of their form. They discern [them].
"Vibhāvento" means making them disappear. For from the moment the sign arises, those modes [of breathing] seem to vanish for one who does not attend to them.
"Assāsapassāse" refers to the various aspects of inhalation and exhalation;
discerning that, or the sign produced by the inhalation and exhalation, "he binds his own mind" means he fixes his own mind by means of that very same establishing.

The meaning is "he enters into. As for those who state the meaning as, "They manifest (*vibhāvayanti*), making manifest (*vibhāvento*), that is, making known what was hidden clear," this would be appropriate from the perspective of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*). This, however, is the meaning here:

because he is endowed with fortitude (*dhiti*), the wise (*dhīra*) yogi, while manifesting the various modes of inhalation and exhalation, understanding them according to their various modes, makes them known and clear.
Or, while calming and pacifying various coarse forms, he fixes his mind upon whatever sign (nimitta) is obtained therein;
thus, by degrees, he binds and settles his own mind.

"By way of color" means by way of the color that appears, as in the case of a ball of wool, a star, a form, and so forth. "By way of characteristic" means by way of its intrinsic nature, such as hardness and so on.
Or [it is so called] because of its characteristics such as impermanence (*anicca*). The connection is: "That sign is to be guarded.
Guarding the sign occurs precisely through guarding the access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*) obtained therein; thus he said:
"Having brought it to growth and increase by means of repeated attention (*manasikāra*)."
233. *Ettha* means "in this" body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*). *Pārisuddhiṃ pattukāmo* means "desirous of attaining," that is, desirous of reaching and desirous of entering into [the path].
Therein, it should be construed as: "desirous of attaining by way of discernment and turning away (*vivaṭṭanā*)," and "desirous of entering into by way of discernment.
The meaning stated briefly is: "having defined name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), he establishes insight (*vipassanā*)."

The passage beginning with “How” is stated in order to show this in detail. Therein, the phrase “Just as,” etc., demonstrates the manner in which the body and the mind are the conditions for the arising of inhalation and exhalation.

“From the smith’s bellows” means from the bellows used by smiths for blowing the fire in the forge. “While being blown” means while they are being blown; the sense is that they cause the air to be taken in. “Tajjamānā” means...
"Corresponding to that. In the phrase "even so," the body made of the four elements (*karaja-kāya*) should be regarded as the smith's bellows, and the mind as the effort [of blowing].
Although inhalation and exhalation are mind-originated, they are said to be "dependent on both body and mind" because they do not occur without the body made of the four elements.

“Of that” means of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). “He seeks the condition” means he investigates and discerns conditions such as ignorance (*avijjā*) by way of the formula: “With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form,” and so forth.
“He overcomes doubt” means he transcends and abandons the sixteen-based perplexity that occurs in the manner of: “Did I exist in the past? and so forth. “Whatever form... [and so on].

"Comprehension by groups" (*kalāpa-sammasana*) is that which proceeds according to the method beginning with "past, future, and present. "In the prior stage" means having arisen in the stage preceding the contemplation of rise and fall (*udaya-bbaya-anupassanā*), which is included within the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*).

"The radiance and so forth" refers to these ten: radiance (*obhāsa*), knowledge (*ñāṇa*), rapture (*pīti*), tranquility (*passaddhi*), happiness (*sukha*), resolution (*adhimokkha*), exertion (*paggaha*), equanimity (*upekkhā*), establishment (*upaṭṭhāna*), and attachment (*nikanti*). Rise...

"Having abandoned": having relinquished the arising of formations grasped through the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*), and having reached the knowledge of the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa*) by contemplating their dissolution alone;

then, becoming disenchanted through the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*) preceded by the contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*); at the conclusion of the practice of the knowledge of desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*), the contemplation of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*), equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), and conformity-knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*).
Immediately after the knowledge of change-of-lineage has arisen, one becomes dispassionate toward all conditioned formations and is liberated by means of the knowledge of the path that has arisen.
For at the moment of the path, the noble one is said to "become dispassionate" and "is liberated. Therefore it was said:

"having reached the four noble paths in their proper sequence. [This refers to] the object of review, which consists of the path, the fruit, Nibbāna, and the defilements abandoned and those remaining.
By way of classification, there are nineteen divisions. For the Arahant, there are nineteen because of the absence of any remaining defilements.

"Of him" refers to the practitioner of the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānakammaṭṭhānika). There is no separate method for the development of the meditation subject, because it is taught by way of the contemplation of feelings, mind, and mental objects following the attainment of jhāna through the first tetrad. "Of these" refers to the three tetrads.

"Experiencing rapture" (*pītipaṭisaṃvedī*) means one whose nature it is to experience rapture thoroughly and repeatedly; or, one for whom there is a thorough and repeated experiencing of that [rapture];

or, one who experiences that [rapture] thoroughly and repeatedly. In this context, while the state of having clearly understood rapture is indeed already indicated by the very inclusion of the term "experiencing," there are nevertheless specific modes by which its experiencing is intended.
To demonstrate this, the word *pati* (back) is included [in the compound], as in: "one who experiences again and again (*pati-pati saṃvedī*) is one who experiences thoroughly (*paṭisaṃvedī*).
Therefore, he said: "In two ways," and so forth. Therein, "How is joy experienced by way of the object? is the interrogative statement.
"He enters the two jhānas accompanied by joy" means that he enters, in succession, the first and second jhānas which are associated with joy. "Of him" refers to...
By that [word]. For this genitive case-ending has the sense of the agent (kattū), in relation to the word "paṭisaṃviditā" (clearly experienced).

"At the moment of attainment" means at the moment of having entered [jhāna]. "By the acquisition of jhāna" means by way of being endowed with jhāna. "By way of the object" means by way of the door of the object;
the joy included within the jhāna that takes that as its object is clearly experienced because the object itself is clearly experienced.

What is meant by this? Just as when someone wandering in search of a snake has identified its lair, the snake itself is effectively captured, because it is easy to seize it through the power of mantras and medicinal charms;
even so, when the object that serves as the abode of rapture is identified, that rapture itself is identified according to its specific characteristics.
"And because it is easy to grasp that [rapture] by way of its general characteristics.
"How is rapture experienced without confusion?"—this should be connected by supplying the words from the previous context.
"At the moment of insight" means at the moment of seeing the object when the wisdom of insight has reached a state of sharpness and clarity. "By the penetration of the characteristics" means...
By means of penetrating both the specific characteristic and the general characteristic of rapture (*pīti*).
For when whatever is the specific and general characteristic of anything is known, that thing itself is known exactly as it is. Therefore he said:
"Rapture is clearly understood through non-delusion."
Now, in order to clarify that meaning by means of the text itself, he said, "For it has been said," and so forth.

Regarding that, what needs to be said about the phrases "by way of long inhalation" and so on has already been stated below. However, while the text there was presented by way of showing mindful performance, here it is presented by way of the experiencing of rapture;
and the experiencing of rapture has indeed already been analyzed according to its meaning. Furthermore, this [is] here...

The summary meaning is as follows: "By way of long inhalation" means that for one who understands by way of the long inhalation which has become the object, that rapture is experienced—this is the grammatical connection.

"Understanding the unification and non-distraction of the mind" refers to the unification of the mind (*cittassekaggatā*), which is included within the jhāna and receives the name "non-distraction," [understood] through the wisdom associated with it.
For one who understands. For just as rapture is experienced by way of the object, so too are the states associated with it experienced by way of the object.

"Mindfulness is established" means that mindfulness associated with the jhāna, by way of the long inhalation, is established upon its object; thus, by way of the object, it is said to be established in the jhāna as well.

"By that mindfulness": by means of that mindfulness established in this way, and because the object has been thoroughly understood through the aforementioned knowledge, that rapture is experienced by way of that object. The meaning in the phrases "by way of long out-breaths," etc., should also be understood according to this same method.

Thus, in order to show the experience of rapture (*pīti*) demonstrated by way of the first tetrad, both in terms of its object and its non-delusion, the passage beginning with “for one who adverts” (*āvajjato*) was stated.
Therein, “for one who adverts” means for one who is adverting to the jhāna. “That rapture” (*sā pītī*) refers to the rapture included within that jhāna.
“For one who knows” (*jānato*) means for one who knows by way of the object at the moment of attainment. Of that...
The connection is: "that rapture is clearly experienced. "Seeing" means seeing after emerging from jhāna by means of knowledge that consists of vision.
"Reviewing" means reviewing the jhāna. "Resolving the mind" means resolving the jhāna-consciousness with the thought, "I shall remain possessed of jhāna for this long a time.
Thus, [this refers] to the mastery over the five powers.
By means of the understanding of jhāna through the gateway of discernment, the experience of joy (*pīti*) from the perspective of its object has been shown.

Now, in order to demonstrate the experience of joy by way of those factors—such as faith (*saddhā*) and the rest—which are included both in jhāna and in insight (*vipassanā*) and the path (*magga*), it is said: "of one who resolves with faith," and so forth.

In this context, "resolves" means for one who has faith; the intention is that this occurs by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). The same method applies to the phrases "exerts energy" and so forth.

"To be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) means to be known by means of highly distinguished wisdom (*paññā*). "Directly knowing" (*abhijānato*) means knowing by means of the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*), which is preceded by the wisdom of insight.
"To be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) refers to the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*) by means of the full understanding through investigation and the wisdom of the path.

"For one who fully understands": the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*) is to be abandoned by means of the full understanding of abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*) and the wisdom of the path (*maggapaññā*).
For one who develops and realizes: the truth of the path (*maggasacca*) is to be developed, and the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*) is to be realized.

However, some here extract the categories such as "to be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) and so forth based on rapture (*pīti*) alone; that is incorrect, for it is the aggregate of jhāna and so forth [that is intended].
Because, having extracted [the relevant portion] from that, it is the discernment of rapture (*pīti*) that is intended.
And here, by the phrase "by means of long inhalation," etc., the experience of rapture through the object is stated according to the first tetrad;
likewise, it is stated by the five terms beginning with "of one who adverts. However, by the phrases beginning with "of one who directly knows what is to be directly known," etc.,...
"From non-delusion. By the phrases "resolving through faith," and so forth, it should be understood that the experience of rapture (*pīti-patisaṃvedanā*) is described both ways:
briefly, by way of the object through serenity (*samatha*), and by way of non-delusion through insight (*vipassanā*).

But why, in this contemplation of feeling (*vedanānupassanā*), is feeling taken under the heading of rapture rather than in its own specific form? It is because of the classification of planes (*bhūmi*) and so forth.
This is in order to show the fourfold contemplation of feeling by breaking it down.

Furthermore, while demonstrating the meditation subject of feeling, the Blessed One—because joy is gross—shows the pleasure associated with it under the heading of "joy" for the purpose of grasping it as pleasure.
By this same method, the remaining phrases are: "experiencing pleasure, experiencing mental formations."
The meaning of these terms should be understood according to the method already given for the phrase "experiencing rapture" (*pīti-paṭisaṃvedi*).

For it is possible to substitute the terms "bliss" (*sukha*) and so forth in place of "rapture," as follows: "In two ways one experiences bliss: one experiences the mental formations [of the second jhāna] and one experiences them by way of the object," and so on;
thus one enters "the three jhānas accompanied by bliss, or the four jhānas," and so forth.
In order to understand the meaning, he said: "By way of the three jhānas," and so forth. By the word "etc.
(*ādi*) in "feeling, etc.," perception (*saññā*) is included. Therefore, he said: "two aggregates.

For the purpose of showing the plane of insight (*vipassanā*), that is, for the purpose of showing the plane of insight by means of the contemplation of miscellaneous formations (*pakiṇṇaka-saṅkhāra-sammasana*), it was stated: "Pleasure: two kinds of pleasure," and so forth; because bodily pleasure is absent in serenity (*samatha*).

This is the cessation described by way of the method of tranquilization. For it was explained in detail regarding the bodily formations with the words, "When this bhikkhu was previously unmastered," and so forth;

therefore, it should be understood according to that same method. In that context, it was presented by way of the bodily formations, whereas here it is by way of the mental formations—this alone is the distinction.

Having thus shown the subsiding of the mental formations by way of extension, the words beginning with “Furthermore” (*apicā*) were spoken in order to show what else remains to be said regarding this tetrad.
Therein, “in the section on rapture” (*pītipade*) refers to the portion taught by the passage beginning with “experiencing rapture” (*pītipaṭisaṃvedī*).
Feeling is stated under the heading of rapture; the intention is that feeling associated with it is stated by the designation of rapture, and not rapture itself.
The reason for this has already been stated above. Regarding the two phrases concerning the mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra*):
these refer to the two passages connected with the mental formations, namely, "experiencing the mental formation" and "tranquilizing the mental formation.

They are called "bound to the mind" (*cittapaṭibaddha*) because they are tied to the mind, according to the statement, "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises]. For that very reason, [they arise] through the mind...
They are called "mental formations" (cittasaṅkhārā) because they form the mind; these are perception, feeling, and so forth.
However, here it is intended merely by way of illustration that perception and feeling alone are meant; thus he says, "feeling associated with perception.
Regarding the phrase "experiencing the mind": here, the experience of the mind occurs in two ways—by way of the object and by way of non-delusion.
And how [is it] by way of object? One enters the four jhānas;

at the moment of entry, through the attainment of the jhāna—and following the method stated in such passages, everything is easily understood—therefore he said: "The experiencing of the mind should be understood by way of the four jhānas.
"Gladdening the mind" means gladdening the mind associated with the jhāna by means of the joy associated with it.
Or, having made that joy the object, he delights with that very joy which has become the object of the insight-consciousness (vipassanā-citta) that has arisen.
The words "rejoicing" (*pamodento*) and so forth are synonyms for that same state, because they are expressions for joy (*pīti*).
"He gladdens the mind with the associated joy" means with the joy-factor of enlightenment (*pītisambojjhaṅga*) that is associated with the jhāna-consciousness.

By nourishing that very same jhāna-consciousness through the conditions of co-nascence and so forth, as well as through the condition of jhāna, by means of the jhāna-ecstasy characterized by elation, and by producing a state of being thoroughly uplifted and overjoyed, one gladdens and rejoices.
"Taking as an object" means taking as an object that sublime ecstasy associated with jhāna; thus, the insight-consciousness proceeding by means of that very [ecstasy]—
The practitioner of yoga, manifesting a state of extreme joy through the rapture that has become his object, is said to "rejoice and exult.
"He places [the mind] evenly" means that he establishes it so that it does not fall even slightly into either the side of dullness or the side of agitation;
rather, by the balanced practice of the faculties or by the attainment of the excellence of concentration, it is neither depressed nor elated, but remains equanimous.
It is "properly established" by reaching imperturbability; thus it is placed by way of absorption (*appanā*).
"By penetration of characteristics" means by piercing through each respective characteristic such as impermanence, that is, by awakening to them moment by moment.

"Momentary one-pointedness of mind" is concentration that lasts for only a single moment. For even that, proceeding uninterruptedly in a single mode toward its object, is [overcome] by its opposite...
Unconquered, as if absorbed, he establishes the mind immovably. Therefore it is said: "Thus, when [the hindrances] have arisen," and so forth.
"Liberating" means separating by way of suppression-liberation (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*), making them distinct; the meaning is that he abandons the hindrances.
"At the moment of insight" refers to the moment of the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*). For dissolution is indeed the ultimate state of impermanence.

Therefore, by means of that [contemplation], the practitioner who contemplates dissolution sees the entire range of conditioned phenomena as impermanent through the gateway of the mind, and not as permanent.

Because what is impermanent is suffering, and because what is suffering is non-self, he contemplates that very same thing as suffering and not as happiness; he contemplates it as non-self and not as self. For that which is impermanent is suffering...
It is not-self; it should not be delighted in. And that which should not be delighted in should not be relished.
Therefore, by following the observation of dissolution, when the conditioned state is seen as "impermanent, suffering, and not-self," one becomes disenchanted with it and does not rejoice;
one becomes dispassionate and does not become impassioned. Thus, becoming disenchanted and dispassionate, first of all by means of the mundane...
By means of knowledge one brings about the cessation of lust; it does not arise, nor does one bring about its origination—this is the meaning.
Alternatively, he is so detached from the conditioned phenomena as they are seen that, by means of his own knowledge, he brings about the cessation of those not yet seen; they do not arise.
He attends only to their cessation, not to their origination—this is the meaning. Practicing in this way, he relinquishes.

He does not take it up. What is meant by this? For this contemplation of impermanence and so forth is called "renunciation as relinquishment" because it completely abandons the defilements along with the formative activities of the aggregates;

and it is called "renunciation as leaping forward" because, through seeing the fault in the conditioned, it leaps forward toward Nibbāna, which is its opposite, by inclining toward it. Therefore, one who is endowed with that [contemplation]...
The practitioner of yoga abandons the defilements in the manner described and leaps into Nibbāna. Therefore it was said:
"At the moment of insight, while liberating and releasing the mind from the perception of permanence by means of the contemplation of impermanence...
[and so on] ...while liberating and releasing the mind from grasping by means of the contemplation of relinquishment, he breathes in and breathes out."

In this context, *aniccānupassanā* (contemplation of impermanence) is the contemplation that "it is impermanent" regarding what is impermanent. This is the name for insight (*vipassanā*) that proceeds by grasping the impermanence of phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.
The phrase "from the perception of permanence" refers to wrong perception (*micchā-saññā*) that occurs toward conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) thinking, "They are permanent and eternal.
It should be understood that by way of the term "perception," the mind and views are also included. This same method applies [to the following terms].

Regarding "in the perception of pleasure" and so forth: "contemplation of disenchantment" (*nibbidānupassanā*) refers to the contemplation that occurs by way of becoming disenchanted with conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).

"From delight" (*nandito*) means from craving accompanied by rapture. "Contemplation of fading away" (*virāgānupassanā*) refers to the contemplation that occurs by way of fading away in that same manner;
thus it is said, "liberating from lust. "Contemplation of cessation" (*nirodhānupassanā*) refers to the contemplation of the cessation of conditioned phenomena.
Contemplation in such a way that formations merely cease and do not arise again in the future as renewed existence is contemplation of cessation (*nirodhānupassanā*).
For this desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*) has now reached its full strength; hence he said, "liberating from arising.
Contemplation occurring in the mode of relinquishing is contemplation of relinquishment (*paṭinissaggānupassanā*). From "taking up" means by way of [viewing things] as permanent and so forth.
"From grasping" means from the grasping of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*); thus the meaning should be understood here. 236.

Regarding "contemplating as impermanent" (*aniccānupassī*)—that is, one whose nature is to contemplate the impermanent, or a "contemplator of impermanence"—here there is a fourfold inquiry: what is this impermanence? how is it impermanent? what is the contemplation of impermanence? and for whom is there contemplation of impermanence?
Showing that it must be "vibhāvita" (made manifest), he said, "It should be known as impermanent," and so forth.
In this context, "permanent" (*nicca*) means stable and eternal, such as Nibbāna; that which is not permanent is "impermanent" (*anicca*), possessing arising and passing away.
In terms of its actual meaning, he said, "The five aggregates are impermanent. Why? Because they have the nature of arising, passing away, and change."

The meaning is: "the existence of arising, passing away, and change. In this context, for conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*), *uppāda* (arising) is their coming into being through causes and conditions, their manifestation, and the acquisition of self-existence after not having existed. *Vaya* (passing away) is the momentary cessation and destruction of those phenomena once they have arisen.

*Aññathatta* (change) is the state of becoming otherwise due to aging (*jarā*). For just as there is a difference in the underlying substance when the state of arising has passed away and the state of dissolution occurs, [so too is there change].

There is no such thing; likewise, even in the state facing dissolution—which is designated as "stasis"—there is no differentiation of the substance wherein the conventional designation "aging" could apply.
Therefore, aging is logical for even a single phenomenon, which is called "momentary aging.
Furthermore, one must necessarily admit that there is no difference in the substance during the states of arising and dissolution; otherwise, [one would have to say] "one arises, another..."
One might conclude that [the aggregates] break up. However, this statement "change-ability" (*aññathatta*) was said with reference to momentary aging (*khaṇika-jara*).
Whatever needs to be said regarding this matter, we shall explain it further on.

Because of the presence of these three characteristics, the designation "impermanent" applies to the aggregates; because of those three characteristics, the designation "impermanence" (*aniccatā*) applies.

Having stated, “Impermanence is the very arising, passing away, and alteration of those [phenomena],” he says “or non-existence after having existed,” etc., in order to show that the conventional term ‘impermanence’ specifically refers to the momentary cessation of phenomena.
In this context, because non-existence is preceded by arising, there is the mention of “having existed.
By this, he demonstrates that the state of destruction is preceded by the state of being cooked (ripened). “In that very manner” means in the very manner of their production.
"By momentary dissolution" means by instantaneous cessation. "Of that impermanence" means of the impermanence characterized as momentary dissolution.
"Endowed with that contemplation" refers to the practitioner who has become possessed of the aforementioned contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).
"Destruction" (*khaya*) is the vanishing of formations; "fading away" (*virajjana*) is their very disintegration, which is fading away (*virāga*); thus, destruction itself is fading away.

“Cessation-decadence” (khayavirāga) is momentary cessation. “Absolute decadence” (accantavirāga) is Nibbāna, because when this is attained, formations absolutely fade away and cease. Therefore it was said: “Cessation-decadence is the momentary destruction of formations;
absolute decadence is Nibbāna. It occurs by way of both these: by way of the contemplation of cessation-decadence through insight, and by way of the contemplation of absolute decadence.

The occurrence of the path should be applied [to this]. Or rather, the occurrence of insight should be understood as being by way of the contemplation of destruction and fading away from the perspective of the object;

and as being by way of the contemplation of absolute fading away through its state of being inclined toward that [object]. However, for the path, the occurrence should be understood as being by way of the contemplation of destruction and fading away due to its non-delusion, and by way of the contemplation of absolute fading away from the perspective of the object. By the phrase "the same method applies," because...

Following the method explained in the passage on the contemplation of dispassion (*virāgānupassī*), it refers by extension to the commentary on the meaning beginning with: "There are two kinds of cessation: cessation as destruction (*khayanirodha*) and absolute cessation (*accantanirodha*).

Therefore, by substituting the word "cessation" (*nirodha*) for the word "dispassion," its commentary should be understood here according to the method stated in this context, starting with: "Destruction is the dissolution of formations."

Relinquishment (*paṭinissajjana*) is the abandoning, relinquishing, or giving up of what is to be abandoned, either by way of its specific factor (*tadaṅga*) or by way of its eradication (*samuccheda*).
Likewise, it is the surrendering of oneself to the unconditioned (*visaṅkhāra*), which is the relinquishment of all acquisitions (*upadhi*);
or, through being inclined toward that and having that as its object, it is the "leaping forward" (*pakkhandana*) into it—this is relinquishment by way of leaping forward.

Regarding the phrase "by way of its own factor" (*tadaṅgavasena*): here, first of all, the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) abandons the perception of permanence by way of abandoning through its own factor.

And while abandoning it, it brings to a state of non-occurrence all those defilements that would arise in the future through the apprehension of things as "permanent," the formative volitions (*abhisaṅkhāra*) rooted in them, and the resultant aggregates (*vipākakkhandha*) rooted in both of those; it does so by way of causing their non-occurrence.

In the same way, the perception of suffering and the other [perceptions] abandon. Therefore he said: “For insight abandons defilements together with the formative activities of the aggregates by means of ‘factor-by-factor’ (tadaṅga) abandoning.
“By seeing the fault in the conditioned” means by seeing the faults such as impermanence in the conditioned formations belonging to the three planes of existence.
"In its opposite state" means by way of its being permanent and so forth. "Inclination toward that" means being intent upon that. "Enters" means it penetrates;

it becomes as if it were penetrating. "He abandons the defilements along with the formative forces of the aggregates" means that when the defilements have been abandoned by the Path, the formative forces and the aggregates rooted in them are rendered subject to non-fruition.
It is said that "the Path relinquishes all of them" because they are called "relinquished" by way of their non-arising together with it.
"Both" refers to insight-knowledge and path-knowledge; for even path-knowledge is called "contemplation" because it sees Nibbāna immediately after, following upon, change-of-lineage knowledge.

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of conjunction, meaning "by way of the sixteen bases" as well as "by way of the internal states and so forth. The phrase "mindfulness of breathing developed" (*ānāpānassati bhāvitā*) should be brought forward and connected [to the rest of the sentence].

237. *Assa* means "of this," namely, of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing. The connection is that its great benefit should also be understood by way of its capacity to cut off discursive thoughts such as sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*).
*Ayaṃ* refers to this concentration of mindfulness of breathing. It is precisely its occurrence upon various and diverse objects [that constitutes its greatness].
The mind’s wandering hither and thither [is what must be restrained].
"True Knowledge" (vijjā) refers to the Path; "Liberation" (vimutti) is the Fruit. Its state as the root is its status as the foundation for insight (vipassanā).
It fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), because that cultivation proceeds by way of the four contemplations, beginning with the contemplation of the body.
They fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment because there can be no fulfillment of the development of the foundations of mindfulness without the development of the factors of enlightenment.
They fulfill true knowledge and liberation because the development of the factors of enlightenment constitutes their culminating point.
"Carimakānaṃ" means of those who are final.
238. "By way of cessation" means by way of ceasing. "The final [moments] of existence" refers to those occurring in inferior existence by way of existence (*bhava*).
Likewise, the "final [moments] of jhāna" are to be understood in the same way. "The final [moments] of death" refers to those occurring at the moment of death, being the very end of everything.
"Therefore" means because they occur in the inferior sense-sphere existence among the three types of existence. "Those" refers to the inhalation and exhalation.

“Before” means below. Since it has been demonstrated in the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* that material phenomena have a lifespan of sixteen conscious moments, it is therefore said: “having arisen together with the sixteenth consciousness.
Alternatively, “before the death-consciousness” means taking the death-consciousness as the limit (the boundary), [the kamma] arises together with the sixteenth consciousness prior to that.
But when the meaning is understood in this way, it is stated that the duration of the in-breaths and out-breaths is seventeen thought-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*).
The connection is made by bringing forward the fact that "these [moments] indeed become manifest to the monk who is devoted to this meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because the object of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānārammaṇa*) has been thoroughly grasped. In order to clarify that very point:
The passage beginning with “of one whose consciousness has ceased” and so forth was stated.
In that context, “the interval of life” means the interval of existence, the limit of the moment of living. “By way of natural law alone” means by its very nature;
the sense is “by way of its own inclination. “Having looked at the moonlight” means, during the bright fortnight at the time of dusk, as if a stream of milk were being poured out from all sides.

Having seen the vault of the sky and the surface of the earth strewn with sand resembling silver plates, he thought, "How delightful indeed is this time and place, so much like my own disposition! How long must this burden of suffering be borne?

Thus, having reflected upon his own life-formations (*āyu-saṅkhāra*), his intention was that they were now exhausted. "Having drawn a line" means having drawn a line across the walking path (*caṅkama*).
"Anuyuñjetha" means he should apply himself; the sense is "he should cultivate.
Commentary on the Recollection of Peace (Upasamānussati-kathā-vaṇṇanā):

"Evam" means in the manner already described for recollecting qualities such as dispassion (*virāga*). "Of that which is reckoned as the allaying of all suffering" refers to that which is designated as "the allaying of all suffering" (*sabbadukkhūpasama*) because all suffering—including its divisions such as the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*)—is allayed therein.

In passages such as “phenomena that are mere designations” (*paññattidhammā*), even that which lacks an intrinsic nature (*asabhāva*) is called a “phenomenon” (*dhamma*) because it is borne and determined by knowledge;
therefore, in order to exclude those [designations], he says, “phenomena are intrinsic natures” (*sabhāvā*). Existence (*bhāva*) is the state of being found in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*);
together with existence they are “intrinsic natures” (*sabhāvā*), meaning they possess a form that is obtainable from the standpoint of the true and ultimate sense. For they, by their own...
They are called *dhammas* because they bear their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); in the sense already stated, they are also called "intrinsic natures" (*sabhāva*).
"Having come together" (*saṅgamma*) means having assembled by way of a coming-together characterized by the convergence of conditions. "Having met" (*samāgamma*) is a synonym for that same term.
"By conditions" (*paccayehi*) means by appropriate conditions. "Produced" (*katā*) means brought into existence. "Unproduced" (*akatā*) means not produced by any conditions whatsoever.
"Made. The reason for the plural form "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhatā*) has already been stated above. "It is declared the foremost" means it is declared as the best;

the letter *m* is used merely for metrical euphony (*padasandhikaro*). That phenomenon possessing its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhammo*), which is characterized by the unconditioned, should be understood as "dispassion" (*virāgo*), because defiled phenomena are dispassioned (*virajjati*) therein.
It is abandoned by the Noble Path as it proceeds having made Nibbāna its object.
Having reached that [state], pride, intoxication, and so forth are said to be abandoned; thus it is said: "Depending on that... they perish.

In this context, "pride-intoxication" (*mānamada*) refers specifically to the pride that proceeds by way of conceiving thoughts such as "I am superior. "Intoxication of manhood" (*purisamada*) is the intoxication arising in dependence upon the male state.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of intoxication regarding birth (*jātimada*) and other such forms should be understood. They are "devoid of intoxication" (*nimmadā*).
"Free from intoxication" (*vigatamada-bhāva*). It is precisely to show this meaning that it is said "intoxication-free" (*amada*). Intoxications are subdued here;
they go to destruction, reaching a state free from intoxication—thus it is "the subduing of intoxication" (*madanimmadana*). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

"Thirst for sensual pleasures" (*kāmapipāsā*) means the desire to manifest sensual pleasures, i.e., craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*). "The abode of the strands of sensual pleasure" (*kāmaguṇālaya*) means that beings adhere (*āliyanti*) to these very strands of sensual pleasure.
“Threefold existence” (*tebhūmaka*) refers to the round of kamma, defilements, and kamma-results within the three planes of existence. This is the unconditioned dhamma.
“For the sake of successive becoming” means for the sake of one birth after another, from one mode of origin to another. “Binding” is the act of knotting; “sewing” is the act of stitching.
Its “departure” and “escape” consist in dissociation from craving; thus he says, “dissociated.”

Having taken as the basis those qualities for which the names "the crushing of intoxication" (*madanimmadana*) and so forth are conventionally established in relation to Nibbāna, he says, "by way of the qualities such as the crushing of intoxication," referring specifically to the qualities of Nibbāna produced in the manner already described;

however, he does not mean [the phrase] "by this, intoxications are crushed," and so on. For those are the qualities of the Noble Path, whereas these are the qualities of tranquility (*upasama*) taught by the Blessed One.
"Was stated" is the connection [of the sentence]. But where was it stated? In the *Asaṅkhata-saṃyutta* and other such collections. Therein, "truth" (*sacca*) means that which is not false.
For Nibbāna is truth in the sense of being non-perverted, because by any method it is exclusively existent due to the absence of the state of non-existence.
Therefore he said: "There is indeed one truth; there is no second. "The further shore" (*pāra*) means that which has become the opposite bank of *saṃsāra*.
For this very reason it is said: “The brahmin has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land,” and, “Few among men are those people who go to the further shore.

It is “very difficult to see” because, due to its supreme profundity and its exceedingly subtle and peaceful nature, it cannot be seen by those who have not accumulated the requisites of knowledge. There is no aging here.

When this is attained, there is no aging for the person; thus it is "ageless" (*ajara*). For that very reason, because it is not subject to aging and the like, it is "steadfast" (*dhruva*) in the sense of being firm.
Because of the absence of the conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) of craving and so forth, it is "without proliferation" (*niṣprapañca*). Because there is no death here, it is "deathless" (*amṛta*).
Because of the absence of defiled states (*saṃkleśadharma*) that produce the nature of misfortune, it is "blissful" (*śiva*). And because it is unafflicted by the four bonds (*yoga*), [it is secure].
It is secure (*khema*). It is marvelous (*abbhuta*) because of its wonderfulness through the state of being free from conditioned formations (*visaṅkhāra*), and because it has never existed before.
It is free from calamity (*anītika*) due to the absence of all misfortunes and evils. It is invulnerable (*abyābajjha*) because of the absence of suffering.

It is purity (*visuddhi*) because it is supremely pure, being exceptionally cleansed of all defilements and stains. It is an island (*dīpa*) because it cannot be overwhelmed by any of the four floods (*ogha*). [It is the refuge] from all the suffering of saṃsāra...
It is a refuge in the sense of protection.
It should be understood that the textual passage beginning with, “And, monks, I will teach you the Truth,” is abbreviated.

By the word “etcetera” (ādi), it includes such descriptions as infinite, untainted (*anāsava*), subtle (*nipuṇa*), undecaying (*ajajjara*), unworldly (*apalokita*), non-demonstrable (*anidassana*), sublime (*paṇīta*), marvelous (*acchariya*), free from calamity (*anītika*), the Dhamma, the jewel, a cave, the ultimate goal (*parāyaṇa*), profound (*gambhīra*), and so forth.

Furthermore, the qualities not explicitly mentioned here are included [in this term]. Because there is neither arising nor passing away for it, it is "endless" (*ananta*), meaning it is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṅkhata-dhamma*).
Because it is not an object for the taints (*āsava*), it is "taintless" (*anāsava*).

Because it is the domain of subtle knowledge, it is "subtle" (*nipuṇa*). Because it is not subject to decay through aging like a conditioned phenomenon, it is "undecaying" (*ajajjara*). Because it is not afflicted by disease and so forth...

It is "looked upon" (apalokita). It is "non-manifest" (anidassana) because it is not cognizable by visual consciousness. It is "sublime" (paṇīta) in the sense of not producing satiety. It is "marvelous" (acchariya) because of its rarity.
It is a "state free from calamity" (anītika-dhamma) because its nature cannot be overcome by calamities and because it is the cause for the state of being free from calamity.
It is "liberation" (mutti) because it is the sign of release from the suffering of saṃsāra. It is a "refuge" (leṇa) because it is a place of shelter for those who view saṃsāra as fearful.

It is the "supreme resort" (*parāyaṇa*) because it is the ultimate goal for those very [beings]. It is "profound" (*gambhīra*) in the sense of being unfathomable because it finds no foothold through ordinary knowledge.
It is "difficult to awaken to" (*duranubodha*) because it must be realized with difficulty and hardship even by those who have performed meritorious deeds.

It is "not within the sphere of ratiocination" (*atakkāvacara*) because it cannot be traversed by speculative knowledge apart from direct realization. It is [so called] because it is to be known and attained only by the wise, such as the Buddhas and others.
The meaning should be understood as "to be experienced by the wise.
It succeeds only for a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka), because through the realization of direct knowledge (sacchikiriyābhisamaya), the qualities of Nibbāna become manifest.

Furthermore, this word *eva* is used in the wrong place [in the compound]; the construction should be "it succeeds indeed" (*ijjhati eva*). Alternatively, it is stated thus because of the attainment of ease (*sukhasiddhi*).
“Only for a noble disciple. For this very reason, he said, “Even though this is so,” and so forth. “By one who respects tranquility” means by one who is inclined toward Nibbāna.

The aforementioned qualities of tranquility are to be brought to mind. What should be said regarding the phrases “he sleeps happily,” and so on, will be made clear in the discourse on loving-kindness (*mettā*).
“He is intent upon what is sublime” because he is intent upon Nibbāna.
The commentary on the exposition of the meditation subjects consisting of recollections is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the eighth chapter.
9. Commentary on the Exposition of the Divine Abidings (Brahmavihāra).

Commentary on the Discussion of the Cultivation of Loving-kindness (Mettābhāvanākathāvaṇṇanā) 240. Regarding "loving-kindness" (mettā), it refers to the divine abode (brahmavihāra). "By one desiring to cultivate" means by one desiring to produce [it]; this is to be connected with the word "should reflect upon" (paccavekkhitabbo). "Sitting comfortably" means sitting not unevenly, but with the legs crossed in the full lotus posture (pallaṅka).
"Why? is a question regarding the reason for the reflection; for one desiring to attain something else, there is a reflection upon the disadvantages and advantages elsewhere.
The intended meaning is: "What is its purpose? Loving-kindness (*mettā*), in terms of its essential nature, is non-hatred (*adosa*).

For it is stated in the description of non-hatred: "friendliness, the act of being friendly, the state of being friendly. Furthermore, by "patience" (*khanti*) here, patience as endurance is intended.
That, however, in terms of its essential nature, consists of the four formless aggregates dominated by non-hatred; thus, when loving-kindness is accomplished, there is the patience of endurance.
He says, "Patience is to be attained," because it is indeed already accomplished [in this sense]. By this, he shows that reflecting upon the benefits of patience is its advantage (*satthika*).
One is "overcome" by the obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*). One has a "mind overwhelmed" by the failure to find an opportunity for the arising of wholesome states.
The danger (*ādīnava*) is to be seen through the act of killing living beings and so forth, because it is the root of harm both in the present life and in future lives.

"Patience is the supreme austerity": patience, characterized by forbearance such as enduring harm from others, is the highest austerity because it serves as the root of right practice, which is characterized by refraining from what should not be done and performing what should be done.
"The army of the power of patience": patience itself is the power of this [army], for it is the supreme blessing;
thus it is called the power of patience. For it is said: "Ascetics and brahmins possess the power of patience. This is because it is capable of dispelling the opposites, such as hatred.
And by that very army of patience, which has become his vanguard, he forms an army of strength.
There is no support superior to patience, for it wards off harm for oneself and others and brings about benefit.
"For the sake of seclusion" means for the sake of suppression. The intention is: "for the purpose of binding oneself through patience."

They are called "faults" (*dosa*) because they corrupt meditative development (*bhāvanā*). "Faults of persons" (*puggaladosā*) refers to persons themselves who are faults. Those in whom meditative development does not succeed, but rather utterly fails, are the ones so described.
"First" means, according to the method of introducing one section from another, the very first of all, without reference to the subsequent sections that will be explained.
One who is to be loved is "dear" (*piya*); its opposite is "unloved" (*appiya*). Briefly, this is of two kinds: one who does not produce benefit (*attha*) and one who produces harm (*anattha*).
"An evildoer. In this context, one who brings about harm to oneself and to those dear to oneself should be regarded as an enemy.

Furthermore, one who fails to bring about what is beneficial for oneself and for those dear to oneself, but instead brings about what is harmful to those who are not dear, and who thus becomes a basis for resentment according to such thoughts as "He has not acted for my benefit," or "He has acted for the benefit of those who are not dear or are unpleasant to me"—[this person is an evildoer].
“Unpleasant” means not agreeable in conduct; the sense is that he is undesirable. “Of a different gender” means one who is dissimilar by way of gender, such as the female gender and so forth.
“Partially” means by way of portions; the sense is “partially,” as in the expression “Tissa’s gift” and so forth.
Now, showing the reason why [these] six types of persons mentioned above should not be cultivated, he says: “For the unpleasant,” and so forth.
In this context, "one who places an unloved person in the position of a loved one tires" indicates that the development [of loving-kindness] is beset with danger due to hatred (*dosa*).
For aversion is the direct opposite of affection, and the development does not reach completion without placing that person in the position of a loved one.
"One who places an excessively dear friend in the position of a neutral person tires" indicates that the development [of loving-kindness] is beset with danger due to lust (*rāga*).

He speaks of the state of being attended by danger because [the relationship] with a very dear friend is a basis for affection rooted in the household life. Therefore he said, “Even in regard to a mere trifle,” and so forth.
A neutral person (*majjhatta*) is one whose nature is intermediate between the desirable and the undesirable; the meaning is that such a person is neither dear nor undear.

One who places [another] in the position of a teacher or in the position of a dear one becomes weary, because in a neutral person there is an absence of both esteem and the quality of being worthy of endearment. Not...
For there is a state of being cultivated even in those who are to be regarded with equanimity, or rather, attractiveness presents itself;
and loving-kindness should first be developed toward one who possesses both endearment and respect. Anger arises because [the object] is not brought into the state of another [suitable] division.

"That very same" refers to the very same dissimilar characteristic. By saying "toward a dear person" without making a distinction, he means "one who shares a similar characteristic. "He engaged in a wall-fight" means:
Having resolved upon virtue, while sitting on a couch inside a room with its doors closed, he was practicing loving-kindness (*mettā*).

Blinded by the passion that had arisen through the medium of that loving-kindness, and desiring to go to his wife, he failed to notice the door and struck the wall, wishing to break through it in order to exit.
Therefore it is said: "Passion deceives by way of the face of loving-kindness."
“And then it is blinding darkness, when passion overcomes a man.

Furthermore, regarding the continuity of the aggregates—which is delimited by grasping and casting off, which belongs to the present time, and which is perceived as if directly before one’s eyes due to its ongoing existence—it is here that the terms “being” and so forth are employed;
they do not refer to [beings] existing in the three times. Thus he says, “But when [someone] has passed away,” and so on.
But why does the development of loving-kindness not succeed when directed toward one who has passed away? Because such a person is an unsuitable object for the exercise of loving-kindness.
Indeed, a deceased individual is no longer capable of receiving the bringing of benefit.

Only where the bringing of benefit can be obtained through practical application, provided that such a possibility exists, is mental cultivation of benefit appropriate. This applies equally to the removal of suffering and the manifestation of joy.

The phrase "this same method" should be understood as indicating that non-reflective contemplation (*anijjhāna*) is prescribed even for the cultivation of compassion (*karuṇā*) and the other [immeasurables] when a person has died.

Elsewhere, it is said that a teacher who was proficient in the jhāna of loving-kindness (*mettā*), being unaware of his own death and desiring to pervade him with loving-kindness, "directs loving-kindness toward the teacher.
Therefore, he said: "My attainment of the jhāna of loving-kindness is indeed proficient. Regarding the term "sign" (*nimitta*):
“Object. “Search” means: “Find out whether the person for whose sake you have merely begun this practice is alive or not”—this is the meaning.
“Practicing loving-kindness” (mettāyanto) means practicing loving-kindness; the meaning is developing loving-kindness. 241.

“Cultivation within oneself” (attani bhāvanā) is for the purpose of being a witness [to one’s own progress]; it consists of various kinds of happiness, such as continuous happiness, blameless happiness, and unadulterated happiness.
Demonstrating that which is found within himself, he says, "I am happy," because of its present occurrence.
Since bodily happiness is not constant, and since such a person has no room for mental suffering, he says "or free from suffering" with reference to the absence of that [suffering].
This connects with the word "am. Likewise in the cases of "free from enmity" and so forth, and especially—

The perception of happiness exists in the absence of suffering. This state of being free from suffering arises because of the absence of hostile persons, of those perceived as enemies, and of evil states;
specifically, it arises from the absence of the distress known as *īti* due to the lack of ill-will (*byāpāda*), and from the possession of blameless bodily happiness.
Showing this, he said: "Free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, happy. "I maintain myself" means being thus established.
"Having offered [it], I maintain my own person; 'I sustain myself' is the meaning.
Such being the case, the connection is that what was stated in the *Vibhaṅga* would be contradicted.

"Such being the case" means if this were so—that is, if loving-kindness (*mettā*) must also be cultivated toward oneself. Having said, "What was stated in the *Vibhaṅga*," [he refers to] the teaching in the *Vibhaṅga*.
Citing a sutta passage that shares the same purport, he said, “And how, bhikkhus,” and so forth. Its meaning will be explained further on.
“That” refers to the statement found in the Vibhaṅga and other texts. “By way of absorption” means by way of the development that leads to absorption.
“This” refers to the statement, “May I be happy,” and so forth. “By way of being a witness” means: just as I, so all beings desire their own happiness.
"Therefore, I must bring about the instilling of happiness in them just as I do in myself"—this is how one establishes oneself as a witness in that regard.
Hence he said, "Even if," and so forth. But why is it that meditation upon oneself does not lead to absorption (*appanā*)?
Because, due to self-attachment, it remains subject to danger. However, for one who has cultivated the meditation on other parts, even there—
There is indeed a breaking of the boundary.
"All directions" means the ten directions without exception. "Having traversed with the mind" means having followed along by way of mental searching.
"He did not find anything anywhere dearer than himself" means that even while searching with every effort, he found nothing superior to himself.
One would not find or see any other being anywhere in any direction more dear than oneself.
Thus, because each individual self of every various being is dear— since no being is found to be dearer than one's own self—
for that reason, one who desires their own welfare [should act accordingly].
"Desiring welfare and happiness for another being—even down to a tiny ant or an insect—one should not harm, nor should one kill, nor should one oppress them; this is the meaning.
"This is the method" means that, having demonstrated how all beings are dearer to oneself than oneself, one should cultivate compassion toward them.

The meaning is that by the Blessed One, when speaking on the basis of ease, he has indeed demonstrated the method for the development of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*) thus: “Loving-kindness should be developed toward beings, setting oneself as the witness.
(242) “For the purpose of proceeding with ease” means for the purpose of proceeding with loving-kindness without difficulty. “Yvāssa” means whoever...

The person would be a practitioner (*yogin*). "Dear" means desired. "Pleasant" means increasing the mind's delight. "Venerable" means worthy of being honored by virtue of specific qualities. "One to be cultivated" means one who should be respected.

"A mere teacher" means one whose measure is that of a teacher in terms of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "affectionate speech and so forth," it includes beneficial conduct and the like.

By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "virtue, learning, and so forth," it includes faith and the like, as well as the practice of the ascetic virtues (*dhutaṅga*) and the application of vigilance (*jāgariyānuyoga*).
The particle *kāmaṃ* is an indeclinable used to illuminate the accomplishment of happiness through acting appropriately and at the right time. By this, he illuminates the following:
a yogi who begins his meditation directed toward such a person acts appropriately, and his meditation therein succeeds with ease;
yet, that yogi should not be satisfied with only that much. Therefore, he said, "Absorption is attained," and so forth. Regarding "the breaking down of boundaries":

The removal of boundaries means not making distinctions such as "I am dear," "neutral," or "an enemy. "Immediately after that" means immediately following that state of being dear, beloved, respected, and venerable;
or, it refers to the immediate sequence after the attainment of loving-kindness (*mettā*) therein.

The connection is that loving-kindness should be developed toward one who is very dear as a friend; [one should apply] the attention to loving-kindness acquired toward those in the position of a teacher to one who is very dear as a friend.
The meaning is "should be brought near. That [loving-kindness] belongs to one who brings about happiness, all the more so because opposing states have been suppressed.

Immediately after the very dear friend, loving-kindness should be developed toward the neutral person, because it is easy to establish the neutral person in the position of a beloved and respected one. And the phrase "from the very dear friend" refers to the preceding stage.
Thus it is said. For from the moment one attains proficiency in mental attention (*manasikāra*), even that [neutral person] stands in the very place of the beloved.

Regarding "from neutrality toward hostile persons": while one is practicing loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward neutral persons, having brought about a state of being dear through the attainment of proficiency in mental attention therein, one immediately thereafter establishes the hostile person in neutrality through meditation; then—
Loving-kindness toward a hostile person should be developed by introducing the state of being dear through the state of neutrality.
And the phrase "toward a hostile person" is stated by referring to the previous stage.

Having made the mind soft and wieldy in each section—namely, among the four categories of persons, the one held in high esteem as dear, the very dear one, the neutral one, and the hostile one—one should first, in the first place...

Having attained mastery over the development of loving-kindness toward a dear person who is an object of affection, one should make the mind pliant and wieldy for the purpose of withdrawing it from that state and directing it toward another part.

Immediately thereafter, by suppressing the quality of extreme endearment toward a very dear friend and fixing the mind on mere dearness, the development should be brought to completion; this too is done by attaining mastery.
Having made it pliant and workable, one should immediately thereafter suppress the state of neutrality toward the neutral person and establish a sense of endearment,
and then apply the meditation. Again, having made even that pliant and workable by bringing it under mastery,
one should immediately thereafter suppress the perception of enmity toward the enemy by means of establishing a state of neutrality.
One who is generating a state of endearment should apply the meditation. Therefore it was said:
"In each subsequent instance, one should apply it"; the meaning is that the jhāna-consciousness should be brought near and generated.
Or else, there is no hostile person, either by the power of karma or by the excellence of current application, who causes absolute harm.

"By way of non-existence. "Because he is of the nature of a Great Man" means because he possesses the character of a Great Man; the meaning is that he has a sublime disposition due to being endowed with qualities such as patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, which have been perfected through long-term cultivation. For one such as this, being all-enduring, does not regard even the transgression of another as even a blade of grass.
Therefore it was said: "Even when others do him harm, the perception of them as enemies does not arise. "By him" means by that yogin. There is...
The connection is with the phrase "hostile person. 243.
"In the case of the preceding persons" means in the case of the preceding persons, such as the beloved and others, who have become the objects of the jhāna.
"Having entered upon loving-kindness" means having entered upon the jhāna of loving-kindness that has been produced by suppressing aversion. By one practicing loving-kindness...
Regarding the phrase "aversion should be dispelled," some here state that the meaning is "having accomplished access concentration.
For them, it would follow that emerging from access concentration must also be intended, because of the statement "having emerged.
Previously, for one who does not give rise to aversion toward that person through non-attention and non-mindfulness, that [dispelling] occurs in a general sense.
The arising and attainment of jhāna by means of suppression have already been described.
Now, however, in order to show the method by which aversion does not arise even for one who recollects or attends to that person, it is said:
