"One should dispel aversion by loving-kindness toward that person. For here, loving-kindness itself is the dispelling of aversion.
This is the intended meaning. "Does not go out" means it does not subside.
"By following" means by pursuing; the sense is "by reviewing. "Should be striven for" means one should exert effort.
And that striving, that exertion, is [to be done] in this manner which will now be explained.
"Ubhatodaṇḍakaṃ" means that which has a staff at both ends; by that [staff]. "Ocarakā" refers to men of base conduct, wicked persons.
"Tatrāpi" means even when their limbs have been entered [by the staff]. "Tenā" means by mental corruption. "Na sāsanakaro":

for the non-doing of all evil is the teaching (sāsana). "Tasseva" means from that as well; this is the genitive case used in the sense of the ablative, and it is also used in the sense of conjunction.
The word *eva* means "even from a person who has first become angry. *Tenā* means "by that anger. *Pāpiyo* means "more wicked.

Some say: "Even though one knows the blameworthiness of anger because it serves as the basis for the persistence of defilements such as resentment (*sārambha*), if one perceives anger as blameless and does not retaliate against an angry person, [there is no fault]. *Ubhinnaṃ* means...
Of two persons. Therefore he said, "of oneself and of another. Alternatively, "of both" means of both worlds;

that is, of this world and the world beyond. "Desirable to enemies" means desired by adversaries. "Producing enmity" means that which is to be done by them. "Angry" means having a disposition to anger.
*Kodhanāyanti* means "this one is prone to anger"; *ayanti* is merely a particle. *Kodhapareto* means "overcome by anger" or "subjugated by another.
*Dubbaṇṇo va hoti* means that even if one is naturally handsome or well-adorned and prepared, one becomes deformed right now through facial distortions and so forth, and likewise in the future.
This is stated to illustrate that this is the certain fruit of being overcome by anger.
Having established the restriction with the words “or ugly,” it is further stated that he is “overcome by anger. “Not possessing abundant wealth” means not having much property.
“Not possessing enjoyments” means being devoid of the means for use and enjoyment. “Not possessing fame” means not having a good reputation.
“The torch of a corpse” means the flame of a funeral pyre; some also say it refers to the firebrand cast out from the cremation mound. “Blazing on both sides” means...
"Burnt at both ends": smeared in the middle with excrement—that is, smeared in the middle portion with the excrement vomited up by a dog or a jackal.
"For the purpose of firewood" means for the sake of wood-work. "It serves neither its purpose nor is it effective.
"I [regard] this as being like that" means I regard this as similar, of such a kind. "This"—refers to what was stated below, beginning with "And he is covetous," and so forth.
The Teacher speaks with reference to what has been stated; therefore, the intended meaning is that one is devoid of virtue due to intense passion for sensual pleasures and so forth.
Here, however, a mind of ill-will (*byāpannacitta*) should be connected with the state of having a corrupted mental intention (*paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappatā*).
The passage beginning "Now, you... and so forth is a demonstration of the manner of self-admonition by means of the scriptural passages as they have been explained.

244. "Whichever dhamma" refers to whichever dhamma of good conduct among bodily conduct and so forth. "Tranquil" means restrained. "Pure" means purified by the removal of the stains of the defilements;
or, it is tranquil because of the absence of the burning of the defilements, and pure because of its blameless nature.
The tranquility of bodily conduct itself should be understood as the state of having restrained bodily action for a long period of time. The same applies to the others as well.
Regarding those modes of conduct of speech and mind:
"He" refers to the person whose conduct of speech is tranquil.
"Skilled in hospitality" means one who is skilled in providing hospitality such that others find no fault. "Gentle" means endowed with a gentle nature characterized by forbearance and patience.
"Easy to speak with" means one whose speech is pleasant. "Greeting" means one whose nature is to greet with words of welcome.

"Open-faced" means not having a frowning face, but rather a face blossomed by joy and gladness. "One who speaks first" means one whose nature is to be the first to address another upon meeting anyone, by way of social courtesy.
He causes the Dhamma to be concluded with a sweet voice.
By way of recitation (*sarabhañña*). Furthermore, one who performs recitation delivers a discourse on the Dhamma with words and phrasing that are rounded, complete, and unconfused.
The intention is that it is made manifest to all people through careful performance. Therefore he said, "For whoever," and so forth. "Having established [conviction]" (*okappetvā*):
"Having placed faith. For faith has the characteristic of conviction (*okappana*). "With attentive ears" means with focused ears;
the sense is that one is desirous of hearing. "Making it a bone," meaning making it a matter of vital importance, or being one who possesses such need.
Regarding the reading, "Not even one is pacified": such a person, passing from hell to hell, remains for a long time.
It is said, "He will fill the eight great hells and the sixteen secondary hells," in order to show that he transmigrates right there.

Among these, the Sañjīva and others are the eight great hells. At each of the gates of the Avīci great hell, four each are placed, making the sixteen secondary hells such as Kukkuḷa and the rest. Compassion should be established toward him because of his state of being a partaker of great suffering.
In whatever person the desire to remove suffering, which is free from harmfulness, is established, there is no room for aversion;
thus it is said: "On account of compassion, resentment is stilled.
And "of this meaning" refers to the meaning stated by the passage beginning with "Whichever phenomenon... and so forth.

245. That which an enemy is able to cause suffering to is called "his own domain" (*visaya*) by way of that [enemy]; this refers to the body of the bhikkhu. Why? For what reason? "His" (*tassa*) means the enemy's.
"In a non-domain" (*avisaye*) means in a sphere where it is impossible for him to produce suffering.

"In his own mind" (*sacitte*) means in his own consciousness. "Causing great harm" (*mahānatthakaraṃ*) refers to the welfare of this world, the welfare of the next world, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*).
By way of violation, it is the cause of great, extensive, and manifold harm, categorized as pertaining to the present life and so forth.
"The cutting off of the root" means that the roots of virtue are indeed shame (*hirī*), fear of wrongdoing (*ottappa*), patience (*khanti*), loving-kindness (*mettā*), and compassion (*anuddayā*);
it is the severing of these. For anger, as it arises, cuts away shame and the other virtues by way of killing living beings and so forth. "Dull-witted" means a blind fool.
“Un-Ariyan action” refers to a great offense committed by an enemy. “Even you yourself” means even you, who are the one [speaking]. “Desiring to cause anger” means desiring to arouse wrath.
“Whether he did it or whether he did not” means regardless of whether he committed the act. “By the production of anger” means by the arising of hatred.
“And suffering for him indeed” means that there is indeed suffering for that offender. “Indeed” (*nāma*) is a particle used in the sense of emphasizing something improbable; therefore—
He shows that the reason for this is not certain. Therefore he said, "Whether you will do it or not," which means "you will either perform it or you will not.
"The path leading to one's own harm" refers to the path of an evil destination (duggati) that brings about one's own ruin. Regarding the phrase "in an improper place":
hatred is what causes harm to the one who is disagreeable to you, whereas an enemy is like a slave because of being subject to his control.
It is impossible to retaliate against that which has already passed. Therefore, cut away that very fault; utterly eradicate it.

"Momentariness" (*khaṇikatā*) means that these [phenomena] possess a moment (*khaṇa*), defined as the duration of their own occurrence, which is delimited by arising and passing away; thus, the meaning is "the state of being subject to destruction in every moment.
"With whom now here are you angry? refers to those aggregates within the continuum of the wrongdoer by whom the offense was committed.
Those [actions] were done, and at that very moment they have ceased entirely. But now, others are present;
toward whom, then, do you feel anger here? For it is not fitting to be angry with those who are innocent—this is the intended meaning. Without him, toward whom would he act?
That is to say, apart from the person who is the object of the infliction of suffering, toward whom could he perform that act of causing pain?

"Let that one who causes suffering cause suffering. "You too are a cause of suffering for him"—thus, since you yourself are likewise a cause of this suffering for him, being equal in your status as a cause of that suffering for both him and yourself, for what reason do you become angry with him and not with yourself? This is the meaning.
246. Because it follows them even into the next world, karma alone is their own property; thus they are "owners of their karma" (*kammassakā*).
The state of being such is "ownership of one's karma" (*kammassakatā*). The term "reviewing" (*paccavekkhaṇā*) is for the purpose of restraint;
and since that restraint concerns future karma, he says, "whatever karma you will do. However, karma that proceeds by way of aversion is "near" because its manifestation is evident.
He said "this too" (*idañca*) to indicate direct perception (*paccakkha*). The word *ca* (and) is used here in the sense of contrast (*byatireka*);
it illuminates the meaning that is being stated in contrast to that karma, by means of its result and outflow (*phala-nissanda*), in the passage beginning with "not even perfect enlightenment.

The connection is "they are not capable. It is called *nerayika* because it is connected to hell (*niraya*), or because it is born there. The intended meaning is that one is besmeared with the dust of hatred, as if covering oneself.
247. One should reflect upon the virtues of the Teacher’s former conduct; moreover, through reverence for the Teacher, one should pacify resentment.
The intention is: "Even when you were a bodhisatta, did your Teacher not fail to corrupt your mind, let alone now that he has attained full enlightenment?
"By one corrupted by the queen" means: having offended against her through misconduct, having transgressed with her. Where...
A corpse is discarded in a cemetery; that is a "raw" cemetery (*āmaka-susāna*). "Being buried" means being dug into the earth.
"Having exerted human effort" means having exerted the strength of one's arms to emerge from the pit.
"By the power of a *yakkha*" means by the power of a *yakkha* whose mind had been won over by the distribution of wealth. "The inner chamber of glory" refers to the dwelling house.
“Āsīsetheva” means that one should form an aspiration for the intended goal in a manner that is rational and blameless.
“Na nibbindeyya” means one should not become despondent, thinking, “Since I have fallen into such distress, how can there be safety for me? For it has been said:
“In times of calamity, O Great King, one’s fortitude must be known. “Yathā icchinti” means in whatever way one desires [to rule] over a kingdom without causing oppression to anyone.
I desired a self established; thus I perceive it as "I am. *Vā* is merely a particle.
"By the King of Kāsi" means by the King of Kāsi, Kalābu. "With thorns" means with iron thorns, together with thorns.
"An old man" means one who has reached advanced age. "Are obstructed" means they cease.
"The time for grasping the mind" means the time for properly taming the mind without giving it an opportunity to indulge in its habitual tendencies.
"With a broad dart" means with a wide dart. "The elephant" refers to a noble elephant. "He slew" means he pierced, or alternatively, he killed.
"Having come to this place, doing such a thing to me does not happen by your own power; therefore, [it was done] by whom, or by which king..."
The meaning is that this is an instigation for one who is intoxicated by power, or for a king.

"Six-colored rays" refers to six-colored beams of light, such as blue, yellow, red, and so forth. Indeed, those elephants are called "six-tusked" (*chaḍḍanta*) because they possess tusks with six-colored rays, not because they possess six tusks.
"Hungry" means starving. "Should eat" means he would eat; or rather, this is the reading itself. "Satiated" means well-fed. "Provisions" (*sambala*).
It is food for the path. Since it is said that it is beneficial for the path by way of its proximity (*upacāra*), it is therefore also called "provisions for the journey" (*pātheyya*).
Looking at that man with eyes filled with tears out of compassion, thinking, "Alas, this blind fool is a betrayer of his friends," [the text says]:
"Do not, O Noble One, [be] mine, O Venerable Sir. Here, *mā* is merely a particle; or, *mā* is a negation, by which—[in the following]—with him...
It prevents the manifestation of such a transformation. "Ayyo me" means "you are my noble one" because of your status as my guest.
"Bhadante" is a term of affectionate address. "Tvaṃ nāmetādisaṃ karī" means "even you have indeed done such a thing.
The construction is: "Even though he was an animal, having become a great monkey, he brought [me] to a place of safety."

"Even when throwing into a basket" means even when kicking with his feet and throwing him into a small basket. "Even when crushing" means even when crushing him in various ways for the purpose of making him weak. "Alampāna" refers to a snake-charmer of that name. "Or yellow" (*pītaṃ vā*): here the word *vā* (or) is used in the sense of an alternative for what has not been mentioned;
by it, he includes [colors] not mentioned, such as white, madder-red, and so forth.
"Following the mind" (*cittānuvattanto*) means following the mind [of the snake-charmer], thinking: "I shall become like what is thought [by him]; may this man thus obtain abundant gain."
"By means of his psychic power (*ānubhāva*), he could turn land into water... [and so on]... or turn it into ashes.
But if, by thus mastering the mind, the supreme goal were not accomplished, then the Blessed One shows the danger (*ādīnava*) he himself had perceived therein.
Therein, 'the supreme goal' refers to the state of Buddhahood. 'By the sons of Bhoja' means by the sons of hunters (*luddaputta*)."
“Aḷāra” is how he addresses that caravan leader by name, who had then liberated him from the hands of the hunter. “Having pulled back” means having pulled the rope fastened to his nose.
“Having completely surrounded” means having encircled him entirely with black *vetta* creepers, rattan, and so forth;
the intended meaning is that these were marvelous [in their power] for enduring what is otherwise unbearable.

It is extremely improper and unsuitable to give rise to a mind of resentment, because it involves the failure to possess the quality of incomparable patience and leads to a departure from the Teacher’s dispensation.

248. The phrase beginning with “Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning” refers to the *anamatagga* word, or those discourses whose meaning is that [word] are called *anamataggiyāni*.
A path traveled by goats is an *ajapatha*. A path traveled by supporting oneself while holding onto stakes driven into the ground is a *saṅkupatha*.
"Saṅkūti" refers to making a long staff in the shape of a hook. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes precipitous paths, difficult roads, and so forth.
"Arrayed on both sides" (*ubhatobyūḷha*) means having both wings tightly armored for the purpose of combat.
The intention is that, having performed other difficult feats, one leaps into mountain fastnesses, river ravines, and the like out of hope for wealth.
The connection is as follows: "He nourished me; he did me a favor; it is not fitting to corrupt my mind toward him"—thus should one generate such a thought.
And this generation of thought is to be understood by way of grasping the past through inference from what is currently seen, namely, the nourishing of children and so forth.
"By loving-kindness" means by that which is designated as loving-kindness, or by that which is accompanied by loving-kindness.
"Liberation of mind" refers to the concentration of the mind. "Cultivated" means practiced with care. "Developed" means increased. "Made much of" means performed repeatedly.
"Made a vehicle" means made like a yoked vehicle. "Made a foundation" means made like a basis for resolve.
"Anuṭṭhitāya" means established. "Paricitāya" means cultivated, having attained mastery through practice. "Susamāraddhāya" means well-accomplished.
"Pāṭikaṅkhā" means desirable, as they are bound to occur. The remainder will follow later. 250.
"Dhātuvinibbhoga" means the analytical separation of the elements by way of the concise grouping of the constituent parts and so forth. "Aparādha" means... [text ends]
Having considered that the person who is not offending is apprehended by way of the phenomena of form (*rūpadhamma*), he said, "Why are you angry with the hairs of the head?
and so forth; for there is no such thing as a person who does not offend apart from the hair and other [constituents].

Now, in order to demonstrate the method of analysis (*vinibbhoga*) solely by means of the produced ultimate phenomena (*paramatthadhamma*), he stated, "Or alternatively," and so forth. [This refers to] depending upon the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*) and the twelve bases (*dvādasāyatana*).
"Depending on" (*upādāya*) means that the word "depending on" should be applied to each [term].
"There is no place for anger to settle" means that just as there is no place for a mustard seed to settle on the point of an awl, nor for a painting in the sky,
so too there is no place for anger to settle upon a person imagined to be "an enemy," because the hair and other parts [of the body] are not objects of anger.
And because of the non-existence of a person who is free from craving.
251. "Sharing" means sharing material goods (*āmisa-saṃvibhāga*). "Of another" means of an adversary. "One of broken livelihood" means one of impure livelihood.
"To him who acts thus" refers to that donor who performs such sharing. "Of the other" refers to the recipient.
“Given by my mother, a female lay follower”—this is the explanatory statement for the phrase “a righteous gain.
By means of that, he demonstrates the purity of its source.
It is “the accomplisher of all aims” because it accomplishes one’s own welfare, the welfare of others, the aim pertaining to the present life, and the aim pertaining to the future life.
It is the producer of all such aims, benefits, and purposes. The givers rise up;
the recipients bow down.

252. "Thus" (*evam*) refers to the modes of self-admonition by means of the aforementioned similes, such as the simile of the saw and the recollection [of the Buddha], and so forth. "Of one whose aversion has been stilled" (*vūpasantapaṭighassa*).
[This refers to] one whose ill will has been dispelled by the power of reflection. "In him too" means even in the person who is an enemy.

By the mention of the "enemy" (*verī*) here, the inclusion of the "unpleasant person" (*appiya-puggala*) should also be understood; for when loving-kindness toward the enemy is established, it is established toward that [unpleasant person] as well.

However, the separate mention of the "dear friend" (*piya*) and the "very dear companion" (*atippiya-sahāyaka*) is for the purpose of showing that the "near adversary" (*āsanna-paccatthika*) is difficult to liberate.

"By way of loving-kindness" means by way of exercising loving-kindness. "Equanimity of mind" means a state of even-mindedness through the promotion of welfare. "Breaking down of boundaries" is that very same equanimity of mind.

"Toward this person" refers to the person who has loving-kindness as their meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "While sitting" is the locative case used to indicate the state of being in relation to another state.
"Welfare and neutrality" refers to those who are dear and those who are neutral. "Fourfold" refers to the four types of persons; "anywhere whatsoever" [refers to the scope of the practice].
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Diversity" (*nānatta*) refers to the various distinctions such as those between the beloved, the neutral, and so forth.

One who is "merely well-disposed toward living beings" is said to be one whose mind is solely intent on their welfare; however, he is not called "one who obtains loving-kindness at will" (*mettāya nikāmalābhī*) nor is he called "virtuous" (*kusalī*).
Why? Because he perceives diversity even with respect to himself and others. But why, then, is this well-disposed person not called "virtuous"?

Because it is the state of being wholesome (*kusalibhāva*) by way of preeminent wholesomeness that is intended here. Furthermore, for this person, the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*) is not distinguished [by success].
Alternatively, one is called "wholesome" because one does not obtain loving-kindness at will, since one perceives diversity in oneself and others;
thus, the meaning here should be understood as: "one is called wholesome because one has a mind intent on the welfare of living beings. This is like the village boundary and so forth.

Because, prior to the development of loving-kindness toward the seven classes of beings such as those within one’s own village, self and the others existed with mutually unmixed boundaries, it is said here that "self and so forth" are called "boundaries"; thus he says, "the four boundaries.
To demonstrate the "intermingling" mentioned in the phrase "they become intermingled," he says, "He pervades equally with loving-kindness," and so on. "Great distinction" means great.

"Distinction" (*visesa*) means excellence or superiority. "By the former" means by one who previously perceived the diversity of self and so forth. "Is not known" (*na ñāyati*) means it is not understood.

253. "The sign" (*nimitta*): just as in the case of meditation subjects such as the *kasiṇa*, the "counterpart sign" (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*)—which serves as the objective domain for *jhāna*—is obtained by way of cultivation through the apprehension of the respective *kasiṇa*-mandala and so forth, based upon the "learning sign" (*uggaha-nimitta*).
It does not stand [before one] in that way; for there is no such thing as a "sign" (nimitta) established here in that manner.
However, this aforementioned breaking down of the boundaries (sīmāsambheda), once attained, is called a "sign" because it is like a sign.

For when that is attained, because of the excellence of the cultivation (bhāvanā), the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are indeed suppressed, the defilements (kilesa) are settled, and the mind is indeed concentrated by access-concentration (upacāra-samādhi).
Therefore he said: "The sign and the access have been attained. "That very sign" refers to the sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta) occurring by way of the breaking down of boundaries.
"Without difficulty" means without trouble; this is because obstacles have already been cleared away all the more so.
"By this much" means by this extent of application to meditation. By this yogi. The meaning of the phrases beginning with "abandoned of five factors" has already been stated above.
“By means of any one of the first jhānas, etc.”—this is stated because those [powers] are common to the transformations that will be explained.
It applies only to one whose mind has reached absorption (appanā), not to one who has merely attained access concentration (upacāra).

Through the attainment of proficiency and strength, and by reaching specific distinctions such as expansion, there is the spreading forth of jhāna by way of directional diffusion, both specifically and generally.
"Various transformations" means having performed various actions.
254. "Accompanied by loving-kindness" (mettāsahagatena) means associated with, conjoined with, and connected to loving-kindness from its arising until its dissolution;

this is the meaning. Furthermore, because it is accompanied by loving-kindness in the manner already described, it is correctly [accomplished] through that method of simultaneous arising and so forth.
Because it has arrived [at the mind], it is therefore said: "endowed with loving-kindness.
Since the word *ceto* (mind) is also used as a synonym for concentration—as in the phrase "higher mind" (*adhicetaso*)—it was stated "with the mind" (*cetasā*) in order to distinguish it from that.
"This" (*etaṃ*) refers to this word. Showing that the encompassing of the directions occurs by way of the encompassing of beings, he said: "of one direction..."
“Based on a being first encompassed [by it]. For beings situated in the various directions are included by the term “directions.
Therefore he said: “It is stated by way of pervading beings contained within a single direction. And pervasion is the contacting of one’s own object by a dhamma that has an object;
it is seeing, grasping, and making into an object through direct experience. Thus he said.
“Pervading” means having touched and made into an object. “Established in the divine abodes” (brahmavihārādhiṭṭhita) means supported by the jhāna of loving-kindness (mettā).

“Thus” (tathā) is a restrictive term; it is a restriction of the form of the simile because it relates to a state that requires such a restriction. “The second” is the pointing out of the thing to be illustrated (upameyya);
for there can be no simile without a thing to be illustrated and its connection with that [simile]. Thus, both of these [are intended].

In order to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “Just as in the east, etc. was stated. Therein, regarding the phrase “likewise the second,” one must supply the words “dwelling having pervaded” to complete the connection. This is also the case for “the third” and “the fourth.

Furthermore, the mention of “immediately after that” refers to the sequence of pervading, not to the sequence of the directions to be pervaded, because the directions have no specifically defined form.

For their status as the second and so forth is according to the sequence of pervasion, not according to their actual form. Therefore he said, "whatever single direction. "Thus" (iti) means in this way;
the meaning is that having pervaded the four directions as described, he dwells having pervaded the upward direction in the same manner. Therefore he said, "by this same method.
This too is an explanation of the meaning of the word "iti" itself. In the text, regarding the words "below" and "across":
The word *pi* is indicated as being elided (*luttaniddiṭṭha*) in order to show this; thus it is said, "also the downward direction and also the horizontal direction.
By this very [statement], it should be understood that the elision of the word *pi* is also demonstrated in cases such as "the second" and so forth.

"In the same way" (*evameva*) is likewise a demonstration of the meaning of the word *iti*. And here, by the term "downward" (*adho*), just as in the case of the hells, the abodes of nāgas, and so on—
It should be understood that by the term "above" (uddha), beings are included wherever they may be in one's own upper direction, such as in the world of the devas; and by the word "etc.
(ādi) in the phrase "neutral, etc.," various distinctions are comprised, such as female and male, noble and ignoble, devas and humans.
"Not wavering even slightly outward" means not falling into even a small amount of distraction away from the meditation subject, nor deviating even a little from the promotion of welfare.

"With all his being" (*sabbattatāya*) means: just as there is a desire for one's own welfare within oneself by means of one's entire selfhood (*attabhāva*), so too [one should practice] loving-kindness toward all beings in every respect.
The meaning is: "he dwells having pervaded. Since it is spoken of in terms of loving-kindness (*mettā*), the word "all" (*sabba*) refers to sentient beings;

and because it is pronounced with a long vowel, he says, "Sabbāvanto means possessing all sentient beings," thereby showing the literal meaning of the term as "the people (pajā) comprised within the aggregate of all sentient beings.
And here, "in every direction" (*sabbadhi*) refers to the directions, while "in every place" (*sabbattha*) refers to the locations.
And it is stated as being non-specific (anodhisopharaṇa) by means of the term "sattodhi" [in the sense of] "all-encompassing through allness.
For it has been said: "for the purpose of seeing without limitation. Terms that convey a single meaning by way of different modes are called *pariyāya*, that is, synonyms.
And the intention here is that words such as "vast" (*vipula*) and so forth are of such a nature. Therefore he said: "Because of the demonstration of such synonyms as 'vast' (*vipula*), etc."

Furthermore, even words already mentioned are taken up again when showing alternative synonyms (*pariyāya*), just as the word *saddhā*, though already stated here as "faith, the act of believing," is stated again in the context of showing synonyms such as the faculties (*indriya*) as "faith, the faculty of faith.

Or, because the word "thus" (*tathā*) or the word "so" (*iti*) was not stated [in the previous summary], [the full formula is given]: "having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness..."
The words *tathā* and *iti* following the phrase "dwells" (*viharati*) do not occur [in that specific formulation] because they refer to the state of pervading and so forth;
therefore, it is said again, "by a mind accompanied by loving-kindness," which is the meaning.
Since stating the very same matter again constitutes a conclusion, he says, "or this was stated by way of a conclusion. But is it not [already] by way of the attainment (*samāpatti*)?

Is this a restatement of what has already been said? This is not a fault, because it is stated specifically for the purpose of completing the description of both the limited and the all-pervading [mettā].

"By the vast" means by the great; and its greatness is due to its taking up the object in its entirety, rather than grasping only a single part of it as is the case with meditation subjects such as foulness (asubha).
Thus he says: "The vastness is to be understood by way of pervasion."

It is called "lofty" (*mahaggata*) because it has reached greatness through such qualities as the capacity to suppress the defilements, or because it has been entered upon by means of the great—namely, sublime zeal, consciousness, energy, and wisdom.
Since this [state] is exclusively of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), it is therefore said to be "lofty by way of plane.

For the conventional usage of the term "lofty" is well-established in reference to the fine-material and immaterial spheres. The phrase "by way of proficiency" (*paguṇavasena*) refers to the prefix *pa-*.
"Multiplied, made much of, and mastered"—the meaning is "by means of its well-developed state.
For it is called "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) because it is impossible to grasp its measure. "By way of having immeasurable beings as its object" means by way of making immeasurable beings its object.

It is "free from enmity" (*avera*) both because it itself is devoid of enmity and because it is the cause for the absence of enmity in those who possess it. Since this pair [of qualities] arises from that...
To show that [he] attains it, it is said: "by the abandoning of the enemy that is ill-will. Because it strikes through the state of mental affliction, it is *byāpajja*—that is, mental unease;
because of the absence of that, it is *abyāpajja*. Therefore he said, "free from suffering" (*niddukkha*).

Furthermore, this state of being free from affliction for him is not due to its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) like that of the fivefold sense-consciousnesses and so forth, but rather from the seclusion from enemies.

Showing [this], he said, "by the abandoning of mental distress. Here, the word "this" refers to the sublime abode of loving-kindness (*mettā-brahmavihāra*) as it has been presented in the *Appamaññāvibhaṅga* and in various passages of the Suttas.
By the word "likewise," there is a classification of its modes (*ākāra*), namely: "in five ways, in seven ways, and in ten ways."

And regarding the transformations (*vikubbanā*) mentioned in the *Paṭisambhidā*, he brings about the absence of division—like that of refined gold—because the teaching has come down through the modes of limited pervasion (*odhisopharaṇa*), unlimited pervasion (*anodhisopharaṇa*), and directional pervasion (*disāpharaṇa*).

However, the only distinction here is that, as in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, the "limited" (*odhi*) of sentient beings is not included. He says "whatever [transformation]" with reference to the transformation itself.

Now, having shown by way of exposition the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-pāḷi* introduced as a summary by means of demonstrating the absence of division, he says “And therein,” etc., in order to provide an explanation of the words not [previously] commented upon (*anuttānapada*). 256.

Therein, regarding the phrase “all beings” (*sabbe sattā*): although the word “all” (*sabba*) may refer to all things in a limited sense, it does not refer to all things in an absolute sense, as in the expression “the knowledge of omniscience” (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), which is defined as “knowing all.
However, [the term here] is delimited by the word “beings” (*sattā*), which refers to one’s own...
Because it exhausts the object without leaving anything remaining, he says: "This is an exhaustive exhaustion. Therein means in that form.

A "being" (satta) is one who is attached or bound by greed through the synonym of desire (*chanda*) and so forth, by way of performing the function of clinging. Alternatively, "therein" (*tatra*) is a locative used in the sense of the instrumental; thus the meaning is "by means of that [greed], such as desire and so forth.

If a being is so called because of being attached (*sattatā*), how can this apply to those free from passion? To this he says: "By a conventional term (*ruḷhīsaddena*)," and so on. It is used by convention among those who are not free from passion.
Or, it is a conventional usage (*ruḷhi*) because it occurs among those who have not yet abandoned passion, due to the continuity of the aggregates bound by the faculties;

or, by extension, it is used for those similar to them who have abandoned passion. Alternatively, having grasped some characteristic (*nimitta*), even when another [object] exists that is likewise endowed with that characteristic, the application of a term to a certain object due to long-standing convention—even in the absence of the actual characteristic—is called a conventional usage (*ruḷhi*), as in the case of "those who go."
Thus, the conventional usage (*ruḷhī*) of the word "being" (*satta*) should be understood in the same way as [the word] "cattle" (*gāvo*).

Alternatively, the designation "being" should be understood as applied to those free from passion (*vītarāga*) by virtue of their past state of existence. Regarding the phrase "due to association with *satva*": here, *satva* means intelligence, energy, or heat;
beings are so called because of association with that, just as a cloth is called "blue" due to association with the quality of blueness.
"Breathing" (*pāṇana*) means that by which one breathes; it refers to inhalation and exhalation (*assāsa-passāsā*). Its activity is "breathing-ness" (*pāṇanatā*); the meaning is:
"by means of that, [namely] through association with inhalation and exhalation. "Because of being born" (*bhūtattā*) means because of being produced by karma and defilements.

Etymologists say "person" (*puggala*) because of filling (*pūraṇa*) and because of falling away (*galana*). For beings, when they are reborn, are as if filling their respective classes of beings (*sattanikāya*), since they fall into every possible state.
And "fall away" (*galanti*) means they pass away (*cavantīti*). For those who have not fully understood the basis (*vathuka*), there arises the designation "self" (*attā*) here;

and since the mind (*citta*) [is also included], it is the "personal existence" (*attabhāva*), which is the body or simply the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*). "That" refers to the pentad of aggregates.

"Having taken up" (*upādāya*) means having grasped, having made the clinging (*upādāna*) the support (*nissaya*). "Because of the occurrence of a mere conceptualization" (*paññattimattasambhavato*) means even though it does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramatthato*).
Because it exists as a mere designation for that which is designated as a "being.

And as for the expression "a being" (*satta*): just as the word *satta*, in the sense already explained, refers to a specific portion [of beings] in its primary sense, yet by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*) it encompasses them all without exception.

"The others too" means the expressions "living being" (*pāṇa*) and so forth; for these too [apply] to those who possess the formless existence (*arūpabhava*), the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), and those endowed with the fourth jhāna and so on.
Because of the absence of inhalation and exhalation, and because of the absence of a person subject to falling into states of deprivation,

these [terms] function only in a limited sense. Having applied [the designation] by way of conventional usage— having, according to that aforementioned convention, superimposed the state of a "living being" or a "person" upon a certain object even though it does not exist there—
if loving-kindness is called "unspecified pervasion" by taking it to mean, in general, synonyms for "sentient beings," then...
Now, with reference to the inquiry as to why [the terms] are stated by means of exactly five aspects, he says “Granted, however,” and so forth. Some, however, have said:
“These words such as ‘beings’ (sattā) and so on were not taken merely for the sake of synonyms, for if they were, it would follow that terms like ‘person’ (jantu) and others should also be included;
rather, they were taken by way of a specific meaning that serves as a characteristic mark. It is with reference to them that he says:
“*Ye pana*,” etc. Therein, “in meaning”: beings (*satta*) in the sense of clinging; living beings (*pāṇa*) in the sense of breathing—such is the meaning.
Showing that for them this [term] is merely a mental construct, he says: “It is contradicted by its being non-specifically pervasive. Why?

Because it would follow that some are beings, some are living beings, and some are persons. Likewise, by not grasping the meaning [correctly], words such as “beings” and so forth are understood as having a limited scope.
The intention is that, instead of grasping the meaning in this way [as limited], one should grasp it as having an unlimited scope according to the method explained previously;
thus he says, "In these," and so forth. "In five modes" means in the five modes of development mentioned in the Pāḷi beginning with "All beings.
"By way of any one" means by way of whichever one [of those five].
257. Now, in order to show the absorption (*appanā*) by discerning it within the twenty-two modes of development (*bhāvanākāra*), the passage beginning with “And here” is stated.

“Free from ill-will” means free from ill-will consisting of mental distress (*domanassa*). “Therefore” means because the distinction of absorption does not arise merely from the analysis of the aforementioned modes;
therefore [it is said]. “In these sections as well” refers even to the divisions such as “May all beings be free from enmity.”

"Whichever [part] becomes clear": although in the preliminary stage one applies attention to various objects through many different modes of mental fixation, at the moment of success in meditation, absorption (*appanā*) occurs by way of whichever part is most familiar and thus most clearly manifest;
this is as it happens in the case of the thirty-two aspects (*dvattiṃsākāra*). Therein, however, the object—
In this context, "the mode of development" (*bhāvanākāra*) is the specific distinction. "Of four" means of four and four; it is stated thus by the elision of the word *byāpani* (extension).
This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

It is expressed according to gender because they are found following those [terms]. As for the third base (*pakati*), although it is not included in the first dyad, it is certainly included in the second dyad and the triad.

Thus, all these together—twenty in the case of non-specific pervasion, twenty-eight in the case of specific pervasion, and four hundred and eighty in the case of directional pervasion—all these [are included]. The neuter designation is used in view of the word *sata* (hundred).
258. Having thus explained the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*), the passage beginning with "iti" is now commenced in order to explain the benefits therein.
In that context, "the rest of the people" refers to those who have not attained the liberation of mind through loving-kindness. "Turning around" means by way of the right side...
They lie on their sides, turning over completely. "Chattering" means making a sound by way of gasping breaths.

"He sleeps happily": here, sleep is twofold: characterized by the stretching out of the back while lying down, and characterized by the occurrence of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) unmixed with kamma-resultant consciousnesses. In both these ways, he sleeps quite happily. Because—
Having lain down slowly, he lies with his limbs properly composed in a pleasing manner;
even when falling asleep, it is as if he has entered a meditative absorption (jhāna). Therefore, it is said: "Having thus slept," and so forth.
Because he fell asleep with difficulty due to not having found comfort at the time of sleep, there is yawning upon waking because of physical exhaustion.
Because there is yawning and tossing from side to side, it is said: "Sighing, yawning, and rolling about, they wake up in pain.
But this person, because he has slept comfortably and lacks bodily fatigue, wakes up free from sighing and the like.
Therefore it is said: "Thus, without waking," and so forth. And the reason for his comfortable awakening is the absence of physical agitation.
He said, "Happiness is changeless.

Regarding the phrase "he sees only auspicious dreams," this is stated with reference to what has been experienced in the past, and because his dreams become auspicious through the intervention of deities and not evil; thus he said, "while worshipping a cetiya..."

"...and so forth. Even when caused by a disturbance of the elements (*dhātu-kkhobha*), his [the Buddha’s] physical form is for the most part auspicious, because the matter born of temperature (*utu*) and nutriment (*āhāra*) generally conforms to the matter born of consciousness (*citta*).
"Like a pearl necklace fastened on the chest" means, as stated by some, like a pearl necklace tied around the neck and hanging down upon the chest.
This may be said with reference to a single-string necklace; however, a pearl necklace consisting of a multitude of various jewel strings [would hang] from the region of the shoulders.
From the waist down to the lower part of the hips, it hangs down and is indeed called "fastened to the chest. "Right there" means right in Pāṭaliputta.
It is possible to sit or lie down because of the safety of that location and the delightful nature of each respective spot.
"The fringe" (*dasā*) refers to the inner fringe, the end of the cloth.

"Living in the performance of duties equally applied" means dwelling in various monasteries while performing the duties that must be carried out with equal application. It is said that the Elder, in whatever monastery he entered, did not think, "I am a guest here," but dwelt there fulfilling the duties appropriate for himself as required.
Others, however, say it refers to dwelling in the abode of loving-kindness (mettā) that is exercised equally toward all beings.
For this elder had already been one who dwelt in loving-kindness even prior to his attainment of Arahatship.

Regarding the phrase "standing in the midst of a forest," it is said that while the elder was wandering about in such a state of balanced mental activity, he once saw a certain delightful forest grove;
having entered a meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) there at the foot of a particular tree, he remained.

Having arisen from that state according to his discernment, he uttered the verse beginning with “As long as I am ordained,” expressing an inspired utterance (*udāna*) born of the joy and gladness resulting from the recollection of his own virtues.
To illustrate this meaning, the first verse, “Standing in the midst of the forest,” was placed [there].
In that context, “roaring” means roaring with the roar of a lion. “Seeking his virtues” means seeking the collection of his own virtues.
Searching and reflecting, they refer to that deity dwelling in the Maṇila tree as "Maṇiliyā"; therefore, that deity also said, "Venerable sir, I am Maṇiliyā.
For, as a general rule, the designation for tree-deities is based on their respective dwelling trees.
“As with the deity of the Phandana tree. “In that very place” means on Cittala Mountain itself.

By the phrase “through the state of having a mind of intense affection,” he shows that even by the mere presence of a mind of intense affection the sword does not strike, let alone through the liberation of mind (cetovimutti) consisting of loving-kindness (mettā).
The mind becomes concentrated very quickly because ill will (byāpāda), from which jhāna has been lost due to some obstacle, has been cast far away.
He becomes concentrated very quickly. Some say this is for the sake of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*). The rest is easy to understand.
And here, although benefits such as sleeping happily and so forth are obtained even by those who have attained jhāna through other meditation subjects—as it is said:
"The sages sleep happily, well-composed within themselves;..."—yet [this practice] is superior.
“The disciples of Gotama always awaken to a true awakening”—and so forth.

Likewise, all these benefits are obtained in their entirety by those who have attained the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), because the divine abodes are the direct opposites of ill-will and the other [unwholesome states].
For this very reason, it was said: “For this, friend, is the escape from ill-will, namely, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness,” and so on.
Furthermore, since beings are led toward suffering by means of ill-will and the like, once the divine abidings (brahmavihāras),
which are the opposites of those states, are established, the leading toward happiness is already as good as attained.
Commentary on the Development of Compassion (Karuṇābhāvanāvaṇṇanā)
259. *Karuṇaṃ* means the divine abode of compassion (*karuṇā-brahmavihāra*). *Nikkaruṇatāya* means through cruelty; the meaning is "through the kind of cruelty described thus:
'Here, someone is by nature prone to harassing beings with his hand, or with a clod, or with a staff, or with a sword, or with one or another [weapon]'.
*Ādīnavaṃ* means fault. It is evil because of the harassment of beings in whatever way [it occurs].
The result [of this] occurs both in this very life and in the future world. For instance, when one harms beings— whether by depriving them of life,
by cutting off their limbs and members, by causing loss of wealth, or by bringing about their lack of gain, lack of residence, harm, ill-repute, or social ostracism,
or even merely by pointing out their faults— that state of negligence of his bears fruit in this very life.
It leads to non-acquisition; it leads to the loss of what has been acquired; on account of it, an evil reputation spreads abroad;
one approaches an assembly without confidence and with a sense of shame; one dies confused; at the breaking up of the body, a bad destination is to be expected;
even if reborn in a good destination among humans, one is of low birth, from a humble family, and is also ugly.

The harmful consequences of cruelty should be reflected upon as being followed by numerous disadvantages, such as: one becomes difficult to look upon, frequently afflicted with illness and many diseases, poorly situated and lacking food and drink, short-lived, and having a meager existence.

Conversely, the benefits of compassion should be reflected upon as being the opposite of those [disadvantages]. Therefore it was said: "The danger of lack of compassion, and the benefit of compassion..."
"And having reflected upon the benefit. By the words "He becomes dear," etc., he first states the reason why one should not begin with beloved persons and the like.
For when one begins to practice compassion toward a beloved person, their state of being beloved does not immediately vanish;

and as long as that state has not vanished, how can there be the practice of compassion? Therefore he said: "He remains in the very place of being beloved. This applies to the other types of persons as well.
The same method applies here. The reason why those who have changed their gender or died are not considered fields [of merit] has already been stated below.
However, in order to demonstrate by way of the scriptural method (*pāḷinaya*) where one should first begin, the passage beginning with "And how, monks...
is commenced. In that context, *duggata* means poor; for such a person, due to the loss of wealth, lacks the means for happiness.
One who has gone to suffering, who has approached it, is called "one who has fared ill" (*duggata*). Alternatively, "fared ill" means having come to a state of being possessed by suffering.
"Ill-endowed" (*durupeta*) means endowed with bodily misconduct and so forth; or, one who stands in darkness by way of [rebirth in] miserable destinies, low families, or inferior forms is "fared ill.
Because of being endowed with bodily misconduct and so forth, one who stands in a state where darkness is the ultimate resort is "ill-endowed. Thus it is in this context.
The meaning should be understood as follows: "Fallen into extreme hardship" means having encountered great difficulty and being submerged in a massive calamity.
"Perhaps indeed" (*appeva nāma*) means "how wonderful it would be.

"Kill him!"—when the king has issued such an order, saying "Kill this thief," they give even hard food... [and so on]... thinking, "While he is about to be executed right now, let him obtain at least this much pleasure. "Well-prepared" means equipped for the experience of happiness.

"By this same method" means by whatever procedure compassion was previously aroused toward a person currently undergoing extreme hardship as described, or one who will experience suffering in the future;
it is by that very same principle. "Toward a dear person" means toward a person worthy of being loved.
This refers to taking into account either the suffering currently being seen or the suffering that will arise in the future.
"Compassion should be practiced"—this is the connection. The same method applies even toward those who are neutral or hostile.

For although the cultivation of compassion for the two types of persons mentioned as its objects is accomplished quite easily, this bhikkhu, having made the cultivation therein more proficient, should next effect the breaking down of boundaries (sīmāsambheda).
Compassion should be developed first toward a beloved person, then toward a neutral person, and then toward a hostile person.
While developing it, one should make the mind supple and wieldy in each successive stage and then extend it to the next.
However, for one who has no hostile person at all, or for one who—due to being of the nature of a great man—perceives even a wrongdoer as a friend, [the sequence proceeds accordingly].
Since it does not arise, one should not even entertain the intention, "My mind has now become pliant toward the neutral person; I shall now apply it toward the enemy.
However, with reference to those for whom such an intention exists, he says, "But if," and so forth.

In that context, "in the manner previously stated" means in the manner stated for one whose meditation subject is loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*); "that [method] in the very manner stated for loving-kindness" means exactly as described for *mettā*.

"It should be pacified" means that this resentment should be pacified by the method described for the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*), namely through the passage beginning with "Then, regarding those previous persons... and "For one who recollects the 'Simile of the Saw' instruction, etc.

Having thus shown the method of cultivating compassion (*karuṇā*)—both toward those currently undergoing great suffering and toward those who are happy but will encounter suffering in the future due to their failure to perform wholesome deeds—
Now, in order to show that this applies even to one who has performed wholesome deeds, the passage beginning with “And whoever here... was spoken.

“Of those” refers to calamities. “Because of not having transcended the suffering of the round” means because of the state of not having transcended the immeasurable suffering of saṃsāra—consisting of birth, aging, and so forth, including the future misery of the states of loss (apāya) which cannot be brought to an end even by the proclamation of the Fully Enlightened One, and which occurs even in the happy destinies (sugati).

“Having cultivated compassion in every way” means: by perceiving the state of being an object for compassion in every respect—whether through the occurrence of suffering, the occurrence of happiness, the non-performance of wholesome deeds, or the performance of unwholesome deeds—one should cultivate the meditation on compassion by directing compassion toward each such individual.
“In the manner already stated” refers to the passage beginning with: “Then, as he repeatedly radiates loving-kindness,” and so forth.
"By the method stated for the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*)": this refers to the sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*) that occurs through the breaking down of boundaries.

"In the same way as stated for loving-kindness" means that just as in the development of loving-kindness, absorption (*appanā*) by way of the threefold and fourfold jhānas was described through such phrases as "without difficulty," and its expansion was described through such phrases as "he dwells pervading one direction," so too here in the development of compassion (*karuṇā*).
The absorption (appanā) should be understood and expanded by means of the threefold and fourfold jhānas;

likewise, the method for its expansion should also be understood—this is the intended meaning. By the restrictive phrase "in the very manner stated," he illustrates this point: that the statement "first, the hostile person should be treated with compassion" is not only contrary to the scripture (pāḷi), but also contrary to reason (yutti). For first...
If anger were to arise in one who recollects loving-kindness, it would not be compassion. One’s own self must also be taken as the object by way of feeling compassion for it;
why, then, is that taken up later? Furthermore, by the phrase “the absorption should be expanded,” this meaning is shown:
that the supernormal powers described in such passages as “he dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by compassion” are accomplished only for one whose mind has reached absorption.
The only distinction in this text [on compassion] is the word "compassion" itself; therefore, without referring to that, it is said, "After that...
should be understood," in order to show that the transformations described in the *Paṭisambhidā* and the benefits described for loving-kindness (*mettā*) are obtainable here as well.
In this context, "after that" means after the transformation described by the phrase "with a mind accompanied by compassion. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Commentary on the Development of Appreciative Joy (Muditābhāvanā) 260. Regarding the phrase "toward dear persons, etc.": it should not be undertaken toward those who are neutral or hostile.

The analysis of the term "development of appreciative joy" (*muditābhāvanā*) should be applied by transforming the grammatical case. The words beginning with "for indeed not" (*na hi*) state the reason for this. In the phrase "by the mere fact of being dear," the word *matta* (mere) [is used].
The meaning is the exclusion of qualifiers (*visesanivatti*).

By this, it indicates specific qualities that serve as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for sympathetic joy (*muditā*), such as having a face constantly radiant due to being reborn with mental joy (*somanassapaṭisandhika*), speaking first, being pleasant to converse with, being open, and being friendly;
the sense is that [the person] is devoid of such specific qualities. By the word "eva" (only/just), however, [it excludes] the beloved person...
It turns away from being overwhelmed by pleasure and so forth, as well as from the occurrence of joy which serves as the cause for sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
For when a beloved person is joyful, delighted, and satisfied due to supreme success, the bhikkhu would find an occasion for sympathetic joy. Indeed, it will be said:
"Or a beloved person," and so forth. At first, for one who recollects a neutral person, equanimity (*udāsīnatā*) becomes established.
Anger arises in one who recollects an enemy. Therefore he said, "How much more so in the case of those who are neutral toward their enemies.
A companion who is like a drunkard in the manifestation of joy is a "drunkard-companion. "Exceedingly joyful" means being exceedingly glad due to the clarity and serenity [of his mind];
for this repetition (*āmēḍita*) refers to that very clarity. Thus, according to the method of the Commentary, from the beginning there is the cultivation of sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
Having shown the basis [of the example], it is now stated as "a beloved person" and so forth in order to show it according to the method of the canonical text (*pāḷinaya*).

Therein, "happy" means one in whom happiness has arisen; the sense is that they have attained happiness. "Adorned" means equipped for the experience of happiness, having prepared the means for happiness.
"Oh, how excellent! shows the manner of prior joy and clear comprehension on the part of that being regarding their prosperity.

"Again, 'it is truly good'" is a demonstration of the cultivation of that joy. Regarding "dear and pleasing," some say that by the inclusion of the term "pleasing" (*manāpa*), even in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), the "dearest friend" (*atippiyasahāyaka*) is intended.

"In the past" means in a past existence within that very same personal continuity (*attabhāva*). "In the future"—here too the same principle applies; for [the feeling] does not exist when one has gone to another state of existence.
The cultivation of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) flourishes. If this is so, how is it with respect to the past and the future? This is not a fault.
For one must grasp them by way of their existing state through the temporal present, thinking, "This very same person was Datta, he was Tissa.
But how can prosperity in the future be an object for this [cultivation]? It is so by means of prophetic declaration and the like, or by inference from the excellence of present application.
Because it should be grasped once obtained.
"Beloved persons" refers to both those who are excessively beloved—namely, those known as "drunkard companions"—and those who are simply beloved.
Both of these types are here called "beloved persons" due to their commonality in being objects of affection. "In succession" means: first the excessively beloved person, then the beloved person.

Regarding the phrase "one who is neutral toward an enemy": having made the meditation subject proficient, supple, and wieldy in each of the four divisions, one should apply it to the remaining ones in the order of their inclusion.

Although the "breaking down of boundaries" consists simply in maintaining an even mind toward these four types of persons—since the boundary is broken by this state—it nevertheless occurs through the development [of that evenness] proceeding in such a way many times, once the former [state] has been established.
Having treated the former as the cause and the latter as the fruit, it is said: "having broken down the boundaries through equanimity of mind.
Alternatively, the state of the boundaries as previously described is itself called the "breaking down of boundaries," hence it is said: "having broken down the boundaries through equanimity of mind.
Whatever else remains to be said here follows the same method already explained above.
Commentary on the Development of Equanimity (Upekkhābhāvanāvaṇṇanā) 261. "Development of equanimity" means the development of the divine abiding of equanimity.

Since the fourth divine abiding is the natural outflow of the preceding three divine abidings, it is therefore said: "by means of the triple and quadruple jhānas obtained in loving-kindness and the others. "Skilled in the third jhāna" means...
It has been well-developed, brought to mastery, perfected, and made proficient through such third jhāna of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra).
For that which is not proficient cannot serve as the proximate cause for the higher jhānas. Furthermore, the mention of the "third" here is according to the fourfold method (*catukkanaya*).
By the phrase "May they be happy," etc., the word "etc. should be understood as including such expressions as "May they be free from suffering," and so forth.
"Sattakelāyana" means "clinging to beings," that is, making them one's own through possessiveness. "Sattakelāyanamanasikārayutta" refers to being engaged with such mental attention;

therefore [the term is used]. Because loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] exist in close proximity to lust, aversion, grief, and joy respectively, they should be understood as behaving in close association with repulsion and attraction as appropriate.
Alternatively, it is because they have attained the state of wishing for their welfare by thinking, "May they be happy, may they be freed from suffering, may they rejoice."

All three [feelings] are in close proximity to attraction (*anunaya*). And when there is its opposite—the provocation of blood—repulsion (*paṭigha*) likewise finds an opportunity here, just as pus does;
thus, it should be understood that repulsion and attraction are in close proximity to them without distinction.
The phrase "because of being gross due to association with joy" is stated with reference to the third jhāna; for one who has emerged from that...

This is the "vision of danger. However, if grossness were being described by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the other [immeasurables], then their grossness would have to be stated as consisting precisely in the presence of applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and rapture (*pīti*), because it is possible for them to be associated with these even in the third jhāna, whereas equanimity (*upekkhā*) is absent from them.
Or rather, they need not be so stated, because here only those [immeasurables] belonging to the third jhāna are intended, and they are defined precisely by the surmounting of each respective jhāna.

Furthermore, even the various meditative states (*jhāna*) such as loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the rest are indeed said to have "transcended" [the lower stages], for the term is used merely as a conventional designation based on their commonality with *jhāna*, just as they share a commonality with one another.

"In the former" refers to loving-kindness, compassion, and gladness. "Because of its peaceful nature" means because equanimity possesses a peaceful nature, being devoid of the aforementioned lack of peace such as partiality toward beings and so forth.
Moreover, this phrase "because of its peaceful nature" should be regarded as a mere illustration. Subtlety (*sukhumatā*).
The excellence [of equanimity], its remoteness from the defilements, its vast fruitfulness, and so forth—these too should be seen as the benefits of equanimity.
"Naturally neutral" means that, without depending on any particular cause, this bhikkhu by his very nature and inherent character stands on the side of neutrality.
"Having looked on with equanimity" means that this venerable one comes and goes solely by virtue of the kamma he himself has performed.
Furthermore, you too have come and will go solely by virtue of the kamma performed by yourself;
it is not possible for anyone to bring you any happiness or remove your suffering through their own efforts.

This cherishing of beings through loving-kindness and so forth is merely what is favorable to the mind. And this is the path traversed by the Buddhas and other Noble Ones, being the unerring way of practice.

That is to say, through equanimity toward all beings; thus, by way of revulsion for the opposing side, one who has developed reverence, esteem, and respect for that person looks upon them again and again with equanimity, and establishes a particularly distinguished equanimity therein.
As he practices in this manner, because of his natural state of neutrality, equanimity becomes firmly established there in an eminent degree.
By the power of meditation (*bhāvanābala*), the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are indeed suppressed and the defilements (*kilesa*) are settled.
He then extends that equanimity (*upekkhā*) toward beloved persons and others. Therefore he said: "Equanimity should be aroused; then, toward beloved persons and others.

In the phrase "one person" (*ekaṃ puggalaṃ*), the word *eka* has the sense of "another," as in such expressions as "some [others] thus assert" (*ittheke abhivadanti*). It is by means of the singular number alone...
And here, a specific number is established; therefore, the meaning here is "another single person. By this, he excludes the self (*atta*).

By the phrase "neither agreeable," he excludes a beloved person and an exceedingly dear friend, or alternatively, the self itself, because of the absence of disagreeableness within the self. By the phrase "nor disagreeable," he excludes an unloved person and an enemy, by way of elimination (*pārisesato*).

The inclusion of the neutral person has been reached. Thus, by the phrase "one person who is neither agreeable nor disagreeable," he shows the neutral person through the method of negating both oneself and those who are dear and so forth.
"By the method stated" refers to the method just mentioned immediately prior, beginning with "that which is his natural neutral state. Of attachment to self...

Because of its powerful nature, even an enemy cannot easily be brought under control due to the state of neutrality (majjhattatā) within oneself; thus, "in these and in oneself" places "oneself" last.
"In the same manner as described for the earth-kasiṇa" means by the method stated for the earth-kasiṇa, beginning with: "This attainment has near-joy as its adversary," and so forth.
For that which was stated below—"having emerged from the third jhāna when it is well-mastered," etc.—[is to be understood here].
That was explained below by way of seeing the danger and the benefit in the first three divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) and in the fourth divine abiding.

This, however, is a demonstration of the manner in which the fourth jhāna arises for one who applies effort toward its attainment after having seen the danger in the third jhāna and the benefit in the fourth jhāna.
Therefore, it is said there: "The sound of earth..."
The passage should be connected as follows: “Having removed that very sign, making it the object, mind-door adverting consciousness arises,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “in the earth-kasiṇa, etc.,” the word “etc. includes the remaining kasiṇas and the sign of inhalation and exhalation.

Granted that the third jhāna arising in the case of the kasiṇas and the breath (ānāpāna) possesses the status of a fine-material-sphere jhāna and so on due to its equanimity being a divine abode (brahmavihāra).
There is indeed a commonality; however, that is not the cause, because the objects are dissimilar. Thus he said, "due to the dissimilarity of the objects.

But is it not the case that the cultivation of the kasiṇas and so forth is one way, while the cultivation of the divine abodes is another, such that there is indeed a dissimilarity between the aforementioned jhānas even by way of their cultivation? This is true; however, the dissimilarity is by way of cultivation.
It is not an absolute cause for non-arising. For the cultivation of loving-kindness and so forth is of one nature, while the cultivation of equanimity is of another.

Nevertheless, the divine abiding of equanimity proceeds by way of a mode of looking on with detachment, having turned away from that [loving-kindness] after touching upon the aspect of wishing for the welfare of beings as it has been directed toward them, by means of the method of exclusion (*vyatirekamukhena*). For he will say thus:
“Beings are owners of their kamma; by whose whim could they become happy? and so forth.
Furthermore, since there is similarity of object here as well, the divine abiding of equanimity succeeds for one who has attained the third jhāna by means of loving-kindness (mettā) and the others.

Therefore it is said: “In loving-kindness and the rest,” and so forth. In that context, “in loving-kindness and the rest” means when loving-kindness and the others are to be accomplished; “by means of loving-kindness and the rest” [refers to the method].
The meaning [is as follows]. The rest is exactly according to the method explained below.
In the commentary on the miscellaneous discussion (pakiṇṇakakathā), verse 262:
"By the supreme Brahmā"—here, there are three kinds of Brahmās: conventional Brahmās (sammutibrahmā), Brahmās by rebirth (upapattibrahmā), and Brahmās by purification (visuddhibrahmā).
“O Kosiya, the crows eat the ripe rice in the field;
I inform you of this, O Brahmā, yet I am unable to prevent them.
Wander forth, O Great Brahmā, while other living beings are still cooking.”
For in such passages as these, by the word "Brahmā," conventional Brahmās are meant:
"Open for them are the doors to the Deathless;
let those who have ears release their faith."
“Perceiving harm, O Brahmā, I did not speak the skillful,
sublime Dhamma among humans.
And in such passages as “Then Brahmā Sahampati,” the word *brahmā* refers to those who are *upapatti-brahmās* (beings born as Brahmas).
From such statements as “He turns the Brahma-wheel,” the term “Brahma” refers to the Noble Dhamma (*ariyadhamma*).
Because they have arisen from that, all Noble Ones (*ariya*) without distinction are called “pure Brahmās” (*visuddhibrahmāna*) by virtue of their ultimate Brahma-nature.
Specifically, however, according to the statement, “‘Brahmā,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata,” the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) is the Supreme Brahmā.

He is called "Brahmottama" because he has reached the pinnacle of excellence through qualities that are supreme even in the world including its devas and Brahmās. Thus, he is the highest among Brahmās;
or alternatively, he is both Brahmā and the highest, hence "Brahmottama," the Blessed One.

When he spoke—referring to the teaching given here and there to those to be trained, beginning with the words "With a mind imbued with loving-kindness"—it was according to the sequence of development (bhāvanā) as previously described. "Iti" means "thus," in the manner just stated.
And having understood and known [them] according to the sequence of the commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*). The "Miscellaneous Discussion" (*pakiṇṇakakathā*) should also be understood:

unlike before, it is not by taking up meanings specific to each respective divine abiding (*brahmavihāra*), but rather, because they are common to all, one should understand the "Miscellaneous Discussion" as that which proceeds by taking up meanings scattered and dispersed here and there.
"He endears" (*mejjati*) is stated by making the Dhamma itself the agent, in order to exclude any other agent besides the Dhamma.

"He feels affection" (*sinehati*): here, affection should be understood as a state of endearment preceded by knowledge that functions in a beneficial manner, being the opposite of harshness caused by malice toward beings;
it is not to be understood in the sense of craving (*taṇhā*), for that is preceded by delusion (*moha*).
This has the nature of non-hatred and is associated with non-greed. But is not craving and its moisture also opposed to ill-will, since they cannot coexist with it?
Even if they do not arise together in the same consciousness, they are not opposed [to ill-will] because they do not abandon it.
One who feels affection (*mejjati*) is a friend; it is a continuity of aggregates (*khandhappabandha*) characterized by an inclination toward welfare.

It should be understood that it is called *mettā* because it is included within that [state], or because it exists toward friends (*mitte*), or because it exists toward dear persons who have become its object, or because this activity of friendship proceeds by way of cleansing (*mejjanavasena*). Regarding the term *karuṇā*:

it "does" (*karoti*), thus it is "compassion" (*karuṇā*). To the questions "What does it do?", "To whom?", and "With what as its cause?", he says: "When there is suffering in others, for the virtuous..."

“Trembling of the heart. “Trembling” refers to a transformation of the mind in the form of an inability to endure [the suffering of others], arising from seeing the suffering of others and desiring to remove it.
Since this occurs only in virtuous persons (sappurisa), he says “of the good” (sādhūnam).
For virtuous persons are called “good” because they accomplish the welfare of both themselves and others. “Destroys” means he causes it to go out of sight; “removes” means he takes it away.
This is the meaning. By this, he shows that "removal" means the warding off of harm. For compassion has the characteristic of proceeding in the mode of removing the suffering of others.
"By way of pervading" means by way of touching, that is, by way of making [the object] its mental support (ārammaṇa);
and here, making it the mental support should be understood as occurring precisely in the mode of removing suffering from those who are suffering.

“*Modanti tāyā*” means that this is a description of the state of being the instrument for the act of rejoicing (*modana-kiriyā*) by means of sympathetic joy (*muditā*). This [instrumental relationship] is established through figurative usage (*upacāra-siddha*);
since there is no agent whatsoever therein apart from sympathetic joy itself, it designates that very [joy] as the agent, saying, “or it rejoices itself.
This too is merely a figurative designation. The phrase “because of the lack of mastery over phenomena” is intended to exclude the state of having mastery.
“Or rather, *muditā* (altruistic joy) is simply the cord of gladness,” so it was said.

*Upekkhā* (equanimity) is an observation arising from a state of neutrality, characterized by the cutting off of partiality toward those who are dear and so forth. Therefore, he said, “May they be free from enmity,” and so on. In that context, the reason for the grammatical designation of the agent as “one who looks with equanimity” (*upekkhati*) has already been stated above.

263. One who is “beneficial” (*hita*) is one who acts for the welfare [of others]; therefore, [loving-kindness] is characterized by the manifestation of a beneficial mode of conduct, in the sense of acting for the welfare of sentient beings.
It has the characteristic of occurring, or the characteristic of causing the occurrence of a beneficial mode. Its function is the bringing about of benefit;
that is, its task is the presentation of what is beneficial to sentient beings, or it is the perfection of such presentation.
It stands as an antidote by way of subduing resentment—which occurs in the form of thinking, "He has done me harm," and so forth—and it becomes an object for knowledge; or, in whatever [context]...
It arises by itself and establishes the subduing of resentment therein; thus, it is "having the subduing of resentment as its manifestation" (*āghātavinayapaccupaṭṭhānā*).

Since it possesses as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) that wise attention which proceeds by seeing the state of being agreeable even in disagreeable beings—by means of a perception of non-disgust toward what is disgusting, let alone in the case of those who are agreeable—it is "having the vision of the state of being agreeable as its proximate cause" (*manāpabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā*).
The "subsiding of ill will" (*byāpādūpasama*) is the pacification of ill will by means of its suppression. "Success" (*sampatti*) is the attainment, the perfect arising.

"Origination from affection" (*sinehasambhava*) is the emergence of the moisture of craving (*taṇhāsineha*). "Failure" (*vipatti*) is destruction; for through the gateway of loving-kindness, passion deceives one.
The meaning regarding the characteristics and other aspects of compassion and the rest should be understood according to this method. We shall explain only the specific distinctions.
It is the mode of removing the suffering occurring for sentient beings. Whether that removal actually takes place or not, it is characterized by the mode of removing suffering;
thus, its characteristic is the occurrence of the mode of removing suffering.
Non-violence (*avihiṃsā*) is the inability and non-endurance of the suffering of others due to the desire to remove it. [It is] non-harming toward sentient beings.

Non-affliction (*aviheṭhana*). It manifests as that; or it stands as the opposite of affliction (*vihiṃsā*), thus it is "manifesting as non-affliction" (*avihiṃsā-paccupaṭṭhāna*). Regarding "the subsiding of affliction" (*vihiṃsūpasama*):
here, beings are afflicted by means of this, or its nature is their affliction; thus it is "affliction" (*vihiṃsā*).
This refers to an arising of a mind of aversion (*paṭigha-cittuppāda*) which functions in the manner of harming beings and serves as the opposite of compassion (*karuṇā*).
Because sorrow deceives by means of compassion, it is said: "Misfortune is the origin of sorrow.
It has the characteristic of rejoicing in the success of others. Its function is to act as the antidote to envy and jealousy.
[It arises] toward the prosperity of beings, toward secluded dwellings, and toward superior wholesome qualities.
It is included under the terms "intolerance," "displeasure," and "aversion. It manifests by way of counteracting that [aversion], or it establishes the pacification of its affliction;
