thus, it is said to have the manifestation of the pacification of aversion (*arativighātapaccupaṭṭhāna*).
Laughter (*pahāsa*) is a state of being exultant and a sense of elation through the influence of worldly joy. Its function is to see beings with equanimity.

The meaning is that its function is to see equanimity alone through an attitude of neutrality toward all beings, including those who are dear and so forth; and its function is to apprehend them with equanimity by way of arising or looking upon them.

Because it does not grasp at the repulsive or non-repulsive aspects among beings, it functions in a manner that pacifies aversion and attachment therein, thereby effecting their suppression (vikkhambhana).

"It presents" means it presents the subsiding of aversion and attraction. Regarding the phrase "the footing for the vision of the ownership of kamma as it occurs," here the word "thus" (evaṃ) refers, by way of contrast,
to the manner of occurrence of the three [immeasurables] beginning with loving-kindness— namely, the modes of bringing about welfare, removing suffering, and rejoicing in success—
and thereby excludes the knowledge of the ownership of kamma as it occurs through the exclusion of those modes.
This shows that the proximate cause for the divine abiding of equanimity (*upekkhā-brahmavihāra*) is not just anything. 264.
Regarding the phrase "the bliss of insight (*vipassanā-sukha*) and success in existence (*bhava-sampatti*)," one should add here "dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra*).
For that too is their common purpose. Likewise, there are eleven benefits, such as "one sleeps happily," and so forth. These...
However, because these have already been explained below, they are not included here.
That by which one escapes or departs is "escape" (*nissaraṇa*); it is that which abandons.
Granted, by means of these [factors], all five hindrances as well as the evil states associated with them are abandoned through suppression, by way of seeing their direct opposites.

However, ill will and the other [hindrances] are mentioned in the Pāḷi. And this being so, the statement regarding the escape from lust should be seen as being well-supported for the divine abiding of equanimity (*upekkhā-brahmavihāra*). 265.

"In these" means among these divine abidings. Loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward beings is practiced by way of perceiving their qualities, such as generosity, kind speech, virtue, and learning, as appropriate.
It proceeds. Therefore it was said: "It has the perception of beings as agreeable as its proximate cause.

Lust also proceeds there by way of grasping at qualities, however they may be, through the seduction of the perception of the agreeable; thus he said: "Because of the commonality of perceiving qualities.
Therefore, because it defiles in an identical manner like an enemy with the face of a friend, lust is the immediate adversary of loving-kindness.
He quickly finds an opportunity for an entrance even through a mere lapse of mindfulness, because loving-kindness is liable to arise toward that object once it has been set aside.

"From there" means from lust, or from the finding of an opportunity for lust. "By way of similarity and dissimilarity" means by way of what is similar, or by way of the dissimilarity of what is similar.
For among beings, one who grasps at an agreeable aspect [finds] a state contrary to that which is similar to loving-kindness.
Ill will is dissimilar to that [loving-kindness]. Therefore, even if it were to find an opportunity, it would take a long time to do so;
thus, like an enemy standing at a distance from a man, it is a distant adversary to loving-kindness. "From that" means from ill will.

"Fearlessly" means without apprehension or suspicion, the intention being that once loving-kindness has gained a foothold, it cannot be easily overcome by ill will. Hence he said, "He will practice loving-kindness," and so forth.
"Of things desired" means of dear things. "Of things lovely" means of things desirable. "Of things pleasing" means of things that increase the mind's delight;
for that very reason, they are called "mind-pleasing" (*manorama*) because they gladden the mind. "Connected with worldly bait" means dependent upon craving.
"Contemplating non-attainment" means being agitated by the thought, "I do not obtain these," due to their non-attainment. "Past" means gone beyond.
“Ceased” means having reached cessation. “Altered” means departed through the loss of its own nature. “Recalling” means reflecting by way of recollecting.
“Worldly” means dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure. By the word “and so forth,” he includes such passages as “of sounds cognizable by the ear,” and so on.
“By way of the commonality of seeing misfortune” means by way of seeing the misfortune of wealth and so forth among those beings.

Compassion arises; when there is improper attention directed toward those very objects for that purpose, sorrow would arise by way of the aforementioned mental distress (*domanassa*), which is the immediate adversary of compassion.
For here, sorrow is spoken of under the heading of mental distress.
Regarding the phrase "due to similarity and dissimilarity": herein, among sentient beings, there is the aspect of compassion which is similar in its desire to remove suffering.

Among those, because the mode of bringing about suffering is of a hostile nature and thus dissimilar [to loving-kindness], compassion—finding an opening through that similarity and dissimilarity—would only find it after a long time;
therefore, like an enemy standing at a distance from a man, it is said to be a distant adversary to loving-kindness.
"Due to the similarity in seeing success" refers to those beings among whom sympathetic joy (*muditā*) proceeds by way of seeing their success in wealth and so forth.
When there is improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) directed toward those very objects, laughter may arise by way of the joy described in the passage beginning with "forms cognizable by the eye.
This laughter is an immediate adversary to sympathetic joy (*muditā*). For here, laughter is spoken of under the heading of joy.
Regarding "similarity and dissimilarity": it refers to the mode of rejoicing toward beings who are delighted by their success in wealth and other such things.
Since discontent (*arati*) is dissimilar (*visabhāga*) to sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which is similar (*sabhāga*), in that it takes the form of non-delight therein,

and since it would take an opportunity only after a long time due to this similarity and dissimilarity, it is said that sympathetic joy has a distant enemy, like an enemy standing far away from a man. "And he is gladdened," etc.,
means that once sympathetic joy is established, even this discontent does not arise.
This was stated by way of showing the qualities that are to be obtained, not by way of showing the suppression of the specific discontent intended here.

Alternatively, it should be understood that discontent was shown as a partial illustration in order to demonstrate that when the discontent which is the opposite of physical and mental seclusion has been suppressed, then the discontent which is the opposite of sympathetic joy (*muditā*) becomes easily suppressible.
"In regard to superior wholesome states" means in regard to the states of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"Of a fool" (*bālassa*) because of his engagement in the dhamma of a fool. "Of one who is deluded" (*mūḷhassa*) because of being utterly confused regarding his own welfare and the welfare of others.
"Of a worldling" (*puthujjanassa*) because of the causes such as the generation of the various defilements (*kilesa*) and so forth. "Of one who has not conquered the flood" (*anodhijinassa*):

either because he has not conquered the floods by means of the paths that conquer the floods, or because the trainees (*sekkha*), who have conquered the floods, have conquered the defilements only partially (*odhisova*). Therefore, this [term] negates the state of having conquered the flood for him.
Because they have not yet mastered the fruition that proceeds beyond the seventh existence, they are "non-conquerors of fruition" (*avipākajina*);

or alternatively, the Arahants are "conquerors of fruition" (*vipākajina*) because they are free from rebirth-linking (*appaṭisandhika*). Thus, he rejects their status as those beyond training (*asekkha*).

Because they are by nature unable to see the danger in delusion—the root of all evil states and the source of manifold disadvantages—they are "seers of no-danger" (*anādīnavadassāvino*). This is due to their lack of both scriptural learning (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*).
“Of the uninstructed”: such a person is, in every respect, called a blind worldling (*andhaputhujjana*).
To demonstrate his state as a blind worldling, it is stated again: “of the worldling. “Of such a kind” means preceded by delusion in the manner described.
“She does not transcend form” means she is not a cause for the surmounting of forms; the intended meaning is that she does not transcend the defilements regarding the object of form.
Equanimity regarding ignorance (*aññāṇupekkhā*) is simply ignorance itself, free from both joy and grief. It is called "similar" by way of not investigating faults or virtues.

Just as equanimity among the divine abodes (*brahmavihārupekkhā*) proceeds solely by way of pure neutrality without investigating faults or virtues—unlike loving-kindness and the others which involve the promotion of welfare toward beings—so too, equanimity regarding ignorance [does not investigate] the faults or virtues existing in beings.
Because it proceeds merely by way of pure equanimity without intending [anything], it is similar [to the divine abiding of equanimity] through its lack of investigation into faults and virtues.
Therefore, because it easily finds an entry point, it is said to have the divine abiding of equanimity as its proximate enemy. Regarding "similarity and dissimilarity":
in the case of the desirable and the undesirable, the mode of neutrality—which is the essence of equanimity—is dissimilar to the modes of proceeding with attachment and aversion toward them.

Attachment and aversion are dissimilar; because they are dissimilar to it [equanimity], those [passions], finding an opportunity through that state of dissimilarity, would take a long time to find an entry point.
Thus, like an enemy standing at a distance from a man, they are said to be distant adversaries of the divine abode of equanimity. 266.
Desire is the wish to act, as stated in the passage, "Wholesome states have desire as their root"; or alternatively, [it refers to] beings.
Because it proceeds by way of a blameless aspiration characterized by the desire to bring about welfare and the wish to remove suffering, it is said that "the desire to act is the initial factor.

For even the divine abiding of equanimity (upekkhā-brahmavihāra) proceeds in the mode of looking on with indifference toward beings who are intent upon their own duties—like a mother—only when the desire for their welfare has not been discarded, as expressed in the words: "In this regard, non-engagement is the unerring path."
“Sons. Regarding the phrase “the hindrances, etc.,” the word “etc. (ādi) should be understood as including the defilements associated with them.

In some instances, even the mention of “beings” is merely a mention of “formations” (saṅkhāra), as in the teaching based on the designation of a person (puggalādhiṭṭhānā desanā), such as “All beings subsist by nutriment”;
it is not so here. Thus he says: “Whether one being or many beings, they are the object by way of the phenomena of conceptual designation (paññatti).”
“By way of the dhammas that are designations” means by way of those dhammas designated as concepts (*paññatti*).

Granted that here, in the context of meditation, there is also the apprehension of happiness and so forth through such phrases as “May they be happy,” nevertheless, that is subordinate—just like the apprehension of the characteristic of impermanence in insight (*vipassanā*) through the thought “All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
It is the designation of a sentient being (*satta-paññatti*) alone that is apprehended as the primary factor.
It should be seen. Or, when access concentration is attained, the expansion of the object is intended here as the accomplishment of the breaking down of boundaries even therein.

Regarding the phrase "having delimited a single dwelling," the construction is: having made a delimitation with knowledge thus, "I shall pervade beings with loving-kindness," one should delimit a single street.
By the mention of the "street," the beings living on that street are included.
Just as they see one direction, so it is in all cases.

267. "The outflow of the kasiṇas" means that the formless attainments (ārūpajjhānas), which are like the result of outflow from the kasiṇa jhānas, are accomplished only through the perfection of the kasiṇa jhānas.
Some say this is because they cannot be accomplished without them. "The outflow of concentration" means...

The outflow of the form-sphere jhāna-concentrations and the three lower formless-sphere jhāna-concentrations is [the attainment of cessation], because it must be acquired only after having successively attained those [preceding states].
The outflow of insight is so called because it is obtainable through the power of insight and because it is to be entered into by means of insight alone.
The outflow of both serenity and insight is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
As it was said: “Because of being endowed with two powers,” and so forth.

By the phrase “the outflow of the preceding three divine abodes (brahmavihāra),” it is shown that the divine abode of equanimity belongs only to one who remains after having attained the three jhānas by way of loving-kindness and the others, and not to anyone else.
To make this same point clearer through a simile, the passage beginning with “Just as” was stated. That which...
What needs to be said here has already been stated above. 268.

"Siyā" (might be) refers to a reflection that might occur in someone in the manner being described. "Ettha" (herein) means that among these, loving-kindness and the others should be understood as the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*);
other meditation subjects are merely practices for one's own welfare. These, however, [are for the welfare of all]: "May all beings be happy..."

By the words beginning with "May they be," [the suttas] refer to those practices that constitute the pursuit of the welfare of others. Therefore, these abidings (vihāras) are supreme because they consist in the correct practice toward sentient beings.

"Brahmas" refers to those born as Brahmas. For they, having become free from mental hindrances through the cultivation of jhāna here [in the human world], are reborn in the Brahma-world; and there, for the duration of their lifespan, they remain indeed free from mental hindrances. Therefore, they are "those whose minds are faultless."

They say, "They dwell [thus]. Or alternatively, *brahmuno* refers to the Great Beings (*mahāsatta*), the Bodhisattvas, whose qualities have been magnified by the fulfillment of the factors that produce Buddhahood—such as the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and so forth—which serve as the causes for all the Buddha-qualities.

For they [act] by seeking the welfare of all beings, by removing what is harmful, by rejoicing in their prosperity, and by maintaining a state of neutrality toward going to or avoiding any destination whatsoever.

And they dwell with minds free from blemish. "In this way" means just as those Brahmās who have been reborn there, or the Great Bodhisattva-Brahmās, are likewise endowed with and possessed of these divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
Regarding the question beginning with "The four," that is, the threefold question starting with "four": [it refers to] by way of the *Visuddhimagga* and so forth.

Here, the "Path of Purification" (Visuddhimagga) is the means for purifying [the mind] from the defilement of ill-will (*byāpāda*) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), specific modes of attention such as the bringing about of welfare (*hitūpasaṃhāra*) are included.

"Āsaṃ" refers to loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the others. "In the immeasurable" (*appamāṇe*) means in that which is devoid of measure. "By which" (*yena*) means by which cause. "That" (*taṃ*) means therefore. The letter *da* is used for the purpose of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).
The phrase "the path of purification for one who is full of ill-will" should be brought forward and connected [to the preceding];
the intention is that it is the direct opposite. This same method applies to the others as well. The intention is that "non-bending" by way of partiality is the mode of neutrality (*majjhattākāra*).
To show by means of a simile that very fourfold attention toward beings which has been mentioned, [it says] "because..."

And the passage beginning with “just as a mother” has been stated. In that context, the word *ca* (and) is used for the purpose of applying the meaning—that is, the bringing about of welfare and so forth—which was already mentioned, to the subject of the simile (*upameyya*).

Alternatively, it means “in turn” or “successively,” referring to the sequence of rotation according to their respective functions. *Abyāvaṭā* means “unconcerned” or “without striving. *Tathā* means “just as.”

The construction is as follows: a mother [should] act with loving-kindness toward her young children and so forth, and likewise toward all beings by means of loving-kindness and the like, being one whose mind is permeated by such acts of loving-kindness.
"Therefore" means: because all defiled phenomena belong respectively to the categories of hatred, delusion, and lust;
and because the means of purification from them is the immeasurables (appamaññā); and because there is a fourfold mental attention toward beings by way of bestowing benefit and so forth.
Therefore, by way of the Path of Purification and so forth, there are only four immeasurables (*appamaññā*). The intention is that one who wishes to develop all four should not do so one by one;
for when including everything, they must be developed in sequence. Regarding "the desire for welfare" (*hitesitā*) as loving-kindness (*mettā*), he says:
"of those who have thus wished for their welfare. Or, "having honored [them]" means: "By this practice, may this person be reborn in hell and so forth."
Or having reflected. The connection is: "it should be practiced by way of the occurrence of the mode of removing suffering.
"Beyond that" means beyond the initial occurrence of the mode of benefit. "Because there is nothing further to be done" means because there is no fourth mode remaining to be performed.
"This sequence" means this is generally the order of their occurrence among these immeasurables (*appamaññā*).
This was said by way of illustration; it does not mean that "their occurrence follows only this sequence and not otherwise.

For there is no fixed rule regarding the order of the three meditations beginning with loving-kindness (*mettā*); any one of them may be developed first. Or rather, it was stated thus according to the order of the teaching.
"Even of a single being" means even of one single being. Because there is no counterpart sign (*appaṭibhāga-nimitta*), there is no grasping of a limited boundary.
And since the apprehension of a "being" occurring by way of conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) is not an apprehension of a limited form and so forth,

it is stated that even loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the other [immeasurables], which have the apprehension of a being as their primary characteristic and take a single being as their object, possess an immeasurable range (*appamāṇagocaratā*) when they reach absorption (*appanā*).
Thus, "not grasping a measure" means, for example, as in the case of a bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*) and so forth, when it has reached a state of extreme bloating and so on.
The sign is apprehended in a limited area, thus without grasping its full extent. "By way of complete pervasion" means by way of pervading without exception.
270. Regarding "by way of escape": here, whatever is the escape from something is precisely its direct opposite.

Just as renunciation is the escape from sensual desires, the formless is the escape from forms, and Nibbāna is the escape from formations, so too is [the escape] from those things accompanied by mental distress.
Loving-kindness, compassion, and gladness—which serve as the escape from ill will, cruelty, and aversion—are not devoid of mental joy (*somanassa*).

It should be understood that by the very mention of "escape," the association of these [three] with equanimity (*upekkhā*) during their preliminary stages is also permitted, because they do not constitute the final escape.
For indeed, the teachers have stated that compassion and gladness occur within twenty-eight types of consciousness-arising (*cittuppāda*).

They desire this. For the equanimity of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra-upekkhā*) does not function without the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*), unlike the equanimity of purification (*pārisuddhi-upekkhā*). For the equanimity of purification never functions without the feeling of equanimity. 271.
"Accompanied by pleasure" (*sātasahagata*) means accompanied by happiness (*sukha*). "Therefore" (*tasmā*) refers to the teaching beginning with "Then you, O bhikkhus," and so forth.

Just as the state of being accompanied by applied thought (*savitakka*) and so forth is understood for all four immeasurables (*appamaññā*), so too is their state of being accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhāsahagata*) understood;
therefore, the opponent’s intention is that all four immeasurables consist of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas. "If this were so" means:

if one includes the matter already stated regarding the fundamental concentration (*mūlasamādhi*) within the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) because it was mentioned immediately after, then such being the case...

The intention is that the contemplations of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) and so forth might also consist of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas, but they do not; for they are taught by way of insight (*vipassanā*).

Anticipating the objection that one might say, "Let the contemplations of the body and so forth consist of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas by way of the development of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānabhāvanā*)," he says, "In the case of feelings (*vedanā*) and so forth," etc.
[He says this] because [the opponent] has grasped merely the shadow of the literal expression (*byañjana*), namely, "loving-kindness..."

The meaning is: having grasped merely the shadow of concentration as it appears from the phrasing in such passages as "my liberation of mind will be developed," yet without grasping the intended sense found in both [passages], namely that the very same mental concentration described by those phrases is also described by the phrases "my mind will be settled internally" and so forth;
for otherwise, the meaning of the sutta would be [contradicted].
One who speaks thus is said to be slandering the Teacher by speaking what is not in accordance with the truth. Therefore, he said: "Do not misrepresent the Blessed One.

272. Showing that one who wishes to avoid this fault [of misrepresentation] should understand that not every sutta has a solely explicit meaning (*nītattha*), and that therefore the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) must be sought from the teacher's family (*garu-kula*), he spoke the passage beginning with "For it is profound," and therein, starting from the beginning...

He said "For this [person]... and so forth in order to show his intention (*adhippāya*). One for whom a teaching of the Dhamma has been requested is "one who has been requested to teach the Dhamma" (*āyācitadhammadesana*);

[the text refers to] that person who has been so requested. "Evameva" is a particle used in the sense of reproach; its meaning is "just as easily. "Internally" (*ajjhatta*) means within the range of one's own experience (*gocarajjhatte*), that is to say, within the objective support of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhānārammaṇe*).
This is because what is called "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittekaggatā*) is comprised within one's own continuity (*sasantatipariyāpannā*).
Therefore, in the commentary on the meaning, it is said: "by way of one's own internal [states].

"The mind will be steady" means that, not being distracted by external objects, it will remain in a state of one-pointedness; for that very reason, it is well-composed, meaning it is properly concentrated (*samāhita*).
"Arisen" means unobstructed. "Evil" means base. "Unwholesome states" refers to sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth.
Unwholesome states (*akusala-dhammā*) are so called in the sense of being produced by lack of skill (*akosalla-sambhūta*).

The construction is: "Having exhausted the wholesome mind by providing an opportunity for them to arise and seize the mind, they will not cease. By this, he states the cause of the aforementioned concentration (*samādhāna*).
"Mere one-pointedness of mind" refers to a concentration that has been merely attained by one devoted to meditation, but which is not well-cultivated.
Furthermore, because it serves as the fundamental cause for the specific types of concentration to be described below, it is called "root-concentration" (*mūla-samādhi*).

This state, which consists merely of one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*), is intended here as "momentary concentration" (*khaṇika-samādhi*), as in such passages as: "I steady my mind internally, I settle it, I unify it, I concentrate it. For just as elsewhere it is said: "Aroused... [and so forth].
"But my energy, monks, was unflagging... [and so on] ...my mind was concentrated and one-pointed.

Having said this, because of the statement beginning with "quite secluded from sensual pleasures," the one-pointedness of mind mentioned first is understood to be "momentary concentration" (*khaṇika-samādhi*); it is the same here as well.
"That very concentration" refers to the root concentration (*mūla-samādhi*).
"Assa" means of a bhikkhu, or of his basic concentration (*mūlasamādhi*). "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) means increasing.

And by "this concentration," it is precisely the basic concentration that is intended. "Thus cultivated": just as fire produced by means of a fire-drill, when increased by means of cow-dung powder and so forth, is still called by the name of the original fire produced by the fire-drill even though it has attained the state of being a "cow-dung fire" and so on; so too here.
This was said because the basic concentration itself is increased by means of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and so forth.

Regarding other objects as well, such as the earth-kasiṇa (*pathavīkasiṇa*) and others: therein, just as through the method of development preceded by the cultivation of loving-kindness, one reaches the fourfold and fivefold jhānas in the earth-kasiṇa and others by way of the states of "with applied thought" (*savitakka*) and so on, [so too does it apply] to the basic concentration.

Meditative development has been explained; thus, having shown the method of development regarding the earth-kasiṇa and others preceded by the development of compassion and so forth, he subsequently taught the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints while showing the method of development preceded by the contemplation of the body and so forth.
Therefore it was said: “Compassion is my liberation of mind,” and so on. If this is so, [then] at the conclusion of the contemplation of phenomena—
Since the meditation subject was already explained for the sake of attaining Arahantship through this teaching, why was it stated again, "Then you, bhikkhu, this concentration with applied thought...
and so forth? It is for the purpose of showing the attainment of the culmination of the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā).
For that [contemplation], while proceeding by way of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā), specifically comprehends the aforementioned jhāna factors.
It is called "having reached the summit. Some say this was stated for the purpose of showing the plane of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "But when, friends... and so forth, shows the comfortable abidings (*phāsuvihāra*) obtainable beyond the attainment of Arahantship.

In that context, *gagghasī* means "you will go. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) refers to the fact that the teaching beginning with "with applied thought" (*savitakkampi*) [is taught] by way of the objects (*ārammaṇa*) of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the other [immeasurables].
This was stated with reference to concentration upon another object, not to the *appamaññās* (immeasurables);
therefore, even by means of another text beginning with "In the same way," that very point is established. Therein, "in the same way" means precisely by way of the threefold and fourfold jhānas.
"In the Abhidhamma" refers to the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*, as well as to various sections of the Abhidhamma such as the *Appamaññāvibhaṅga*.

273. "By way of the 'beautiful as supreme' (subhaparamā), etc. Here, the word *subha* (beautiful) is used with the elision of the latter member of the compound, referring to the beautiful liberation (*subhavimokkha*) spoken of thus: "He is intent upon the beautiful alone" (*subhanteva adhimutto hoti*). The word *parama* has the sense of excellence.

That which has the beautiful liberation as its supreme, excellent, and ultimate limit is "the beautiful as supreme" (*subhaparamā*), namely, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettācetovimutti*); beyond that, there is nothing further to be accomplished by it.
The meaning is "it does not exist. Since it is an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) meaning that is intended here, the bliss of insight (*vipassanāsukha*) and so forth have no place in this context.
These specific qualities are distinguished from one another, let alone from others. Therefore he said:
"The distinct excellence of their power should be understood as being unlike one another. "Having distinguished" means having made them mutually distinct.

"By way of being the decisive support for this or that" means by way of its status as a decisive support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) through the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) for this or that liberation, such as the liberation of the beautiful (*subha-vimokkha*).
Now, in order to demonstrate this matter more clearly, it is said: "Of one who dwells in loving-kindness" (*mettāvihārissa*), and so forth.
The connection is: "He applies his mind to this one who dwells in loving-kindness. "Through familiarity with what is not repulsive" (*appaṭikkūla-paricayā*).

This is because, through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*), one has become thoroughly habituated to perceiving any object whatsoever—even that designated as a "sentient being"—solely in its aspect of non-repulsiveness.

Consequently, whatever object arises before him, even if it is of a conditioned (*saṅkhāra*) nature, presents itself solely in its aspect of non-repulsiveness, let alone in its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
Thus, his mind proceeds toward it fearlessly, out of a sense of delight, thinking, "It is not repulsive."
And because one is well liberated from adverse states with ease, the term "liberation" (*vimokkha*) is used as a synonym for that jhāna.
Therefore he said, "In regard to things not repulsive," and so forth. Furthermore, the meaning already stated applies here:

for one who gives rise to resentment toward a conscious object with the intention of acting harmfully and so on, there is a familiarity with the repulsive; likewise, even toward unconscious things such as wind or heat, resentment arises due to that same familiarity with the repulsive.
It is to be made manifest. "Nothing beyond that" means that there is no supporting condition for any further liberation beyond that liberation of the beautiful (*subha-vimokkha*).

It is called "striking" (*abhighāta*) because one strikes with it; that which has a staff as its striking is "staff-striking" (*daṇḍābhighāta*); that which has that as its beginning is "staff-striking and so forth" (*daṇḍābhighātādi*);
and that which has the visible form (*rūpa*) of staff-striking and so forth as its sign is "the sign of the visible form of staff-striking and so forth" (*daṇḍābhighātādirūpanimitta*).
But what is that? He says: "the suffering of beings. The meaning is: the suffering arising for beings, caused by the physical body (*karajarūpa*) and produced by blows with sticks and so forth.
For one who dwells in compassion, the danger in form is well understood because of the sign of form;
the intention is that both suffering and compassion have the nature of being unable to endure the suffering of others. Therein—in space—the mind leaps forward.
The total absence of forms is their opening up and disappearance.
Regarding the passage beginning with "by this and that," the construction is as follows:

for the yogi who contemplates the consciousness of joy arisen in beings who are gladdened by various causes of gladness such as the attainment of wealth, [he thinks], "It is truly good that this being is gladdened."
Because it arises through the occurrence of sympathetic joy (*muditā*), the mind becomes familiar with the grasping of consciousness by means of seeing joyful consciousness.

"Attained in successive order" means attained through the cultivation of detachment from the fine-material realm (*rūpavirāga*) by way of the sequence of attaining fine-material-sphere jhānas in any kasina other than the space-kasina (*ākāsakasiṇa*).
It has the sign of space as its object; thus, it is "that which has the sign of space as its range" (*ākāsanimittagocara*).

"In that first immaterial-sphere consciousness whose objective domain is the sign of space": "he directs his mind" means leading the mind of development toward the attainment of the second immaterial sphere;
the sense is "cultivating it in that manner. "Therein" means in that first immaterial-sphere consciousness.
"Mind" refers to the consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness. "Enters" means it penetrates it and settles there by way of liberation.
"Because of the absence of mental application (*ābhoga*)" means because there is no mental application (*ābhujanā*) by way of such things as the aspiration for happiness,

"May they be happy," and so forth. While the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the rest, proceeding by way of the aspiration for the happiness of beings, takes beings as its object through the medium of apprehending ultimate reality (*paramattha*),
the development of equanimity (*upekkhā*), however, not proceeding in that manner, takes beings as its object solely by way of looking on with indifference (*ajjhupekkhanā*).

Because it takes an object, he said: “For one who dwells in equanimity, the mind becomes free from the suffering of grasping at what does not exist, owing to its being turned away from grasping at ultimate realities such as pleasure and pain.

But is it not the case that even the divine abode of equanimity (*upekkhā-brahmavihāra*) is [attained] precisely through the gateway of grasping ultimate realities by way of negation, according to such passages as: “Beings are owners of their karma; by whose whim would they become happy? and so forth?
"Does it take sentient beings as its object? "That is true; however, that occurs during the preliminary stage of meditation (*pubbabhāga*).
But at the time of reaching the culmination, it takes sentient beings as its object solely by way of equanimity (*ajjhupekkhanavasena*).

Thus, its occurrence is specifically directed toward objects that do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*). And the suffering inherent in grasping what does not exist is [overcome] by way of equanimity."

It should be understood that this is because, upon reaching absorption (appanā), it is characterized by being the head of the seven graspings free from misapprehension (*aparāmāsa*). The rest is exactly as stated in the method already described.

274. "All these" means all these immeasurables (*appamaññā*). "Of giving and so forth" refers to the qualities that produce a Buddha, such as giving and the rest, when they have reached the state of perfections (*pāramī*).
"Of all wholesome states" refers to all blameless states; [this applies] to the thirty-two...
Of the perfections, of their causes—the factors conducive to Buddhahood—and of all things that possess a beautiful nature.

Indeed, there are no mundane phenomena superior in power to the qualities that produce a Buddha; regarding the Buddha-qualities, it is simply not possible [to speak of anything higher]. "Fulfilling" means causing them to increase.
For just like the foundations (adhiṭṭhānāni), the immeasurables (appamaññā) are the cause of the growth of all the perfections.
"Those who bring about fulfillment. By the passage beginning with "Through the disposition toward welfare," he shows this meaning:

because their own mental continuum has been thoroughly prepared by the four immeasurables—by way of demonstrating that the sublime abodes (brahmavihāras) such as loving-kindness (*mettā*) serve as the foundation for the sublime abode of equanimity (*upekkhā*)—the Great Bodhisattvas are capable of fulfilling the perfections (*pāramīs*) such as giving, and not otherwise.

The statement, "this should be given, this should not be given," is to be regarded as a mere illustration, because it must be said that one gives "without making a distinction such as 'this should be given' or 'this should not be given.
For the perfection of giving is free from conceptual differentiation regarding the recipient or the object to be given. As it has been said:
“Just as a jar that is completely full, when turned upside down,
vomits out its water without remainder and does not retain anything there.
This phrase “of all beings” should also be connected with the words “the source of happiness” and “giving.”
Thus, by means of the gift itself, as well as by the act of giving, it is stated that Great Beings are of great benefit to the world;
likewise, this is because of their dedication [of merit]. For the purpose of illustrating that point, although it was said "without making a distinction," it was further stated "of all beings.
"Of them" means of all beings. Regarding the word "injury" (*upaghāta*), here too [the phrase] "without making a distinction" applies.

Having brought [the words] together, they should be connected. Herein, this is the construction of the words: "Without making distinctions and avoiding harm, all beings undertake virtue (*sīla*), which is the source of happiness for all beings.
For the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*) is free from conceptualization regarding beings and time;
its fruit is indeed dedicated solely to the welfare of the world. "They resort to renunciation" means they enter the homeless life (*pabbajjā*).
For one who has gone forth, virtue is fulfilled in every respect, whereas it is not so for a householder.
Here too, this should be connected by bringing in the phrase: "the cause of happiness for all beings without making distinctions.

Indeed, Bodhisattvas do not undertake the life of renunciation or formally adopt the precepts by making a distinction of time; and this is merely an illustration, as it also applies to the cultivation of jhāna and other forms of renunciation.
Because it is desirable. That it is the source of happiness for all beings is according to the method already stated above. This same principle applies to the remaining [qualities] as well.
"In regard to the beneficial and the harmful" means in regard to what is advantageous and what is disadvantageous. "For the sake of non-delusion" means for the destruction of delusion.

"They purify wisdom" means that by hearing what has not been heard—such as the bases of knowledge (*vijjā-ṭṭhāna*) practiced through yoga—and by clarifying what has been heard, they shake off the notions of "I-making" (*ahaṃkāra*) and "mine-making" (*mamaṃkāra*).
They purify their knowledge. For the perfection of wisdom is free from the conceptualization of "I" and "mine.

"For the sake of welfare and happiness" means solely for the purpose of increasing the welfare, happiness, and so forth, of sentient beings. "Constantly" means continuously, without interruption, and unmixed with opposing factors.
"They arouse energy" means so that unarisen welfare and happiness may arise in sentient beings, and what has already arisen may further increase.
Thus they exert themselves. For the perfection of energy (vīriya-pāramitā) is devoid of contraction and expansion.
By the phrase "having attained the state of a hero," he shows their capacity to restrain those who have transgressed.
"They forgive various kinds of offenses" means they endure the manifold wrongs committed against them in a manner that cuts to the quick. They are free from the conceptualization of self and other.
For the perfection of patience (*khantipāramitā*) is the endurance of faults.
"Not deceiving their promise" refers, by way of the common characteristic of non-deception, to the non-practicing of all ignoble speech.

The perfection of truth (*saccapāramitā*) is indeed being free from false conceptualization regarding what has been seen and so forth, whether promised or not promised. [They are] characterized by unwavering resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
The perfection of resolve (*adhiṭṭhānapāramitā*) is the firm establishment in the qualities such as giving that have been undertaken, characterized by an unshakable resolve and commitment;
and it is the correct persistence in those qualities that produce a Buddha once they have been undertaken. "In them" means among sentient beings.
"Unwavering" means not to be shaken by opposing factors. "Thus" means in the manner already described, such as the disposition toward the welfare of sentient beings. As...
And the perfections have the divine abodes as their foundation; likewise, they also have the foundations [of the fourfold resolve] as their foundation. For it is thus:

through the practice of the perfections for the sake of benefiting others according to one’s promise, there is the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*); through the relinquishing of their opposites, there is the foundation of generosity (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*);

through the pacification of one's own mind by means of the perfections, there is the foundation of peace (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*); and through skill in the means of benefiting others by means of them, there is the foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*).
In this way, each perfection (*pāramitā*) should also be applied individually as appropriate. This is the summary here;
however, whatever needs to be said regarding the perfections in detail should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Cariyāpiṭaka-vaṇṇanā* within the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
For fear of excessive prolixity, we have not elaborated upon it. The same applies to the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*) and so forth. These alone—
"They are" means "these indeed are"; such is the construction.
The commentary on the description of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) is concluded.
Thus ends the commentary on the ninth chapter.
10. Explanation of the Description of the Formless (Āruppaniddesavaṇṇanā). Explanation of the First Formless State (Paṭhamāruppavaṇṇanā) 275.
Regarding the phrase "among those taught": this refers to "the four formless states" as they were thus taught; here, the locative case is used in the sense of selection. Therefore he said:
“Regarding ‘in the four formless states’ (*ārūppesu*): therein, that which is formless (*arūpa*) by way of seclusion from form (*rūpa*) is the formless meditation itself (*ārūppa-jhāna*).
However, here it is the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) for that purpose that is intended. The connection is: ‘one who desires to develop that [formless state] arouses the fourth jhāna.

‘Based on form’ (*rūpādhikaraṇa*) means ‘with form as the cause. For in this context, the word *adhikaraṇa* has the sense of ‘cause,’ as in such expressions as ‘based on sensual pleasures’ (*kāmādhikaraṇa*).”
In the sense of punishing, "staff" (daṇḍa) refers to clubs and the like. Taking up such an object with the intention of harming others is "taking up the staff" (daṇḍādāna).

A weapon (sattha) is so called in the sense of cutting beings; it is a missile. Quarreling (bhaṇḍana) is strife (kalaha). Hostility (virodha) is conflict (viggaha). Dispute (vivāda) is contention through various arguments.

"This" (etaṃ) refers to the aforementioned taking up of the staff and so forth. "In every way" (sabbaso) means without exception. In the formless realm (ārūpe), that is, in the state of being formless.
Or in the formless existence (*ārūpa-bhava*). "Of forms alone" means of those very forms whose dangers have been seen, and not of the formless; this is the intended meaning.
"For the sake of disenchantment" means for the purpose of becoming disenchanted by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*). "For the sake of dispassion" means for the purpose of fading away from passion.

"For the sake of cessation" means for the purpose of ceasing. All of this is said with reference to transcendence (*samatikkama*). By the word "etc. in "taking up the staff, etc.," [the other items are included].

It should be understood that all harmful things, such as taking what is not given and so forth, are comprised within the cause of form (*rūpa*), and it is not only those mentioned here in the text that are so included.
"Corporeal form" (*karajarūpa*) is stated to show its suitability as the basis for the aforementioned disadvantages;
the meaning is "gross form. "Disadvantage" (*ādīnava*) means fault. "Of that" refers to form. "Light" (*āloka*) is simply a particular kind of color; thus, [the term] occurs there [in that sense].

Having removed the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta), it may be possible to grasp the space sign (ākāsanimitta); however, this cannot be done by removing the limited-space kasiṇa (paricchinnākāsakasiṇa).
For the removal of that [limited-space kasiṇa] can only occur through the sign of form (rūpanimitta). Therefore, he said: "In nine, excluding the limited-space kasiṇa.
Some, however, say: "In eight, excluding even the light kasiṇa (ālokakasiṇa)," but regarding its exclusion:
No cause is seen; the material form of the hand has transcended it because there is no objective support for it.

If this is so, why is it said, "by way of the fourth jhāna"? Is it not the case that the first jhānas and so forth also proceed by way of having no objective support, since they have the counterpart sign as their object?
This is true; however, [the fourth jhāna] is distinguished by its peaceful nature due to the abandoning of the coarse factors.
Because it has been thoroughly transcended by means of the fourth jhāna, which has attained imperturbability, it is said to be "by way of the fourth jhāna.
Some say this is because of the cessation of inhalation and exhalation and because of the transcendence of the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu);
however, that is not the reason, since other mind-originated material phenomena still arise, and because the lower jhānas do not lead to the transcendence of the sense-sphere.
“Only its counterpart” means only the counterpart of the material form of the fingernail, because it is possible to grasp the sign [of the mark] there.
Regarding the inquiry, “And that is not called ‘similar’; therefore, what is the point of transcending it?”—it is with reference to this that “How?
Just as... and so forth was said. Therein, “how” is a question expressing a desire to explain. “Just as” is a particle used in the sense of a simile. “A painted figure” (lekha-citta) refers to...
The mind [is directed] toward a line that has been prepared with black pigment and so forth. "A fissure between fruits" means a gap.
"Having seen" means having seen from afar. "Engaging in similar forms, sounds, and activities" means employing similar forms, shapes, and sounds.
"By way of the object" means: "My eye is beautiful, my body is firm, my requisites are handsome."

Thus it is by way of making [the object] the focal point (*ārammaṇakaraṇa*). "The time of possessing derived matter" (*karajarūpasamaṅgikāla*) means the time when one is endowed with both the bodily form of one's own personal existence (*attabhāvarūpa*) and the objective form (*ārammaṇarūpa*).
"That too" (*tampi*) refers to the *kasiṇa* form as well; for this accusative case is used here in the sense of the genitive. The construction is:

"just as there is a desire not to see fear and terror, so too there is a desire to transcend [them]. And this is a general term for the aforementioned disenchantment (*nibbidā*), dispassion (*virāga*), and cessation (*nirodha*).
For it is said that these three were described because they lacked the desire to see fear and terror. It is told that once a dog, having merely been struck by a boar in the forest, fled;
at a time when he could not yet see forms, he saw a cooking pot from afar and, perceiving it to be a boar, fled in fear and trembling.
Also, a man who was terrified of goblins, in the middle of the night in an unfamiliar place, [saw] a headless corpse...
Seeing the palm trunk, terrified by the perception of a *pisāca* demon, trembling and fainting, he fell down; it is with reference to this that it was said:
"Just as pigs... [and so on]... should be understood.
(276) He says "Thus" (*evaṃ*) in order to conclude the meaning of the simile as previously stated. "He" (*so*) refers to the practitioner of yoga (*yogāvacara*). In that *jhāna*...
The connection is with the phrase "he sees the danger. "Form" (rūpa) refers to the kasiṇa-form.

"From the peaceful liberation" means from the formless jhānas; for those [jhanas] are designated as "peaceful liberations" in such passages as, "Those peaceful liberations which, having transcended forms, are formless," and so forth.

The establishment of their peacefulness is to be understood from the tradition of the lineage (anussuti). By the word "just as" (yathā), through the particle *eva*, it indicates in what manner this...

The fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere has two factors; likewise, it is shown that the immaterial attainments also have two factors by way of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind, but not merely the state of having two factors as in the case of the third jhāna.
Is it not the case here too that there is merely the state of having two factors due to the difference in planes?
This is not a fault, because the relationship between the simile and the subject of the simile involves different bases.

"Therein" means in that fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). "Longing" means expectation. "Having exhausted" means having worn away that jhāna by seeing its danger; the meaning is, having become free from expectation.
Since attention to it as peaceful necessarily implies attention to it as sublime and subtle, he said: "having attended to it as peaceful and infinite. "Having spread out" means...
Or rather, having expanded it as it was increased, or having spread it out by way of expansion. "By that" means by the kasiṇa-form.
"He removes the kasiṇa" means he takes away the kasiṇa-form, such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth, which has become the object of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere.
Showing the method of removal, however, he said, "While removing," and so forth. Therein, "he rolls up" means he withdraws it.
"Aññadatthu" means "absolutely. "Neither emerges" (*neva ubbaṭṭati*) means it does not rise up. "Does not turn away" (*na vivaṭṭati*) means it does not revolve back.
"Of this" (*imassa*) refers to this kasiṇa-form. "Non-attention" (*amanasikāraṃ*) means not attending to, not thinking about.

"And depending on attention" (*manasikārañca paṭicca*) means by relying on the meditative attention that develops [the thought] "space, space. This is what is meant: of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere...

When one does not attend to the kasiṇa-form as the object in its entirety, but instead attends to the space touched by it as "space, space," and when that [space] appears as space through the power of meditation, then one is said to have "removed" (ugghāṭeti) the kasiṇa;
and that [kasiṇa] is said to have been removed by him. Therefore he said: "the mere space revealed from the kasiṇa."
“...is discerned. All this—these three kinds—is indeed one, because they are merely different modes of expression.

Why was it said, “they suppress the hindrances”? Is it not the case that the hindrances have already been suppressed at the very moment of the access concentration (upacāra) of the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and from that point on, they no longer manifest as obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna)? If they were to [manifest] again, [it would be impossible].

Could one fall away from jhāna? As for what some say—"There are indeed subtle hindrances suppressible by formless jhānas, and it was with reference to these that this was said"—that is merely their own opinion.

For there is no such thing as specific abandonment (odhiso pahāna) in the sublime wholesome states, as there is in the supramundane wholesome states. Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the fine-material sphere and the formless spheres...

The distinction such as the state of having a sublime fruit and so forth should be understood as being due to the specific nature of their development—that is, by way of being more continuous and more refined within those very same [factors], such that each subsequent one is superior to each preceding one. However, the statement "they suppress" is spoken by way of praise;
for elsewhere too, the abandoning of what has already been abandoned below is mentioned in reference to what follows above. As for those who say... [all]
They say that this was stated because wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*) are the opposites of all unwholesome states;

however, those [who say this] must state the reason why the suppression of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa-vikkhambhana*) is not mentioned in the access concentration (*upacāra*) of the second jhāna and so forth.

"Mindfulness stands firm" means that mindfulness, having the sign of space as its object, remains properly well-established. And here, by way of the term "mindfulness," [those factors] conducive to access jhāna are [implied].
He shows the application of their respective functions for those [meditations] with faith as the fifth. "By access" means by access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*).

"Here too" is a collective reference to the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), for that is associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*). "The rest" refers to the passage beginning with "the remaining [meditations] belong to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*).
Whatever remains to be said here that has not yet been stated should be understood according to the method explained in the exposition of the earth-kasiṇa (*pathavī-kasiṇa-niddesa*).
He said: "In the same manner as described for the earth-kasiṇa.
Having thus extended by reference (*atidisa*) what is common to that [practice], he now said, "But this is the distinction," and so forth, in order to show what is specific.

Regarding the phrase "the front of vehicles, baskets, water-jars, etc.": the front of vehicles such as covered litters (*oguṇṭhana-sivika*) and the like is the "front of the vehicle" (*yānamukha*); the basket (*putoli*)...
The mouth of a small door is a "putoḷimukha"; the word *mukha* (mouth) should be applied to each term, as in "kumbhimukha" (the mouth of a jar).

Space itself is [defined] by its delimitation as the opening of a vehicle and so forth. "By means of preparatory attention" (*parikammamanasikārena*) means by means of attention that serves as the preparation, namely, access concentration (*upacārajjhāna*).
For "preparation" (*parikamma*), "conformity" (*anuloma*), and "access" (*upacāra*) are not different in meaning. Looking [at it].
By means of the eye of the formless-sphere jhāna.

"In every aspect" means by way of seeing the faults in all material phenomena—such as the sign of form through the taking up of a staff, its arising, and so forth—as well as in the signs of form such as the earth-kasiṇa and the jhānas that have them as their object. In those very things...
Or [it is called "form"] by means of the abandoning of attachment to forms and so forth, or by the desire not to direct the mind toward them.

The fine-material jhāna (*rūpajjhāna*) is also called "form" through the elision of the latter member of the compound, as in "he develops the path for rebirth in the form realm" (*rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti*), just as "existence in the form realm" (*rūpabhava*) is called "form. For "one possessing form" (*rūpī*) means one who has attained the fine-material jhānas.
The object, namely the kasiṇa-form, is also called "form" through the elision of the former member of the compound, just as in the case of "Devadatta."
“Given. “He sees forms”: the meaning is that he sees the kasiṇa-forms with the eye of jhāna. “Therefore”:
because, through the elision of the latter member and the elision of the former member respectively, the designation “form” (rūpa) is seen applied to the form-jhāna and the kasiṇa-forms;
therefore [it is so called]. “Perception of form” (rūpasaññā): this is the perception associated with that [jhāna] regarding the form-jhāna. And of that which has it as its object...
By the word "and" (ca), it includes the aforementioned fine-material-sphere jhāna;

thus, it shows that the designation "perceptions of form" (*rūpasaññānaṃ*) in the Pāḷi is made by means of a collective singular compound (*sarūpekasesa*). "Dispassion" (*virāgā*) is because of loathing. "Cessation" (*nirodhā*) is because of the cessation [of perceptions] through the suppression of the desire and lust that obstruct them.
To make this very meaning clearer, the passage beginning with "What is meant? (*kiṃ vuttaṃ hotī*) was stated. Of that...
Or rather, the construction here should be made thus: "The cessation of all things without remainder through dispassion in every aspect.

The statement, "For one who is not dispassionate toward the object, there is no transcendence of perception," is said because these jhānas are to be attained by transcending the object, not by transcending the factors (of absorption).
Furthermore, in this context, the transcendence of perception occurs through the transcendence of the object.
Without [the former], the latter does not exist; therefore he said, "When perceptions have been transcended, the object has indeed been transcended.
This is to be connected with the phrase "it was stated without [explicitly] saying...

In the expressions beginning with "of one who has attained," the term "attained" (*samāpanna*) is used in reference to wholesome perception (*kusalasaññā*), "arisen" (*upapanna*) in reference to resultant perception (*vipākasaññā*), and "dwelling in happiness in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*) in reference to functional perception (*kiriyasaññā*).
For the jhānas of an Arahant are specifically a dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*). If one asks:
"If the transcendence of the object that brings about the transcendence of perception was not mentioned in the *Vibhaṅga*, then why is it included here?", he says "But because... and so forth.
This commentary on the meaning has also been made by way of the transcendence of the object, as in the passage beginning: "And this is a designation for that which has that as its object."
The intention is that, as in the *Vibhaṅga*, it does not merely speak of the surmounting of perception.
278. "By striking" (*paṭighātena*) means by the striking together, the meeting of the sense organ and the object.

In the phrases beginning with "the subsiding" (*atthaṅgama*), each preceding term is a synonym for each succeeding one; therefore, the subsiding of perceptions of resistance occurs at the time of possessing the jhāna.
"Non-arising" (*anuppatti*) is stated as "Granted, these... and so forth, in order to demonstrate by way of inquiry the reason for their apprehension right here.
It is for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in those who are practicing. Of these perceptions of repulsion. Here, in the discussion on the first immaterial attainment (*āruppa*).
The statement is by way of their disappearance.

Or rather, instead of praising and extolling [the jhāna], it is said "or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth to show that the cessation of perceptions of resistance (*paṭighasaññā*) is stated here precisely because it must be mentioned in this very context.
In that regard, the non-existence of a phenomenon possessing its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) occurs either through its abandonment by its opposite or through the absence of its conditions.
Among these, for one possessing the fine-material jhāna (*rūpajjhāna*), there is the non-existence of perceptions of resistance.
Showing that [the absence of perception] is due merely to the non-existence of conditions and not to the attainment of an antidote, he says "even though," and so forth.

Therein, "those" refers to perceptions of aversion (*paṭighasaññā*). "Fine-material" refers to fine-material-sphere jhāna. "Of one who has attained" means of one who, having attained it, abides therein.

The construction is: "even though they do not exist. It is not the case that they do not exist because they have been abandoned; at that time, perceptions of aversion do not exist by way of their state of being abandoned.
“They do not exist indeed. Regarding this, he states the reason: “For development pertaining to the fine-material sphere does not lead to dispassion for the fine-material [realm].
Anticipating the objection, “But aren't perceptions of resistance also immaterial phenomena (arūpadhammā)?”, he says: “And their occurrence is dependent upon the material.
Furthermore, “this development” refers to the development of the immaterial [sphere] (arūpabhāvanā). “To maintain” means to ascertain. “Here” means...

In the formless jhānas, immovability (*āneñjatā*) is established through such terms as "imperturbable volitional formations" (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*). Furthermore, their nature as peaceful liberations is stated in passages such as, "Those peaceful liberations which, having transcended forms, are formless.

(279) Due to the thorough abandoning of perceptions of resistance (*paṭighasaññā*) by means of cultivating the antidote preceded by the vision of faults, even by a great [amount of...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated here.*

One does not emerge from the formless attainments because of sound. However, emergence from all fine-material-sphere attainments would not be possible due to the lack of complete abandonment [of sound].
Yet, even the first jhāna cannot endure even a slight sound; therefore, it is said that for one who has attained it, sound is a "thorn.

In the absence of the development of the formless, there is the arising [of rebirth] after death for those capable of such rebirth, characterized by the perception of form and the perception of resistance.
As long as the manifestation of one's own karmic result continues, so long is there said to be both transcendence and subsidence by means of bringing about the state of non-arising.
Regarding perceptions of diversity, however, those that do not arise in that particular existence because they depend exclusively on form do not arise due to the absence of opportunity;
they do not fail to arise because of being obstructed by the development of the formless attainments, for some of them do indeed arise since they are not obstructed.

Therefore, non-attention toward them is said to be non-adverting and non-reviewing; or rather, it is the non-performance and non-entry of the life-continuum consciousness within the range of the impulsion that establishes [the mind].
And by means of that, through the surmounting of forms which are the causes for the attention to perceptions of diversity, the stability of concentration [is attained].

The phrase beginning with “in brief” was stated in order to demonstrate this. Furthermore, the praise of the attainment of the base of infinite space is described by these three terms for the purpose of generating enthusiasm and providing encouragement to the listeners.

For there are those who hold unwholesome views and ask, “What benefit is there in a perception that functions in space, which is devoid of all objects of regard? It is in order to turn them away from such wrong graspings that this was said.
The benefit of *jhāna* is stated by these three terms. For upon hearing this, it will occur to them:
"Since this attainment is indeed so refined, come now, let us make an effort to produce it. (280) *Assa* means of space.
*Uppādanto* is the very arising (*uppāda*), and likewise *vayanto* is the passing away (*vaya*). For [space] is a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*).
Because it arises without having previously existed and perishes after having existed, it is delimited by rise and fall.

Space, however, because it is a phenomenon lacking intrinsic nature (asabhāvadhamma) and because both those [characteristics] are absent in it, is said to be infinite. Since the space delimited by the "unblemished space" (ajaṭākāsa) is not intended here, he says: "Space means the space cleared by the kasiṇa.
That by which the kasiṇa is removed is the "kasiṇa-clearer" (kasiṇugghāṭa); that very thing...

"Emergent from the kasiṇa": by way of attention (*manasikāra*) as well—meaning, by way of the preparatory attention that occurs in the mode of infinite pervasion, because there is no grasping of a boundary due to the mere grasping of the seclusion from form—it "pervades infinitely.

Because the boundary is not grasped, having made it infinite, one touches [the object] with the contact of jhāna preceded by the contact of the preparatory stage. Just as [one touches] only the tip of a lotus stalk...
"Medicine" (*bhesajja*); likewise, *ākāsānañcaṃ* is derived from *ākāsānantam* by changing the letter *t* of *parassa* (of another) to *c*.

Because it is the basis for the occurrence of jhāna, the object is said to be "its base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being a foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*), since the word *āyatana* is seen to have the meaning of a foundation.
Furthermore, the word *āyatana* is also appropriate here in the senses of cause, source, birthplace, lineage, and dwelling place.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Base of Infinite Consciousness (Viññāṇañcāyatana-kathāvaṇṇanā) 281.
One who has attained mastery (*ciṇṇavasībhāva*) is so called because he has practiced, cultivated, mastered, and gained proficiency in the characteristics of mental adverting and so forth.

By that mastery thus attained. Because it cannot be reached without transcending the perception of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-saññā*), [and] because of the active engagement of the attention and perception associated with that [perception].

It is said that they are "enemies of the neighboring fine-material-sphere jhānas" because they bring about a state conducive to decline, and because by transcending them alone, the transcendence of the others that must be transcended is accomplished.

Furthermore, because they bring about successive distinctions through development that has entered the right path, and because their sublime nature is established, the second immaterial attainment is more peaceful in its essential quality than the first immaterial attainment; thus he said: "But not..."
For he will say, "They are more refined, each subsequent one than the preceding here," as in the case of the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*).
One should not simply attend to or develop it as "infinite, infinite";
rather, one should attend to it as "infinite consciousness, infinite consciousness," or simply as "consciousness, consciousness."

"In that sign" means in that sign consisting of consciousness, namely, the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment (*paṭhamāruppaviññāṇa*). "Directing the mind" means causing the mind of meditation (*bhāvanācitta*) to proceed.
"In consciousness pervading space" refers to the first immaterial consciousness proceeding as an object by pervading the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa.
"Enters" means it proceeds by way of absorption (*appanā*). Even though it is a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*),...

Because it lacks the cultivation that transcends the object, this [attainment] reaches absorption (appanā), just like the fourth immaterial attainment. As for the method of absorption here, it is according to the method already stated:

in the preliminary stage of this second immaterial jhāna, there are three or four access-thought-moments (javana) belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), which are associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity. Then, as stated in the passage beginning, “The fourth or fifth [moment] belongs to the immaterial sphere,” and so forth...
The meaning is that it should be understood according to the method explained for the first immaterial jhāna, or else by the method of absorption (appanānaya).
Even with respect to an object that is a dhamma possessing intrinsic nature, the jhāna reaches absorption through the development of transcending the object; thus it attains immaterial absorption.

This is to be understood according to the method stated in the *Maraṇānussati-niddesa*: "In that case, there is merely the transcending of the object of the jhāna that has already reached absorption."

282. "In every way" (*sabbaso*) means: in the first immaterial realm (*ārūpa*), by way of seeing all faults—such as "being an adversary to the proximate fine-material jhāna" and "having an insubstantial nature"—or by way of abandoning attachment to it and the absence of desire to advert to it;

or else, the meaning is that it is "entirely" (*sabbaṃ*), without remainder, according to the divisions of wholesome, resultant, and functional [states]. This meaning is according to the method explained above.

"It can be known," he said; "the phrase 'all' is exactly as previously explained. Since the state of the jhāna being the base of infinite space was explained below by way of an external-object compound (*bāhiratthasamāsa*), he said, "By the method stated before, the jhāna itself is the base of infinite space.
However, to demonstrate that for the object it is by way of a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*), he said, "The object also... and so forth. Therein:
“‘In the same manner as before’” is said with reference to the establishment of the terms stated as “there is no end to it,” and so forth.

The phrase beginning with “likewise” is stated to show that the meaning of the word *āyatana* (base) is applicable here in the sense of a place of origin (*sañjātidesa*), just as it is in the sense of a foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
In this context, “place of origin” (*sañjātidesa*) means that which is originated (*sañjāyati*) therein; thus, the place itself is the origin.

Jhāna is [achieved] by the non-occurrence [of the mind]; the object is [achieved] by non-attention. Or else, both may be applied to both. For it is possible to understand the meaning as follows: there is non-adverting even for jhāna;
or, non-attention is the non-introduction of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousness by means of the impulsion (javana) that leads to it;
and for the object, non-occurrence is the non-functioning of the mind by way of taking it as an object. Thus the sense is established.
Having combined them by means of a collective designation (*sāmaññaniddesa*) or by the method of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*),

the first formless-sphere consciousness is called "infinite consciousness" because it must be attended to as "infinite" precisely through its own mode of pervading the previously [envisaged] infinite space that was made its object; thus, it is stated again "by way of attention."
Or it is said, “or infinite,” the intention being that this is by way of attending to it in its entirety. Therefore he said:
“Attending to it without remainder, one attends to it as ‘infinite. Showing that this very same meaning is stated in the *Jhānavibhaṅga*, he said:
“But what is stated in the Vibhaṅga,” and so forth. The meaning of that text should be understood in this way.
"He attends to that very space pervaded by consciousness as the consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness.

However, this meaning appears more appropriate: he attends to that very space pervaded by consciousness—that is, to the aspect grasped by it—in such a way that the consciousness pervades that [space] as infinite.
For the space that the practitioner of the first formless attainment [pervades] with consciousness...
It pervades the infinite. One who possesses the second immaterial attainment is said to "pervade the infinite" when he attends to that consciousness together with its mode of pervading.
Here, "infinitude" refers to the mode of pervading the infinite by way of mental attention; it does not mean the absence of a limit to its arising, as is the case with space.
“‘It has no end, thus it is infinite’—he said only this much.
By the phrase “a conventional term,” he shows that the word *viññāṇañca* is established in the sense of the compound *viññāṇānañca*.

Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows: consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is made infinite (*añciyati*) by the second formless absorption; it is taken as an object in the manner described, and thus it is called *viññāṇañca*. The rest...
"It has the meaning already stated" means he said, "The remainder is exactly like the previous [section].
Regarding the commentary on the discussion of the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana):
whatever in the third immaterial meditation subject is similar to what was stated above should be understood according to the method already explained.

We shall explain what has not been stated before. In that context, "of that very [consciousness]" means of that very consciousness by depending upon which the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*) occurred. But what is that? He says: "of the consciousness of the base of infinite space.

By this, he shows that there is no object for the third formless absorption other than that. By the phrase "of that which has become the object," he indicates that the consciousness of the second formless attainment is not its object.
He turns back. "Absence" (*abhāva*) means non-existence. "Emptiness" (*suññatā*) means hollowness. "The mode of seclusion" (*vivittākāra*) means seclusion (*viveka*).

With these three terms, he speaks of the very disappearance of the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment (*paṭhamāruppaviññāṇa*). Having said, "It should be brought to mind," the passage beginning with "That consciousness...
is stated in order to show the method of bringing it to mind. Therein, "without bringing it to mind" means [not bringing it to mind] in every respect.
"Without having done" means without having reflected. The word *vā* has the sense of non-restriction; by it, he shows that the purpose is accomplished even by one of the three modes.
"In that sign" means in that sign for the arising of jhāna, which consists in the absence of the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment.
"Pervading space" means occurring after having pervaded space. Alternatively, the reading is *ākāsaphuṭe*. "In the state of being empty, secluded, and absent."
This is stated for the purpose of grasping that specific mode by which it has been cultivated—namely, as emptiness, seclusion, and non-existence.
Alternatively, "in the state of emptiness, seclusion, and non-existence" refers to the state of non-existence characterized by emptiness and seclusion;
by this, he demonstrates only the absence of destruction, not prior non-existence and so forth.
"For in that absorption-consciousness" means: when the consciousness associated with the jhāna of the base of nothingness is occurring by way of absorption;
or, when the aforementioned absorption-consciousness has arisen in that state of non-existence (natthibhāva) which is reckoned as the disappearance of the first immaterial attainment.
The connection is: "that bhikkhu dwells perceiving only non-existence. It is like a man who, having gone somewhere and returned...
The construction is: "He sees only emptiness; he sees only the state of non-existence. "That place" refers to that location where they have gathered.
By the phrase "having disappeared through preliminary attention," he shows that its disappearance is due to the absence of making it an object of cognition, not because it has perished.
Here is the application of the simile: just as that man [sees] those who have gathered there...
Having gone after seeing the community of monks, he returns and sees that place as empty of monks when all the monks have departed for some business;
yet he does not see the reason for their departure from there either.

In the same way, this practitioner of yoga, having previously seen the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment with the eye of the jhāna of the base of infinite consciousness, [sees it thus].

Thinking "it does not exist afterwards," when that [consciousness] has departed through the preliminary mental attention (*parikamma-manasikāra*), he dwells perceiving its very non-existence with the eye of the third formless absorption (*tatiyāruppa-jhāna-cakkhu*);
he does not investigate the cause of its departure, because such an absorption lacks that kind of directed application (*ābhoga*).

Regarding the phrase "having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness" (*sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma*), whatever is to be said there should be understood according to the method explained below.

284. By explaining the meaning of the term “non-existence” (*natthi*) as the state of being empty (*suñña*) and secluded (*vivitta*) through various methods, the words “empty” and “secluded” are also implicitly included.
The repetition (*āmeḍita-vacana*), however, is intended to show the mode of cultivation. To demonstrate that this very same meaning has been stated for this term even in the *Vibhaṅga*, it was said:
“And what [is stated] in the *Vibhaṅga*,” and so forth. In that context, “he causes that very consciousness to cease” means:
The meaning is: "that very same first immaterial-sphere consciousness which was previously attended to as 'infinite consciousness.
For it is that very object which, like the sign of form in the case of the first [jhāna], is made non-existent by the third immaterial attainment.
"Comprehension by way of destruction" refers to the contemplation of dissolution; for that [contemplation] sees only the dissolution of conditioned phenomena.
With the intention that [consciousness] receives the description beginning with "he also causes consciousness to cease," he says: "It is stated as being like the comprehension by way of destruction.
