"Assa" refers to the reading. Again, "assa" refers to consciousness. "Abhāveti" means he makes it non-existent;
he acts in such a way that it does not stand before knowledge, by means of non-attention. For that very reason, he "vibhāveti," which is to say, he brings about its state of disappearance.
It acts or destroys so that it is no longer seen; thus, it causes [the object] to disappear or to go into concealment (*tirobhāva*).
"Not otherwise" means that the meaning of this passage is exactly as stated, and not otherwise—that is, there is no inconsistency in this sense.

"Of this" refers to the absence of consciousness in the first immaterial realm (*paṭhamāruppaviññāṇābhāva*). "Anything whatsoever" (*kiñcana*) means even a little bit. It refers to the state where the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of a phenomenon has almost entirely vanished.

He said, "There would be nothing but its dissolution," meaning, "there is not even a mere residue of its dissolution remaining. For if even a mere residue of dissolution remained, it would still possess something belonging to it (*sakiñcanatā*).
And by "nothing belonging to it" (*akiñcana*), he refers to the complete disappearance of consciousness in every respect, without grasping at any mode whatsoever.
The rest is exactly as previously explained.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Base of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (285).

"But it is not peaceful" means that while the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is particularly peaceful because it has reached a state of extreme subtlety in its remaining formations, this attainment of the base of nothingness is not peaceful because that [subtlety] is absent. This which...
Because they must be maintained by conditions among the aggregates, and because they are the root of disease, they resemble a disease;

because they are associated with the sting of suffering and so forth, they resemble a boil; and because they produce affliction and so forth, they resemble a dart. That perception exists when there is [the mind], not when it is absent;

thus it is said: "Perception is a disease, perception is a boil, perception is a dart. And herein, that [perception] performs its function effectively for the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*).
Gross perception is to be understood. Not only perception, but the inclusion of feeling, volition, and so forth, should also be seen;

however, the description is made by way of the headword "perception. "This is peaceful" means it is peaceful because it is devoid of perceptions similar to diseases and other conditions that produce a state of non-peace.
For that very reason, it is sublime. But what is that? He says: "neither-perception-nor-non-perception. By this designation, he refers to the jhāna associated with it.

“Disadvantage” (*ādīnava*): here, disadvantage should be understood as the presence of perceptions similar to disease and so forth, and not merely as being opposed to the neighboring base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*).
“Above” means in the fourth formless realm. “That very same” means that very same [perception]. “Has occurred” means it has proceeded, been produced, or been employed.
“In that sign” means in that sign of meditation consisting of the attainment of the third formless realm. “Mental” means the mind.

Having taken the phrase "the mind itself is mental" (*mano eva mānasam*) to mean either the mental state of meditative development (*bhāvanā-manasikāra*)— for that indeed exists in the mind and is thus called "mental"— or,
because the factors associated with jhāna conform to the jhāna, they too receive the designation of "attainment" (*samāpatti*);
therefore he says, "in the four aggregates comprised within the attainment of the base of nothingness," the intention being that these [aggregates] constitute the objective support (*ārammaṇa*).
286. As it has been stated, because non-existence (*ākiñcañña*) serves as the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), this meditation has that as its sphere or cause;

thus, the meditation is the "sphere of nothingness" (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as follows: since non-existence itself, acting as the object-condition, is the cause of the meditation, the object is the "sphere of nothingness.
The rest here should be understood according to the method explained below.
"By means of which perception it exists" means by the presence of such a perception. For that [perception], because it lacks the function of a sharp perception, cannot be called "perception";
yet, because it does not transcend the essential nature of perception, it cannot be called "non-perception.
The meaning is: "because of its existing. "That" refers to that jhāna. In the phrase "to show that first," "that" (taṃ) refers to that [jhāna].
The meaning is: together with its practice, the aforementioned perception, and the means for its attainment.
For by one who extracts the Dhamma by way of the person—saying "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient"—perception is extracted by way of that which possesses perception;
otherwise, it should have been extracted as "the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Furthermore, that practice is where it occurs.
To show how it proceeds, it is said: "He attends to the base of nothingness as peaceful; he develops the attainment with a residue of formations.
For the base of nothingness is the locus for the development of the fourth immaterial attainment, while the attainment with a residue of formations is its mode of proceeding.
"Yatra hi nāma" means "in that which indeed. "Natthibhāvampi" means even the emptiness of consciousness.
The intended meaning is that it is likewise subtle. "By way of having a peaceful object" (*santārammaṇatāya*): that which has a peaceful object is "peaceful-objected" (*santārammaṇā*);

the state of being such is "the condition of having a peaceful object," by means of which [it is so called], not by way of the continuity of the jhāna. For the third immaterial attainment is not more peaceful than the fourth immaterial jhāna. The objector [says]:
"If one attends to it as peaceful, there would be no seeing of its danger (*ādīnava*) therein. And if there is no seeing of its danger..."
Showing that there would be no transcending [of the lower stage] at all, he said: "If one attends to it as peaceful, how does transcending occur?
The other replied with the solution: "By way of not desiring to attain [the higher stage].

By this, he shows that there is indeed the vision of the danger [in the lower stage]. He makes the very same point already stated by the words "For he... and so forth even more clear. In that regard, in which...
One should possess the practice of adverting to, entering, and so forth, regarding the delight in jhāna.

However, that [practice] is entirely absent in the third immaterial state; showing that there is merely the act of making it an object because of the absence of other [states], he said, "Even though," and so forth.
"He goes having completely transcended" means that, not regarding even a blade of grass as a livelihood for those craftsmen, he simply passes beyond them.
"Sā" refers to the practitioner. "Taṃ" refers to the third formless attainment (*tatiyāruppasamāpatti*).
"By the method stated previously" means by the method stated as "Tranquil indeed is this attainment," and so forth; thus, he attends to it as tranquil.

The construction is: "He reaches that perception (*saññā*) by which he is called 'neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient' (nevasaññīnāsaññī), and is said to develop the attainment of the remaining formations (*saṅkhārāvasesasamāpatti*)."
For the teaching is given by way of the term "perception" (*saññā*). "Extremely subtle" (*paramasukhuma*) means having reached the highest degree of subtlety.

"The attainment with residual formations" (*saṅkhārāvasesasamāpatti*) refers to an attainment in which only a mere residue of formations remains due to that supreme subtlety. Therefore he said: "formations that have reached an absolutely subtle state.

"Absolutely" (*accanta*) means having gone beyond the end (*anta*). It is that beyond which there is nothing more subtle; thus it is called "formations that have reached the furthermost limit of subtlety."
This is the meaning. For, starting from the access concentration of the first jhāna, as cultivation proceeds like a saw, formations are gradually brought there to their final stage;
beyond that, there is only cessation, not the occurrence of formations.
Therefore it is called "the attainment with a residue of formations."
287. Regarding that which consists of four aggregates: "In the ultimate sense" means in the sense of the ultimate reality distinguished by the specific qualities of the wholesome and so forth.
Since it is intended here specifically as the foundation for the training in higher wisdom, he says: "The states of consciousness and mental factors of one who has attained [jhāna] are intended here.
"Due to the absence of gross perception" refers to the fact that, although there is the perception belonging to the resultant state of the fourth formless attainment...
The perception of the fourth immaterial wholesome state is gross compared to the perceptions of insight, the path, and the fruit; nevertheless, "grossness and subtlety" must be understood relatively.

This is because, unlike the perception included within the five-aggregate existence, there is no gross perception in the four-aggregate existence as there is in the three lower planes; thus it is called "subtle" because it has reached a state of extreme subtlety where only a residue of formations remains.
Because it exists by way of its subtle perception (*saññā*). In the phrase "neither-perception" (*nevasaññā*), the negative particle *na* has the sense of non-existence;

in the phrase "nor non-perception" (*nāsaññā*), the negative particle *na* has the sense of "other than," while the vowel *a-* has the sense of non-existence alone—the meaning being "neither perception nor non-perception. "Being included" (*pariyāpannattā*) means because of being contained within [the realm] by way of being a part of it.
"Therein" (*ettha*) refers to the fourth formless realm (*ārūpa*). In the second interpretation of the meaning, "neither-perception" (*nevasaññā*)...

In this context, the negative particle *na* has another meaning. Likewise, in the phrase "not non-perception" (*nāsaññā*), both the negative particle *na* and the vowel *a* have another meaning; thus, by these two, the very absence of perception is shown.

Since its inclusion within the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) implies its status as a base (*āyatana*), it is said to be so "in the sense of a foundation" (*adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena*), because it serves as a supporting condition (*nissayapaccaya*).
But what is the reason why such a perception arises here? With reference to this inquiry, he says, "Not only," and so forth.
It should be understood that this teaching is given by way of the perception (*saññā*), as in the passages beginning with "beings of diverse bodies and diverse perceptions.
Thus, this is the meaning: even for a phenomenon (*dhamma*) that must be said to exist by its own nature (*sabhāva*) based on some particularity, [it is designated] in this way.
The meaning expressed by the statement "it does not exist" is based on the presence of some specific distinction (*visesa*).

When he said, "Venerable sir, there is oil," he spoke with reference to its being unwholesome (*akappiya*); when he said, "Venerable sir, there is no oil," he spoke with reference to its not filling the tube. Therefore, he said: "In this regard, just as... and so forth.
If the function of perception (*saññā*) is the cognizing of an object, then since this [mind-consciousness] is identical to perception, how could it not be able to perform that function?

He said: "Like the function of burning," and so forth. Because it has reached a state of extreme subtlety with only a residue of formations remaining, it is unable to perform the function of clear perception;
for that very reason, it is not easily grasped by knowledge. Therefore he said: "It is also unable to produce disenchantment.
"One who has not made a resolve" means one who has not made a resolve for insight—that is, one in whom the course of comprehension has not been set in motion.
“An ordinary insight-worker” (*pakativipassaka*) means one who possesses insight by nature.
Having entered into insight by way of the aggregates and so forth, he is able to develop insight into the phenomena occurring at the sense doors together with the doors and their objects;

however, in order to show how he is able to do so, the passage beginning with “He too” was stated. “By means of the comprehension of groups alone” refers to [the stage] included within the fourth immaterial consciousness-arising.

"Insight into groups" (kalāpasammasana), which is termed "insight into the method," consists in grasping phenomena such as contact and so forth together as a single unit—without analyzing them—and contemplating them as a group or a collection.

"Insight into phenomena one by one" (anupadadhammavipassanā) consists in contemplating those same phenomena such as contact and so forth after having analyzed them, grasping each individually according to its own specific nature by way of impermanence and so forth.
Thus, it has reached such subtlety that even the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) could not [fully comprehend] it step by step.
The meaning is: "not to be seen with insight.

"Of the elder" means of a certain elder. "By others too": here is another simile—once, it is said, a certain brahmin saw a man standing holding a pleasing earthenware vessel and asked him, "Give this to me."
"A vessel," he said. Intending that it had been soaked with liquor, he replied, "It is not proper, venerable sir, to give it; there is liquor in this.
The brahmin addressed a man standing near him, saying, "In that case, give this man some to drink.
The other replied, "There is none, venerable sir. In this context, just as the brahmin, taking into account the unsuitability [of the recipient], said "there is," even though...
Because it is not present there in the sense of being something to be attained, it follows that one must say "it does not exist"; it should be understood that the same applies here as well.

But why is no mode of cultivation mentioned here, as was done in the previous cases with the phrases "infinite space," "infinite consciousness," and "there is nothing whatsoever"? On this point, some have said: "The mode of cultivation..."
The term "name" refers to the mode of occurrence of access jhāna upon its respective object; and here, the object consists of the phenomena of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*).
When these are apprehended, they may be taken either by way of one primary phenomenon or all of them together.
In that regard, under the first alternative, the apprehension of consciousness follows; thus, in the mental attention "consciousness, consciousness":
In the first case, the fourth formless attainment would result in being the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*).

In the second case, however, because the meditation has as its object entirely the phenomena of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), if one attends to it as "nothingness, nothingness," it would either be the base of nothingness itself or have non-existence as its object.
In no way can the state of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) be obtained. Thus, this is not a valid reason for such a meditation.
Because it does not proceed [by itself]. For the development of the fourth immaterial state does not proceed by contacting the base of "consciousness is nothingness"; what does it contact then?
It contacts the continuity (*santati*) of the third immaterial state.
If this is so, why is it not included as "peaceful" (*santa*) in the Pāli text? Although it is not included as such in the Sutta, it is [so stated] in the Vibhaṅga.
But it has indeed been included. As it was said: "He attends to that very base of nothingness as peaceful; he develops the attainment with a residue of formations.
Now, why is the mode of development not mentioned in the Sutta as it is in the Vibhaṅga?

It is because of the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*) and because of the elegance of the teaching (*desanāvilāsa*). For those who are to be trained, just as in the case of the three lower formless attainments [where one thinks] "space is infinite," "consciousness is infinite," and so on—
"consciousness, there is nothing"—in this way the mode of development is grasped; even when that [mode] is not thus grasped, they penetrate that meaning.

It is with reference to them that the teaching was given in the Sutta in that manner. And for those who follow the method of the Suttas, the summary teaching in the Abhidhamma’s *Suttantabhājanīya* is likewise.
However, as for those to be trained who penetrate that meaning only when it is explained by way of analysis—
They penetrate [the truth], and it is by way of them that the mode of development is stated in the *Vibhaṅga*.

However, the Blessed One, the Lord of Dhamma, the Perfectly Enlightened One, knowing the various ways in which the Dhamma should be taught, adopts the mode of development in some instances and does not adopt the mode of development in others.
And that teaching is solely for the purpose of training those who are to be trained; such is the meaning here.

The "Grace of the Teaching" (desanāvilāsa) refers either to the teaching of the Suttas as a discourse by way of a method (pariyāyakathā), wherein the modes of development (bhāvanākāra) are not included;
however, the teaching of the Abhidhamma is a discourse that is non-methodical (nippariyāyakathā), wherein the modes of development are included.
Thus, one should understand the reason for the inclusion and non-inclusion of the modes of development in this context.
Others, however, say: "The mode of development is not mentioned in the Sutta for the purpose of showing the distinction in the fourth immaterial attainment;

and this distinction is produced by gradual development. That gradual development, moreover, is generated by the sequence of abandoning, because the jhānas must be attained through the surmounting of what is to be abandoned. For it is thus: by way of seclusion from sensual desires and so forth, the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, the fading away of rapture, and the disappearance of pleasure and pain."
The fine-material-sphere jhānas have been taught by way of the transcendence of the perception of form and so forth, and the immaterial-sphere jhānas likewise.

Furthermore, it is not only the jhānas, but indeed all virtue and all wisdom as well, that are taught by way of demonstrating the transcendence of states to be abandoned, because they must be accomplished through the abandoning of opposing states. For thus:
“Having abandoned the taking of life, he abstains from taking life”—by such passages is the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*) shown;

“Having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics”—by such passages is the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) shown; “Neither for sport, nor for intoxication”—by such passages is moderation in eating (*bhojane mattaññutā*) shown;
“Here, a bhikkhu, having abandoned wrong livelihood, maintains his life by right livelihood”—by such passages...
Purity of livelihood; the practice of wakefulness as expressed in the passage beginning, “Having abandoned covetousness for the world, with a mind free from covetousness”;
and the development of the perception of impermanence for the sake of uprooting the conceit ‘I am’—for, Meghiya, in one who perceives impermanence, the perception of non-self becomes established;
one who perceives non-self proceeds to the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am,’ and through the destruction of the taints, attains the taintless liberation of mind.

"Having realized for himself through direct higher knowledge in this very life the liberation by wisdom (*paññā-vimutti*), he enters and dwells therein"—by such passages, wisdom is taught precisely by way of the abandoning of opposing states (*paṭipakkha-dhamma*).

Therefore, when the Blessed One teaches the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), he does so by way of demonstrating the transcendence of those states that must be abandoned, beginning with "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (*vivicceva kāmehi*).
Thus it was said: "By way of seclusion from sensual pleasures and the rest, the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, rapture, fading away, and the disappearance of equanimity..."
"The fine-material-sphere jhānas have been taught; the immaterial-sphere jhānas [have been taught] by way of the surmounting of the perception of form and so forth.

In this context, just as the first fine-material-sphere jhāna is [free from] the hindrances such as sensual desire and their associates because it is endowed with states such as faith—which, like applied thought (vitakka) and the rest, have attained through specific development a nature that is sharp, clear, and courageous—so too...

Because it suppresses unwholesome states, it has attained the status of a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*); compared to sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmāvacaradhamma*), it is subtle, refined, peaceful, and sublime.

However, the second jhāna and those following it, through the excellence of their development (*bhāvanāvisesa*), reach a state that is even more subtle, more refined, and so forth, due to the abandonment of gross factors. The same applies to the formless-sphere (*arūpāvacara*) [states].

The first jhāna, occurring through the cultivation of dispassion toward form, reaches a state of calm and subtlety with respect to all fine-material-sphere phenomena— both in terms of the continuity of its object and the continuity of its factors—

just as it does with ordinary, limited phenomena. For by virtue of the calmness of its object, the phenomena that take it as their object also possess a calm nature, just like those phenomena that have supramundane states as their object.

Furthermore, although there is no difference in terms of its nature as a phenomenon (*dhamma*) or in its state of loftiness (*mahaggata*), the formless attainment (*ārūppa*) is indeed more peaceful than the fourth fine-material-sphere attainment even in terms of its constituent factors (*aṅga*),
which is why it is described as the "peaceful liberation" (*santavimokkha*). However, the second formless attainment and those following it become progressively more peaceful—

more peaceful, and most peaceful— than the first formless attainment and so forth, both in terms of their constituent factors and their objects (*ārammaṇa*), due to their association with specific distinctions in cultivation (*bhāvanāvisesa*).

This specific kind of self-development, beginning from the access concentration (*upacāra*) of the first jhāna, brings about the state of peace and subtlety of each respective jhāna by means of transcending what is to be abandoned at each stage; it reaches the state of extreme subtlety of the remaining formations (*saṅkhārāvasesa*) in the fourth immaterial attainment (*catutthāruppa*).
From that point, the fourth immaterial attainment becomes the object for insight (*vipassanā*) by way of the "insight into phenomena as they arise one after another" (*anupadadhammavipassanā*).

Even for one who is naturally gifted with insight (*pakativipassaka*), approaching [this state] does not become a condition for the arising of disenchantment (*nibbidā*), because the remaining formations have reached a state of extreme subtlety;

likewise, while it itself proceeds among the phenomena of the third immaterial attainment (*tatiyāruppa*), it is unable to discern them as they truly are, just as other jhānas are unable to discern their own respective objects.
It merely proceeds by way of a mere mental engagement (*ārambha*) with them.
In that case, since it is unable to remain even as an object due to its lack of distinct manifestation (*vibhūtākāratā*),

how could it possibly serve as an object? Therefore, seeing that its function is unmanifest (*avibhūta-kicca*), the Teacher, after describing the mode of development (*bhāvanākāra*) in the three lower stages,
stated the mode of development in the Sutta for the fourth formless attainment to demonstrate that such a mode is not available here.
He did not speak because it was a teaching given by way of a method (*pariyāyadesanā*).
However, since there is indeed a mode of occurrence (*pavatti-ākāra*) of a dhamma that possesses an object (*sārammaṇa*) toward its object,

the *Vibhaṅga* states, "He attends to that very base of nothingness as peaceful," in order to show that this [attainment] has reached an exceedingly subtle state, due to its being a teaching according to the nature of the dhamma (*yathādhamma-sāsana-bhāvato*).

Alternatively, in the *Vibhaṅga*, it is stated that "one attends to it as peaceful" by way of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*), because at that time the object is still unmanifest for the meditator.
However, in the Sutta, the mode of development is not taken by way of absorption (*appanā*) because [the object] is then unmanifest.

For some meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) are unmanifest at the beginning, such as the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) and so forth; some are unmanifest in the middle, such as mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).
Some [meditation subjects] are for both purposes; how so? Such as the recollection of peace (upasamānussati) and so forth.
However, the fourth formless meditation subject (catutthāruppa-kammaṭṭhāna) is not clear at the conclusion because the object remains unclear even when the peak of development is reached.
Therefore, in order to show this distinction regarding the fourth formless realm, the Teacher did not include the mode of development in the Sutta, not because it is entirely absent.
The conclusion here must be reached.
288. Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discussion:
"Of peerless form" means by virtue of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide aura, the jewel-treasure, and so forth.

The word *rūpa* refers to his physical body (*rūpakāya*) which is unique due to its other qualities (*guṇa*), or it signifies intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), as in such passages as "that which in the world is a lovely form, a pleasant form" (*yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ*).

Therefore, "one of matchless form" (*asadisarūpo*) means one of matchless nature; by this, because it illustrates the possession of specific qualities such as the ten powers (*dasabala*) and the four grounds of self-confidence (*catuvesārajja*), the Teacher’s excellence of the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*) is also shown to be peerless. "Thus" (*iti*) means in the manner described above.
"In that formless realm": the "Miscellaneous Discussion" (pakiṇṇakakathā) should also be understood.

As before, this does not refer to meanings specific to particular jhānas; rather, because it concerns common factors, the Miscellaneous Discussion is to be understood as proceeding by taking up meanings that are scattered and miscellaneous across various contexts.
289. "By transcending the sign of form" means by transcending the counterpart-sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) known as the kasiṇa-form.
"By transcending space" means by transcending the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa.

"By transcending the consciousness that has occurred in space" means by transcending the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment (āruppa), not by transcending the consciousness of the second immaterial attainment. It is because of transcending that [first].
For that indeed is its manifestation. Indeed, in the manifestation of the consciousness of the second immaterial state, that [consciousness] itself would be transcended, not its object;
and it is not logical to transcend the manifestation of a non-object simply by seeing a fault in the object.
And in the Pāḷi: “Mindful he enters the base of infinite consciousness... mindful, having emerged, that very consciousness...”
It is said, “he eliminates it,” but it is not said, “he eliminates that very base of infinite consciousness,” nor is it said, “he eliminates that very [base].
However, in the passage, “having attained the base of infinite consciousness, ‘consciousness is infinite,’” two things are mentioned:
the object, which is the consciousness, and the base of infinite consciousness itself. From whichever of these two, or from whatever state, he has emerged—
Since the connection with the word "that" (taṃ) would follow from that very [word] specified as the exertion,

the mention of "consciousness" (viññāṇa) is for the purpose of excluding the base of infinite consciousness; thus, it is stated that there is a transcendence of the non-existence of the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment itself.

"Even though this is so" means even when there is no deficiency in the constituent parts. "More excellent" (*suppaṇītatarā*) means very much more excellent; or the meaning is that they are beautiful and more excellent.

Even though there is equality in the number of the four palace floors and the cloths, and in their state and measure, yet there is a distinction in the successive strands of sensual pleasure and the excellence of the pleasant touch and so forth.

By the phrase "just as," and so forth, he shows this meaning: although these four attainments are equal in their state of being formless (*ārūpya*) and in their constituent factors (*aṅga*), there is nevertheless a progressively more distinguished state of being more excellent and so on, established through a specific excellence of cultivation (*bhāvanāvisesa*).
This superior quality is demonstrated by the words "just as," etc.
291. *Nissito* means standing in dependence. *Dūṭṭhitā* means not properly established, or established in suffering.
*Tannissitam* means dependent on that; the meaning is "the place. Alternatively, *tannissitam* means the person standing in dependence on that person who is attached to the pavilion;
this is the meaning. For [if one were] outside the space, separated from and without that person who is attached to the pavilion—
Just as space is the locus for consciousness fixed in space, so too, when that [consciousness] has departed through seclusion, the third immaterial state is its locus.

(292) It indeed takes that as its object; because of the absence of anything else, it thinks "this is it. Thus, even though its danger has been seen—namely, that this base of nothingness has as its object the departure of the consciousness that had the near-space as its object, which was itself the adversary of the neighboring base of infinite consciousness—it is nevertheless not peaceful.
This is the jhāna of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Because there is no other object of such a kind capable of serving as an objective support, and because of the non-attainment [of such], he indeed takes that very thing as his object.
The phrase "the Lord of all directions" is stated for the purpose of showing that he is one to whom people have nowhere else to turn. "Vutti" means livelihood; "vattati" means he lives. 293.
Regarding the passage beginning with "ascended," this is the summary of the meaning: just as some man [might climb] a long ladder many fathoms in height...
Having ascended it, standing on its upper part, he clings only to the side of that ladder because of the lack of any other support;
and just as one who has ascended the peak of a mound of earth or a mixed mountain clings only to its summit;
and just as one who has ascended a mountain or a rocky crag, being unable to find anything else, clings to himself while trembling.
It clings just to the knee; likewise, this fourth immaterial jhāna proceeds by clinging to that third immaterial state.
Whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the description of the immaterial states is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the tenth chapter.
11. Commentary on the Exposition of Concentration:
Commentary on the Development of the Repulsiveness of Nutriment.

294. As for "enumeration" (*uddesa*): because it is intended as a summary for those whose wisdom is mostly dull or middling, and because a burden that has been taken up must necessarily be carried, he said:
"The exposition of the development of the perception of repulsiveness regarding food—thus enumerated as 'one perception'—has now arrived.
In this context, the word "perception" (*saññā*) occurs in the sense of a state characterized by perceiving, as in "perception of forms," "perception of sounds," and so forth.
In such passages as “the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering,” it occurs in the context of insight (vipassanā);

in such passages as “the perception of the bloated corpse or the perception of the form of the skeleton—do these states have the same meaning or different meanings? it occurs in the context of serenity (samatha).

Here, however, it should be understood as the preliminary work for serenity; for the apprehension of the repulsive aspect in nutriment, or the access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) developed thereby, [is what is intended].
Here, what is intended is the "perception of repulsiveness in nutriment. In that context, regarding the nutriment in which the perception of repulsiveness is to be developed,
the passage beginning with "it nourishes, thus it is nutriment" is commenced in order to analyze all nutriment— by way of its functions, classifications, dangers, and similes—
in connection with that [perception], for the purpose of generating penetration and dispassion.

In this context, "it brings" (*āharati*) means that by way of being a condition for arising or for persistence—designated as the nutriment-condition—it brings its own fruit, produces it, and maintains it;
such is the meaning. It is called "morsel-made" (*kabaḷīkāra*) because it is made into morsels;

this is stated by way of its physical basis (*vatthu*), but in terms of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), it should be understood as having the characteristic of nutritive essence (*ojā*). And it is "morsel-made" in the sense already explained.
"And nutriment" refers to edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*). This same method applies to the others as well. It "touches," thus it is contact (*phassa*).
For although this is a non-material phenomenon (*arūpa-dhamma*), it occurs precisely in the mode of touching the object. Thus, it is said to have the characteristic of touching.
It "volitions," thus it is volition (*cetanā*); the meaning is that it directs itself toward the object together with its associated states.
Volition dependent on the mind is mental volition (*manosañcetanā*). It is consciousness (*viññāṇa*) because it cognizes by way of conceiving rebirth.
Thus, in this context, the nutriments should be understood according to their general meaning and their specific meaning.
But why are only these four stated? Are other phenomena not conditions for their own fruits? They are indeed not non-conditions; however, these—
And thus they are both "as it is" and "otherwise": even though their status as conditions is equal, they are "additional conditions," and for that reason they are called "nutriments" (*āhāra*).

How so? For among these, the first, while itself acting as a condition—according to its suitability—for the factors included within the same group (*kalāpa*), brings forth the materiality consisting of the octad of nutritive essence (*ojā-aṭṭhamaka-rūpa*);
the second brings forth the three types of feeling; and the third [brings forth] the three realms of existence.
It brings about rebirth-linking; the fourth [nutriment] brings about mentality-materiality at the moment of rebirth-linking. Therefore, he said: “Edible food,” and so forth.

And here, when the nutritive essence—divided into that born of karma and so on—obtains its conditions, it maintains two or three successions and brings about the materiality consisting of the eight factors beginning with nutritive essence.

The nutriment of contact, divided into that to be experienced as pleasant and so on, brings about the three types of feeling according to what is appropriate. The nutriment of volitional formations, divided into meritorious volitional formations and so on...

It should be understood that the nutriment of mental volition brings about rebirth-linking—both with consciousness and without consciousness—as appropriate among the three types of existence, such as the sense-sphere existence;
and the nutriment of consciousness brings about, at the moment of rebirth-linking according to conditions, both mind (nāma) and matter (rūpa), as well as the psycho-physical complex (nāmarūpa).
Alternatively, these very phenomena are called "nutriments" in the sense of being supports. For just as physical food [sustains the body], so too do these sustain the continuity of existence.
It is a condition for the material body by way of being its support; likewise, the immaterial nutriments are conditions for associated states.
For it has been said: "Edible food is a condition for this body by way of nutriment-condition;
the immaterial nutriments are a condition for associated states and for the material phenomena originated by them by way of nutriment-condition."
Another method: edible food is called nutriment because it is a specific condition for the internal continuity, and likewise the three factors beginning with contact are called nutriments.
For among beings who subsist on edible food, edible food is the specific condition for the material body;
contact is the specific condition for feeling in the mental body; mental volition is the specific condition for consciousness; and consciousness is the specific condition for name-and-form.
As it is said: “Bhikkhus, just as this body is sustained by nutriment, it persists dependent on nutriment;

without nutriment, it does not persist. So too, with contact as condition there is feeling; with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness; with consciousness as condition there is name-and-form.
Regarding “craving for edible food”: it is craving that is attached to edible food. That is a danger because it brings about what is harmful. For one who is infatuated...
For the enjoyment of food leads to what is harmful. The locative case here has the sense of "cause" (*hetu*); the same applies to the remaining cases.
"Craving" (*nikanti*) means longing or desire-attachment (*chanda-rāga*). It is called "fear" (*bhaya*) because one fears it; thus, craving itself is fear, which is "craving-fear.

Due to the cause of physical food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*), this desire-attachment in these beings is a fear, a terrifying thing, [which brings about] harm divided into categories such as those pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*).
Because it is the cause of the entire suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*). For this very reason, it was said:
"Bhikkhus, if there is lust for material food, if there is delight, if there is craving, consciousness becomes established there and grows," and so forth.

Approaching (*upagamana*) is the convergence and conjunction with the object by one whose perversions (*vipallāsa*) have not been abandoned; it is the arising of contact to be experienced as pleasant, and so on.
It is fearful because it is not liberated from the three kinds of suffering. Therefore he said:
“Monks, dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises; with that feeling as condition, craving arises... [and so on] ...this is the origin of this mass of suffering.
In this context, *upapatti* means that by means of it one is reborn (*upapajjati*) in various states of existence, or it is the act of being reborn (*upapajjana*).
Rebirth is terrifying and fearsome because one is not liberated from the calamities rooted in rebirth. Therefore, he said:
"Bhikkhus, when an ignorant person performs a meritorious volitional formation, his consciousness becomes oriented toward merit.
When he performs a demeritorious volitional formation, his consciousness becomes oriented toward demerit," and so forth.

"Rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi*) means the linking together from one existence to another; it is "fearful" and "terrible" because there is no liberation from the sufferings associated with the signs of rebirth-linking.
Therefore, he said: "Bhikkhus, if there is lust for the nutriment of consciousness, if there is delight, if there is craving, then consciousness becomes established there and grows," and so forth.
He should be instructed by means of the simile of the dog’s meat, for the sake of enjoyment free from desire and lust;
for in this way, there is no fear of attachment therein. Just as a flayed cow is devoured by creatures wherever she goes, so too, when there is contact (*phassa*), feeling (*vedanā*) arises;
and since feeling should be regarded as a dart of suffering, one should contemplate the danger in contact.

He said, "The nutriment of contact (phassāhāra) should be illustrated by the simile of the flayed cow," because for one who sees that there is no fear of being approached by a passer-by, there is no fear of rebirth.

He said, "The nutriment of mental volition (manosañcetanāhāra) should be illustrated by the simile of the pit of glowing embers," because for one who sees that all states of existence (bhava) are completely ablaze with eleven fires and are like a pit of glowing embers, there is no fear of rebirth. Consciousness (viññāṇa) is like a thief.
"Because it leads to misfortune, feeling is difficult to endure, like being struck by a blow"—seeing this correctly, one has no fear of rebirth.
Thus he said: "The nutriment of consciousness (viññāṇāhāra) should be illustrated by the simile of the hundred spears.
Having thus elucidated the danger in the nutriments by way of their functions and so forth, [the author] now [explains] the nutriment intended therein.
Having extracted [the relevant points], the passage beginning with "But among these... was stated in order to show the method of mental attention (manasikāra) regarding the repulsive.

Since "edible food" (kabaḷīkāro āhāro) is mentioned even in the description of derived matter (upādāyarūpa), he said "divided into what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted" in order to distinguish it from that;

or rather, this is a statement of its constituent parts. Therein, "divided into what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted" means the classification according to what is to be eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted.

Because there is no desire to express a distinction of time, it is said as "milk" [without specifying when it was milked]. The restriction "material food" (kabaḷīkāro āhāro) should be understood as excluding contact-food (phassāhāra) and the rest;
likewise, it should also be seen as excluding nutriment consisting of essence (ojāhāra).

For here, only food that has a physical basis is the subject of the meditation (kammaṭṭhāna); thus, the meaning here should be understood as: "it is called food (āhāra) because it is consumed (āharīyati)."
“It nourishes, thus it is nutriment”: this meaning, however, should be understood by way of the nutritive essence (*ojā*) that has been produced.
“In this meaning” means in this meaning known as the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). “Perception has arisen” refers to the development of meditation by way of the term “perception” (*saññā*);
for he will say later: “But by way of grasping the aspect of repulsiveness,” and so forth.

"Having mastered the meditation subject" means having made the meditation subject well-mastered, well-attended to, and well-retained both in terms of the textual doctrine (*pariyatti-dhamma*) and its meaning (*attha*).
Therefore he said: "Without missing even a single word of what has been learned.
In this context, "of what has been learned" means from the teacher's instruction. "Even a single word" means even a single term, or even a single section, or even a mere portion; such is the meaning.
Why is it said, "in ten aspects"? Is it not because of the absence of a final livelihood;
because of the arising of agitation, greed, and so forth regarding the gain or loss of alms-food; because of the production of indigestion when eaten;
and because of the breeding of worms? For this has been said: "This is the end... [and so on].
“Monks, among ways of livelihood, this is the lowest: namely, the life of a beggar. This, monks, is a curse in the world:
‘You wander about as a beggar, with bowl in hand. Not having obtained almsfood, one is anxious;
and having obtained almsfood, one consumes it while being greedy, infatuated, and obsessed, seeing neither the danger nor possessing the wisdom for escape. “Having eaten...”
And food sometimes brings death or death-like suffering to someone;
moreover, thirty-two species of *ukkocaka* worms, thirty-two species of *takkoṭaka* worms, and maggots live in dependence upon it.

It is said in reply: First of all, the state of being one who lives on the refuse of others is for the purpose of purifying the defilements of the mind through application to a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
One should certainly keep in mind: "May I not become like a brand from a funeral pyre.

Likewise, one must prevent the arising of agitation, greed, and so forth regarding both the failure and success in obtaining alms-food; this is because such states do not exist for one who possesses perfectly pure virtue and is reflective.
The drowsiness caused by food is not necessarily present, or it should be understood as being included within the category of consumption. [This refers to] the breeding of worms.
However, it should not be included, or even if it were included, there would be no restriction here by the phrase "in ten ways.
Or rather, the inclusion of the others here should be understood according to this same method, since the intended meaning here is the contemplation of repulsiveness as it occurs.
For instance, things such as the excrement of a house-lizard, mouse-dung, and lac-insect dung are included because they are possible occurrences.
It is not exclusive. The same should be stated for seeking and so forth, as applicable.

In the cases of "going" and so on, returning is also included under "going" because it shares the same nature as going. Just as approaching a hall for returning [from a journey] and so forth, in the case of seeking, there is a common repulsiveness due to treading upon places containing impurities, seeing and smelling what is unsightly and foul-smelling, and enduring such things.
"By way of going" means by way of going toward the alms-village for the purpose of wandering for alms. "By way of seeking" means by way of wandering about the alms-village for the sake of alms.
"By way of enjoyment" means by way of consuming the food. Both [food and the body] are supported by both;
even though they occur together, being established by the power of karma, they do not exceed their respective boundaries.
It is called the *āsaya* (seat/receptacle) because it settles, stays, and remains there without confusion; it refers to the bile and other secretions that reside above the stomach (*āmāsayo*).
This syllable *ā* has the sense of a boundary; thus, it is "from the seat" (*āsayato*). It is called the *nidhāna* (storehouse) because food, having been eaten, remains accumulated there;
it is the stomach (*āmāsayo*), thus "from the storehouse" (*nidhānato*). "From the uncooked" (*aparipakkato*) refers to what is known as the small intestine (*gahaṇī*).
"Because it is not yet matured by the heat of kamma-born fire. "Matured" means because of the state of having been digested as food once eaten.

"As a fruit" means produced [from that digestion]. "As an outflow" means because it trickles out in this and that direction. "As a smearing" means because it smears everything completely. The construction is:
"In all these respects, the repulsiveness of food should be reflected upon. This is according to the sequence of the accomplishment of their respective functions.

Furthermore, while this sequence beginning with "going" has been established [in order], the "smearing" (sammakkhana), although it occurs among such things as consumption, is placed last because it is especially repulsive by way of its natural outcome (nissanda). 295.

Regarding the phrase "of such great power," they say it refers to the great power of the practice to be described hereafter, which is accomplished through the maintenance of the meditation subject at all times and so forth.

Showing that a practitioner of yoga (*yogāvacara*) should practice in this way by placing the excellence of the Dhamma (*dhammasudhammata*) foremost, he said, "In such a teaching of great power," and so forth.
Here, the word *nāma* should be understood as expressing esteem. The construction is: "Having gone forth, one should go facing toward the village.
Furthermore, this reflection on the act of going and so forth by the practitioner is not for his own sake alone.

Then, demonstrating that even those who have not yet received formal instruction [can attain this], he took up the two watches of the night with the words beginning, "the whole night. "Pariveṇa" means the courtyard of the pariveṇa.
Regarding the phrase "in the twentieth or thirtieth watch," some say that the division of the watches here is according to the present continuity [of the meditation];

others, however, say it is by way of the "hot seat" (*uṇhāsana*). For the development that has not yet reached the suppression of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) [is characterized by] the joy of pervading (*pharaṇapīti*).
Because of the absence of sitting, he does not dispel physical fatigue at all; thus, there is indeed a shifting of the postures.
The mention of "twenty or thirty times," however, is according to the time of going for alms as previously observed.
Alternatively, from the act of walking up to the attention given to the smearing [of the body with clay] constitutes one round; having thus attended to the meditation subject twenty or thirty times.
"Uncongested by people" means free from the crowding of people; by this, he shows that they are not crowded, have little noise, and have little clamor.
For that very reason, they are "blissful through seclusion," being desirable due to the separation from people, or rather, conducive to the practice of meditation in seclusion.
Because they are endowed with shade and water, they are cool. Because they are pure, they are delightful regions of the earth.
The first two [phrases] are statements of the causes for the latter two. "Noble" means faultless. "Delighting in seclusion" means delighting in the practice of jhāna.
Although the dwelling place of practitioners of yoga is indeed well-swept and well-scrubbed, it might sometimes even become so after they have left it;
therefore, this is stated to show the possibility of its becoming repulsive through the contemplation of its loathsomeness.
It should be understood that the passage beginning with “surrounded by foot-dust, dung, gnats, and so forth” has been stated.

Therein, “bedspread” (paccattharaṇa) refers to a covering such as a felt rug (cimilika) or similar material that is spread upon the ground for the purpose of protecting the skin. “Jatukā” refers to small bats.

“Because of being defiled” (upahatattā) means because of being contaminated. “From here and there” (tato) means from various places. Regarding the phrase “sometimes even by owls, pigeons, and so forth,” the word “sometimes” (appekadā) applies here as well.
The word *padaṃ* (place) should be brought forward and connected [to the preceding]. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "water, mud, etc.," rubbish and so forth are included.
The "monastery lane" (*vihāraracchā*) is the path leading from the courtyard into the monastery grounds.
"In the hall of reflection" (*vitakkamāḷake*) means in the hall where one reflects, thinking, "Where indeed should I go for alms today? and so forth.
“Village road” means the path leading from one village to another. “Stump-and-thorn road” means a road possessing stumps and thorns.
“It must be looked at” indicates that going [on such a road] is characterized by looking.
“By one concealing a boil,” and so forth, is an instruction regarding the proper conduct, showing that the lower robe and other garments should be worn with such an intention.
It is like one suffering from a tumor covering the tumor for the purpose of warding off the perils of wind, heat, and so forth.
Alternatively, by bringing in another instance of the word *gaṇḍa*, it should be connected as "covering [it] as if it were a tumor.
This is because of the statement: "Monks, 'tumor' is a designation for these five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*)."

“Tumor” (*gaṇḍa*) is a synonym for the personal existence (*attabhāva*), specifically because the body of form is joined with the sting of suffering, because it exudes impurities, and because it becomes bloated, putrid, and split open through arising, aging, and dissolution. “Wound-cloth” (*vaṇacoḷaka*) is a piece of cloth used to cover a wound.

“Having taken out” means having removed it from its bag. “Even corpses” (*kuṇapāni pi*): the word “even” (*pi*) is used in the sense of censure; such things as these should also be regarded [as foul].
"Are occurring" means that this [food] is possible there as well, when considering its possibility.
"Should be endured" means it should be tolerated, because otherwise food would not be obtained. "At the village gate" means near the village gate or within the threshold.
The intention is that they should be looked at by one who looks only a yoke’s length ahead, standing after having passed through the village streets.
“Bedspreads and so forth” refers to bedspreads and the like that are defiled by the excrement of house-doves and other such things.
“Ending with many corpses”: here, one should include even the looking upon village streets crowded with people dressed and robed improperly;
for that too is indeed repulsive. “Aho vatā” is a particle used in censure. “Bho” is an address to the Dhamma. “To this extent indeed... [is the phrase].
Food is repulsive; the meaning is that even the act of going for its sake is thus disgusting and difficult to endure.
296. "Repulsiveness of going" (*gamanapaṭikkūla*) means that going itself is repulsive. In the phrase "even having endured" (*adhivāsetvāpi*), the particle *api* has a cumulative sense;
by this it is meant: "There is no liberation by this much alone, but beyond this there is also a vast, entire [state of] repulsiveness."
The phrase "it must indeed be endured" summarizes what is to be described as repulsive. "Clad in the outer robe" means with the body covered by the wearing and arrangement of the *saṅghāṭī*.
"Wherever" means in whichever streets. "Even down to the flesh of the calves" means even as far as the region of the flesh of the calves.
"In a muddy puddle" means in mud mixed with water. "A single robe" means...
With one hand, he holds his wrapped robe. It is called *macchadhovana* because fish are washed in it; thus, it refers to water.
The word *sammissa* (mixed) should be connected with each term individually.

*Oḷigalla* refers to places where muddy water from leftovers, feces, filth, and so forth flows out, which may even be filled up to the knees with impurity. *Candanikā* refers to [places for] mere leftovers, urine, feces, and filth.
The places where it is deposited. "From what" means from vomit and so forth. "Those flies" refers to the blue flies that move in swarms there.
"They settle" means they remain.
"Even while giving," etc., refers to the fact that even though some may act with care due to their faith, [the object] remains unfit for the practice of reflecting on its repulsiveness.

However, this was undertaken merely to demonstrate the manner of practice characterized by lack of faith and lack of diligence. "They remain silent" means they will abandon [the teaching] on their own and depart.
"Go! means "Get out. "Hey you! is a term of address used with disregard. "Shavelings" is a disrespectful way of addressing them.
"They speak" means they converse. He says, "like a wretched person," because of the state of being one who lives a life of extreme poverty.
"Having walked for alms in the village, one should depart.
(297) "In that regard" means regarding that food contained in the bowl.

It is something to be felt as shameful, thinking, "Does he perhaps wish to give me what is left-over?"—thus one might suspect it—or because sweat is trickling due to the heat of the food, or because of the monk's own state of feverish distress.

The intention [is as follows]: "Even food that is dry and hard" means even food that is hard because it is dry, let alone when it has been moistened with buttermilk, sour gruel, and so forth—this is the intention.
By means of that moisture, he speaks of its repulsiveness due to its being soaked.
"In that" refers to the alms-food. "With its beauty entirely destroyed" means with its beauty completely ruined. "Starting from the middle" means...
Starting from the middle of the tongue. "Tooth-dirt" is the impurity of the teeth.
"Crushed and smeared" means crushed by both sets of teeth and smeared with saliva and so forth.
And for such [a tooth], whatever excellence of color, excellence of odor, and excellence of preparation it previously possessed, that entirely perishes; however, its taste might still remain.
Or it does not blow; thus he says: "It is a specific conditioned state (saṅkhāra) whose color and fragrance have vanished.
"In a dog’s trough" means in a bowl for feeding dogs. "Like a dog’s vomit" means like the refuse spat out by a dog.
Because it has passed beyond the range of the eye, it must be swallowed; this explains its extreme degree of repulsiveness.

298. "Consumption" (paribhoga) means swallowing. The connection is that this food, as it enters within, becomes supremely loathsome, like thick madhuka oil smeared [on the body]. "Within" means inside the stomach.

He says "as it enters" because the food has not yet reached its place of storage—that is, it has not yet arrived at the stomach—but is already mixed with bile and other humors. It is distinct from both the stomach and the intestines.
“Regarding ‘what is called its receptacle,’ he says ‘because’ and so forth, referring to the apprehension [of it]. A bile-receptacle is simply bile as its receptacle.
It is said to be ‘excessive’ because the world is for the most part deficient in merit. Thus, ‘by way of its receptacle’:

having entered inside while being repulsive, it becomes exceedingly repulsive when mixed with even more repulsive things such as bile; thus should the repulsiveness by way of its receptacle be contemplated.”

299. Regarding the phrase "from a storehouse" (*nidhānato*), the same principle applies here as well. "It" refers to the nutriment. "By one ten years old" means by a being who is ten years from birth. "In a place" (*okāse*) means in the location designated as the stomach (*āmāsayasaṅkhāte*).
300. "Of such a kind" (*evarūpe*) means of this sort; the meaning is: resembling a latrine pit that has not been cleaned for ten years up to a hundred years.

"A storehouse" (*nidhānaṃ*) refers to the state of being something to be stored. "In the manner already described" (*yathāvuttappakāre*); however, if it is as already stated by the phrase "by one ten years old," and so forth...
“Of this kind” means *yathāvuttappakāra* (of the aforementioned kind); [it refers] to that. “In the supreme darkness of night” means in the great gloom that makes it exceedingly dark.
The connection is: “Having reached a state of extreme loathsomeness, he stands in a place that is extremely foul-smelling and disgusting.
To the question “Where? Like what? he says: “Just as if,” and so forth. In a pit drenched by a black cloud—that is, by rain falling many times—...
"Having frolicked over some kind of impurity, it might vanish" refers to the seizing of an unseasonal cloud.
The mention of bits of grass, leaves, and mats is for the purpose of showing that even though they are mixed with what is foul, they attain the state of being foul.

"Covered with foam and bubbles produced by the heat and boiling caused by the body's fire" means covered with a mass of foam and bubbles arisen from the state of being thoroughly boiled and cooked by the power of digestion. "Uncooked" means because of its state of being uncooked.

301. "Like mineral ores of gold, silver, and so forth" means: just as when the ores of gold, silver, and so forth are smelted according to the proper method, they are said to release the gold, silver, and so forth and attain the state of gold, silver, and so forth—this [food] is not like that.
Rather, this food, when ripened by the body-fire, releases froth and bubbles; it is called *saṇha* because [the essence] is made subtle therein.

“*Saṇhakaraṇī*”—having been ground on a grinding stone bearing that name, it enters the state of feces just as yellow clay is placed into a small bamboo tube merely for the sake of its color and shape;
having entered the state of urine, it fills the bladder. This is the construction [of the sentence].
It is like the fuel-portion of the stomach and the worm-eating portion [of the intestines].
And it is not yet manifest. The portion of the essence is made clear by its result, yet those [parts] share the nature of being unripened;
therefore, setting those aside, only the portions produced from dung are shown here.
Showing that what is called "repulsive" must necessarily have a repulsive result, he says, "When it is fully ripening," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "nails, teeth, and so forth," it should be understood that by the word "and so forth" (ādi),

one includes not only the skin and other parts mentioned in the discourse on the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra-pāḷi), but also the eye-secretion, ear-secretion, dental impurities, filth arising from the body,
and other such impurities (asubha) that are excluded from the thirty-two divisions; thus he says, "various corpses."
303. *Nissandamāno* means flowing out; the meaning is "trickling down. Regarding the phrase "in this manner and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes:
nasal mucus from the nose, saliva from the mouth, and occasionally vomiting bile, phlegm, or blood;
excrement through the anus; urine through the urinary tract; and sweat and grime from the pores of the entire body—such types of impurity.
He embraces [them]. "On the first day"—this is said with reference to the day of the discharge. Therefore he says, "discharging on the second day.
"With a distorted face" means with a face contracted due to disgust; therefore he says, "loathing it.
"Becoming abashed" means becoming dejected, thinking, "I am even nursing this! "Reddened" means as cloth is by dye.
He is "enamored" (ratto) by way of the transformation of the mind through desire and lust.

He is "greedy" (giddho) because, by his very nature of longing and intense craving, he has become greedy and fallen into greed. He is "infatuated" (gadhitō) because, being as if bound by its state of being difficult to release, he is tied fast to it.

He is "infatuated with" (mucchitō) because, through craving for flavors, he has fallen into a swoon or delusion. He is "dispassionate" (viratto) because he is free from lust. He is "distressed" (aṭṭīyamāno) because he is suffering.
*Harāyamāno* means being ashamed. *Jigucchamāno* means loathing.
*Navadvārehi* is stated by way of the prominent large openings; it flows out even through the pores of the skin.
*Nilīyati* means hiding oneself by not showing oneself, or shrinking away. *Evaṃ* refers to the entry through a single opening.
There is emergence in many ways through many doors; namely, entering with joy born from the manifestation and entry of what was hidden, and emerging while feeling abashed;
entering with passion, and emerging without passion—these are the modes [of its occurrence].

304. Regarding the phrase "even at the time of consumption," the word "even" (pi) indicates that the food causes revulsion even when it has merely entered the opening of entry, let alone when it has undergone digestion, reached maturity, and [exited through] the other openings. This is the food.

"For the purpose of removing the stench" means for the purpose of eliminating the foul odor. "By the body-fire" means by the bodily heat accompanied by the digestive fire (*gahaṇiteja*). "Foam-topped" means...
"Having repeatedly produced froth. "Having boiled" means having reached full maturity. "Leaping up" means jumping about.
"Phlegm and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," one includes bile and other humors. "Excrement and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," one includes sweat, filth, and the like.
"These openings" refers to the mouth and other orifices. "A certain [person]" says this with reference to the urinary passage. However, those who are by nature clean...
Having washed the mouth and so forth, they wash their hands again. "Again, some" refers to the anus.
"Two or three times" means either twice or thrice. And here, the repulsiveness of going and searching for the purpose of food is called the repulsiveness of food.
This is because the act of consuming depends upon it, while the receptacle and the storehouse are connected to it.
One should also understand this distinction: that for others, the state of being a consumer of worms is likewise to be included among the secondary characteristics (vikāra). 305.

"That sign" refers to the sign of meditation—the object of focus known as physical nutriment—which appears by way of its repulsive aspect to one who repeatedly brings it to mind according to the modes already described; it is not the learning-sign or the counterpart-sign.
For if the learning sign (uggahanimitta) were to arise there, the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) would also have to arise.
And that being the case, there ought to be absorption (appanā) attained through jhāna; yet it does not occur. Why?

Because of the diversity of the modes of development and because the meditation subject is profound by virtue of its nature as a real phenomenon (sabhāvadhamma). Therefore he said: "Of physical nutriment..."

"Because of the profundity of the nature of phenomena (*sabhāva-dhammatā*). For here, although the development (*bhāvanā*) proceeds by way of the aspect of repulsiveness, those very phenomena upon which the designation "edible food" (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) is based are themselves repulsive; it is not the designation that is so.

Thus, even through the gateway of grasping the aspect of repulsiveness, the development proceeds by taking only the phenomena as their own-nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*) as its object; and since phenomena as own-nature...
Because of its profound nature by its very essence, absorption (jhāna) is unable to enter into it. Indeed, it is because of this profound nature that the first two Truths became difficult to see.

If the mind is concentrated by access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), why is the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) designated simply as "perception" (saññā)? To this he says: "But by way of grasping the aspect of repulsiveness," and so forth.
Now, in order to show the benefit of this meditation, the passage beginning with “And furthermore” was spoken.
“Craving for flavors” means craving that has as its object flavors such as sweetness and so forth. “Contracts” means it shrinks back because it remains fixed upon the manifold repulsiveness therein.
“Recoils” means it withdraws; it does not spread out. “Turns back” means it desists. “One who desires to cross the wilderness” means...
It has the purpose of crossing over the great wilderness of famine. "Free from intoxication" (*nimmada*) means being devoid of intoxication through pride (*māna*) and the like;
it should be understood that by the mention of the absence of intoxication, the absence of playfulness, adornment, decoration, and so forth is also implied.
"By way of the full understanding of physical nutriment" refers to [the contemplation of] physical nutriment as repulsive in form, according to the method already stated.

By means of the door of knowing through delimitation: "lust pertaining to the five strands of sensual pleasure" is so called because it is connected to the five strands of sensual pleasure in the sense of not transcending them, or it is lust that has those as its object.
It goes beyond full understanding (*pariññā*) and transcendence.

For when craving for flavors (*rasataṇhā*) has been rightly removed, craving for forms (*rūpataṇhā*) and the rest are also necessarily removed, due to reaching the excellence of moderation in eating. Mindfulness (*sati*).

And since the object is indeed transcended when the subject has been transcended, he said: "By way of the full understanding of the five strands of sensual pleasure, he fully understands the aggregate of form.

For when full understanding is reached regarding the sense-base of visible forms and so forth, those things that serve as their supports and the sensitivities (pasāda) that grasp them are also easily brought to full understanding.
By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "unripened and so forth," the receptacles and stores are also included.
The inclusion [of all parts] should be understood. In this context, what is uncooked is simply the undigested food (udariya).

By the mention of the "receptacle" (āsaya), the inclusion of bile, phlegm, pus, and blood is established; by the mention of the "cooked" (paripakka), that of feces and urine; and by the mention of the "fruit" (phala), the inclusion of all [parts] beginning with head-hair is accomplished.
Thus he said: "The development of mindfulness directed to the body also reaches fulfillment. "By the perception of foulness" means by the meditation on foulness (asubhabhāvanā).

The meaning is: "the practice of the development of the impurity of the insentient. He has entered upon the conformable way because, by grasping the aspect of repulsiveness, he clearly perceives the body's state of being impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome.
"This practice," however, refers to this development of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment.
"Ending in the Deathless" means culminating in Nibbāna; it refers to what is termed the development of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment.
The meaning is that, having made access concentration the foundation and having developed insight, one attains Nibbāna.
The commentary on the development of the repulsiveness of food is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the development of the analysis of the four elements.
306. “One definition”: thus, the exposition of the development of the previously mentioned definition of the four elements has been reached.

This is called the “exposition” (uddesa) because it serves as the basis for the subsequent detailed explanation (niddesa), owing to the predominance of weak or medium wisdom; and it is said so because a burden that has been brought must necessarily be carried.
In this context, although there is a distinction in the definitions due to the difference in their objects, they are treated as one by virtue of the commonality of being a “definition.”

However, having unified that [process], it is stated as "a single definition. Alternatively, although there is a difference in the objects during the preliminary stage, because the accomplishment of the purpose lies in its having a single object, it is stated as "a single definition.

For instance, even though for a yogi performing the meditation on the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra), attention initially proceeds separately toward each individual part, [the process is still considered one].
But later on, at one moment, the accomplishment of the purpose occurs in only one part, not in all; so it is here as well.

Herein, it might be argued: "Just as in the meditation subject of the thirty-two aspects, attention proceeds without differentiation by way of the commonality of repulsiveness, so too here, attention should proceed without differentiation by way of the commonality of being elements."
Is it said that "one [mode of] definition" proceeds because of this? No, it is not so.
For in that case (the meditation on repulsiveness), from the point of transcending conventional designation (*paṇṇatti*), attention must be applied everywhere solely by way of repulsiveness;

but here, the elements (*dhātu*) are to be attended to by way of their individual intrinsic nature and specific characteristics, not by way of the generality of being elements. Therefore he said: "by way of discerning the individual intrinsic nature..."

"...a conclusion. Or rather, one should see that the phrase "one defining" was stated in order to show that there is a single meditation subject called the "definition of the four elements" (*catudhātuvavatthāna*), which is unmixed with the other thirty-nine meditation subjects.
Why was it said, "The exposition of the development of the definition of the four elements," when indeed the definition of the four elements...?
What is development (*bhāvanā*)? It is true that it is development; however, the initial discernment (*vavatthāna*) occurs once, whereas its repeated practice is called "development.
This distinction is stated by way of a difference in terminology. But how can development be defined, given that its nature transcends the range of words?

This is not a fault, because the term "development" is applied here to the sense of "cultivation. For in this context, the sense of "cultivation" refers to the grasping of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
“Development” (bhāvanā) is what is intended here.
“By way of discerning the specific nature” means by way of apprehending the individual characteristic, such as hardness and so forth.
For this meditation subject does not, like the earth-kasiṇa and other meditation subjects, involve the discernment of a mere conceptual designation.

It does not proceed by way of discerning colors such as blue, like the meditation subjects of the blue-kasiṇa and so forth, nor does it proceed by way of discerning the general characteristics of formations—such as impermanence and so on—like the meditation subject of insight;

rather, it proceeds by way of discerning the specific intrinsic nature of earth and the rest. Therefore it is said: "by way of discerning the specific intrinsic nature," [referring to] hardness and so forth.

The meaning is: "by way of apprehending the specific characteristics. "Ascertainment" (sanniṭṭhāna) should be understood as the determination by knowledge, not the determination of the [mental factors] included under the general category, nor the determination of applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth. "Attention to elements" (*dhātumanasikāra*) means attention directed toward the elements;

the meaning is: cultivation and attention directed toward the four elements. It is called "action" (*kamma*) because it is to be performed; it is for the sake of the particular states of happiness of the practitioner.

It is called a "meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhāna*) because it is a basis (*ṭhāna*) due to its causal nature; it is the work of yoga (*yogakamma*) proceeding by way of clearly discerning the individual characteristics of the four great elements.
Therefore he said: "Mindfulness of elements, the meditation subject of the elements, and the analysis of the four elements are one in meaning.
Why was it stated that "this analysis of the four elements has come down in two ways"? Is it not [the case that...]?
Is it not the case that because [the elements] were presented in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga* neither too concisely nor too diffusely, one should say they were "presented in three ways"?
No; for even there, the internal elements were included in their entirety through their classification, and the external elements were also taken into account.
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "presented in two ways," it does not mean that they were presented in exactly two ways.
A restrictive rule (niyama) should be adopted; however, since [the method] has already been presented in two ways, the inclusion of the third type is thereby established.

Furthermore, that which is neither too concise nor too detailed should be understood as being included either by way of repetition in the phrase "both concisely and in detail," or by the word "and" (ca) itself.
Alternatively, that which is by way of a method neither too concise nor too detailed...
The detailed portion that is obtainable by way of rejecting excessive brevity has been stated as "it comes in two ways," having included it within the method of detailed exposition.
By doing so, this statement—"it comes in detail for one of not very sharp wisdom who takes the elements as his meditation subject"—is also supported. [This refers to] "in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna."
And this should be regarded as merely an illustration, since it is presented in exactly the same way in such discourses as the *Satipaṭṭhāna* and the *Kāyagatāsati*.
In the *Rāhulovāda*, that is, in the *Mahārāhulovāda*; and in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*, that is, in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta* and in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga* of the Abhidhamma.
Granted that in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna* the teaching comes down surrounded by a simile according to its meaning, yet a simile is intended only so far as—

The phrase "for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the object of comparison" means that after first showing the simile, the Pāli beginning with "Just as... was introduced in order to clarify the meaning of the object of comparison (*upameyyattha*).
But why is the exposition of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) given here by way of the elements (*dhātu*), and there [in the *Mahāhatthipadopamasutta*] even by way of the four great elements?
It is for the purpose of demonstrating the emptiness of beings; here it is by way of the elements, and there too because of their manifest nature due to their grossness.

It should be understood that this exposition of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is presented by way of the great primary elements (mahābhūta) in order to conform to the conduct of certain people who are to be trained.

In this context, regarding the terms "earth element" and so forth, the meaning of "element" (dhātu) is the meaning of "individual essence" (sabhāva); the meaning of "individual essence" is the meaning of "emptiness" (suññata);

and the meaning of "emptiness" is the meaning of "absence of a sentient being" (nissatta). Thus, earth itself is an "element" in the sense of its individual essence, emptiness, and absence of a sentient being.

The earth element (*pathavīdhātu*). The same method applies to the water element (*āpodhātu*) and the others as well. "Earth element" is the element that serves as the foundation for co-nascent material phenomena;
likewise, "water element" is the element of cohesion; "fire element" is the element of maturation;
and "air element" is the element of distension—such is the compound here, and its meaning should be understood in this way. This is the summary.
The detailed exposition, however, will follow later.
