Regarding the phrase "of one with sharp wisdom" and so forth, the word "thus" (evaṃ) refers back to the text as it has been shown.

He said "of one with sharp wisdom" because the detailed teaching is intended for one whose wisdom is not excessively sharp. Just as one who is worthy of a pair of garments is called "one who possesses a pair of garments" (*vatthayugika*).

Thus, one who is worthy of the meditation subject of the elements (*dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna*), or who employs the meditation subject of the elements, is called a "meditator on the elements" (*dhātukammaṭṭhānika*); [the text refers to] that meditator on the elements.

"Expert" (*cheka*) means skilled according to the respective conventional designation, as in the case of a newly born animal possessing a tail, hooves, horns, and so forth, which is a collection of parts such as bone, flesh, and the like.
The term "cow" (*gāvī*) applies when [the carcass] is not divided; it does not apply when it is divided.

However, when it is divided, the terms refer to the specific parts such as bone, flesh, and so forth—one who knows this is [so called]. A "cow-slayer" (*goghātaka*) is one who kills cows for the sake of a livelihood.

An "apprentice" (*antevāsī*) is one who lives near him by way of performing work, because he lives depending on him. "Having pierced through" means having pierced another at one spot. Of the great path...
"In what is reckoned as the middle place" means in that which is reckoned as the point where the four great roads intersect.
Since those four great roads appear as if they have converged after coming from the four directions, therefore that place is "the crossroads of the four great roads" (*catumahāpatha*);
in that crossroads of the four great roads. They dissolve, break apart, and divide, thus they are *bīla*, meaning parts.
Having changed the letter *va* to *ba*, and the letter *i* to *ī*. Indeed, in order to show that very sense of "a part," it is said: "having made a division (*koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā*).

Although the word *ṭhita*—as in "standing" (*ṭhito vā*) and so on—is used elsewhere to mean either being endowed with the posture (*iriyāpatha*) known as standing, or the cessation of movement because the root *ṭhā* signifies stopping, [here it refers to] being endowed with the remaining postures after setting aside walking.
However, in this context, "awakening" (bodhaka) is intended to mean that which awakens to the mode of occurrence of the material body (rūpakāya) in whatever way it may be; thus he says:

"Because it exists in any one of the four postures (iriyāpatha), it is 'as-it-is' (yathāṭhitaṃ). Therein, "by way of mode" (ākārena) means by way of the mode of occurrence of the material body, such as standing and so forth.
For standing and the rest are so called because they are the bases for the occurrence of bodily activity designated as "posture" (īryā).
They are called "postures" (*iriyāpathā*). "As it stands" (*yathāṭhita*) means as it occurs. Here, "intention" (*paṇidhāna*) is intended to mean precisely the place as it has been stated;
thus he said, "Because of its standing as it is, it is 'as intended' (*yathāpaṇihita*). Alternatively, "standing" (*ṭhita*) indicates the body's association with the posture known as standing.
"Intended" (*paṇihita*) indicates its association with the other postures. Alternatively, "standing" refers to the material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) comprised by the body.
"At each respective moment" means the demonstration of their persistence according to their own specific functions.
"Placed" (*paṇihita*) should be understood here as meaning "placed in various ways" (*pakārato nihita*) by those respective conditions through the function of conditions.

"By way of elements" (*dhātuso*) means having separated each element—such as the earth element and so forth—from the others. "Contemplates" (*paccavekkhati*) means he looks back upon them individually (*pati pati avekkhati*).
Having analyzed [the matter] with the eye of knowledge, one sees it.

Now, in order to demonstrate by way of explaining the meaning of the essence (bhāvattha) that very same meaning which was stated in the Pāḷi by way of explaining the literal meaning (*saddattha*) through the passage beginning with "Just as a skilled [butcher]," the text says, "Just as for a butcher of oxen," and so forth.
In that context, "of one who is rearing" means for the purpose of increasing and nourishing the flesh.

[It refers to] one who is being raised on things such as *kuṇḍaka* (gruel), rice, cotton seeds, and so forth. "Dead" (*mata*) means having been killed and then dead; "dead" (*mata*) also means merely dead.
For this very reason he said, "at that very moment. The designation "cow" does not disappear;
for even when the cow is merely dead, the configuration of those limbs and parts upon which the conventional designation "cow" is based has not yet perished.
"Bilāso" means having made a hole after hole. "Vibhajitvā" means having separated the flesh from the mass of bones, or having divided the flesh thus separated into portions.
For this very reason it is said: "The perception of flesh occurs. This refers even to one who has gone forth but whose meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is not yet mastered.
"Resolution of the compact" (*ghanavinibbhoga*) means the resolving apart of what is compact by way of continuity, collection, and function.
Analysis. "Reflecting by way of elements" means reflecting by way of elements after having performed the aforementioned resolution of the compact mass.
Regarding "the perception of a being": they say this is the perception of a being that occurs by way of the view of self;

however, it is indeed appropriate that even the conventional perception of a being should disappear at that time, because of the thorough accomplishment of the resolution of the compact mass according to reality. For when this is so—
The meaning of the simile conforms to and accords with the meaning of the thing illustrated by the aforementioned similes. Therefore he said:
"By means of the elements alone does consciousness become settled.
(307) Having thus shown the places where the meditation subject of the elements has been presented in brief, [the author now] shows the places where it has been presented in detail.
The passage beginning with “But in the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta,” etc., was stated in order to show this.

By the word “thus,” he concludes only the detailed derivation of the meditation subject on the elements from the Rāhulovāda and Dhātuvibhaṅga suttas; he does not conclude the entire method of teaching, because that method of teaching is presented there in other ways as well.
"Therein" means in that aforementioned discourse on the simile of the great elephant's footprint. "Internal" (*ajjhattika*) refers to those factors included within the continuity of a sentient being.
By both terms—"internal" (*ajjhattaṃ*) and "personal" (*paccattaṃ*)—the dharma belonging to each respective individual is expressed; thus he says, "Both are designations for what is one's own.
However, because they are included within one's own continuity, by way of their becoming something to be grasped as "self," [they are called internal].
“Internal” (ajjhatta) refers to that which occurs with reference to oneself. It is “individual” (paccatta) because it is included within this or that particular continuity of existence.
For this very reason it is said: “It is internal because it occurs within oneself; it is individual because it occurs in dependence upon each respective self.
“Hard” (kakkhala) means rigid. Because it serves as a support for co-nascent states by way of its stiffened nature, it is therefore called “stiff” (thaddha).
It has been stated. "Hard-going" (*kharigata*) means gone into, included within, or having the very nature of what is hard (*khara-sabhāva*);
this is the meaning. However, because it appears in a harsh manner due to its hard nature, it is called "rough" (*pharusa*);
therefore he said, "the second is a term for the mode. That which is "clung-to" (*upādinna*) is the group of eight [bases] belonging to the body.
However, with reference to its being produced by kamma, it is both *upādinnam* (clung-to) and *anupādinnam* (not clung-to).

To show that all of this is indeed *upādinnam* in the sense of being taken up, grasped, and adhered to by craving and so forth, it is said: "‘Clung-to’ means firmly taken up," and so on. Therein, the construction is:
"that which is grasped as ‘mine’ is adhered to as ‘I’. The phrase *seyyathidam* is an expression of inquiry indicating a desire to explain.
He asks: "What is that?"—the meaning being "what is it? *Tato* means "afterwards.
*Taṃ* refers to the earth element shown here through its internal and other divisions. *Dassento* means "showing" by way of analyzing the physical basis (*vatthu*).
Although the brain is included within the marrow of the bones and is not mentioned separately in this text (*pāḷi*), it is [treated] in twenty aspects in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
In order to show that [the earth element] has been fully completed, it was taken separately; thus, including that as well, he said:
"It should be understood that the earth element is demonstrated in twenty aspects by inserting the brain among the portions of the earth element," because of its preponderance of stiffness.
By the phrase "or whatever else there may be," the brain is [included] in the Pāḷi.

The inclusion is to be understood. Therefore, here the phrase "or whatever else there may be" should be understood as referring back and forward [to the preceding and following sections], in accordance with the statement:
"Having included the brain, the earth element is described in twenty aspects, or whatever else there may be.
Furthermore, the phrase "or whatever else there may be" should be applied to the remaining three groups.
"In three parts" means in three kinds of parts; for those are not merely three portions.
"By way of trickling forth" means by way of its nature to flow. "It spreads" (*appoti*) means it extends. "It reaches" (*pappoti*) means it attains;

and this is said with reference to the water together with its constituent elements (*sasambhāra*). For, by way of trickling forth, it extends to various locations reckoned as earth together with its constituent elements.
And it reaches [its place], or rather, by way of its specific characteristic.

For that [water element] also, by virtue of being a co-nascent condition—such as the mutual and support conditions—for the other three elements, binds, adheres to, and prevents the scattering of each respective location known as the remaining three elements;
thus, by means of its state of trickling established through its fluid nature, it is worthy of being called "it fills" (*appoti*) or "it pervades" (*pappoti*).

“By way of heat” means by way of sharpness, that is, by way of keenness. “In the manner stated” means in the manner stated regarding the water element—namely, as being of various kinds by way of being originated from kamma, and so forth. “Agitated” means disturbed. “Becoming heated” means overcome by heat.
“Decays” means it becomes worn out. The occurrence of aging in this body, which is obtained by way of the fire element, [is here described] by way of manifest aging.
To show that these [states] are to be understood, the passage beginning with “deficiency of the faculties” (indriyavekallatā) was stated. The distinction between these is as follows:
*santāpa* is the state of heat resulting from exceeding the body’s natural temperature; *paridāha* is a great burning that occurs by way of consuming the body.

Furthermore, the phrase “by which one ages” (*yena jīrīyati*) is also appropriately interpreted to mean that one ages through the diseases of decay such as those occurring every day (*ekāhika*). A hundred times...
Having heated it repeatedly and then thrown it into cold water, the clarified butter (*sappi*) that is extracted is called "clarified butter washed a hundred times" (*satadhotasappi*).
"Eaten" (*asita*) means consumed. "Chewed" (*khāyita*) means masticated. "Tasted" (*sāyita*) means experienced as flavor.

"It undergoes proper digestion" is said with reference to a digestive faculty (*gahaṇī*) that is balanced; however, improper digestion should also be understood by way of that same faculty when it is unbalanced.
“By way of the state of nutritive essence and so forth” means by way of nutritive essence (*rasa*), blood, flesh, fat, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, and semen.

“Separation” means the state of being distinct, the state of being mutually dissimilar. For when food, classified as what is eaten and so forth, undergoes transformation, there arises nutritive essence;

depending upon that, the element of nutritive essence (*rasadhātu*) comes into being—this is the meaning. In this same manner, everything should be understood following the sequence: “from the transformation of nutritive essence, blood,” and so on.
"By way of blowing" means by way of moving or by way of going with speed. Regarding "vomit, spittle, etc.," here the word "etc.
(ādi) should be understood as including the winds that cause the occurrence of belching, spitting, and so forth. Regarding "feces, urine, etc.," the word "etc.
should be understood as including those things that expel bile, phlegm, lymph, and all manner of foul odors. Although the word *kucchi*...
Regarding the term *udara*, since the word *koṭṭha* refers to the interior of the intestines, the remaining portion of the abdominal region is here referred to by the word *kucchi*;
thus he says, "winds lying in the *kucchi* are the winds outside the intestines.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "bending, stretching, etc.," all bodily activities such as looking forward, looking aside, lifting up, and putting down are included. "Inhalation and exhalation..."
By the phrase "mind-originated," it is shown that inhalation and exhalation do not occur apart from the body;
for there is no possibility of a mind-originated phenomenon existing externally. If this is so, how is the statement to be understood:
"Exhalation is the air exiting through the nostrils; it proceeds by touching the tip of the nose in one with a long nose, and the upper lip in others"? That [statement]...

It should be understood that this is stated by way of the mind-originated [matter] occurring in the mode of exiting [the womb], and the temperature-originated [matter] occurring in the continuity [of existence].
"In all cases" is said with reference to the exposition of the three elements beginning with the water element (*āpodhātu*).
Therein, in the exposition of the water element, by the phrase "or whatever else," the [matter] produced from cohesion is indicated; in the exposition of the fire element...

Regarding the natural heat of the body, in the description of the air element (*vāyodhātu*), the inclusion of the wind that produces skin-knots, boils, and so forth—which permeates the network of veins here and there—should be understood.
The winds that produce flexing and other such movements are indeed mind-originated (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*).

If this is so, how is the statement "the first five are originated by four" to be explained? For it is not only the winds that produce flexing and so forth which follow along the various limbs and members.
“Vātā,” and then “atha kho tadaññepi” (and also others besides those), thus there is no contradiction.

“Iti” is a reference to the manner already described. Therefore he said, “by twenty modes,” and so forth. “Ettha” means in this element meditation subject (dhātukammaṭṭhāna) as it has been presented in detail.
By this, it is shown that this commentary is not only for the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta.
Thus it is shown that there is indeed an exposition of the meaning for both the *Mahārāhulovāda* and the *Dhātuvibhaṅga* suttas.
The same method applies to the way of development (*bhāvanānaya*) as well. For it has been said: "In this way, [it is explained] in the *Rāhulovāda* and the *Dhātuvibhaṅga* too.

(308) Regarding the phrase "in the way of development": it means in the method of development; that is, in the procedure of development by which the cultivation of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) succeeds.
The meaning [is as follows]. "Therein" means in the meditation subject of the elements (*dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna*).

Since this meditation subject has come down in two ways and has been taught in two ways according to these two types of persons—namely, "one of sharp wisdom" and "one of not-very-sharp wisdom"—therefore, their application of attention (*kammaṭṭhānābhinivesa*) to that meditation subject must also be twofold.
To show that first, [the text says]: "For one of sharp wisdom..."
The passage beginning with “of a bhikkhu” is commenced. Regarding the phrase “the body hairs are the earth element,” the word *iti* here has the sense of “beginning.

Thus, “the detailed discernment of the elements” means the detailed discernment of the meditation subject of the elements in forty-two modes, starting with “head hairs are the earth element, body hairs are the earth element,” and so forth.
“From prolixity” means from slowness or from being gradual. That which...

"The characteristic of rigidity" means the quality of hardness, which is the characteristic of rigidity found in the hair and so forth. The same method applies to "the characteristic of cohesion" and the others as well.
"One who attends to it thus" refers to one who engages in attention merely by way of these characteristics, without touching upon the physical basis.
"His" refers to one of sharp wisdom. "The meditation subject becomes clear" means that which serves as the locus for the practice of yoga becomes manifest.

That very characteristic becomes manifest; or, because that characteristic is well-established, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) consisting of the attention directed toward it becomes manifest and clear.
This is because one of sharp wisdom, through the proficiency of his faculties, has a preference for what is concise.
For one whose wisdom is entirely dull, even the development of meditation does not succeed.
He said: “Not for one of non-sharp wisdom. “Thus he gives attention” means that he gives attention in brief according to the method already stated.
“Darkness becomes unmanifest” is to be construed as follows: because it does not appear, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) becomes obscure, making [the mind] as if blind.
“By the former method” refers to the method previously stated, beginning with “Head-hairs are the earth element,” and so forth. By the grasping of the physical basis (vatthu).

When one attends to it in detail, the meditation subject becomes clear to one whose wisdom is not excessively sharp, because of his lack of quick comprehension and his preference for detailed exposition.
Now, in order to illustrate the aforementioned point by means of a simile, it was said: "Just as in the case of two bhikkhus," and so forth. Therein:
"The opening of the *peyyāla*" means that which serves as the beginning or the gateway for the *peyyāla* recitation—either the first instance or the second instance.
"Having expanded" means having recited it in its entirety without omission. "By way of both ends" means by way of grasping the beginning and the end of each respective instance.
"Merely touched by the lips" means merely the contact of the lips. [This is] as in the case of one of sharp wisdom when turning over a text.
A bhikkhu may prefer the concise method and not the detailed one, while another may prefer the detailed method and not the concise one;
this should be understood as the application of the simile even to the method of development (*bhāvanānaya*).
Therefore—because the concise method is suitable for one of sharp wisdom, and the detailed method is suitable for one whose wisdom is not excessively sharp—therefore [it is said].

Since the preliminary duties such as the purification of virtue must be fulfilled by one who wishes to devote himself to a meditation subject, and since those have been described in every aspect below, they are not treated here.

However, because meditation succeeds only for one whose body is secluded and whose mind is secluded, and not otherwise, [the author] shows both of these, saying: "By one who has gone into solitude..."
"By means of seclusion," he said. Therein, "having gone into solitude" (*rahogata*) means having gone to a private place;

the meaning is that one has approached a place conducive to meditation alone. "By means of seclusion" (*paṭisallīnena*) means having restrained the mind from various objects one by one and having settled it upon the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*); the meaning is that the mind is closely concentrated thereon. [He should contemplate] his entire material body...
"Having reflected" means: attending to one's own entire physical body—above the soles of the feet, below the tips of the hair, and across to the skin—as consisting of elements;
and since this body is composed of the four great primary elements, reflecting upon it by way of those four great elements thus:
"In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element."

The meaning [is as follows]. Now, in order to show the method of mental attention regarding those elements by way of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and their modes of appearance (*upaṭṭhānākāra*), it was said:
"That which in this body... and so forth.
Therein, "the state of stiffness" states the characteristic; for the earth element has the characteristic of hardness (*thaddhatta*). "The state of rigidity" [is likewise stated].

The mode of manifestation (*upaṭṭhānākāra*) means the mode that should be grasped by knowledge. Fluidity is the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of the water element because its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is to flow;
cohesion is its mode of manifestation. Heat is the characteristic of the fire element because its intrinsic nature is warmth; maturation is its mode of manifestation.
Distension is the characteristic of the air element because its intrinsic nature is to provide support; movement is its mode of manifestation.

The mode of appearance; and the "mode of appearance" refers to the clear manifestation of knowledge by way of the elements performing their own respective functions. Why, then, is both mentioned here?
It is due to the inclination of individuals. For to some who attend to the elements, they become graspable as intrinsic natures;
to others, they become graspable by way of performing their own functions—that which is called their "taste."
In this regard, the yogi, while attending to the elements, first discerns each one individually according to its specific characteristic and its function.
Therefore it was said: "Whatever rigidity or hardness there is in this body... [etc. ...having thus discerned the elements in brief.
Therein, "having discerned" means having discerned the elements by their characteristics through knowledge that acts as a discerning agent.
Or having discerned and grasped it by way of its taste. This, first of all, is the application to the meditation subject in the method of development in brief.
Having thus discerned the elements: "In this body there is the earth element, which is the state of hardness or rigidity;
the water element, which is the state of fluidity or cohesion; the fire element, which is the state of heat or maturation..."
"Or is it the air element's state of distension or its state of motion?
In this way, by attending to the elements together with their characteristics and so forth, one should repeatedly bring them to mind and attend to them for a hundred times, a thousand times;
they should be struck by reasoning and thoroughly investigated by applied thought. As he attends to them in this manner, regarding those characteristics and so forth—
When [the earth element] appears very clearly, one should grasp that alone, set aside the other,
and practice mental attention together with it by way of "earth element, water element," and so forth. For one who attends in this manner— gradually,
neither too quickly nor too slowly, warding off distraction, transcending mere designation, and relinquishing when it no longer appears— [the meditation succeeds].
Skill in attention should be practiced through these ten aspects: by way of characteristic and the three types of discourses.
Therein, "by way of sequence" means according to the order in which it was learned from the teacher, and that is precisely the sequence of the teaching itself.
One who attends to it in this sequential manner should not attend too quickly. If one attends too quickly...
For if one attends to the meditation subject again and again without interruption, the meditation subject remains unmanifest and does not bring about distinction.
Therefore, it should be attended to neither too quickly nor too slowly. Just as it should not be too quick, so it should not be too slow;
for if one attends to it too slowly, the meditation subject does not reach its conclusion.
It does not become a condition for special attainment. Men traveling along a path who go either too fast or too slow should be cited here as examples.

"As to warding off distraction": having abandoned the meditation subject, the mind's distraction toward external, diverse objects must be warded off; for when there is external distraction, the meditation subject declines and is lost.
In this context, a person traveling along a one-foot-wide path should be cited as an illustration.

Regarding "transcending the description" (*paṇṇatti-samatikkamana*): having transcended the description such as "this is the earth element," one should fix the mind upon the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) themselves.
Thus, for one who has abandoned the description and directs attention only toward the characteristics such as hardness, the characteristics...
They appear very clearly and distinctly. Through this repeated attention, his mind gains cultivation.
The entire body of form appears as mere elements—empty, insentient, and soulless—like a machine revolving back and forth by means of its string.
However, if he also applies attention externally, [the same occurs].
Then, as humans, animals, and other beings wander about him, they appear having abandoned their mode of being as sentient creatures and appearing merely as an aggregate of elements;
the actions performed by them appear as if they were being set in motion by a machine made of elements;
and the food, drink, and so forth swallowed by them appear like an aggregate of elements being cast into an aggregate of elements.

It becomes established. Then, even if his mind has attained such familiarity, if—due to over-exerted energy—it does not enter the method of development through agitation, or due to overly slackened energy—through idleness—if it does not enter the method of development, then one should apply energy and concentration according to the method taught in these three suttas:
the *Adhicitta-sutta*, the *Anuttara-sītibhāva-sutta*, and the *Bojjhaṅga-sutta*.
[These] should be performed. Therefore it was said: "And three discourses.

Now, when one has thus applied evenness of energy and directs attention toward that very characteristic, at which time the faculties such as faith and the rest proceed having attained evenness and become well-purified, then—due to the distancing of lack of faith and so forth—by means of the seven powers that have reached an especially high degree of strength...
Having gained support, the jhāna factors such as applied thought (vitakka) and the rest become more prominent and manifest;
because they are the direct opposites of those states, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), along with the evil qualities associated with them, are suppressed.
At this point, he has attained access concentration (upacāra-jjhāna) which takes the characteristic of the element as its object. Therefore it was said: "Again and again, the earth-element..."
“The water element... [and so on] ...access concentration arises.

In this context, the word *matta* has the sense of excluding qualifications; thus, by means of that [term], one excludes those specific qualities—such as “a being” or “a soul”—which non-Buddhists and the worldly masses imagine exist in this personal existence (*attabhāva*) despite their non-existence there, being merely products of conceptual construction (*vikappanāmattena*).

They superimpose [a self], and this [contemplation] turns that back. Therefore he said: "as being without a sentient being (nissatta) and without a life-principle (nijjīva). "To be adverted to" means it should be brought to mind.
"To be attended to" means the characteristic of the elements (dhātulakkhaṇa) as being merely elements should be established in the mind again and again by way of cultivation.
"To be reviewed" means that very characteristic of the elements should be looked at repeatedly and individually, by one who has achieved success in cultivation.
It should be seen directly, one after another, with the eye of knowledge.
"As he is thus striving" means as that yogi is devoted to meditation in the manner described,
and therein, through his practice of heedfulness, through his practice of constancy, through his cultivation of what is suitable, and through his discernment of the sign of serenity.
By means of the continuous practice of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), by living without regard for body or life, and by not falling into despondency midway,
he should intensify his cultivation and remain steadfast with great exertion, applying effort, application, and striving correctly.
"Sustained by the wisdom that illuminates the analysis of the elements" refers to earth and the other [elements].

Through the non-abandonment of the wisdom of development—which has the function of illuminating by means of the manifestation of the individual essences and characteristics of the elements—at its beginning, middle, and end, there arises a sense-sphere concentration that is merely access, having reached its peak because it has grasped [the object] from all sides without attaining the state of the sublime (mahaggata).

It should be understood that the term "access concentration" (upacāra-samādhi) is used here in a conventional sense; for concentration that moves having approached absorption (appanā) is what is meant.
This is access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*); there is no absorption (*appanā*) here.
However, it is described in this way because such concentration possesses the same characteristic [as absorption]. But why is there no absorption here? The reason for this is stated:

"because its object is a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva-dhammārammaṇattā*). For when the object is a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature, due to its profound depth, absorption-jhāna does not arise unless there is a specific distinction in cultivation (*bhāvanā-visesa*).

Furthermore, supramundane jhāna reaches absorption by way of the sequence of development for purification, while the formless attainments reach absorption by way of the development that transcends the object; this point has already been stated in the description of the recollection of death.
Thus, having shown the meditation subject on the elements by way of comprehending the four elements without distinction within the material body, [the text continues:]

Now, in order to show briefly the method of attention to the elements (dhātumanasikāra) as it appears in the Sutta by way of analyzing the bones and so forth therein, the passage beginning with “Or else” is commenced. Therein, the connection is: “These four parts which have been mentioned.

Just as the conventional designation “house” arises depending on wood, creepers, grass, and clay, which exist according to their respective conditions and are distinguished by their arrangement; [so too here].

There is nothing there called a "dwelling"; rather, the designation "body" exists in dependence upon bones, sinews, flesh, and skin, which function as distinct arrangements according to their respective conditions. Herein, there is no self or soul;
it is shown to be merely space enclosed by those [elements]. This teaching is intended to demonstrate the emptiness of beings.
He said, "While analyzing [the body], it is for the purpose of showing the absence of a sentient being," and so forth.
Therein, "dependent on bones" means depending on the more than three hundred varieties of bones that stand elevated in successive order, such as the heel-bone and others.
"And sinews" means the nine hundred varieties of sinews that stand binding together that very collection of bones. "Flesh" refers to that same collection of bones...
It is flesh of nine hundred varieties of cuts that remains after being smeared [with blood].
"Skin" refers to the thick skin that stands enveloping the entire body, covered by the shadow of the wing-like scales.
In all instances, the word *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). "The space is enclosed" means, for example, as when it is established by means of walls, foundations, and so forth.
Just as the wood, the binding creepers, the plastered clay, and the thatching grass— these elements such as wood and so forth—
surrounding the space both inside and out, come to be designated as a "house" (agāra) and receive the conventional name "dwelling" (geha);
even so, the space situated inside and outside, surrounded by the aforementioned bones and other parts, is likewise [designated].
The bones and so forth, being derived from [the four great elements], come to be designated simply as "form" (rūpa) and receive the conventional designation (vohāra) of "body" (sarīra).

Just as in the world a house constructed depending on materials such as wood comes to be designated as a "house" and is called a "Khattiya’s house" or a "Brāhmaṇa’s house," so too this [body] is conventionally referred to as a "Khattiya’s body" or a "Brāhmaṇa’s body"; there is no [substantial entity] here whatsoever.
The intended meaning is "a being" or "a soul.
The construction is: "having repeatedly dissected those four parts.

"Following each respective interval" means following the gaps between those respective parts—namely, between the bones and the sinews, between the sinews and the flesh, and between the flesh and the skin.
"With the hand known as knowledge" means with the hand of wisdom. "Having analyzed again and again" means having repeatedly disentangled [the parts].
Alternatively, "having analyzed again and again" means having performed an analysis by means of the hand of knowledge that follows each individual part, such as the bones and so forth.
"In these" refers to one's entire material body, which has been divided into four parts and analyzed as previously described.
Regarding the four parts beginning with bone: "in the same manner as before" means by the very method previously stated, namely, "whatever rigidity there is in this body," and so forth.
As for the method of cultivation that should be explained here, it should be explained in the same manner as that stated in the immediately preceding method.
However, when brought forward from the detailed exposition as "the determination of the four elements," it should be applied accordingly. Thus, in the manner now being described:
The method of development (bhāvanā-naya) is to be understood. Why was it said, "Having mastered the elements (dhātu) by way of forty-two aspects"?

Is it not the case that, from the beginning, the elements do not consist of thirty-two aspects? This is not a fault, because the elements themselves are to be mastered under the heading of their physical bases (vatthu).
In the manner described—by means of the five factors such as being neither too far nor too near from the village that serves as one's resort (gocara-gāma)—...
"In one who is endowed with" and so forth refers to the aforementioned types [of persons]. "By one who has performed all duties":
he is called "one who has performed all duties" because all duties—such as the severing of impediments and so on—have been performed by him;

this indicates that for such a person, the purification of virtue and other preliminary tasks have already been accomplished prior to the undertaking of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "From the concise summary of the requisites": by this, the mental expressions are brought together.

The equipment (*sambhāra*) is the cause for that [perception]. What, then, is this? It is earth and so forth. For among the twenty modes such as head-hairs and so on, the conceptual designation "earth" occurs by taking rigidity as its basis, because it functions with earth as its sign.

Therefore, in that context, what is called the "earth-equipment" consists of the head-hairs and so forth together with their specific existence; thus they are "with equipment" (*sasambhārā*). This applies also to the water-element portion and the others.
The method is the same. "The concise summary with its constituent parts" means the summary together with its requisites;
the construction is: "it should be developed from that concise summary with its constituent parts.

Having discerned the four elements, beginning with earth, respectively within the twenty, twelve, four, and six sections, the definition of elements (dhātu-vavatthāna) is [achieved] by way of the concise summary with its constituent parts.
This is the development (bhāvanā). Therefore he said: "Here, a bhikkhu [contemplates] in twenty parts," and so forth.

"By way of analysis together with the constituent parts" means: by way of analyzing the constituent parts—the hair and so forth—without taking the twenty parts beginning with hair as a single whole as was done previously, there is a defining of them individually as the earth element. This applies to the water-element parts and the others as well.

The same method applies here. Regarding "by way of a summary of the specific characteristics" (*salakkhaṇasaṅkhepato*): it is called a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) because one is characterized by it;

that is, the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena, which in this context refers to stiffness and so forth. Therefore, because they possess such characteristics as stiffness, they are "with their characteristics" (*salakkhaṇā*), namely the forty-two modes beginning with head-hairs.
"By way of a summary" of these means: [the following is said] regarding the twenty beginning with head-hairs.

Having taken the parts together as one and having defined therein the fourfold characteristic, such as hardness and so forth, meditation is "meditation by way of the summary of characteristics. This same method applies to the parts of water and the other elements.

"By way of the analysis of characteristics" means by way of the classification of the head-hairs and so forth, which possess their own respective characteristics such as hardness; that is, among the forty-two modes consisting of the head-hairs and so forth.
The development [of insight] occurs by way of defining the four characteristics—such as hardness and so forth—for each [of the elements].
Thus, in order to explain the method of development taught in these four aspects, the passage beginning with “How does one develop it together with its requisites and in brief?
is commenced. And herein, just as a person of sharp wisdom, because of that sharpness, possesses the capacity to discern the nature of others...

It is twofold by way of having sharp faculties and dull faculties. Therein, the first method is stated briefly by way of one with sharp faculties, and the second by way of one with dull faculties. Thus there is also the person whose wisdom is not excessively sharp.
Therein, by way of the person who has clear faculties, [the exposition is given] through the brief summary of constituent parts and the brief summary of specific characteristics.

And thus the method of development (bhāvanānaya) has been demonstrated. However, it should be understood that for one whose faculties are not very keen, the method of development is demonstrated by way of analysis with constituent parts (sasambhāra-vibhatti) and by way of analysis according to specific characteristics (salakkhaṇa-vibhatti).
As he defines them in this manner, the elements (dhātuyo) become clear to him because of his thorough discernment of the elements. Now, as for the procedure of development here:
This should be understood in the same manner as explained below.
"Of one" refers to a person whose faculties are not overly sharp. "Developing thus" means developing by way of both the detailed and the concise methods.
That sevenfold method by which, having mastered [the practice], one becomes skilled is called "skill in mastery."
...is called [the knowledge], or the knowledge produced by that. In this way, skillfulness in attention should also be understood.
Regarding the "thirty-two aspects": this refers to the thirty-two types of parts, beginning with head-hair, which have been discerned by means of attention to the elements.
And the phrase "in the thirty-two aspects" is stated because there is no defining of the fire-element and air-element parts by way of color and so forth. All of that therein...

“The method stated should be performed”: from the instruction on skill in learning beginning with “by means of speech and mind,” up to the phrase “by way of successive releasing, etc.,” the entire method of development (bhāvanā-vidhāna) that has been set forth must be carried out and accomplished.
“By way of color, etc. means by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation. And this [method] is by way of color, etc.
Since attention is common to both the attention to the elements and the attention to their repulsive colors as its preliminary stage,
it was said, "At the end, attention should be exercised in this way," in order to show specifically the attention to the elements already produced.
(311) "These states are devoid of mutual concern and reflection" refers to these [states], such as the skin enveloping the skull.

When these phenomena, which are the primary elements and their derivatives, are designated as "hair," they are empty of any mutual intention or reflection such as, "Hair has arisen in me," or "We have arisen here.
By this, he demonstrates that there is merely the elements (dhātu), due to the lack of agency in both cause and fruit;
and by that, it is shown that even intention and reflection are likewise devoid of agency.
It must be seen. For those [aggregates] do not arise, nor do they become conditions, by being directed toward or reflected upon as such and such causes.
"Iti" (thus) is a reference to the manner already described. "Acetana" means non-conscious, or devoid of volition (*cetanā*).
"Abyākata" means included within the category of the indeterminate (*abyākata-rāsi*). "Suñña" means empty of a self (*attasuñña*).
Therefore it is "insentient. It is "stiff" because it possesses the characteristic of stiffness. Therefore, it is the earth element;
such is the way attention should be applied—this is the connection. This applies in all cases. 312. Regarding the phrase "in the place of an empty village":
here, the mention of an "empty village" is for the purpose of showing that, in the ultimate sense, the body is devoid of an experiencer.
313. *Madhukaṭṭhika* means the seeds of the *madhuka* tree.
314. By the term "stone mortars," stone slabs placed to serve as supports for the pillars of a house are intended. 315.
The inclusion of "fresh cowhide" is for the purpose of showing its similarity to [the aforementioned objects] in terms of having a foul odor and other such qualities.
316. Because the flesh-muscles are for the most part thick, there is a great amount of clay required. 317.
"In the walls and rafters" means in the wooden posts that serve as the foundation for the walls of a hut made of split wood. 318.

Just as the state of being a support belongs to the heel-bones and so forth, the state of being supported by them also belongs to the ankle-bones and so forth; this is established even without deliberate attention.
For the sake of clarity, after stating "standing with the heel-bone and the ankle-bone lifted up," and so forth, it was further said, "resting upon the head-bone and the neck-bone," and so forth.
319. Regarding "in rotten reeds, bamboo shoots, etc.": this refers to rotten reeds, bamboo stalks, and the like.

321. The assembly of breast-bones is called the "breast-bone cage" (*uraṭṭhipañjara*) because it resembles a cage. An old chariot cage is cited as an illustration in order to demonstrate its instability.
322. "The pair of twin flesh-masses" refers to a pair of flesh-lumps. 323.
Because the *kilomaka* (pericardium) is white in color, it is described as "wrapped in rags" (*pilotikapaliveṭhita*), with "rags" (*pilotika*) being used as an illustration.
It has been stated. In the same way, regarding the statement "the kidneys and heart do not know the flesh throughout the entire body," it should be construed as follows:
the kidneys and heart do not know, "We are covered by the concealed pericardium," nor does the flesh throughout the entire body know, "I am covered by the concealed pericardium."
324. *Koṭṭhamatthakapassaṃ*: the upper side within the interior of a granary.
325. *Dvinnaṃ thanānamantare*: between the two breasts; that is, in the middle of the two breast-regions, and the breast-region should be understood here in its internal sense.
327. *Ekavīsatiantabhogē*: in twenty-one places where the inner circle is bent down and up.

328. Since the food that has been consumed and remains in the stomach is intended here by the term *udariya*, he said: "The *udariya* is what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, remaining in the stomach.
331. *Ābaddhapitta* (bound bile) is like circulating blood and like bodily heat; its function is bound to kamma-born materiality. Thus he said:
"The *ābaddhapitta* is bound to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) and remains pervading the entire body. By the statement regarding its being "bound,"...

This indicates that while the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) exists, [the body] certainly exists; however, it should not be understood as being exclusively born of kamma (*kammaja*), like the life-faculty itself.
"In the gall-bladder" (*pittakosa*) means in the receptacle of bile, which resembles the shell of a large *kosāṭakī* gourd. "Become liquid" (*yūsabhūta*) means become essence (*rasa*). 332.
A cesspool (*candanikā*) is a place for discarding used water, fetal waste, and so forth; [it refers to] within such a cesspool.
333. Since "prior residence" (pubbāsayo) belongs only to certain individuals of dull wisdom, he said, "pubbo is unconfined in its location," with the intention that it is not common to all. 334.
"Like bile" means like uncongealed bile. "The entire body" refers to every part of the body connected to the life-faculty (jīvitindriya).
"Moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs"—here, the liver is moistened by filling its lower portion.
It should be understood that the others moisten them by trickling down upon them little by little.

The comparison regarding the moistening of clods of earth and so forth below is intended merely to show the commonality of the lack of agency in both the moistener and the object to be moistened, not to show a commonality of location;
for some of the things to be moistened by the accumulated blood are indeed below [the moistener].
The state of being situated above something has been shown in the description of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*).
The construction should be understood as follows: the lower part of the liver does not know, "Blood is situated upon me," and the kidneys and so forth do not know, "Blood is situated moistening us."
336. *Patthinnasineha* means fat that has attained a state of rigidity and density. The construction is: "flesh throughout the entire body.
And this is said with reference to a stout body. Although fat possesses both rigidity and density, it is not as firmly bound together as flesh;
therefore, it is called "rigid broth" (*patthinnayūsa*). For that very reason, it is classified as a portion of the water element (*āpokoṭṭhāsa*).
337. "In young palm-stalk wells filled with water" refers to the cavities of young palm-fruit stalks that have been cut off at the tip while still containing water. 338.

It should be understood that the oil contained in a rinsing-water vessel (*ācāma*) is cited as an illustration to clarify the commonality of non-exertion (*abyāpāra*) by way of its pervading its own substrate. 339.
[This refers to] the sour and sweet tastes, etc., which are the conditions for the production of saliva.
343. Having applied attention to the head-hairs and so forth, one should apply attention to the fire-element portions by changing the grammatical analysis;
this is how it should be connected. "By which one is warmed" means that by which the body is warmed is the function of warming.
"Fire" is the very mode of grasping that [function], expressed as a noun. The same method applies to the phrases "by which one ages," and so on.
"By way of in-breath and out-breath" means by way of the state of the air entering within and exiting from the nose.

"For one whose attention proceeds in this manner" refers to the attention directed toward the meditation subject as it proceeds, according to the mode described above, in its detailed analysis together with its constituent parts.
"The elements become evident" means that because they have been discerned in detail, the elements become manifest. Here too, the method of development is as explained below.
It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. 345.

"In those very [parts]" means in those same twenty components (*koṭṭhāsa*). Regarding the characteristics of maturing and the characteristic of distension, here too the phrase "in those very [parts]" should be brought forward and connected.
Again, "in those very [parts]" means in those same twelve components; this is the meaning. And herein, regarding the components beginning with hair—
Because they are easily discernible there due to their state of agitation— just as the water element and others are in bathing powders and the like—
the phrase "right there the characteristic of cohesion," and so forth, was stated. However,
considering that the air element and others are not as easily discernible within the fire-element factors such as heating and so on, [it was said] "by that..."
It is said to be "indivisible," not "in that very place. If this is so, how can it be said to be "in that very place" regarding the divisions of air?
For even the divisions of air, such as upward-moving winds and so forth, come to be apprehended in a lump-like form;

however, this is not the case for the divisions of fire, such as the heat that warms and so on—thus, there is no fault here. In that context, "by that" means by that fire. "Indivisible" (avinibbhutta) means...
"Inseparable" (*avinābhūtaṃ*) means either that it occurs by way of being included within each respective group.

"One who defines in this way" refers to one who defines the elements (*dhātu*) by way of their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*) and in brief, according to the manner described. "By the method stated" refers to the method stated below, beginning with the words, "As he is thus striving...
(346). "Even while developing in this way" refers to one who develops [the meditation] after having discerned the elements by way of their specific characteristics and in brief.
"By the method stated previously" means by the method stated in the section on development (*bhāvanā*) under the detailed analysis of constituent parts.

"In this way" means just as in the case of head-hairs, so it is for all [the other] sections. "In all sections" refers to the remaining forty-one types of sections; thus, herein the discernment of one hundred and sixty-eight elements has been explained.
As for the procedure for development here, it is exactly according to the method stated below.
Now, in order to show the method of attention directed toward the elements (dhātu) by way of their etymological meaning and so forth,

the passage beginning with "By way of the etymological meaning" is stated. Therein, "by way of the etymological meaning" means that since the initial grasping of the meditation subject occurs through words—
that is, because its meaning must first be grasped via the medium of words— therefore, the elements must also be attended to by way of their etymological meaning.
"Stated as groups": this is stated because, having discerned the elements both specifically and generally according to the meaning of the words, they function as a mass rather than individually;

therefore, their attention as groups is also stated. Since those groups have the dimension of atoms (*paramāṇu*), [the text speaks] of the earth element and so forth included therein within a single [atom].
In order to show the measurable extent of the body, the necessity of attending to it by way of its particles (*cuṇṇa*) was stated.

However, since this attention to the particles occurs by way of their aggregation (*saṅghāṭa*), attention by way of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth was stated to show that the specific form [of the elements] as they have emerged must be discerned.
For one who discerns the elements by way of their characteristics, there is the analysis according to their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇavibhatti*).
Regarding the application of mindfulness to the meditation subject: since, when the elements are being discerned by way of the forty-two parts,
this distinction must be known— namely, "so many are temperature-originated, so many are mind-originated, etc."— therefore,
attention is described by way of their origin.

In order to show that even for those [elements] whose origination has been thus fully understood, a discernment of their specific and general characteristics must be made by following the sequence of sounds,
"attention according to diversity and unity" is stated. In order to show that although these [elements] are inseparable in terms of their specific characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*),
they are nevertheless "inseparable in location" (*padesa*) because their positions cannot be pointed out individually, "according to separation and non-separation" is stated.
Attention has been explained. Furthermore, even though they function inseparably, some [mental factors] are similar to certain [objects] while others are dissimilar;
thus, this distinction must also be discerned. To show this, attention has been explained in terms of similarity and dissimilarity.

Moreover, among the elements that are both similar and dissimilar, those that are internal are endowed with such specific functions, whereas those that are external are the opposite; this distinction must be discerned.
Attention is described by way of distinction between the internal and external in order to show [this].
Attention is described by way of inclusion in order to show that the specific inclusion of elements—such as their grouping according to genus and so forth—must also be discerned.

Attention is described by way of condition in order to show that the elements must be discerned also by way of their mutual support through their respective functions, such as sustaining and so forth.
It was said [thus]. In order to show that the elements are to be discerned by way of their non-affliction, attention by way of non-attention was stated.

In order to show that the elements are to be discerned by way of the specific nature of their own conditioning factors and by way of the specific nature of their state as conditions, attention by way of the analysis of conditions was stated. Thus, regarding the discernment of these thirteen aspects:
The reason should be understood. "By means of modes" (*ākārehi*) means by ways or by causes. 347.

Therein, "because it is spread out" (*patthaṭattā*) means because of its manifoldness; thus, by way of etymology (*niruttinaya*), he states the meaning of the word: it is "earth" (*pathavī*) because it is manifold (*puthubhāvato*), for "earth" (*puthuvī*) is the same as "earth" (*pathavī*).
Alternatively, it is "earth" (*pathavī*) in the sense of spreading out (*patthanaṭṭhena*), since it extends itself by way of being a foundation (*patiṭṭhābhāvena*).
The meaning is "he attends upon. The meaning of the word *appoti* has already been stated above. *Āpīyati* means it is dried up; some say it means "it is drunk.
They say, "But this meaning is appropriate in the sense of the primary element (the earth-element)," yet it is indeed appropriate even in the sense of a characteristic.
For that [element] also proceeds as if being drunk by the other three elements through its mode of parching and drying what is harsh. *Appāyati* means...
"Brūheti": for the water element has the function of moistening. "Tejati" means it consumes; the meaning is that by its state of sharpness, it heats the other three elements.
"Vāyati" means it moves; the meaning is that it causes the collection of elements to go to another location by acting as the cause for their arising in a different place.
Having thus explained the specific meanings of the terms, he now speaks of them in general terms with the words "But without distinction... and so forth.

It has been said. As for "because they bear their own characteristics" (*salakkhaṇadhāraṇato*): just as that which is imagined by the heretics—such as "primordial nature" (*pakati*) or "self" (*attā*)—does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), so it is not with these. Rather, these are called "elements" (*dhātuyo*) because they bear their own characteristics and intrinsic nature.

As for "because of taking up suffering" (*dukkhādānato*): this is because they burn with suffering. For these elements, being established as causal factors, [are like] the elements of iron, copper, and so forth.
They burn with manifold kinds of suffering in saṃsāra, such as iron and copper. "As the locus of suffering" means:
because they are merely the site for the occurrence of no small amount of suffering, and because they lack mastery;

or else, because beings, acting as the causes, undergo that suffering through these [aggregates], and once it has been thus undergone, it is deposited and placed within them—thus, "as the locus of suffering."
The elements (*dhātuyo*). Furthermore, this meaning has already been stated as: "The meaning of 'element' (*dhātu*) is the sense of being devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*).
For it was with the purpose of uprooting the perception of a "living soul" that the Blessed One gave the teaching on the elements in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, this person consists of six elements.
Thus, by way of the etymological definition, both specifically and generally, the intrinsic characteristic of the elements is made clear; therefore he said: "In this way..."

"They should be brought to mind according to their meaning by way of both the specific and the general. Furthermore, attention (manasikāra) should be understood in the manner already explained above, after having discerned the elements (dhātu) through the gateway of their meanings. 348.
"By modes" (ākārehi) means by ways. Alternatively, they are called "modes" (ākāra) because the elements are manifested or seen therein; thus, they are constituent parts (koṭṭhāsa).

"Through the combination of eight factors": because of the coming together (samavadhāna) of the eight factors—color and so forth—which are distinguished by the specific conditions mentioned above, and because they exist simultaneously through a particular mode of arrangement;
it is on account of this that there is the conventional designation (sammuti), which is merely a name (samaññāmatta), namely "hair. "Through the analysis of those very same [factors]":
because of the analytical separation (vinibbhujana) of those very same factors, such as color and so forth.
For just as the eight factors beginning with visible form (*vaṇṇa*) are found to exist in the ultimate sense when analyzed by wisdom as distinct from one another,
so too are head-hairs not found to exist in the ultimate sense as something distinct from visible form and the other factors. Therefore,
when those phenomena upon which the conventional designation "head-hairs" is based have been separated out individually, there is no such thing as "head-hairs."
“Convention” (sammuti) means merely a conventional expression (vohāramatta).
The phrase “merely a collection of eight factors” is stated by taking the color and other qualities—which serve as the basis for the designation “hair”—as a unity;
it is not because those [factors] themselves constitute a mere collection of eight things. Regarding the section on hair produced by kamma:
The same applies to the root of the hair; thus it should be understood accordingly for body-hair and the other [parts] as well.
Regarding the phrase "the group of ten dhammas": here, the fire-element portion that ripens what has been eaten and so forth should be called "the group of nine dhammas.
Now, if these portions beginning with the hair consist respectively of groups of eight, nine, and ten dhammas, then why [is it said] that one should attend only to the elements such as earth?

He said, "But by way of prominence," and so forth. Since this attention to elements has as its sole purpose the eradication of the perception of a living being (*sattasaññā*), and since the analysis of phenomena (*dhammavinibbhoga*) leads preeminently to the eradication of the perception of a living being, therefore the classification of phenomena should be understood in this way with respect to the constituent parts.
For here, the undigested food in the stomach (*udariya*), excrement (*karīsa*), pus (*pubba*), and urine (*mutta*) are temperature-originated (*utusamuṭṭhāna*).
The fire that digests what is eaten and so forth is originated by kamma; the wind of inhalation and exhalation is originated by consciousness. Thus, six [elements] have a single origin.
Sweat, tears, spittle, and snot—these four—are originated by both temperature and consciousness. The remaining thirty-two are originated by all four [causes].
Among these, in the portion of fire that digests what is eaten and so forth, there is one group consisting of the life-nonad (*jīvitanavaka*). In the others, which have a single origin...

In those [groups] originating from temperature (*utu*), each one is an octad originating from consciousness (*citta*); in those originating from two [factors], there are two octads each according to temperature and consciousness;

in those originating from four [factors], there are three octads each originating from temperature, consciousness, and nutriment (*āhāra*); in those originating from temperature and consciousness, there are ninefold groups including sound (*sadda*);
in the eight instances of the fire and air elements, there are eight ninefold groups including life (*jīvita*); and in the remaining twenty-four instances...
When taken as a unity, without analyzing the physical body— which consists of two sets of ten-fold material groups (the body-decad and the sex-decad) plus the eye-decads,

ear-decad, nose-decad, tongue-decad, and heart-base-decad found in the fleshly portions designated as the eye and so forth— there are one hundred and forty-seven material clusters (*rūpa-kalāpa*) from the perspective of material classification;
however, when the components of these constituent parts are further divided, there are more than one thousand five hundred materials.
When the differentiation of their constituent parts is grasped, the incalculable diversity of material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) should be understood.

Thus, although these forty-two sections are divided into many types by way of the analysis of phenomena, they should be defined solely by way of the four elements through the apprehension of their predominance.
Therefore he said: "But by way of predominance... [they] should be brought to mind. Herein, the method of bringing them to mind is as follows:
It should be understood in the manner already stated.
349. "By a middling measure" means by a middling dimension obtainable in a body of middling height and circumference.
"Being grasped" means being grasped after having been encompassed by wisdom. "Reduced to powder by the breaking up of atoms."
In this regard, some say: "An eighth part of a finger-breadth is a barley-corn (*yava*); an eighth part of a barley-corn is a louse-egg (*ūka*); an eighth part of a louse-egg is a nit (*likkhā*);
an eighth part of a nit is a chariot-dust particle (*rathareṇu*); an eighth part of a chariot-dust particle is a water-dust particle (*tajjārī*);
an eighth part of a water-dust particle is an atom (*aṇu*); and an eighth part of an atom is what is called an ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*). Thus it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
However, it is stated: “Seven grains of rice measure one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*); seven *ūkā*s measure one grain of rice; seven *likkhā*s measure one *ūkā*;
thirty-six chariot-dust particles (*rathareṇu*) measure one *likkhā*; thirty-six *tajjārī*s measure one chariot-dust particle;
thirty-six *aṇu*s measure one *tajjārī*; and thirty-six atoms (*paramāṇu*) measure one *aṇu*. Therefore:
A "subtle atom" (*paramāṇu*) is defined as being even a thirty-sixth part of an *aṇu*;

it occupies a portion of space, is beyond the range of the fleshly eye, and is an object of perception only for the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). With reference to this, it is said: "grounded and pulverized into subtle atoms," meaning they have been reduced to a state of fine powder through the aforementioned divisions of atoms.
"Become subtle dust" means that for this very reason, they have attained an exceedingly subtle state of dust.
“Doṇamattā siyā” means sixteen *nāḷis*. Here too, the phrase “by the medium measure” (*majjhimena pamāṇena*) should be brought in and connected.
By that [measure], they say: “A *kuḍuva* is four handfuls by nature; four *kuḍuvās* are a *nāḷi*; sixteen *nāḷis* of that *nāḷi* are a *doṇa*;
and that, moreover, is twelve *nāḷis* of the Magadha *nāḷi*. “Collected” (*saṅgahitā*) means as follows:
It does not scatter; thus, by way of binding, they are taken as being gathered together.
"Guarded" means protected in such a way that it does not fall into a state of dampness or sliminess through the influence of the water element, which has the nature of trickling.
"Distended" means made to be extremely distended by the cohesive wind (*saṅghāta-vāyu*). "It does not disperse nor perish" means that even though it has become like fine dust...
The earth element, having received conditions from the water, fire, and air elements— which have the functions of binding, ripening, and moving—
becomes moistened by moisture, ripened by heat, and brought to expansion by air; like flour-dust,
it does not scatter here and there nor fall apart, but rather becomes a compact mass and exists in various ways.
It becomes something that can be grasped. Therefore he said, "not being scattered," and so forth. In this context, *vikappa* means division.

Although the fire and air elements also possess a physical form because they are material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), the kind of density found in the earth and water elements is not found in the fire and air elements;
thus, due to the absence of such a state of mass, there is no breaking into powder therein.
It is not extracted. For even in the presence of water, fire, and wind together with their constituent elements, the state of being measurable is simply not obtained.
"Having reached the state of broth" means having attained the condition of broth, that is, the condition of fluidity. For that very reason, it has the mode of being cohesive.
"It does not drip" means it does not flow down. "It does not leak" means it does not overflow. This demonstrates the state of being thoroughly saturated by the water element.
It is stated [thus] because it has the nature of nourishing.
By the phrase "having become the mode of heat," he shows that even the ordinary heat in the body occurs by way of that very fire element which is designated as the digestive organ (*gahaṇī*).
"It ripens" means it causes digestion; for it properly [digests] whatever food has been eaten.
By means of transformation, it serves as the cause for the perfection of the tastes and so forth; thus it is said that it "ripens" and "stirrs up" this body.
For this very reason it is said: "it does not show a state of putrefaction.

The fire element is a specific condition for the excellence of bodily color, which is supported by karma and caused by clarity of mind, let alone for the perfection of material form produced by temperature and nutriment.
It is said that it brings about the perfection of color, referring to the fire element as previously described.
Regarding the phrase "characterized by motion and distension": here, some say that "motion" (samudīraṇa) means pushing or impelling, while others say it means drying up.
"Distension" (vitthambhana) is the causing of rigidity in the other three elements; some call this "compression" (uppīlana). By "that" [is meant] that which has the characteristic of distension.
Regarding the air element (*vāyodhātu*): "The other" refers to that which has the characteristic of motion. For it has the nature of pushing; therefore he said, "struck evenly.

And "striking evenly" is the state of being the cause for the production [of the material aggregate] in another location. "Impact" refers to production in a location even closer [to the original]. "He causes to roll" means he causes it to revolve.
Now, by way of conclusion, that purpose for which the attention to the powder was introduced:
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “Thus it is indeed” was stated. Therein, regarding the phrase “a machine of elements”:

just as a mechanical figure functions by means of a thread even though there is no agent (kattā) present, so too does a machine composed of elements proceed by way of the mind; here, the method of attention (manasikāra) should also be understood according to the manner already described.

350. Although the characteristics and other qualities of the four elements have already been explained here and there below, nevertheless, in order to show the method for grasping the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) by way of a separate treatment after having demonstrated them in their entirety, the passage beginning with “By way of characteristic, etc.

is commenced. In this context, that by which something is characterized is a “characteristic” (*lakkhaṇa*); she whose characteristic is hardness is “one whose characteristic is hardness” (*kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇā*).
But is it not the case that solidity itself is the earth element? True, this is so;

nevertheless, although the phenomena are non-different because they possess the nature of being perceived or unperceived as sound, this description is made by means of a distinction established through conceptual designation (*kappanā*). For in this way, there occurs an understanding of the specific meaning.
Alternatively, it is called a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) because it is characterized (*lakkhīyati*); thus, the element which is characterized by being solidity is the "solidity-characteristic."

In this way, the meaning here is to be understood. The same method applies to the remaining [mental factors] as well. "Having the function of establishing" means having the activity of providing a foundation for co-nascent states.
For that very reason, because it presents itself to knowledge in the mode of receiving [those states], it is said to have "receiving as its manifestation.
However, its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is not mentioned here as being distinct from other phenomena, because it exists as a common property.

Or it is like a remote cause. Or, for example, in the commentaries on the *Dhamma-uddesa-vāra* and other sections, after showing how taste and so forth act as conditions for others, the "proximate cause" (*padaṭṭhāna*) is cited for the purpose of demonstrating that they possess such conditions; but it is not so here.

Here, however, because the inquiry is intent upon elucidating the unique and specific characteristics of the elements (*dhātu*) that are not shared with anything else, the proximate cause is something distinct from those other phenomena.
It should not be lifted up; it must be seen [as such]. Its function is to nourish (*brūhana-rasa*); that is, its role is to cause the co-nascent states to increase.
For it is said that it demonstrates their state of being refreshed. Its manifestation is cohesion (*saṅgaha-paccupaṭṭhāna*);
just as external water acts for bathing powder, so too does it manifest as the cohesion of the co-nascent states. Its manifestation is the provision of softness (*maddava-anuppadāna-paccupaṭṭhāna*).
Like an external fire, it has the manifestation of providing softness to co-nascent phenomena such as lacquer and iron.
*Abhinīhāra* (projection) is the state of being the cause for the emergence of a mass of elements in another location, or rather, it is their extraction, like a sprout from a seed. 351.
They are produced by temperature alone because they do not arise through the influence of karma and so forth. Those produced by temperature and mind sometimes arise from temperature.

"Sometimes from consciousness" means because they arise from consciousness at certain times. "The remainder" refers to the twenty-four remaining parts beginning with head-hairs—namely, the first three portions of fire and the five portions of air—which makes thirty-two in total.

"All of them" means that all these arise from four origins (samuṭṭhāna) by way of kamma and so forth; for even in the case of head-hairs and the rest, those parts not separated from the flesh arise only from kamma, nutriment, and consciousness.
352. "By way of diversity and unity" means by way of particularity and generality. For the mutual dissimilarity of phenomena is diversity (*nānatta*), while their similarity is unity (*ekatta*).
"Of all four" refers to all four [truths]. "From their own characteristics, etc."—*salakkhaṇa* is one's own characteristic;
[the phrase] is "from that, the own-characteristic, etc. By the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of taste, manifestation, and also qualities such as softness, smoothness, and roughness.
The summary should be understood. Why was it said, "of those that have become diverse by way of being originated from karma, etc."?
Is it not the case that, by way of being originated from karma and so forth, there is a unity and commonality among the four elements? No;
it was said thus with reference to such distinctions as: "the elements originated from karma are indeed distinct from those originated from temperature (utu) and so forth."
By way of expression, it refers to these elements (*dhātu*). Their characteristic is being affected (*ruppana-lakkhaṇa*), their intrinsic nature is being affected (*ruppana-sabhāva*).
What, then, is this so-called "being affected"? It is that which is the production of a different state when opposing conditions such as cold and so forth come together;

or, when those conditions are present, it is the state of being the cause for the production of a different state even while [the element] itself remains existent—that is "being affected. "Because they have not passed away" means because they do not abandon [their own nature].

And here, "great manifestation" (mahantapātubhāva) should be understood by way of the elements together with their constituent parts; likewise, "great transformation" (mahāvikāratā) by way of the element that is the common characteristic of the great primary elements (mahābhūta);

"great pervasion" (mahāparihāratā) and "the state of existing as something great" (mahattavijjamānatā) are by way of both. With reference to the word *bhūta*, the neuter designation "these" (*etāni*) is used.
They are "great" because they have manifested as a collection consisting of many hundreds of thousands of groups of material qualities (*rūpakalāpa*).
And because they arise in a continuous stream, immeasurable in number, and extending for many yojanas in length and breadth.
"Four nahutas" means four times ten thousand. They appeared as large as the bodies of devas, dānavas, and others, measuring three gavutas and so forth.
Herein, this is the etymological analysis: they are called "great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*) because great beings (*mahantāni bhūtāni*) have been born and produced therein.
Alternatively, it is a "great marvel-maker" (*mahābhūto*) in the sense that he displays many different kinds of marvels, displays many wonders, and displays many astonishing feats;

or, it is a "great marvel-maker" because there are great marvels (*mahantāni abhūtāni*) therein. Or, they are "great beings" (*mahābhūtā*) because spirits (*yakkha*) and so forth are great by their very nature (*jāti*); thus they are "great elements."
Or rather, this term "great primary" (*mahābhūta*) should be understood as being conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) with respect to them.

However, earth and the others are called "great primaries" because they are deceptive and because their specific locations cannot be pointed out, just like the actual great primaries. The neuter gender has been employed here because the word *bhūta* possesses both genders.

In that context, "deceptiveness" refers to their appearing as having the nature of blue and so forth, while they themselves do not possess the nature of blue and so forth; for they are indeed devoid of the nature of male, female, and so on.

And having offered [the oblation], there is the manifestation of the forms of woman, man, and so forth. Likewise, because they do not exist either inside or outside one another, yet persist in dependence upon one another, their location cannot be specified.

For if these elements were situated inside one another, they would be unable to perform their respective functions due to the lack of mutual penetration; if, on the other hand, they were situated outside one another, they would be separate and distinct.
If that were so, the doctrine of their indivisibility (*avinibbhutta-vāda*) would be undermined; therefore, they cannot be pointed out as separate locations.

Even so, by means of their respective specific functions such as providing a foundation and so forth, each of the three acts as a support for the other three, whereby they function as conditions through such relations as co-nascence (*sahajāta*).
Thus he said: "And it is not the case that they do not stand supported by one another."
"From the agreeable" means from those things that are captivating and full of charm. "By way of color, shape, and movement" refers to colors such as black or dark-brown;
shapes such as broad, gaping, or thin; and movements such as the waving of hands or eyebrows.
"The characteristic of its own essence" (*sarasalakkhaṇa*) means a characteristic that constitutes its intrinsic nature, or its inherent nature together with its specific function.
Regarding the term *mahāparihāra*: explaining the meaning of the words here, he says, "by the great... [they are] beings; or, beings that have great maintenance (*parihāra*).
In that context, regarding the latter sense, the word *parihāra* from the second member of the compound has been elided from the first member, and thus it is called *mahābhūtāni*.
