The phrase "tathā hi" (for thus) means "precisely because of the great magnitude of that transformation. To demonstrate that transformation, the passage beginning with "from the earth" was stated.
Therein, "accimato" refers to fire. "One hundred thousand koṭis" means one single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) consisting of one hundred thousand koṭis;
he speaks thus by treating all of it as one, in its capacity as the field of his authority. "It dissolves" (*vilīyati*) [due to] the downpour of clouds that cause calamity.
Like salt in urine, it goes to dissolution and falls apart. "By the agitated" means by the disturbed.
"It scatters" means it disperses and falls apart.
Having shown the magnitude of the transformation in non-clung-to (anupādinnaka) things, he says "stiffened," etc., showing it in clung-to (upādinnaka) things. Therein:
The word *vā* in the phrase *kaṭṭhamukhena vā* has the sense of a simile (*upama*).
Just as one bitten by a snake with a wooden mouth becomes rigid, so too, through the disturbance of the earth element, that body becomes like one with a wooden mouth;

the meaning is that it becomes rigid as if a wooden mouth had been placed upon its face. Alternatively, the word *vā* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). That [restriction] is: "through the disturbance of the earth element..."
The word “or” (*vā*) should be brought forward and connected in this way. This is the meaning here:

even when bitten by a woodpecker, the body becomes rigid solely through the disturbance of the earth element; therefore, that body is never dissociated from the earth element, remaining as if it had entered the mouth of a woodpecker.
Alternatively, the word “or” (*vā*) has the sense of indefiniteness; in that case, the meaning is: by a woodpecker...
The bitten body either becomes rigid or does not, depending on the power of mantras and medicinal herbs;
however, when devoid of such mantras and herbs due to the disturbance of the earth element, that body becomes entirely rigid, like a piece of wood placed in a fire.
"Putrid" means decomposed. "Scorched" means completely heated, with a burning sensation having arisen. "Cut through" means all around.
It is cut, shattered, and pulverized into atoms, like the body of the Venerable Elder Upasena.

Regarding the term *mahābhūtāni* (the great elements): it should be understood as an analysis (*niddesa*) formed by eliding the second member of the compound in the phrase *mahāvikāravantāni bhūtāni* (elements possessing great transformations), thus becoming "the great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*).
Even though [the elements] such as earth and so forth are well-known to the whole world, one should describe them according to their true nature, having abandoned misconceptions.
They are called "great" because they cannot be discerned without great effort; for their nature is difficult to comprehend.
Indeed, they are easy to understand once one has stood regarding them as "not great," but upon seeing their difficulty to grasp, one realizes, "Oh, these are great!
Alternatively, they are "great elements" (mahābhūtāni) due to reasons such as being a portion of the great elements.

Indeed, these elements are called "great primaries" (mahābhūtāni) for the following reasons: because they are a portion of the great primaries, because they share the commonality of being great primaries, because they depend upon the great primaries, because they have the nature of great primaries, and because they culminate in the great primaries.
In this context, "because they are a portion of the great primaries" means that in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, regard this as 'the primary' (bhūta),'", they are mentioned without distinction.

The pentad of aggregates is called “the primary element” (*bhūta*). Among these, that pentad of aggregates which occurs in the sensual existence, the fine-material existence, the five-aggregate existence, and in certain percipient existences, deserves to be called the “great primary element” (*mahābhūta*) because of its vast scope.
However, the four elements beginning with earth are merely partial constituents of that great primary element.

“They are called ‘great elements’ (mahābhūtā). For linguistic conventions that apply to wholes are also seen to apply to their parts, as in the expressions ‘the ocean was seen’ or ‘the cloth was burnt. They are called ‘elements’ (bhūtā) because derived matter (upādārūpa) exists dependent upon them;
thus, they are the four primary constituents beginning with earth. Furthermore, this designation ‘element’ applies to these [four] because...”
Because they do not exist for any other purpose, because they are the unerring basis for derived matter (*upādārūpa*), because they are of great benefit to the world,

and because they serve as the support for the eye, the ocean, and so forth, they were designated by the conventional term "great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*). "Dependent upon the great elements" means dependent upon those that are great,
of great power— such as kings beginning with Mahāsammata and Mandhātu, and deities beginning with Sakka, Vepacitti, and others.

They are called the "great elements" (*mahābhūtā*) because they are the great beings (*mahābhūtā*) due to being the support for all beings and creatures—whether they be asuras, the Great Brahmās and other Brahmās, or, by virtue of their qualities, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples.
For their body consists of the four great elements. "By way of the state of being great elements" means by way of the state of having many elements.
For this term *mahā-sadda* (great sound) is seen in the sense of plurality in such expressions as "the great multitude has assembled.

Furthermore, the elements (*dhātu*) such as earth and so forth exist in immeasurable varieties even within a single individual existence (*attabhāva*). Therefore, because they are great, numerous, and divided into many hundreds of thousands of types, they are called "great primary elements" (*mahābhūta*).
[The phrase] "up to the end of the great primary elements" refers to the great primary element.
Because it reaches its conclusion by way of that [verse]:
“Time devours all beings, including itself;
and the being who devours time devours the cooker of beings.”—

In such passages as these, one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is called "one who has come to be" (*bhūta*). For he, because the conduit to existence has been severed and because he will not undergo rebirth in the future, is called "one who has come to be" in an absolute sense;
the others are not, because they have not transcended the conventional designation of "those who will come to be.

It is precisely this "one who has come to be" who is here called a "great being" (*mahābhūta*) by way of honor, just as one speaks of a "great one whose taints are destroyed" or "Mahāmoggallāna. And of these...

For these elements (*dhātu*), which proceed by way of continuity within the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there is no reaching of an end other than in the continuum of the aforementioned great primary element (*mahābhūta*).

Therefore, because the primary elements have reached their end [within that continuum], the term *mahābhūta* is used by eliding the word *bhūta* from the first member [of the compound *mahābhūtabhūta*]. Thus, these elements are called "great primaries" (*mahābhūta*) because they are a portion of the great primary element, and so forth.

It should be understood as follows: since earth and the other elements possess their specific characteristics—such as hardness or trickling—without ever abandoning their general elemental characteristics, it is said, “because they have not transcended the characteristic of an element.
For a particular cannot exist by abandoning its general characteristic, nor does a general characteristic function independently of its particulars. Thus, they say:
“Because it looks toward its own ultimate meaning, it does not abandon its particularity along with its commonality;
because it gives rise to doubt, it grasps both as having a single meaning even when they are equal.

And by the “retention of their own specific characteristics”: by that very retention of their own specific characteristics through which they are called “elements” (*dhātu*), they are likewise called “phenomena” (*dhamma*).
They are called both ways because they are manifested precisely as being devoid of a sentient being and devoid of a soul. For this very reason it was said:

“This person, O bhikkhu, consists of six elements; he dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena. Because the moment of form does not exceed the moment of the immaterial [states], it is said to be “conformable to its own moment.
“By sustaining” means by remaining; the meaning is by continuing.
"In the sense of destruction" means by way of momentary dissolution. "In the sense of fear" means by way of being fearful due to the oppression of arising and passing away, and so forth.
"In the sense of being pithless" means by way of being devoid of a self as its core.
353. "These arise together": these four elements arise together and proceed together, at the same time.
Even when present in their minimum extent, within each pure octad produced by temperature, consciousness, or nutriment, or within the life-nonad produced by kamma—
each such group being inseparable from its location and having no distinct, assignable place for itself—
the earth element exists there as the basis for the other three elements. For wherever earth exists as the foundation for the other three elements, right there...
The others [the remaining three elements] exist in relation to that [earth element] by way of binding, ripening, and moving.
This same method applies to the rest as well. 354. The intention is that the first two are mutually similar because of their heaviness.
And here, one might ask: does not lightness also exist in earth? For indeed, it is said of it: "hard, soft, smooth, rough, heavy, light."
Is it not the case that even here lightness is indeed obtained? No, because what is intended is weightiness in the primary sense (*nippariyāya*).

For weightiness itself is spoken of figuratively (*pariyāyena*) as the "lightness" of the earth element when compared to something heavier, just as coolness is [figuratively spoken of] in relation to the fire element.
If this is so, how is there "lightness of matter"? This too is simply the mode of lightness (*lahutākāra*) in the manner already described.

Because they are obtained by way of dependence. For the characteristics of delimitation and change are not found in an ultimate sense, since they are merely specific states of produced material phenomena (*nipphanna-rūpa*).
Therefore, with reference to the weightiness established in the ultimate sense, it is said:
"The first two are similar because of their weightiness. By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), he concludes this point of being "similar. "Two" [refers to the first two].
However, this [term] should be brought over and connected here with "the latter" just as it was with "the former.

The intended meaning is that they are dissimilar by virtue of their being heavy or light. And just as with the states of being heavy or light, so too should similarity and dissimilarity be applied by way of the states of being drinkable or undrinkable.
355. "Internal" refers to those internal [bases] mentioned below; the meaning is that they are included within the continuum of a sentient being.

Regarding "the bases of consciousness, the intimation, and the faculties": this refers to the six bases of consciousness beginning with the eye, the two types of intimation (bodily and vocal), and the female faculty, male faculty, and life faculty.
As for those who say, "The 'bases of consciousness' includes the heart-base," for them, by the inclusion of the term "faculties" (*indriya*), [the heart-base is already accounted for].
The inclusion of all eight material faculties should be understood. Regarding the phrase "of a nature contrary to what was stated":

this is said because, just as for the external elements there is a reversal of the previously stated conditions—namely, their total lack of dependence on the bases of consciousness, the intimation, and the faculties, as well as their absence of postures—so too is their fourfold origination; it is not, however, like the case of characteristic matter.

Because there is no other source of origin for them, they possess temperature-originatedness (*utusamuṭṭhānatā*). Furthermore, it may or may not be stated that the internal elements are the support (*nissaya*) for lightness and the other [qualities], for their characteristic is the grasping of intimation (*viññatti*). 356. "By the others" means by the water, fire, and air elements.

"Included in one" means included in one by way of inclusion through genus (*sajātisaṅgaha*). For the inclusion of things belonging to the same genus is "inclusion by common genus. Therefore, he said: "Because there is no difference in their mode of origination."
357. “Being a foundation for the three great primary elements, it is a condition”:
this means that by way of cohesion, those three great primary elements with which it is grouped, by way of maturation, they are maintained, and by way of motion, they are distended;
for those three great primary elements co-nascent with itself, it acts as a foundation and, precisely because of that, serves as a support by way of upholding.
Or, acting as a foundation in the manner already described, it becomes a condition by way of co-nascence and so forth.

This same method applies to the remaining [elements] as well. 358. Although it was shown above that these phenomena lack mutual attention and reflection, nevertheless, showing that the discernment of the meditation subject should be performed separately according to this very method:
He said, “The earth element is here,” and so forth. In that context, the word *ca* (and) has the sense of inclusion;
by it, he indicates that this too is one mode of attention (*manasikāra*). “Here” means within these elements.

By stating, “I do not know ‘I am the earth element’ or ‘I am a condition,’” he demonstrates the absence of any mental application (*ābhoga*) regarding his own function, just as there is none regarding his own self.
The phrase beginning with "the others too" was stated in order to show that, just as for the benefactor, there is also an absence of mental application (ābhoga) for those things to be benefited.
"In all instances" means in all elements (dhātu); therein also, in all [instances] distinguished by the functions of self and the things to be benefited.

"359. By way of the analysis of conditions" means both by way of the analysis of the conditioned phenomena (paccaya-dhamma) and by way of the analysis of the state of being a condition (paccaya-bhāva). "By way of condition" (paccayato).

For by this [previous section], the state of being a condition for the other three elements—by way of their respective unique roles such as providing a foundation for earth and so forth—has been stated.

Here, however, the analysis of the state of being a condition is stated in its entirety for those phenomena from which earth and the other elements arise, as well as for earth and the others themselves;
this is the distinction between these two modes. "Kamma" refers to wholesome and unwholesome [volitional action].
Kamma that produces material form. "Consciousness" refers to any consciousness that produces material form. "Nutriment" refers to internal nutriment that produces material form.

"Temperature" refers to any temperature; in its essential nature, it is the fire element (*tejodhātu*). The restrictive term "kamma alone" is used for the purpose of showing the absence of confusion regarding the origins [of material phenomena];
by this, it is indicated that even for certain things not born of kamma, kamma serves as a contributory condition (*pariyāyapaccaya*) in a figurative sense. For he will say accordingly:
“Conditioned by kamma, mind-originated,” and so forth. Now, one might ask: must there not also be a condition other than kamma for those things originated by kamma?
There must be; however, because that [condition] falls within the category of kamma, the restriction was made in order to exclude other counterparts.
Therefore he said, “not mind and so forth. Regarding the phrase “of those originated by mind and so forth,” this is also the meaning here.
It should be stated according to what is appropriate. "The others" refers to those other than consciousness and so forth. "Productive condition" is said with reference to its status as a producer;

however, as for the actual condition, it is specifically the kamma-condition. For it has been stated: "Wholesome and unwholesome volition is a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for resultant aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma."

"Of the rest" refers to those things originating from consciousness and so forth. "Is a condition by way of the indirect method (*pariyāyato*) as a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*)" means that because the *Paṭṭhāna* teaches the decisive support condition only for non-material phenomena, there is no decisive support condition for material phenomena in the direct sense (*nippariyāyena*).
However, because of the statement in the Sutta, "relying on a person," and "relying on a thicket of forest," according to the method of the Suttanta...
It should be understood that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). Regarding the statement "consciousness is a producing condition" (*janaka-paccaya*):

it is said that consciousness is a producing condition by virtue of its being an originator, while acting as a condition through its modes of co-nascence, support, nutriment, and so forth. The same method applies to nutriment and temperature as well.
Having thus shown the analysis of conditions among the elements (*dhātu*) by way of the conditioning factors such as kamma, etc., [the text now proceeds] to those things originated thereby...
Demonstrating the classification of conditions by way of the elements as well, he first states them in brief with the words, "The great primary element originated by kamma," and so forth;
then he explains them in detail with the words, "Therein, the earth element originated by kamma," and so forth.
Therein, "the earth element originated by kamma" refers to the earth element born of kamma, which was mentioned generally in the phrase "the great primary element originated by kamma."
In relation to the three elements— water, fire, and air— which are born of kamma and arise simultaneously with the kamma-born [matter],

they are related to those [elements] that assist them by way of conascence, mutuality, presence, and non-disappearance conditions, as well as by way of support, because they assist those elements, serve as their basis, sustain them from their arising until their dissolution, and because there is no absence of them.
It is a condition, and like kamma, it is a condition for them not by way of being their producer, because it does not originate them.

Although here the state of being a support is already included by the mention of the "support-condition" (*nissaya-paccaya*), the phrase "by way of being a support" is used to show this specific distinction:
that the function of the earth element, which is not shared with anything else, is the state of being a support for its co-nascent phenomena.
And it is stated separately as "and. The same method applies to the phrases beginning with "by way of binding" (ābandhanavasena). Regarding the phrase "of the thirty-two great elements":
the term "continuity" (santati) is used because the four great elements—arising from temperature, consciousness, and nutriment—are not intermingled with one another, but proceed without interruption;
thus, the inclusion of the word "continuity" refers to this uninterrupted occurrence. The state of being a foundation for the earth element is [the function] of those [elements] that are co-nascent.
He said, “Of phenomena alone,” meaning “not by way of being a foundation. The same principle applies to the phrases “not by way of binding,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “herein,” this refers to those great elements originated by kamma. Since it is easy to apply the method of the lineage (tantinaya) in such passages as “the earth element originated by consciousness [is related] to the other [elements] originated by consciousness,” he extends the application by saying, “In ‘consciousness-nutriment’... the same principle applies.”

Regarding the phrase "and moreover, in those [elements] proceeding by way of conditions such as co-nascence," the word *ca* (and) has the sense of conjunction, while the word *pana* (moreover) has the sense of specification.
By means of both, it illuminates this meaning: that the elements, while proceeding by way of the aforementioned conditions such as co-nascence, proceed with this specific distinction.
Now, in order to show that distinction, he spoke the verse beginning with “dependent on one. Therein, the construction is as follows:
dependent on one element, three elements proceed in four ways; dependent on three elements, only one element proceeds in four ways;
and dependent on two elements, two elements proceed in six ways. As for the meaning, it concerns earth and the other [elements].
When each one acts as a condition for the other three, those three being the conditionally arisen, this is one tetrad;
when each of the three acts as a condition for the other one, that one being the conditionally arisen, this is another tetrad:

namely, the first and second with the third and fourth, the first and third with the second and fourth, the first and fourth with the second and third, and the second and third with the first and fourth.
In the case of these two pairs acting as conditions, the fact that the other two pairs arise in dependence upon them constitutes one set of six.

Thus, for those factors proceeding in four ways by way of being conditions and in six ways [by way of being related], the analysis of the conditions and the conditionally arisen should be understood respectively according to the sequence of single, dyad, and triad, and triad, dyad, and single. And this—

The state of being a condition occurs by way of the conditions of co-nascence, mutuality, support, presence, and non-disappearance; and even therein, it should be understood specifically through the aspect of mutuality.
It is with reference to this that it was stated in the section on "Dependent" (paṭicca): "Dependent on one great primary, three great primaries arise;
dependent on three great primaries, one great primary arises; dependent on two great primaries, two great primaries arise."
By the word “etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase “advancing, retreating, etc.,” the inclusion of physical actions such as taking up and letting go should be understood.
It is a condition for pressing because it is established by way of the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*) through the action of striking.
“That” refers to the earth element itself. It follows the water element (*āpodhātu*), [indicating] the subordinate status of the water element therein and the predominance of the earth element.
And because it has a preeminent function both in establishing—as it does in being the state of support—it is the condition for that establishment, which is the placing of the foot;
such is the connection. "Of the casting down" means of the downward placement.
And in that regard, since the water element possesses a heavier intrinsic nature, its activity is preeminent; thus he says, "the water element follows upon the earth element."
Likewise, in the statement "the fire element has an upward movement," the subordinate nature of the air element to it during lifting is expressed.
Since the air element, which moves horizontally, possesses a predominant function in drawing back and thrusting forward, the subordinate nature of the fire element to it is understood.
In this context, *atiharaṇa* (drawing back) is the moving of the foot toward the place where it was standing; *vītiharaṇa* (thrusting forward) is moving it forward from that position.
“Carrying away even a little distance” means taking it away or moving it across; “carrying away while looking” refers to the same.
“By each single door” means by each of the thirteen modes of discerning the elements as analyzed in such passages as “the earth is so called because it is spread out,” and so forth.
“This is that access concentration”: how, then, is this a synonym for “definition”? [It is so called] because it defines the object through the various aspects of the elements.
He said, "Of the four elements," and so forth.
Now, in order to show the benefits of this meditation, "And furthermore," and so forth was stated.
"He plunges into emptiness" means that by seeing the mere nature of the elements, one defines the body of form as being non-self, and following from that—
Since the fact that even the group of mental names (*nāmakāya*) is soulless is clearly evident, he penetrates the emptiness of self in every respect and becomes established therein.
He eradicates the perception of a "being" means that for that very reason, he uproots and eliminates the inaccurate perception that occurs in such ways as "a being," "a person," "a woman," or "a man.
Not directing his attention toward the conceptualization of wild beasts, spirits, ogres, demons, and so forth...

Because he has clearly seen the mere nature of the elements (dhātumattatā) even in the mental continuum of another as if it were his own, he—like one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava)—endures and overcomes fear and terror without forming such conceptual constructions (vikappa) as "these are wild beasts like lions and tigers" or "these are spirits and demons.
For it is stated that the failure to fall into such aforementioned conceptualizations is the cause for enduring fear and terror. *Ugghāta* means elation or exultation.

Suppression is the occurrence of a state of dejection. Furthermore, one becomes possessed of great wisdom because of correctly effecting the resolution of the compactness of the body by way of its elements.
Thus it is said that this meditation subject is conducive to those of an intellectual temperament;
or else, the intention is that one whose destiny is a happy rebirth [attains this] due to the immaturity of the faculties.
The commentary on the hidden meaning of the "Exposition of the Analysis of the Four Elements," which is adorned with nineteen methods of meditation, is finished. 361.

Questions concerning the essential nature and other characteristics, beginning with "What is concentration?", are for the purpose of understanding its divisions according to their essential nature and so forth. From the perspective of essential nature and so forth...
For when the classification of what has already been known is being stated, it is easy to understand because the detailed exposition follows the concise summary;

and since the method of the concise summary is subsumed within the method of the detailed exposition, it was said: "in order to show the detailed exposition and the method of development of concentration.
Alternatively, by means of the passage beginning with "What is concentration?", the various classifications of concentration itself are shown, as is its development and its benefits.
It is said, "in order to show the detailed method of development," with the intention that [the path] is indeed dependent on the method of development (*bhāvanānaya*).

"In every way" means both by way of performing all the preliminary duties for development, such as the severing of obstacles, and by way of elucidating the development of all meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Having stated, "It is fulfilled," the passage beginning with "It is twofold indeed" was spoken in order to clarify that very state of fulfillment.
The concentration intended here is mundane concentration (*lokiya-samādhi*). "In the ten meditation subjects" refers to those ten meditation subjects previously described as "conducive to access.
"In the consciousness preceding absorption" means in the moments of consciousness prior to absorption (*appanā*).

In the mental arisings of the preliminary stage of the eight meditative absorptions (*jhāna*). "One-pointedness" refers to one-pointedness both in the cognitive process with a single adverting consciousness and in the cognitive process with multiple adverting consciousnesses.

"In the remaining meditation subjects" refers to the thirty meditation subjects stated to be "conducive to absorption. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the benefits of concentration.
362. "Visible state" (diṭṭhadhamma) refers to the personal existence that has become directly manifest; dwelling in happiness therein is "dwelling in happiness in the visible state.
Granted, by the phrase "having attained," only absorption concentration (appanāsamādhi) is indicated;

however, since the inclusion of access concentration (upacārasamādhi) would also occur through the word "one-pointed mind" (ekaggacitta), the term "development of absorption concentration" is stated in order to exclude that.
"But these," it says, "are the states of jhāna developed by outsiders; they produce mere one-pointedness of mind.

In the discipline of the Noble One, in the teaching of the Blessed Buddha, they are not called 'effacement' (sallekhā), because they do not constitute the practice for the effacing of the defilements.
However, in the teaching, even non-harming and so forth are indeed effacement, because they serve as the basis for the supramundane.
It "constricts" because of its defilement by craving, corruption, and so forth, within the process of saṃsāra, which is an extremely constricted state—the ultimate point of confinement.
"By way of attaining the opportunity" means by way of attaining the opportunity reckoned as the ninth moment, which is fit for the acquisition of the goal.
For, due to the rarity of that [opportunity], one who does not attain even absorption (appanā) fails to attain it.

A person who is full of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) performs the work of insight (vipassanā) while remaining in access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) alone, thinking, "I shall quickly transcend the suffering of saṃsāra.

"The basis for direct knowledge" (abhiññā-pādaka) means that which serves as the foundation and the support for the types of direct knowledge such as the supernormal powers (iddhividhā). "It exists" refers to the method already described.

Here, the word *iti* has the sense of "manner"; by this, the phrase "in this manner, according to the method already stated" includes the other direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) as well, in their already described mode.
"Whenever there is a basis" means whenever the causes for attaining direct knowledge established in a previous existence are present.
For the attainment of direct knowledge requires a specific qualification, which is called the "prior cause. This does not refer to the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Mastery. Therefore the Blessed One said: "When there is a basis.

"To be realized by direct knowledge" means that which is to be realized by the distinguished wisdom (paññā) whose divisions will be explained below. "Of the Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma that is both to be developed and to be fully understood.
The construction is: "he inclines his mind toward the realization of direct knowledge. "Right there, right there" means...
Regarding each and every dhamma that must be realized: one who is capable of being a witness, by virtue of direct personal experience, is "capable of being a witness" (*sakkhibhabba*);
the state of being such is "the capacity for being a witness" (*sakkhibhabbatā*).

Even though the aspiration for existence (*bhavapatthanā*) has not yet arisen with respect to those various karmas leading to existence, it occurs simply through the fact that the karma has been performed and accumulated.
Showing that the task of aspiring for existence (*bhavapatthanākicca*) is accomplished, he said, "or not aspiring. One who goes together and proceeds with another is a *sahabya*, meaning a companion;

however, here what is intended is one who enters into the same state of existence (*ekabhavūpaga*). The state of being such is *sahabyatā*; [the text says] "that *sahabyatā*. Now, considering the objection:

"Is it only the cultivation of absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*) that has the benefit of specific states of existence, or is it the other as well?"—he said, "even the cultivation of access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*)," and so forth.

“Nibbāna” means the extinguishing (*nibbuti*) of the three kinds of suffering. Although the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*) exists within material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), it is as if non-existent due to the absence of consciousness.
Therefore, he said, “We shall dwell in happiness. “By means of the sixteen modes of knowledge” refers to these:
the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, non-self, disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, relinquishment, and turning away (*vivaṭṭānupassanā*).
"By eight and by eight noble path and fruition knowledges"—thus, by sixteen.
"By nine modes of concentration practice"—this is by way of the five fine-material jhānas and the four immaterial jhānas; thus, by nine. Some, however, [say]:
"The four fine-material jhāna-concentrations, the four immaterial jhāna-concentrations, and the access concentration for both..."
They say that by making [the first] one, there are thus nine.

"In the application of the development of concentration" means: in the practice (*anuyoga*) of the development of concentration, or in the yoga known as the development of concentration. "Yoga" is said to be development (*bhāvanā*). As it is said: "From yoga, indeed, much is born.
(363) By the word "and" (*pi*) in "concentration and joy," virtue (*sīla*) is included.
The commentary on the Exposition of Concentration is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the eleventh chapter.
The first part is completed.
